# PREFACE

Gabriel Garcia Marquez reportedly told Gerald Martin, who wrote his biography: “Each of us has three separate lives: our public, private, and secret lives…” I was very much aware of the distinction between private and public life, because my life was shaped by the tension between the two. The memoirs you are about to read are simply the story of what I lived through along the axis of that tension. I believed that my secret life was an inseparable part of my private life and hoped to tell as much of it as possible. But as the writing progressed, I realized the need to draw the line between private and secret life as carefully as I could. Perhaps because I could hurt others even more than myself, my secret life will not be part of these memoirs; if I live long enough, it may become the subject of another, fictional book.

Fatma was the protagonist of my entire life—public, private, and secret. In all three of my lives, the greatest role always belonged to her. The celebrated English novelist Iris Murdoch wrote in her first novel, “To find a person inexhaustible is simply the definition of love.” Fatma was my inexhaustible, indeed ever-growing love. Because I lived my life anchored to Fatma, I am the luckiest person I know. On the days when I felt happiest, when I told her, “My dear Fatma, you gave me heaven on earth!” I was expressing my most heartfelt emotions.

Yes, I can say that Fatma, too, chose to live her life anchored to me; she shared her private, public, and secret life with me. Did she regret it? Yes, from time to time… I have no doubt that she deserved a more fulfilling life, one with less hardship, sorrow, and suffering. I am sure that if she had had the opportunity to attend the schools she desired and to pursue a profession she loved, her life might not have been anchored to mine, and she might have led a happier existence. As she always said, perhaps it was for the sake of our daughter Elvan that she did not leave me. Perhaps one of the things that made my love for her immortal was that I was never certain of her love. She showed her devotion to me through her actions.

Fatma and I lived a shared life that lasted 55 years. For that reason, I did consider naming the book My Life with Fatma. But however much we shared, this is my life story. Our 55-year partnership, five years of which I was forced to spend apart from her, came to an end in a completely unexpected way on October 6, 2018, when my Fatma suffered a brain hemorrhage and suddenly departed in the office of Prof. Dr. Hasan Yazıcı, my friend of 60 years and her doctor of 20 years. During roughly the last six months we spent together after my release from Silivri prison, we had resolved never to look back, never to speak of the past, and to live our remaining years thinking only of each other. It was not meant to be… During our last days together in Ayvalık, she had promised that once we returned to Istanbul she would tell me about myself. That, too, was not meant to be. Consequently, the memoirs you are about to read have, regrettably, remained very incomplete.

Despite all the adversities I have been through, I believe I lived a life worth writing about. The fundamental reason for this is that I spent nearly all of my adult life with Fatma, the most beautiful woman and the most flawless person I have ever known. With her intelligent, sensible, sensitive, realistic, grounded, cool-headed, capable, honest, sincere, self-assured, dignified—in a word, noble—character, Fatma gave me so much; she was one of the two women who made me who I am, even more so than my mother. I owe her a great deal; above all, the brilliant children she raised, my Elvan and Acar, and my brilliant grandchildren Defne and Leyla…

On October 10, 2018, the day we laid Fatma to rest, we gathered around a table on the terrace of her house in Çamlık with close friends who had come to share my grief. “If I could have foreseen that Turkey would come to this, I would have lived my life very differently,” I said. I was not unaware that this was a pipe dream, but what I meant to express was this: If I could go back to the beginning, I would have devoted my life entirely to Fatma; like her, I too would have wanted not two but four children; I would not have stayed apart from her for a single day, let alone five years. The response from my friend Nuri Çolakoğlu at the table was: “Why do you say that!.. You’re writing your memoirs. When you’re done, you’ll look at the book and say, ‘What a life I’ve lived!’…” I don’t know if that will be the case, but this much is certain: I am writing my memoirs for myself and for Fatma; to record how happy she made me; how powerless I was to make her happy; and what we shared together—first and foremost for my children and grandchildren. My memoirs do not aim to bear witness to the domestic and world politics of the long era I lived through; they merely describe the effects of these on my own life.

Yes, I could have named this book My Life with Fatma. But however much we shared, this is my life story… The other day, while I was chatting with Fatma’s nephew Cenk, the son of my late sister-in-law Ayşe, he said, “Uncle, you have a story… I wish I had a story too…” Inspired by him, I decided to give my memoirs the title I Have a Story.

# CHAPTER I / HOW I BECAME WHO I AM

The foremost factor in making me who I am was undoubtedly the family I was born into. It would be fitting to begin the story of my family with the person who perhaps played the greatest role in it: my maternal grandfather, Halit Remzi Bey. What I know about him is very limited. Who his parents were, whether he had any siblings—I do not know. As far as I know, his interesting story goes as follows: He was born in 1868 in Üsküp (Skopje); he attended the Mülkiye Rüştiyesi in Salonica, a school that Atatürk also attended for a time. He entered business life at a young age. He worked as a contractor on the construction of the Salonica quay. He later joined the Ottoman Public Debt Administration (Düyun-u Umumiye, 1876–1939) as an official. His first wife, whom he married in Salonica, contracted tuberculosis and passed away shortly after the birth of their son Celal (the grandfather of writer and translator Celal Üster).

In the early 1900s, Halit Bey was appointed head of the Public Debt Administration for the district of Midilli (Lesbos), and moved to the city of Midilli, bringing along his son Celal and Celal’s Greek nursemaid Eleni. The town notables wasted no time in finding him a new bride through the traditional matchmaking custom. He married Rasime Hanım in a religious ceremony. When it became apparent on the wedding night that the bride was intersex (hermaphrodite), he divorced her and returned her to her family. What befell him caused a great stir in Midilli; satirical songs were composed about him: “O plane tree, mighty plane tree / Every bird comes to perch on it / Neither girl nor boy / Halit Efendi, my heart aches for that one…” (For the preservation of these lyrics, as for most of what I know about our grandfather Halit Bey and our grandmother Nazire Hanım, I am indebted to the matchless memory of my cousin on my aunt’s side, the painter Gaye Baykal-Kazancıgil, who was as close to me as a sibling. May she rest in peace.)

The search for a new wife for Halit Bey began. This time he said, “I won’t marry without seeing her first…” A scenario was accordingly devised: the approved new bride candidate, Nazire Hanım—“the Customs Officer’s daughter”—clad in her black çarşaf, rode in a phaeton with her aunt’s daughter Şaziment (or Şaziye) Hanım, passing slowly through the courtyard of the central mosque. Halit Bey watched them from a window overlooking the courtyard, and immediately took a great liking to Nazire on account of her ample bosom, deciding to ask for her hand from her father, Osman Bey, the customs director of Midilli (originally from the village of Kalunya).

About Halit Bey’s lineage we know nothing, but about Nazire Hanım’s we have some information. Her maternal line goes back several generations to Hacı Ahmet Ağa of Midilli. The Ağa had three children (İshak, Ayşe, Ahmet). Of these, Ayşe also had three children (Hanife, Münevver, Adile). Münevver Hanım married Alaybeyi Ahmet Bey and bore five children (Nimet, Hüsnü Esma, Hatice, Süveyde, Ahmet). Of these, Hatice Hanım married Hafız Ahmet Bey and they had two daughters (Rıfat, Faika). Faika married “the Customs Officer” (Customs Director) Osman Bey, originally from the village of Kalunya, and they had four children (Zihniye, Cavit, Nazire, Servet). Of these, Nazire—my maternal grandmother—married Halit Remzi Bey of Üsküp and had three children (Remzi, Şefika, and my mother Sabiha). My mother’s aunt Servet Hanım also had three children (Şaziye, Aziz, Meseret). Of these, Şaziye Hanım (the maternal grandmother of Ottoman cultural historian Prof. Dr. Çiğdem Kafesçioğlu and architect Murat Kafesçioğlu) was the cousin mentioned in the marriage story of Nazire Hanım that I related above.

## From Midilli to Harput

Halit Bey and Nazire Hanım married in 1903. Their first child, my late uncle Remzi (Karatal), was born in 1904 in Midilli. The following year, Halit Bey was assigned by the Public Debt Administration to Kemah (then part of Adıyaman province, today part of Erzincan). The family moved to Kemah with their belongings loaded onto mules, on a long and adventurous journey via Ayvalık. My late aunt Şefika (İpekel) was born in 1906 in Kemah; at one year of age she came down with ringworm of the scalp (tinea capitis). Halit Bey took his daughter to Istanbul for treatment. There, Şefika was successfully treated with “hacamat” (cupping—a procedure involving the extraction of bad blood from the body). Two years later, Halit Bey was transferred, this time to Harput (Elazığ). My late mother Sabiha was born there in 1908. Remzi and Sabiha both developed “Oriental sores” there. Both would bear scars from the sores that, once healed, were believed to become beauty marks.

Halit Bey’s next post in the Public Debt Administration was the directorship of the Istanbul Fish Market. The family settled in a house with a garden near Zeyrek. In the evenings, Halit Bey frequented the small unlicensed back-street taverns known as “koltuk meyhaneleri” with the well-known writers of the day, foremost among them his friend the author Ahmet Rasim. After a while he resigned from his post and entered the world of commerce; he partnered with Halil Bey, nicknamed “Moskof” (“the Muscovite”), to export lemons to Batumi. Halit Bey and his family moved, presumably on the eve of the First World War, to Ankara, settling in a house with a garden in the “Armenian quarter.” Their neighbors were the (Vehbi) Koç family, who ran a grocery shop. During the “Deportation” (Tehcir) of 1915–16, Halit Bey and Nazire Hanım hid two Armenian girls in their attic for months; they later converted them to Islam and arranged their marriages.

Halit Bey’s business in Ankara was army food supply contracting, primarily “kavurma” (preserved meat). For a time he worked at the “Yeni Gün” newspaper, which Yunus Nadi had begun publishing in 1920. A man with a great passion for classical Turkish music who spoke Greek and French well, Halit Bey arranged for his daughters Şefika and Sabiha to take violin and oud lessons (from the Greek Aleko) as well as French lessons from a French lady. When the Greek occupation army reached as far as Eskişehir, Halit Bey, who was in İnebolu on business, summoned Nazire Hanım to leave Ankara immediately and join him. Nazire Hanım, together with the President of the Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation Mustafa Asım Bey and his family, traveled by horse-drawn carriages over the Ilgaz mountains—where bandits roamed—and reached İnebolu.

## Ayvalık

Victory was won in August 1922. Upon the news that a population exchange with Greece was to take place, Nazire Hanım traveled several times from Ankara to Midilli; she gathered documents relating to the properties she owned there; after the exchange, these documents enabled her to be allocated a house and several hundred olive trees in Ayvalık. The family was now bound for Ayvalık; it was there that they celebrated the proclamation of the Republic on October 29, 1923. Shortly afterward, Halit Bey was appointed mayor of Ayvalık by the single-party government. During his five-year tenure, among other things he had the city’s first electricity plant built along with a cinema hall where silent films were shown. He had some of the stone pine trees planted that still adorn the hillsides of the city today. He organized Republic Day balls attended by İsmet İnönü and Kazım Orbay, among others. According to family lore, he was removed from the mayorship in 1928 because of his project to build a quay where ships could dock. The owners of the barges that transported the region’s principal products—olive oil and soap—to ships were opposed to the construction of the quay.

Halit Bey had been initiated into Freemasonry during his years in Salonica. In his political views, he felt an affinity with the Unionists (İttihatçılar) and later with the Kemalists. His religious convictions were weak, perhaps nonexistent. (According to my mother, he was “an atheist.”) His wife Nazire, by contrast, was devoutly religious, praying five times a day, never going out without her çarşaf. When angry at her husband she would complain, “That wretched Freemason… He made my children irreligious…” Nevertheless, at Nazire Hanım’s insistence, the Ramadan and Sacrifice festivals (Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha) were duly celebrated in the family. Halit Bey did not fast but did attend the festival prayers. During his mayorship, until the state monopoly administration was established in 1926, he also produced “Ayvalık” brand rakı, cognac, and wine at 74 Dereboyu Avenue.

In those years, the family’s chief entertainment was hosting fasıl (classical Turkish music) evenings at home, with the participation of neighbors and relatives. Şefika and Sabiha would play the oud, kanun, and piano at these evenings and sing. Another amusement for the family and their friends was holding séances. Nazire Hanım believed that the spirits summoned at these séances truly came to visit. For Halit Bey, it was merely entertainment. Because of the fright these sessions caused her as a child, my mother Sabiha was never able to stay home alone for the rest of her life.

Sabiha, the beloved youngest child of Halit Bey and Nazire Hanım, was a very beautiful girl. Nazire Hanım was determined to betroth her to their relative Salih (Komili) Bey. Although Halit Bey was not at all in favor, the engagement took place in 1925. However, at a ball that Sabiha attended with her father, she danced with a guest (who had come “from Atatürk’s circle”). Thereupon Salih’s brother Necmi Bey (father of Halis Komili, a former president of TÜSİAD) told Salih, “Your fiancée danced with a stranger…” When Salih reacted furiously, Halit Bey declared, “I don’t want such an uncivilized son-in-law…” and immediately broke off the engagement, returning the gifts. Although the deeply upset Sabiha insisted for a while that she would not “take off the ring,” she soon forgot the matter. In 1926, she married Ahmet Saim Bey, the son of one of the wealthiest families of Midilli. On August 16, 1928, the couple’s daughter (my eldest sister) Sumru was born.

Sadly, Ahmet Saim Bey contracted tuberculosis a year later and went alone to Davos, Switzerland, for treatment. In 1930, a week after undergoing surgery in a hospital in Vienna, he passed away at the age of only 22 and was buried there. His grave would later be searched for by family members but never found.

Approximately a year after Halit Bey died of a heart attack in Istanbul on February 7, 1931, at the age of 63, the 53-year-old Nazire Hanım also passed away. Despite their very different personalities, she had been bound to her husband with a great love; unable to bear the grief of losing him, her heart simply stopped.

Having lost first her husband, then her father, then her mother within two years, Sabiha was left a widow with her two-year-old daughter Sumru. She was so beautiful that five handsome young men from the Ayvalık gentry proposed marriage to her. But she fell in love with Ahmet Muharrem Bey—born in Serres (Greece), nicknamed “the Handsome,” four years her junior and only 21 at the time—whom she visited at his soap factory (at 1 Gülbahar Street) to sell tickets for a ball organized by the Ayvalık Philanthropic Society. “If I could live three years with this man, it would be enough for me!” she used to say. This encounter paved the way to their marriage.

## Serres

Ahmet Muharrem Bey belonged to the largest landowning family of the city of Serres in Greek Macedonia, whose population, as Mark Mazower recorded in his book Salonica, was two-thirds Muslim before the Balkan Wars. Located 80 km north of Salonica, Serres is the place where Sheikh Bedreddin of Simavna—the subject of Nazım Hikmet’s famous poem—who rebelled against the Ottomans with his egalitarian ideas, was hanged in 1420. Ahmet Bey’s paternal lineage traced back to Halil Bey, the brother of Muharrem Bey, Governor of Alexandria, who was the son of Çorbacıbaşı Hüseyin and the nephew and son-in-law of Mehmet Ali Pasha of Kavala (Muhammad Ali, the founder of modern Egypt).

The agricultural lands and real estate of the very wealthy and childless Muharrem Bey were consolidated in a waqf—an Islamic endowment—established in Alexandria (the Muharrem Bey Waqf). When Halil Bey returned from Alexandria to his hometown of Serres toward the end of the 19th century, the management of the waqf passed to his brother Hasan Berto. Over time, Berto transferred the waqf’s assets to himself. (Our relatives on my father’s side, the Alantar brothers, tried hard in Egypt to claim our shares; they even asked me in 1983 to obtain a court ruling confirming we were heirs. Unfortunately, their efforts came to nothing.)

Halil Bey, who returned from Alexandria to Serres, had four sons (Mahmut Pasha, Hacı Osman, Hacı Ali, Hacı Mestan). Hacı Ali Bey, to whom Sultan Mahmud II had granted nine estates as fiefs, also had three sons (Muharrem, İlyas, İbrahim Pasha). İlyas Bey is our ancestor on the paternal side. As famous for his miserliness as for his wealth, İlyas Bey owned some 20,000 dönüm (roughly 2,000 hectares / 5,000 acres) of land in the villages of Radiloz and Oteligos between Serres and Drama; he also sponsored wrestlers who competed at Kırkpınar. (I will tell the story of meeting one of these wrestlers, a white-bearded old man, later on.)

İlyas Bey had seven children from four wives (Ali, Ziba, Siyavuş, Ata, Behiye, Aliye, Tayyar). Of these, Ali Bey had two children (Baise and Muharrem); Muharrem Bey was my grandfather. (One interesting thing I learned about my father’s grandfather Ali Bey was that he sided for a time with Tepedelenli Ali Pasha, the Governor of Ioannina who rebelled against the Ottoman state.) Ali Bey’s brother Tayyar Bey also had three sons: İlyas, Yahya, and İhsan (Alantar). I am glad I had the opportunity to know these three nephews of my father; all three, whom I called “uncle,” became people I loved dearly. (İlyas and Yahya were not at all religious, but the youngest brother İlyas, when I visited him in Adapazarı near the end of his life, would reveal to me that he belonged to the Kadiri Sufi order.)

I learned the family genealogy I have recounted above primarily from Yahya Alantar, with whom I had a close relationship (and whose influence made me a Beşiktaş supporter at the age of five or six). My Uncle Yahya read my columns in Milliyet and greatly enjoyed them. In a letter of his that I kept, he wrote that he found some of them comparable to the editorials of Şükrü Baban in Yeni Sabah and Nadir Nadi in Cumhuriyet. He described my refusal to deny that I was a Marxist in my youth as “a noble stance.” Despite the heavy cost it imposed on the family, he was in favor of the 1923 population exchange with Greece; “otherwise we would have ended up like Lebanon,” he used to say.

Another detail from that letter that struck me greatly was his mention of the sense of “reticence, of hiding” that having sided with Tepedelenli Ali Pasha—who rebelled against the Ottoman state—had instilled in the family. According to information I obtained from another relative (Nurhan Gençel Bey) about our paternal ancestors, our lineage had initially embraced the Alevi faith before later choosing Sunnism.

Now let me turn to the roots of my father’s maternal side: My paternal grandfather Ali Bey married his son Muharrem to Mukaddes Hanım, the daughter of Agâh Efendi, the Mevlevi Sheikh of Serres. Agâh Efendi had inherited his sheikhdom from his grandfather Şükrü Bey (the earliest known ancestor on my paternal grandmother’s side), through his father Osman Bey. When Serres fell under Bulgarian occupation during the Balkan Wars, Agâh Efendi fled in 1913, taking with him his wife Güllü Hanım, his daughter (my paternal grandmother) Mukaddes Hanım, his son-in-law (my grandfather) Muharrem Bey, and their one-year-old son (my father) Ahmet—first to Salonica, then to Edirne, and shortly thereafter to Istanbul. (My father’s only sibling, Fahire Hanım, had died in childhood.)

The family took refuge in the Mevlevi lodge in Kasımpaşa. When Agâh Efendi realized he would never be able to return to Serres, his heart, consumed by grief, gave out. Muharrem and his wife Mukaddes, who had suffered various traumas during the migration, faced great hardships in the new homeland to which they had been uprooted. Whereas they had been very wealthy in Serres, here they fell into dire poverty. My grandfather Muharrem Bey fell ill while working as a laborer at the Agricultural Equipment Agency in Adapazarı to support his family, and died at a relatively young age. My paternal grandmother Mukaddes Hanım, unable to recover from the effects of the massacres she had witnessed, suffered a mental breakdown after her husband’s death; she was committed to the Bakırköy psychiatric hospital by her sisters (Üftade and Zehra Hanım) who lived in Istanbul. She died there in the late 1930s.

My father Ahmet, left an orphan, was taken in by his aunts Üftade and Zehra, who lived in Laleli, and by his father’s aunt (who was childless) Aliye Hanım and her husband, the retired captain Salih Bey, who lived in Anadoluhisarı. After the population exchange agreement, my father came to Ayvalık in 1926, at the age of only 14, together with his aunt Üftade. (Aunt Üftade, whom I vaguely remember, was a very pleasant person. She was the wife of Colonel Saadettin Bey, who fell as a martyr in Shkodër; she was widowed before they had even spent a year together and never remarried.) As a result of his aunt’s application, my father was allocated, as an exchangee’s entitlement, five to six thousand olive trees—mostly in Ayvalık with some in Yalova Esenköy—along with a soap factory, oil warehouses, and a house (at No. 80 on Sefa—later Barbaros—Avenue) in Ayvalık. The property allocated to my father as an exchangee corresponded to only a very small fraction of what the family had owned in Serres. There had been considerable corruption in the allocation of property to exchangees. Some had bribed the allocation commissions to acquire far more property than they had owned in Greece. Having attended Istanbul Erkek Lisesi while staying with his great-aunt, Ahmet settled in Ayvalık in 1930, when he turned 18, to take actual possession of his property and build a life there. Because he was very handsome and impeccably dressed, the people of Ayvalık soon nicknamed him “Handsome Ahmet Bey.” He took part in community life; among other things, he served as president of the İdmanyurdu Sports Club, supported by partisans of the ruling Republican People’s Party (CHP). Supporters of the Free Republican Party (Serbest Fırka), meanwhile, backed Akınspor. When a brawl broke out between the two clubs’ supporters in August 1939, both clubs were shut down.

## Ahmet and Sabiha

Many families and young women had their eye on the very handsome and quite wealthy Ahmet Bey. But Ahmet chose Sabiha, the famously beautiful widowed daughter of Ayvalık’s first Republican-era mayor Halit Remzi Bey. Sabiha, who had gone to meet Ahmet Bey on the pretext of selling a ball ticket, used to say, “I would give ten years of my life to be with this man.” They married in 1934 and took the surname Alpay in accordance with the law enacted that year. Their wedding was held at the house (now the Bonjour Guesthouse) of Süeyde Hanım, the mother of Sabiha’s first husband (and father of her first child Sumru), the late Ahmet Saim Bey.

Ahmet and Sabiha built a very happy partnership in the first ten years of their marriage. They began living winters in a rented apartment in the Kaptan family’s building in Ayvalık, and summers in the small house in the resort neighborhood of Çamlık that Sabiha and Sumru had inherited from Ahmet Saim Bey. Their first child, Olcay (my second-eldest sister, wife of the late Ünal Karacan, an engineer and Istanbul Technical University (İTÜ) graduate), was born in 1935 in that house; their second child, my elder brother Acar (whom we lost in a tragic traffic accident in 1977, father of former TÜSİAD president Ümit Boyner and of Cihan Alpay), was born in 1938 in İzmir. Ahmet Bey was a true gentleman. He was a husband in love with his wife and a father devoted to his children. He was extremely affectionate toward his children, including his stepdaughter Sumru. He was a man who loved to read; the works of Nazım Hikmet were among his bedside books.

Sabiha Hanım, in her own words as a result of a “stray bullet,” became pregnant again six years after Acar. She considered having an abortion, but the doctors would not allow it, saying it was too late. Ahmet Bey, for his part, had decided that their third child would also be a boy and had already chosen the name: “We placed the order—Şahin is coming from America!” he would say. (This must have been a reflection of the admiration for the United States prevalent toward the end of the Second World War.) In those years, the Alpay family spent the winter months in the apartment building that their family friend and Çamlık neighbor Mustafa Lütfü Kaptan had built on the seaside in Ayvalık. The Kaptans lived on the third (top) floor; the Alpays, their tenants, on the second (middle) floor.

In those years, the population of Ayvalık consisted almost entirely of exchangees who had been settled there, mainly from Midilli, Crete, and Greek Macedonia, pursuant to the Lausanne Treaty signed between Turkey and Greece in 1923. The treaty had subjected approximately 1.2 million Greek Orthodox living in Turkey—including the Karamanlıs, some of whose mother tongue was Turkish—and approximately 400,000 Muslims living in Greece, including Cretans, some of whose mother tongue was Greek, to compulsory exchange. The Kaptan family, the Alpays’ neighbors, were one of a handful of Black Sea-origin families who had come to Ayvalık through internal migration from the Trabzon region before the exchange. The Kaptans’ story, too, helps one understand what kind of place my hometown Ayvalık was—and, more importantly, what kind of place Turkey was in its transition from Empire to Republic.

## My other family: The Kaptans

The second milieu that was perhaps as influential in making me who I am as my own family was the family of Fatma—my love, and my wife. The pioneer role in the Kaptan family’s settling in Ayvalık—then still entirely a Greek city (known to the Greeks as Kidonia, or more commonly Ayvali)—was played by Salim Bey from the village of Hamandos (now Aydoğdu) in the Sürmene district of Trabzon. Salim Bey was a ship captain. He was a commercially astute “Black Sea lad.” He grew wealthy through trade between Trabzon and Romania. In the course of his travels he learned Romanian and even served as an interpreter at the Ottoman consulate in Constanţa. When he married his fellow villager Rukiye Hanım, whether she could wear the modern wedding dress her husband had ordered from Bucharest became a great subject of debate in Hamandos, but in the end the dress was worn.

Salim Bey was not a man of conservative inclination (presumably because of his openness to the world), and this trait would be passed down to the Kaptans to a great degree. Before the First World War, he moved to Istanbul and settled in Sarıyer to expand his business. Rukiye Hanım bore him two daughters named Fatma and Leman. When Istanbul was occupied, Salim Bey moved his family to Manyas. He opened a grocery shop there. According to family memory, he played a role in bringing weapons by ship to the nationalist forces (Kuvva-yı Milliye). When he learned that Çerkes Ethem intended to abduct his beautiful daughter Fatma, he packed up everything, loaded his family onto horse-drawn carts, and migrated to Ayvalık (presumably in 1918), at a time when the War of Independence had not yet been won, the Republic had not been proclaimed, and the population exchange with Greece had not taken place.

When he settled in Ayvalık—where only the district governor and security forces were Muslim and the rest of the population was Greek—there was only one other Turkish-Muslim family living in the city. The only village inhabited by Turks was Araplar (now Mutluköy). In other words, Salim Bey was in a sense the pioneer of Muslim settlement in Ayvalık. His daughters Fatma (who would pass away a few years later, at the age of 16) and Leman learned to read and write at the Greek school they attended in Ayvalık.

After the proclamation of the Republic, Salim Bey turned to olive oil and soap trading between Ayvalık and Istanbul. Because his wife Rukiye could not give him a son, he took a second wife, the widowed Hanife Hanım, also from the village of Hamandos. His first wife Rukiye Hanım would be deeply upset when she learned of this marriage from others. Hanife Hanım, whose husband had been killed during the 1877 Russo-Turkish War, had buried three children who died of typhus on the road as she fled westward from Trabzon. She bore Salim Bey the twins Kenan and Neriman in 1920, and İsmet in 1925. (Kenan Kaptan was one of the founding partners of Pak Maya. İsmet Kaptan studied agricultural engineering in Italy and, after serving as İzmir Fair director, became one of the founding partners of Ege Seramik.) Living in Ayvalık with his two wives housed in two separate homes on the same street, Salim Bey sold hardware and (in the words of his late son Hakkı Kaptan, who told me all this) “maritime supplies” at the shop he had opened, while searching for a reliable partner to handle the Istanbul side of his commercial operations. His brother Mehmet (known by the nickname “the drunken womanizer”) recommended Mustafa Lütfü Bey, a hardworking “Black Sea lad” from Vakfıkebir who was then engaged in trade at the Oil Wharf in Eminönü, Istanbul.

Mustafa Lütfü of Vakfıkebir had been conscripted during the First World War, sent first to the Albanian front and then to the Syrian front, and had served as Cemal Pasha’s headquarters sergeant. He fought with distinction on the Palestine and then the Galician (Romanian) fronts, was wounded in the forehead and leg, and received a veteran’s certificate. Upon his discharge, he divorced the wife he had married before his military service with a curt “You are divorced”—the traditional repudiation formula; he married for a second time in Istanbul, to Mahmure Hanım, a fellow Black Sea native. When Mahmure died young of tuberculosis, their six- or seven-year-old son Hakkı was left motherless.

Salim and Mustafa Lütfü agreed in the 1930s to form a partnership. Salim Bey, whose original surname was Erol, and Mustafa Lütfü Bey, whose was Kodalak, both changed their surnames; together they adopted the surname Kaptan, fitting for their Black Sea origins. Salim Kaptan married off the 32-year-old Mustafa Lütfü Kaptan to his elder daughter (from his first wife Rukiye), the 16-year-old Leman. Mustafa Lütfü in turn married his son Hakkı from his first marriage to Neriman, daughter of Salim Bey’s second wife Hanife Hanım. The Kaptan family’s kinship relations, which even many Ayvalık residents found difficult to untangle, were based on the fact that a father (Mustafa Lütfü) and his son from his first wife (Hakkı) married sisters born of the same father (but two different mothers)—Leman and Neriman. Despite their Black Sea origins, the Kaptans had little attachment to conservative values, whether in terms of religiosity or traditionalism. The adventures that had carried them from the eastern Black Sea to the northern Aegean had played a role in their adapting to the not particularly conservative values of the Ayvalık community, composed as it was of exchangees.

Salim Kaptan died in Istanbul in the early 1940s, where he was being treated for cirrhosis; he was buried in the Sarıyer cemetery, beside his first daughter Fatma. After his death, Mustafa Lütfü Kaptan took over the management of the Kaptan firm, and his son Hakkı Kaptan from his first marriage took on the accounting. Hakkı, who had wanted to become a history teacher and remained passionate about history throughout his life, was forced to take on the role of his father’s accounting director after graduating from Galatasaray Lycée and the Higher School of Commerce. Mustafa Lütfü Bey’s second wife Leman bore four children: the eldest a boy (Suat), the other three girls (Bingül, Ayşe, and Fatma, in that order). Suat contracted tuberculosis in 1946 and died at only 18, plunging the family into mourning.

Mustafa Lütfü Kaptan was a very hardworking businessman. He invested the money he earned from the construction materials trade he had established with his father-in-law Salim Kaptan in the olive and soap business. Over time he came to own thousands of olive trees, an olive oil factory, a soap works, warehouses, and numerous properties. He had Ayvalık’s first apartment building—three stories—built on the seaside. He gave the two-story house he had purchased in Çamlık, originally belonging to Greeks, to his son; in its large garden he had a two-story house built for himself. By the 1940s, the “Black Sea lad” from Vakfıkebir who had fought for years on various fronts in the First World War and earned a veteran’s certificate had become one of the wealthiest businessmen in Ayvalık. He remained true to his roots and always employed seasonal “Black Sea lads” at his workplaces. In 1956, at the age of 65, he decided to learn to drive; he took the exam and obtained his license. However, shortly afterward, he died in an accident while driving his jeep to Burhaniye to inspect a farm he was considering purchasing. His wife, my future mother-in-law Leman Hanım, was widowed at 49.

In early 1944, there was great commotion in the Kaptans’ three-story seaside apartment building in Ayvalık. Leman Hanım went to Istanbul to give birth to her fourth child and on February 14 brought her third daughter, Fatma Nur, into the world. Shortly afterward, Sabiha Hanım, the wife of the Kaptans’ tenant on the middle floor, Ahmet Alpay, also went to Istanbul to give birth to her fourth child and on April 18 gave birth to her second son, Şahin. Both mothers returned to their hometown soon after giving birth. Thus, by a twist of fate, Fatma and Şahin—who would marry in 1965, when they turned 21—found themselves under the same roof in the very first days of their lives. One might say that my life with Fatma began right there.

## The mental crisis that shook the family

Let us return to the Alpays: Ahmet and Sabiha were very happy together, but their happiness did not last long. Ahmet Bey was under the influence of various traumas caused by the upheavals that had begun with the Balkan Wars, which had uprooted his family. Following the Capital Tax Law enacted in 1942, he had filed an income declaration of 1.5 million liras and been assessed a tax of 10,000 liras. He suffered great distress over how he would pay this amount and the anxiety that if he could not, he would be sent to Aşkale. From that date onward, he fell into an increasingly chronic mental crisis.

My mother, with the best of intentions, had moved the household to Istanbul for my father’s treatment; following the advice of certain relatives and doctors there, she first sent my father, under medical supervision, to a clinic in Paris. My father escaped from the clinic, climbed onto a train car, managed to reach Marseille and apply to the Turkish consulate there, and with the consulate’s help boarded a ship and returned to Istanbul. Upon his return he endured the agonizing electroshock treatments prescribed by doctors in Istanbul, but when he heard that brain surgery was being considered, he fled the house and took refuge with his aunts, turning hostile toward the woman he had once loved—my mother. What is both deeply saddening and thought-provoking about these events is that a case of depression that could in later years have been managed with medication alone led, as a result of the coercive methods employed, to the disintegration of the family.

As a result, my father, with the help of his aunts Üftade and Zehra, was freed from guardianship, divorced my mother, and began a solitary life that would last until the end of his days. The last time I recall seeing him in our house in Teşvikiye was in 1950, the year I started primary school. He would later settle in Ankara, where until the 1960s he ran a shop in the Maltepe district selling Ayvalık olive oil and soap. He would then return to Ayvalık and live on the income from leasing the olive groves he owned. Until his death on September 9, 1981, at the age of 69, when his heart stopped, both my siblings’ and my own relationship with him remained very limited. His closest companion was a small dog he named Fidel (faithful).

“A woman worthy of seven novels”

For the reasons briefly described above, I essentially grew up as the child of my mother, who passed away on January 24, 1992, at the age of 84. My mother, described by one relative as “a woman worthy of seven novels,” led a very unfortunate life as a result of the upheavals of Turkey in the first half of the 20th century in general and of those in her own life in particular. She was widowed from her first husband at only 22. Although she divorced my father at around 40, she never remarried; she devoted herself to her children. Her greatest entertainment was card games. She was one of the best bridge players in Ayvalık. She was a very affectionate but, when necessary, authoritarian mother. She raised her children with love and ensured they received a good education.

I owe her gratitude for ensuring I attended the best schools despite the limited financial means she had after divorcing my father. Another matter for which I owe her gratitude is her encouraging me from an early age to help her with housework. When needed, I went to the market, washed dishes, and cleaned. I believe these experiences helped me acquire the ability to adapt to all manner of circumstances later in life.

The fundamental pillar of our family was undoubtedly my mother. She herself had only a primary school education, but perhaps under the influence of her father, who was quite educated and experienced, she placed great importance on her children receiving a good education. She ensured that all four of us attended Istanbul’s best schools and learned English. My eldest sister Sumru finished middle school and my second-eldest sister Olcay finished high school at the American College for Girls in Arnavutköy. My elder brother Acar finished middle school at Robert Academy in Bebek and high school at Işık Lisesi in Nişantaşı before going on to Istanbul University’s Faculty of Law. I, as I will recount in detail later, attended middle school at the English High School for Boys in Nişantaşı, high school at Robert Academy in Bebek, and university at Ankara University’s Faculty of Political Science.

My mother’s great influence on my upbringing certainly had a political dimension as well. She greatly admired Atatürk. I believe all Turkish and Muslim families forced to emigrate from the Balkans believed they owed their finding peace in the “motherland” Turkey—where they took refuge after so much suffering and pain—to his capable leadership. My mother had been more influenced by her father Halit Bey, who held positivist views, than by her devoutly religious mother Nazire Hanım. Her religious sentiments were not at all strong. I remember that shortly before she passed away, she asked, “Şahin, I wonder, do heaven and hell really exist?”

Despite having grown up in a Mevlevi family, religious beliefs played virtually no role in my father Ahmet Bey’s life either. Among my mother’s relatives, I knew no one who was devout. Among my father’s relatives, however, there were religious people. Aunt Üftade, whose officer husband was martyred in Shkodër during the First World War, prayed five times a day but only covered her head. Dudu Bengi Hala, a distant relative of my father who lived alone in Bursa, occasionally visited us in Ayvalık, and never married, was the sole “devoutly religious” person in the family—she fulfilled all the obligations of Islam and covered herself from head to toe. The relatively devout member of our nuclear family was my eldest sister Sumru, who never neglected fasting during Ramadan until her final years and whom I occasionally witnessed praying.

In short, I grew up in an entirely secular family, far removed from conservatism, and quite “modern” by Turkish standards. I received no religious education. During the 1955– 60 period when I attended middle school, religious instruction was elective, not compulsory. My mother readily agreed to my request to be exempted from religion class. Her secularism did not, however, prevent her from placing a miniature Quran in the inner pocket of my jacket, in the belief that it would help me succeed in exams. The family environment must have played a significant role in shaping my views on religion during my youth. In my mature years, I would come to see having received no religious education in a society where religion plays such an important role as a significant deficiency. My consolation on this score was that some of my devout friends nonetheless attributed to me the moral qualities one would expect to find in a religious person.

I cannot say that either my father or my mother were conscious Kemalists in the sense of being wholly committed to Kemalist ideology, to authoritarian secularism and identity politics, but both admired Atatürk. They were Kemalist in the sense of seeing women and men as having equal rights and of respecting education, science, and differences in religious belief. As I mentioned above, I believe they felt they owed their finding peace and security to the Turkish Republic founded under Atatürk’s leadership. Perhaps the fact that Atatürk, like them, was a child of Rumelia also played a part in their devotion to him. Despite their families having been subject to the compulsory exchange, neither my mother nor my father instilled in us children any form of hostility toward Greeks or foreigners. What my mother said about the exchange was this: “It was a time of war. In war, both sides committed great crimes against each other. But the war ended, and the enmities were left behind…”

The Turkish-Greek peace that began in 1930 and would last until 1955 may have played a role in her acquiring this understanding. In the 1930s, until the island fell under Nazi occupation, mutual friendship visits took place between the notables of Ayvalık and Midilli. Unlike in Crete, there had been no conflict or war between Greeks and Turks, between Orthodox and Muslims, in Midilli. I had heard from elderly “Islanders” that when the Turks migrated from Midilli to Ayvalık, they were seen off in tears by their Greek neighbors; and that they were able to take their movable possessions, right down to their flocks of sheep, across the water.

My late mother held a worldview that could be described as far from nationalism, cosmopolitan and humanist. Her influence was in that direction. It was she who instilled in me the awareness that people are of equal worth regardless of their nation, religion, or language. I can say that her influence was decisive—even before the schools I would attend—in my developing from childhood onward a mentality open to the world and to different nations and cultures. I believe that the policies of Kemalist Turkey to turn a new page and consign the past to oblivion played a role in the fact that I never heard from either my mother or my father any narrative about the suffering and traumas experienced by their families when they were exiled from their homelands. Not having probed their memories on these subjects has been one of my greatest regrets.

My eldest sister Sumru, who passed away in 2011 at the age of 83, also played a very great part in my upbringing. I can say she was a half-mother to me. When, in 1950, she married my much-loved late brother-in-law Özbek Cömert (1925–2010), the son of Ali Cömert, one of Ayvalık’s leading businessmen, I apparently wanted to go with her. My second-eldest sister Olcay (Karacan), with the love and affection she showed me throughout her life, became one of the people closest to me in life. My late elder brother Acar Alpay was my role model. From how to shave to how to cut one’s nails, how to wash one’s hands, how to tie a necktie—I learned many things from him. With his rich library and his passion for literature, he was the one who instilled in me a love of reading. He showed me great love; he approached me as a guardian and protector. He must also have spoiled me somewhat, because as a child I enjoyed provoking him and going against him. Perhaps the most important example of this is that despite his being a fervent Fenerbahçe supporter, I became a Beşiktaş supporter from the year I started primary school, influenced by a relative. Even this my brother took in good grace. I will recount in detail the great role he played in my fate and my life later on. In short, my siblings and I were always bound to one another with great love and solidarity. My late mother’s sheltering our divided family under her wing, and the strong love and solidarity that developed among us as siblings, laid the foundations for the deep attachment I feel to my family.

Had my parents not divorced when I was only six, had my father been able to sustain his initially successful business career, I too might have had a “normal” life—one that would not have strayed beyond the framework drawn by the established order, like that of most of my school friends. Growing up in a divided family directed me and all my siblings toward marrying young and founding families of our own. Having grown up virtually fatherless may have played a role in my gravitating toward unconventional views and choices, toward knowledge rather than money as a source of power, and toward the search for an alternative social order. The fact that, while holding views that could generally be described as Kemalist (statist-nationalist) under my family’s influence until middle school, I then moved toward socialism and eventually its totalitarian varieties from high school onward, may also be related to this. Growing up in a fractured family whose financial situation was rapidly deteriorating may have engendered in me, on the one hand, a distinct sense of self-confidence and the ability to stand on my own feet, and on the other, a feeling of exclusion from society. My tendency to avoid being at the very forefront in almost every milieu I found myself in, preferring instead the position of the important figure in the background—the “éminence grise”—may also be related to this.

## My Hometown Ayvalık

Ayvalık, where I spent the greater part of my childhood and nearly all my summer holidays, is an exceptional place not only for its lace-like coves, its islands, its magnificent beaches, and its paradisiacal natural setting where olive and pine forests intertwine, but also for its architecture, which reflects its character as a prosperous Greek city based on agriculture and trade in the 19th century. Ayvalık, or Kidonia in Greek, was a quite wealthy settlement during the Ottoman period when it was inhabited almost entirely by Greeks. This character was in significant measure related to its having an autonomous structure during the period from 1773 to 1821, when the Greek independence movement triumphed. As one of the trade centers between the Anatolian hinterland and European countries, it bore the identity of one of the Ottoman Empire’s gateways to the West. Indeed, nearly all the major Western powers maintained a consulate here. Until the religion-based compulsory population exchange between Turkey and Greece under the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne, only Greek Orthodox Ottoman citizens lived here, apart from state officials and gendarmes.

Perhaps the best descriptions of what Greek Ayvalık was like before the exchange are the vivid portrayals in the memoir titled “Anatolia and Syria a Century Ago” by Dr. Şerafeddin Mağmumi. The articles of the modern Greek historian, (my late friend) Oxford University history professor Richard Clogg, are perhaps the most important witnesses to late-19th-century, pre-exchange Ayvalık. The books of my late friend Ahmet Yorulmaz are indispensable reading on life in post-exchange Ayvalık.

With the exchange, all of Ayvalık’s Greeks were subjected to compulsory migration to various parts of Greece, primarily Midilli; in their place, Turkish-Muslims from three main regions were settled. The largest group were those of Midilli origin; the second largest were Cretan exchangees, settled primarily on Cunda Island. The third group, considerably smaller than the others, consisted of those who, like my father, came from Greek Macedonia—mainly the Serres, Drama, and Kavala regions. Ayvalık in the 1920s and 1930s was, one could say, the embodiment of the modern, European Turkey that the Kemalists envisioned. A few families whose origins traced to freed black slaves in Midilli, one or two families of Dobruja-Romanian origin, and a small number of Kurdish families driven from the East, some of whom began fishing in Cunda, completed post-exchange Ayvalık society.

After the Second World War, Bosnians fleeing Tito’s communism in Yugoslavia were settled in Küçükköy, just near Sarımsak Beach. Ayvalık, where I spent a significant part of my childhood and youth, thus had a cosmopolitan character, composed of immigrants from very different regions of the dissolving empire, all of them Muslim. Over time, these immigrant groups intermarried and merged. Although Ayvalık gradually lost its character as a city of exchangees with the internal migrations that began in the 1970s, it continues to be a city of immigrants. (It is known that of today’s population of around 70,000, only 5,000 were born in Ayvalık.)

The years I spent entirely in Ayvalık can be counted on one hand. When I was only three or four, my family moved to Istanbul, partly for my father’s treatment and partly to ensure the children could attend school there, and began spending winters there. Only the 1953–54 school year, when I attended third grade of primary school, did I spend entirely in Ayvalık. For me, Ayvalık was my hometown where I spent summer holidays at our summer house in Çamlık throughout my childhood; after marrying Fatma, it became our shared homeland as well. I always felt I essentially belonged there.

The Ayvalık that began to take hold in my consciousness was, in those years, a city where Greeks no longer lived but which was, in its entire architectural fabric, still a Greek city. The magnificent buildings left by the Greeks, including the monastery in the Çamlık square, which would be demolished in the 1950s and 1960s, were still standing. With the city’s historic structures being placed under the protection of the Monuments Board in the 1970s, the city’s historical character was preserved to a degree. With its cosmopolitan social milieu formed by immigrants from different cultures, its natural setting of unparalleled beauty composed of lace-like coastlines and islands intertwined with the Aegean, and its urban environment based on the distinguished Greek architecture of the 19th century, Ayvalık profoundly influenced both my intellectual and my spiritual world. I believe that not only the values instilled in me by my family and the schools I attended, but also Ayvalık’s community and environment nurtured in me the idea—which would take root from my youth onward—that people of all nations and religions deserve equal respect and that all of humanity constitutes a single community.

## Çamlık

Ayvalık, in yet another respect, gave rise to my resentment of a class-based society. In the years I grew up, the general picture of social stratification in the town was as follows: most of the olive-owning proprietors lived in Çamlık, most of the middle class including civil servants lived in Sefa or Orta Çamlık, and those who lived by their labor lived mostly in the town center. The Çamlık neighborhood where my family lived was the settlement of the Ayvalık bourgeoisie, primarily those engaged in olive cultivation, olive oil and soap production and trade. The people of Çamlık were, in their dress, values, and behavior, a quite European community. They had as secular a culture as was possible in the Turkey of those days; religion did not play an important role in their lives.

In Ayvalık, which until the 1950s was one of Turkey’s wealthiest and highest tax-paying districts, many of the Çamlık families (including mine) had one foot in Istanbul or İzmir; they spent part of the year there and had their children schooled there. Most lived in houses left by the Greeks and employed servants, usually of village origin. Many families had young girls from impoverished villages who had been entrusted to the wealthy out of desperation and put to work as domestic servants. From the 1960s onward, as the production of alternative cooking oils—sunflower oil foremost among them—became widespread, Ayvalık’s wealth and with it the general prosperity of the Çamlık families would go into decline. There is no doubt that the reactions stirred in me by Ayvalık’s marked class differences played an important role in my embracing socialist ideas at university age.

I should open a parenthesis here and touch upon the story of Cemile—which could be the subject of a novel in its own right—a nine- or ten-year-old girl whom a woman from one of the impoverished mountain villages of Balıkesir brought and entrusted to my mother in the late 1950s. To her credit, my mother looked after Cemile well; she hired a tutor to teach her to read and write, provided for her every need, raised her as a complete urbanite, but at the same time also had her running every errand. Cemile was as good-natured as she was dignified. In her youth she had a love affair with a young man from the Çamlık upper class, but as might be expected, she was abandoned. My mother was planning to marry her off to a well-mannered young man who worked as an apprentice at the pharmacy of her in-law Osman Bey in Istanbul. Cemile would not agree. Presumably sometime in the late 1960s, Cemile, by then in every respect a complete city dweller, said, “I want to return to my village,” and when she insisted, word was sent; her mother came and took Cemile back to her village. In time we would learn that she had married and had children.

Years later, on a summer day in the early 1980s, Cemile turned up with her children. From head to toe—in her dress, her speech, her manner—she had become a villager again, had returned to her origins. That she said she had made a great mistake in returning to the village, that she regretted it, was perhaps the saddest aspect of her story. My mother said she could stay and not go back to the village if she wished, but Cemile said, “I have a husband, children—it is no longer possible…” She was right. She left and was never seen again. As one of the most unsettling events of my life, it has never lost its place in my memory. On one occasion, I had (shamelessly) struck Cemile because I caught her smoking. Even though she forgave me, the guilt I felt left a mark on my soul. Cemile was only one of the village girls given to Çamlık families as “besleme”—girls raised in the household as unpaid servants. They must have been among the factors that prepared the resentment I would feel toward a class-based society.

Ayvalık, with its natural beauty, its architecture, and its social fabric, is an exceptional place that can give the impression of being somewhere outside Turkey. As with most people from Ayvalık, it has lodged itself in my very being. I always wanted to go to Ayvalık at the first opportunity. In the years I was forced to stay away, I ached for it. Going to Ayvalık filled me with joy, leaving filled me with sadness. It was a peerless place to experience childhood. Çamlık was for me a place as safe as the womb. There, we lived in a house (now number 179) originally belonging to Greeks but later expanded. With the neighborhood boys—foremost Yusuf (Kaptan), two years older than me, and Azmi (Heper), a year younger and a distant relative—we played cowboys, soldiers, pilots, truck drivers, and so on in the wooded area behind our houses. With the neighborhood girls, especially Fatma and Emine (Kaptan), we played house, doctor, telephone, and so on. Swimming several times a day from the piers in front of our houses; fishing for hours under the blazing sun with rods made of reed and nylon line; sitting on the piers and greeting the long-nosed Austin municipal bus that came twice a day from Ayvalık along the dusty road with the refrain we had composed beginning “The blue bead is coming…”—these were the aspects of my exceptionally happy childhood that overshadowed every adversity.

## Nilüfer Hatun Primary School

My family had moved to Istanbul in the mid-1940s, when I was, I believe, only three years old, partly to ensure the children attended school there and partly so that my father could receive the treatment he needed. We lived in a large rented house on Operatör Raif Bey Sokak in Şişli. I am surprised that I remember the interior partitions of this house, the décor of the rooms, the corridor where I rode a tricycle, the garden where my brother, six years my senior, got up to mischief with his friends, and that I have some vivid memories relating to the neighbors. For we left that house in 1948, when I was only four, and moved to a rented apartment on the third floor of the Umur building on Hüsrev Gerede Caddesi in Teşvikiye. In 1949, my mother enrolled me in a nearby nursery, but gave up on sending me when I reacted with great protest. In the 1950–51 school year, I was enrolled at Nilüfer Hatun Primary School (formerly “Primary School No. 15”) on Şakayık Sokak in Nişantaşı.

My teacher at this school was (may she rest in peace) Müveddet Hanım, who took us from the first grade and graduated us in the fifth. (I do not remember her surname.) She must have been about 60 at the time, but she was a simply magnificent teacher because she managed to keep a class of 80 students under control and succeeded in teaching reading, writing, and arithmetic while also instilling a certain discipline. She was the first teacher to encourage me to study, to read and learn, to be a good student. The most important piece of advice she gave me, which would never leave my mind for the rest of my life, was this: “Remember, children, you are first and foremost human beings, then Turks, then Muslims…” These words of hers were, I believe, a summary of the official identity policy that Turkey began pursuing in the 1950s upon joining the Western alliance, based on the core idea that “We are not Central Asians but Anatolians; we are the heirs of all civilizations that have passed through Anatolia…” It was a succinct expression of the policy implemented during the phase that Etienne Capeaux, in his book examining the evolution of Turkey’s identity policies, aptly titled “From the Turkish History Thesis to the Turkish-Islamic Synthesis,” described as the “humanist” phase.

My first acquaintance with the press, in which I would spend many long years, came in 1950, when I started primary school and learned to read. I remember following with great interest the news in the Hürriyet newspaper, which had just begun publication that year and was being delivered to our home, about the Turkish soldiers going to fight in Korea. I can say that my interest in events at home and in the world began in those days. In the summer when I finished second grade, we were forced to vacate the apartment in the Umur building, I believe at the landlord’s request.

Fatma enters the stage

I spent the 1952–53 school year in Ayvalık, staying with my eldest sister Sumru, who had married two years earlier and had begun living with her husband and small children in the expanded family house in Çamlık, and attended the Cumhuriyet Primary School. In those years the Cumhuriyet Primary School was housed in a building of magnificent architecture that greatly impressed me, one that had housed a college during the Greek era. Consisting of a courtyard with a small pool in the center and classrooms opening onto the courtyard, the building, like many other splendid buildings left by the Greeks, was demolished by the municipality in the late 1950s (for reasons I can perhaps only describe as vandalism). Today in its place stands a school building constructed in the Black Sea architectural style with a concrete courtyard. Because it holds precious memories of my childhood, its present state strikes me as very sad.

The beginnings of my interest in my childhood playmate, the neighbor girl Fatma—with whom I played house during summer holidays in Çamlık—date back to the 1953–54 school year, when we attended third grade together at Cumhuriyet Primary School. We were only nine or ten years old. There was something that excited me about this slender, fair-skinned, rosy-cheeked, blonde girl with greenish hazel eyes. I would sulk at her, then find a way to make up. Six or seven years had to pass before I became conscious that I was in love with her and dared to declare my love. In the summer of 1960, when I had just finished middle school, while swimming from the pier in front of the Kaptans’ house—two houses down from ours—in Çamlık, as we always did, one day the other children had gone and Fatma and I were left alone. I was in the three-sided enclosed “cabin” at the end of the pier; she was in the sea. I summoned all my courage and said, “Fatma, I think I’m falling in love with you…” She was not expecting it at all… She was very surprised and could only manage, “That’s just how it seems to you…” And I said, “Yes, it definitely seems that way to me!..”

We were both sixteen. At the time, Fatma was seeing a young man from the same neighborhood, two or three years older than us. She was therefore quite bothered by my beginning to pursue her. Despite her wounding my pride many times, I could not give her up. Perhaps one reason I could not escape her allure, besides her beauty, was her personality, which had begun to manifest itself as early as primary school. This personality was reflected in the composition she wrote on April 20, 1956, when she was in the fifth grade, on the topic “What do you want from your parents?” In the composition, which I discovered about ten years ago among papers kept in our house in Çamlık, she had written the following: “1) I want there to be no fighting at home. 2) I want them to give me the right to speak at home. 3) I want them not to beat me. 4) I want them to allow me to spend money. 5) I want them to tell me what is going on at home. 6) On my holidays, I want to go to the places I like and play. 7) I want them to love me. 8) I want them not to embarrass me in front of my elders and juniors. 9) I want my mother and father to be kind-hearted and cheerful. 10) I very much want them to send me to college. Grade: 5, Age: 11, Written by: Fatma Kaptan, Address: Gümrük Caddesi, Balıkhane Sokak, No. 5, Ayvalık.”

Our classroom teacher at Cumhuriyet Primary School, Muhsine Hanım (a close friend of Leman Kaptan, who would later become my mother-in-law), was a kind-hearted, likable person and a teacher of very gentle character. The most important event of that year for me was being in the same class as Fatma. Fatma and her cousin Emine (Kaptan) were my girl classmates. That year I also made two close male friends, both now deceased. Osman, the son of Enver Örnek, who ran a guesthouse and restaurant in Çamlık, and I got into a great deal of mischief together. Osman was a very smart boy. After finishing Galatasaray Lycée he spent a few years in Belgium but was unable to continue his studies. When the Çamlık girl he was in love with left him, the brilliant future expected of him never materialized. For many years he worked at the reception of İzmir’s most famous hotel. In later life he married a girl much younger than himself; they had a daughter. He drank rakı and smoked heavily. He developed lung cancer at only around 60 and passed away.

My other friend, Dinçer (Görç), belonged to one of a handful of black-skinned families of Midilli origin in Ayvalık. The ancestors of these families had been sold as slaves from Africa to Midilli, then converted to Islam and freed by their owners. Dinçer, who had a slight stutter, was the son of “Arap” (“the Arab”) Bayram—a huge man who hated talking and was famous for his drunkenness, a truck driver who worked for my brother-in-law Özbek. Dinçer’s importance to me was that, until university, he was my first friend from the lower classes and the only friend of a different race. Because I was close friends with Dinçer, in the face of Ayvalık’s sharp class differences and the division between “those above” and “those below,” I felt almost privileged, different from everyone else. He had become my confidant. I could easily share with him thoughts and feelings I could not share with others. In later years Dinçer attended the technical high school in Ayvalık, became a skilled lathe operator, and emigrated to Germany. He returned a few years later and worked at the shipyards in Maltepe, Istanbul. He married a white girl. A few years after retiring and settling in Cunda in the 1990s, he fell ill and died.

## Nişantaşı, Gaye Apartment

In 1954, when my mother purchased an apartment at No. 34 Valikonağı Caddesi in Nişantaşı, Istanbul—in the Gaye Apartment building—I returned for the fourth grade to Nilüfer Hatun Primary School and to Teacher Müveddet. Teacher Müveddet was pleased that the student in whom she saw promise had come back. She frequently held me up as an example to the class. Her encouragement played a great role in my developing the habit of studying and, above all, a curiosity for learning. May she rest in peace. My closest friend in the class was Hamit (Dalkılıç), the son of a military officer. I remember that during nearly every recess, Hamit and I would pace the school garden, conversing with a show of expertise about the news we had read in the papers. We were conscious that we were far ahead of the rest of the class in our knowledge of Turkey and the world.

Many years later, in the early 1990s, I looked up Hamit, a friend who had left a mark on me, and found him through the telephone directory. He had studied at Istanbul University; he was working somewhere as a civil servant. He was perhaps dejected at not having achieved the career he had hoped for. When I called to meet again, his telling me that “we have walked very different paths and can no longer be friends” both greatly surprised and saddened me. I never saw him again, but as my first close intellectual friend, he never left my mind.

In the 1950s, Nişantaşı was a far more multicultural, cosmopolitan neighborhood than it is today. The Greeks had not yet left, nor the Jews, nor the remaining Armenians.

In the six-story Gaye apartment building at the intersection where Valikonağı and Rumeli Avenues meet, besides us there lived another Turkish and Muslim family (the Ferhatoğlu family from Edremit), an Armenian family (“Monsieur Garbis”), and a Jewish family (“Monsieur Jak”). We had very good neighborly relations with all of them. Our Armenian doorman Aram Efendi lived in the basement with his adult daughter Stella. The delicatessen at the front of the basement (which became Konak Pastanesi after the 1960s) was run by “Yorgo Efendi,” a Greek. The taste of the tongue-and-pickle sandwiches my brother and I bought from him is still on my palate. The image of the Greek delicatessen seller who set up his counter in the doorway of the apartment building across from ours on winter evenings, selling cured bonito, has also lodged itself in my memory.

When I returned to Istanbul at the end of September from Ayvalık, where I had gone for summer vacation in June 1955 after finishing primary school, I would learn what had happened in Istanbul on September 6–7. From that date on, our non-Muslim neighbors would leave the apartment building one by one. I was filled with mixed feelings. I was caught between the nationalist sentiments instilled by school, newspapers, and the radio on the one hand, and the humane values imparted by my family and close circle on the other. I was aware that what had happened was related to the Cyprus question. I had listened to radio reports about demonstrations where the cry of “Either partition or death!” was raised. I recall that what took place in the year I turned twelve stirred in me an indescribable unease. I can say that the September 6–7 events—which went down in history as the assaults and looting targeting non-Muslims by crowds whipped into a frenzy by nationalist provocations and handed clubs—were the first event to awaken in me the thought that something was wrong in Turkey. Years later, I would learn from the statements of retired General Sabri Yirmibeşoğlu, head of the Special Warfare Department, that the savagery of September 6–7 had been carried out through a “magnificent organization” spearheaded by the state itself.

## English High School for Boys

It was time for middle school. My mother, who herself had only been able to attend primary school and had always seen her highly educated father as a role model, placed great importance on her children receiving a good education and learning foreign languages; she had begun having me take English lessons in the fifth grade of primary school. Perhaps partly encouraged by this, I wanted to attend the English High School for Boys (hereafter EHSB), which was just a few streets away, and learn good English. Due to increasing demand, EHSB had in recent years begun admitting students by examination. My mother must not have been very confident I could pass the exam, for she would say, “If you can pass, wonderful… Otherwise I’ll enroll you in Şişli Terakki…” I passed the exam with a middling score among the 35 students admitted that year and was overjoyed. From 1955 to 1960, I studied there for a total of five years—two years in the (English) preparatory program and three years in middle school.

EHSB was an exceptional school, one of the finest secondary education institutions in Turkey in those years. In the preparatory classes, we received intensive English instruction from British (English, Scottish, or Welsh) teachers. The science courses were also taught in English, again mostly by British teachers. Courses in the social subjects were taught in Turkish by distinguished Turkish teachers. The school’s headmaster was English, his deputy Turkish. Classes of 30–35 students made it possible for teachers to engage more closely with their pupils. I need not elaborate on what learning English—a language that over the course of the twentieth century became the world’s lingua franca—gave me. Knowing proper English is a privilege even today; in my youth, it was all the more so.

I can say that thanks to learning good English, my frame of reference transcended Turkey’s borders; I entered the world’s sphere of influence. There is no doubt that this had a profound effect on my intellectual development and, consequently, on my destiny and life story. EHSB’s contribution to opening me up to the world was not limited to the English I learned. There I came to know teachers and students from foreign nations; I had many friends from minority communities. Nişantaşı’s multicultural, cosmopolitan atmosphere was experienced even more intensely at school. The foundations of my belief—one that would grow stronger over time—that all people are of equal worth regardless of language, religion, or race were laid here.

I can say that I acquired the skills of expressing myself by speaking before audiences and communicating easily with others by taking roles large and small in the plays staged by EHSB’s theater club (the Dramatic Society), starting from the preparatory years. I played the lead role (Shylock) in Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice. In our graduation year, I performed in Bernard Shaw’s Androcles and the Lion. I remember being very happy when the English teacher who wrote a review of the play for that year’s school yearbook wrote, “And particular mention must be made of Alpay’s speech which was to my mind the best in the play…” The inclusion in the school’s 1960 yearbook of a poem I adapted from Shakespeare’s As You Like It—a tribute to our teachers that could be described as a panegyric, titled “As We Like Them”—had also made me quite proud.

At EHSB we received a very good education not only in terms of coursework but also in standards of conduct. The school had an educational philosophy that encouraged competition among students in every area. The report card we received at the end of each term was in the form of a large booklet. Grades were given out of a hundred, and according to the average, each student’s class ranking for that term was recorded. The school’s policy of encouraging competition played a major role in my rise from the bottom ranks in the preparatory years to the top ranks in middle school. Although I took not the slightest pleasure in mathematics or the sciences, by studying hard (by “memorizing” or “cramming”) I managed to earn high marks even in those subjects, and thereby succeeded in winning the favor of our mathematics teacher Isaac De Leon—may he rest in peace. Unfortunately, however, I was unable to catch the attention of our physics teacher Clifford Ellison, who would later also be my teacher at Robert Academy.

In the social subjects, from the first year of middle school onward, I was among the most successful students in the class. The encouragement of our teachers—all of them now departed—above all our English teachers Robert T. Shade and Godfrey Goodwin, our geography teacher İsfendiyar Erkut, our history teacher Muazzez Yazgaç, and our Turkish teacher Tahir Alangu, was a tremendous source of motivation. The Scotsman Mr. Shade and İsfendiyar Bey, with their seriousness and the authority they commanded, became role models for me. I can say that the competitive drive instilled at EHSB left a mark on me that would last my entire life.

Another important dimension of education at EHSB was athletic activities. Because I had grown up by the sea in Ayvalık, I was a good swimmer. But I had no particular talent in any of the other sports I played. Athletic activities, especially football, created a great atmosphere of fun and competition and reinforced attachment to the school. For five years, every Wednesday afternoon and every Saturday morning, we were bused to the large sports grounds on the Hill of Eternal Liberty (over which the E-5 highway now passes). As members of one of four teams to which we were automatically assigned on the day we enrolled, we carried on a fierce competition for five years. As right-back Alpay of the red-and-white Charnwood House football team (left-back was Tayfur Altay, who remained a close friend), I tried to play as well as I could but never rose above mediocre. (However, as I will relate later, the football I learned at EHSB would be enough to make me one of the two star players of the school team at the Webb School of California, where I would go on an AFS scholarship in the 1961–62 academic year, alongside the Filipino Carlos Perez-Rubio.)

I made some of my closest friends at EHSB. Foremost among them was certainly Ömer Madra, who enrolled in the school a year after me and was also a distant relative on my mother’s side. In the pages ahead, you will read about the striking parallels between our life stories, brought about by a friendship that deepened not only at school but during the summer holidays we spent together in Ayvalık, the place of our origins. I should relay some of my memories of Ömer from the middle school years: With our tremendous curiosity about Western pop music, we would press our ears to the radio and compete over who heard a newly released song first; playing disc jockey, we would record pop music programs onto my brother-in-law Özbek’s hulking but in those years exceedingly rare tape recorder in Ayvalık.

We went to a dance class in Beyoğlu to learn to dance. Our instructors were the couple Gönül and Erdoğan. Since it was mostly Erdoğan Bey who worked with us, we would laugh a great deal at the sight we presented while partnering him in dances ranging from the slow and swing to the cha-cha and waltz. At the time, we were both smitten with Ömer’s neighbor girl in Nişantaşı, Gülsün (Kamu). I had also quite fancied Nazlı (Ilıcak), a family friend’s daughter to whom Ömer introduced me. (Perhaps sixty years later, when I revealed this secret to her, Ilıcak would say with a mischievous expression, “Darn! If only I’d known…”)

The epitome of EHSB students’ cosmopolitan character was our classmate Godfrey Scotchbrook. Godfrey had a very interesting story. His father, an officer, had been posted at Britain’s military attaché office in Istanbul during the Second World War. While staying at a guesthouse run by a Greek lady, he had fallen in love with the young daughter of the house and married her. Shortly after the birth of Godfrey, the product of this marriage, the war ended and his father was recalled to London. Major Scotchbrook, after purchasing tickets for the ship that would carry his wife, son, and mother-in-law to Britain, set off for London on a military aircraft and tragically lost his life when the plane crashed. Godfrey grew up without a father and was educated partly in Istanbul (at EHSB) and mostly at schools in England. Now the owner of a very successful consulting firm in Hong Kong, Godfrey never lost his interest in Turkey. Since we decided, years after graduation, to revive our relationships as EHSB classmates, we get together every time he comes to Istanbul. (Godfrey has promised to tell me his life story.)

The closest among my classmates was Metin (Kılıçlı). (I will return to the interesting story of our friendship in due course.) I recall that in the conversations Metin, Salamon (later Selim Razon), and I had during our lunchtime walks from the school to Maçka Taşlık, political topics also came up, though my interest in politics was still very limited. Until the student demonstrations of April 1960, I had no negative attitude toward the ruling Democrat Party (DP).
