Tayfur Altay, Mehmet Atakan, Nedim Demirelli with whom I shared a passion for pop music, Ahmet Kutman (with whom I would later make the AFS journey to the United States), Yavuz Sökmen, Mehmet Soyarslan—the only classmate who like me was a Beşiktaş supporter—the late Ümit Tolun who like me was from Ayvalık, Şefik Yüksel whose path would cross mine on various occasions throughout life, Vahit Çelikbaş, Marcel Erdal, Alp Pekuz, Mehmet Önkal, and of course Godfrey Scotchbrook—all became friends with whom I have kept up ties despite the passage of so many years. Fifty-three years later, in 2013, we came together with these friends and even prepared a yearbook commemorating our school memories. This much is certain: among all my schools, EHSB was the one to which I felt the greatest attachment.

Among the publicly recognized figures I came to know during the EHSB years and with whom I maintained a friendship, I can name from the upper classes Ergun Göknel, Rıza Türmen, Faruk Birtek, Osman Ulagay, Ahmet Yücekök, Murat Belge, Niyazi Dalyancı, and Müfit Özdeş; and from the lower classes Celal Üster (my maternal uncle’s grandson), the late ambassador Nabi Şensoy, Reha Uz, and Mehmet Arda. Nearly all of them went on to distinguish themselves in their careers. My EHSB friends bestowed on me a nickname that stuck even after I transferred to Robert Academy: “Dayı” (Uncle). This nickname was inspired by the fact that I was among those in our class whose voice deepened earliest and who grew tall earliest (only to level off quickly afterward), and by my habit of standing up to students in the upper classes—that is, my “dayılanma.” I may well have acquired the habit of challenging authority when necessary in those years.

## A Turning Point: 1960

My last year at EHSB, the 1959–60 academic year, became one of the turning points in my life. My elder sister Olcay had married Ünal Karacan, a civil engineer and graduate of Saint Joseph and then İTÜ, in 1958 and moved to Germany. My brother Acar, who had been studying at Istanbul University’s Faculty of Law while also managing the pharmacy run by his future father-in-law Osman Çokay in Nişantaşı, had also left home. My mother, whose financial situation had been deteriorating as her income dwindled steadily after her divorce from my father, decided in the early months of 1960 to rent out the Nişantaşı apartment and move to Ayvalık, to be near my sister Sumru. As a result, I spent the remainder of that year living with my maternal aunt Şefika and her husband Hamit (İpekel) in 2nd Levent.

The İpekels were avid readers of the newspaper Cumhuriyet, subscribers to Akis magazine, and staunch supporters of the CHP. While staying with them, I too began reading Cumhuriyet and Akis. By spring, relations between Prime Minister Adnan Menderes’s Democrat Party (DP) and İsmet İnönü’s opposition Republican People’s Party (CHP) were growing increasingly tense, and the country was experiencing a deep political polarization. Every evening, the state radio would read out the long lists of those joining the Fatherland Front, spearheaded by the DP.

Then, on April 28–29, large-scale demonstrations by university students against the government took place in Istanbul and Ankara. We followed the news about these demonstrations—in which my brother also took part—with great excitement. Rumors had spread, later revealed to be fabricated, that the police had killed some of the demonstrating students and ground them into mincemeat. My aunt’s anger toward the DP government was growing by the day. On the morning of May 27, 1960, I was preparing to go to school for the graduation ceremony when we learned from the radio that the army had seized power and a curfew had been declared. I remember feeling deeply disappointed that the graduation ceremony could not take place. I would later learn that I had graduated third in my class.

The coup of May 27, 1960, was the first of the military interventions my generation would witness. My relatives in Istanbul, above all the İpekels and my brother, had greeted the coup with joy. In their view, the army had said “enough” to the increasingly authoritarian, dictatorial DP government. As far as I remember, I too was mostly under their influence. The news coming from the Ayvalık branch of the family, however, was bad. Ali Cömert, my sister Sumru’s father-in-law, was the region’s most prominent businessman. He had extensive olive groves; factories processing olive oil, soap, and cotton (ginning); and a large farm where various crops were cultivated. He was like the Ayvalık branch of the DP government. Banks competed to extend him credit. President Celal Bayar, when he visited Ayvalık, had been hosted at his seaside mansion.

Though he was somewhat overbearing toward those who worked for him, he was a man I found quite endearing with his large build, paternal manner, and “islander” (Lesbos) accent. The fun days we spent with the other children of the family during summer holidays on his farm in Altınova, full of fruit trees, hold an unforgettable place among my childhood memories. Witnessing “Uncle Ali Bey’s” eyes fill with tears as he gazed at the lights of his homeland Lesbos from the balcony of the farmhouse at night had given me much to think about.

The May 27 intervention paved the way for Ali Cömert’s bankruptcy. The military government imposed price controls on olive oil; banks cut off credit and demanded immediate repayment of debts. As if this were not enough, when his two barges carrying tons of olive oil to the Oil Wharf at Eminönü in Istanbul sank in the Sea of Marmara, the Cömert firm was first forced to seek a composition with creditors and ultimately went bankrupt. Ali Cömert lost his entire fortune. The considerable number of olive trees my sister Sumru had inherited from her father were also sold by the bankruptcy estate, since they had been mortgaged against the loans taken out by her father-in-law. In short, May 27 had brought ruin upon the family of my eldest sister, to whom I was deeply attached. My beloved brother-in-law Özbek, a graduate of Galatasaray High School and the Istanbul Faculty of Economics, not only lost his position as heir to what was perhaps Ayvalık’s wealthiest family but was tried on charges of fraudulent bankruptcy brought by creditor relatives and sentenced to two years in prison. After his release, he would make a living as an accounting manager at his uncle’s company.

In my final year at EHSB, it became clear that the school’s high school science section would be closed. Most of my classmates thereupon decided to continue at Robert Academy in Bebek. Although I had not the slightest interest in science courses and all my attention was focused on the social subjects and literature, I decided to take Robert Academy’s entrance examination, partly out of a desire to follow my close friends and, more importantly, because we no longer had a home in Istanbul and I needed to attend a boarding school. That year, for the first time in Robert Academy’s history, students were admitted through an examination that even its own middle school graduates were required to take. It caused a stir that those from EHSB, myself included, placed at the top of the entrance exam. And so, from the 1960–61 academic year onward, I became a boarding student at Robert Academy. Great changes in my life awaited me.

## At Robert Academy

Robert College, founded in 1863 by American Protestant missionaries, was the oldest American educational institution abroad; it was at that time one of Turkey’s most prestigious and influential educational institutions. The institution had a coeducational college (Robert College, RC) in Bebek, a boys’ high school (Robert Academy, RA), and a girls’ high school in Arnavutköy (American College for Girls, ACG). (In 1971, the college section would be nationalized and become Boğaziçi University, while the high school sections would be merged on the Arnavutköy campus and begin offering coeducational instruction under the name Robert Lisesi.)

Having changed homes and schools quite frequently since childhood, I had little difficulty adapting to the new environment, new friends, and new teachers. I was placed in the dormitory on the top floor of the building then known as Anderson Hall, where some thirty students slept. Boarding was enjoyable in itself. The school’s campus was of a beauty rarely matched anywhere in the world. I was no longer among the concrete masses of Nişantaşı but in the midst of extraordinary nature, looking out over the Bosphorus from the hills of Bebek. I was seventeen. With the help of the school’s educational approach, which reconciled discipline with freedom, I had begun to feel like an individual. On weekends, I could go down to the city, to the cinema, the theater, or the tavern with friends. Courses were taught by highly qualified foreign and local teachers and demanded a great deal of study. The teacher who appreciated me most was our Turkish literature teacher, the late Münir Aysu. The school offered opportunities to participate in a wide variety of extracurricular activities. My main interest, however, was theater. I joined the Drama Club (Robert College Players) and took a supporting role (the judge) in Ayn Rand’s The Night of January 16th, staged that year.

Founded as a Protestant missionary school, Robert College had in the Ottoman period served primarily the empire’s non-Muslim subjects. With the Republic, it had transformed into a completely secular educational institution, serving an overwhelmingly Turkish-Muslim student body. Looking back years later, I have thought that the education we received at foreign-founded schools, both EHSB and RA, made us quite privileged in the country but left us considerably deficient in the context of Turkish culture. To give a pointed example, in English literature classes we read passages from the New Testament and the Old Testament, but in Turkish literature classes the Quran was never a subject in any way.

My interest in politics was virtually nonexistent; I was hardly interested in anything beyond literature. The most important event of my first year at RA, from my standpoint, was learning of the existence of an organization called the American Field Service (AFS). AFS offered scholarships to high school students from nearly every part of the world to stay with a host family in the United States and attend their senior year there. (AFS had been founded during the First World War to assist in the evacuation of wounded and dead Americans from the battlefield, and had assumed an entirely new role after the war ended.) I told my mother and my brother of my intention to apply for an AFS scholarship. We decided it would be a good idea for me to apply. My brother and I filled out the application forms together. I sat for the oral selection exam conducted by former AFS scholarship recipients. I was not very hopeful, but I managed to become one of five students from RA to win the AFS scholarship that year. Two of them were close friends who had come from EHSB (Ahmet Kutman and Yavuz Sökmen), and another was the late Mustafa Gürsel, who would in time become one of my closest friends.

As summer approached, it became clear where I would be going: I would attend the Webb School of California, a prestigious private school in the town of Claremont near Los Angeles, and stay with the family of Gordon A. Wilson, the school’s dean of students. When I learned that the school was an all-boys boarding school, I was deeply disappointed. The hope of studying at a coeducational school alongside American girls had been one of the things that made the scholarship attractive. I had always attended boys’ schools. Apart from Fatma, the girl next door in Çamlık, no girl had truly caught my eye. When I learned that Webb was the most prestigious school on the West Coast of the United States, attended by the children of celebrities, I would find little consolation in that.

## Summer of 1961

I passed my first year at RA on the Honor Roll. At the end of June, I went to Ayvalık for a short stay to see my mother, my father, and my sister before the trip to America. There I learned that Ömer (Madra) had also passed the entrance exam and transferred from EHSB to RA, which made me very happy. The great event of the summer of 1961, however, was that Fatma—the girl I had lost my heart to since primary school and whom I believed to be the most beautiful girl in the world—unexpectedly showed me favor. She had fallen out with the other one and was turning toward me for the first time. My love blazed… I lived the most beautiful days of my life up to that point during that July. Fatma was beauty itself… Sadly, just a month later, at the end of July, I had to set off for the United States. I can say that this was the first of the conflicts between my private and public lives that would persist throughout my lifetime. My heart wanted to stay with Fatma; my mind favored going. I cannot forget the great heartache of parting from Fatma. And yet, it never crossed my mind to give up going. We were very young, and I was very curious about America. But I would not make this mistake again…

# CHAPTER II / OPENING UP TO THE WORLD

In the first days of August 1961, we departed Istanbul for New York on a large four-propeller aircraft filled with roughly a hundred male and female students who had won AFS scholarships that year. For the first time, I was going abroad, to spend a year with people I did not know, living on the other side of the world. My soul was filled, on the one hand, with the pain of separation from Fatma, and on the other, with curiosity about the new world. I suppressed some of my anguish by chatting with newly made friends along the way. (It was on that journey that I met my dear friend Güven Nil from the German High School, whom we lost in 2001. I will describe Güven’s place in my life later.) The plane made its first refueling stop at Shannon airport in Ireland, and its second at Gander airport in Newfoundland in eastern Canada. At Gander airport, an ultramodern structure for its day, I felt to the marrow of my bones that I was stepping into a world that was entirely new, in every sense, and very different from anything I had known. This feeling would become even more striking when we landed at New York’s Idlewild airport (its name before it was renamed JFK in December 1963).

We spent a few days in New York before being sent off to our host families. While trying to explore New York by walking its streets with friends, I felt as if I were being crushed beneath the skyscrapers. When I looked out over the city from the top of the Empire State Building, then the tallest of those skyscrapers, I was seized by a great fear. It was there that I first realized I had a fear of heights. As we wandered the city, we nearly got run over, since until then we had never encountered such a thing as a road where pedestrians were forbidden. The terror of cars hurtling toward us is still in my mind. Finally, AFS officials put Yavuz Sökmen and me on a plane bound for Los Angeles. This would be my first trip on a jet aircraft. I had taken off toward an unknown, exhilarating future. We landed at Los Angeles International Airport as night was falling.

I remember as if it were yesterday the excitement aroused by the boundless lights of Los Angeles spreading across a vast expanse as seen from the plane, and the apprehension of being about to meet the completely foreign people with whom I would soon be staying. Father (Gordon) and mother (Mollie) Wilson met me at the airport. White-haired Father Wilson, who walked with a limp due to childhood polio, showed great warmth and was trying to help me acclimate to the new environment. He told me that at Webb he served as dean of students and also taught ancient Greek history, classics, and English; that his interest in Turkey stemmed from this; and that he had visited Turkey in the late 1950s. When they applied to AFS to host a foreign student, they had indicated that a Turk would be their preference. His wife Mollie was a homemaker. They had five children—three girls and two boys—and two dogs.

After a brief dinner stop upon leaving the airport, we headed east in the Wilsons’ car along the widest roads I had ever seen, approximately 150 kilometers to the town of Big Bear Lake in the San Bernardino Mountains; we reached the summer house located on the shore of the eponymous lake (which had disappeared that year due to severe drought). I stayed there until the Webb School in Claremont opened in September. I met the family’s five children: in order, Bettie, eight years my senior; Gordie, five years older; Jackie, three years older; Tom, three years younger; and Barbie, six years younger. Bettie had married Marty and settled in Oakland. Gordie and Jackie no longer lived at home since they were away at university. The family did not have a member my own age, as AFS rules required, who was supposed to help me adjust. Tom attended Webb School and Barbie was in primary school. I knew that Webb was a private boarding school for boys, and that in this respect I would be in a different position from the other Turkish students.

The weeks I spent at Big Bear were quite difficult.

I was experiencing the deep sorrow of being separated from Fatma only a few weeks after winning her love. The Wilsons were doing everything they could to help me adjust. Father Wilson, taking Tom along with us, drove me on a trip lasting more than two weeks that extended all the way to Oregon. I saw San Francisco for the first time then. It was then that I discovered the incredible beauties and national parks of Northern California. There I rode a jet boat racing across a river. In Yosemite Park, I drove through tunnels carved through the trunks of redwood / sequoia trees.

When we returned from the trip, in the time remaining before school opened, Jackie offered to teach me to ski in the mountains; Tom, to teach me to ride the horses tethered in the garden. Jackie and Barbie wanted to take me ice-skating. I accepted none of these very thoughtful offers. I remember saying exactly this: “Thank you so much for thinking of ways to entertain me. But I’m afraid of getting injured. I don’t want to take risks. Because this year is very precious to me…” At the Wilsons’ summer house in Big Bear Lake, a classical music record collection and a world literature library that struck me as incredibly rich were helping to soothe, if only slightly, the ache that parting from Fatma had carved into my heart.

## Letters to Fatma

Fatma and I had only been able to be “sweethearts” for a few weeks in June–July 1961. I missed her desperately, and I was anxious that she might leave me in my absence. Several times a week, I was writing and sending her pages and pages of letters expressing my love and longing. She was responding with answers that grew increasingly infrequent and brief. In one letter she wrote, “It never would have crossed my mind that I’d call you my sweetheart…” Finally, in a short letter in January 1962 in which she wrote that she would be going to Ayvalık for the holiday, she said, as if preparing the ground for a break, “You’ll find someone prettier than me there…” A few weeks later, she stopped writing altogether. I understood that she had gone back to the other one.

I did not keep the letters she sent me; I destroyed them in hurt and anger. I had asked her to do the same. I cannot describe the astonishment and joy I felt when I learned, years later, that my Fatoş had kept all but the first two of the sixteen letters I wrote to her between August 7, 1961, and May 14, 1962… For her having kept them showed that even though she had ended our relationship and returned to the other one, she had preserved me somewhere in her heart—or (at the very least) could not bring herself to destroy my love-filled letters. (And yet in the last letter I sent, I had written in capital letters, “IF YOU NEVER WANT TO SEE MY FACE AGAIN, DISPOSE OF MY LETTERS…”) When I began writing my memoirs, I reread these letters with great excitement. The letters not only expressed the great love I felt for Fatma but also reflected my thoughts during that period.

The most obvious conclusion I drew from these letters was that I had probably frightened Fatma with them and perhaps encouraged her to give up on me even if she did not want to… As a fledgling “existentialist,” reading Sartre, Camus, Kierkegaard, and so on as best I could, and perhaps partly driven by a desire to seem interesting, I was writing her variations on “the meaninglessness of life”: “I find the world utterly meaningless and living unnecessary… What do you expect from a phony man like me in such a phony world? Am I committing a great crime by tying you to myself?.. You are free! You don’t have to wait! Never force yourself! Don’t give up on yourself, on your feelings! One is responsible only for oneself!… Perhaps among your suitors there is someone who wants you, needs you more than I do. Perhaps you want them more too. Why should I stand in your way then…” But then: “No one can love you the way I do… I’m going crazy for you.”

In these lines there were traces both of my superficial existentialism and of the insecurity I felt, forcing her to make a choice (“either the other one or me”): “Know this: life with me will not be one of those lives you see lived around you. If you wish to live that way, look to rid yourself of me… I am an unknown person… Which one am I… Should one fear this person… I hate living a balanced life… You can expect any kind of action from me… I know that I am not a normal person…”

My atheism, which I was discovering and taking pride in at the time, was also reflected in the letters: “I need you to love me more than to believe in God… I told you from the very first day that I wanted to live my whole life with you…” In what I wrote, there were also hints of my uncertainties about what I wanted to do and become in the future: “I don’t know which university I’ll attend… If I say now that I’ll study literature, it’s certain to change tomorrow… Maybe I’ll be forced to work in some wretched science field.” About the United States: “I don’t want to study here… but I should leave the door open, I’ll try to get a scholarship. In that case, either we’ll need to get married right away or I don’t know what will happen…” (As I will relate later, I would win a full scholarship to study in the US but would give it up so as not to be separated from Fatma once again.) And then there were these lines, worth recording: “In the future, perhaps I’ll write the story of what passed between us; only as a keepsake for my children, of course… I had never thought until now that I would have children; but I suppose they’ll benefit from what I’ve been through.”

There were also a few lines in the letters about politics in Turkey. Since my connection to the country had been almost entirely severed, I was writing the following about Menderes’s execution (in September 1961), which I had probably learned about from my elder brother’s letters: “Zorlu and Polatkan don’t matter, but when will we ever see someone like Menderes again… How can you not grieve for the second most important person after Atatürk?.. As for İnönü, I will say this: I take comfort in being part of the generation that will write history. We will deliver his eternal punishment…” (My view of İnönü would change over time, and I would come to see the positive aspects of his legacy as well.)

## Claremont

About a week before the Webb School opened at the start of September, we moved to the Wilsons’ home in Claremont, near the school campus—a spacious, extremely modern, single-story house built a few years earlier, with a large living room, six bedrooms, and four bathrooms. I settled into Jackie’s room. Before school opened, the classrooms needed to be cleaned. Mr. Wilson asked whether I would like to do the job and earn a little money. I gladly accepted; for the first time in my life, I performed physical labor and earned money. Like his own children, I too called Mr. Wilson “Dad.” He treated me well enough to make this feel natural. Mother (“Ma”) Wilson, who was of a reserved nature, perhaps could not show the same degree of closeness, but it was obvious in everything about her that she was a very good person.

When school opened, my introduction to the class went as follows: It was the custom, apparently, for senior students to gather on Sunday evenings, with a different student giving a talk each week. Mr. Wilson told me that because my name came first in alphabetical order, and because this would also be a good occasion to introduce myself to the class, the school administration thought it fitting for me to give the first talk. I agreed. I began my talk by sharing information about my family and my homeland: I was the child of a family from Ayvalık. My father and mother had been settled in Ayvalık under the compulsory population exchange agreement between Turkey and Greece in 1923; they met and married there. My father was born in the Greek city of Serez. My mother was originally from the island of Lesbos, just across from Ayvalık…. The moment I said, “My mother comes from Lesbos; she is a Lesbian…” a terrifying storm of laughter erupted in the classroom. I could not understand what had happened, but without missing a beat, I continued my talk.

When my talk was over, one of my classmates came up to me and introduced himself. A dialogue ensued between us: “Şahin, I don’t think you know what the word ‘lesbian’ means…” / “Doesn’t it mean someone from Lesbos?…” / “In English, with reference to the island’s famous ancient female poet Sappho, it is also used to mean a woman who loves women…” This amusing incident had two consequences: The ice between me and my classmates, who had jumped to the conclusion that I was a very witty person, melted on the spot… And thus began the friendship, which has lasted to this day, with Tor Krieger, who came over and explained to me what the word “lesbian” meant. Tor became one of my closest friends in life.

I should open a parenthesis here and touch on Tor’s interesting story: After Webb, he studied comparative literature at Wesleyan, one of the prestigious universities in the US. He spent his sophomore year at the Sorbonne in Paris. During this time, he developed a passion for philosophy. He was among the founders of the Wesleyan chapter of Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), one of the important student organizations of the New Left movement, which took a critical view of American democracy. After graduation, prompted by his atheist beliefs, he decided to deepen his knowledge of religious matters. With his first wife, whom he married in 1966, he volunteered among Native Americans as part of the Domestic Peace Corps program. (He would go on to marry two more times and live with three more partners, and from these relationships would have two children, a daughter and a son.)

He was admitted to the doctoral programs in divinity at both Columbia and Harvard. In the meantime, he was drafted to be sent to Vietnam. He filed for conscientious objector status to avoid going, but since this right was recognized in the US only for members of religious groups, he had to wage a great legal battle and go into hiding for several months. He joined the Peace and Freedom Party, which opposed the war and fought for fundamental rights. When Columbia and Harvard refused his request to transfer from the divinity to the philosophy doctoral program, in deep indignation he gave up on an academic career. He never lost his interest in literature and philosophy, but he decided to make his living as a carpenter, and so he did. He is one of the most intellectually formidable people I have known in life.

Tor came to Turkey on several occasions to see me. The first time, at the end of the summer of 1966 while he was in France, he drove to Istanbul in his old-model Volkswagen after a rather adventurous journey crossing Europe from one end to the other. He went to Robert Academy, the only address he had; there he learned that I might be in Ayvalık, and by asking around, he found me. We were able to spend a few days together in Ayvalık and Istanbul… Our second meeting came many years later. In 1995, when I happened to be in the US, he came to New York to see me. Later, he came to Istanbul in 2005 and to Ayvalık in 2007; he was our guest for a week or two. Our last meeting took place in Santa Rosa, where I went to visit him in September 2015 and stayed as his guest for a week. We continue our friendship through correspondence.

Returning to Webb: The Wilson family treated me extremely well. Mr. Wilson was a true gentleman, and his wife a true lady. Father Wilson, together with his son Tom, made his second visit to Turkey in the summer of 1966. They drove to Ayvalık from Switzerland; together, we made a three-week journey through the Aegean, the Mediterranean, and Central Anatolia that also helped me get to know Turkey. From 1970 until I wrote to them again in 1974, we lost touch. In 1975, he was planning to come to Turkey with his wife, but sadly he did not live long enough. (I will relay my most important memory of him later, when the time comes.)

After Father Wilson’s death, Mother Wilson and I corresponded several times a year until her passing in 2015 at the age of 104. Nearly every New Year and on my birthday, she would send me small dollar checks enclosed in letters. With that money, I acquired many books. I had the opportunity to visit her in Big Bear Lake, where she had settled, twice: on my own in 1985 and with Fatma in 1988. Jackie and her husband Bob; before them their son John; Gordie’s daughter; and Tom and his son all came to Turkey. Among the Wilsons, my “intellectual companion” turned out to be Gordie, who shortly after Webb opened was in a serious car accident and had to stay home for several months. His misfortune was my good luck. I think he too has not forgotten the pleasure of our conversations, in which my consciously or unconsciously existentialist ideas clashed with his radical libertarian views. We are still in correspondence.

Webb School was one of the most prestigious private secondary schools in Southern California. (It still is. It has grown considerably and has also begun admitting female students.) Among my classmates were members of very wealthy and well-known families. (For example, the sons of the famous actor Robert Mitchum and of the family that owned Parker Pens were among them.) A number of my classmates showed me great warmth and invited me to their homes during holidays. You can imagine how happy it made me that some of those who took little interest in me that year later came to Turkey to visit me, and from 2007 onward became devoted readers of my columns in Today’s Zaman.

Without exception, all the teachers at Webb treated me very well. The most interesting was our English teacher, Lachlan P. MacDonald, a fairly well-known short-story writer. I always received As in his courses. I was successful in all the courses I took except one. In the chemistry laboratory, when everyone else’s experiment came out blue while mine came out red, I was considerably embarrassed. I gained quite a bit of sympathy by distinguishing myself as one of the school’s best football players (!). Our football coach always played me in the starting eleven. However, in a match in which we were defeated 7–0 by a high school team in Northern California that we visited as part of the private schools league, I had to ask to be taken off the field after the seventh goal. The one who showed me the most favor was the elderly track-and-field coach, who put me on the A team despite my finishing last in the trial races.

What I disliked about Webb School was that, just like EHSB and Robert Academy, it was an all-boys school. Ulla, a Swedish girl who like me had come on an AFS scholarship and been placed with a family in Claremont, attending the local public high school, nearly swayed me when she said, “If you came to my school, you’d have a great time with the girls here…” Mr. Wilson would talk me out of this enthusiasm by telling me that such a transfer would be very difficult. Being an all-boys school was not the only thing that bothered me at Webb. The instruction was entirely secular, but the Webb family who had founded the school were devout Protestants. Every morning at eight o’clock, all students gathered at a chapel on campus, sang hymns, and listened to talks on subjects unrelated to religion. Partly because I came from a Kemalist family and was gradually developing critical views toward religion, being required to go to the chapel every morning irritated me considerably. I asked to be exempted, but my request was denied on the grounds that the gathering was not religious in nature, that I was not required to speak, and on other grounds. There was no recourse but to sit in the chapel in silence, with a sullen expression conveying my displeasure. Yet this experience would help me grasp the role religion played in American society.

What I loved most about Webb, however, was riding down to the town of Claremont every Saturday on the geared bicycle the Wilsons had given me, passing through the orange groves (none of which remain now). Claremont was a quintessential college town: at the time it had no fewer than five universities. For this reason, there were bookshops with rich collections. From these I would purchase quite a number of books on existentialism and bring them back to Turkey. The most noteworthy book I acquired was, without a doubt, Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels’s famous Communist Manifesto. In the year I attended Webb, I took my first step into Marxism by reading this book. I would later produce one of the first Turkish translations of it as well.

I had experiences at Webb that deeply affected me. One day Mr. Wilson told me that a Turkish doctor named Osman, living in Pasadena, had called him; the doctor had heard that they were hosting a Turkish student and wanted to meet him if possible. When Wilson asked, “The doctor would like to invite you to dinner at his home—would you go?” I gladly accepted. Osman Bey came one evening in his car, picked me up, and took me to his house. On the way, he explained that he was originally from Adana and had settled here after studying medicine in the US. When we arrived at the house, I saw that there were eight or ten other guests besides me; from their names, I gathered that most were Armenian. I was the first to speak up and introduce myself. After explaining the purpose of my stay in the US, I asked them what had brought them to the US and what they did. The Armenians told me that their elders had been expelled from Turkey through forced deportation and had emigrated to the US via Lebanon, and that they themselves had been educated here and entered various professions. I was in shock!!! I was hearing of the “Deportation” for the first time. I sensed that they were deeply wounded on this subject, and I did not press the matter further.

After returning home, I told my mother about the Armenians I had met in Pasadena and asked whether what they had told me was true. She then told me that it was true; that the Deportation had taken place while they were living in Ankara; and that her father had hidden two young Armenian girls in the attic of the house for a time and then arranged for them to convert to Islam and be married. I asked reproachfully, “Mother, why did you never mention any of this to me before?!” It had never occurred to her (!)… It was then that I came to understand how impenetrable the veil that Republican Turkey had drawn over the past truly was. The truth was that neither my father nor my mother had properly told their family stories; what I managed to learn, I mostly learned later, by asking relatives.

Love at First Sight

The year I spent at Webb also taught me what is called “love at first sight.” At a graduation party held on the yacht of one of our very wealthy classmates, anchored near Catalina Island off the Los Angeles coast, I met Linda Ann Wesson, who attended Azusa High School. We had both come to the party with different dates, but almost the moment we saw each other we were smitten, and before long we had thrown ourselves into each other’s arms. When I met her, unfortunately only a few weeks remained before my departure from Claremont, and we only managed to see each other a few more times. The Wilsons were quite worried about the consequences of the stormy love affair I was living through. In truth, in those days the thought of returning to America just to be with (to marry) Linda even crossed my mind.

Our farewell was very sorrowful. On the way back and after returning to Istanbul, I wrote Linda quite passionate love letters. However, after a while, perhaps thinking that our relationship had no future, I asked her to burn all my letters. In her reply she wrote: “I once spoke of a certain ‘magic.’ I used this word to describe what I felt when I was with you. You had the ability to make me feel there was no other world besides ‘our’ world. You made me forget so many things—being with you was like being outside all of humanity. I first experienced this at the party where I forgot who I was with and put everything aside and listened to my heart. Burning your letters would be a great loss for me, because they are so beautiful—I have difficulty believing they were written to me alone. There is nothing else to say; you said it all. And I don’t think I could express it any better with my limited understanding and intelligence. But this too is true: the things we shared are still so beautiful to me that no matter how much time passes, it is impossible for me to forget. I am so grateful to you for the happiness you gave me; it is very hard to get used to the idea that I will never find that happiness again. Şahin, I will never forget you, never. Please don’t forget my feelings for you; you made your choice. Always and forever, Linda.”

I hope to tell the full story of our “love at first sight,” which lasted perhaps a month and was spent going back and forth a few times between Claremont and Azusa, in “Human Landscapes from My Life,” which I plan to write in the future. This much is certain: had I not been consumed by my true great love, my love for Fatma, Linda might never have left my mind. During visits I made to California years later, I wanted to look up her phone number in the directory and call her, but I could never muster the courage.

## Back Home

At the beginning of July 1962, I said farewell to the Wilsons and to Linda and set off on a journey organized by AFS. As AFS scholars who had spent the year in Southern California, we piled onto a Greyhound bus; starting from Los Angeles, passing through the northern states of the US, we made a trip lasting approximately a month that took us to Washington, D.C., and from there to New York. Nearly every evening, we were guests of a different family in a different state. There were students from many nations on the bus, most of them European. Getting to know them, as well as the students in the families that hosted us, was both great fun and very educational. In Salt Lake City, the capital of Utah, the family I stayed with was in the funeral business. The way John, the boy my age in the family, left me behind and rushed headlong off to work when word came would remain in my mind as a tragicomic anecdote. My closest friends on the bus, those with whom I spent the most time, were two Dutch girls around my age. One of them, Beatrice, developed a crush on me; while studying at university in Amsterdam and working at her father’s shipping company, she would (fruitlessly) insist that I marry her.

The Greyhound journey was an extraordinarily rich experience in terms of forming an understanding of the diversity of the United States and the world. When we arrived in Washington toward the end of August, we toured the White House together with all of that year’s AFS students. Hundreds of students gathered in the White House garden. President John F. Kennedy, with Jackie at his side, addressed us. I had never before been so close to a political leader. As I listened, I reflected that I was face to face with the most powerful leader in the world. The Kennedys were truly a very handsome couple, and Jackie was a very beautiful woman; together they were deeply impressive. (JFK’s assassination would coincide with my first days at Ankara University’s Faculty of Political Science, and I would be deeply saddened by it.)

By the time we arrived in New York to embark on the return journey from Washington, I had begun to consider myself a “citizen of the world” who now knew Americans and Europeans alike. Cosmopolitan, universalist, humanist values seemed to have seeped into me a little more deeply. From New York, I flew to Zurich on a plane carrying Swiss and Austrian students. There I was met by my elder sister Olcay and my mother, who was visiting her at the time. After staying as a guest of my sister and brother-in-law for about ten days in the small town of Pratteln, my mother and I boarded a train from Geneva to Istanbul. After an adventurous and exhausting journey of about a week through Italy and Yugoslavia, we reached Istanbul at the very end of August 1962.

When I returned home, my elder brother told me what had happened in the country during my absence. The military junta that had come to power on May 27, 1960, had executed Prime Minister Menderes, Foreign Minister Fatin Rüştü Zorlu, and Finance Minister Hasan Polatkan in September 1961. Following the general elections held in October, the Republican People’s Party and the newly established Justice Party had formed a coalition government under the premiership of İsmet İnönü. Military Academy commander Colonel Talat Aydemir and his associates had attempted an unsuccessful coup in February 1962 and been pardoned. The question that arose in my mind in my first days back in the country, and that perhaps would determine my fate, was this: “Why was the US so rich and free, while my country Turkey was so poor and so far from freedom?” By the time I returned to Robert Academy in September 1962 to complete my senior year, the idea that some things needed to change in Turkey had begun to gnaw at my mind.

As I began my senior year at Robert Academy, my self-confidence had grown and my sense that I could steer the course of my life had strengthened. I was staying in a three-person room in the building called Theodorus Hall. My roommates were Ahmet Kutman, who had been one of my close friends since EHSB, and Güven Nil, with whom I had made the AFS journey and who upon return had transferred from the German High School to ours—someone I was very fond of despite our relatively short acquaintance. I should open a parenthesis here and say a little about Güven.

After finishing RA, he attended Robert College and became a mechanical engineer. After working at various firms for a time, in the 1980s he made a great deal of money through the company he founded, taking advantage of the export mobilization ushered in by the January 24th decisions. Believing that the future lay there, he invested his earnings in agriculture. First in Sakarya, then in Gallipoli, he established vineyards for winemaking, olive groves, and almond orchards. His pride and joy was the Sarafin Farm in Gallipoli. He had discovered the place while touring the region, driven by his deep curiosity about the history of the Battle of Gallipoli, and had purchased it. Together with Ahmet Kutman, who had taken over Doluca Wines after his father’s death, they began producing Sarafin-brand wines, perhaps the finest in the country.

Güven was extraordinarily intelligent, extraordinarily sensitive, and a voracious reader. He was a good athlete and passionate about basketball. He played guitar. The popular music trio of Güven, Münir, and Mürüvvet was quite well known in school circles. When he died of a heart attack while playing basketball in February 2001, I simply could not believe it. His loss was one of the greatest I have suffered. He had become very close to me. Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, he was the friend I saw most often and with whom I was most in intellectual agreement. He read my columns in Sabah and Milliyet without fail and would call to share his thoughts. He was insistent that I write my memoirs; he would say he was prepared to invest quite a lot of money in a film based on a screenplay derived from them. He believed that democracy would take hold in Turkey, that the Kurdish question would soon be resolved, and that the PKK would lay down arms and join democratic politics. Had he lived, he too would have suffered the same disappointments as we did.

Among my teachers in the senior year, the one I probably respected the most was Godfrey Goodwin, from whom I learned a great deal and under whom I took classes in classical music history at EHSB and in the history of visual arts at RA. After his retirement, Goodwin settled in London, and I had the chance to see him again only briefly, in Istanbul, a few years before his death, when he came for the launch of one of his new books. The obituary published in The Guardian upon his passing said: “Godfrey Goodwin, who has died aged 84, was best known for his ‘History of Ottoman Architecture.’ First published in 1971, this book remains in print and is one of the standard reference works on the subject, documenting the British scholar’s deep love of Turkey.” (September 6, 2005)

Among the teachers who supported my intense interest in literature in my final year at RA, one was our Turkish literature teacher Münir Aysu, and the other was our English literature teacher Charles Klopp. The late Münir Bey had a tremendous memory; he never forgot the countless students he had taught and kept track of what they were doing. We met on various occasions until the 2000s. Klopp, who would later specialize in Italian literature and history, mentioned in the foreword of his book Sentences: The Memoirs and Letters of Italian Prisoners from Benvenuto Cellini to Aldo Moro (1999) that a distant source of inspiration for the book was a student of his who, while he was teaching at Robert Academy in Istanbul in the 1960s, had told him, “In the future, I might go to prison because of my political views.” That student was not me. For at that time, my interest in politics was not yet at a level where it could bring to mind the possibility of going to prison for it. What I was thinking at the time was that I might one day become a good novelist.

“Reflections”

1963 was the year my love of literature peaked. I did not merely read intensively; short stories and numerous poems I wrote in English were published in the school’s literary magazine “Spectrum,” for which Mr. Klopp served as advisor. I was also one of the editors of that year’s yearbook (Reflections ’63). I prepared the section containing brief profiles of the graduating class and wrote many of the entries myself. The late Mustafa Gürsel and Mehmet Araslı said that in the profiles I wrote about them, I had practically read their characters and futures. The profile about me was written by my close friend from EHSB, Metin Kılıçlı, who said: “Known by almost everyone by the nickname ‘Dayı’ (Uncle), Şahin possesses the ability to communicate effectively with his friends through his powerful written and oral expression… Thanks to his intensive reading and talents, he promises to be a writer for future generations.” (p. 30.)

Metin’s prediction did not come true. In 2006, in Stockholm where I had gone for the Nobel Prize ceremony, I said to Orhan Pamuk, wanting to express my admiration and partly because I genuinely thought so, “Orhan, you are the only person in my life I’ve been envious of…” Sadly, he misunderstood. He must have thought of those who resented him out of jealousy and adopted a hostile stance, for he replied, “Şahin, you couldn’t possibly be jealous of me…”

I graduated from Robert Academy on the “High Honor” list. Outside of classes, I was one of the most active students. Hüsnü Özyeğin, who would later become one of Turkey’s most successful businessmen, was elected president of the school’s Student Council, and I was elected vice president. My friendship with Hüsnü, who would become the most famous member of our class, would grow closer in later years. In addition to the yearbook, I contributed to the school’s literary magazine “Spectrum.” One of my closest friends in the Book Club was Cem Kozlu, who was then in his first year of high school (and would later become one of our school’s most famous graduates, the CEO who paved the way for Turkish Airlines to become one of Europe’s largest carriers). Cem, who also served for a time as an executive at the Komili company and thereby established a connection with Ayvalık, remains one of my closest friends today.

As at EHSB, I became one of the active members of the Drama Club at Robert College. In the first term, I performed in William Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar. Güven Nil played Caesar, Mehmet Atakan—another friend whose friendship began at EHSB and continued throughout life—played Marcus Antonius, and I took on the role of Marcus Brutus. In Alejandro Casona’s Trees Die Standing, staged by the ACG Players (the American College for Girls Players), I appeared on stage with Nevra Şırvan Serezli (who would later become a famous actress) and Evin Sander İlyasoğlu (who would gain renown as a music critic), among others. In the second term, I appeared as Dr. Bauer in a play about the life of Sigmund Freud (whose title I cannot recall), in which the lead roles were shared by the late Ali Taygun and Mürüvvet Somuncuoğlu.

When I graduated from Robert Academy in June, I shared with Hasan Yazıcı—who would in time become one of my closest friends—the trophy awarded to the school’s most successful student in both academics and extracurricular activities, established in the name of the late Kaya Kaynar, the child of a family from Ayvalık who had died at a young age. During our school years, I had not been close to Hasan. Our friendship, which continues to this day, essentially began when I returned home from Sweden in the early 1980s. After completing his degree at the Cerrahpaşa Faculty of Medicine, Hasan went to the US and specialized in rheumatology. Today he is one of the world’s leading experts on Behçet’s disease; he also gained renown for the battle he waged against plagiarism in Turkey. I will return to the story of our friendship in the pages ahead.

One of the events that left its mark on me in my senior year was a trip organized by the “Social Services Club” near the end of the school year to Talas College, also an American school, in which students from the Arnavutköy and Üsküdar American girls’ colleges also participated. The most important aspect of the journey, which we made by train to and from Kayseri, was that it was my first trip east of Ankara. It was on this occasion that I first encountered what was called a “village.” The poverty I witnessed in the villages of Kayseri gave me a jarring sense of the scale of social injustice in the country. I can say that one of the foundations of my leftism, my socialism, which would accelerate during my university years, was laid on that trip. After the trip, I fell seriously ill; diagnosed with scarlet fever, I spent ten days in the school infirmary with a temperature reaching 43 degrees Celsius. I cannot forget my late elder brother’s coming to visit me nearly every day to boost my morale, and the tenderness he showed. Because of this illness, I was unable to sit some of my final exams and completed high school through make-up exams taken afterward.

Another unforgettable memory from the final year at the College was the turmoil in May caused by Colonel Talat Aydemir’s second failed coup attempt. I had been unaware of Aydemir’s first attempt in February 1962 because I was in the US at the time. My elder brother had told me that he had received no punishment for that attempt and had merely been forced into retirement. This time, Aydemir was tried before a military tribunal together with his principal accomplice Major Fethi Gürcan, sentenced to death, and executed in June 1964. After the successful military coup of May 27, 1960, we had now witnessed an unsuccessful coup attempt in May 1963. We were becoming ever more closely acquainted with the military’s political role.

“Columbia”

From my standpoint, one of the most important matters of 1963 concerned the question of where I would attend university. Like many of my classmates, I was planning to go to the United States. I took the examinations required to apply to American universities; with the aim of studying in the social sciences, I applied for scholarships to several of the US’s elite universities, foremost among them (also on Mr. Wilson’s recommendation) Columbia University in New York. Yet I was not without hesitations. In those days, the only means of communication, let alone with the US, even within Turkey, was by letter. The possibility that if I went for four years I might not be able to come home every summer was unsettling.

On the other hand, I had also been influenced by new ideas. The discourse of the Workers’ Party of Turkey, which was reaching our ears with increasing intensity, was providing a fairly clear answer to the fundamental question that had arisen in my mind on the way back from the US: “Why is the US so rich and free, while Turkey is so poor and so devoid of freedom?” Because we were being exploited under the yoke of an alliance of American imperialism and its domestic collaborators, the comprador bourgeoisie and the big landowners… To change the country’s fate, it was necessary to free ourselves from the imperialist yoke and build socialism… Seen from this perspective, going to the US to study looked like a kind of “treason against the homeland.”

On one of the last days at school, I ran into Nuri Çolakoğlu, who had graduated a year earlier and was attending the Faculty of Political Science in Ankara, and with whom I had not been particularly close until then. Nuri, who would later become one of my closest friends, subjected me to a kind of barrage of persuasion: What was I going to do going to the US… Like him, I could study at the Faculty of Political Science and become a diplomat, I could have a good career… Turkey’s future was being charted in Ankara, at the Faculty of Political Science… I must also have been considering the possibility that even if accepted at American universities I might not receive sufficient scholarships, for I applied to sit the entrance examinations for the Philosophy Department of Istanbul University’s Faculty of Letters, for its Faculty of Economics, and for Ankara University’s Faculty of Political Science.

Toward the end of June, news came that I had been accepted to Columbia University in New York to study sociology. I had also won a full four-year scholarship, including a work-study position at the university library during the summer months. The scholarship I won offered the opportunity to study at one of America’s most prestigious universities without my family having to spend a single penny. It was one of the best scholarships won by Robert Academy students that year, perhaps the very best. I suspected that the reference letters written by the Webb School teachers, including Mr. Wilson, had played a major role in this. A few weeks later, I received information about which dormitory, which room, and which roommate I would have at Columbia University. The time had come to prepare for the journey to New York. Flying was unthinkably expensive. Most students were making the journey to New York on cargo ships, a trip lasting roughly a month. With my elder brother’s help, I too reserved a place on a cargo ship to depart in August.

## I Went to Ayvalık and My Life Changed

In the first days of July 1963, I went to Ayvalık to see my mother, my father, and my elder sister Sumru, and to holiday for a few weeks, before a separation that would last years; had I not gone, my life might have followed an entirely different path. I went to Ayvalık and my life changed… There I ran into Fatma. The previous summer, we had ignored each other. This time, it was different. We came together. After finishing Işık High School, she had been studying in the Pedagogy Department of Istanbul University’s Faculty of Letters for two years. She had definitively separated from “the other one.” My love for her—which had never died, only been suppressed—immediately blazed anew. My love was not unrequited. I was madly in love with Fatma; she loved me too. The world was mine! We decided to get married right away. (As I will recount later, on March 20, 1964, we would become engaged with rings we bought and put on at the Grand Bazaar, and on November 29, 1965, we would marry in Ankara and build a home.)

Right in the middle of these extraordinary summer days when I was reunited with Fatma, my closest friend from Webb School, Tor Krieger (as I mentioned above), turned up, having driven thousands of kilometers in his Beetle Volkswagen. He had been attending a school in Paris for a year and had seized the opportunity to come to Turkey to see me before returning to America. I was bewildered about what to do in the face of my reignited love for Fatma: Was I going to go to Columbia, or wasn’t I? Could I leave Fatma and go once again? It was a terribly difficult decision… I returned to Istanbul with Tor, who had met Fatma and understood the difficulty of my decision. The results of the Istanbul University entrance exams had been announced. Tor and I went to Beyazıt to see the results, which at the time were posted on bulletin boards. I was very happy to have placed third in the Philosophy Department of the Faculty of Letters. I was quite upset, however, to find myself only on the reserve list for the Faculty of Economics; there must have been a mistake. This was the first and last failure of my educational life.

A few days after Tor returned to France, the results of the Faculty of Political Science entrance exam also arrived in the mail. I had placed somewhere near the top of the list. I did not hesitate much: My future was now charted… I decided not to go to New York. I would go to the Faculty of Political Science, become a diplomat, and marry Fatma; period! As in the famous poem by the American poet Robert Frost, “The Road Not Taken,” two roads had diverged before me. I (contrary to the poem) took “the one more traveled by,” and (as the poem says) “That has made all the difference…”

Fatma greeted my decision not to go to the US with her characteristic cool-headedness, but she did not hide her satisfaction. We were going to get married. I wrote a letter to Columbia informing them that “due to family reasons, regrettably” I would not be able to come, and reiterating my thanks for the scholarship. And so the New York chapter closed. Interestingly, the idea of marrying Fatma and going together never arose; probably out of fear: In that case, Fatma would have to join me later, and once again a long separation would be necessary. I did not want to risk being apart from her yet again. Yes, in later years, I did occasionally ask myself why we had not gone to New York together. (This was theoretically possible, since Fatma had inherited from her late father the means to comfortably finance it.) Nevertheless, I would ultimately conclude that the decision to go to Ankara rather than Columbia was, in the final analysis, despite everything, the right one.

The person most pleased by my decision not to go to the US was my mother. She would not be separated from her beloved son for years. She was also glad that the reason was Fatma. Fatma was the daughter of a family she knew, her neighbor and playmate Leman Kaptan; she was a fine bride-to-be. Interestingly, my father was pleased as well. When I told him I had given up going to the US and was thinking of marrying Fatma, he said, “Whoever she may be, if she is someone you love, everything in life is worth doing…” He also said he would help me as much as he could with getting married, but his promises would not be kept.

Mr. Wilson, who had been a great support in my winning the Columbia scholarship, made no reproach. The one who was deeply vexed by my not using the scholarship was Cornelius Bull, the headmaster of Robert Academy at the time. About a year after my graduation, I had gone to the school on an occasion I cannot recall. Hearing that the students were assembled in Albert Long Hall, I headed there. When I eavesdropped from the doorway, I heard Bull saying from the podium: “I hope none of you does what Şahin Alpay did and turns down a rarely won scholarship for the sake of a girl!..” That I should appear there at the very moment Bull was speaking about me was an almost unbelievable coincidence… I turned away from the door and quickly left the school.

After spending what were perhaps the most dramatic days of my life with Fatma in Ayvalık until October, I set off for Ankara. My mother had spoken with my maternal uncle Remzi Karatal, who lived in Ankara, and they had agreed that I would stay in the apartment on the ground floor of their building, which belonged to my aunt Perihan’s elder brother, who was in America at the time. Thus my housing problem for the first year was solved. A year later, my elder sister Olcay and my brother-in-law Ünal decided to settle in Ankara after returning home from Switzerland, and they began living in the Karacan family’s apartment on Selanik Street. In my second year, I was their guest. In the third year, Fatma and I would get married. In this way, my university life was quite separate from that of the Faculty of Political Science (Mülkiye) students who lived in dormitories. Throughout the first two years, nothing occupied my mind besides being with Fatma. I went to Istanbul nearly every weekend. Fatma was in her third year studying in the Pedagogy Department of Istanbul University’s Faculty of Letters, staying with her late maternal uncle İsmet—also known for his tenure as Director of the İzmir Fair—and his wife Aysun Kaptan; she too sometimes came to Ankara.

Finally, one spring day in 1964, during one of her visits to Istanbul, my mother and I went to visit my future mother-in-law Leman Kaptan, who was at the time visiting her middle daughter Ayşe in Kadıköy. My mother asked, “Leman, these children have decided to get married—what do you say?..” And when Leman Kaptan replied, “Since they’ve decided between themselves, there’s nothing to be done…” the path to our marriage was opened. On March 20, 1964, Fatma and I went to the Grand Bazaar; we bought a pair of wedding bands and became engaged right there on the spot. At that point, we intended to have the official wedding ceremony when I finished university. But we would not be able to hold out that long…

# CHAPTER III / BECOMING A REVOLUTIONARY

The winter of 1963-64 in Ankara would be the harshest winter I would ever experience. Since the Faculty of Political Science (SBF) had opened its doors to such a crowded class for the first time due to Ankara University’s first centralized entrance examination, classes were held in a sports hall without any heating during the harsh winter conditions. We were simply freezing… The conditions of the apartment I lived in were the complete opposite: it was excessively hot and humid because it was on the lower floor of the sauna operated by Dr. Hami Koçaş.

Nuri Çolakoğlu and I had become inseparable friends. With his encouragement, I joined the SBF Theater Club. Thus, my acting that had begun in the preparatory classes at EHSB continued at SBF. I played the lead role, Harrison Fish, in the play “The Last Hour of Harrison Fish” written by Juan Areola. The play, directed by Nuri, was performed one evening at the French Cultural Center in Kızılay and another evening at Gazi Education Institute in January 1964. Among those who had roles in the play were Deniz Gökçe (who would later become a well-known economics and sports writer), the late Cenk Duatepe (who held critical positions in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and served as Turkey’s Ambassador to Damascus during the period when Abdullah Öcalan was expelled from Syria), and Necati Utkan, Tansu Okandan, and Ayşe Aksoy (who would later serve as ambassadors).

The faculty member who left the greatest impression on me during my first two years at Mülkiye was undoubtedly Mümtaz Soysal, who was then a newly appointed associate professor and taught the course “Introduction to Constitutional Law.” Soysal had represented the CHP in the constitutional commission of the Representative Assembly established to draft the new constitution after the May 27 military intervention. He was also among the founders of the magazine Yön, which was published between December 1961 and June 1967 and served as the voice of the nationalist left movement in the post-May 27 period, along with Doğan Avcıoğlu, İlhan Selçuk, and İlhami Soysal (all now deceased). After the March 12, 1971 military intervention, he would be accused of “communist propaganda” in his textbook titled “Introduction to Constitutional Law,” sentenced to approximately 7 years in prison by a martial law court, and serve 14 months. The truly impressive aspect of Soysal’s lectures was his delivery that captured the complete attention of students. Being influenced by his ideas led me to develop an increasing interest in what was written in Yön magazine. My conversations with Nuri increasingly focused on the discourses of TİP (Workers’ Party of Turkey) and Yön magazine.

## Between two fires

I can say that the foundation of the tension between my private life and public life, which I could describe as being “between two fires,” was laid in the summer of 1965. That summer, while continuing to experience my passionate love with Fatma and making plans to marry at the end of that year, I was simultaneously developing an increasingly intense relationship with TİP and the idea of socialism. That summer, I participated in the meetings of the Ayvalık TİP district organization and in the election campaign it conducted in the villages of Ayvalık for the elections to be held on October 10, 1965. On that occasion, I would learn for the first time that some of these villages were inhabited by Alevis, whose existence I had not been much aware of until then. That summer, Ömer and I covered the Ayvalık-Çamlık asphalt road with TİP slogans that we wrote in oil paint.

The story of my friendship with Ömer could be the subject of a book in itself. I am also related to Ömer through the distant kinship between his paternal grandmother Beraat Madra and my maternal grandmother Nazire Hanım, both of whom were of Lesbos origin. Neither of us knows exactly when our friendship began. But he too had entered EHSB one year after me, in 1956, and our friendship had grown closer in Ayvalık where we spent our summer holidays. When we were in middle school, our passion was to press our ears against radios and listen to American-British pop music through the static, competing over who heard the new songs first. I reunited with Ömer in Ayvalık in the summer of 1964, after not seeing him for a long time because he entered Robert College one year after me and graduated one year later, and because I had spent my sophomore year in the USA. He was planning to go to France to study cinematography. It was not very difficult for me to dissuade him from this “empty and meaningless” career idea and convince him to study at SBF like me, “to become a diplomat and serve the Turkish state.” Just as Nuri Çolakoğlu had persuaded me to go to Ankara and study at SBF instead of going to New York to study sociology at Columbia University…

Our lives with Ömer would continue to follow an astonishing parallelism. I married Fatma at the end of 1965, he married his classmate Tanju at the end of 1966. My first child (Elvan) was born in 1968, his first child (Cem) in 1969. Like me, he began his Ankara adventure with the SBF Theater Club, then like me joined the socialist youth movement, the Fikir Kulübü (Ideas Club), TİP, and the Aydınlık movement. We lived through the disappointments of revolutionary politics together. After the March 12, 1971 military coup, he went to prison while I fled abroad. After the September 12 military intervention, while I was not admitted to universities, he resigned from his position at SBF. Our journalism period began with me starting to work at Cumhuriyet, and shortly after, him at Milliyet… I will return to the long history of my friendship with Ömer as appropriate.

## We are getting married

On November 29, 1965, Fatma and I got married in Ankara. Our wedding ceremony was held at the marriage office located in the Türkocağı building in Ulus. Fatma was the most beautiful bride I had ever seen, wearing the most beautiful wedding dress I had ever seen. The famous marriage registrar Mr. Müctaba Yetişen performed our ceremony with great solemnity, giving the occasion a sublime atmosphere. He spoke as follows (I quote verbatim since it is a now-abandoned form of discourse):

“You have previously informed us in writing of your decision to marry each other. Upon this request of yours, we conducted the necessary examinations. We investigated your civil status. We made the announcement according to the provisions of our Civil Code and marriage regulations. There is no obstacle to your marriage. It has been determined that you are legally eligible to marry. Now, please state verbally, before me and your witnesses, the wish you have communicated to us in writing. Do you wish to marry each other? Mr. Şahin Alpay, do you wish to marry Miss Fatma Nur Kaptan? - Miss Fatma Nur Kaptan, do you wish to marry Mr. Şahin Alpay?… You have stated before me and in the presence of witnesses that you wish to marry each other. By virtue of the authority vested in me, I inform you that your marriage has been legally contracted. I have registered your marriage in the marriage registry. I will also notify the population administration for it to be recorded in the civil registry. May it be auspicious and blessed.”

After Fatma and I, along with our witnesses my maternal uncle Remzi Karatal and Fatma’s brother-in-law (at that time) Arman Onaran, signed the marriage register, Mr. Mücteba stood up. We stood up with him. He continued his speech: “With this ceremony, from this moment on, your marital union has been established. You are obligated to ensure the continuation and happiness of this union toward each other, and as husband and wife, you are bound by fidelity and mutual support to one another. You will bear the responsibility of jointly caring for the sustenance and upbringing of your children. The husband is the head of the union. The proper sustenance of the wife and children belongs to him. The woman is her husband’s helper and advisor to the extent of her ability in ensuring mutual happiness. The woman looks after the home. The husband represents the union. For the permanent needs of the household, the woman also has the right to represent the union just like the husband. From this moment when your marital union has come into being, I remind you of these obligations imposed by our Civil Code as duties that must be observed as long as your life continues, and I wish you health and happiness.” (I found the late Mr. Mücteba’s standardized speech text in the late Güngör Uras’s column dated July 16, 2000.)

Our marriage was celebrated with a dinner reception at my elder sister Olcay and my brother-in-law Ünal’s home on Selanik Avenue, attended by most of our close relatives who could come to Ankara and my close friends from Robert College and SBF: Ömer Madra, Nuri Çolakoğlu, Erdal Yavuz, and Ümit Hassan. A girl of Fatma’s beauty and worth certainly deserved to be married with a magnificent wedding… Undoubtedly, if her father had been alive, he would have allowed his precious little daughter neither to marry me nor to marry without a proper wedding. Indeed, years later, we would both feel regret and sorrow for not having had a wedding ceremony. Around midnight, Fatma and I headed to the attic apartment we had rented in the Güneş building in Maltepe. And what do we see: the elevator was broken! Unfortunately, I was not strong enough to carry Fatma in my arms seven floors up.

We were both still 21 years old. This was considered a very early marriage for the male side in urban families of those years. Among my classmates, no one got married earlier than me. (Interestingly, I would later learn that my close friend from Webb, Tor Krieger, also had the first of his three official marriages that year.) The most important factor in our hasty marriage was certainly that we were experiencing a passionate love; but I think an equally important factor was that Fatma had grown up without a father since age eleven due to her father’s death, and I had grown up without a father since age six due to my parents’ divorce. I think for this reason we both felt the need to have a home as soon as possible. The small rented apartment on the top floor of the ten-story Güneş building in Tandoğan became our first home.

Fatma had completed her fourth year in the Pedagogy Department of the Faculty of Letters at Istanbul University; she would graduate if she passed the remaining few final exams. At that time, we thought she would pass the exams sooner or later and graduate. However, over time she gave up on the idea of graduating and getting a diploma. Unfortunately, I acted very selfishly and did not object to this. We thought: I was going to become a diplomat anyway, and therefore she would not be able to work. My plans to become a diplomat encouraged us to establish a traditional type of family where the man worked and had a career, while the woman took on the role of housewife. Another factor that played a role in Fatma eventually dropping out of university was that she had not enjoyed studying pedagogy. With her strong intelligence, sound logic, and sensible and cool-headed character, she could have been a first-class medical doctor. However, her mother had not encouraged her to get a good education; she had wanted her to marry someone from Ayvalık who would look after her properties at as early an age as possible.

Our marriage was made possible by the income Fatma received from the olive groves she had inherited from her father. My mother, who herself was barely making ends meet, could hardly contribute to our budget. Did living on Fatma’s income create any discomfort for me?.. Honestly, it both did and did not. Because, above all, there was no other way for me to marry her. On the other hand, I consoled myself thinking this was anyway a temporary solution, a kind of educational scholarship my beloved was providing me. I had now moved on to the third year; I was studying successfully in the Diplomacy and Foreign Relations Department. In any case, I would graduate in two years and start working at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs… My beloved thought the same.

During the more than two years from the summer of 1963 until we married in the fall of 1965, I can say that only Fatma occupied my mind; marrying her and being with her at all times had become my main aspiration. In those years, Fatma was studying at the Faculty of Letters at Istanbul University; she was staying at the home of her uncle İsmet and aunt Aysun in Taksim-Talimhane. While studying in the first and second years at Mülkiye, I went to Istanbul most weekends to see Fatma. However, from the spring of 1965 onwards, developments began to occur that were preparing a life for me without Fatma. When I returned from the USA to Turkey, the seed had been planted; I had begun to believe that the left movement, then represented by the Workers’ Party of Turkey (TİP), would find remedies for the poverty, injustices, and restrictions on freedom in Turkey that tormented my conscience.

“Dönüşüm”

My entry into the leftist youth movement came through the magazine Dönüşüm (Transformation), whose first issue was published in April 1965 and which only produced 5 issues. The pioneers of this first magazine published by leftist youth in the 1960s were Ataol Behramoğlu, İsmet Özel, and Abdullah Nefes, childhood friends from Çankırı (all three would become famous as poets). The magazine, prepared in a room in the editorial office of the journal Sosyal Adalet which served as TİP’s publication organ, was owned by Ataol Behramoğlu, while Ümit Hassan (my friend from Robert College who was then, like me, studying at Mülkiye) served as its managing editor. I believe I joined the editorial board at Ümit’s suggestion. Among the editorial board members, I also knew Hüseyin Ergün, the President of the SBF Fikir Kulübü (Ideas Club). The editorial board of the magazine, which published in line with TİP ideology and featured articles by TİP leaders, included, in addition to those mentioned above, İsmet Özel, Alper Aktan, Kurthan Fişek, Yurdakul Alpay, Aslan Sonat, and myself. Dönüşüm also engaged in polemics with Yön, the magazine of the left outside TİP. Ataol Behramoğlu had written an article titled “A response to a magazine with a clear direction” in response to a criticism of TİP published in Yön.

All 45,000 copies of the first issue of the magazine, which attracted considerable interest and was published on April 22, 1965, were sold. Copies reached not only Istanbul and Izmir but also some provinces of Anatolia. The attacks organized by right-leaning students under police protection against the young people selling the magazine in Kızılay and Ulus also contributed to the interest it generated. From these attacks, which were the first examples of the right-left conflict that would grow among students, my share was a few punches to my head in Kızılay. These attacks disturbed the TİP leadership, which (in Hüseyin Ergün’s words) “did not want fighting and brawling,” and the magazine was asked to cease publication, which it did.

Since I was still keeping my intention to become a diplomat at that time, I had written in the first Dönüşüm under a pseudonym. I remember that my article signed “Salim Altay” targeted American cultural imperialism. I was uncomfortable with my Robert College graduate and AFS scholarship background alongside the leftist identity I was acquiring. The main event reflecting this discomfort was my resignation from the membership of the association (whose name I no longer remember) established by young people who went to study in the USA on AFS scholarships, by writing an angry protest letter. I recall that I shared the leadership of this “action” with the late Yalçın Yusufoğlu, who was one of the founders of the Turkish Socialist Workers’ Party (TSİP), the first socialist party organized after March 12. (Just as years later we would talk and share our disappointments with the left movement.)

Dönüşüm, which served to establish communication among leftist youth groups, began to be published again in late 1966. This time Abdullah Nefes took on the ownership and editorial directorship. After the closure of the journal Sosyal Adalet, Dönüşüm II, which acquired the identity of TİP’s publication organ, published a total of 7 issues, from the 6th to the 12th.
