This time, those on the editorial board included, besides Nefes, Behramoğlu, Ergün, and myself, Doğu Perinçek, Atilla Sarp, Osman Sakalsız, Ayhan Başaran, Murat Koğacıoğlu, Nuri Çolakoğlu and Ömer Madra (who joined at my suggestion), and Sinan Cemgil (one of the founders of THKO who was killed by the gendarmerie in the Nurhak mountains in May 1971). I also met Doğu Perinçek on this occasion. I would write in the second Dönüşüm under my own name. My articles in Dönüşüm reflect the transition in my political ideas from roughly nationalist-statist-secularist Kemalism to roughly TİP socialism. (Unfortunately, I was unable to find copies of either the first or second Dönüşüm. More than fifty years later, at our meeting in Ankara in April 2016, even Abdullah Nefes, who passed away in 2021, would say that he had no copies of the magazine left.)

Turkish Labor Party Ayvalık branch

My interest in politics, socialism, and especially TİP intensified in the summer of 1965. Those I met in Ayvalık who had been arrested and imprisoned in the 1951 Turkish Communist Party trial and members of the TİP district organization played an important role in this. As far as I remember, the key figures were tailor Ali Çolakoğlu, a former TKP member, and his son Mustafa Çolakoğlu, also a tailor, who was active in the TİP Ayvalık district organization. Ali Çolakoğlu introduced me to the “old guard”: the late Ahmet Bilge, who was then working as a contractor and had taken on the restoration of the mansion left by Greeks two houses away from our home in Çamlık, his partner Güner Eliçin (father of journalist Işın Eliçin), and old Ahmet Usta, a shoemaker from Cunda, or rather from Crete (whose surname I don’t remember). Through Mustafa Çolakoğlu, I had also met the main members of the TİP district organization: watchmaker Hüseyin, gardener Hasan, grocer Fethi (Namlı), electrician Işık, and salt merchant Muvaffak.

In the summer of 1965, I frequently got together with the people I mentioned above. I participated in the election campaign the TİP district organization conducted in the villages of Ayvalık during the 1965 elections. As I described above, Ömer Madra and I wrote fiery slogans against American imperialism and in favor of socialism in oil paint on the asphalt of Çamlık, Ayvalık’s “bourgeois” neighborhood and our own. Although Fatma found what I was doing strange, she had adopted a benevolent perspective. Starting from our engagement period, she had begun to develop the principle of not interfering in my public life. She probably thought “he must know what he’s doing.”

In the 1965-66 academic year, I was studying in the third year at SBF in the Diplomacy and Foreign Relations department. Nuri Çolakoğlu, whom I had met at Robert College and who had played a major role in my going to Ankara, and I were inseparable. Nuri had failed that year and had come to the same class as me. We frequently got together at the attic apartment on İzmir Street where he lived with his girlfriend Sezi (Ergun), who was then a TRT programmer and would later become his first wife. We had divided the courses between us. I would attend some and take notes, he would attend the others. This way we could devote more time to our other interests.

## Peace Association

My first step into socialist youth organizations was with the Peace Association, of which I was among the founders in December 1965, about a month after my marriage to Fatma. Among the founding members of the association, I remember Hüseyin Ergün (the first president of Fikir Kulübü), Alper Aktan, Kutlay Ebiri, Ahmet Ali Arlı, Sami Urfalı, Ömer Madra, Tuğrul Eryılmaz, Necmiye Alpay from the Faculty of Language, History and Geography, and Henri Çerniyak, my friend from Robert College who was studying at ODTÜ. (Çerniyak later emigrated to Israel and, I believe, started working for Mossad.) On the first board of directors of the association, besides Kutlay Ebiri who was elected president, there were Sema Erder (whose beauty attracted the attention of many of us), Ayhan Başaran, my classmate from Robert College Erdal Yavuz, and myself. At that time, I was closely following leftist literature and felt great affinity for TİP, but perhaps because I had not yet abandoned the prospect of becoming a diplomat (which I had promised Fatma), I had neither joined Fikir Kulübü nor registered with TİP.

The Peace Association defined its purpose in its founding declaration as follows: “The principle of peace at home, peace in the world outlines the main lines of the association’s work. The association is against any behavior that could endanger peace.” The vast majority of the association’s founders and members were students from and around the SBF Fikir Kulübü. Some members were also members of TİP. The association served as a kind of “front organization,” functioning to recruit left-leaning youth to Fikir Kulübü membership. Years later, when asked about his memories of the Peace Association, Hüseyin Ergün said: “It was an initiative started by bourgeois and aristocratic youth…” President Kutlay Ebiri remembered the association differently: “I know that there were no aristocrats among us, except perhaps Sami Urfalı. There were one or two wealthy (Ömer Madra, Şahin Alpay) or middle-class (Erdal Yavuz) College students. I was living on a 250 lira per month scholarship from the Ministry of Finance, and I was sending the money I saved to my mother.” (See: Pınar Selek, Barışamadık, İthaki Özyürek Publications, Istanbul, 2004, p.274)

Kutlay said the following in a letter he wrote to me years later (in early 2016): “The idea to establish the Peace Association came to me from the fact that the SBF Fikir Kulübü was somewhat too closed in those years and the negative atmosphere created by some whose heads were in the clouds (meaning quite radical leftists) like İsmet Özel. Our aim in founding the association was to attract more Mülkiye students to the left and to emphasize anti-imperialist themes (especially against the Vietnam War). We contacted Bertrand Russell, prepared panels with brilliantly printed photographs against the Vietnam War that he sent, and soon 50-60 students who had not really thought of joining Fikir Kulübü joined the association. We also opened the Istanbul branch under the presidency of my high school friend Fahrettin Yağcı.” Founding president Kutlay Ebiri and the late Fahrettin Yağcı from Istanbul University Faculty of Economics would both do economics doctorates on government scholarships in England after graduating from the faculty and become experts at the World Bank. (Both were among my close friends in the club of those disillusioned with the belief in socialism.)

Kutlay was a distant relative of Altay Egesel, the notorious chief prosecutor of the Yassıada Trials. What he said about the association’s founding process gives an idea about our confusion: “…Russell’s efforts regarding Vietnam and his universal fame had appealed to us… We looked at the guerrilla and liberation movements in Latin America with sympathy, we studied them, but we never thought of applying their methods in Turkey. We were of the view that there were serious differences between the class character, striking power, and political spectrum positioning of Latin American armies and those of the Turkish army.” (Selek, pp. 272-273.)

An internal conflict reflecting “the spirit of the times” occurred in the Peace Association. The supervisory board, of which Sema Erder was also a member, expelled Kutlay from the association on the grounds that he had “deviated from the revolutionary line and turned the association into a supporter of the junta.” This was perhaps a harbinger of the “who is the real revolutionary” competition that would grow and eventually lead to revolutionary youth being at each other’s throats. Years later, Kutlay explained this incident to Selek as follows: “I think the junta supporter image came from me telling my friends what my distant relative Altay Egesel said when I occasionally went to visit… Egesel was very much involved with the junta supporters at that time. This was probably a habit from before May 27…” After Kutlay’s expulsion, Ayhan Başaran took over the association presidency, and later Erdal Yavuz. Cengiz Çandar became Erdal’s vice president. (Erdal and Cengiz would be among my lifelong friends.) The association was closed after the March 12, 1971 military intervention.

## Two Nuris

I had achieved my goal, married the girl I loved, and set up a home of my own in Ankara. I now had the opportunity to engage more closely with the political subjects I was being educated in and was quite curious about. Indeed, the 1965-66 academic year, the first year of our marriage, would be a turning point in my life.

It was late March 1966. One day Nuri Çolakoğlu came to our home in Maltepe-Tandoğan. Mahir Çayan, the newly elected president of Fikir Kulübü, had called him and broached the subject: Fikir Kulübü wanted to win the SBF Student Association elections to be held in April. For this purpose, they had decided to nominate Nuri, a Robert College man, whom they believed could attract votes from a wider circle of students. However, Nuri had not accepted the proposal, using his engagement with the Theater Club as an excuse; he had suggested me instead on the grounds that I could be even more successful.

I remember being excited when Nuri brought up the subject. Being the presidential candidate of Fikir Kulübü at Mülkiye, the main headquarters of socialist-revolutionary youth, was no small matter. Nuri introduced me to Mahir Çayan, whom I would meet for the first time. Mahir made a very positive impression on me. I was proud of the offer he made. Still, I asked for permission to think about it for a day or two. I talked with Fatma. Since she didn’t know where this could lead, and mainly because of her attitude of leaving decisions about myself to me as she almost always did, she did not take a position for or against. If she had taken a position against, could she have changed the decision I would eventually make? Perhaps…

When it became known in our circle of friends that Fikir Kulübü had offered me the candidacy, Nuri Yıldırım, one of the few Robert College graduates at Mülkiye and one of my lifelong friends (later ambassador), came to my door unexpectedly. A very bright future awaited me as a diplomat; if I accepted the offer, became Fikir Kulübü’s candidate, and especially if I were elected Association president, I would ruin my future. I was facing quite an ironic situation: while one Nuri from Robert College was opening a path for me, another Nuri from the same school was insistently warning me not to take that path. My interest in politics was growing steadily. The urge to prove myself must have prevailed, because after some thought I accepted the proposal and became Fikir Kulübü’s candidate for SBF Student Association president. I was more or less aware that if I were elected, my plan to become a diplomat would come to an end. For this reason, I began to think of a future for myself as a faculty member at SBF. After my candidacy was announced, without further delay, I registered as a member of the TİP Çankaya District organization, then headed by my brother-in-law, the late Ünal Karacan, my sister Olcay’s husband. (My brother-in-law would later, angered by my going over to the ranks of the “proletarian revolutionaries,” strike my registration from TİP, so I would not need to resign.)

I won, by a single vote, the election between me and Şükrü Tufan, the candidate of the Hür Düşünce Kulübü (Free Thought Club), which brought together students close to the Justice Party and had been established by Celal Güzel, Mehmet Keçeciler, Abdülkadir Aksu (all of whom would later become ministers) and their friends. The fact that I won the election as a “Robert College student” who did not stay in the dormitory because he was married, who was rarely seen at the faculty, who did not know many people at school, who was called “bourgeois,” and who was rumored to “own half of Ayvalık” was truly a miracle. Cenk Duatepe, a fourth-year student who was the election committee chairman and a Fikir Kulübü sympathizer, would explain to me how this was possible: “When we noticed that the rightists were stuffing the ballot boxes with plenty of fake votes, we also took precautions…” (When Duatepe passed away on March 26, 2010, Milliyet newspaper reported: “Duatepe had served as Turkey’s Ambassador to Damascus during the period when terrorist Abdullah Öcalan was expelled from Syria and played an active role in the process that ended with Öcalan’s extradition to Turkey.”)

The SBF Fikir Kulübü, composed of TİP-leaning students, was winning the Student Association elections for the first time. Upon the announcement of the results on April 20, club members and sympathizers held jubilant celebrations inside the faculty. Various revolutionary marches were sung, including “The Internationale” and the famous march of the Italian communists “Avanti Popolo.” These demonstrations had tragi-comic consequences. Upon a denunciation by some right-wing students, two of the friends who sang these marches were tried without detention for nearly 5 years on charges of “communist propaganda,” in the language of the indictment against them. One of them was our friend İsmet Özel (later a famous poet), who was a very dogmatic Leninist at the time but adopted a rather dogmatic Islamism from the second half of the 1970s onwards, and the other was Erdal Yavuz (later a professor of economic history), one of my closest friends from high school to this day.

Although they were acquitted in 1971 due to insufficient evidence, the Court of Cassation overturned the decision on grounds of incomplete investigation upon the prosecutor’s objection. The court finally decided at the end of 1972 to acquit Özel based on the unanimous decision of the SBF Board of Directors that no action was necessary under the disciplinary regulations, and to interrogate Erdal Yavuz when found, as he had not come to give a statement after the reversal. Had the Court of Cassation’s final acquittal not come in time, this ongoing case would very nearly have prevented Erdal from going to Strasbourg University to do his doctorate on the scholarship he had won from the Ministry of Finance, and we would not have been able to join him there a while later.

The election won by a single vote and through a fraud for which I bore no responsibility played a decisive role in deepening my politicization. The majority of the Student Association board of directors, of which I was president, consisted of Fikir Kulübü members. Among them, I remember Erdal Yavuz, Nuri Çolakoğlu (who would later become a journalist-writer), and Tuğrul Eryılmaz, as well as Ali Külebi, Erçin Odman, Suat Asutay, Atilla Vural, and Özkan Mert. İstemihan Talay from the Social Democracy Club (who would become DSP Mersin/İçel MP for the 18th-21st terms and Minister of Culture in the 55th-57th governments) and Esat Güçhan from the Hür Düşünce Kulübü (who served as Tekel General Manager and Wrestling Federation President for a while) were also among those who entered the board by breaking through the Fikir Kulübü list.

The day after the election, on April 21, 1966, we visited Anıtkabir as the board of directors. I wrote the following in the memorial book: “Immortal Atatürk, the Supreme Leader of our people in our National Liberation War! We are the owners and guardians of the Turkish regime, of the Turkish revolutions!” My views at that time, I believe like those of many of my leftist friends, were a strange mixture of Kemalism in the sense of nationalism-statism-secularism and a kind of “soft” socialism meaning state-led development, land reform, and distancing from the West, which TİP advocated in its early years. Atatürk was respected as a great revolutionary among leftist youth at the time. Indeed, the picture of “Mustafa Kemal wearing a kalpak at Kocatepe” in my study at home would not come down from the wall until 1970…

## Turkish left in the 1960s

With my election to the presidency of the association, which we would soon rename “SBF Student Association,” I began to participate more actively in the leftist youth movement. For the purpose of understanding the place I envisioned for myself within this movement, it would be useful for me to provide a general description of the left in Turkey in the period from the second half of the 1960s to the March 12, 1971 military intervention. I would like to emphasize that the summary description you will read below has no claim beyond reflecting my understanding.

During this period, the Turkish left was essentially divided into four currents. The one that initially carried great weight was TİP, established in 1961. One of the rival currents consisted of intellectuals and politicians gathered around the “Socialist Culture Association” founded by Doğan Avcıoğlu and the magazine Yön (1961-67) that he began to publish. The other was the National Democratic Revolution (MDD) movement led by former communists. In addition to these, there was also a leftist youth movement that harbored various tendencies within it.

After Mehmet Ali Aybar was elected chairman in 1962, TİP began to increase its influence among left-leaning intellectuals and youth. Along with Aybar, sociologist Behice Boran, economics professor Sadun Aren, and newspaper columnist Çetin Altan were the party’s leading spokespersons. In its program adopted at its first congress in 1964, TİP spoke of “development by the non-capitalist path” as an intermediate stage on Turkey’s way to socialism and of a “second war of liberation for independence.” TİP received 2.9% of the votes in the 1965 elections, its first election, and won 15 parliamentary seats thanks to the proportional representation system in effect and the distribution of votes according to the National Remainder method. Emboldened by this electoral success, party spokespersons began to speak of “socialist transformation.” From the summer of 1966, Aybar began to speak of the inseparability of the struggle for national independence and the struggle for socialism. The success of the independence struggle in underdeveloped countries was only possible by ending the power of the comprador bourgeoisie and landlords who collaborated with imperialists. The idea of a struggle to be waged simultaneously for national independence and socialism was also supported by the party’s other leading figures.

The group referred to as MDD supporters, whose spokesperson was Mihri Belli, opposed Aybar’s theses at TİP’s second congress in November 1966 and put forward the thesis of a two-stage revolution. In the first stage, the goal was the National Democratic Revolution (MDD), that is, gaining national independence by ending the power of imperialist and domestic collaborators and eliminating feudal remnants through land reform; the socialist revolution could only come on the agenda after this. The great majority at the congress supported Aybar’s theses, but the first signs of division within the party were also seen. Complaints began about Aybar’s dominance and the lack of democracy in the party.

The ideological split in TİP emerged following the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968. While Aybar strongly opposed the invasion, he began to speak of the need for a socialism that included liberal democratic institutions, “socialism with a human face.” He called on socialists to read the works not only of Karl Marx and Vladimir Ilyich Lenin but also of Karl Kautsky and Eduard Bernstein. He argued that the democracy inherent in socialism could be realized for the first time with “Turkish socialism.” While Aybar’s theses were supported by people like Çetin Altan, Şaban Erik, Rıza Kuas, and Tarık Ziya Ekinci, Behice Boran, Sadun Aren, and the party’s general secretary Nihat Sargın opposed them.

Boran argued that, contrary to what Aybar claimed, human history was not a history of struggle for freedom but of class struggles; Şaban Erik argued that Aybar’s views meant a revision of scientific socialism. Despite fierce opposition, Aybar emerged successfully from the third congress held in November 1968 as well. One of the congress resolutions emphasized that “Turkish socialism” was a completely independent current and that socialist parties and states should respect each other’s independence. At this congress, a resolution describing TİP as “socialist” was adopted for the first time. Immediately after the third congress, Çetin Altan, who had been one of his supporters until then, published an article criticizing Aybar’s authoritarian attitudes. When Aybar demanded his expulsion from the party, Altan claimed that Aybar accused everyone who opposed him of being a “Moscow communist.”

Intra-party divisions negatively affected TİP’s work considerably after the third congress. At the extraordinary congress convened in December 1968, Aybar said that he had been advocating “individualist socialism” since 1945 and that if TİP came to power, it would preserve the institutions of liberal democracy. Aren accused Aybar of imposing his own views on the party, and Altan accused him of authoritarianism. The “National Democratic Revolutionaries” directed harsh criticism at both Aybar and the Aren-Boran faction. Before the general elections on October 12, 1969, Aybar’s supporters also split among themselves: the trade unionists who were among the party’s founders opposed the method used in determining parliamentary candidates. The party’s vote share dropped from 2.9 percent to 2.65 percent, and as a result of the abandonment of the national remainder method in the distribution of parliamentary seats, TİP could only win 2 seats. The election results were interpreted by MDD supporters as proof that the struggle for socialism and the struggle for independence were different from each other and as a defeat of the thesis of coming to power through parliamentary, democratic means. The MDD thesis began to spread especially among leftist youth. Opponents demanded that Aybar, whom they saw as responsible for the electoral failure, step down from the chairmanship. Aybar resigned from the party in November 1969.

At the fourth congress held in October 1970, the Aren-Boran faction dominated the party. When a resolution was adopted stating that advocacy of MDD theses was incompatible with TİP membership, MDD supporters were purged from the party through forced resignation or expulsion. The Aren-Boran faction continued to adopt Aybar’s theses that the struggle for independence could not be separated from the struggle for socialism and that power would be achieved through democratic means, but they claimed to advocate “scientific socialism” against his “individualist/democratic” understanding of socialism. According to them, socialism was a “mode of production” based on public ownership of the means of production and a planned economy. Following the March 12, 1971 military intervention, the Constitutional Court would decide in July 1971 to close TİP not on the grounds of “communist propaganda” but on the grounds of “separatism” by mentioning the existence of Kurds in the east of the country in a resolution adopted at its last congress.

“National Democratic Revolutionaries”

According to the “proletarian revolutionaries” opposing TİP, whose leading spokesperson was Mihri Belli (one of the former central committee members of the TKP), the revolution in Turkey would be two-staged; the National Democratic Revolution (MDD) stage and the Socialist Revolution (SD) stage were separate from each other. Turkey was politically and economically dependent on Western imperialist states, primarily the USA, and the remnants of feudalism were hindering socio-economic development. The first task of revolutionaries should be to ensure national independence and to eliminate feudalism. The establishment of socialism was a later goal. Belli first developed these views in the summer of 1966 in Yön magazine, and after 1968 in Türk Solu and Aydınlık magazines. According to Belli, besides the comprador bourgeoisie, there was also a national bourgeoisie in Turkey; even if it could not be made to join the MDD, at least it could be neutralized. The Kemalists were representatives of the national bourgeoisie.

Belli directed two fundamental criticisms at the TİP leadership: 1) By confusing the MDD and SD stages, it was alienating important allies from the movement. 2) Coming to power through peaceful and democratic means was an illusion. TİP’s program was only compatible with MDD goals. Belli saw no difference between Aybar and the Aren-Boran leadership, speaking of the “opportunist Aybar-Aren clique.” The MDD supporters, on the other hand, supported the invasion. Belli argued that the Kurdish question (that is, the question of the suppression of Kurdish citizens’ identity rights) would be solved when MDD was achieved and equal rights were granted to all citizens of different origins.

Differences of opinion arose among MDD supporters who characterized themselves as “proletarian revolutionaries” on the question of who would lead the revolution. Belli initially (in the 1966-68 period) argued that the vanguard would be assumed by the “military and civilian intellectual stratum” (the fashionable concept of the time), which he characterized as “the most conscious section of the petty bourgeoisie,” but later changed his views and adopted the view that the vanguard would be assumed by “the proletariat and poor peasants, the most revolutionary forces of society.” His making this change was influenced by criticisms that he was engaging in “petty bourgeois tailism” by drawing closer to the views advocated by the magazine Devrim edited by Avcıoğlu. In the autumn of 1970, an attempt by Belli to establish a legal party “to lead the MDD” together with Hikmet Kıvılcımlı (a former TKP member) and his supporters, as well as the faction led by Mahir Çayan among leftist youth, came to nothing. Belli fled abroad after the March 12 intervention. After returning to the country with the 1974 political amnesty, he founded the Turkey Labor Party with his supporters in 1975, but the party was closed by the Constitutional Court on grounds of “separatism.” Belli would pass away in 2011.

## “The Junta Supporters”: The Yön-Devrim Circle

The leftist group that was perhaps the most influential on Turkish politics in the 1960s was the current that published the magazines Yön (1961-67) and later Devrim (1969-1971). A narrow circle that included names like Mümtaz Soysal, İlhan Selçuk, and İlhami Soysal alongside Doğan Avcıoğlu acted as its spokesperson. It never claimed to become a broad-based movement, but the magazines it published had widespread influence among intellectuals. In its declaration published in its first issue dated December 20, 1961, signed by about 150 intellectuals, Yön magazine advocated the implementation of “a new and progressive type of statism.” “New and progressive statism” essentially envisaged a planned public sector, a mixed economy system, and land reform. In 1962, the magazine pioneered the establishment of the Socialist Culture Association, which adopted the aim of advocating “Turkish socialism.”

The Yön writers, especially Avcıoğlu, essentially advocated the following ideas: Turkey had gained political independence under Atatürk’s leadership but had not gained economic independence. The path to economic independence, rapid industrialization, and development passed through an “anti-imperialist and anti-feudal national liberation revolution.” Turkey should leave the NATO alliance and join the non-aligned movement. The current multi-party system served the power of “reactionary classes consisting of comprador bourgeoisie and feudal landlords” and prevented the necessary reforms from being made. For revolution, an alliance of progressive forces including the “vital forces,” that is, the left wing of the military-civilian intellectual stratum, trade unionists, revolutionary youth, and the small and medium bourgeoisie, needed to be established. The vanguard of the revolution should be the military and civilian intellectual stratum. Avcıoğlu placed great hope in the Turkish army, which he saw as very different from the armies in the West and Latin America that served the ruling classes. The army, composed of officers from poor families and committed to Kemalist principles, was one of the most important forces of the revolution. Revolutionary youth would play the leading role in the national liberation struggle.

Relations between TİP and Yön magazine were never friendly. Although some TİP executives initially supported the magazine, others opposed the establishment of the Socialist Culture Association. The Yön circle also opposed the socialist slogans that TİP began to use after the 1965 elections on the grounds that they alienated the progressive sections of the bourgeoisie from the revolution. TİP under the Aren-Boran leadership, on the other hand, saw the “Center-Left” movement in the CHP as the main rival.

Avcıoğlu ended the publication of Yön in 1967 and wrote Türkiye’nin Düzeni (Turkey’s Order) (1968), one of the most influential books among intellectuals of that period. In October 1969, he began to publish Devrim magazine. With Yön magazine and Türkiye’nin Düzeni, the intellectual infrastructure of the “national liberation revolution” had been prepared, and now it was time for action to realize it. Avcıoğlu and his friends, together with officers of various ranks, longed for a left junta that would come to power through a military coup. They also secured the support of army and air force commanders. Revolutionary youth undertook the task of preparing public opinion for the coup through bombings, robberies, and kidnapping actions from the first weeks of 1971.

The junta known as the “Cemal Madanoğlu junta” planned to seize power on March 9, 1971. However, its activities were being closely monitored by MİT (National Intelligence Organization). The coup attempt came to nothing when two force commanders switched to the other side at the last moment after receiving information from MİT that they would be purged if the coup succeeded. Three days later, on March 12, 1971, the TSK (Turkish Armed Forces) high command declared martial law and had a government loyal to itself formed. In the atmosphere of repression following the kidnapping and killing of Israeli Istanbul Consul General Efraim Elrom on May 22, Avcıoğlu, İlhan Selçuk, İlhami Soysal, and some officers including retired general Cemal Madanoğlu (who had been a member of the National Unity Committee that seized power on May 27, 1960) were detained by martial law authorities.

The members of the “Madanoğlu Junta” remained in detention for a few months, but the military court decided on their release in 1973. What played a role in this was that an investigation of the coup attempt in all its details would have revealed that some force commanders had also been involved. Deniz Gezmiş, Yusuf Aslan, and Hüseyin İnan were tried by military courts on charges of attempting to abolish the constitution, sentenced to death, and executed in May 1972. Hasan Cemal, one of the managing editors of Devrim magazine, wrote the story of the March 9 coup attempt, which had remained covered up until then, with all its details in his book Kimse Kızmasın, Kendimi Yazdım (Don’t Let Anyone Be Angry, I Wrote Myself) (Doğan Kitapçılık, 1999). Doğan Avcıoğlu dedicated the rest of his life to writing comprehensive works including Türklerin Tarihi (History of the Turks); he developed stomach cancer and passed away in 1983, when he was only 57 years old.

Political historian Mete Tunçay would make the following assessment about him in the article he wrote upon Avcıoğlu’s death: “Avcıoğlu was a Revolutionary from the very beginning. What he understood by Revolution was Turkey entering a socialist line through the intervention of a well-intentioned, progressive military junta. He experienced the denial of these expectations twice, but he did not give up or back down… He simply did not want to understand that Turkey was too developed to be taken further by an army intervention… It is clear, I think, that the military socialist regimes established in some African countries are not at all something to be envied for a fairly advanced country like Turkey. Doğan Avcıoğlu never accepted that being a democrat was a necessary, though not sufficient, condition for socialism. In this respect, he should be seen within the tradition of ‘enlightened despotism’ in the history of political thought. May God forgive his faults.” (“After Doğan Avcıoğlu,” Yapıt, Issue 47: December-January 1983, pp. 93-95.)

## The revolutionary youth movement

During the 1966-71 period, youth organizations were an important part of the left movement. Fikir Kulübü was first established at Ankara University’s Faculty of Political Science in 1956, by mostly conservative-leaning academics. However, from the mid-1960s onwards, it came under the domination of socialist-leaning youth and spread to universities in major cities. In 1967, the umbrella organization Fikir Kulüpler Federasyonu (FKF - Federation of Ideas Clubs) was established. FKF members initially consisted almost entirely of TİP-leaning university students, but from 1968 onwards, the SD (Socialist Revolution) - MDD (National Democratic Revolution) split was reflected in the organization’s ranks as well. In January 1969, MDD supporters took over the leadership of FKF and expelled the others from the organization. At its congress in October 1968, FKF took the name Devrimci Gençlik Federasyonu (Dev-Genç -Revolutionary Youth Federation). Members felt an affinity for Marx, Engels, Lenin, Stalin, Mao, Fidel Castro, and Che Guevara alike.

Students belonging to Dev-Genç eventually split into two main currents. The first sought the magic formula that would bring the revolution in books, while the second sought it in “revolutionary action.” Under the influence of the international climate of the second half of the 1960s, the first were mainly inspired by the literature of the Proletarian Cultural Revolution in China, while the second were inspired by Latin American revolutionaries. (See Igor P. Lipovsky, The Socialist Movement in Turkey: 1960-1980, Leiden: E.J. Brill, 1992.)

“Proletarian Revolutionaries”

A group of young people, former TİP members who adopted the MDD strategy, began to publish the monthly magazine Aydınlık Sosyalist Dergi (ASD - Enlightenment Socialist Magazine) from November 1968. The founding editorial board of the magazine included Doğu Perinçek, Şahin Alpay, Erdoğan Güçbilmez, Atıl Ant, Gün Zileli, Oral Çalışlar, and Cengiz Çandar. The ASD circle later merged with the circle around the magazine “Türk Solu,” which Mihri Belli and his friends had begun publishing in Istanbul some time earlier. Vahap Erdoğdu, Seyhan Erdoğdu, and Münir Aktolga joined the editorial board representing the Mihri Belli circle. However, differences of opinion emerged between the ASD circle and the Mihri Belli circle due to different assessments regarding the attitude to be adopted toward Mao Zedong Thought and the political line represented by Devrim magazine. The magazine’s editorial board split in two in October 1970. Since the publishing license was under Münir Aktolga’s name, the magazine came under the control of Belli supporters in January 1971, while the other editorial board members (later joined by Halil Berktay) began to publish the magazine under the name Proleter Devrimci Aydınlık (PDA - Proletarian Revolutionary Enlightenment).

There were also different views among the youth in PDA ranks. After intense debates, Maoist ideology was generally adopted. In its January 1971 issue, the magazine declared that it adopted Marxism-Leninism-Mao Zedong Thought as its guiding ideology. A group from the magazine circle founded the illegal Turkey Revolutionary Workers’ and Peasants’ Party (TİİKP) in May 1969. After the March 12, 1971 military intervention, while a group from this circle was sent to Palestinian Resistance Movement camps for military training, some sought to settle in rural areas among peasants, and others began to publish an underground magazine called Şafak (Dawn) in cities. TİİKP members also split in late 1971 among groups directing accusations of “opportunism, revisionism, tailism” and other charges at each other. The faction led by İbrahim Kaypakkaya split off and founded a party called the illegal Turkey Marxist-Leninist Communist Party (TKP-ML) and its armed wing, the Turkey Workers’ and Peasants’ Liberation Army (TİKKO). By the end of 1972, members of all groups on the Mao line were arrested by security forces and imprisoned. Kaypakkaya died under torture in May 1973.

Turkey People’s Liberation Party-Army The group of young people gathered around Aydınlık Sosyalist Dergi and dominating Dev-Genç, led by Mahir Çayan, Ertuğrul Kürkçü, Yusuf Küpeli, and others, remained attached to Mihri Belli for a while but then split off and began to publish a magazine they called Kurtuluş (Liberation). Roughly speaking, organizations that took the armed revolutionaries in Latin America as their model, focoism in its different branches (THKO) and urban guerrilla (THKP-C), engaged in armed actions. Mahir Çayan from the THKP-C group, Dev-Genç president Ertuğrul Kürkçü, and those with them (Hüdai Arıkan, Cihan Alptekin, Nihat Yılmaz, Ertan Saruhan, Ahmet Atasoy, Sinan Kazım Özüdoğru, Sabahattin Kurt, Ömer Ayna, Saffet Alp) kidnapped two British and one Canadian technician serving at the NATO base in Ünye on March 27, 1972. On March 30, 1972, they were surrounded by security forces in the village of Kızıldere in Niksar. When they refused to surrender, all except Ertuğrul Kürkçü were killed. Kürkçü remained in prison for 14 years until 1986; in the 2000s, he was elected to the TBMM (Grand National Assembly of Turkey) in the ranks of the Halkların Demokratik Partisi (HDP - Peoples’ Democratic Party).

Turkey People’s Liberation Army (THKO)

The group of direct action youth led by Deniz Gezmiş, who stood out during the student demonstrations in Istanbul in the spring and summer of 1968, organized around the Devrimci Öğrenci Birliği (DÖB - Revolutionary Student Union). This group’s views were close to the ideology of the Yön-Devrim magazines published by Doğan Avcıoğlu. In 1970, together with Hüseyin İnan and Yusuf Aslan, Deniz Gezmiş founded the Türkiye Halk Kurtuluş Ordusu (THKO - Turkey People’s Liberation Army). THKO engaged in violent actions such as bank robberies and kidnappings aimed at creating public opinion for the leftist military coup that the “Cemal Madanoğlu junta” planned to carry out on March 9, 1971. After the coup attempt failed, Gezmiş, İnan, and Aslan were captured and tried in a martial law court.

Sinan Cemgil, one of the group’s members, after the March 12, 1971 memorandum, went up to Nurhak Mountain near Elbistan with his friends and established a guerrilla camp. The group’s members, who had set out to raid the NATO Kürecik Radar Base, were surrounded by security forces upon a tip-off from villagers and were killed in the clash that broke out on May 31, 1971. Meanwhile, the sentencing of THKO leaders Gezmiş, İnan, and Aslan to death by the military court and their execution on May 6, 1972, represents the end of the revolutionary youth movement known as the ’68 generation.

## SBF Student Union

Having drawn the general picture of the left movements that were suppressed by the March 12, 1971 military intervention above, I can now return to my own adventure in this context… I was aware that my candidacy for the presidency of the SBF Student Association as Fikir Kulübü’s candidate and winning the election meant the end of my plan to become a diplomat. After graduating in June 1967, I turned my attention to an academic career for a while. At that time, I was acquainted with and occasionally met with Mete Tunçay, who had become an associate professor at the faculty with his work Türkiye’de Sol Akımlar 1908-1925 (Leftist Currents in Turkey, 1908-1925), and Alaaddin Şenel from the same department. Both were left-leaning faculty members. Nermin Abadan, who had recently become a professor, also showed me considerable warmth and counted me among her most successful students. Under these conditions, I thought I could become an assistant at the History of Political Thought chair headed by Yavuz Abadan.

When Yavuz Abadan passed away around the time I graduated from the faculty, Bülent Daver, who was an associate professor at the time, took over the chair. Daver, most likely in order to prevent a “registered communist” like me from entering, did not hold an assistantship examination that year despite there being a vacant position. He also gave hope for a while to Ömer Madra, who graduated a year after me and was, like me, “registered,” before giving up on holding an examination. Thereupon, Ömer took the examination for the International Law chair headed by the late Seha Meray and passed. Becoming an assistant at the History of Political Thought chair would eventually fall to Ümit Hassan (our classmate from Robert College), who was perhaps less “registered” than us and who suffered considerably under Daver.

One of the first things I did after being elected president of the SBF Student Association was to write an article, published in the newspaper Akşam in the “Thoughts of Thinkers” section right next to Çetin Altan’s column titled “What the Devil Bids You See,” reflecting my ideology at the time, which was a mixture of Kemalist secular nationalism and TİP socialism. Cengiz Çandar entered the faculty in 1967, when I was a senior, and immediately joined Fikir Kulübü; his account of having been left “in awe” when Mahir Çayan introduced him to me, under the influence of having read this article, would be quite a source of laughter between us years later.

One of the first acts of my presidency was changing the name of the SBF Student Association from “Talebe Cemiyeti” to “Öğrenci Derneği.” This was a requirement of our Kemalist advocacy of pure Turkish. During my presidency in the period after the 1966 summer break, I increasingly acquired a deeper Workers’ Party identity. The harmony in ideas ensured a smooth relationship between me and Fikir Kulübü president Mahir Çayan. (Mahir’s saying that he “sensed MDD sympathies” in my article published in Akşam was perhaps a sign of what was to come.) As the Fikir Kulübü majority on the SBF Association board of directors, we invited none but TİP leaders to speak at the faculty. Mehmet Ali Aybar, Çetin Altan, Behice Boran, and Sadun Aren spoke in turn in the large meeting hall. It was the year before 1968; boycott actions had not yet spread to universities. The first boycott took place at SBF in 1967, during my presidency of the association. We refused to attend classes in reaction to the faculty administration’s limiting the number of exams that could be taken before being expelled from school. Our dean, the late Prof. Dr. Aziz Köklü, was an extremely gentlemanly and soft-natured person. We ended the boycott in favor of students by cooperating with him.

What was expected from the association administration was, naturally, work aimed at meeting students’ needs. It was certain that the administration I headed was quite inadequate and unsuccessful in this regard. I had assigned myself entirely political tasks; I had left the conduct of the association’s other, normal functions to the other Fikir Kulübü member friends on the board of directors. Unfortunately, the result was that Fikir Kulübü’s candidate (Tuğrul Bayaz) lost the board of directors elections held in April 1967. We handed over the administration to the board headed by Uluç Gürkan, the candidate of the Center-Left group who won the elections.

Immediately after my graduation from the faculty in June, a public prosecution was brought against the administration I had headed, seeking 1-5 years’ imprisonment on grounds of corruption in the accounts. I remember feeling extremely ashamed of this and losing sleep over it. The case must have been seen as having a political dimension, as our defense was undertaken by the late lawyer Halit Çelenk, a person I loved and respected very much, who at that time handled revolutionaries’ cases. I was so happy when the white-haired judge found the evidence against us insufficient and gave an acquittal verdict in the case where the treasurer member and I were defendants…

A noteworthy event occurred in the autumn of that year. I had graduated and was unemployed. I enrolled in SBF’s graduate program. On this occasion, when I went to the faculty one day, I ran into Mete Tunçay. “Mete abi” told me that the Turkish Political Science Association had secured financial support from Americans for some translations, that in this context Karl R. Popper’s two-volume book The Open Society and Its Enemies would be translated into Turkish, that he would translate the first volume on Plato, and he suggested that I translate the second volume on Friedrich Hegel and Karl Marx. The only thing I knew about Popper in those days was that he was a thinker who criticized Karl Marx quite severely. Of course, I firmly rejected the proposal. How could “Mete abi” think I could endure such a humiliation?!.. This is one of the most ironic events of my life. Because Popper would be the thinker who perhaps influenced me the most in my post-socialist period. Decades later, when Taraf newspaper asked, “Who is your hero?” I would unhesitatingly say “Popper”…

## Doğu Perinçek and I

From the end of 1967, my friendship with Doğu Perinçek, who had a steadily rising profile within the revolutionary youth movement and served as FKF president from February to the summer of 1968, began to deepen. Through him, I met many Law Faculty members, including the late Uğur Mumcu and Ergun Özbudun, with whom my friendship has continued to this day. The first product of my growing closeness with Perinçek was two jointly signed articles published in the April 15 and May 15, 1968 issues of Forum magazine. Forum had begun to be published in 1954 by a group that included, primarily, Professor Aydın Yalçın and well-known professors of the time such as Bahri Savcı and Turhan Feyzioğlu, as well as politicians like Bülent Ecevit and Ziya Müezzinoğlu; professors like Cahit Talas, Muammer Aksoy, Şerif Mardin, Mümtaz Soysal, Sadun Aren, and Haluk Ülman had also begun to contribute to the magazine after a while. The intellectual father of the magazine, Aydın Yalçın, had joined the Hürriyet Party formed by those who left the Democrat Party due to its turn toward authoritarianism, and after May 27, the Yeni Türkiye Party, one of the parties established to replace the DP; he was an academic who was not at all acceptable in Mülkiye circles due to his liberal tendencies or anti-left views.

Forum magazine, which had lost the influence it once had in the mid-1960s, had tilted toward the left through a process of which I know nothing. The one who invited us to write there was the poet Hasan Hüseyin Korkmazgil (1927-1984), whom I had met in TİP ranks and who took on first the art and then the general editorship of the magazine from 1968. Our jointly signed articles with Doğu Perinçek published in Forum were the first signs of our turn toward becoming MDD supporters. It was also I who introduced Doğu to Mihri Belli, whom I had met during my visits to the Sol Yayınları (Left Publications) office. We had now come to give credence more to the biweekly Türk Solu magazine that Belli and his supporters had begun to publish in Istanbul than to Yön magazine.

In the article titled “The first step toward alliance” published in the May 15, 1968 issue of Türk Solu, written by me, the following was said:

“The May 27 revolution is, without doubt, a movement of the secular and democratic Turkish bourgeoisie against the power of the Imperialism-Comprador-Landlord alliance of 1950, which came out of the ballot box and abolished our country’s independence and surrendered our people to imperialism. It is obvious that the 1961 Constitution brought by the May 27 revolution… is an obstacle to the Imperialism-Comprador-Landlord alliance that the counter/revolution has reinstalled in power through the ballot box, and that it has allowed the development of anti-imperialist and democratic forces in Turkey… The task before socialists (italics mine: we are not yet speaking of socialists or revolutionaries) is to unite all national and democratic forces… that will realize the establishment of a national democracy in Turkey. In light of this task, in the current revolutionary stage, the closest allies of socialists are the military-civilian intellectual stratum who have demonstrated with all their behavior that they are the greatest obstacle to imperialism.” (p. 3)

These lines reflected well the mindset I held in those days, one that would soon undergo rapid change. According to our understanding at that time, the May 27, 1960 military intervention was the secular and democratic Turkish bourgeoisie’s challenge against the reactionary alliance of imperialists and domestic collaborators. With the 1965 elections, the alliance of reactionaries had come to power again. The task falling to “socialists” was to unite the forces that would realize national democracy; their closest allies were the “military-civilian intellectual stratum” (represented by the Yön magazine circle).

My articles published in leftist magazines were increasingly drawing me into the “revolutionary” movement in my public life. Developments in my private life, however, were in a very different direction.

## Elvan is coming

Fatma had become pregnant in a way we had not really planned; she was expected to give birth at the beginning of April 1968. I had no objection to having a child, but I desperately needed a job and income. Refet Erim, the secretary general of TÜBİTAK, was the brother of my classmate Feryal from Mülkiye (who would marry my classmate Emiri Mikelay from EHSB). Through Erim, whom I had met in Ayvalık where he spent his summer vacation with his family, I started working at TÜBİTAK at the beginning of March as a “researcher” with a meager salary. This was the first job I ever held for a wage.

I shared an office with Gülören, the wife of Uğur Cankoçak (the late trade unionist, one of Mehmet Ali Aybar’s close friends), whom I had met in TİP ranks. During the three months I worked there, Cankoçak, who dropped by frequently, and I had plenty of conversations about socialism. Interestingly, through them I met Erdoğan Teziç there, who was then still an associate professor and would later become rector of Galatasaray University and president of YÖK (Council of Higher Education). Those who hired me knew that for me, with quite a good education by Turkish standards, this would only be a temporary job. I, too, had my eye on finding a job at a university.

Our daughter Elvan came into the world a few days earlier than expected, at noon on March 31, 1968. Since my mother and mother-in-law, who had come to Ankara to welcome the birth, and my elder sister Olcay, who lived in Ankara, had gone to a women’s matinee at a nightclub, I was the only one with Fatma during the birth. When the nurses brought our baby to the room where I was waiting excitedly, I spent a long time alone with her. My daughter was the most beautiful of all the babies I had ever seen; she was a living synthesis of my beloved and me. I had become a father under conditions where my future showed great uncertainty. I cannot forget the happiness I felt that day, despite my anxieties about the future… When I went out to the street to get the news to my mother and mother-in-law, I ran into Cengiz Çandar face to face. Cengiz, my close friend with whom I would share many things, was the first to visit Fatma and Elvan at the hospital. Later, I ran to the apartment of Nuri Çolakoğlu, with whom I was then inseparable, on İzmir Street to give him the news. Nuri was not home. I wrote a note and stuck it on the door: “Fatma gave birth to a girl!..” Nuri would keep this piece of paper for years.

Shortly after her birth, Elvan developed jaundice. Despite all of Fatma’s objections, I insisted on showing Elvan to Dr. Sevim Belli, a pediatrician and Mihri Belli’s wife. (Apparently Fatma prioritized professional competence, while I prioritized ideological competence…) When Mrs. Sevim said that the baby’s blood needed to be changed, Fatma (probably out of maternal caution) firmly decided to take the child to another, “normal” doctor. In the end, it turned out that a blood change was not necessary, and the jaundice, which is sometimes seen in newborn babies, passed on its own after a short time. A lesson was emerging from what we experienced: one should not confuse ideology with health.

The growing tension between my private life and my public life had now acquired a new dimension. I was in love with my wife and I also loved my newborn daughter very much, but the idea of dedicating myself to revolution was also increasingly attracting me. I was beginning to receive increasing signs that I was being dragged toward an impasse. Good news would come from Doğu Perinçek, who was completing his doctorate in those days. Doğu was trying to get me into the Law Faculty as an assistant, but there was a staffing problem there. Thereupon, Doğu introduced me to Prof. Dr. Bülent Nuri Esen, the head of the Constitutional Law Chair who also taught at the Faculty of Education; he also succeeded in convincing him to take me on as an assistant at the Constitutional Law and Human Rights Chair he headed at the Faculty of Education. Esen was at that time one of the Law Faculty’s staunch Kemalist professors who was opposed to the Justice Party and close to the CHP, and he was distinguished by his patronage of “left”-leaning academics. (I will tell the story of how he would disappoint me later.)

In May 1968, I started working as an assistant at the Faculty of Education; I was placed in the office of Esin Konanç, who would later become a professor and RTÜK member. Together with Perinçek, we founded a “Marxist Study Group” in which faculty members and assistants from the three neighboring faculties (Political Science, Law, Education) also participated. Among its members, I remember Erdoğan Güçbilmez, Türkkaya Ataöv, Cem Eroğul, Kurthan Fişek, Nuri Çolakoğlu, and Ömer Madra. Unfortunately, during the three years until May 1971, when I would be dismissed due to “absenteeism” and during which I increasingly acquired the identity of “professional revolutionary,” I made almost no contribution to the faculty. I cannot say that I felt any inner unease because of salaries I did not deserve on the grounds that I was working for “the revolution.” Meanwhile, I enrolled in SBF’s graduate program after passing the entrance exam in the autumn of 1967; in the autumn of 1968, I also passed the doctoral qualifying examination. The doctoral courses provided an occasion for me to come together years later with Rıza Türmen, whom I had known as “head boy” at EHSB. Mümtaz Soysal, who was then an associate professor, and I agreed that I would write, under his supervision, a doctoral thesis on “foreign schools in Turkey and their political effects.” However, this project would remain on paper.

Another important event for me in 1968 was being tried for “communist propaganda” because of a book translation. I continued to meet occasionally with Erdoğan Berktay (who used the pseudonym Erdoğan Başar), one of the “old guard” whom I had met through Sol Yayınları and found very respectable. He was the father of Halil Berktay, who was two classes below me at Robert College and was studying at Yale University in the USA. He lived in Tandoğan, at an address close to our first home in Maltepe, with his wife Yegan Hanım, who was a very pleasant person. In those days, the distance between Erdoğan Berktay and Mihri Belli reflected the division among the “old guard”: Belli favored solidarity with the Yön circle, Berktay with TİP; but it was the former who was proving influential.

Mr. Erdoğan, who had left Sol Yayınları due to the same division and founded Anadolu Yayınları, had suggested that I translate Sartre’s book titled Jean Paul Sartre Describes Cuba (from the English translation titled “Sartre on Cuba”) into Turkish, and the book was published later that year. Our esteemed novelist Adalet Ağaoğlu was doing a program on TRT Radio at that time where books were also reviewed. At the beginning of 1969, she invited me as the Turkish translator and Türkkaya Ataöv, who was then an associate professor, as the commentator to the program where Sartre’s book was discussed. Some time later, a prosecution was brought over the program under Article 142 of the Turkish Penal Code, that is, on the charge of “communist propaganda.” The case resulted in acquittal some time later.

“Annus Mirabilis”

Another important event of 1968, which would later be called “Annus mirabilis / Year of miracles” and during which student and youth uprisings against the established order would occur in almost every corner of the world including Turkey, in the West and the East, was the decision that Doğu Perinçek—who was elected president of the Fikir Kulüpleri Federasyonu in March of that year but removed from the presidency in July because he stood close to the MDD line—and I made to publish a monthly theoretical magazine. Doğu, who probably thought of the magazine as a tool for the role he wanted to play in the revolutionary movement, suggested that its name be taken from “Aydınlık” (Enlightenment), which Şefik Hüsnü Değmer had published in 1921, as a reference to the tradition of the communist movement in Turkey. The first editorial board meeting of Aydınlık Sosyalist Dergi was held in late September at the home of Ergun Göknel, whose name was not mentioned in the magazine because he was doing his military service at the time, whom I had known as a few classes senior to me during my student years at EHSB, who had studied chemical engineering in Germany and returned to the country (who would later become İSKİ general manager, be tried on charges of corruption and serve time in prison).

In addition to Doğu and myself, Erdoğan Güçbilmez, a close friend of Doğu’s who was then an assistant with a doctorate at SBF, and Ergun Göknel attended the founding meeting. Later, students whom Doğu had met during his FKF presidency would also join the founders: Atıl Ant from the Ankara Law Faculty, Gün Zileli from DTCF, and Cengiz Çandar from SBF, as well as, presumably to emphasize the magazine’s pro-MDD character, Vahap Erdoğdu, known for his closeness to Mihri Belli, his wife Seyhan Erdoğdu who was an assistant at ODTÜ (who would enter the CHP Party Assembly in 2010 and rise to vice chairmanship), and ODTÜ student Münir Aktolga… Interestingly: In those days, Doğu Perinçek and I were so close that I would say to Fatma: “I love and appreciate Doğu so much that if we ever fall out, I would be very surprised…” (In time we drifted so far apart that the like of it is rarely seen.)

The first issue of the magazine was published in November 1968, after a summer that was stormy for the left movement due to the boycotts at universities in the spring and then the debates that arose over the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in August. With this magazine, we had drawn quite close to the MDD line. As the Aydınlık editorial board, we visited Mihri Belli at his home. Belli was very impressed by the cadre and expressed his satisfaction by saying “This is it…” (The “it” he meant was probably the hope that MDD would succeed.) As in the rest of the world, the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia had also caused differences of opinion within the left in our country. The most pronounced of these occurred within TİP ranks. The TİP leadership, which initially opposed the invasion collectively, soon showed signs of division. While Aybar openly opposed the invasion, Behice Boran and Sadun Aren adopted the opposite view. The invasion had also caused bewilderment within the Aydınlık editorial board. Since I had started paying attention to what was happening in China, it would not be long before I took a stance against the invasion.

In those days, I was both devoting myself intensively to reading leftist literature and also doing translations. The book People’s Army, People’s War by Nguyen Van Giap, the legendary commander of the Vietnam People’s Army, was published by Sol Yayınları in 1968. Also that year, I had done the translation of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels’ Communist Manifesto, which was published by Bilim ve Sosyalizm Yayınları (Science and Socialism Publications), founded by Süleyman Ege. Probably because I didn’t have the courage to give my name as translator at that time, the pseudonym “M. Ardos” was used in the first book, and Süleyman Ege’s name was written as translator in the second.

My growing curiosity about Marxist-Leninist literature played a role in my approaching the MDD line. When I read Lenin’s book State and Revolution, I experienced the event (expressed by Orhan Pamuk in what has now become a cliched famous sentence) of “I read a book and my life changed…” Revolution could only succeed through the seizure of the state through armed uprising. I had now begun to see the socialism represented by TİP as a kind of “freshwater socialism”—tame and watered-down. Our ideas were rapidly changing, becoming increasingly radicalized. Years later, I would write about those days as follows: “The idea developing at Mülkiye was socialism. First Çetin Altan’s Swedish and Kibbutz Socialism, then Mehmet Ali Aybar’s Turkish Socialism… I discovered that the most genuine of these was Karl Marx’s socialism. For young people like me who knew foreign languages and were curious about reading, it was now time to discover the socialist literature that was forbidden (and therefore very attractive). Reading Lenin was a completely different experience. When I finished reading State and Revolution, I now considered myself a true socialist. I had found ‘the key to heaven on earth.’ Just at this time, the salvos of the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution in China began to be heard in Turkey, and it was time to discover Mao. Some friends had discovered local syntheses of nationalism and Marxism, some had discovered Castro, Che Guevara, Focoism, Tupamaros.” (Milliyet, May 23, 1991.)

The SBF Foreign Relations Institute library was a rich treasure trove for leftist youth. It was possible to find many sources there, from the complete works of Lenin and Stalin to Peking Review, the English-language weekly publication of the Chinese Communist Party. However, the books of Mao, about which I had begun to feel great curiosity, could not be found anywhere. I think it was the spring of 1969; I wrote a letter to Mr. Wilson, the head of the American family with whom I had spent the 1961-62 academic year in the USA, to approximately this effect: “Dear Mr. Wilson, the books of Chinese leader Mao Zedong that I am very curious to read cannot be found in Turkey. I know that the Selected Works are published by Lawrance & Wishart Publishing House in New York. If possible, could you send me those books as this year’s birthday present?” The reply from Mr. Wilson was approximately as follows: “Dear Şahin, I am not of the opinion that there is anything worth reading in those books. However, since you want to read them, I am ordering them for you right away…”

Indeed, Mao’s 5-volume Selected Works was delivered to our door by the postman a few weeks later. I well remember how excitedly and curiously I took the books out of their packages and began to read them while underlining. There were two noteworthy aspects of this event: 1) Mr. Gordon Wilson, whom I had begun to see vaguely as a role model during the year I stayed with them, was a fairly liberal-minded American committed to the Protestant faith who generally voted for the Democratic Party in presidential elections. Although he did not approve of it in any way, he had not hesitated to send me the books, thinking that I had the right to satisfy my curiosity. (His wife Mrs. Mollie Wilson, although she generally voted for the Republican Party, would not refrain, in her later years, from participating in the anti-Vietnam War demonstrations held every weekend in the small town of Big Bear Lake where she lived.) 2) Thus, Mao Zedong Thought came to one of its first followers in Turkey through the USA, quite ironically.

Now that I had begun to read Mao at the original source, I was rapidly moving toward adopting both his theory of MDD as armed revolution based on the strategy of encircling the cities from the countryside under the leadership of the working class party, and his theses that the Soviet Union, which had failed to create socialist man, had turned into a bureaucratic dictatorship and was revisionist and social imperialist.

One of the important contributions to this during the winter of 1968 and spring of 1969 was my correspondence with Halil Berktay, who was then a senior at Yale, one of the leading universities in the USA. In this correspondence, we shared commentaries suggesting that the most advanced expression of Marxism-Leninism was found in Mao Zedong Thought. Our correspondence may have played a role in Halil’s decision to return definitively to Turkey in the summer of 1969, giving up his plan to do a doctorate at Yale (and his girlfriend, the daughter of a very beautiful and very wealthy American family, to whom he read Nazım Hikmet’s poems in spontaneous translation), despite his father’s opposition as far as I know. (Unfortunately, these letters were not preserved.)

That summer I introduced Halil to Doğu Perinçek. According to what Halil related years later, one of the first things Doğu said to him was “Unlike Şahin, we don’t openly take sides in the China-Soviet dispute, we adopt the Ho Chi Minh stance…” At that time, Mihri Belli and his followers, that is, most of the former members of the communist party called “old guard,” had also adopted this stance.

Becoming an “MDD supporter”

From the spring of 1968, I had believed in the necessity that the socialist revolution in Turkey must first pass through the MDD stage. My first article as an MDD supporter was the article titled “What is the non-capitalist path?” which appeared on page 6 of the October 1, 1968, issue 46 of Türk Solu magazine, which Mihri Belli and his friends had been publishing in Istanbul for some time. In the article, I was saying that there was no debate that the path to be followed by socialists in countries with a “semi-colonial, semi-feudal” structure like Turkey was MDD, but that there were two different theses regarding the leadership of MDD: 1) I explained the “First Thesis” defended by Moscow as follows: “Revolutionary democrats” consisting of intellectuals and officers who had lost hope in capitalism would lead national liberation movements, and the revolution would follow a “non-capitalist path” leading to the industrialization of society and the quantitative and qualitative strengthening of the working class. This would give rise to an increasingly powerful working class power alternative against the power of these ‘revolutionary democrats.’” 2) The most important, distinguishing element of the “Second Thesis” represented by Beijing was that MDD must be based on the organizational and ideological leadership of the working class, not the “revolutionary democrats.” The guarantee of transition from MDD to socialist revolution lay here. Apparently, the second thesis seemed more convincing to me.

The section on the world in the article titled “The World, Turkey and Revolutionary Struggle” (pp. 1-17), which explained the views of the magazine’s founders and appeared in the November 1968 first issue of Aydınlık, was written by me. Like many of the editorials, this article was largely a joint production of Doğu and myself. The points that caught my attention when I read it about half a century later were: - In addition to the Soviet-China (and Albania) dispute in the socialist camp, the existence of those who did not take sides in this dispute (the parties of Cuba, Vietnam, and North Korea) was pointed out. (p. 6) - It was claimed that ideological disagreements among socialist countries did not affect fundamental policies, and, as an example that could be cited, it was mentioned that the liberation struggle in Vietnam was supported by both Moscow and Beijing. (p. 8)

- It was mentioned that Czechoslovakia had “come to the threshold of counter-revolution with a movement that began under the name of democratization” (p. 6); it was said that “the current that imperialists blessed as ‘liberalization in socialism’ was a counter-revolution contrived by revisionist Dubček and his cronies.” (p. 9)

All of this was a sign of the debate “Who is right: Moscow or Beijing?” which would continue for some time in Aydınlık ranks, or of the avoidance of taking a position on this issue. Although my own conviction strongly leaned toward Beijing, it was apparent that I was trying to accommodate the indecision in the ranks.

“We can only learn from books”

My first signed article in Aydınlık was titled “Revolutionary Theoretical Education” (Issue 2, December 1968). In the article, which listed the books that “scientific socialists” should read and which had a quote from Lenin placed at the beginning—“Without revolutionary theory there can be no revolutionary movement”—I said: “One cannot become a socialist without participating in the revolutionary struggle, but one can never become a socialist without knowing revolutionary theory. No one can call themselves a socialist without reading, without knowing scientific theory, without applying this theory to practice. What makes a person a socialist is not being of working class origin, but having adopted working class ideology, that is, scientific socialism. We can only learn scientific socialism from books. For this reason, we will read books (emphases in the text)… A revolutionary book is a revolutionary weapon. For this reason, today in China millions of people point to the book of scientific socialism as the most powerful weapon against all the weapons of imperialism…” (p. 146)

Continuing: “A class acquires the quality of being a class through the coexistence of two subjective and objective elements. The objective element of being a class is the place that class takes in the production process, its situation in terms of ownership of the means of production. For example, the proletariat, which has nothing to sell but its labor power and is employed by the capitalist in exchange for wages and exploited through surplus value, in this state possesses the objective element of being a class; in this state it is a class in itself. The proletariat only becomes a class for itself by adopting its own ideology, that is, scientific socialism, and only by acquiring this quality can it attain the power to turn the wheels of society forward. The proletariat that does not possess working class ideology cannot play its revolutionary role and remains under the political, economic, and ideological domination of the bourgeoisie and merely becomes a tail of the bourgeoisie.” (p. 148) “The working class movement is inconceivable without a cadre of socialist intellectuals, whether of working class or bourgeois origin, who will provide ideological leadership to the working class and are equipped with scientific theory. The development and success of the working class movement depends on the existence of a cadre of vanguard intellectuals who have organized ties with the working masses, who are in ideological solidarity with the working class, and who participate in working class action.” (p. 149)

This article pointed to the following matters that dominated my understanding at the time: 1) I was now speaking of “scientific socialism,” the socialism based on Marx and Engels’ “discovery of the laws of development of societies,” not of the socialism represented by TİP or any other kind; 2) By revolution I understood a Leninist one, that is, a revolution of the type that would violently, by force of arms, overthrow the bourgeois state through a popular uprising under working class leadership; 3) I was saying that there could be no revolution without intellectuals equipped with “scientific socialism” theory raising the consciousness of the working class and making them a class for itself; 4) I had come a long way in adopting Mao Zedong Thought: I was referring to the “Little Red Book” as “the book of scientific socialism”; 5) If, as Lenin foresaw, socialist consciousness was to be brought to the working class by intellectuals, I was emphasizing the need for serious intellectual preparation. I was complaining about the inadequacy of “socialist consciousness” around me, especially among university students; 6) Probably to indicate the importance of people like me, I was strongly emphasizing the role of intellectuals in the revolution.

My article titled “19th Century Trade Treaties and Their Effects on Ottoman Social Structure,” published in the April 1969 issue 6 of Aydınlık, essentially developed the thesis that trade treaties made with Western states, starting with the 1838 Baltalimanı treaty with Britain, played a role in “the emergence process of Turkey’s semi-feudal, semi-colonial structure that has continued to this day without fundamental change.” When I read it about fifty years later, the main points the article indicated were as follows: 1) Doğan Avcıoğlu’s book Turkey’s Order had convinced me. I understood the process that began with the Tanzimat not as modernization but as a process of colonization. (After abandoning Marxism, the opposite would seem correct to me.); 2) Claiming that 1960s Turkey was in a semi-colonial and semi-feudal structure, as I did in this article, was an expression of trying to understand the country not through facts but through ideological clichés, by imitating analyses specific to other countries (China).

The editorial written by me titled “Let Us Steel the Revolutionary Ranks!” published in the October 1969 issue 12 of the magazine was like a harbinger of the splits that would occur among pro-MDD youth. I think the quote I made from Stalin’s book translated into Turkish as “On Right and Left Deviations” in the introduction of the article reflected my diagnosis about the source of the emerging differences of opinion: “…there is a long or short period during which one must work with all one’s might to convince the masses of the correctness of our policy. This period cannot be skipped. To think that this period can be skipped is foolishness. It can only be overcome and eliminated through patient political explanation and exposition conducted among the masses.” (Translated by: M. Ardos, Ankara: Sol Publications, p. 53)

In the article, I was criticizing the “left deviation” emerging among revolutionary youth, that is, hasty revolutionism (called “adventurism”) and the tendency toward violent actions, and I was saying: “In Turkey, the proletarian revolutionary movement is engaged in the struggle to raise the consciousness and organize the proletariat, the vanguard force of MDD.” This could be “a right deviation in the form of neglecting” the struggle, as well as “a deviation that appears to be ‘left’ but is essentially right in the form of engaging in actions that destroy alliances… terrorist and anarchist actions disconnected from the masses are not a deviation but directly individualist petty bourgeois revolutionism.” (p. 424)

In the same article, reference was also made to the basic argument I had developed in the article titled “The proletarian revolutionary line is the mass line” published a month earlier in the September 16, 1969 issue 96 of Türk Solu magazine: “The intellectual and youth segment of the petty bourgeoisie constitutes the main social source of both proletarian revolutionaries and Kemalist revolutionaries. The proletarian revolutionary movement is just beginning to take steps beyond being a movement of socialist intellectuals of petty bourgeois origin. Neither MDD nor the socialist revolution can succeed unless revolutionary theory is made the property of the masses. Making calls for struggle in the sharpest form while the masses have not yet been made conscious is adventurism, a ‘left’ deviation…” (p. 6)

“Objective and subjective conditions”

In addition to my criticisms of “adventurist” actions “disconnected from the masses,” the “left deviation” emerging among revolutionary youth, the arguments I put forward in my article on Doğan Avcıoğlu’s book “Turkey’s Order” published in the October 1969 issue 12 of ASD, especially the thesis that the proletariat in Turkey did not have the conditions to lead the national democratic revolution, paved the way for a split in the magazine’s editorial board. Since it expresses my views at that time well, I quote at length from this article below:

“The national democratic revolution is a preparation for the socialist revolution. It is necessary to make a correct distinction between the national democratic revolution and the socialist revolution, and at the same time to correctly combine these two… National democratic movements only turn into a national democratic revolution after the leadership of the proletariat and its party is established. Because national democratic struggles conducted under the leadership of the petty bourgeoisie will not achieve lasting victories. The proletariat that provides leadership in the national democratic revolution will not stop halfway after the power of all national classes under the hegemony of the proletariat is secured, and will immediately proceed to the socialist revolution, relying on its own organized forces conscious of the necessity of revolution. If the proletariat has monopolized leadership in the national democratic revolution, consolidated the worker-peasant alliance, and the joint power of the national classes has been established, a peaceful transition to the socialist revolution will be possible. The bourgeoisie will not be strong enough to resist either politically or economically. The immediate task before the national democratic power in this transition period is to manage the progress from capitalist ownership to socialist ownership over the basic means of production through state capitalism. The transition period will end with the completion of the socialist transformation over the ownership of the basic means of production. After this, the stage of building socialism will begin…” (p. 463)

Continuing: “The socialist revolution is a process of revolutionary transformation in all political, economic, and ideological fields. In the political field, it is a process of consolidating working class power. In the economic field, it is a process of transition from private ownership to collective ownership, to large-scale socialist production. In the ideological field, it is a process of relentless struggle against bourgeois ideology, bourgeois habits, and bourgeois culture. Until the victory of the socialist revolution in the ideological field, that is, until the completion of the socialist revolution in the superstructure as well, it is not certain whether socialism or capitalism will ultimately prevail…” (p. 464)

## The question of leadership in revolution
