Continuing: “In Turkey, the proletariat today does not fully possess the objective and subjective conditions to lead the revolution. The main task of proletarian revolutionaries today is the struggle to bring the proletariat to these conditions. This is the essence of the proletarian revolutionary line. Why is the proletariat not in a position to lead the revolution today? The objective conditions that the proletariat must have in order to gain leadership in the revolution are as follows: First, the proletariat must exist as a class, that is, as a mass of proletarians who have nothing to sell but their labor power. It must be concentrated mainly in the industrial field where large-scale capitalist production takes place. Only in this way will it be able to acquire the conditions necessary for organizing and coming under discipline. All ties with the peasantry and private property must be completely severed.

“However, the Turkish proletariat today is mostly semi-proletarian in character. The existence of the working class’s ties with the peasantry constitutes an advantage in terms of establishing the worker-peasant alliance that forms the basis of the revolutionary united front. However, its ability to take advantage of this depends on the existence of the subjective conditions for the leadership of the proletariat. The subjective conditions for leadership are: the vanguard section of the proletariat gaining class consciousness, that is, assuming the task of building socialism; fully grasping that the road to socialism passes through national democracy; organizing on the ideological basis of scientific socialism together with intellectuals who have adopted scientific socialism as a guide to action, and establishing the party that will lead the class and its allies. However, the Turkish proletariat today lacks these subjective conditions. Today, the conscious sections of the proletariat are still in the stage of economic struggle and are waging a democratic struggle so that the democratic rights that entered the constitution and laws through the struggles of the petty bourgeois military-civilian intellectual stratum can genuinely be exercised. Today, the Turkish proletariat lacks a vanguard party…” (pp. 464-465)

(Looking back from today, that is, from 2022, the above lines seem to me, although they cannot be accepted as a creative application of M-L-MZT, quite realistic and based on a concrete analysis of concrete conditions.)

Continuing: “Today in Turkey, the struggle of proletarian revolutionaries and the proletariat to gain leadership in the revolution is being waged. Under these conditions, Avcıoğlu’s statement that ‘At the present stage of development of our country, nationalist revolutionaries appear to be candidates for playing a leading role once again’ is not wrong, at least for a while. It is possible to influence the flow direction of class struggle, to chart its course, when we are in a position to guide the masses, when the masses have acquired political consciousness. We cannot give direction to the class struggle on our own, from where we stand, with the subjective intentions and wishes in our heads. The proletariat will not become the vanguard just because we want it to. Only if we work to give political consciousness to the proletariat and all national classes, if we can awaken the masses, if the revolution is based on the political consciousness of the masses, can the national democratic revolution succeed. Only if we wage the struggle to bring the proletariat to class consciousness can the proletariat attain the conditions under which it will lead the revolution.” (p. 465)

Continuing: “If we proceed from the concrete analysis of concrete conditions and do not deviate into idealism, we see that the military-civilian intellectual stratum will play an important role in the revolutionary movement in Turkey for some time to come. Even today, the main struggle nationwide is taking place between collaborators and this force. Proletarian revolutionaries are only just now, and mainly based on the youth movement, taking part in the struggle. Let us not exaggerate the opportunities provided to proletarian socialists by the youth movement being an important democratic force… let us not forget that we are still in the stage of the unorganized struggles of proletarian socialist intellectuals and let us keep our feet on the ground.” (p. 466)

Continuing: “We proletarian socialists struggle for the proletariat to gain class consciousness and thereby gain leadership in the revolution so that national democratic movements can turn into a national democratic revolution. This struggle cannot be accomplished without the vanguard party of the proletariat. For this, we will defend to the end the political, ideological, and organizational independence of the proletariat in the revolution…” (p. 474) “To leave the proletarian movement without organization, without a vanguard, to attach it to the tail of the petty bourgeois revolutionary movement, is in the final analysis not to be for complete and definitive victory against imperialism, to submit to imperialism, to compromise with it… The conditions for turning the proletarian movement into a mass movement in Turkey are increasingly maturing. The Left Kemalists must take this movement into account.” (p. 475)

Continuing: “Today, the struggle for both the proletariat and the petty bourgeoisie to attain their own parties is one of the main conditions for united action among revolutionaries… Those who argue that the national front can be established within a single ‘revolutionary party’ representing the revolutionary united action, by undermining genuine revolutionary united action, will have prepared the eventual defeat of the national front.” (p. 474) Avcıoğlu’s idea of “first revolution, then securing popular support ‘as soon as possible’ is idealist. Revolution can only be real if it is based on organized popular support, that is, on conscious masses… The belief that revolution can occur with the desire of a few people is the essence of all types of petty bourgeois revolutionism.” (p. 475)

My article ended with these sentences: “Proletarian socialists believe that revolution can only occur when the masses become aware of its necessity and voluntarily join the revolutionary struggle with the will and determination to achieve it. Therefore, we will patiently convey the correct ideas specific to the proletariat to the masses and struggle to make our movement a mass movement. We can only achieve success if we base the revolution on the masses, not on a handful of people, not on a few individuals. Let us make these principles, this mass line policy prevail in all revolutionary ranks, whether proletarian socialist or Kemalist. Then we can be sure that our revolution will reach victory.” (p. 477)

The following excerpts from the long two-part article titled “Why is the opportunism of Aybar and Aren the same?” published in Türk Solu issues 106 and 107, dated November 25 and December 2, 1969, shortly after issue 12 of Aydınlık, also help in understanding the views that dominated my mind at that time:

“All the opportunists, from Aybar supporters and Aren supporters to Küçükömer and Divitçioğlu, are of the opinion that the further one goes in hostility to the military-civilian intellectual stratum, the more ‘socialist’ one becomes. According to them, the authoritarian regime of the military-civilian intellectual stratum based on an army that fought a national liberation war against imperialism is fascism… any regime based on the army is fascism… democracy is the opposite of dictatorship… there can be no such thing as dictatorship of the majority, democratic dictatorship… Atatürk’s regime was authoritarian, but at the same time it was the power of the majority, the most democratic regime Turkey has experienced. The administration of the National Unity Committee was also authoritarian, but it was incomparably more democratic than the rule of imperialism and its collaborators, a tiny minority, represented by the reactionary-parliamentarist DP and AP…

“It is no coincidence that the views of the opportunists plaguing the socialist movement are also seen exactly in the rightist ideologues plaguing the Kemalist movement. We ask Ecevit and the like: are they also calling the Atatürk and National Unity Committee governments fascism like the opportunists? But they dare not openly accuse Him of fascism. They cannot, because in our country the strength of the forces committed to the cause of national liberation cannot be determined by looking at the seats in parliament. Atatürk is still today the symbol of revolution around which all national liberationists, whether socialist or Kemalist, rally… Whoever opposes this symbol of revolution today is in the final analysis in the camp of imperialism and collaborators.” (Issue 106, p. 10)

I was also writing the following about leadership in the revolution: “National democratic movements can only turn into a national democratic revolution with the realization of the revolutionary ideological, political, and organizational leadership of the proletariat… According to the Arenist opportunists, since the working class exists, it is ‘objectively’ the vanguard in the revolution. The objective existence of a class cannot mean that it automatically possesses class consciousness. Today in our country, the most conscious sections of the proletariat are in the position of a class fighting for economic and democratic rights, with the majority under the influence of the most reactionary ideologies; it has not yet risen to the position of a class for itself. To claim under these conditions that the proletariat is the vanguard in the revolution is to sweep under the rug the struggle that will bring the working class to the conditions of leadership, and objectively to oppose the leadership of the working class in the revolution.” (Issue 107, p. 11)

“The Eastern question”

One of the most interesting aspects of the article I quoted above is the section titled “The Eastern Question,” which generally reflects the Aydınlık circle’s view of the Kurdish issue: “Another possibility that cannot be ignored is that a reactionary Kurdish movement under the leadership of Kurdish feudal lords will be pitted against a revolutionary government through imperialist provocations. Both our own history and experiences in neighboring countries are sufficient to show this… Today, for all revolutionaries of Turkey, the struggle against both Turkish and Kurdish chauvinism is one of the important tasks of our national democratic revolution struggle. Because all the people of Turkey, whether Turkish or Kurdish, are under the pressure of imperialism and feudal remnants, and the path to liberation is to stand shoulder to shoulder in the same struggle. The chauvinist tendencies widespread especially in the military cadres of the military-civilian intellectual stratum must definitely be eliminated through an intense ideological struggle. We must not allow imperialism to divide the people of Turkey!” (p. 476.)

## My ideology at the end of 1969

As of the end of 1969, the views I advocated with the claim of applying Marxism-Leninism-Mao Zedong Thought to Turkish conditions, which are also reflected in the quotes I made above, may be summarized in the following points:

1) Turkey has a kind of capitalist social structure under the yoke of imperialism, semi-colonial in nature, harboring feudal remnants. It is under the domination of imperialism and its native collaborators, that is, the comprador bourgeoisie (intermediary to and partner in the country’s exploitation by the imperialists) and the landlords.

2) In the absence of a bourgeoisie of national character, the petty bourgeois-origin military-civilian intellectual stratum that assumed its role liberated the country from the yoke of imperialism through the national revolution led by Mustafa Kemal Pasha and the Kemalists. However, the parliamentary democratic regime adopted in 1950 resulted in the collaborators of imperialism, that is, the reactionaries, seizing power. The May 27, 1960 military intervention objectively represents the resistance of the military-civilian intellectual stratum against the power of the reactionaries. The regime established by Atatürk was authoritarian, but democratic in terms of representing the interests of the majority; so is the National Unity Committee established with the May 27 intervention. Atatürk is the symbol of revolution around which all national liberationists, whether socialist or Kemalist, rally. (Atatürk’s role in Turkish history is likened to the role played by Sun Yat-sen, who led the transition from empire to republic in China.)

3) Just like the 1920s, the 1960s are essentially the scene of the struggle of three political lines: Kemalists, Reactionaries, and Socialists. The Kemalists are divided into two wings: the national revolutionary Left Kemalists, whose spokesman was Doğan Avcıoğlu and who were represented by the magazines Yön and Devrim, and the opportunist parliamentarist Right Kemalists represented by Bülent Ecevit as spokesman in the CHP. At the current stage, the task of proletarian revolutionaries is to form a united front with the Left Kemalists against both the Right Kemalists and the opportunist, parliamentarist Socialists represented by Aybar and Aren.

4) The task of proletarian revolutionaries is, on the one hand, to maintain a relationship based on the principle of both friendship and criticism with the national revolutionary Left Kemalists, and on the other hand, to organizationally and ideologically build the working class movement and make it Turkey’s main revolutionary, vanguard force. The guarantee of transition from MDD to socialist revolution lies here.

5) However, under present conditions, the working class does not have the objective and subjective conditions necessary to lead the revolution. Objectively, it continues to maintain its ties with the peasantry and has not been able to go beyond being a class in itself. In terms of subjective conditions, it has neither attained scientific socialist consciousness nor has a vanguard party equipped with this ideology. Under these conditions, the Left Kemalists are candidates for playing a leading role in the revolution, even if temporarily. Just as not supporting the nationalist revolutionary movement on the grounds that the proletariat is not the vanguard is a kind of opportunism, so not working for the leadership of the proletariat and completely surrendering the revolution to the initiative of nationalist revolutionaries is another kind of opportunism.

6) For the working class movement to attain the consciousness and organization necessary to gain leadership of MDD requires revolutionaries to carry out patient and long-term construction work. Proletarian revolutionaries believe that revolution can only occur when the masses become aware of its necessity. For this, they must patiently wage the struggle to raise the consciousness and organize the masses. The concept of “mass line” expresses this. To flee from this work, to argue that there is a hasty, shortcut road to revolution, is a left deviation.

7) There is no Kurdish issue (referred to as “the Eastern question”) independent of the national democratic revolution, which is the common cause of Turks and Kurds. A reactionary movement to be led by Kurdish feudal lords incited by imperialists undermines the MDD struggle. Turkish and Kurdish revolutionaries should be in the same camp and should fight together against chauvinist nationalism and the chauvinist tendencies in the military-civilian intellectual stratum (Kemalist) ranks.

Looking back approximately half a century later, I can gather the main characteristics of the views I adopted in those years in the following points:

1) I was trying to directly apply the revolutionary theories developed for China or Third World countries with semi-colonial, semi-feudal structures to Turkey. Time would show how empty this effort was, how far removed from reality.

2) With the courage given by my youth and ignorance, I was belittling the efforts of Aybar, Divitçioğlu, Küçükömer, and even Avcıoğlu to understand Turkey’s unique class and power structure and to develop a unique revolution and socialism strategy.

3) My views were not without some realistic aspects either: a) During the import-substitution development period extending from 1962 to 1976, both real wages and support prices for agricultural products were on an increasing trend. There was no demand for (national democratic or socialist) revolution among the Turkish people. There never was later either. b) According to Marxist theory, the working class envisioned to lead the socialist revolution was quantitatively weak and maintained its ties with the peasantry, and according to the same theory, did not have the consciousness and organization necessary to make a revolution. In short, the observation that the working class did not have the “objective and subjective conditions” to lead the revolution within the context of said theory was not far from reality. c) Therefore, within the context of the same theory, my thesis that if Turkish revolutionaries or communists were to mobilize Turkish workers and peasants first for a national democratic, then a socialist revolution, this required a long-term, patient effort of consciousness-raising and organizing was also not wrong.

The stance of the majority in the Aydınlık editorial board (including myself) who acted independently of Mihri Belli against both the “left deviation,” that is, tendencies to form rural and/or urban guerrillas, and the “right deviation,” that is, Belli and his circle who seemed to have pinned their hopes on the success of the Avcıoğlu junta, in other words “juntaism,” drew the reaction of both groups targeted. The majority in Aydınlık began to be accused of “pacifism, revolutionary empty talk, revolutionary in words but conservative in reality.” The thesis I put forward that the “objective and subjective” conditions necessary for the working class to lead the revolution did not exist also began to be shown as the theoretical basis of the majority in Aydınlık’s “right deviation character, pacifism, tailism…” (The most detailed effort on this subject would be made by Mahir Çayan in the article titled “On the nature of the new opportunism,” which appeared in the 20th issue of Aydınlık Sosyalist Dergi, published in June 1970, 6 months after the split.)

## Aydınlık splits

The emerging differences of opinion led to a split in the Aydınlık editorial board at the end of 1969. The trio of Vahap Erdoğdu, Seyhan Erdoğdu, and Münir Aktolga, who took a stance close to Mihri Belli, took control of the magazine by taking advantage of Aktolga’s having assumed ownership. The others, including myself, began to publish “Proleter Devrimci Aydınlık” (PDA - Proletarian Revolutionary Enlightenment) from January 1970. PDA was called “White Aydınlık” by its opponents in reference to its cover color, while ASD was called “Red Aydınlık.” “Red Aydınlık” was characterized by the majority publishing PDA as the publication organ of the “Unprincipled Unity Front” (consisting of “Adventurists” and “Tailists”). However, this “front” would also disintegrate at the end of 1970 when Mahir Çayan, Ertuğrul Kürkçü, Yusuf Küpeli, and Münir Aktolga took a stance against the Belli circle, which they characterized as “right deviation,” and left “Red Aydınlık.” (Çayan would explain the reason for their departure from ASD in a pamphlet titled “Open Letter to Aydınlık Socialist Magazine” published by Kurtuluş Yayınları in January 1971.)

The response of the PDA circle, and mine in particular, to Çayan’s accusation of “right deviation” was an article about 40 pages long titled “The Working Class and the National Democratic Revolution” (PDA, No. 3-17, March 1970, pp. 353-392). In summary, I was saying: “In the current period, there are essentially two wrong tendencies. One of these is the tendency that aims to keep our developing revolutionary movement within the limits of a youth movement, that cannot grasp the importance of establishing revolutionary ties with the worker-peasant masses and working among the masses, that cannot see that our main task is to raise the consciousness of and organize the worker-peasant masses… that gives a secondary place to political consciousness and ideological solidity among militants, and that tries to pass off the petty bourgeois ideology expressed in Regis Debray’s book (I mean Revolution in the Revolution) as scientific socialism…

“The second wrong tendency argues that the national democratic revolution can be achieved without the leadership of the working class and its party, takes the leadership of the working class to mean ‘the vanguard role of socialists,’ separates the democratic revolution from the socialist revolution with a ‘Great Wall of China,’ relies primarily on petty bourgeois intellectuals rather than its own forces for the revolution, and sees the divergence between true Marxists and modern revisionists in our age as ‘a divergence over nuclear strategy.’ We must wage a struggle on two fronts against these wrong tendencies.” (pp. 354-355.)

With this article, I was also raising the banner of Mao Zedong Thought against “modern revisionism” in my own way: “In the period we are in today, proletarian revolutionaries are engaged in an intense worldwide struggle against modern revisionism, and Mao Zedong Thought has elevated Marxism to a brand new stage, to the stage of Marxism of our era in which imperialism is rapidly advancing toward a worldwide collapse and the forces of socialism are rapidly heading toward a worldwide victory…” (p. 355)

“Faced with the revelation that the views they defend are views that have been condemned in every theoretical-practical respect internationally, some circles that have panicked (especially meaning the Mihri Belli circle) want to prevent the international ideological debates from being known in our country and thereby prevent the level of consciousness in the ranks from rising. For this, they put forward the claim that the international debate is being used to create ‘an artificial split’ among revolutionaries in our country. There is a tight unity between the revolutionary struggles of the world proletariat and the Turkish proletariat. Without fighting against the wrong views that have emerged worldwide, there is no way to bring the Turkish proletariat to success. Every national democratic revolution struggle inevitably comes face to face with modern revisionism and cannot advance without purging it from its own ranks.” (p. 356)

In the same article, I explained the splits in the international communist movement with a diagram as follows: Proletarian revolutionary line = National democratic revolution = “Without party leadership, there can be no revolution… Working class leadership is necessary…” / Modern revisionist line = Non-capitalist path = “It would be good to have a party, but it’s okay without / Working class leadership is good but not necessary…” / Castro-Guevara-Debray line = Socialist revolution = With or without a party = The leader is the Foco representing the alliance among all the toiling classes. With this diagram, I was implying/claiming that in Turkey, PDA represented the proletarian revolutionary line; Mihri Belli and his circle the modern revisionist line; and Mahir Çayan and his friends the Focoist line. (p. 367)

Against the criticisms directed at my views on “objective-subjective conditions,” I also made this defense: “The objective reasons that delay consciousness-raising and organizing are not important from the perspective of our consciousness-raising and organizing struggle. It is a factor that needs to be taken into account in grasping the current level of consciousness and organization, but it is not important from the perspective of our practice, our action, our political line. We want to state this definitively.” (p. 373) Mahir Çayan would respond to this article of mine as well in the article titled “On the nature of the new opportunism” published in the June 1970 issue 20 of ASD, with arguments similar to those in his previous article.

The “old guard” who published Türk Solu magazine in Istanbul had initially taken a stance supporting PDA due to their reaction to the “adventurist-Focoist” circle following the split in Aydınlık. Indeed, my article titled “The only consistent national liberationist current is the proletarian revolutionary current!” would be published in Türk Solu. (Issue: 123, March 24, 1970, pp. 8-10). In this article, I criticized Mihri Belli’s views, which I interpreted as surrender to “petty bourgeois radicalism,” as follows: “In Turkey, the army under the command of petty bourgeois radicals has until now been the executor of progressive movements and may be so in the future as well. But just because petty bourgeois radicals realized progressive movements by using the power of the army, proletarian revolutionaries cannot be asked to be militarist…” (Here I was referring to Belli’s call for proletarian revolutionaries “not to be anti-militarist” in his article titled “Turkey’s Reality” in issue 64 of Türk Solu.)

A topic that played a role, albeit secondary, in the split in ASD was the stance to be adopted toward “Mao Zedong Thought.” In the editorial board, Halil Berktay and I defended the Mao line. I was also pleased with parting ways with Mihri Belli and his circle, who adopted the “not taking sides” stance (characterized as the Ho Chi Minh stance) on ideological differences in the international communist movement. However, the majority consisting of Perinçek and others in PDA was not resolute on this matter. (Indeed, there was some truth in Cengiz Çandar’s statement, even years later, that “I was never a Maoist.”)

The first step toward the PDA circle accepting Mao’s thought at least in words was the article published on the occasion of Lenin’s 100th birthday, signed by the editorial board, titled “Living Lenin” (PDA, Issue: 4-18, April 1970, pp. 436-438). In the article, there was mention of “Mao Zedong, Lenin’s greatest follower, who has creatively developed Lenin’s thought in our time…” I had written the article, but because of this article, Çandar, who had assumed the managing editorship of the magazine, would be sentenced to 7.5 years in prison.

## Hikmet Kıvılcımlı’s influence

After parting ways with Belli, it appeared that Perinçek had become anxious that we had broken from the tradition and entirety of the socialist movement, that there was no authority left to rely on. For this reason, every time he went to Istanbul, he would visit Hikmet Kıvılcımlı and make efforts to bring him together with the PDA movement. The attitude to be adopted regarding Kıvılcımlı’s ideology would lead to tension between Perinçek and me, and gradually to my loss of confidence in him.

The first event in this context occurred on the evening of May 22, 1970. Mustafa Kuseyri, one of the SBF students, was accidentally shot and killed by his close friend Nejat Arun while playing Russian roulette. The incident, which showed how dangerous familiarity with weapons was becoming, was covered up by revolutionaries with the claim that “fascists killed him,” and Arun disappeared. On that tragic day, Nuri Çolakoğlu and I were in Antalya, where we had gone for a weekend getaway with our wives. We were shaken by the news of the death of Kuseyri, a friend we loved dearly. The day after Kuseyri’s death, a “Respect for the Constitution” march was organized in Ankara to condemn fascism; many faculty members from the SBF and Law faculties participated in the march. (Hasan Cemal would relate the following about this incident in his book titled “Let No One Be Angry, I Wrote About Myself”: “One of those who knew the inside story of the Kuseyri incident at that time was Doğu Perinçek. I will never forget, that day as the march was starting in front of the Law Faculty, he leaned toward my ear and said to me, ‘Is what you are doing acceptable?’; ‘It wasn’t fascists who killed Kuseyri…’”) However, neither Perinçek nor any other friend from the PDA circle told me the real story behind the incident. I would learn the truth that Kuseyri was accidentally shot by his friend while playing with weapons months after the incident.

Perinçek was not from a working class family. (His father Sadık Perinçek, a retired judge, had served as a member of parliament from Erzincan for the Justice Party.) In April 1970, he had married Sırma Ersanlı (Osman Ulagay’s ex-wife), with whom he had been friends for some time. Sırma could not be considered a working class child either. In short, there was no difference between us in terms of our class origins. However, the signs that Perinçek was beginning to see and characterize me as “an unreliable bourgeois” were increasing.

One evening in late summer 1970, at the apartment on Kızılırmak Street where we were living at the time, we met with Perinçek and a few friends from the editorial board—which ones, I can no longer remember. At one point Perinçek said: “If an illegal revolutionary party, a communist party had been founded, what would you do?..” I remember answering as follows: If a communist party had been founded, I would probably have known about it. On the other hand, I don’t think the revolutionary movement, consisting of some intellectuals and university students in Turkey, which has not yet reached the working people, has come to the stage of organizing… The second part of the answer reflected my sincere opinion. The view I also developed in my writings was this: For the revolution, the party of the proletariat is absolutely necessary, but for this, a long, patient construction work reaching the working masses needs to be done. The first part of the answer, however, reflected my naivety in the face of Perinçek’s cunning…

As I would learn later, Doğu and some friends from the editorial board had decided to establish a “Leninist party” after the split in the magazine and the break with the Mihri Belli circle, and had begun working in this direction. In the statement Perinçek gave to the police after his capture in the summer of 1972, he would say that he, Ömer Özerturgut, and I had founded the Türkiye İhtilalci İşçi Köylü Partisi (TİİKP - Turkey Revolutionary Workers’ and Peasants’ Party). The fact that Özerturgut was in Germany and I was in the Palestinian Resistance Movement at that time had led him, perhaps to protect the others, to speak this way. In reality, my becoming aware of TİİKP’s existence and my membership in TİİKP would come much later, after I began to be sought by security forces following the March 12, 1971 memorandum. My being invited to join the organization much later reflected the increasing mutual distrust between Perinçek and me.

## Who is more revolutionary

The competition of who was more radical, more revolutionary among the revolutionary youth groups continued. An important development for the PDA movement in this context was our coming into contact with the ideas of the monthly theoretical organ of the Communist Party of India Marxist-Leninist, “Liberation” magazine, and its leader Charu Mazumdar. Because this party, founded in 1967, had begun its first actions in the village of Naxalbari in the West Bengal region of India, the members of this movement were called Naxalites. The “Maoist” friends studying at Robert College’s upper division, especially Garbis Altınoğlu, had met an Indian student and begun avidly reading the articles signed by Charu Mazumdar (Charu Majumdar) in the “Liberation” magazines they obtained from him. They also delivered these magazines to me. I too began avidly reading Mazumdar and making translations of his articles to be passed from hand to hand. His article titled “Let’s make the 1970s years of liberation” that I translated was also published in PDA’s August 1970 issue, numbers 8-22. The article stated:

“We must prepare the material necessary for waging a revolutionary war. What is our war material? Is our war material dynamite, explosives, and firearms? Of course not. The essential material in a revolutionary war is human beings… Once people are equipped with revolutionary theory, that is, Mao Zedong Thought, they become thousands of atoms and Chairman Mao’s more powerful spiritual atom bombs… Comrades, a heavy responsibility rests on our shoulders. Let us overcome all hesitation and remember Chairman Mao’s teaching: True revolutionaries are those who voluntarily ‘shoulder heavy burdens.’ Think of our country’s poor and landless peasants and the limitless poverty, endless oppression, and crushing misery that have brutally crushed them for thousands of years and continue to crush them. Comrades, it is you who possess the magic weapon that will put an end to the exploitation and oppression that crushes them, that will bring happiness to tens of millions of our citizens—Mao Zedong Thought. Nothing can be more sacred and valuable than giving one’s life for this great cause, and we are fortunate to be among those who sacrifice everything for this great cause. This is why we are Communists, followers of Chairman Mao. The war of annihilation launched by our party and led by the poor and landless peasants must be advanced toward the goal of establishing Red political power in various regions, and this war must spread to all provinces and all of India. Thus, the poor and landless peasants will gain self-confidence, become politically conscious, and develop their creative powers through guerrilla warfare.” (pp. 334-335.)

The method Mazumdar proposed for communists was, in summary, this: Revolutionary intellectuals would “proletarianize,” purify themselves of all their bourgeois aspects, melt into the poor and landless peasants, become one of them, and together with them lead the revolution that would advance through the annihilation of class enemies, that is, landlords and rich peasants. Firearms were not needed to annihilate class enemies; weapons like knives, arrows, spears, and so on were sufficient. The use of vehicles like automobiles, tractors, and trucks on roads would be strictly avoided; one would walk. The landless and poor peasants would become politically conscious through this war of annihilation and be equipped with Mao Zedong Thought…

In short, the Naxalites proposed a quite violent, brutal class war. It may be hard to believe, but the Naxalite movement that Mazumdar (1918-1972) started has managed to survive to this day and spread to some regions of India, although it has remained quite marginal. It may be hard to believe today, but the path to revolution that Mazumdar proposed seemed quite logical to me in those days. However, I thought that a long preparatory period would be needed to make revolution in Turkey through this method, that is, by annihilating class enemies in rural areas using weapons other than firearms. But Mazumdar was right: To proletarianize, to purify oneself of all bourgeois aspects and habits; to dedicate oneself entirely to the revolution was the indispensable condition of being a revolutionary.

The Mazumdar thought that I was pioneering the spread of was leading me into an ever-growing dilemma: The tension between my public life and my private life was increasingly growing. How was I going to make revolution while continuing to live like a bourgeois? The conflict between my increasingly radicalized understanding of revolution and the ideal of dedicating myself entirely to the revolution on one side, and my great love and attachment to my wife and daughter on the other, was preparing the ground for the decisions I would have to make in the near future.

The publication of one of Mazumdar’s articles that seemed publishable in Turkey of those days was a step toward the acceptance of Mao Zedong Thought by the PDA circle. I remember placing on the last page of the magazine this quote from Mao, which I believed also reflected my own thoughts: “We must completely purge from our cadres the ideas that we can win easy victories through lucky coincidences without waging a hard and arduous struggle and paying for this struggle with our sweat and blood.”

The real, serious sign of the adoption of Mao Zedong Thought by the PDA circle was reflected on the cover of the magazine’s November 1970 issue, number 25. On the cover celebrating the magazine’s entering its “Third Year,” alongside the profiles of Marx, Engels, Lenin, Stalin, and Mao arranged side by side—which was then the symbol of Mao supporters—was this quote (which I found and translated from Peking Review): “Invincible Marxism-Leninism-Mao Zedong Thought is the powerful weapon of the proletariat for learning about the world, transforming it, and advancing history. When Marxism-Leninism-Mao Zedong Thought is fused with the hundreds of millions of revolutionary masses and with the concrete practice of people’s revolution in all countries, it will bring forth the inexhaustible revolutionary power that will crush and shatter the entire old world. Then victory will belong to the peoples of the world.”

“Down with Soviet Social Imperialism!”

Partly emboldened by the cover of PDA’s November 1970 issue, Maoist-leaning friends, most of whom were studying at Boğaziçi University and İTÜ (Istanbul Technical University) in Istanbul, organized a meeting one day at the end of November at İTÜ’s Gümüşsuyu campus. At this meeting, for the first time in Turkey, a poster with “Down with Soviet Social Imperialism!” written in large letters was hung on the podium. Shortly after I began my speech amid the protest shouts of THKO and THKP-C sympathizer militants in the hall, some were seen drawing their weapons and beginning to fire at the ceiling. It never occurred to me that things would go so far as killing me, but it became clear that it would be impossible for us to continue the meeting; we had to end the meeting and leave the hall. The incident was a sign of the extent to which Mao Thought was not accepted among revolutionary youth.

In the days after the meeting was adjourned, some friends from our circle conveyed: When asked what he thought about the “Down with Soviet Social Imperialism!” slogan being chanted at the meeting organized at İTÜ, Doğu Perinçek had said “This is Şahin’s personal opinion, it doesn’t bind me…” When I returned to Ankara a few days later, I would see that Perinçek was sincere in this statement: The walls of the meeting room at PDA’s headquarters on Adakale Street were decorated all around with “Long Live Hikmet Kıvılcımlı Thought!” posters. It appeared that Perinçek, who had seemingly become anxious that the PDA movement had broken from the communist tradition after the split with Mihri Belli and his circle, had been in contact with Hikmet Kıvılcımlı in Istanbul for some time and had concluded that getting closer to him would benefit the movement. Indeed, in one of the last issues of PDA, an evaluation article on the program of the Vatan Partisi (Homeland Party), which Kıvılcımlı had founded, would be published with the signature of “Program Preparation Committee.”

As I mentioned before, I did not think that Kıvılcımlı had views different from Mihri Belli, nor that he expressed his ideas in an understandable language. The “Long Live Hikmet Kıvılcımlı Thought!” posters at the PDA headquarters had further eroded my already shaken trust in Perinçek. Under these conditions, I began to think that I could not continue to remain in the PDA circle. When Perinçek returned to Ankara, I told him that the Kıvılcımlı posters disturbed me greatly; that we needed to make a decision about which one to follow—Mao Zedong Thought or Kıvılcımlı Thought—and that I wanted an editorial board meeting to be held at the first opportunity for this purpose.

The meeting was probably held in the first days of December 1970.

Perinçek opened the meeting by stating that I had requested an evaluation of Kıvılcımlı and his ideas, and called on the board members one by one to explain what they thought on this matter. I don’t remember if all members of the editorial board were there, but everyone in the majority present took the floor and expressed positive views of varying degrees about Kıvılcımlı’s ideas. The one who went furthest in this matter and surprised me considerably was Halil Berktay. Banging his fist on the table, he said that Kıvılcımlı was the thinker who had made the greatest contribution to historical materialism, one of the main teachings of Marxism, since Friedrich Engels. I think the thought that Halil had assumed the role of a kind of “Doğu’s Suslov” first crossed my mind there. (Mikhail Suslov was the party ideologue who supported the policies of Soviet Communist Party leaders, especially Leonid Brezhnev, with fatwas taken from Marxist-Leninist literature.)

When my turn came to speak, I said that I did not agree with Kıvılcımlı’s views in any way, and that if the PDA movement was determined to follow these views, there was no reason for me to remain there. Perinçek had the last word and said the following: “Democratic centralism applies in our movement. Everyone has the right to express their opinion. We may all be wrong, only one of us may be right. Şahin is one of the founders of this movement and his departure from among us is unthinkable…”

“Mao! Mao!”

I felt that we were heading toward a period full of uncertainties. It was becoming clear that the Avcıoğlu junta would attempt a coup in the near future. I did not know what kind of developments this would lead to, but it was very clear that extraordinary days awaited Turkey. Perinçek had not won me over with his words at the last meeting, but there was nowhere I could go after leaving PDA. I no longer trusted the circle I was with, especially the person in the leadership position, but I was committed to the idea of revolution. Whatever was going to happen would happen… At that time, I poured out my troubles about the situation to Erdoğan Güçbilmez and Ömer Madra, the two friends I saw as closest to myself in Ankara. Their trust in Perinçek had also been shaken. (Indeed, Güçbilmez went to military service, hoping he could escape the trouble that was felt to be approaching, but it didn’t work; after March 12, they would arrest and imprison him while he was doing his military service.)

Perinçek and his friends’ “flirtation” with Hikmet Kıvılcımlı was of necessity short-lived. Because Kıvılcımlı, just a few days after the PDA editorial board meeting I mentioned above, in his article titled “Mao! Mao!” published in ASD on December 15, 1970, mocked those who advocated Mao’s ideas and said the following: “To pretend to be a Maoist in Turkey today is to confuse Turkey with the Ottoman Empire that was 50 years behind…” (In truth, he might have been right about this.) Kıvılcımlı did not stop there; in his article titled “The army has drawn its sword!” published on March 13, 1971, just one day after the TSK High Command issued its memorandum to the Demirel government on March 12, 1971, he called on the army to seize power directly.

A few weeks after the March 12 memorandum, Ferit İlsever, one of Doğu Perinçek’s most trusted friends, said he wanted to meet with me privately. We met. He said that our movement had established a party named TİİKP, and that he had been assigned the task of “organizing” me into this party. Without asking whether I wanted to become a member, he informed me that a cell had been formed consisting of me along with student friends named Abdurrahman Taşçı and Serhat Hürkan, and that I had been appointed cell secretary. İlsever, when we met I believe the day after May 22 when Prime Minister Nihat Erim announced that “Operation Sledgehammer” would be conducted against leftist organizations, informed me that our assignment location would be Çukurova, that I had been assigned as the party’s regional coordinator, and that we needed to proceed to the assignment location as soon as possible. Our mission was to settle among the region’s poor peasants and raise their consciousness and organize them on the path of revolution.

I did not believe in the slightest that a communist party consisting of a handful of intellectuals and students could be established, or that such a party could make revolution. As certain as I was that a long period of consciousness-raising and organization was needed for this, I believed in revolution. Even though I did not know Çukurova at all, had never gone there before, there was nothing to do but try to accomplish the given task. I don’t remember what excuse I made up for Fatma, but saying I was going on a trip for a few days, I kissed her and my daughter Elvan and left home. I did not know whether I would be able to return home again.

“What is this kid doing among you?”

On April 20, we met with my cell comrades and set off for Adana. After staying in Adana at an inn where porters usually lodged for 1 lira per night (in 1971 values), we headed to the Çukurova villages. Abdurrahman, assuming we might receive a warm welcome there, first suggested we go to Yenice village in the Karataş district where Yılmaz Güney’s family had migrated from Siverek and settled. We did so. We found Güney’s father. The old man we spoke with in a coffeehouse under the curious gazes of the villagers asked what we were looking for there. We began to play the role we had decided on beforehand: I was an assistant at Ankara University Faculty of Education and was conducting research on the sociological structure of Çukurova. Those with me were university students helping me. I was twenty-seven years old, and my circumstances and appearance suited the role quite well. It was certain that Abdurrahman also looked like a university student, but Serhat, who was perhaps only in his first year of university at the time, looked at most 16-17 years old. Güney’s father asking “What is this kid doing among you?” would later make us burst into laughter… The situation was clear; it would not be possible to settle in that village. It was evident from their every manner that the villagers were very uneasy.

This time we headed to the mountain villages to the east of Karataş. According to Abdurrahman, the chances of finding shelter there might be greater. In the first village we reached, the villagers did not find the story we told very convincing. They said they knew the gendarmerie was after revolutionary youth; they could only host us for one night on the condition that we leave the next morning. They offered bread, bulgur pilaf, and ayran. I could hardly sleep that night. There was a full moon in the sky. Looking toward the plain, one could see night lamps or candles burning everywhere among the crops. We would learn that the villagers were collecting snails to be exported abroad.

The next morning, we set off without really knowing where we were going. After walking quite a bit, we took a break near a village, in a place like a sheepfold. Loud radio sounds were coming from the sheepfold where MHP posters were hung. The date was April 26, and the radio was announcing that martial law had been declared in 12 provinces, primarily Ankara, Istanbul, and İzmir. I panicked… I told my cell comrades that it would be good for us to return to Ankara as soon as possible, otherwise the gendarmerie would catch us. Abdurrahman said he saw no reason to return to Ankara; he implied that he saw my attitude as defeatism. I swallowed it. We began walking toward Karataş. Behind us, a tractor driven by a villager was coming. I suggested to my friends that we ride this tractor to the nearby village. Abdurrahman refused very firmly. Referring to the Mazumdar literature, he reminded us that revolutionaries could under no circumstances make use of motor vehicles… I had fallen into the pit I myself had dug: So you’re the one who translated and spread Charu Mazumdar’s teachings!… I couldn’t help but laugh inwardly. Worried that I would be accused of treachery if I insisted on getting on the tractor, I kept silent; the tractor passed by us, and we continued walking.

From Karataş to Tunceli

It soon became clear that the first thing the villager driving the tractor did was to alert the muhtar (village headman). For when we reached the village named Kızıltahta, we saw that the muhtar was waiting for us with a large group of villagers, shotgun in hand. They sat us in a coffeehouse and surrounded us. Our story of conducting sociological research did not seem convincing to the muhtar in the least. He merely said that according to the instructions they had received, they were obligated to report suspects to the gendarmerie. After a while, two gendarmerie NCOs arrived in a jeep, took us, and brought us to the gendarmerie station in Karataş. I don’t think the gendarmerie commander there believed our sociological research story either, but when he couldn’t find our names on the list of those wanted by martial law despite all his searching, he released us a few hours later.

From Karataş, we went by bus (Abdurrahman no longer objected) directly to Tarsus. There, in a house, as I remember, we met with friends from the PDA circle, primarily Ferit İlsever and Oral Çalışlar. Ferit, my boss within the organization, gave us the order to make our second attempt at settling in villages in the Pazarcık plain of Kahramanmaraş. We headed there. Unfortunately, our Pazarcık adventure also yielded no results. Upon hearing news that villages where revolutionary youth went were being raided by the gendarmerie, after being able to shelter for only one or two nights in villages where it was clear we were unwelcome, we returned to Tarsus, the regional headquarters (Oral Çalışlar’s hometown). Ferit gave us the order to make our next attempt in the villages of Dersim/Tunceli.

Since Serhat had left us, we continued on with Abdurrahman. When we arrived in Tunceli center on May 6, we could feel that the atmosphere was not very favorable for going out to the villages. We learned the location of Kurdish writer and politician Kemal Burkay’s house. Mr. Kemal, whom I knew from the TİP ranks, bless him, hosted me in his home that night despite all our “ideological” disagreements. He advised us that Tunceli was not at all safe and that we should leave there as quickly as possible. As soon as I left Burkay’s house in the morning, I was surrounded by plainclothes police and taken to the Police Directorate. The police also brought Abdurrahman, who had been staying at a hotel that night, shortly after.

For the Police Chief, I adapted the sociological research story to Tunceli. It was obvious that the Chief did not find the story convincing, but like the gendarmerie commander in Karataş, when he couldn’t find our names on the list of those wanted by martial law, he directly called the Ankara martial law command. When he couldn’t get any information from there that we were wanted either, he released us, admonishing us to return to Ankara as soon as possible. He would very much regret this a few days later, for in the first wanted list of 19 people announced by the Ankara Martial Law Command a few days later, that is, at the end of May, I was also on the list along with Doğu Perinçek from the PDA group and Erdoğan Güçbilmez (who had left the movement in November 1970 and decided to go to military service).

We returned to Ankara. I went straight home and embraced Fatma and Elvan. Fatma had grown quite cold toward me; she sensed that our life together was nearing its end. She had adopted an indifferent attitude to what we were experiencing. The situation was very different for me: I was attached to my wife and daughter with all my heart, but a fate I could not control was taking me away from them. On the one hand, I was committed to the idea of revolution and socialism; on the other, I saw the country as very far from revolutionary conditions. Moreover, my trust in the people I was acting with had been greatly shaken. I was aware that we were being dragged toward an impasse. I no longer had any chance of escaping from this. I would go wherever fate took me.

Elvan was three years old. I was not a loveless or conscienceless father. On the contrary, not knowing when I could be together again with my wife and daughter whom I loved so much was deeply painful. A great weight had settled on my heart. At that time, we were living in a flat in the Çim Apartmanı building on Tunus Avenue. Fatma had sold the three-story house in Ayvalık left to her by her father (in which we had both been born) and bought this place. (How I would later regret that we had let go of that three-story house in which we had both been born…) In my last days at home, when I took my dear daughter to nearby Kuğulu Park, the thought that I might be doing this for the last time seared me inside.

On May 10, I met for the last time with Ferit İlsever, for whom I felt deep antipathy. İlsever told me to ask Fatma to give ten thousand lira as aid to the “movement.” (I would comply with this order too…) On May 22, 1971, as soon as the Ankara Martial Law Command announced the “wanted” list, I said goodbye to Fatma and Elvan and left home. I began hiding in the homes of colleagues that Sezi, the wife of Nuri Çolakoğlu, worked with at TRT. I moved between two or three houses. Interestingly: People I had never met before were taking the risk and accepting me into their homes. I owe them gratitude to this day. As for some friends I thought were close turning me away at the door with apologies, to tell the truth, I was hurt but understood. The owners of the last house, where I would stay for quite a long time—Mustafa, a TRT employee and leftist sympathizer, and his wife—were not staying at their home at that time, for a reason I don’t remember. (Perhaps they had vacated the house for me.) In the apartment where I stayed alone, I behaved as if I were not there at all; I made no sound, didn’t turn on lights or the radio. My connection to the world consisted only of Mustafa who occasionally came and went bringing me food. Once, there was a knock at the door. When I looked through the peephole in the door, I saw that the visitor was a soldier with epaulettes and became quite worried. Fortunately, after knocking on the door a few times, he left. He was a friend of Mustafa’s…

## TİİKP’s directives

One day Halil Berktay showed up. Not as two friends who had known each other for years, but with the attitude of two “party members” in a subordinate-superior relationship, he conveyed to me the orders of TİİKP, that is, of Doğu Perinçek. I was to join the Palestinian resistance movement and receive armed training there. We would go together with Atıl Ant and Cengiz Çandar. Atıl would be the cell secretary, Cengiz the member responsible for external relations, and I would be an (ordinary) member. When he said we would join the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine organization under the umbrella of the Palestinian Liberation Movement, I asked if they were aware that the organization’s leader Nayef Hawatmeh was a well-known Trotskyist. It appeared he was not very aware, but he merely said “We are aware… You will convince them, win them to the correct views…” Before leaving, he reminded me that if we were captured, I should be prepared to bite off my tongue if necessary but not talk under any circumstances. He said he himself had been putting out cigarettes on his arms in preparation for bad days. (When he was captured in the summer of 1972, he too would give one of the most detailed statements to the police.) I asked him to send Fatma to me so I could see her one last time. He left after telling me what day and where to meet with Atıl and Cengiz.

(Years later, in 2023, during a conversation, Gün Zileli told me that when he asked Doğu Perinçek “Why did you send them to Palestine?” he received this answer: “They were going to be a burden to us anyway; let them go and do whatever they do there…”)

When Fatma came to where I was staying a few days later (June 26), my heart was pounding as if it would leap out of my chest. I remember saying to her approximately the following: “I’m very sorry my love… I’m in love with you as on the first day; I’m attached to you and my daughter with all my heart, but unfortunately, I’m being sought by martial law. For this reason, I will have to leave Ankara soon… I don’t know when we can meet again. Embrace my daughter for me, take good care of her…” I also had the shamelessness to say: “The revolutionary movement is going through extremely difficult days. I have one last request from you; I would be very happy if you could give ten thousand lira to the comrades…” (My face turns red whenever I remember this. I would learn that Fatma gave the money in question.) Fatma never asked where I was going or what I would do. When I hugged her for the last time before leaving, she was rightfully quite cold. I felt to the bone that she had neither the intention nor the hope of seeing me again. I will never forget the pain, sadness, and sorrow I felt inside when the door closed and she left. But I had deserved it… (However, my brother-in-law—my wife’s sister’s husband—would tell me, a few days before her death, that even in that summer of 1971 full of unknowns, Fatma had not given up on me.)

# CHAPTER IV / IN THE PALESTINIAN RESISTANCE MOVEMENT

In the early evening of June 27, 1971, we met with Atil and Cengiz at the home of the late theater actor Erkan Yucel (1944-1982) in Sihhiye. Atil had dyed his hair platinum red, presumably to avoid being recognized. He looked comical. It was obvious from his demeanor that he was very pleased about being appointed cell secretary. Both of them seemed quite cheerful, behaving as if they were in a university cafeteria. I, on the other hand, was not in good spirits at all. We were heading into the unknown. Shortly after, Nuri Colakoglu came to deliver some necessities to us travelers. He was acting like a “revolutionary comrade” rather than a friend of many years - that is, ice cold. Perhaps he was doing this to avoid giving the meeting a dramatic atmosphere, I thought.

After spending that night at Yucel’s house, the next morning we set off toward Antep on a Cayiragasi bus, sitting in seats far apart from each other. On the bus, we met Saim, who, we were told, would guide us across the Syrian border and help us join the Palestinian resistance movement. As the bus left Ankara, I felt I was experiencing one of the most dramatic moments of my life. The folk song blasting from the radio, which the driver had turned up to full volume, went like this: “I am swept away by the winds of my fate / O horizons, I say, there is a journey to tomorrow / Though separation has appeared, my beloved does not hold my hand / Today I am a guest to the evenings of exile…” The lyrics of the song perfectly reflected my state of mind.

How had Perincek made the decision to send us to Palestine? According to what Cengiz told me later, after Cengiz was sentenced to 7 years in prison because of the editorial titled “Living Lenin!” that I had written, Perincek decided to send Cengiz first, asking him to research which organization under the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) umbrella would be appropriate to join. Cengiz found the Democratic Popular Front led by Hawatme to be suitable, as it appeared to be the “most revolutionary.” (I don’t think Cengiz had any idea about the organization’s Trotskyist identity at that time.) It was decided that Atil and I would join Cengiz, and contact was made with Saim, a tea-stall keeper and smuggler from Tarsus whom Oral Calislar knew, to organize our journey.

## In Akcakale

When we arrived in Antep, we hired a taxi under Saim’s guidance and went on to Akcakale. There we stayed at the house of one of Saim’s relatives, located close to the border, until dark. When darkness fell, we set off in a jeep toward the border. When the jeep suddenly broke down, we walked the remaining 300-400 meters in plain sight of the crowd sitting in the surrounding coffee houses - we were worried they might report us, but they apparently concluded we were smugglers and paid no attention - and took shelter in a hay barn near the border. From there, guided by a dark-skinned Kurdish youth who was clearly a master smuggler, we walked toward the railway that marked the border.

On the night of June 29, 1971, the full moon shining brightly in the sky illuminated the plain almost like daylight. As we were advancing along the railway, we were suddenly startled by the command “Squad halt!” About 20-30 meters ahead of us, a squad of gendarmes was resting on the ground. It was obvious from their demeanor that they had been informed about our crossing in advance and appropriately rewarded. They paid no attention as we passed in front of them; we continued walking and crossed into Syria at what we would learn was one of the villages of Tel Abyad. Sami, who spoke Kurdish and Arabic fluently, asked the villagers to call a taxi; we immediately set off toward Aleppo with the taxi that arrived. At midnight, we stopped in Raqqa and bought drinks.

When we arrived in Aleppo, our driver found, by asking around, the office of the organization whose full name was the Democratic Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (hereafter abbreviated as DC). It was clear that no one there knew we were coming, but we were still welcomed warmly. They seemed familiar with young people coming from Turkey. At the office, each of us was given a “mukatil” (fighter) identity. Atil was given the name Musa (I don’t remember his second name), and I was given the name Selim Tariq. Cengiz, by his own choice, took the name Zekeriya and (in honor of his father) Ihsan. Now we had a semi-official identity to carry with us, and we believed we had achieved a relatively safe status.

We set off from Aleppo to Damascus in the same taxi. We stopped at the facilities of a dam along the way and ate at its restaurant. There, a comical situation occurred that could have been very costly, potentially resulting in imprisonment in Syria - Atil mistook an officer among the customers for a waiter and waved him over with his hand. (We would later learn that some people who were caught after crossing the border spent months in prison. One of them was my friend Mufit Ozdes from the English High School.) When we reached Damascus in the late afternoon, we began searching for the DC office, which we knew was near Shara el Baghdad (Baghdad Street) in the El Ezbekiye district. We mistook the Baath Party Headquarters for the address we were looking for. Fortunately, the taxi driver went and found out it was not the address we were looking for. We finally found it: the DC office was located in the basement of an apartment building, accessed by stairs. As if it wasn’t surprising enough that the office of the “mighty” DC was in a cramped basement apartment, it also turned out that the few people there had no idea we were coming. It was clear that our joining the Palestinian resistance movement had not been organized with much care. Still, I was grateful that we had made it this far without being caught by either Turkish or Syrian security forces.

## Malula

It was a great stroke of luck that Dr. Omer, whom Cengiz knew from Ankara and who was a graduate of Ankara University Medical School and spoke Turkish very well, happened to show up at the DC office - this helped get our affairs in Damascus on track. Dr. Omer showed us enough warmth to host us at his home for several days; he made us feel right at home. He also gave us the good news: “You’re lucky, the training starts in a week…” He took us to a famous dessert shop in the city center. I cannot forget the shambaba sweets (a syrup-soaked dessert) he treated us to. (That day while walking in the streets of Damascus, we saw Mihri Belli from afar. Cengiz and Atil went to greet him; I didn’t feel like it at all.) The greatest feast in Damascus, however, was the lunch we had at a shabby restaurant near the DC office, run by a Christian Syrian named Abu Muhammed. The menu consisting of omelette, hummus, fava, shepherd’s salad, and flatbread is perhaps my most striking memory of Damascus.

On July 4, 1971, we were sent to the camp near the town of Malula, located about 60 km northeast of Damascus, where the Arameans, one of the ancient Christian ethnic groups, lived, to receive guerrilla training. As soon as we arrived, when the staff there equipped us with khaki military uniforms and French-made cafe-au-lait colored boots (which had become famous in Ankara through Deniz Gezmis and his comrades), we felt that we were truly taking a step toward becoming guerrillas. The approximately 30 people other than us three Turks were all young Arabs, some Palestinian and some of Iraqi and Lebanese origin, mostly poor and unemployed. Among our Arab comrades, all using code names, one character I cannot forget was the Lebanese Abu Fen. He distinguished himself from the others by knowing a few words of English and by the great importance he attached to himself. He told anecdotes about his friendship with Arafat and Hawatme.

Initially, we communicated with our Arab comrades through sign language. Over time, our Arabic vocabulary expanded. By the end of the approximately nine months I stayed in Syria, I would learn enough Arabic to engage in political discussions, albeit with great difficulty. However, this Arabic, picked up entirely by ear, would quickly evaporate after I left Syria. Among us, only Cengiz, because he stayed in the Palestinian resistance movement for nearly three years, would be able to retain his Arabic language skills even though he never learned to write it.

The Malula training camp was set up in a valley stretching between a steep cliff on one side and a gently sloping hill on the other. In the makeshift hut in the valley were the camp commander’s office and the space where the elderly camp cook Abu Vahit stored provisions and cooked meals. Right in the middle of the camp was the physical training area called “halaka” (Arabic for “circle”), where the toughest exercises were performed. Just above the Halaka was the hill where “theoretical” training took place - weapons, explosives preparation, and guerrilla tactics - with a “shajara,” a large plane tree, in the center. Further up the hill were the cave-like shelters where we spent our nights, shivering in the desert cold during summer months.

A few days later, a Syrian captain (with the code name) Abu Veyl arrived at the camp to manage the training program. He was a dark, tall, handsome young man and a sharp soldier. He spoke perfect English. Although not every day, he was usually at the camp during the daytime, supervising the training, and returned to Damascus at night. (Perhaps for this reason, the Arab comrades spread the legend that Veyl had a very beautiful wife.) When he was absent, the camp command was taken over by Abu Fadil, a stern but not unpleasant blue-eyed blond Arab. Over time, Zekeriya and I developed a certain friendship with Veyl and had conversations with him.

At Malula, we received “mukatil” training until the beginning of September, that is, for more than a month. Training began by waking up at 6 am, running approximately 10 km up and down the valley, followed by physical exercises until 8. Afterwards, we usually had breakfast consisting of flatbread with accompaniments like cheese, olives, and canned sardines, alongside well-steeped, dark-red Ceylon tea, immediately followed by the distribution of Du Maurier brand long filtered cigarettes. Those cigarettes, dangled before us like bait, were our greatest luxury. Between 9 and 13, Palestinian instructors gave lessons on topography, weapons, tactics, etc. Following lunch eaten between 13-14, weapons training took place under the shajara - which scorched our lower bodies in the sun while chilling our upper bodies in the shade - ranging from Kalashnikov machine guns to shoulder-fired bazookas, until 18. After dinner, from 20:00 onwards, political meetings or night exercises were held. Meanwhile, at any hour of the day or night, we would be invited to the “halaka” to crawl under barbed wire.

About two weeks later, friends from Turkey began arriving at the camp, and within a few days we became a group of at least 15 people. Among those who came were Sabetay Varol (code name Adil) from Istanbul Technical University (ITU) and Ismet Tufanyazici (Faris) from Ankara Law School, both close acquaintances of mine. A few evenings later, at sunset, someone with a Che Guevara appearance arrived - bearded, wearing a beret, with a machine gun on his shoulder. His arm was in a cast from being wounded in the Black September of 1970, when the Jordanian army attacked Fatah and inflicted heavy casualties. The arrival was Halit Sait, an experienced Turkish “mukatil.” (Years later, we would learn that his real name was Mumtaz Celtik; he was a volunteer fighter who, fed up with things, had left Thrace on his own, crossed into Syria alone, and joined Fatah.) His joining us gave our group an even more authentic guerrilla identity.

Not everyone could adapt with equal ease to the challenging conditions at the Malula training camp, which were nothing like the university cafeterias of Ankara and Istanbul. Thinking that I would be there for a long time, perhaps years, I made an effort to adapt to the environment as best I could. My concern about not breaking down psychologically also demanded this. I ran at the front of the group during the ten-kilometer morning runs and threw myself into military training wholeheartedly. On one hand, this helped me adapt to the conditions and forget myself; on the other hand, I was (in my mind) setting an example for others as a role model. Through these efforts, I soon became the informal military leader of the group.

Perhaps another factor that played a role in my showing this motivation was my resentment at Perincek having appointed Musa to the leadership of the group (presumably finding me unreliable). Our friend Musa was clearly the one having the greatest difficulty adapting to the conditions. He shirked the training as much as possible and set a negative example for the group with his undisciplined behavior. During our first nights at the camp, while trying to cope with the desert cold in the cave where we were placed, Musa’s selfishness in pulling our blankets - Zekeriya’s and mine - onto himself had greatly surprised and angered us. As the days progressed, the difficulties Musa was experiencing began to manifest in various ways. After a while, Zekeriya, who had not shown his hand on this matter until then, and I began discussing Musa’s negative behaviors among ourselves.

Crawl!

My whole body had started itching. I concluded that I was sick. One day in late July, with Abu Veyl’s special permission, I was taken to Damascus, to the hospital where Dr. Omer worked. (I remember meeting Comrade Memduh, one of the top leaders of the DC and the Palestinian resistance movement, there. We would have contact with him on various occasions later on.) The diagnosis was clear: I had lice. They advised me to wash and sent me back to camp. As soon as I returned, I asked “Refik” (meaning comrade) Abu Fadil for permission to wash. “Carry water from the hill, heat it, and wash…” he said. Under the barely concealed mocking gazes of my friends, I did exactly that. Honestly, it was the most laborious but also the most enjoyable bath I ever had in my life. I felt better than I had since arriving at the camp. After washing, I put on the brand new, spotless underwear that Abu Suphi had specially brought out of storage for me. I was extraordinarily relieved… I was happy… But barely half an hour had passed when the “icma” (assembly) order was given at the ‘halaka’; then came the command to “Crawl!”

under the barbed wire… All my efforts to get clean had been wasted… I got the impression that Comrade Fadil did this partly to rub my nose in it, perceiving me as the leader of the Turkish group, and partly to emphasize the intensity of the training; I deeply resented it. As for the lice, they would continue to exist on me, pleasantly making me itch, until I washed months later at my elder sister’s house in Ankara.

One day, when we climbed the hill where the fountains were located to carry water to the camp as usual, we saw that there was a makeshift detention facility there, containing about 10-15 people dressed in guerrilla clothing like us. We would never learn what crime these people had committed to be there; a few days later they would disappear from there. We couldn’t help but notice that they were wearing Mao badges on their collars. “I told you these people (the DC) were Trotskyists!…” I couldn’t help but mutter. Where had they sent us?..

One day a major night exercise was held. The most delicate, most dangerous part of the exercise, conducted on the surrounding hills under the light of the full moon, involved placing explosives in a cave-like target, lighting the fuse, and then quickly returning to the trench. The first task was assigned to Zekeriya. I knew that although Zekeriya had excellent control of his feet (he played football well), he didn’t have much control of his hands. I worried. How would he carry out this task?! Under my anxious gaze, Zek (his shortened name) placed the explosive in position, lit the fuse, returned to the trench, but the expected explosion did not occur. It was clear he had failed to ignite the fuse. Comrade Fadil ordered Zekeriya to go back and light the fuse again. We held our breath… After Zekeriya repeated the action and hurriedly jumped back onto those of us in the trench, I was the one underneath him. My head hit the ground, my glasses flew to one side. I don’t know what I would have done if they had broken. I complained quite a bit. Fortunately, the explosion occurred this time.

The training program at Malula was completed with a major exercise lasting three days and three nights. We walked 30-40 km over mountains and hills; we performed various maneuvers along the way and used different weapons. After this exercise, which was like a graduation exam, in the first week of August we were suddenly loaded into jeeps and transported to the village of Jaba in the Golan Heights, located right across from the city of Quneitra under Israeli occupation. On the way, we stopped at the city of Daraa; there each of us was given a Kalashnikov machine gun. We had now become “mukatils.”

The commander of the Jaba camp, Comrade Halit, was a man of 30 to 35 who spoke poor English and was chubby, likeable, and rather naive, to a degree quite at odds with his post. At first we thought he was an important figure, but over time it became clear he was not at all. Since we had completed military training and become mukatils, at Jaba we focused on ideological training. Days began with a run on a route parallel to the Quneitra border, with afternoons dedicated to ideological training. The training had become quite lax compared to Malula. Our presence there didn’t seem very meaningful. Our leader Musa had completely fallen apart. He hardly participated in the runs or the training; he sat cross-legged puffing on his cigarette… The girls from the neighboring village waving from afar seemed very attractive to us. We hadn’t completely disconnected from worldly interests, you understand… In September, the moonlight at Jaba was something else entirely. During the full moon, the stars seemed close enough to touch. It reminded me of moonlit nights in Ayvalik and made my heart ache. What were Fatma and Elvan doing, I wondered? Would I ever see them again?

One day we found the opportunity to go from Jaba to Damascus to demonstrate our Maoism. Our leader Musa, Zekeriya who was responsible for external relations, and I as the third member of the executive cell visited the Chinese Embassy for “official contact” through a connection Zekeriya had established. We told the officials there that we were Turkish revolutionaries following Chairman Mao’s path. After exchanging good wishes, we returned to the camp with many small red plastic-covered books (“Quotations from Chairman Mao”), other literature from Beijing, and boxes of Chinese tea as gifts. This visit made us quite proud, especially Musa.

## Rashidieh

In mid-September, we were loaded into jeeps again and after bidding farewell to Comrade Halit, we crossed into Lebanon via hidden dirt roads winding through the hills. For a while, we stayed in tents at the Bir Hassan refugee camp in Beirut. Through another arrangement prepared by Zekeriya, Musa, Zekeriya, and I put on civilian clothes and went down to the city for two days, staying at a hotel. On one of these days, we took a walk through the city center, where Maronite Christians were concentrated, including the city’s most famous street, Shara El Hamra. The stores selling the most famous French brands reflected the high level of prosperity prevalent in Beirut in those years. On the street, elegantly dressed men and women walked alongside soldiers and guerrillas with weapons on their shoulders.

One evening we went to a cinema in that elegant neighborhood. The beauty and elegance of the women we saw in the cinema hall was dazzling… This was civilization, and how far we had fallen from it… The second evening, Musa and Zekeriya decided to go to a brothel; I didn’t want to. When they returned and told us what had happened to them (!), we laughed until we couldn’t breathe… I don’t remember laughing that much during the entire Palestinian adventure.

One day we were hastily taken from Beirut to the DC camp set up right next to the refugee camp in the town of Rashidieh, located in the south of the country, near the city of Tyre and about 15 km north of the Israeli border. The camp consisted of tents set up on a wide beach stretching along the Mediterranean coast and dug trenches. The natural surroundings were extraordinarily beautiful; it was as if we had come to a corner of paradise. Behind us were lush green hills covered with palm, banana, and pine trees, and before us stretched the deep blue Mediterranean. The scenery both gave me a measure of peace and drowned me in pain and sorrow. Much time had passed since I left Ayvalik. Looking at the horizon, I wondered whether, if I set out onto that vast sea in a small boat, I could reach my homeland and be reunited with my wife and daughter.

What was Fatma doing, I wondered? Had she completely erased me from her heart? (When I found the answer to this about two years later, in a letter Melek Ulagay sent me on October 2, 1973, before Fatma had come to Stockholm, how sad and at the same time how happy I had been: “After martial law, during certain periods in the winter of 1971, I stayed at your house in Ankara with Fatma. Despite all the wrong behaviors our friends showed toward her in those days, Fatma’s trust and love for you, the strength of her own character, had deeply impressed me. The strength that many people who claimed to be revolutionaries could not show, Fatma showed alone by persisting to the end. She believed that one day she would meet you. Now that many obstacles have been overcome, it is very sad that you still cannot meet.”)

At the beginning of October, a new group of friends from Turkey joined us. Among those who came were Ali Mercan (code name Sami), whom I knew from Ankara, and Ahmet Ozdemir (Saban) from Istanbul, whom I would meet there and come to love very much. We visited the Palestinian refugee families in the camp at their makeshift homes.
