The ordinary Palestinians, whose cause we felt great affinity for but whose existence we had only known theoretically until then, were living in great poverty and deprivation; they were surviving mainly on aid from the United Nations, Arab countries, and some socialist bloc countries. My deep sympathy for the oppressed Palestinian people, expelled from their homeland, would deepen considerably with what I saw and experienced here. The only heartening sight I encountered at the camp was the blonde, shapely Italian nurse in her early twenties who was working as a volunteer at the health clinic. She seemed as beautiful as a film star to me, and I was smitten…

We witnessed dramatic events at the Rashidieh camp. One of these occurred among the many Iraqi volunteers who joined the camp a few days after us. One afternoon, while I was in the trenches dug into the beach, I was startled by a gunshot that went off very close by. One of the Iraqis had pressed his Kalashnikov to his stomach and pulled the trigger. It was clear that the young man, far from his homeland, unable to adapt to the conditions, could not bear the distress he was suffering. My own inner turmoil, caused by the conflict between my public life and my private life, also peaked at Rashidieh. It was, I suppose, in the hope that the storm raging inside me could only end this way that I informed Comrade Fadil, who had come from Malula to take command here, that I wanted to volunteer for the first “operation” against Israel. I thought I could resolve the contradiction between my commitment to the revolutionary cause and the love and longing I felt for my wife and daughter by giving my life for the cause of the oppressed Palestinian people. (Sabetay, who witnessed this request, would tell me years later when we met how surprised he had been by it.) However, not only was no operation against Israel carried out during our time at Rashidieh, but we would not witness any combat during the approximately nine months I spent in the Palestinian Resistance Movement. It was as if an “invisible hand” was protecting me…

Rashidieh was also where we came closest to armed combat. One night the alarm was raised; we took positions on the beach, ready for combat. In the open Mediterranean, Israeli commandos were coming toward us, firing illumination flares as they pursued Palestinian guerrillas returning from an operation against Israel. We watched as the pursuit approached the shore; we thought our end might be near. However, after a while the illumination flares stopped, and the pursuit ended. We never learned what happened, but the Palestinian guerrillas must have either been captured or killed.

With the friends who joined us at the beginning of October 1971, we had become a group of at least twenty people from Turkey. Meanwhile, two more “Halits” had joined the camp - one a blond Irishman, the other a black Haitian. “Halit the Irish” was a member of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), fighting for Northern Ireland to join the Republic of Ireland. “Halit the Haitian” was a member of one of the leftist organizations fighting against the dictatorship of Papa Doc (Francois Duvalier). It was exciting to find comrades who spoke English, coming from distant corners of the world. Their presence emphasized the internationalist nature of our environment. Those of us who knew English had plenty of conversations with them about world revolution.

While Musa’s leadership completely hollowed out at Rashidieh, my de facto leadership became firmly established. Most of those who newly joined us also recognized me as their leader. I shared my tent with a young friend with the code name Ismet, about whose real identity I only knew that he was from Bakirkoy and a graduate of Capa Education Institute, who inspired great confidence. We had hung in our tent a photograph of Chairman Mao together with Marshal Lin Biao, the hero of the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution, who was expected to succeed Mao upon his death. This was an expression of our recognition of the Chinese Communist Party as the vanguard of world revolution. (I would learn much later that Lin Biao, who allegedly attempted a military coup against Mao and when unsuccessful tried to flee to Moscow, had died when his plane crashed en route. What I would learn over time about the internal struggles in the Chinese Communist Party and the tragedies experienced in China under the communist regime would play a role in the collapse of the Marxist-Leninist paradigm in my mind.)

“Chairman Mao died”

One day we received news from Palestinian friends that “Chairman Mao” had died. As the now natural, de facto, and military leader of the group, I requested that a memorial ceremony be organized. A squad of our friends lined up and fired a salute into the air with their Kalashnikovs. We tried to relieve the grief caused by “Chairman Mao’s” death in this way. The camp residents apart from our group from Turkey watched the show we staged with curiosity and amazement. Shortly afterward, we would learn that the news was not true and that Mao was alive. The Palestinian comrades had probably made up the news of his death to mock our Maoism.

In mid-October, we were informed that we would be relocating. Around October 15, we were transferred to empty land in the heights of the mountainous village of Aita El Foukhar, located east of the Lebanese Mountains running parallel to the Mediterranean, near the Syrian border. We built a camp with the tents we set up. After a while, another group of friends from Turkey and Germany joined us. Thus our group, perhaps reaching 30 people, had never been this large; the number of Arab or Palestinian guerrillas alongside us had also never been this small. This place had now become a camp that the DC had essentially allocated to those of us from Turkey. Since there was no official from the DC present, I had become the de facto commander of the camp. The situation was somewhat strange…

The first dramatic event I experienced at Aita El Foukhar was the arrival of our friend Ayhan Ozer from Ankara. Ayhan, an engineer who was a graduate of ITU, was married and had recently had a child. Dogu Perincek must have decreed that he too, like me, needed to separate from his wife and child in order to “proletarianize,” to be freed from bourgeois ways. One evening, I was alone with Ayhan (whose code name I don’t remember) on dish-washing duty. I thought he might be in great distress. Deciding to open up to him, perhaps as a consolation, I said something like this: “Ayhan, we have something in common. Both of us came here leaving our wives and children behind. Yes, we have dedicated ourselves to the revolution, but that doesn’t mean we have been purged of our feelings for our loved ones… Sometimes we may need to share our troubles…” His response was very harsh. He said something like: “Comrade Selim, we have dedicated ourselves to the revolution and we should no longer look back, we must forget the past!…” I had been severely rebuffed. He must have been right…

(Long after I left the Palestinian resistance movement, when we met in Amsterdam, I would learn from Cengiz that Ayhan had suffered a severe mental breakdown. The comrades had been forced to hand him over to the Turkish Embassy in Beirut; his family came and took him back home. About ten years later, in the mid-1980s, we got together in Istanbul. One day he came to see me at the Cumhuriyet newspaper where I was working at the time. We talked privately. He had retired and was not working anywhere. He said he was still a socialist and revolutionary, but that he regularly performed his prayers and went to the mosque. Praying was good for his soul… I never saw him again. In 2014, I read in the newspapers that he had passed away in Ankara and that his funeral was conducted by the Workers’ Party, of which he was a member, led by Dogu Perincek. He remained in my memory as a living example of how people break when their psychology is strained too much.)

We had formed a management committee under my leadership, consisting of friends who had known each other for a long time. News came that some friends, primarily Musa, but also including Saban (Ahmet Ozdemir) and Ismet (whom I valued greatly), had been called back to Turkey. When we were at Rashidieh, we had conveyed our complaints about Musa’s behaviors “completely incompatible with being a revolutionary” to the “party inspector” (Muzaffer Orucoglu) who had been sent there. (When we learned that Musa was appointed to head the organization’s Istanbul operations upon his return, we would not be too surprised. For the story of Orucoglu, who later settled in Australia and became a painter and novelist, see: <http://www.muzafferorucoglu.net> )

I pulled aside Ismet, whom I valued greatly and who was still a young man in his early 20s, and spoke to him privately. I strictly warned him not to forget that the revolutionary movement was in a period of self-defense, to absolutely refuse if he was asked to participate in bomb or armed attacks, and to focus his energy on organizational work. (Unfortunately, what I feared would come to pass: Some time after returning home, Ismet was given the task of throwing a bomb at the Israeli Embassy in Cankaya. On the way, the bomb exploded in his hand and he died. When I learned this, I was deeply pained. By coincidence, Omer Madra, who was passing by there at that time, would later tell me that he came upon the scene of this incident.)

Aita El Fukhar

One day in mid-November, the snow suddenly set in. I had always had a kind of snow phobia; when it snowed, an unexplainable anxiety would fill me that we would be unable to find food or get to a doctor. Perhaps partly because of this, when the snow depth gradually reached a meter and our food supplies dwindled significantly, I gathered the committee and proposed abandoning the camp and retreating down to the village of Aita El Fukhar. My proposal was accepted. Except for one, the few Palestinians did not object either. Only one said he would absolutely not leave the camp based on the decision of us Turks and set up a tent for himself. (When the snow let up and the sun came out, the image of him sitting on the chair he placed in front of his tent, listening to melancholy songs on his radio, is still before my eyes today.) We oiled the weapons and other valuable equipment, put them in containers and buried them in the ground, and one day in late November we descended to the village. My first task there was to go to the church and speak with the priests. I told them we had taken refuge there fleeing from the snow, and asked them to support us until help arrived from our organization.

They showed us a half-finished reinforced concrete building for us to stay in; they gave us water and food. We lit a fire to warm ourselves; the friends picked each other’s lice, starting with Adil who had the most, and burned them crackling in the fire. A few days later, finally an official from the DC arrived. Although they were the ones who had left us out on the mountain, they were not very understanding about our having abandoned the camp, but a day or two later we were informed that we would be moving to a new camp. We were first taken by jeeps to Beirut, to the Burj El-Barajneh Palestinian refugee camp. A few days later, we were transferred from there to near the Nahr Al-Bared camp just north of Tripoli. We began to shelter in the camp consisting of tents we set up by the seashore.

In December 1971, we followed the developments of the India-Pakistan war, which resulted in Bangladesh gaining its independence from Pakistan, on a small transistor radio we had somehow acquired. We stayed at that camp for about a month; we welcomed 1972 there. The DC officials had left us completely on our own here as well. Our number had dropped to around 15 after some had returned to Turkey. Military and physical training activities were increasingly replaced by conversation and even playing football in the wide area by the river. The feeling that our presence there was gradually losing its meaning was spreading among us. We began to think that the time had come for the veterans of the group to return to Turkey - that we had learned what we could learn in the Palestinian Resistance Movement and could go back.

An important development occurred at Nahr Al-Bared. A Kurdish friend with the code name Sadik, a student at Capa Teachers’ College, pulled me aside and said he wanted to return to the country and continue his education. I raised the issue with the management committee consisting of old friends. A couple of them said we couldn’t allow him to return to the country, that if he were caught he would give information about us to the security forces. Some even argued that he should be killed. I was shocked. In short, I said, “Being a revolutionary is entirely voluntary work, we have no right to force anyone into it, we have no authority to take anyone’s life. I am taking responsibility and we are sending Sadik back home with the first group to return.” (Years later, one day in late 1975, on the ferry from Kadikoy to Karakoy with Sabetay, we ran into Sadik, whose real name I didn’t know. He saw us and came over to us smiling. He hadn’t been caught, had finished school, and was working as a teacher in Istanbul. I cannot express how happy I was to see him safe and well and happy.)

Finally, due to our deep doubts about the commitment of the TIIKP (the Revolutionary Workers’ and Peasants’ Party of Turkey), and primarily of Dogu Perincek, to Marxism-Leninism-Mao Zedong Thought, we decided to leave TIIKP and, upon returning to Turkey, join the Communist Party of Turkey - Marxist Leninist, which we had learned was founded by Ibrahim Kaypakkaya and his friends. Initially, Sabetay, Ismet and I would return, while Cengiz would stay in Lebanon for now to maintain our external relations. Cengiz contacted the Kurdistan Democratic Party representatives in Beirut to secure the necessary support for our safe return to Turkey. We conveyed our decision to return to the DC officials. They were helpful in every way. They must have also thought there was no longer any reason for us to stay at their camps.

In mid-February 1972, Sabetay, Ismet, Cengiz and I crossed into Syria via mountain roads in a jeep provided by the DC. Our first stop was Malula. No trace remained of the training camp; only the hut that had once been used as the administration building and for storing provisions still stood. Friends who had come from Germany had stored the large amount of clothing they had brought with them here, thinking it would be needed by those returning. We put on the civilian clothes we found there. We were taken by the DC to the Yarmouk camp, the largest camp housing Palestinian refugees in Damascus, and settled in a small house. At a meeting we held there, the four of us decided to establish what must have been the umpteenth Communist Party of Turkey (Marxist-Leninist) organization. All of us except Cengiz would return to Turkey and join Kaypakkaya. I kept expressing the view that this was a time not for attack but for preserving forces, that there was nothing we could do during martial law except protect ourselves. The decisions we made certainly reflected our distrust and reaction toward Perincek and his circle, but I think they also expressed an attempt to calm the anxieties forming within us about the future, a search to not be left without purpose. We felt in our bones that we were walking toward an uncertain future.

## From Damascus to Qamishli

The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) organized our return journey from Damascus to Turkey. It was clear that the DC and the KDP had cooperated to ensure that upon our return we would engage in armed struggle against the military regime in Turkey. Cengiz, who conducted contacts with them, had informed us that we would fly from Damascus to Qamishli in northeastern Syria, and from there cross the Tigris to enter Turkey. We received a bag full of hand grenades and a bag of pistols, given to us to take along and use. One day in mid-February, we went to Damascus airport in vehicles provided by the KDP. After embracing and saying farewell to Cengiz, we headed toward the (Dakota model) plane that would take us to Qamishli, with the bag full of hand grenades in my hands and the bag with the pistols in Faris’s hands.

Just as I reached the plane’s stairs, the handle broke off in my hand and the bag dropped to the ground with a thud! Without showing any reaction, I picked up the bag from the ground, pressed it to my chest, and climbed the stairs.

The sight we encountered on the plane was striking. Everyone except us was a Turkish pilgrim returning from the hajj, dressed in special pilgrim’s garments. We sat in different places from each other. Throughout the journey, I tried not to talk to those sitting next to me. After about an hour of flight, the plane landed in Qamishli at the Turkish border. We were waiting curiously to see what would happen now. Looking out the window, I saw several cars approaching the plane’s stairs. Clutching the bags, we got off the plane, and as soon as we got into the waiting cars, we quickly left the airport. It was clear that the KDP and the Syrian Mukhabarat (intelligence organization) had cooperated to have us secretly delivered to Turkey.

The cars first took us to a house in Qamishli. After spending one night there, we were moved to a village on the banks of the Tigris. The KDP officials said they would take us across from here to Turkey. The three of us gathered. Taking into account the dangers of crossing with the bags in our hands, I suggested that we wrap up the weapons inside them and bury them in a pit, to come back and retrieve them when we found the opportunity. The friends agreed with this idea. We did so. Whether we would find such an opportunity was doubtful, but we had no doubt that crossing the border with these would be very dangerous.

On the night of February 21, 1972, brightly illuminated by the full moon, we descended to the banks of the Tigris, and a giant, elderly Kurdish smuggler took us across one by one to the opposite shore, carrying us on his back when necessary and loading us onto a raft made of boards placed on tractor inner tubes. I remember admiring his strength and skills. Throughout this entire activity, the cigarettes glowing in front of the border post on the Turkish side showed that the gendarmerie was aware of our arrival and was content to just watch. It was clear that the necessary money for them to turn a blind eye had been paid.

When we found ourselves in Turkey, the initiative suddenly passed to Ismet. I was somewhat bewildered. He suggested we hide among the rocks on the other side of the road until morning; we did so. When morning came, we went up to the asphalt road running along the shore and began waiting for minibuses coming from Silopi and heading to Cizre. None came by at all. We decided to slowly start walking toward Cizre. We walked past the border posts, which were set up at quite frequent intervals. Nobody paid any attention. It was clear that all of them knew we would be passing through. Finally, a minibus came from the Silopi direction and stopped to pick us up. The driver’s pointed questions implied that he believed we, in our suits, were smugglers.

The minibus was stopped by gendarmes on the Cizre bridge and identity checks were conducted. We showed the fake identity papers we had used when going from Turkey to Syria. I don’t know if the gendarme sergeant at the bridge was also informed, but we passed through the not-too-strict control and continued on our way. In Cizre, we boarded a bus going to Mardin. Faris suspected he had run into an acquaintance at the bus station, but we paid no attention… Once the bus started moving, perhaps owing to the sense of ease that came from having survived so many ordeals, I began to feel like an ordinary, “clean” Turkish citizen. Even though I was “wanted,” I felt a quiet joy inside for having returned to my country. Taking on the role of a pharmaceutical company employee, I chatted with the rather talkative villager sitting next to me, using my imagination to its fullest about what I was doing there.

From Mardin, we went to Diyarbakir by minibus and spent the night of February 22 at a hotel there. The next day, traveling by bus via Ergani and Elazig, we reached Malatya, our intended destination. We had addresses (I don’t remember how we obtained them) that we hoped would enable us to reach Ibrahim Kaypakkaya. Ismet volunteered to go to these addresses. Adil and I waited at the bus station. On the walls of the bus station hung posters showing those wanted by security forces - I suspected I was among them but avoided approaching to look closely. When Faris returned a few hours later with the information that all those addresses had been raided by security forces, we decided we had no choice but to continue to Ankara. A vague joy stirred inside me. When I arrived in Ankara, perhaps I could see my beloved and my daughter…

How I had missed them!…

When we got off the bus in Ankara in the morning hours of February 24, our paths separated. Ismet and Sabetay continued to Istanbul; I got in a taxi with the few liras left in my pocket and went to my elder sister Olcay’s house on Kizilirmak Street. When my sister opened the door and saw me, she didn’t know what to do from shock and joy… I saw my niece Sedef, whom I had left as a baby, for the first time as a 2-year-old child. I will never forget: with her blue eyes and blonde hair, she resembled a fairy. My sister immediately notified Fatma. How I had missed her!.. She stayed with me for two nights. We decided it would not be right for her to show me Elvan. One afternoon, Omer and Tanju also came to see me. The day I was to leave, I don’t know how I found the strength to tell Fatma that my fate was bound to the revolution, that she should now consider herself free… Was I sincere, or was it that a hope, however small, of being reunited with her had not yet died inside me? Fatma received it with her usual composure. Were storms raging inside her, or had she come to believe that the expected end had come? I could never read what was going through her mind…

After staying at my sister’s for three nights, washing and getting rid of the lice and getting new clothes, on the night of February 28, 1972, I set off for Istanbul by bus. I remember we crossed the Bosphorus by car ferry. As soon as I got off, I called my elder brother from a phone booth. He was very excited. He said he had been terribly worried and that I should immediately come to his house on Kore Sehitleri (Korean War Martyrs) Street. I did so. My sister-in-law Ayla had taken my young nephews Umit and Cihan to her mother’s so they wouldn’t encounter me. My brother and I embraced like never before… How happy he was to see me… But he was very worried; he feared what seemed inevitable - that I would eventually be caught and imprisoned. With all his love and devotion to me, he didn’t even consider the dangers my presence posed for him. I told him I would be leaving soon and just wanted them to host me for a few days. I was determined not to abandon the revolutionary cause - or I was convincing myself of this, wanting to believe it.

I stayed at my brother’s until March 4. That day I met with Omer. Omer took me to the home of our mutual friend Alev on Asmali Mescit Street in Tunel. Alev (Seref) was married to Taner at the time and pregnant with her daughter Su. Without hesitation, she agreed to shelter me for a while. The next day, I went to the house of Adil Ovalioglu and his friends in Baglarbasi, which we had agreed upon as the meeting place with Sabetay and Ismet (we had learned that Adil had joined Kaypakkaya). Adil and I agreed that our primary issue was the matter of shelter. He said he would make some contacts. We would decide together in the coming days what we would do. A few days later, at the agreed place and time in Tepebasi, I met with Sabetay and we went to a coffee house in Kadikoy to talk over with Adil what we would do. Adil was saying that there were some caves in the Bingol countryside, that we could spend the martial law and heavy pressure period by hiding there. I don’t know whether he himself was fully convinced of this, but I certainly was not; it would soon become clear that Sabetay wasn’t either. Indeed, he did not come to our appointment on April 1.

# CHAPTER V / I CHOOSE FREEDOM

With Sabetay’s disappearance, a new chapter opened in my life. I made a decision that had probably been forming in my subconscious for some time. I went to my elder brother and asked him to help me escape to Europe. He encouraged me, saying, “I’ll do everything I can, and that’s what I should do.” Through him, I sent a message to Fatma. The essence of my message was this: “My love, I have wronged you; don’t pay me back in kind; forgive me… I’m going to escape to Europe, and I want you to come join me. I’m giving up revolutionary activities. I will never, ever leave you again, never, ever hurt you… Please, please come to Istanbul immediately, we need to talk…” How did I convince myself of a scenario that seemed completely unrealistic to achieve under the prevailing conditions? What probably made this possible was the desperation I was in, and the glimmer of hope awakening within me that I might escape the dead end I had fallen into. And my dear brother was fueling this hope: “Whatever it takes, I’ll send you abroad…” he said. I felt as if I had been reborn. I was now a different person… A great burden had been lifted from my conscience… I no longer had any practical involvement with revolution and revolutionary activities, even if ideologically I still had some connection.

(In the following section, I made use of notes I took during my first days in Stockholm, where I would seek refuge. This is why I am able to give exact dates.)

## Drunk with happiness

I continued staying with Alev. Since she and her husband Taner were on bad terms at the time, he wasn’t staying at home, only dropping by occasionally. Alev showed me one of the greatest friendships I have ever witnessed by sheltering me for days. Yes, she too was a “leftist” sympathizer, but the solidarity she showed had nothing to do with political stance; it was entirely about friendship and companionship. This would be one of the experiences that made me realize the deep distinction between being ideological comrades and being true friends.

My dear Fatma came and stayed with me for three nights at Alev’s house between March 19-21. I practically threw myself at her feet; I begged her to give me one last chance. She was uneasy, but surprisingly, she wasn’t saying “It’s over, I’ve closed the chapter on you”…

Did she think I was deluding myself, or was she also hopeful that we could be together again?.. I wasn’t sure, but because she hadn’t ended our relationship, I was flying with happiness even though the future was completely uncertain. My love for her was more intense than ever. The plan we agreed upon was this: My brother would somehow obtain a fake passport for me, I would escape abroad with it, and have Fatma and Elvan join me. My Fatma came again on April 7 and stayed with me for a few more days. I now trusted that she hadn’t abandoned me. I believed that one day I would be reunited with her and my daughter.

On March 30, I was shaken by the news. Security forces had surrounded and killed Mahir Cayan, Cihan Alptekin, and their comrades in the village of Kizildere in the Niksar district of Tokat; only Ertugrul Kurkcu had survived the massacre and was captured alive. Although we had had arguments that reached the level of serious accusations, Mahir was an old friend of mine. (Fatma had found only him likeable among my leftist friends.) Unfortunately, the competition among young leftists over “who is more revolutionary” was costing the lives of comrades who had dedicated themselves to the cause of a more just Turkey and had also been swept up in the dream that armed revolution was possible.

After that date, I would stay alternately at two houses: My brother’s mother-in-law Aunt Mueyyet and father-in-law Osman (Cokay) Bey accepted me into their home as if there were nothing unusual about it, as if there were no danger. The apartment of Fatma’s close friend from university, Konca, and her husband Erdal (Aktulga) in Atakoy became my second home. (I owe a lifelong debt of gratitude to these people.) Omer came to see me in Atakoy. We talked at length about our troubles. He too had experienced disappointments and had completely broken away from the revolutionary movement. I told him about my plan to escape to Europe; he thought it was right. We parted with an embrace. Unfortunately, not long after, he would be arrested along with Altan Oymen and others on charges of “hijacking a plane” and would spend more than two years in prison in Ankara, being tried in the TIIKP (Revolutionary Workers’ and Peasants’ Party of Turkey) case, until he was released with the 1974 amnesty.

On April 15, I met with Ahmet Ozdemir (Saban), who had contacted me through my brother, in the then-empty lot in front of the Hilton hotel, overlooking Dolmabahce. Saban was one of the comrades who had returned from Palestine before us. He was one of the most pure-hearted, decent, and idealistic friends I have ever known in my life, someone I loved dearly. He suggested we go together to Syria, and from there to Lebanon, to rejoin our comrades. I told him I was determined to escape to Europe and seek refuge in one of the countries there. (This would be my last meeting with him. Ahmet managed to return to Syria and from there to Lebanon. But this was a very unfortunate success. Sadly, he would be one of the comrades killed in the raid by Israeli commandos on the Nahr Al Barad camp in February 1973. Seeing how deeply saddened I was when I learned of this in Stockholm, my Greek friend Anestis Kombokis, with whom I was sharing a house at the time, painted on a piece of wood, in memory of Ahmet, a small torch that would burn forever. This painful memento still stands in my bookcase today.)

On April 17, I met with Adil Ovalioglu somewhere in Dolapdere. He told me that Saban had gone to Elazig and would head south from there to cross the border. He repeated his suggestion that we settle together in the caves of the Bingol mountains. I told him I had made my final decision and would escape to Europe, and we said our farewells. When I returned to Alev’s house that evening, I found Omer and Tanju waiting for me. On April 18, we celebrated my 28th birthday together. This would be my last time seeing them until we met again in 1975.

Days were passing but my hope that my brother would find a way to obtain a fake passport for me was not fading. I had lost contact with Sabetay. I didn’t know what had happened to him. (Years later, when we met in Istanbul, he would tell me that he had escaped abroad with a fake passport his brother had obtained by bribing the police heavily, and had sought refuge in France.) I was left alone. Months had passed since my return home in early March, June had arrived, but my brother had made no progress in obtaining a passport. One night while I was staying at the Cokays’ house, my sister-in-law Ayla sat me down. She reminded me that she had lost hope they could help me escape, that the protection they were providing me was creating an increasingly dangerous situation for them, and asked me to fend for myself as soon as possible. She was absolutely right…. I told my brother that I had no choice but to try to return to the Palestinian resistance movement. My dear brother again said to me, “If you can’t manage it, come back…” There was nothing I could do but set off saying farewell to my Fatma, farewell to my Elvan, farewell to my hopes and dreams.

The only thing I could do now was to return the way I had come to Cizre, from there somehow to Syria, and from there to Beirut, to rejoin Cengiz. I felt deep regret that I hadn’t met up with Saban to go together. Even if I would eventually be caught, I had to try. My brother was very upset, but he too had nothing left to say. He had been unable to find a way to smuggle me to Europe. I put the fake identity card I had used when first going to Syria in my pocket and on June 18 set off by bus via Adana, Gaziantep, Urfa, and Mardin toward Cizre. From there, I would somehow find a way to return to Syria the same way I had come.

I spent the first night on the bus. On the second day, the bus I was on was stopped by police between Urfa and Mardin. Everyone on the bus except me was a villager. With my suit and tie, I had a conspicuous appearance. The police officer conducting the identity check immediately approached me. I showed my ID; I said I worked as a marketing employee at a pharmaceutical company and was going to Mardin. The police officer thanked me and returned my ID. (As I had tested and would test on other occasions, my appearance left the impression that I was someone completely “innocent / clean.”) It was unnerving to see so many military vehicles pass us as the bus made its way toward Mardin.

In Mardin

On the night of June 19, I arrived in Mardin and went straight to a hotel near the bus station that had caught my eye (the Yildiz Palas), and immediately shut myself in my room. I couldn’t sleep for a long time, but then exhaustion took over and I fell asleep. I woke up at 8 in the morning and immediately got up and went to the bus station. Hawkers were announcing buses going in two directions. One was shouting “Cizre -Silopi!”, the other “Antep, Antep!”… A deep anxiety descended upon me that if I got on the Cizre bus I would be caught in a short time, and without thinking much, almost instinctively, I bought a ticket for the Antep bus. When the bus started moving, there was a relief inside me as if I had survived a great ordeal. A peace filled me similar to what I had felt during the Cizre-Gaziantep bus journey at the end of February (and similar to what I would feel later, in January 1981, when being transported from the police detention center in Izmir Basmane to the military detention center in Narlidere). I began chatting comfortably about this and that with the citizen from Mardin sitting next to me, as if I were a “normal” person. I couldn’t believe I could do this. Apparently, I had become thoroughly frightened that I would be caught if I continued toward Cizre…

Returning to Istanbul the way I had come, I arrived in Kadikoy late on June 21. I went to a random hotel on Rihtim Avenue and immediately withdrew to my room. I had made my decision: I would get up early the next morning, go to Adil Ovalioglu’s house in Baglarbasi, and surrender myself to him so that he could take me to the caves in the Bingol mountains. I had no other choice. My only concern was that I might not find the house, whose location I only vaguely remembered… On the morning of June 22, 1971, I left the hotel and walked to the Kadikoy ferry pier. I bought a cheese sandwich, a glass of lemonade, and a copy of Milliyet newspaper from the buffet. When I opened the newspaper, the headline story I encountered was titled “The Trunk Murder!” The summary of the news was this: Bogazici University student Banu Erguder had been detained by police in Pasabahce; when the trunk she was carrying, which she said contained her books, was opened, the dismembered corpse inside was found to belong to Adil Ovalioglu, who was wanted by the police… I was horrified!.. If I had gone to Ovalioglu’s house without buying the newspaper and reading the news, I would probably have been greeted by the security forces with “Welcome, Sahin Alpay!” and interrogated about the murder. (The police investigation would conclude that Ovalioglu had been killed by Zeynel Altindag, one of the “Maoist” youth at Bogazici University whom I had also known at one point, due to an intra-organizational dispute.) By sheer luck, I had escaped another disaster…

Without thinking too much, I swallowed my pride and decided to call my brother. (I don’t know why it never occurred to me to go and surrender to the police. I was probably afraid of spending many years in prison and falling among Dogu Perincek and his comrades again. If I had surrendered, I couldn’t have known that I too would be released like the others with the 1974 amnesty.) I crossed to the other side by ferry, to Kabatas, and called my brother from the first phone booth I found. My dear brother had been very upset about my departure, hadn’t slept for days; he was overjoyed that I had returned safe and sound. They had closed up the house on Kore Sehitleri (Korean War Martyrs) Avenue and moved to his father-in-law’s house in Zincirlikuyu. He told me to come there in the evening, that he would be waiting for me. “Whatever it takes, I’ll make sure you escape to Europe,” he said… My sister-in-law Ayla, contrary to my expectations, was also pleased about my return. I remember as if it were yesterday what an enormous boost of morale my brother’s words gave me. That night (and for days afterward) I stayed at the home of my sister-in-law’s sister Ayhan and her husband Altan (Demirkol). They sheltered me in their home as if there were no risk involved, as if I were an ordinary guest. I cannot put into words my debt of gratitude to the friends and relatives who took the risk of hiding me. (In this context, you can imagine how moved I was when I learned that my elder sister Sumru’s elderly father-in-law Ali Comert had sent word saying, “Let him come, I’ll hide him on the farm.”)

I started looking for new friends who would hide me in their homes and help me escape. The first thing that came to mind was to look for Metin (Kilicli), a close friend from middle and high school. I hadn’t seen him for a long time, but I had no doubt about his friendship. The year we graduated from Robert College, his father had passed away, and the responsibility of supporting his mother and two sisters had fallen on his shoulders. For a while, he had bet on horse races by closely studying the horses’ performance and had, incredibly, won considerable sums of money. Later, he had started working as an assistant to a director in Yesilcam (the Turkish film industry), and in the meantime had had a great love affair with the director’s wife. Metin, who was one of the brightest minds in our class and should have studied on scholarship in the USA to become a physicist or chemist if circumstances had allowed, had studied architecture at Mimar Sinan University, calculating that he could only support his mother and sisters by working as a contractor after his father’s death. I learned he was living in Atakoy. I somehow found his address and knocked on his door. He was quite surprised to see me. He didn’t invite me inside, but said the following through the crack in the door: “I live here with my mother and two sisters. I can’t put them in danger. But I’ll help you in any way I can other than sheltering you.”

At Metin’s suggestion that I could stay at hotels there until I found a safer place, I went to Kumburgaz. With the fear that I could be reported and caught at any moment, I stayed there for a few nights at a place called “Marmara Family Pension.”

Metin and I started thinking together about how I could escape to Europe. We had heard that our close friend from middle school, Sefik (Yuksel), was a senior executive at THY (Turkish Airlines). Metin was saying, “If Sefik gives you his passport, I’ll make the necessary modifications to it, and you can go.” He tracked down Sefik and conveyed my request. Sefik’s answer was (of course, and quite rightly) negative. (According to what Sefik told me when we met years later, when Metin received the negative answer, he had lashed out at him saying, “What kind of man are you! How could Sahin have trusted you enough to send me to you!..” and had caused Sefik sleepless nights.)

I didn’t lose hope. I continued waiting for my brother to find an opportunity. Since I couldn’t find a place to stay in Istanbul, at the end of June I went to Erdek via Bursa; I stayed there for a few nights (in a very anxious state of mind) at a place called “Deniz Hotel.” Playing the role of a young man vacationing alone was quite unsettling, and I was quite afraid of being caught; but there was nothing to be done. At the beginning of July, I returned to Istanbul and started staying at Ayhan’s again. There was good news!.. My brother was about to buy a passport… I had photographs taken to use in the passport and took them to Metin. But this time the news was discouraging: The man had changed his mind! But my brother continued searching… On July 7, I went to Cinarcik via Yalova to stay for 3-4 days. I stayed at a hotel called “Manolya Palas.” In the oppressive heat, overwhelmed with anxieties about what would become of me, I spent terrible nights. One day I ran into Sanar (Yurdatapan), an old acquaintance of mine. Bless him, he said he would help if there was anything he could do.

On July 14, hope was born again: My brother had found a police officer who would secretly get me on a THY plane going to Frankfurt; (the man was asking for 15 thousand liras, which was no small amount for that time). My brother went to Ayvalik to talk to Fatma. Fatma immediately put up 8 thousand and promised to send the remaining 7 thousand. In preparation for the operation, a ticket was purchased for the plane departing on July 30 for 3,200 liras. However, when the man raised his demand to 20 thousand liras, the operation was abandoned. (This was perhaps my greatest stroke of luck. Out of desperation, the cost of this adventure I would have embarked on without even a fake passport could have been very high.) On the night of July 30, I was staying at (our dear friends) Konca and Erdal’s (Aktulga) in Atakoy; I watched the plane on which I was a ticketed passenger take off without me.

On August 9, I met my brother Acar. “A new opportunity has arisen. We can buy a passport, and you can travel abroad at any moment, but we need to find 10 thousand liras to pay for the passport,” he was saying. It occurred to me that I could ask my high school friend Ahmet (Kutman) for a loan. Metin and I called Ahmet. Bless him, Ahmet gave the money saying, “You can pay your debt when you have the means in the future.” The man demanded an additional 2 thousand liras to also give his identity card along with the passport. I met with my classmate from high school, Riza (Asi), and borrowed 2 thousand liras from him as well. (These two loyal friends would refuse when I wanted to repay my debt three years later.) This problem was also solved. Then, on August 15, my brother announced the big news: The person who agreed to let me use his passport and identity card in exchange for money was a bartender acquaintance. His condition was that the passport and identity card be returned to him after the job was done.

## A true friend

I was flying with joy!.. Now it was time to adapt the passport to me, that is, to change the photograph and forge the embossed and inked official stamps on it. There was not the slightest doubt about who could do this. This was exactly a job for Metin. I handed over the passport I received from my brother to Metin. I was locked away in the Demirkols’ apartment in Etiler. The hosts were on vacation. As long as I was in the apartment, I could not turn on the lights or make any noise. Altan would come every few days to bring food. There was no choice but to endure any and all conditions.

About a week later, word came that Metin was waiting for me at a friend’s architecture office in Osmanbey. When I arrived at the office, Metin had mounted my photograph on the authentic passport and had also taken care of the embossed stamp. Under my amazed and excited gaze, he drew the reverse image of the inked stamp with a ballpoint pen on an eraser and, with great composure, using his one chance, perfectly set the inked stamp in place as well. The passport I needed to leave the country was now ready. I was finally going…

(Here I want to open a parenthesis and tell a bit about Metin: When I returned to the country in 1975, I found him working as a contractor. We started meeting frequently. He had married his girlfriend from university, Nuray, and they had a daughter, Ozge. Because his business wasn’t going very well, after a while he started working for a close friend’s construction company; reluctantly, he took on responsibility for the company’s operations in Libya. I was working at Cumhuriyet at the time. One morning in April 1986, concerned by news that the US had bombed Libya, I called Nuray. Surprisingly, there was no sign of anxiety in her voice. A little later she said, “Let me put someone on for you.” Metin had sensed that the bombs were coming and had managed to return to Istanbul by boarding the last plane out!.. This was another demonstration of Metin’s intelligence and resourcefulness.

However, Metin was as unlucky as he was smart and resourceful. The year he graduated from high school, his father, who was a tailor, died leaving considerable debt, which darkened his future. His misfortunes continued. When the company he worked for abandoned its operations in Libya due to the war, Metin had started overseeing the company’s construction projects in Istanbul. One day Nuray called; she said Metin had broken his hip by falling into an elevator shaft and had narrowly escaped cracking his skull. When I went to visit him at the American Hospital, he was quite exhausted. He recovered over time, but his health problems continued. A year or two later, he had to have part of his stomach removed due to an ulcer.

It was he who would react most strongly to my starting to write for Zaman in 2002. He believed not in democracy but in secularism and looked upon religious beliefs with suspicion. It upset me greatly when he said that, had he known I would one day start writing for Fethullah Gulen’s newspaper, he would never have supported me; but our friendship was not shaken. This time he had started working at a brokerage firm owned by a friend; meanwhile, he was again betting on horse races. Then he started battling prostate cancer. The treatment was successful. I called him when I was released from Silivri in 2018. He said he was very upset about my imprisonment. His daughter Ozge had gotten married and settled in Canada. He said he was going to Montreal to look after his grandchildren. He returned from there. Our friendship continues.)

Meanwhile, Fatma had shared the developments with her maternal uncle Ismet Kaptan (the former general manager of Izmir Fair) and his wife Aysun, and they had said they definitely wanted to see me. I went to their apartment in Atakoy where they were living at the time. I explained my escape preparations with complete openness. Uncle Ismet asked me to give him the passport. He would show it to Nihat, the director of the Istanbul Police Department’s 4th Division (Passport Division), who was his blood brother from Galatasaray High School, and make sure there was no problem with me setting off with it. (This is what family solidarity was all about!..) A few days later, the answer came:

Mr. Nihat had been amazed at the “uniqueness” of the modification made to the passport and had said, “It’s come out perfect; he can go with this comfortably…” After receiving this assurance as well, there was no obstacle left to my setting off…

## Bosfor Tourism

Now it was time to organize the journey. My brother and I made the plan together: the safest way for me to travel would be by bus. I would go to Munich by the comfortable Bosfor Tourism bus, then continue to Geneva by train. There I would apply for political asylum in Switzerland. There would be advantages to seeking refuge in a country at the center of Europe. Moreover, my elder sister Olcay’s sister-in-law Mrs. Ayhan lived in Geneva with her Swiss husband; she could be of help throughout the application process.

My brother bought my ticket from Bosfor Tourism for me to set off on the morning of August 20, 1972. A day or two earlier, we had gone to a store in Pangalti and bought a gray suit for me to wear on the journey. On the night of August 19, there was feverish activity at the Cokays’ house with my brother, my sister-in-law, and her late mother Aunt Mueyyet participating. My hair was dyed black so I wouldn’t be recognized on the road. Aunt Mueyyet gave me strong anti-depressant pills to use during the journey to suppress my excitement. It was decided that my brother and sister-in-law would follow my bus in their car, so they would know whether or not I had made it through safely. (What would happen if I didn’t make it safely??? I didn’t even want to think about it…)

On the morning of August 20, my brother, my sister-in-law, and I set off for Taksim. The bus was departing at 9:00. We said our farewells excitedly and I boarded the bus. While boarding, I thought I saw Nedim (Demirelli), a close friend from middle school. Had he seen me too? Even if he had, I was sure he wouldn’t say anything. (Years later I learned that he hadn’t seen me.) I was more excited and tense than I had ever been on my previous “fugitive” journeys. As soon as the bus started moving, I swallowed one of the pills Aunt Mueyyet had given me. The bus made a rest stop halfway to Edirne; I got out and had a glass of tea. The pill had taken effect and I had begun to feel like a “normal” passenger. It was great luck that there was no one sitting in the seat next to me; there was no need to make unnecessary small talk.

When we arrived at the Kapikule border crossing, the bus hostess began collecting passports under my amazed gaze. So (hooray!) I wouldn’t have to go to passport control in person… As the hostess took my passport, she said, “You can go out to the garden while waiting.” Concerned that staying on the bus might raise suspicion, I immediately did so. (Meanwhile, my brother and sister-in-law were watching what was happening from a distance; but I wasn’t aware of this.) After a while, the hostess invited the passengers back to the bus and returned the stamped passports one by one. I couldn’t believe it!.. I had sailed through passport control without the slightest hitch. Just as the bus was about to cross the border, it stopped. A police officer came inside and told us to take out our passports. After checking them one by one, he wished us a good journey and left… The barrier at the border lifted and our bus crossed to the Bulgarian side…

Farewell Dogu Perincek!

I was beside myself with joy… The operation had succeeded or was about to succeed. The thought that the Bulgarians might become suspicious and take me off the bus did cross my mind, but the Bulgarian police collected our passports, stamped them, and (thank goodness) returned them. While waiting, I went to the bathroom and there, quite literally and in actual fact, I did a belly dance for joy; I remember shouting inwardly, “Farewell Dogu Perincek, farewell Mihri Belli…” My managing to escape from Turkey was a true miracle. I would learn later: About ten days after I left, my brother had been interrogated by the political police: “We’ve received reports that you’ve been in contact with your brother… Do you know where he is?” My brother had been able to say with a clear conscience, “I have no information.” What if this interrogation had happened before I left? Then we would inevitably have had to cancel the whole operation; I would have had no choice but to go and surrender to the police.

(I always believed I was “God’s lucky servant.” I could only explain surviving so many ordeals with this… Sabetay told me when we came together years later: His brother had also smuggled him abroad. Although he had never made such a request of him, his brother, presenting him with a fait accompli, had enabled him to escape to France by paying large sums to a gang within the police. So we owed our salvation to our brothers, to our families… My dear Fatma would say she was very amazed that I could have asked my brother for such risky help. When I learned of Sabetay’s escape story, my conscience was somewhat relieved. I wasn’t the only one who had put his brother at risk…)

When the bus set off toward Sofia, I had already begun to feel like a free person… So much so that I was daring to chat with those sitting in the adjacent seats. This time I had become “an accountant going to visit relatives in Germany”… We passed through Bulgaria without stopping and entered Yugoslavia. I was sailing through passport controls without a hitch. We stayed one night in the city of Nis (in today’s Serbia). After a rest stop in Belgrade, we continued to Maribor (now in Slovenia); we stayed there for one night too. Then, passing through Austria, on to Munich!

## The Americans are bewildered

That evening, after a dinner of a sausage in bread and a beer at a place resembling a train station, I went to a random hotel. As I had done in Mardin, anxious not to be seen around, I immediately went to bed and slept. In the morning, I got up, went to the station, and bought a train ticket to Geneva. There were two American young men in the compartment I settled into. While I was deep in conversation with them, the Swiss passport police arrived. The fact that after looking at my passport they thanked me and returned it greatly surprised the Americans: How had a Turk’s passport been returned without being examined, without being questioned, and moreover with thanks?.. (If only they knew the passport was fake!..) To be honest, I too was a bit surprised but extremely pleased.

When I arrived at the Geneva station on August 23, I immediately went to the office that helped find hotels. Soon I had a room at the address “Hotel Kaufmann, Boulevard des Tranchees 48.” My next step was to use the address I had to go to the home of Ayhan (my brother-in-law’s elder sister) and her husband Guy. There was no answer at the door. After several attempts, I knocked on the neighbor’s door. Since I didn’t know French, it was only with great difficulty that I learned the homeowners hadn’t been in the city for some time. But the neighbor woman was kind enough to give me Guy’s sister’s address. When I arrived there, a great disappointment awaited me: His sister was saying that Guy and Ayhan had gone to Turkey… In all my naivety, I thought for a while that maybe they would return to Geneva after learning I had arrived here. I was wrong. I would later find out that as soon as they heard I was coming to Geneva, they had left the city for fear that I would knock on their door.

What was I to do now? Out of concern that I might encounter an unfavorable situation, I didn’t want to approach the Swiss police without someone knowing of it and being able to bear witness. I was afraid that something might go wrong and I would be sent back to Turkey. (Of course, this was an entirely meaningless worry, but it reflected my psychology in those days.) Meanwhile, some nights at the hotel where I was staying, I could hear Turkish conversations. In the mornings, I would see Cumhuriyet newspapers thrown in the trash bin in the corridor. Since many Turks lived in Switzerland, I saw nothing surprising in this.

My brother and I started corresponding by letter. I wanted two things: The money I had with me was about to run out; what would I do?.. It would be good if Fatma’s cousin Ahmet, who lived in Strasbourg, came and took me to France. The answer came: Ahmet would come at the first opportunity and take me to Strasbourg. I would go to a friend of Ismet Kaptan’s who lived in Geneva and get 500 dollars from him. And that’s what I did. While waiting first for the Ayhans, then for Ahmet to come, I walked the streets of Geneva for about 20 days. Out of old habit, to avoid arousing suspicion, I would leave the hotel early in the morning and return late in the evening; to save money, I lived on sandwiches all day. My biggest entertainment was watching broadcasts about the Munich Olympics that were taking place at the time on screens in shop windows. This is how I learned of the Palestinian guerrillas’ attack on Israeli athletes on September 5-6. I remember being troubled, thinking that these actions would turn Western public opinion against the Palestinians. This was also one of the first signs of my beginning to take a stance against armed struggle, against weapons in general.

## Ahmet Kaptan

Ahmet Kaptan showed up at my hotel on September 11. I was flying with joy. His first question was: “Do you realize where you’ve been staying?!” I didn’t. It turned out that the Turkish Consulate General in Geneva was in the building adjacent to my hotel… This was the reason for the Turkish conversations I had heard, the Cumhuriyet newspapers I had seen… Apparently, I had even avoided looking carefully at my surroundings.

On the afternoon of September 12, Ahmet and I departed for Basel to catch the train going from there to Strasbourg. We encountered a big problem at the border: The French police were asking what work I did, how much money I had, why I wanted to go to France, etc. As usual, I said I was an accountant and would return to Turkey after visiting my nephew Ahmet for a few days. The police asked me to show how much money I had on me. After paying the hotel bill, I only had about 200 dollars left… The police curtly told Ahmet, who said he would take full responsibility for me, “You can pass, but this person cannot enter France…” I was at a loss as to what to do. The thought began to cross my mind that I would have no choice but to apply for asylum in Switzerland. With minutes left before the Strasbourg train departed, the police chief appeared. Ahmet managed to convince him, and we ran and boarded the Strasbourg train at the last moment. I breathed a deep sigh of relief… My skill (!) at crossing borders through illegal means had shown itself once again.

I started staying at Ahmet’s one-room apartment in Strasbourg. Ahmet worked at a restaurant at night and slept at home during the day. Therefore, I would leave the house as soon as he arrived in the morning and walk the streets of Strasbourg until evening. I had no idea what I would do: First of all, I decided to find Erdal Yavuz, a friend from high school and university who I knew was doing his doctorate at Strasbourg University. Despite Ahmet sending word here and there, we couldn’t get any information about where Erdal was living. The only thing being said was that he hadn’t been seen around for a long time…

Days later, information came that Erdal was living somewhere on General De Gaulle Boulevard. From that moment on, I started walking up and down that boulevard, reading the names written on apartment doors one by one. On September 22, I came across the name Taner Beygo on the door of one of the multi-story apartment buildings. I was tremendously happy. I had met Taner while he was working as an assistant at Istanbul University Law Faculty, through my friend Bulent Tanor. I had also heard that he had started working at the Human Rights Commission in Strasbourg. Without hesitation, I rang the bell. When Taner opened the door and saw me in front of him, he was stunned, but immediately invited me in and introduced me to Duygu, who was (at the time) his wife. We talked at great length. The most important information he gave was that Erdal was living in the building just behind. He was saying I could seek asylum in France. He promised to discuss this matter with his acquaintances at the European Human Rights Commission. A door of hope had opened.

## Oblomov Erdal

It was late. I waited until the next day to go to Erdal. When he opened the door and saw me in front of him, Erdal’s shock was even greater than Taner’s. We embraced… He hadn’t left the house for about forty days; while his girlfriend Irene worked, he was taking care of the housework, cooking, sweeping the house, and in the meantime playing chess, backgammon, or bridge with friends who came and went. He still hadn’t completed his doctoral studies. When we were in high school, I had nicknamed him “Oblomov” (after Goncharov). His state that day fit this description perfectly. (Erdal and Irene got married after a while and had a son they named Devrim [Revolution]. I remember teasing him saying, “You made your revolution at home too!”) That very day I moved in with Erdal and stayed as their guest until I left Strasbourg.

Taner, whom I saw a day or two later, had discussed my situation with a Czech judge named Vasak who worked at the Human Rights Commission. Vasak had said he would soon go to Paris and discuss the matter with the Interior Minister; he had instructed me to wait for him before making an asylum application. He had also mentioned that an assistantship and doctoral opportunity at Strasbourg University could be arranged for me. I was so hopeful that I would immediately write to my brother and Fatma that the possibility of staying in France had arisen.

A day or two later, Taner came with this information: The French Interior Minister had preferred not to have heard about this matter. Given this, Vasak recommended that I go to Sweden, where I could easily obtain asylum. He had written down the phone number and home address of Associate Professor Goran Melander, a human rights expert at Lund University, and sent it to me. The goal had become seeking asylum in Sweden, which had never crossed my mind until that day. The fact that I would be able to contact Melander, and that I saw this as a safeguard, played a role in my being immediately convinced. There was someone who would help me in Sweden. Moreover, I knew that Sweden was a country governed by social democrats, following a policy of neutrality, quite civilized, and with very beautiful women too. Taner and I started planning the trip to Sweden. Once again without delay, I informed my brother and Fatma that my route had turned to Sweden.

Meanwhile, Taner told me that Prof. Dr. Bulent Nuri Esen, who was my department chair at Ankara University Faculty of Education and who had taken me quite under his wing at the time, was in Strasbourg; however, when he mentioned me to him, Esen had firmly stated that he did not want to see me. I wasn’t surprised by this. But I wasn’t without doubts about whether the information Taner conveyed to me fully reflected the truth. Why hadn’t he arranged for me to meet the Czech judge? Was he directing me to Sweden to get rid of me? But if that was the case, I owe him gratitude. Because as I will describe in detail below, my affairs in Sweden would go smoothly, and my life would settle into order in a short time. (As I later learned, Sabetay’s asylum application to France had not been easily accepted at all. The French police had asked him to inform on Turks, or failing that, on Latin Americans; because he refused, he had to wait a year for his application to be accepted.)

## On the way to Sweden

On October 26, 1972, I set off from Strasbourg toward Sweden. Taner and his wife drove me to Karlsruhe, the nearest German city, in their car, which had diplomatic plates and was therefore not subject to passport control. There, after buying a thick jacket that would keep me warm in Sweden’s harsh winters (with the money I got from Ahmet), I bid farewell to the Beygos and boarded the train that would take me to Kiel. I remember that Duygu, Taner’s wife, had tears in her eyes as we said goodbye and warmly wished me good luck. I think it had seemed to her as if I were setting off on a journey with an uncertain end.

I spent one night at a hotel in Kiel, which seemed very cold and repellent to me, almost reminiscent of Germany’s Nazi past. The next day, I went by train via Lubeck to Travemunde. On Friday, October 27, when I arrived in Malmo in the evening hours on the German ferry I boarded from there, I was extraordinarily excited.

Now the moment of truth was at hand.

# CHAPTER VI / A REFUGEE IN SWEDEN

I had arrived in the country where I would apply for asylum and, if all went well, spend years of my life. When I said I had come to see Associate Professor Göran Melander from Lund University, thinking this would provide security if anything went wrong, and that I would return to Turkey in a few days, the passport police immediately stamped my entry. The customs officer asked me to open my small bag. I was prepared: I had bought a Playboy magazine in Travemünde and placed it on top of the items in the bag. The customs officer made a few jokes about the Playboy and let me pass. When I stepped into Malmö, I could barely contain my joy. The blue-flamed torches lining the avenue from the ferry to the city center told me I had arrived in the land of the Vikings and filled me with hope.

I immediately found the train station and bought a ticket to Lund, only about 20 km away. I would later learn that the small city of Lund housed one of the country’s most distinguished universities. While waiting for the train, a rather well-dressed young man carrying beer bottles in a plastic bag sauntered toward me and said something. When I said I didn’t know Swedish, he asked in quite fluent English if I had a few kronor (Swedish currency) to spare. When he got no result, he didn’t insist. This would be my first encounter with the gentleman beggars of Sweden, or rather of the Nordic countries.

## Panic in Lund

My first task in Lund was to find a hotel. I had just started settling into my room when the receptionist woman came upstairs and asked something in Swedish, and I panicked. Had she noticed my passport was fake? Had she notified the police? I hastily said I had to leave immediately and fled the place. I found another hotel. When I realized I had left my bag containing my shaving kit in the previous hotel room, I reluctantly went back to retrieve it. The poor woman had no idea what was going on; she was looking at me in astonishment. This was the first of the senseless panics I would experience in my new country. I wouldn’t feel safe until my asylum was granted.

Saturday morning, my first task was to call Melander. The phone rang but there was no answer. So I spent some of my limited pocket money and took a taxi to his address. Dog barking responded to my persistent ringing of the doorbell. The Melanders weren’t home. I thought I might learn where they could be from the neighbors across the street. I knocked on the door of the villa directly opposite. The door was opened by a white-haired lady of about 80 who was very courteous. After telling me in fluent English that she didn’t know the Melander family and that they might have gone to their summer house, she invited me to have tea with her, and I was so shocked I almost swallowed my tongue. My state of mind wasn’t at all suitable for accepting the invitation; I politely thanked her and left. However, after walking a few steps, I knocked on the elderly lady’s door again to ask a question that came to mind, though I don’t remember what it was now.

She didn’t know the answer to my question, but she said: “You didn’t want to have tea with me, but please wait here a moment, there’s something I want to show you…” She had surprised me again. I waited curiously. Shortly after, she appeared with a small pot containing a single newly bloomed flower. “I’ve been taking great care of this plant for months. It finally bloomed today. Unfortunately, I have no one to share my joy with. That’s why I wanted to show this to you…” she said. I was shaken. As I would mention in an article I wrote for the German newspaper Die Zeit about “what being European means to me,” this incident told me that loneliness among the elderly was a serious problem in Sweden. From my perspective, however, it was a sign that things would go well for me in Sweden.

## Associate Professor Melander and his unforgettable wife

There was no chance of seeing Melander until the beginning of the week. Nothing was disturbing me at the hotel where I was staying. I had relaxed a bit. On Saturday, I took the train to Malmö. Before exploring the city, I went straight to the post office and mailed the fake passport and identity card I had used to the address in Beirut where my elder brother wanted them sent so they could be returned to their owner. A great weight had been lifted from my shoulders. The following Sunday, I killed time wandering around Lund. The beauty of the Swedish girls I encountered on the streets was simply dazzling. Exchanging a few words with one of them at a café had done me good.

Early Monday morning, I grabbed the phone. Melander immediately invited me to his home and welcomed me very warmly. He knew I was coming. (Apparently, the Czech judge in Strasbourg had informed him.) He introduced me to his wife, who had Elizabeth Taylor’s complexion and eye color, but was perhaps even more beautiful than her. They served coffee and cake and listened to my troubles. Melander said in summary: Getting asylum from Sweden won’t be a problem for you. If you wish, you can apply right here. Finding an opportunity to do a doctorate at Lund University won’t be difficult either. But “I think you would prefer to drown in the ocean rather than in a lake…” Therefore, I recommend you go to Stockholm. You can be sure I will follow up on your asylum application.

Yes, I also thought it would be wiser to go to Stockholm and that I could find broader opportunities there. I thanked the Melanders warmly, left, and that night of October 30th, I departed for Stockholm by train. As soon as I arrived in the city in the morning, following Melander’s directions, I went to the Police Headquarters building located in Kungsholmen, within walking distance of the station. Young and beautiful girls were handling applications at the reception. I approached the most beautiful one and said directly that I wanted to seek asylum in Sweden. She didn’t seem to have encountered an extraordinary request at all; she directly asked for my passport. When I said I didn’t have a passport, she said without any surprise, “please wait a moment.” Shortly after, 2-3 police officers came, took me to one of the upper floors; there they took almost all my belongings and locked me in a room, paying no attention to my insistent requests to call my lawyer (meaning Melander).

“Everyone must answer for the crimes they commit”

In the room where I was placed, a young man who appeared to have passed out from alcohol or drugs was lying on a bed on the floor. Then the young man’s lawyer or visitor came, and they talked about something. The man didn’t respond at all to my request for help in contacting my lawyer. After a while, a police officer came and took me to a room on a lower floor. A white-haired, stern-looking, rather heavy commissioner interrogated me. When I said I wanted political asylum, he said, “Everyone must answer for the crimes they commit,” and added, “We don’t need people coming to Sweden to work either.” When I said I hadn’t come to work but was seeking political asylum, he said, “I served in Cyprus, I know what liars the Turks are…” (This would be the first and last ill treatment I would encounter in Sweden.) My soul darkened. I spent that night in detention almost without sleeping, fearing I would be deported to Turkey the next day. That was the impression the commissioner had given.

But the opposite happened. Early in the morning, police officers came; they ignored me as I walked toward them saying “I want to speak with my lawyer,” told me in English that I was being released following instructions from the State Immigration Office (Invandrarverket); they returned my belongings and just let me out onto the street. I was flying with joy… I was very happy, but what would I do now, how would I find shelter, how would I feed myself?! I thought: If I were in Turkey, I would go to the student association at the university and ask for help. That’s what I did. I found the address of Stockholm University Student Association (Stockholm Universitets Studentkar) in the phone book. At the association’s reception sat a blonde girl who again struck me as stunningly beautiful. When I explained my situation, she told me I had come to the wrong place, wrote down the address of the nearest “social bureau” (a name I was hearing for the first time) on a piece of paper, and explained how I could get there by metro. I had now learned to use the metro and was able to get help from people in finding addresses. Were Swedes good people, or was my good English helping? Both seemed possible.

I found the address at Medborgarplatsen; I explained my situation to an elderly female clerk. She wanted to see my passport, and when I said I didn’t have one, she wasn’t surprised at all. After immediately calling the Police Headquarters and getting information about me, she said I would receive a certain amount of financial assistance each month until my asylum application was concluded, and that she could find me a place to stay if I wanted. I accepted, flying with joy. Before I left, she reminded me that I needed to go to the Police Headquarters twice a week to sign in.

## Parkgatan 20

I went to the address Parkgatan 20, near Friedhemsplan metro station. An elderly Swedish couple, Mr. and Mrs. Erik Öhman, were renting out a furnished room in their apartment. After listing one by one the conditions I needed to follow while using the room in their fluent English, they left me alone. I sensed this would be a temporary solution. I can’t forget the nightmare I had the first night I stayed there: I was in Istanbul. I was surrounded by police in the house where I was hiding. I woke up in a sweat… When I looked out the window and saw the trees in the park in front of the house, I remembered I was in Stockholm. This would be the first and last nightmare I would have in Sweden.

On one of the days I went to sign at the Police Headquarters, they informed me that I needed to be there for an official interrogation on November 6th at 2 PM. I went there on the given day and time. I was taken into a room. The police commissioner who came to interrogate me said, “By law, we have to interrogate you. I will ask ten questions. You are free to answer them or not. You know English, but by law, I must have a Turkish interpreter with me. If you need, you can ask for his help,” and introduced the Turkish university student Doğan Tüney who was with him.

He was extremely polite. I gave detailed answers to all his questions except one. When I said I wouldn’t answer the question about how and with whose help I escaped from Turkey, the commissioner said, “If I were in your place, I wouldn’t answer this question either.” I would later run into this commissioner in Stockholm city center and we would greet each other. I would become friends with the interpreter Doğan Tüney, who had confined himself to listening to the interrogation. A few weeks after this interrogation, my asylum application was accepted; the obligation to go to the police station was lifted. I received the Swedish Alien’s Passport that I would use as identification from then on from the State Immigration Office. This passport allowed me to travel without a visa to many Western European countries. I wasn’t a Swedish citizen, but now I had a proper Swedish passport in my pocket. I now felt completely safe.

## Tomas Hammar

Doğan Tüney was a political science student at Stockholm University. When I asked him who could help me pursue a doctorate at Stockholm University, he unhesitatingly gave me the name of Associate Professor Tomas Hammar and wrote his phone number on a piece of paper. How valuable Doğan’s recommendation would be would soon become apparent. The next morning, I called Hammar; I explained my situation. He said he would be waiting for me on November 10th at 2 PM in his office on the 8th floor of Building A at the university’s Frescati campus. What was happening?!.. I could only describe my experiences in Sweden as the English say, “Too good to be true.”

I had a long meeting with Hammar. I told him that I was a graduate of Ankara University Faculty of Political Science; that I had passed the doctoral qualifying exam there and reached the thesis stage, but when I started being sought by the military regime that seized power in 1971 due to my articles published in leftist magazines, I had to flee the country and sought refuge in Sweden. (I wouldn’t mention to anyone in Sweden for many years, including Tomas, that I had joined the Palestinian Resistance Movement. I was concerned—perhaps completely unnecessarily—that this could have consequences against me.)

The proposal Hammar made that very day was unbelievable: A major research project on the political values and behaviors of immigrants living in Stockholm was being prepared at the Political Science Department of Stockholm University. The project, called “Political Resocialisation of Immigrants” (PRI for short), envisioned conducting a comprehensive field study on the variables affecting immigrants’ adaptation to Sweden’s political culture. Since the government was preparing to grant immigrants voting rights in local elections, the research, expected to be financed by the Central Bank, was important not only academically but also politically.

It had been decided that the research would cover Finns and Yugoslavs as the largest immigrant groups, as well as Poles who consisted entirely of political refugees. He said they were debating whether to include Turks or Greeks, who mostly consisted of economic migrants, and if I agreed to join the research team, the decision would be made in favor of Turks. In that case, I could be admitted to the doctoral program “through the back door” without taking the highly competitive entrance exam. The expected funding from the Central Bank needed to come through for the research to begin. Therefore, I had time to decide.

I simply couldn’t believe that such a proposal was being made to me as soon as we met, trusting only what I told about who I was and my education, my word, without any documentary evidence in my hands. Had I come to paradise on earth??!! I was facing an offer I couldn’t refuse. Was the happy future heralded by the flower that had bloomed that very day at the elderly lady’s home in Lund coming true?

There was some hesitation in me regarding the offer I received. Since I generally tended toward theoretical work, the idea of undertaking empirical research based on interviews didn’t seem very appealing. Additionally, I was being asked to write an undergraduate thesis to be able to work on the research.

Due to my hesitations, during the months when the project was expected to start, I did consider studying Sinology, that is, Chinese culture and history, also utilizing my background (?!) on China. I even contacted the relevant department at Stockholm University for this purpose and learned that I could be accepted. Fortunately, on one hand the difficulties of learning Chinese scared me, and on the other hand, strong reservations expressed by both Fatma and my elder brother would dissuade me from embarking on this adventure.

While waiting for the PRI Project to start, I thought it would be very wise to learn the language of the country (where I might stay for years, perhaps until I died). The Swedish government provided free Swedish courses for immigrants. At that time, courses were organized by the Workers’ Trade Union Confederation (ABF), the Civil Servants’ Trade Union Confederation (TBV), and other public education organizations. Completely by coincidence, I enrolled in TBV’s Swedish courses.
