After attending full-time courses for about five months, I took the Swedish proficiency exam at Stockholm University in April 1973 and passed. My knowledge of English played a major role in this, as Swedish is a language close to English grammatically and close to German lexically.

## Üstünel and Abadan

At our second meeting in spring, Hammar asked if I knew the Turkish professor Besim Üstünel, who was a visiting faculty member in the economics department located just one floor above the political science department; he said things would be easier if I could get a letter from him confirming I was a graduate of the Faculty of Political Science. I was very happy to hear this. Üstünel had been my professor. There was no way he wouldn’t know me, because I had served a quite eventful term as president of the student association at the Faculty of Political Science. I immediately went upstairs and knocked on Üstünel’s door. He recognized me immediately when he saw me and asked how I was. I explained that I would be doing a doctorate by working in a research group, but since I didn’t have my diploma with me, I needed a letter stating that I was a graduate of the Faculty of Political Science. He said he couldn’t provide such a letter without giving any reason. I was surprised.

It was apparent that he saw supporting a “Maoist” as dangerous. Honestly, I wasn’t expecting this. Still, I thanked him and left, and of course I never saw him again. When I explained what happened, Hammar was also surprised; he said he would discuss the matter with department head Prof. Elias Berg. Berg, who hadn’t even seen my face until that moment, unhesitatingly signed the letter confirming I was a graduate of Ankara University Faculty of Political Science. Thus my diploma problem was solved. I don’t think I need to say what this incident told me about the general quality of Swedish and Turkish academics. (Years later, when I returned to my homeland and started working at newspapers, I met Üstünel on various occasions. He was quite friendly. I didn’t see the need to tell him that Elias Berg, who didn’t know me at all, had signed the letter he had refused to sign.)

I have another memory that makes one think about the quality of Turkish academics; let me tell it since the occasion has come. I think it was late 1979, early 1980. I was about to finish my doctorate. Prof. Dr. Nermin Abadan-Unat had come to Stockholm to attend an international conference on migration and had met Hammar. When Hammar mentioned me, Mrs. Nermin had said I was one of her former and best students at the Faculty of Political Science and wanted to see me. So we met at a reception Hammar gave at his home. Mrs. Nermin asked how I was and said complimentary things about me. We parted amicably.

The quite strange part Hammar told me later: Some time afterward, they met at a migration conference in another European city. Tomas told Mrs. Nermin that although they wanted me to stay in Sweden and continue working in the department, I was insistent on returning to my homeland. He asked if, in that case, she could help me get into a university in Turkey. The answer he received was: “Şahin is known as a Maoist: Therefore, unfortunately, I cannot help him…” Upon my return to the homeland, I met Mrs. Nermin a few times but never let on that I knew about this answer. I never wrote about these memories on any occasion. When I shared it with him, Hasan Cemal was surprised; he insisted, “Let me write about it…” but I didn’t let him either. I’m recounting these memories here because they give a good idea about the intellectual class’s fear of the state in Turkey.

Coming to my first year in Stockholm: I was friends with Doğan Tüney, whom I had met during the police interrogation, for a while; through him I also met a very interesting person. This was Hans Von Frankenstein, Doğan’s womanizing buddy. Hans was a real member of the world-famous Frankenstein family. He had lived in Istanbul, where his father was stationed, for a long time during his childhood and had gone to school there. It was quite interesting to meet, in Stockholm, a Frankenstein who spoke Turkish like a native and knew Turkey very well.

I was corresponding frequently with Fatma and my elder brother. I was very excited because I would be reunited with my wife and daughter sooner or later. I wanted them to come as soon as possible, because it had become clear that I would have a secure future in Sweden. I kept writing to Fatma insisting she come as soon as possible, that if necessary she could leave Elvan with her mother for a while. Fatma, partly thinking about the dangers that traveling with the Alpay surname might cause, and perhaps partly wanting to see whether I had “reformed,” was determined to divorce before coming to Stockholm and take custody of our daughter Elvan, who was only 6 years old.

## Letter from Fatma

In one of her first letters after I informed her that an opportunity had arisen for me to work at the university, she said: “The news in your letter is wonderful. You can’t know how happy it made us. We feel relieved and I’m now looking at our future with hope… You know I’ll come to you but I think we shouldn’t rush. We’ve been patient for so long, being a bit more patient will be good for all of us. I find it more appropriate to come without causing trouble. We waited 18 months; waiting 4-5 more months won’t matter. I didn’t like the idea of leaving Elvan either. If I leave her, she’ll be devastated… Besides, my mother won’t accept it. I can’t trust her either. Also, you know they won’t give me a passport… it would cause us trouble. The only thing left for me to do is divorce. I know you don’t want us to separate. It scares you, doesn’t it? That’s why you’re racking your brain and suggesting other ways… You’re so sweet and amazing. I love you, don’t worry, that’s why I can’t break away from you, haven’t you realized yet? Stay faithful to me, I want you.” (22.11.1972)

I’m copying here some excerpts from her subsequent letters reflecting her unique personality, without changing a letter: “Your loneliness makes me very sad. I can imagine what state you’re in… You must find a solution as soon as possible… You must do something until we come. I believe you’ve imposed certain prohibitions on yourself. You must lift these prohibitions. Even if you don’t feel like it, make friends with a girl. You can establish such a relationship as soon as possible. What’s important for me is you. I want you to stay healthy. You’re making even small matters into problems. These may not last either. You can be angry at me for everything I’ve written. But I don’t want you to be upset and get caught up in new thoughts about me… If you think I want you to make me do what you want to do yourself, you’ll make me very sad. Because I know you, I have to write these things too. Nothing and no one can change your love for me anymore. I believe in you. I want you to believe in me too. Nothing can shake my faith in your love and affection. The rest doesn’t matter. You are mine… The decision about the work you’ll do and the field you want to work in is yours. Whatever you want, whichever you find beneficial, make your decision.” (March 2, 1973)

In another letter she said: “Apparently you’ve made everything dependent on my coming. I write in every letter that I’ll come to you. You must believe me… But I can’t leave Elvan… The child isn’t happy like everyone else’s child. There’s a big void in her life. Even though she doesn’t want to show it, I’d have to be stupid not to understand. I can’t describe her uneasiness to you… She cries every time I leave the house and says don’t go. Every time I leave, she thinks I won’t come back and is scared… I can’t be separated from Avoş [her pet name for Elvan] even for a few months. I have to think more about my child. I know there are a few possibilities to bring her to us. But I don’t act on possibilities. Especially in this environment… I don’t want to write more about this. And I don’t want you to say ‘leave Elvan and come’ in every letter.

I’m not unaware of the state of your love for me. Yours, as you write, has ceased to be love and has become an obsession, a sickness… You take everything to extremes. I know you very well. A few years ago you also idolized certain people. I told you then too that what you were doing wasn’t right. After some time, for whatever reason, they would lose their greatness in your eyes and fall to zero. That’s the kind of man you are—so passionate, with a rich inner world, and also a bit inconsistent…

You’ve probably made me the sole purpose of your life these days. I would have wanted to always be the same thing for you. Then you would have been the same thing for me too… I don’t forget what you said to me in front of your friends. (In the days leading up to March 12th, I had said “If the revolutionary struggle requires it, I’ll leave you” and I had done just that…) When you set aside your feelings, what you said showed how honest you are. None of your friends could be as honest as you…

I want to spend my life with you, and very happily too. I can’t live with anyone else but you. I’ve compared you with many people… I find you superior to all of them. You always won. (Don’t get spoiled please.) I can’t know a second person with your qualities. Because there isn’t one. I accepted most of what you did to me in the old days as childishness. I believe the same things won’t happen again. The fact that your ideas have changed while your essence hasn’t is enough for me to believe in you. I don’t want your essence to change. I love and appreciate your human side (because it’s so strong).

Please don’t forget what I want from you. The first and most important of these is to love living life. And enjoy living. Life is very beautiful. For us, it will be even more beautiful from now on. I love living very much. I’m very attached to life. You should love it even more. Because you will give me pleasure. In return, I will make you love life too… If you love life, you’ll find many things to love, and thus you’ll love me normally too. You know me. I’m a normal person. I have no superior qualities. I think, what do I have to be loved this much? Then I say, since my husband loves me that way, I must have superior qualities. For this reason, I’m afraid of developing a complex. I see myself as superior to everyone. It’s not a good thing of course. So you see, my love, thanks to you, I’ve already started to get complexes. Will you get rid of them?… You don’t find me silly, do you?“ (March 29, 1973)

The divorce drags on

Fatma would do what she set her mind to. But as the divorce dragged on, her morale was deteriorating: “The lawyer said we’ll get a decision in September. I’m agreeable to that too. I’m afraid of it dragging on even more. I received your letter, which says”come” from beginning to end. How many times have I written to you, my love. I can’t leave my daughter and come. I’m sorry, but I can’t think of being separated from her (unless God separates us). You seem to forget that I’m a mother. Motherhood and fatherhood are not the same. She’s the creature I gave life to… My priority is my daughter… Maybe I’m upsetting you but you need to appreciate me too. She’s very scared that I’ll leave her… Let’s put these aside. Who could she stay with? The mothers are getting old. You know your mother’s attitude already. And mine now needs to be taken care of… I don’t want to write these things again… I’m tired of hearing the same things and writing the same things. Besides, I’m not like I used to be. If they had told me I would become like this, I wouldn’t have believed it. My health isn’t good, nerves are terrible. In short, my situation is awful… my morale is zero too. I’m bored, bored, bored… How much longer will I have to swallow things. You’ve all ruined me as a family. And I was very patient… This is quite an unpleasant letter but I’m determined to show myself as I am. I have nothing left to give for morale. I need it now. I wish you patience and good luck.” (19.06.73)

What she wrote was frightening me. Was I losing her? Her letter a month later increased my worries even more: “Coming to your doctorate issue; you may have given up. You say you can’t give another year. You want to learn a new language and direct your studies that way. You’ve reached 30. Make your own decisions. I’m tired of making decisions… I also want you to be someone who makes the right decision for me. I’m tired of thinking. I don’t want to think about anything. Besides, your decision didn’t surprise me. You are you. No matter how much you want to change, it means you can only go so far. I don’t have much to say about this. I also can’t say I like it. But I’ll still say do what you want. What’s important is that you work on something you feel passionate about. I wish you healthy good days. I’ll write when I find the opportunity.” (14.07.1973)

Another three months had to pass, and the divorce case had to be concluded, before the letter that relieved my worries arrived: “My dear love, I don’t understand where you got the idea that you lost me… You still haven’t understood that I love you, apparently. If I didn’t love you, I wouldn’t have done any of the things I did, you know. You really screwed me over. Since I’m still thinking of coming, there must be some reasons, right, my darling. If I had thought of leaving you, I would have started building another life for myself long ago… I can’t think of someone else until living with you becomes impossible. I miss you. My love who is both mature and still a child. You’re a sweet man. You’re not an easy type to find. That’s why I didn’t even see the need to look. I want to come as soon as possible now. I’ll take care of the passport issue after the elections. (If they don’t give it, I’ll be devastated.) I don’t even want to think of such a possibility.

I want to set out at the end of November. Some days I’m full of joy, some days I walk around with a long face. Damn this goiter, it’s causing me a lot of trouble. You’ll give me a beautiful life, won’t you. The past years have worn me out. Your life-filled wife isn’t like she used to be anymore. I don’t want the desires inside me to be destroyed. I’m fighting my unwillingness toward life. I want to enjoy everything like before, to be joyful, to truly live. I love living very much. I want to not care about anything. I believe I’ll gain these by your side… If I can’t gain them, then I’ll be destroyed, my love. I believe in you. I want our life to continue like the early days of our marriage. You’ll give me such a life, won’t you? We have the right to be happy now. We’ve suffered so much, my love.

I went to the doctor for the goiter. I learned that it’s not very serious and can pass quickly with treatment… I’ve dropped to 50 kg. I’m like a model but my nerves are terrible. The lines on my face have increased. But don’t worry, I’m beautiful. I’m still a conceited person. What do you say. I’m right, aren’t I?.. So much time has passed that even if I had no special qualities, I must seem very pleasant to you. When will you become a doctor? You know I won’t be a worker’s wife… My sweet love, you’re no longer my husband. Isn’t that funny. Get ready to struggle with me. I’ll make you suffer a lot. My anger is at its peak by the way… Your daughter and I kiss you thousands of times. (She kisses your photos secretly.)“ (09.10.1973)

## Letters from my elder brother

The letters from my elder brother were quite upsetting to me. (His story, which is also reflected in these letters, doesn’t fit into my story. I will write his story separately.) Shortly after I left the country, they had a car accident, fortunately no one was hurt. He wasn’t happy with his life at all. He was having financial difficulties. As if that weren’t enough, the person from whom he had bought the passport for me kept asking him for money. In one of his first letters to Strasbourg, he wrote: “Oktay has worn me out. I have no patience left. I want to end my relationship with him as soon as possible. The cost to me has come to twice the amount we committed, and not only have I received no financial help from anyone, but I’ve been in a very difficult situation due to the financial burdens caused by the accident afterward.” (28.10.1972)

Oktay wouldn’t leave him alone: “It was the last days of April. Oktay came to me. He said he would go to Germany as a worker. The financial side of the affair came to about 4 thousand lira. Since he had no money, I had to provide this too. I had to find 4 thousand lira. I had only been at the job for three days. I asked the boss, got an advance, and the passenger flew on May 14th. With all his sins, he was a good kid… I don’t begrudge him a thing…” (24.05.1973) Oktay said in the letter he sent him from Germany: “I finally came to Germany and started working… for once I wanted to see you without asking anything of you, but it wasn’t meant to be… I thank you again and again for your sacrifices in every way…”

In almost every letter, I expressed my debt of gratitude to him, which I could never repay: “At a moment when everyone, everyone had given up hope on me and abandoned me to my fate, if I hadn’t had a gem of a brother like you, everything would have been over for me. If a rebirth was possible for me, I owe it entirely to you.” His response was: “I was proud of you throughout my life. Because I found in you everything I felt I lacked in myself… I was proud even of your political ideas. Perhaps I wasn’t a man of that struggle. Life’s winds had steered me in another direction. Sometimes I had been against you too perhaps. The reason was the environment. They were pushing me to talk like that. Though I didn’t want to, I was saying the things they themselves couldn’t say—they were putting the words in my mouth… I simply acted as an elder brother to a brother whose very existence made me proud. If I couldn’t have shown it, I would never have forgiven myself for the rest of my life… If something had gone wrong and I had been caught, it would have caused the loss of many things I valued in my life. But rest assured I would never have felt regret.” (07.04.1973)

I also wrote: “The pain of the burdens I’ve placed on your back, both spiritually and materially, weighs on me. And the fact that I can’t do anything to help you other than sit and express my distress in letters crushes me spiritually, crushes me… Believe me, the guilt I feel often makes me say this: The water jug should have broken on its way to the water. What did this wretched self of mine, this selfishness, have that was worth so much trouble?.. The solution was always an honorable death that I longed for but never happened. Perhaps the closing of this file would have been better for all of us, all of us. You’ll say, it’s easy to say these things now. True… I apologize for everything I put you through. Despite everything, forgive me. I didn’t want to rub salt in the wounds of the various troubles you’ve encountered in life. But it’s easy to say these things now. Forgive me.” (13.06.1973)

He was changing jobs frequently in an effort to improve his financial situation. At the same time, he was expressing his desire to emigrate to Sweden if it were possible. But with my warnings about the unfavorable conditions, he was aware of how difficult this would be. In one of his letters, he said, “When I started thinking very seriously about coming to Sweden to work, I realized I couldn’t do it…” He finally fulfilled his desire to come to Stockholm and see me during a trip to England for the company he worked for, between November 2-5, 1973. Seeing me having rebuilt my life pleased him greatly. And perhaps he envied it.

What he wrote upon returning to Istanbul reflected his disappointments about his own life: “You write that you saw me in a very good mood in Stockholm. True. I was. But it was temporary. I was happy. I had come to see you for three, even 2.5 days… Not to harass you by telling my depressions… I tried to appear as I should be… For several years now, deep down I haven’t been the Acar seen from the outside. I know the reasons for this very well. There was an Acar in my ideal, my friend. No matter what I did, I couldn’t become that Acar. Various incidents, coincidences, impossibilities, and mistakes I sincerely made thinking they were right at the time. And mistakes… They distanced me so much from that ideal Acar that, since it’s no longer possible to go back and start over, I have to continue the fight as a type I never wanted to be. Helplessness. The more one struggles, the more one is dragged into the swamp… Your wife, your siblings, worst of all even your children can’t know you well… for a thinking person like me, it’s a disgrace… I’ve entered such a cycle that I can’t turn back… Actually, I don’t know how to turn back. A new year is coming… it would have been good to start life in another country and build it as I wanted again. But even dreaming of it is forbidden to me.”

Karin and Gunnar

Fatma’s divorce, getting passports, and coming to Sweden would take until January 1974. Among the noteworthy things that happened to me until she came were the following. My sister-in-law Ayla sent me a letter with the addresses and phone numbers of their Swedish acquaintances Karin and Gunnar, and informed them that I would call them. Partly so as not to embarrass my sister-in-law, I called Karin and went to visit their home in the far south of Stockholm. Karin and Gunnar were a couple in their 70s. They had been in Turkey as journalists to follow Ecevit’s election campaign and had somehow met my sister-in-law in the meantime. They received me very warmly. They were good people. Their twin children, daughter Pia and son Pier, were still of high school age. It was obvious they had become parents quite late. (Gunnar would commit suicide a few years later, unable to bear the cancer pains.) Karin helped me find a more suitable place to stay. Meanwhile (even though she knew I was married with a child), she wanted me to befriend her daughter Pia. I wasn’t very keen on this idea.

The place Karin found for me by looking at newspaper ads was an address in the Tensta-Rinkeby area, densely populated by immigrants from Turkey and quite far from the city center. A young Polish woman in her 30s, whose name I don’t remember, was renting out a small independent unit consisting of one room and a bathroom-toilet across from her own apartment. Tensta didn’t have a metro in those years; one commuted by bus. I had started attending Swedish courses. Because I was somewhat bothered by the distance of the house and somewhat by my landlady’s expectations of companionship, I asked Karin to find me a different place.

## Östermalmstorg

The new place she found was this time right in the heart of the city, at Jungfrugatan 5 in Östermalmstorg, one of the most prestigious neighborhoods. Since the address was very attractive, I immediately called the landlord and went to visit. A middle-aged Swedish woman named Ulla was working as a night secretary at the country’s best-selling newspaper Dagens Nyheter. She had started living separately from her husband and needed someone who could stay at night with her young son and daughter, who attended elementary school. She wasn’t asking for rent for the room I would stay in. She must have liked me, because she said, “Many people applied, but if you want, I can give you the room.”

I had now started living in the heart of the city. However, as days passed, it became clear that this arrangement wouldn’t work either. Doing a kind of babysitting for the children was difficult. Ulla was introducing me to her drunk husband as if I were her boyfriend. Then one night she opened my door and jumped on me naked. I barely escaped. I had to find a new place as soon as possible. I met two Greeks in the Swedish courses. One of them, Yorgo, who sat right next to me, one day addressed me in Turkish after avoiding it for a long time. He had learned village Turkish from his mother, who was a Karamanlı / one of the Karamanlides (subjected to forced migration to Greece under the 1923 population exchange agreement; Turkish in mother tongue, Greek Orthodox in faith).

I quickly became friends with the other Greek, Anestis (Kombokis). Anestis was around my age. He had aspirations of being a painter and would never give up on this aspiration. He was like-minded in many ways. He lived in an apartment near the police station in Kungsholmen with his Swedish girlfriend at the time, a nurse named Anna. (He would later marry two Swedish women and divorce the second one, who gave him three children.) Through him, I met many Greeks. The friendship I established with Kostas Ladopulos, his wife Margareta Mellberg whose father was Swedish and mother was Greek, his brother Dimitris, and their circle confirmed the observation that Turks become friends with Greeks abroad.

## Fred Krimgold

I had interesting teachers in the Swedish courses. The first, Emma, was an extremely pleasant, intelligent, cultured, middle-aged woman. She had mixed-race children from her Black Sierra Leonean husband. My Swedish teacher after Emma, with whom I had established good dialogue, was even more interesting: Anna, who was only in her twenties, came to me during a coffee break on one of the very first days of the course and said that her American friend named Fred had been in the same class with a Turk named Halil Berktay at Yale University. She asked if I knew Berktay… The world was truly small. Shortly after, Anna introduced me to Fred (Krimgold). Fred was an architect specializing in disaster engineering. He was doing his doctorate at Stockholm Technical University (Tekniska Högskolan) and was interested in disaster problems in Turkey. He lived in the old town, Gamla Stan, in a historic building near the Slussen bridge (Skeppsbron, No. 46). As soon as we met, he immediately offered to rent me a room in his apartment. I suspected that behind the warmth shown at the time by Fred, who is still my friend, lay his aim of using Anna’s interest in me to get closer to her. Fred achieved his desire a few years later and managed to marry Anna; although their marriage didn’t last long.

From May 1973, I rented one of the rooms in Fred’s apartment. The greatest benefit of meeting Fred would be meeting through him (the late) architect Dinç Gürs and his Finland-Swedish wife Bambi (Barbro), who would be our lifelong friends. (There is a Swedish minority in Finland that makes up about 5 percent of the population. Swedish is one of the official languages.)

## Anna von Celsing

Anna had a very interesting identity. Her lineage went back to Gustaf von Celsing, one of Sweden’s first ambassadors to the Ottoman Empire in the 18th century, and his sons Gustaf and Ulric von Celsing. (Her father was also Sweden’s ambassador to Argentina at the time.) When the von Celsings returned from Istanbul, they placed the items they brought with them in their estate in the town of Biby, about 130 km southwest of Stockholm, on about a thousand dönüms (roughly 100 hectares) of land. Anna took me to Biby by car one weekend. The lower floor of the estate was full of the Celsings’ belongings. The decor evoking 18th century Istanbul was exciting. (As I learned later, when the Celsing family faced financial problems, they put the property up for sale in 2001. Various furniture and other items including 103 watercolor and oil paintings inside were first offered to the Turkish, then Swedish culture ministries. Unfortunately, when no positive response was received, it was sold to the Orientalist Museum in Doha, Qatar for 30 million dollars.)

That day Anna also took me to the historic Katrineholm castle near the Celsing estate, protected by the Swedish culture ministry, which housed many oil paintings related to the Ottoman Empire. The painting depicting the Ottoman dynasty tree was the one that stayed in my memory the most. What I saw that day was quite impressive for me, who knew nothing about the history of Sweden-Turkey relations other than Demirbaş Şarl (“Charles the Fixture,” as the Turks called Charles XII), who took refuge with the Ottomans and was “the Swedish king fed from the treasury.” When I went with Anna to visit her sister and the sister’s Austrian husband, who lived near Drottningholm, where the Swedish royal family’s summer palace is located, I had the opportunity to meet the world-famous sculptor İlhan Koman, who was living with his wife on a boat. He showed me around his sculpture studio that he had set up in a cave. His Swedish wife whom I met was quite drunk. Koman’s works, however, were admirable.

After taking classes at TBV for about five months from December 1972, I took the Swedish proficiency exam at Stockholm University in May 1973 and passed. I had started speaking Swedish haltingly. Since I didn’t want to continue living on social assistance, I applied to the employment office to work during the summer months. In April 1973, I started working at an ice cream factory owned by the Glasbolaget company in the Nacka district, not far from Slussen pier. I wrote to my elder brother, “I’ve finally joined the international working class! I get up at 4:30 in the morning, get on the bus at 4:48, start work around 5:35… When work ends, I’m limp as a rag…”

## Female urologist

Most of the factory workers consisted of young girls, mostly Finns. The relatively heavy work was handled by a small number of male workers from various countries. The work I did consisted of dipping ice cream-filled cones placed on a metal tray coming out of a giant refrigerator into chocolate sauce. The cold air that the refrigerator blew toward my lower body had a price. When I started having difficulty urinating, I had to go to the hospital. They referred me to a female urologist. In quite an embarrassed state, I explained my problem. She asked me to lie on the examination table and expose my penis. After examining it thoroughly, she determined that my penis had caught cold and prescribed medicines that made me recover quickly. I was quite embarrassed while the urologist, who was a very beautiful woman, held my penis and examined it. I was getting to know another aspect of Swedish culture that didn’t recognize the boundaries I was used to from my homeland.

In the fall of 1973, I started working on the pilot project of the PRI research. I started commuting by train a few days a week to the city of Södertalje, about 30 km southwest of Stockholm. There I interviewed about 50 randomly selected citizens of Turkey registered as residents there. What was surprising was that most of them were Assyrians from Mardin and Midyat. Many said they had fled to Sweden not from the military regime but from Kurdish oppression, and they had no complaints about the military. On this occasion, I was learning an aspect of Turkey I didn’t know, that there was a dense Assyrian population in the Southeast, and that some Kurds had driven a significant portion of them out of the region through various forms of pressure. (I would later learn that Assyrians fleeing from Turkey had also taken refuge in other European countries, especially Germany.)

In the fall of 1973, Dinç Gürs offered to hand over to me the Turkish courses he was giving at TBV. Of course, I accepted with pleasure and continued this work for several terms. I could now mainly teach the lessons in Swedish, but since all the students knew English, I was using a Turkish textbook prepared in England and could resort to English when necessary. We held the courses in a high school building in the evening hours. The walls of the classroom I used were decorated with, among other pictures, photographs showing in what ways women’s genitals could be shaved. I was getting to know yet another aspect of Swedish culture.

I met interesting people in my Turkish courses. One of my students, most of whom consisted of Swedish women married to or friends with Turks, was Ann-Marie, wife of the famous photographer Lütfü Özkök. A Finn married to a Turkish lady and a Hungarian-born architect (Adrian) who came to the courses out of admiration for the musicality of Turkish were among the others who stayed in my mind. But the one who impressed me most among the students was definitely Madeleine. One evening when she opened the door and entered just as the lesson was about to start, the attention of all 15-20 people in the class focused on her. A strikingly beautiful woman with her white skin, green eyes, blonde hair, tall stature, elegant black outfit, and graceful posture—I can say she was the most beautiful woman I saw in Sweden.

## Dinç and Saygun

At the end of courses that lasted about twelve weeks, it was customary for the teacher to have a farewell dinner with attending students and their spouses. I was quite surprised when Madeleine showed up at the dinner at the end of that term with her Kurdish architect husband, who barely came up to her shoulder and was far from handsome. I learned at that dinner that they had been married for a long time and had three sons. When I learned during a Stockholm visit after returning to Turkey that Madeleine had suddenly left her husband and children and settled in America with her young Swedish lover, I honestly wasn’t too surprised. The fact that almost all of the Turks or Greeks I knew who were married to Swedish women, with one or two exceptions, eventually divorced their spouses gave me an idea about the institution of marriage in Sweden.

Dinç had opened a clothing store near Odenplan, one of Stockholm’s main squares. Besides the Turkish courses at TBV, he had also handed over to me the job of teaching mother tongue classes to children of immigrants from Turkey. In those years, the Swedish administration was committed to the ideal of a multicultural society; in this context, immigrant children were granted the right to take mother tongue lessons. (Literacy lessons were also given to immigrant women from Turkey who needed them.) My most striking memory from the mother tongue teaching I conducted for a few months was this: When I realized one of my students was Kurdish, I asked his father, whom I had the opportunity to meet, why he enrolled his son in Turkish rather than Kurdish mother tongue lessons. His answer was simple: “We’re thinking of returning to Turkey in a few years. When we return, Turkish, not Kurdish, will be useful for his work…” I know that in the following years, for the vast majority of immigrants from Turkey regardless of their origin, the dreams of returning to the homeland were not realized; and that the number of families who wanted their children to receive mother tongue education steadily declined.

Thanks to Dinç, I also met Saygun Kuyumcu, who would become one of my lifelong friends. Saygun’s story is interesting enough to briefly mention here. He had completed his secondary education in Egypt, where his mother’s second husband was stationed (at Turkey’s Alexandria consulate), and learned Arabic well. He later settled in Istanbul and started studying at Robert College, but finished high school (like all unruly students) at Yeni Kolej. Later, in Sweden, where his path somehow led him, he married Eija, a Finn, and they had two children.

When I met Saygun, he was teaching mother tongue and physical education to Turkish children at a high school in Tensta-Rinkeby. Toward the end of the 1970s, even before we did, he and his wife decided to take the children and return to Turkey. However, due to the increasing violence in the country, they regretted it two years later and returned to Stockholm. In 1979, I was looking for a rental house in Istanbul. Saygun told me to talk to his late mother Mrs. Nermin, and if I could convince her, she could rent us her apartment in Akatlar. We were able to rent Mrs. Nermin’s apartment only after her death in 1985, unfortunately, and we lived there for exactly 33 years until my Fatma’s death in 2018; our children grew up there. To this day, I’m amazed at how Saygun, one of my closest friends (originally Circassian), can still be so Turkish and equally Swedish. He is like the embodiment of multi-identity/multiculturalism.

Through one of my students in the TBV courses, I also met Zeynel Çelikel, who would become one of my closest friends in life. Years later, Zeynel divorced his Swedish wife and returned to Turkey; first he settled in Datça, then in Keremköy near Ayvalık… I will tell his quite dramatic story in “Human Landscapes from My Life,” which I plan to write if I live long enough.

## Stockholm

My time in Sweden was approaching one year, and my impressions were accumulating. How right I was to come to Stockholm. Stockholm was a very orderly city with wonderful nature, intertwined with forests and the sea. It lay on the shore of an archipelago of some 22 thousand islands and islets. Swedes lived in prosperity. They owed this prosperity to the Social Democratic Party, which had been in power since 1932. The social democrats had achieved a good synthesis of liberal economy and democracy. Step by step, my respect for Sweden and Swedes was increasing.

Swedes were a highly educated society. Income distribution was quite fair. The strong position of women in society was very impressive for someone like me coming from Turkey. The equality in male-female relations, sexual freedom, and the prevalence of cohabitation instead of marriage quite surprised me. The Protestant Swedish Church was under state control, but there was complete freedom of belief. Unfortunately, I would learn too late that everyone, including immigrants, had to pay church tax (unless they objected). The separation of church and state, promised by the Social Democrats, would only happen in 2000. Yes, Swedes were quite cold people, but they were very honest and polite. The prevalence of suicides, despite how happy they seemed, was ironic. One reason for this could be the harshness, length, and darkness of winters; but the rapid urbanization experienced in the 20th century had also led to social isolation, people becoming distant from each other, and alienation.

The process of radical change in the paradigm (the macro theory) I carried in my mind for trying to understand the world had begun. This process continued until the late 1970s. In my first years in Sweden, I was aware that “real socialism,” that is, “scientific socialism” as practiced in the world, had major problems, but I thought these stemmed more from implementation issues. Perhaps the best witness to this is the late architect Oğuz Öztuzcu, whom I met in Stockholm (again through Dinç) and who would become one of my lifelong friends. I had met him and his wife at the time, Duygu, shortly before Fatma came to Stockholm. As Oğuz often reminded me, in the first days after we met in 1973, I would say that I was a communist and that I believed the world revolution would happen someday. I remember that we had quite a lot of exchange of ideas about Marxism and real socialism with Ishtiaq Ahmed from Lahore (Pakistan) and Gautam Navlakha from Mumbai (India), whom I met at the university. (Their stories will certainly be the subject of “Human Landscapes from My Life” that I plan to write.)

## I find Sabetay and Cengiz

In October 1973, Sabetay’s response to the letter I sent after finally learning his Paris address had arrived. He described his incredible encounter with Cengiz in Paris like this: “I had no contact with any Turks until I ran into Zekeriya with my eyes wide open in amazement at a cafe I frequented. You can imagine what state of mind I was in…” About his political views, he also wrote: “I haven’t lost my belief in the revolution for a moment. But I’m not ready to enter a long, complex struggle that requires endurance. Even the effort I need to show to create the conditions seems daunting to me, and more than anything, after what we experienced in the past, I’m afraid of taking wrong steps that will be repeated every day…” These lines well reflected our common thoughts and feelings of those days. Sabetay remained one of my closest friends in terms of our intellectual adventure.

I started corresponding with Cengiz. In his first letter, he said, “You can’t know how happy I was with your letter. Since we parted, I kept thinking with a bitter feeling whether we would ever meet again. For more than a year, I’ve been sending various news to the homeland trying to find you” (24.09.1973). His second letter ended like this: “Remember that you’re not alone, that there’s a group of people who love you, and among them is Zek, who loves you from the heart, who has known you as his most dear, most beloved comrade for two years, and who reserves a special place for you above everyone else.” (02.10.1973)

Cengiz’s letters had made me extremely happy. Contrary to what I feared, all the time that had passed and all the different experiences we lived through had not distanced us from each other, but on the contrary, had brought us closer. In one of his letters, he summarized well what we had been through: “My dear, one or two books, five or ten strikes, ten or fifteen demonstrations and hop, we found ourselves on the threshold of armed struggle! This Turkish revolutionary movement was just like the upstart who’s never seen anything before—honestly, looking at it now.” (22.10.1973) Our ideas would follow quite different paths over time, but Cengiz and I always remained very close friends.

I learned from Cengiz’s letters that we had been sentenced to death by the TİİKP (Revolutionary Workers’ and Peasants’ Party of Turkey) as turncoats who had betrayed the revolution. (Many years later, it would be possible to meet the person who was assigned to execute me and learn the story. Oğuz had joined the TİİKP ranks while doing his physics doctorate at Birmingham University in England on a state scholarship, and had abandoned the doctorate to become a full-time revolutionary. When he received the assignment, he tried to find me for a while, then gave up on it. He had decided to return to Turkey and was caught and imprisoned for a while. When I met him, he was living with his wife somewhere in the hills of İznik.) Cengiz, like me, had escaped execution: He had encountered the TİİKP member assigned to kill him in a house in Paris and had managed to convince him of the meaninglessness of this execution. Apparently, the execution sentences issued against us didn’t have much of a serious side.

The days of the Marxist paradigm in my mind were numbered, but it would still take another year or two for it to reach the point of collapse. Perhaps the final point of my communism would be when I stepped aside and stood in a moment of silence upon learning from a newspaper headline in the Stockholm metro in September 1976 that Mao Zedong had died.

In October 1973, when Fred had to vacate the apartment in Slussen, I moved to Anestis’s apartment at Hjarnegatan 2 in the Kungsholmen district. I must share an unforgettable memory from my days there: One night when I lay down to sleep, I heard such vulgar screams from the room directly above that it gave me the impression someone was being murdered. I woke Anestis in concern and said, “Anestis, I’m worried, I think they’re slaughtering a woman upstairs…” His reply was: “Don’t worry, my friend, that woman gets slaughtered every night…” I don’t remember ever laughing so much at my own naivety.

## My hope for reunion

In September 1973, my hope of soon being reunited with my Fatma and my Elvan grew. My Fatma wrote in her letter informing me that the divorce case had concluded and she had obtained custody of Elvan: “Our case is over, my love. I got the decision too. You’re forbidden to marry for one year. But not me. Funny, isn’t it?.. Not many people know we got divorced. I don’t really tell anyone. It somehow feels shameful to me…” (26.09.1973)

However, she thought it would be risky to set off immediately after the divorce decision. After another two months passed, she applied for a passport in early December 1973. In her last letters before coming, she wrote: “I want to live without thinking about anything anymore. I’m tired, you know?.. I have a world of problems in my life. I don’t know how I’ll solve them. It’s best to just let everything take its course… I’m not closing up the apartment for now. The people I know here will probably take care of it while I’m there… My first attempt for the journey was to have my photograph taken. This week I’ll officially start the passport process… The other day Avoş asked me again when you’re coming. He won’t come, let me get you a new father, I said. I don’t want one, she said. I won’t call him father, she said. Then what will you call him, I asked. I’ll call him uncle, she said. Then she asked me, what will you tell my father if he comes. I’ll say I waited, he didn’t come, so I got someone else… Then I’ll go with my father, she said… Seeing she was getting really upset, I said don’t worry, I’ll take you to your father. My little one relaxed. The shameless thing also said she loves you more. How much she must miss you, right? Who knows what she thinks about you. I’m very curious about how you’re doing there. We have a very sweet daughter. And she’s getting more beautiful. It won’t be easy to hold her back. She’s an incredible feminine creature. She doesn’t resemble me at all… I’ll give you more definite news in my next letter. Hopefully it will turn out well. I don’t know what I’ll do if they refuse. I’m even afraid to think about it. May all the luck be ours…” (02.12.72) And finally: “I can give you the good news now. Today we got our passports. I’m letting you know immediately… I’ll come after New Year’s… I’m so happy, my life.” (20.12.73)

My excitement had reached its peak… I had been longing for my Elvan since April 1971, for my Fatma since July 1972. My struggle to bring my family back together was finally bearing fruit… I had made my preparations, and in early November, with Tomas’s help, I had rented one of the apartments in the Lappkarsberget (Lappis) housing complex in the university district of Frescati, available to teaching staff. The two-bedroom apartment with all modern comforts at Professorslingan 45/4 would be the Alpays’ first home in Stockholm, where they would stay until May 1975.

I was keeping my relationships in Stockholm limited to as few people as possible. Until I settled in Lappis, I didn’t have a phone of my own. The consequences of getting a phone were immediately apparent. One of the first days I was staying in Lappis, the phone rang; the voice on the other end said: “Şahin abi [elder brother, a respectful form of address], I’m İsmail, Hanife’s brother. How are you?..” I couldn’t collect myself at first. Who was this İsmail? He reminded me. He was a young fellow townsman from Ayvalık whom I hadn’t seen for many years. I had met his sister Hanife and İsmail in our youth when they worked for Ömer Madra’s grandmother, and I hadn’t seen them for a long time. He had been working as a deckhand on cargo ships for a while. He had heard from his sister Hanife that I was in Stockholm, and when his ship happened to stop in Stockholm, he had wanted to look me up right away. But how had he obtained my phone number? “I went to the central station, asked the first Turk I ran into. He pulled it right out and gave it to me…” can you believe it?! It turned out later: the person İsmail had run into was the husband of one of the Swedish students attending my Turkish courses.

Stockholm Central Station, like for all immigrants, is full of memories for me too. At one point, I did freelance interpreting work for extra income. I would usually meet the people from Turkey I was going to help at the “meeting point” right in the middle of the station, and from there we would head to wherever we needed to go. Once, as soon as I entered through the station door, the compatriot I was going to interpret for stopped me, saying “Hello, Şahin Bey…” In astonishment, I asked how he had recognized me immediately. His answer was, “I recognized you by your walk, abi…” Apparently, I had no chance of hiding my Turkishness.

## The day I had dreamed of

As I waited to greet Fatma and Elvan at Arlanda Airport on January 15, 1974, my heart felt like it would stop from excitement. The day I had dreamed of had finally come. I hadn’t seen my daughter for about 3 years, my wife for about 2 years. Finally, they came through passport control… First, I embraced Elvan. She had grown so much; to me, she was the most beautiful girl in the world… She was only 6 years old but extraordinarily mature. My beloved, now 30 years old, seemed even more elegant and more beautiful than ever. I cannot describe with what happiness I embraced them…

In our first weeks together, my Fatma seemed distracted and troubled. After about three years, as she began living with me again in a completely different environment, she must have had doubts about whether our relationship would work… There were things she wanted to discuss with me. It took a few months for us to talk through all these things and for her to conclude that our relationship could continue. Elvan’s happiness with her new life gradually played a role in convincing her to stay with me.

My little Elvan showed an incredible ability to adapt. One of the first things I did when renting the apartment was to secure a spot for Elvan at the nearest kindergarten. Just a few days after she arrived in Stockholm, I took her to the nursery she would now attend five days a week. They had said that at least for the first week, the mother or father would need to come with the child. Just a few minutes after meeting the caregivers and other children at the nursery, she came over and said, “You can go, dad…” which both surprised and delighted me greatly. The warmth of the nursery’s reassuring, motherly caregiver Else Marie played a big part in Elvan’s quick adaptation, but the main thing was my dear daughter’s extraordinary ability to adapt, which she would display throughout her life. Learning Swedish didn’t take long either. In the first days in front of the color television we had bought and started watching, Elvan would say “What’s he saying?.. What’s he saying?..” waiting for me to translate, but a few weeks later she started answering the phone in Swedish. One weekend, she answered those calling for me like this: “Pappa inte hemma, han stadar… / Dad’s not home, he went to clean…” I was proud of Elvan’s speed in learning Swedish.

About two months after they came to Stockholm, Fatma described my relationship with Elvan in a letter she wrote to my elder brother and sister-in-law: “Little Elvan has lost the concept of father in three years. Because she was very small before, the concept probably never took hold. For Elvan, Şahin is a friend named father… She loves him, scolds him, and argues with him. She sees herself as equal to her father. The funniest part is that both of them report their complaints to me. I often laugh because the situations seem so strange. I’m the authority at home. When coming here, I had decided to hand this responsibility over to Şahin, but it’s an impossible thing…”

She also reflected her impressions of Stockholm: “I really liked the location of the apartment and Stockholm. It’s especially good that where we live is comfortable for children. Having the nursery across from us makes things easy for Elvan… I stayed home for days from morning to evening and it was starting to get to me. Starting the Swedish courses was positive in this regard. I met people of various nationalities; I should add that most of them are funny types. For now, I’m both having fun and learning something at the courses. Yesterday we entered the third week since I started the course. As you can imagine, I still show no signs of speaking. My conversations with classmates in class are like Tarzan’s; a mix of Turkish, English, and Swedish. I laugh a lot at my words afterwards. Last night a young boy selling eggs and potatoes came to the door. If you had been with me and heard me bargaining, I would have been good material for you… When I tell Şahin, he laughs a lot at the states I get into. Everything here is comfortable and nice, but not having friends creates a very big void in my life. Although the people here are helpful, they are very foreign types to me. I like Stockholm but I don’t love it. I don’t know if I’ll be able to get used to it here. I’ll only be able to answer all these questions after a long time. It probably wouldn’t be right for me to speak definitively about such matters these days…

“Dear Acar, why are you thanking me? I wanted to come here. I thought of all three of us when making this decision. I can’t decide whether I did right or wrong. But this path seemed right to me… As for my health, it’s zero. I’m falling apart in every way. I don’t seem to have a healthy spot. I’ve had gastritis in my stomach for a long time. It’s probably going to turn into an ulcer soon. I haven’t started treatment yet. We’re waiting for the residence permit so we can get it done cheaply… I need to wake up at 7:00 tomorrow. One of my great pleasures was waking up late. Of course, I’ve been deprived of that since starting the courses. What would it matter if they started at 10:00 instead of 8:30!…” (19.03.1974)

As the days passed, Fatma, like Elvan, gradually began to adapt to the new environment. She was enjoying herself and having a good time at the Swedish lessons. As she met Turkish friends, she also began to embrace Stockholm. When summer came, our new life together fell into place and never experienced another upheaval.

Are you from inside or outside?

In June 1974, my nephew Ahmet, the son of my elder sister Sumru, who was attending university in Belgium, came to join us, taking advantage of the work permit and earning opportunity granted to foreign students in Sweden during the summer months. First, he worked as a waiter for a while at a cafe near the central station. When he addressed the Turkish young men he was serving in Turkish, they were surprised and asked: “Are you from inside or outside?..” The young people Ahmet encountered were from the Kulu district of Konya, like the majority of Turks living in Stockholm in those years, and they were actually asking: “Are you from Kulu or not?..” This anecdote of Ahmet’s was a clear expression of how Turks living in Stockholm at that time were divided into “Kulu people and others.”

Since the Turkish courses I was teaching had ended, schools had closed, and the Södertalje pilot research was completed, I had to find a new job. I never wanted to live on welfare from the social office. Together with Ahmet, we found a rather heavy but well-paying job; we started doing factory cleaning. On one of the days I wasn’t working, Ahmet was late leaving the factory when evening came and got locked inside. When he informed me of the situation by phone, I was annoyed at his delay and simply told him to find a way out. Thereupon, Ahmet jumped over the iron railing surrounding the yard, and while jumping, his little finger got caught on the sharp point of the railing. Fortunately, the people around helped get him to the hospital. When I got there, the doctors said they unfortunately had to cut off the tip of his little finger. I cannot forget the sorrow and guilt I felt for not immediately going to help him… My only consolation was that this incident had not ended in a much more disastrous way.

As her mood gradually improved, it would become clear that Fatma’s health problems were not physical but psychological. Although she couldn’t make much progress in the Swedish courses, she was having quite a good time. The lifelong friendships we formed with the couples Dinç and Bambi Gürs, Oğuz and Duygu Öztuzcu, Saygun and Eija Kuyumcu, Zülfü and Ülker Livaneli, and Sait and Gülder Koçaş made the greatest contribution to Fatma’s adjustment to life in Sweden. Thanks to them, we had many beautiful days in Stockholm.

One of my unforgettable memories from our first days in Lappis was the young man I encountered in the courtyard in the middle of the housing blocks. I was surprised when he called out to me with a fluent “Merhaba!” in Turkish. Because with his blonde hair, blue eyes, and height of at least 1.80 meters, he resembled a Swede; but he was a genuine, dyed-in-the-wool Turk, and then some, who had been living in Stockholm for years. Nurgun and I quickly became friends. He showed great warmth; he helped me solve everyday problems. He was very capable. In the following years, he had managed to work three different jobs simultaneously and get elected to the municipal council from the Social Democratic Party, but in the meantime, he had to close the pide (Turkish flatbread) shop he opened because he couldn’t give it proper attention. We would be sad to hear years later that his Swedish wife Lotta, who was a very kind-hearted person and put up with all his eccentricities, couldn’t take it anymore and divorced him.

## The 1973 elections

The general elections held in Turkey on October 14, 1973 unexpectedly and as a result of parliamentary mathematics led to the formation of a coalition government between Bülent Ecevit’s Republican People’s Party (CHP) and Necmettin Erbakan’s National Salvation Party (MSP), with Ecevit as prime minister. It had become clear that a period of relaxation would open in the country’s political life. My elder brother was writing that a political amnesty was being discussed and that my return to the country might be possible in the not-too-distant future. I was astonished. I was writing to my elder brother: “The political news from Turkey is heartening. To be honest, it never crossed my mind that Ecevit could win the elections or form a government and pass an amnesty. That’s how far we are from being able to understand Turkey…” (03.02.1974) I would continue to remain far from understanding Turkey.

The general amnesty law adopted on May 18, 1974 excluded political convicts. However, upon CHP’s application, the Constitutional Court expanded the amnesty in its July 2 decision to also include political prisoners based on the principle of equality. Shortly after this, the law granting university graduates the opportunity to do military service as short-term reserve officers was also passed. Doing only 4 months of military service starting from July 1975 and being discharged as a reserve officer was an opportunity not to be missed. Still, I had hesitations. I was writing to my elder brother: “Almost everyone I know abroad has decided to return. Fatma’s attitude is ‘I can’t guarantee that I’ll always be with you either here or in Turkey. Nor can I decide for you. Don’t ask me anything, decide what you’ll do yourself…’ I suppose the best thing is to benefit from the amnesty, do the military service, and then return to Sweden. But the dangers also make me think… The chauvinist nationalist atmosphere stirred up because of Cyprus doesn’t make me optimistic. If I’m going to spend even one day in prison, let’s not bother with this. If I come, I should be able to return to Sweden within 6-7 months and continue my doctorate. If they don’t give me a passport to return, all my efforts will be wasted…”

## From Damascus to Amsterdam

Cengiz Çandar had managed to cross from Beirut to Europe at the end of 1973 and had received political asylum from the Netherlands. We had been corresponding for a while. To see him and decide together what we would do, I went to Amsterdam by train between September 11-15, 1974. We had said farewell in Damascus in February 1972, under extraordinary circumstances; about two and a half years later, we met in Amsterdam… In the few days I stayed with him, we took stock of what we had been through. After Sabetay and I returned to Turkey, he had gone through very difficult days in Beirut. Eventually, he had found a way and managed to make it to the Netherlands. However, he had no intention of staying there. He was absolutely determined to benefit from the amnesty and return to the country.

After talking with Cengiz, my decision to return to the country was not delayed. Upon returning from Amsterdam, I talked with my doctoral thesis supervisor Tomas Hammar and we agreed: I would be appointed as a research assistant for 6 months starting October 1, 1974, and I would take leave from the university from April 1975 until the end of the year to do my military service and return to duty. I would join the doctoral courses upon my return. In the letters I sent to my elder brother in those days, I was writing: “Despite having had to save my own skin at one point, feeling great distrust of the revolutionary movement of Turkey and being worn down by the pressure of fascism, I neither turned my back on my people nor was my belief in the rightness and legitimacy of the cause to which I devoted my most productive years shaken. My judgment about myself is that I was not a fighter worthy of this cause…” (19.09.1974) “I suppose one needs to have a different nature than mine to be able to live for a long time somewhere other than one’s homeland, provided one doesn’t go to prison…. Despite speaking the language and loving Sweden, I feel more foreign now than ever. I can see at most 3-4 more years of my life in this country… The idea that even if one is to die, it should be among one’s own people is gaining strength… I suppose I’m getting over the shock of the first half of my life…” (09.11.1974) These lines indicated that while I was preparing myself for returning to Turkey, on the other hand I had definitely left behind the period of revolutionary activism.

In early October 1974, my mother-in-law Leman Kaptan came to visit us in Stockholm and stayed for about a month. This visit was also an opportunity for me to regain her affection. In early November, Fatma returned to Turkey with her mother, taking Elvan as well, to rent out her apartment in Ankara, and stayed for 5-6 weeks. Before she set off, we discussed all the matters related to our relationship and fortunately decided to face the difficulties together. This was a sign that she had decided to “continue” with me. Partly to celebrate this, we went to Frankfurt for two weeks between December 23, 1974 and January 6, 1975; we were guests of Alev Şeref and her then-husband Necmettin Baykal.

According to news from Turkey, those returning to benefit from the amnesty were not encountering difficulties. The State Security Court had dismissed the case in which I was also tried. There was no longer any obstacle to my return. On February 24, 1975, I applied for a passport at the Stockholm Embassy. I received the passport, valid for 3 months with the note “must return to the country by June 1” for those benefiting from the amnesty to return to Turkey, from Consul General Burhan Ant, whom I knew from Mülkiye. On April 2, 1975, Fatma, Elvan and I departed for Istanbul by Scandinavian Airlines (SAS). Dinç and Zeynel came to see us off at Arlanda Airport. I was very excited. In my eagerness to board the plane as soon as possible, I had gone ahead leaving Fatma and Elvan behind. During the journey, I was eaten up inside. For the first time in a long while, I was going to my country, and legally at that. But there was also some anxiety within me: Would it be possible for me to leave the country again?..

After embracing my elder brother and sister-in-law who met us at Yeşilköy Airport, we continued by plane to Izmir and from there by taxi to Ayvalık. After reuniting with my mother, father, elder sister, brother-in-law, and other relatives whom I hadn’t seen for more than four years since 1970, I set about handling the necessary matters for my military service. Due to a piece of misinformation, I was only able to obtain the required health report in the final days of the allotted period, which made me quite anxious. Because I had always been in Turkey illegally in the period after March 1972, I had a certain apprehension in everything I did, an anxiety within me of encountering a setback at any moment. It would turn out that this anxiety was not at all unfounded.

## Çanakkale is impassable

It became clear that I would do my military service in Çanakkale, a few hours by road from Ayvalık, at the 116th Gendarmerie Private Training Regiment Literacy School. Our conscription for short-term service was postponed from July 1 to July 15; we would be discharged 15 days earlier than expected, on September 15, doing about 70 days of net military service. Probably no one had done such short and such comfortable military service since Turkey was founded. We were lucky in this regard. (Especially for Cengiz and me, who had previously done serious “military service”…)

On July 15, we gathered at the barracks gate. We lined up before the captain (Sabri Arıkan). The captain, calling names one by one for roll call, paused after reading my name and scrutinized me carefully (under the astonished gazes of the others). It was clear he had been informed about my identity. About half of those sent to Çanakkale were Mülkiye graduates, most of the others were Police College graduates; most of my squad consisted of old friends. Our commander, by virtue of his tall stature, was (academic) Zafer Toprak. The squad members consisted of (my revolutionary comrades, journalists-writers) Cengiz Çandar and Ömer Madra, (academic-writer) Gündüz Vassaf, (journalist) Şefik Kahramankaptan, (journalist and later one of President Recep T. Erdoğan’s chief advisors) İlnur Çevik, and relatively young Mülkiye graduates (diplomat) Cengiz Aslantepe and (finance inspector) İlkay Bayram. We did military service alongside (former THY general manager) Cem Kozlu, (professors) Ömür Sezgin, Şevket Pamuk, Sabri Sayarı, (the late) Murat Sertel, Hasan Köni, Süleyman Gedik as well as (journalists) Koray Düzgören, Okay Gönensin, and Edip Öymen, all friends of mine. Mesut Yılmaz (ANAP party leader between 1991-2002 and three-time prime minister) and (state minister) Mehmet Ali İrtemçelik were also politicians doing their “national service” with us in Çanakkale. I would meet both of them later.

The regiment’s dormitories were of a quality that could be called comfortable. About 300 of us reserve officer candidates collected money among ourselves and had showers installed in bathrooms where we could bathe with hot water every day. The training we received essentially consisted of plenty of marching and firing 3-5 rounds with M1 rifles left over from World War II; it would not be an exaggeration to say that most of the time was spent idling. It was clear that the Turkish Armed Forces’ only expectation regarding us was to get rid of the “bekaya,” that is, the conscripts who were in a state of draft evasion, as soon as possible.

From the very first day, when I got the signal that the Turkish Armed Forces had their eyes on me, I tried to be as disciplined a soldier as possible. I never joined the trio of Cengiz Çandar, Ömer Madra, and Gündüz Vassaf, who escaped from the regiment almost every weekend to go drinking in town. In fact, one weekend they went to Ayvalık without me and ate and drank with Fatma while gossiping about me. But in the end, they got caught and spent a week in detention in a chicken coop-like place set up on one side of the regiment. However, for some reason, when being discharged, while all of them got “excellent” for “conduct and behavior,” the grade assigned to me was “average” despite all my disciplined behavior; even though the captain said he had been watching me from the first day and had seen no fault of mine.

As soon as I was discharged, I set about getting a passport. How would the foreign travel ban against me be lifted? The CHP-MSP coalition government formed after the 1973 elections had fallen from power in September 1974 following Ecevit’s resignation, and in April 1975 a coalition government known as the “Nationalist Front,” consisting of AP, MSP, MHP, and CGP under Süleyman Demirel’s leadership, had been formed. Getting a passport seemed difficult. I set up camp in Ankara and started looking for connections. Fatma’s late maternal uncle (one of the founders of the Pakmaya company) Kenan Kaptan had a friendship with the Director General of Security Celalettin Tüfekçi; he sent me to him with a request for help. Tüfekçi behaved quite politely, but ultimately no result came from this contact. Weeks, months were passing, and I didn’t know how I could solve the problem. Time was slipping by, and my return to Stockholm was being delayed. My thesis supervisor Tomas Hammar, whom I informed of the situation, said in his letters: “We’re happy to hear from you. If a problem arises, we’ll do whatever is necessary for you to come here… In the letter I received from the Swedish ambassador, he writes that he’s in contact with you and can testify that you worked at the university. Write if there’s anything I can do… We’re completing preparations for the research. We have a little more time for you to come…”

## Rıza Türmen

During an Ankara visit, I ran into Rıza Türmen, who was then a first secretary at the Foreign Ministry (he would become a judge at the European Court of Human Rights between 1998-2008). We knew each other from the English Boys’ High School. We had reconnected at doctoral courses at Mülkiye and become friends. When I explained my problem, he said he had an acquaintance at MİT (the National Intelligence Organization) and could learn from him whether I had any hope of getting a passport. After two days spent in anxious waiting, I visited Rıza and his wife Dr. Tomris Türmen (Executive Director of the World Health Organization between 1992-2006) at their home. The news Rıza gave made me jump for joy. The MİT official he had spoken with had said “as far as we’re concerned, there’s no obstacle to him getting a passport.” Rıza didn’t stop at just giving this information, he also offered advice: I could see Deniz Baykal, who had served as Energy Minister in the previous CHP-MSP government, and ask him to help me get a passport. Baykal must have had some closeness with Oğuzhan Asiltürk (MSP), who retained the Interior Ministry seat in the new government… Following his advice, I immediately called Deniz Baykal. Baykal graciously gave me an appointment right away; I visited him at CHP headquarters.

I knew Baykal from my years studying at Mülkiye; at that time he was a young faculty member who showed warmth toward leftist students. I explained to him that I was doing doctoral studies at Stockholm University, had returned to the country under the general amnesty and done my military service, but couldn’t manage to get a passport. Although he didn’t welcome me with the warmth he had shown in the Mülkiye years, he took an interest. He told me to see Mehmet Can, a Mülkiye graduate who had served as Minister of Customs and Monopolies as well as Minister of Justice, and was then a CHP deputy for Adana, saying he would solve my problem. Mehmet Can received me very warmly at his home. After speaking with Asiltürk on my behalf, he called me and said I could get my passport. I didn’t know how to thank him. I also called Baykal and thanked him heartily. Despite there being no legal obstacle, I had managed to get a passport after about four months of effort and only thanks to connections at the highest level. I was walking on air with joy…

I immediately informed Tomas Hammar of the news and asked for his help (as usual) regarding a place to stay upon our return to Stockholm. In early January 1976, we flew to Stockholm as a family. At Arlanda Airport, just as they had seen us off, Dinç Gürs and Zeynel Çelikel met us. We settled into the apartment at the Wennergren Center (where mostly foreign academics were hosted for short periods) that Hammar had arranged for us to stay temporarily. Hammar welcomed me with joy. From February 1, 1976, I started my research assistant position at Stockholm University’s Political Science Department. On the day I started work, finding on my desk a letter from my father saying “Welcome to Sweden” both surprised and delighted me. Hammar would do me another favor: With his encouragement, I applied for the non-repayable state scholarship given to doctoral students and obtained the right to benefit from this scholarship for 4 years from April 1, 1977 to April 1, 1981. We immediately enrolled Elvan, who had started elementary school in Ayvalık, in the nearest elementary school to our home. Her teacher was Barbro (“Babba”), a very sweet and very beautiful young woman. Unfortunately, she was an unlucky woman. A few years later, we would learn that she had died in a traffic accident.

## Renewing our vows

In one of the first letters I wrote to my elder brother after returning to Stockholm, I said: “After staying in Turkey for eight months and being together with you for a long time, this place seemed so strange to me… But I feel very at ease. If I hadn’t benefited from the amnesty, it would have been a terrible mistake. Seeing my presence here as temporary also gives such comfort. I’m thinking of staying for as short a time as possible and returning after getting the greatest possible benefit. Life isn’t life without the sun… When I reach the stage of writing my doctoral thesis, that is in early summer 1978, Fatma and Elvan will return, and I’ll return in the fall. We’re determined to return to the homeland and settle in Istanbul.” (As I’ll explain later, Fatma, Elvan, and our family’s new member who would be born on March 11, 1978, our son Acar, made a permanent return to the homeland in the fall of that year, due to a decision of ours that was not at all sound. I, on the other hand, would travel back and forth to Stockholm and suffer greatly until I completed my work in April 1981.)

## The PRI research project

The team that would carry out the PRI (Political Resocialisation of Immigrants) research project headed by Associate Professor Tomas Hammar at Stockholm University’s Political Science Department had been determined. Ko-Chih Tung, of Japanese-Chinese mixed heritage, would take on coordination in the project; Markku Peura would be responsible for Finnish immigrants, Stepan Udovich for Yugoslavs, Andrej Berkowicz for Poles, and I for immigrants from Turkey. The comparison group section of the research regarding Swedes would be done by the Swede Birgitta Ornbrant. The academic assistantship of the project was undertaken by Andrej’s wife Halina; the administrative secretariat by another Pole, Wojciech Luterek. I would like to briefly mention the very interesting life stories of my project colleagues here.

The project director, my doctoral thesis supervisor Tomas Hammar, is without doubt the smartest, most knowledgeable, best, and most honest person I have known in life. He is one of the most important figures in my life. His offering me a job in the research project he would start as soon as he met me shaped my future. Tomas was an associate professor during my years in Sweden; in the early 1980s, he was appointed to Sweden’s first professorship in migration research. I have detailed above how he supported and looked after me. Tomas’s interest in migration and immigrant issues stemmed from his parents. His family had an interesting story. His father and mother had opened a folk education center (Birkagårdens folkhögskola) in Stockholm and had taken a close interest in the problems of those who fled the Nazis and took refuge in Sweden during World War II. Tomas’s wife Stina was an academic who had studied pedagogy and literature; had developed theories on dreams, myths, and fairy tales; and had published books on these subjects. (We lost Stina, to whom I owe gratitude for her warmth, in 2020. I remember her with respect.)

The person I met through the PRI research project and who would become my lifelong friend was Ko-Chih Tung. His Japanese father had married a young Chinese woman who was a member of a Mandarin family and an expert in Chinese philology while serving as a marine biologist in Manchuria under Japanese occupation; the couple had three sons, one year apart, with Ko-Chih, born in 1944, being the eldest. When the war ended in 1947, the Soviets had occupied Manchuria and taken the Japanese there prisoner, including Ko-Chih’s father, deporting them to Siberia. The father was released after a while and managed to take his wife and sons and return to Tokyo, where he was the sole heir of the influential Tanaka family. After some time, following a conflict between the Japanese mother-in-law and the Chinese daughter-in-law, the Tanaka family rejected their daughter-in-law and grandchildren (whom they disparaged as “Mao’s seeds”). The Mandarin family to which the mother belonged had never recognized the marriage to a Japanese man from the occupation army.

Ko-Chih’s mother had managed to subsist in Tokyo with her sons for a long time by teaching Chinese philology courses at Japanese universities. During this time, as a result of a crisis she went through, she attempted suicide by jumping in front of a train with her children, but the eldest son Ko-Chih grabbed her arm at the last moment and prevented the attempt. Taking advantage of an opportunity that arose in the early 1960s, she emigrated to Hawaii with her sons, obtained US citizenship, and through hard work ensured that each of her sons studied at the best American universities. Ko-Chih had married Margareta, a Swede he met while studying political science at Dartmouth College, settled in Sweden, and begun doctoral studies at Stockholm University like me. Being a qualified statistics expert, he was in the position of chief assistant for the research. Ko-Chih would become one of my foreign friends whom I loved and admired very much and with whom I gradually developed a close relationship.

Perhaps the person with the most dramatic story in our research group was the Pole Andrej Berkowicz. Andrej had been expelled from the Polish Communist Party during the campaign it launched in the late 1960s to purge Jews from its ranks, and had found the remedy in taking refuge in Sweden with his wife Halina. I would become friends with Andrej and have the opportunity to follow what happened to him during my various visits to Stockholm in the 1980s. During my visit in 1982, I learned that Andrej, who was approaching 70, had recently divorced Halina and married a young Polish woman who had taken refuge in Sweden. When he invited me to his home for a dinner with plenty of vodka, I met his young and beautiful wife, who was carrying in her arms their son Adam, then only a few months old. During my visit to Stockholm about a year later, I had learned that Andrej’s Parkinson’s disease had progressed considerably. What I learned during my Stockholm visit two years later was even more distressing. Andrej, saying “my illness is progressing, I want to buy an apartment for my wife and child, but I don’t have enough money,” had borrowed large sums from many acquaintances including Hammar and Wojciech, then gone to Bangkok and squandered the money there on Thailand’s famous prostitutes. When he returned to Stockholm, he told the creditors who wanted him to pay his debts, “God has never treated me well… I’m sorry for you, but I have no money left to give…” and had passed away some time after this.

Perhaps the one with the most interesting story among the Swedes I knew in Stockholm was Beatrice Ceyhan, who was my student in the Turkish courses I gave at TBV. She had met her Turkish husband while he was studying architecture in Stockholm, they had fallen in love and married.
