Unfortunately, a few years after their son Metin was born, her husband had committed suicide after going through a severe psychological crisis. Beatrice, who remained faithful to the memory of her beloved husband, never married again and never lost her interest in Turkey and Turkish. She frequently visited Turkey and her husband’s relatives. She was also one of the rare Swedes who hosted Fatma and me in their home. After I returned to the homeland, we continued to correspond with her for many years.

Let me come to one of my closest friends I made in Stockholm. One day in 1975, my home phone rang. The caller was a young Turk studying at the university. He said he got my number from someone who knew me and that he absolutely wanted to meet me. His voice was so convincing that I couldn’t say no. We met. While studying at METU, he had been detained for participating in boycotts, a case had been opened against him at the State Security Court when “banned publications” were found in his locker at the dormitory, and when he was finally sentenced to 2 years and 4 months in prison, he had decided that leaving the country would be the right thing to do. He had sought asylum in Sweden and started studying journalism in Stockholm. His name was Yavuz Baydar. The elder brother-younger brother relationship that began with him would turn into a close friendship over the years, and Yavuz would be in my life in one way or another in every period.

## Turks in Stockholm

From January 1976, while continuing with doctoral courses on one hand, I also embarked on the fieldwork of the PRI research on the other. I was quite successful in the courses; I passed all exams on the first attempt. I left only one exam for the end so I could continue to use the state scholarship. What surprised me most was receiving one of the highest grades in the statistics exam, probably because I had studied quite hard for it.

In the field research, we conducted detailed interviews with a random sample of 265 citizens of Turkey residing within the municipality of Stockholm, covering their socio-economic conditions as well as their political values and behaviors. I personally conducted 30-40 of these, while Turkish students we specially trained administered the others. After the September 1976 elections, in which for the first time in Europe immigrants were granted the right to vote in local elections, I also conducted phone surveys with about 80 people from Turkey, asking which party they had voted for and why.

My doctoral thesis, which I wrote based on the research findings, was published in Swedish in 1980 by the LiberFörlag publishing house under the title “Turkar i Stockholm: En studie av invandrare, politik och samhälle” (Turks in Stockholm: A Study of Immigrants, Politics and Society). I wrote the thesis in English; but Hammar suggested it be published in Swedish on the grounds that it would receive much broader interest from relevant circles. The translation was done by Göran Licke, one of my students from the Turkish courses I gave at TBV. I added a long Turkish summary at the end of the book (titled “Turks in Stockholm: A Social and Political Study on Immigrants”). I thought I would have the opportunity to publish English and Turkish translations of the thesis in the future. Unfortunately, after returning to Turkey I would have to leave my academic career and work at newspapers for a long time, and I would find neither the time nor the desire to return and deal with my doctoral thesis.

The results of the research were interesting. I won’t go into a detailed explanation of them here. After the forty-odd years that have passed, as well as the quantitative and qualitative changes in migration from Turkey to Sweden, these findings have little validity for today. However, I can mention a few findings (that perhaps still remain valid): As expected, those from Turkey were seen to be less “adapted” to Swedish society compared to immigrants from other countries. When I examined their values and behaviors in roughly three groups (Urban origin with high school and higher education / Urban origin with relatively low education / Rural origin with low education), the following findings stood out: Almost all of them were quite satisfied with their life in Sweden in terms of material conditions, but quite dissatisfied in terms of non-material conditions. While the majority maintained the tendency to return to the country, the proportion of those who thought they were permanent was also rising. The most striking finding in terms of their political socialization was undoubtedly that while the vast majority had voted for right-wing parties in the last election they had taken part in back in Turkey, 80% voted for left (social democratic and democratic left) parties in the 1976 local elections when they voted for the first time in Sweden. It appeared that most voted for left parties because they believed they would better serve the interests of immigrants.

## Our wonderful neighbors

In our new home, we had neighbors with very interesting stories whom we loved very much. We frequently met with the Italian Fabio Manzetti and his Norwegian wife Margrete, who lived right across from us, with their four adorable small children (three girls and one boy) born one year apart. Fabio served us the best pasta sauces we ever ate, and Margrete the best coffee we ever drank. Fabio was a faculty member at Stockholm Handelshögskolan / School of Economics, Sweden’s equivalent of the London School of Economics. We had quite enjoyable conversations with him on political and economic matters. (Fabio and Margrete would be greatly affected by our decision to return to Istanbul in late 1978 and would shortly after move to Milan.

However, they regretted it because of the air pollution in Milan and emigrated to Oslo a year or two later. The couple’s life in Oslo was not very happy. Fabio, who got bored with economics and took up horse training, would divorce Margrete after a while and marry a young Norwegian woman.)

In the apartment right next to the Manzettis lived an Iranian couple, Mustafa and Efi Tabatabian, with their newborn baby girl. They were very lovable people. We also developed a close friendship and neighborly relations with them, and ate their pilaf. Their life after we left unfortunately also brought them separation. The family was torn apart following the Islamic Revolution in Iran in 1979. Mustafa, who admired Khomeini, returned to Tehran. The last information I obtained about Efi, who sympathized with the leftist People’s Mojahedin organization, was that she was among the Iranians who stormed the Iranian Embassy in Norway.

We essentially lived among our Turkish friends. The Gürs, Öztuzcu, Livaneli, Kuyumcu, and Koçaş couples were the friends we saw most frequently. We also established lifelong friendships with Zeynel Çelikel and his wife Kerstin; with Haluk Soydan, who was then living in Uppsala, and his (now late) wife Lillian. When friends who came from Turkey and stayed for short periods were also taken into account, we had in a way become part of the Turkish ghetto.

Zülfü Livaneli had also taken refuge in Sweden as a victim of March 12. We were among the first to hear some of the compositions he made in Stockholm that would earn him fame far beyond Turkey’s borders as a musician. One weekend while Zülfü was preparing to give his first concert in Stockholm, we went shopping with our wives to get his concert clothes. As a result, Zülfü would long wear the stage outfit Fatma chose—a white shirt and a black vest—at his concerts in Turkey as well.

We had a funny experience with Zülfü. Following an advertisement, we applied in September 1976 to make programs in the Turkish section of Swedish Radio. Ulla, the Swedish wife of the late Demir Özlü, who had settled in Sweden in those days, was also among those in charge of that section. Looking at our resumes, we believed they would hire us for the two open positions. However, when it became clear that this was not the case and that they would make us compete with other applicants, we withdrew (being a bit arrogant about it).

One innovation that Stockholm brought to our lives was Fatma starting to work outside the home for the first time. In the Tensta-Rinkeby area, where immigrants from Turkey were concentrated, she worked in kindergartens on one hand and gave literacy lessons to women from Turkey on the other. And thus she had an income that contributed to the family budget more than mine.

Now confident that I had won her heart back, I declared my love to her once more and proposed that we renew our vows. Our marriage was officiated by the Mülkiye graduate and Stockholm Consul General Burhan Ant on March 31, 1976, the day we moved into our new home in Stockholm, which was also Elvan’s eighth birthday. Dinç was Fatma’s witness, Oğuz was mine. It was one of the happiest days of my life. On the same day, we moved into our three-bedroom apartment at Professorslingan 35/3 (which I found with Tomas Hammar’s support). My affairs in Sweden had now completely fallen into place. However, I had started to see our presence in Sweden as temporary.

## We are drowning in sorrow

In July 1976, upon the invitation of the Gürses, we went on a trip to Finland together with the Livanelis. The trip took us to Helsinki, and from there to the town of Ekenäs in the region where Finns of Swedish origin lived, which was Bambi’s homeland, and we met Bambi’s mother and father; from there we went to the island owned by Bambi’s father. We had a great time. Bambi would later tell us: Fatma, whose beauty Bambi’s father admired, had started to adorn his dreams… I would very much agree with Bambi’s late father. She always adorned my dreams too…

We also had plans for after Finland. After returning to Stockholm and staying one night, the next morning we were to set off for Amsterdam, where Ömer was on a 3-month scholarship from the UN, to see the Madras. Our train tickets had been purchased. However, when we came home after Finland, I found a letter in the mailbox from my father sent from Ayvalık. The letter contained my mother-in-law Leman Kaptan’s death notice that appeared in the newspaper and my father’s brief condolence note. My dear Fatma was understandably very, very upset by this sudden news of death. Leman Kaptan had passed away on July 20 while we were in Finland and had been buried the next day. We cancelled the Holland trip and the next day, taking Elvan as well, we all flew to the homeland. My elder brother met us at Yeşilköy; we continued to Ayvalık via Izmir by plane. We visited Leman Kaptan at her grave. I loved my mother-in-law. (I agree more than ever today with her judgment about me that I “have intelligence but no common sense.”) I returned to Stockholm a few days later, Fatma and Elvan a few weeks later.

Four months passed. One morning in November 1976, the phone rang. A woman from Ayvalık whom I barely knew and had never spoken with on the phone before was calling and saying: “Şahin Bey, Bingül, Hasan, and Neriman had a very terrible accident in Susurluk last night while returning from Istanbul. Very terrible… Do you understand???…” A car driven by a chauffeur had crashed into a truck parked by the roadside without any warning signs near Susurluk; Fatma’s brother-in-law Hasan Önen and her maternal aunt Neriman Kaptan had died at the scene, and her elder sister Bingül, who had been taken to a health center while still conscious, had died there from internal bleeding. The driver had managed to survive the accident with injuries. You can imagine what a heavy blow this was to all of us, but especially to Fatma. Again we immediately went to the homeland. Again my elder brother met us at Yeşilköy. Again we continued to Ayvalık via Izmir by plane. Three funerals at once—it was heartbreaking. This time Fatma was completely shaken. Sorrows would not let go of us. I didn’t know how to console her. After staying in Ayvalık for a few weeks, we returned to Stockholm.

Tension was escalating in Turkey both between right and left groups, and within left groups. Ömer described the situation in Ankara in his letter as follows: “Around 1972, we were in a position to more or less influence events, or at least we thought so. Now everything is very different: I seriously doubt whether we even have the power to analyze developments or make predictions, let alone have any influence… When taking Cemo to gymnastics, if there’s a rally in an area on our route, we have to detour for kilometers; if I have to leave school a bit late, at an hour when darkness is falling, I jump into the car and race home with my heart pounding, constantly scanning all around; even in the middle of the day, watching out for places where young people are somewhat concentrated and staying away from them; constantly complaining with friends at school and home that ‘Boy, the situation is so bad, there’s no security left’… That’s how our life passes.” (February 13, 1976) “I seriously doubt whether we even have the power to analyze developments or make predictions, let alone have any influence…” These words of Ömer’s were a most apt expression of how far we were from understanding the country in which we were born and raised.

During the May Day celebrations on May 1, 1977, when a few gunshots were fired in a clash between two opposing groups in the packed Taksim Square, 5 people were killed by bullets and 29 were crushed to death in the panic that ensued; hundreds were injured. This grave incident triggered developments that would escalate with mutual killings between right and left and result in the military coup on September 12, 1980. I had started to think that returning to Turkey would not be possible… On May 2, my elder brother called from Istanbul. He had thought that I might have suspected he could have been in the square and worried about him, although this had never crossed my mind. He told me what he knew about what happened in Taksim. He said how happy he was that we had escaped from Turkey. After sharing our sorrow over the state of the country, we hung up the phone.

## A very dark day

On May 6, 1977, toward noon, the phone rang. My sister-in-law Ayla was calling from Istanbul: “Şahin, we lost Acar…” she said. I couldn’t believe my ears… It didn’t occur to me that the word “lost…” would mean death… In his last letter, he had written that he had started working as sales manager for a company that produced forklift machines and how pleased he was with his job and the company allocating him a car. He had finally found some peace. However, on the morning of May 6, he had set off in his car to go to the company’s factory in Kartal; when he reached the Soğanlık intersection, he was crushed under a bus coming from the İzmit direction that had swerved into the opposite lane to avoid hitting a minibus that suddenly appeared in front of it… The accident had made the news in the next day’s Hürriyet newspaper. Under the photo of the car reduced to a pile of metal, it said: “The car that the bus entering the wrong lane smashed to pieces ended up like this. The body of Acar Alpay, who was driving the car and died terribly trapped in the pile of scrap, could barely be extracted…”

His watch had stopped at 9:22, the moment of impact. Had he lived, he would have turned 39 on July 16. His daughter Ümit was 13, his son Cihan was only 10. From my childhood on, he had been a compassionate elder brother to me, had made it possible for me to escape to Sweden—meaning he had given me back my life and my family. I remembered what he had written in the letter he sent in late 1973: “A new year is coming… it would be good to start life in another country and rebuild my life as I want. But even dreaming of it is forbidden for me…” Despite how much he longed for it, I couldn’t support the idea of him coming and settling in Sweden. If I could have, he might be unhappy now, but he would be alive. My heart was bleeding. This was yet another blow to my mother, who had already suffered every misfortune imaginable. We buried my mother’s eldest son on May 8, “Mother’s Day.” I tried to pull myself together by walking the streets of Istanbul for three or four weeks. My relationship with my elder brother had been more than that of siblings. In this relationship, he was always the giver, I was the taker. (I will tell his life story, which cannot fit here, in the book “Human Landscapes from My Life” that I am planning.)

I took leave from the university and we stayed in the homeland for about three months. Bless them, Tomas and Stina came to Istanbul in early June to show solidarity in our difficult days. With them, we first went to Kulu via Ankara and visited the home region of most of the people from Turkey living in Stockholm. The people of Kulu had built gleaming houses with the expectation that they would return one day and equipped them with all modern appliances. But very few would be able to return. From Kulu, we went to Konya and visited the tomb of Mevlana (Rumi). From there, we came to Ayvalık again by bus via Antalya, Denizli, Aydın, and Izmir. I would be grateful to the Hammars for life for this visit they made to console and distract me.

Our sorrows would not end… Shortly after the Hammars returned to Sweden, Ömer and Tanju along with Alev and Necmettin came to Ayvalık to see us. Their visit helped me considerably to recover. In mid-August, around the time Elvan’s school was opening, we returned to Stockholm. About a month later, on the morning of September 19, the phone rang again. It was Ömer on the other end. He said Tanju had died. I went into shock… This was the fourth phone call announcing the sudden death of someone close to us… Tanju, a dear friend of ours whom I likened to French film actress Jeanne Moreau, had fallen ill shortly after their return from Ayvalık to Ankara and had said farewell to life at only 32 years of age, diagnosed with colon cancer. Her two sons, Cem born in 1969 and Ege born in 1976, had been orphaned. The life of Ömer, my closest friend, was becoming very difficult. He insistently prevented me from going to Ankara to attend the funeral.

## Ecevit in power

After returning from Turkey, I focused on writing my doctoral thesis. Events that would affect our future were taking place in the homeland. The Taksim events of May 1, 1977 had triggered the decision to hold early general elections. In the election held on June 5, Bülent Ecevit’s CHP won 213 parliamentary seats with 41.4 percent of the vote, but could not achieve the majority needed to govern alone in parliament. Thereupon, the Second Nationalist Front government was formed as a coalition of AP, MSP, and MHP under Süleyman Demirel’s leadership. However, when CHP won the local elections held on December 11, 1977, the balances began to change; when a group of deputies left AP, the government had to resign on December 31. Ecevit formed the new government on January 1, 1978, with the support of 10 deputies who had left AP and remained independent, in return for giving each of them a ministry. We welcomed this development with great joy in Stockholm. We believed that under Ecevit’s rule, Turkey would leave political tensions behind and find stability. Hope was awakening that the time to return to the homeland would soon come.

Fatma was pregnant. Upon the death of my elder brother, my cousin Gaye’s husband Dr. Aykut Kazancıgil (Gaye being my maternal aunt’s daughter) had advised that a baby would lift our spirits shaken by the tragedies we faced. We had decided; if the child to be born in March was a girl, we would give her late elder sister’s name (Bingül), if a boy, my late elder brother’s name (Acar). In those days, the sex of babies couldn’t be known in advance. After a healthy pregnancy, Fatma gave birth to our son Acar on March 11, 1978. She gave birth at the hospital in Danderyd, one of Stockholm’s most exclusive neighborhoods. The doctors allowed me to watch the birth process while holding Fatma’s hand. When the nurse, placing Acar in an incubator so his body temperature wouldn’t drop, said, “You have a healthy, handsome son…” I was on top of the world. It was one of the happiest days of my life. Ten years later, I had become a father again and now I had a daughter and a son. But even during those days she stayed in the hospital, I managed to upset my dear Fatma: by saying I was very sad about the death of a communist leader whose name I can’t even remember now… She nearly threw me out of the room she was in. But she was so happy to have given birth to Acar; she would look at him again and again saying “I can’t believe this beautiful baby is mine.” The birth of Acar had reconnected us to life.

After a while, Fatma and I began to think that since the political situation in Turkey was hopeful and I was close to completing my doctoral thesis, we could now make a permanent return. Meanwhile, Oğuz and Duygu had returned; Zülfü and Ülker were also planning to return. We calculated that Fatma could take care of the baby more comfortably in the homeland; and if I stayed alone, I could finish the thesis faster. Unfortunately, almost all our calculations would prove wrong. In October 1978, together with the Livanelis, we loaded our belongings that we could take into the country duty-free into a freight car. Fatma took the children and returned to the homeland on the Stockholm-Izmir flight that SAS was operating at the time. Until we learned that the freight car had gone to Izmir instead of Istanbul due to a dispute, we remained in suspense about what happened to our belongings. I won’t tell of the difficulties I encountered in getting our belongings cleared from Izmir customs with the help of a customs broker found by Fatma’s maternal uncle İsmet Kaptan, obtained in exchange for bribes, storing them in Ayvalık for a while, and then transporting them to Istanbul.)

## Alone again in Stockholm

After Fatma and the children left, I didn’t vacate the apartment we were living in; I shared the rent with Gunilla, my student from the Turkish courses. The plan didn’t work out as expected; life away from Fatma and the children was terribly difficult. Levent, Gunilla’s boyfriend who was doing his doctorate at Grenoble University in France, was also coming and going to Stockholm like me. We would socialize with him. Meanwhile, to dispel my distress, I would sometimes play chess with him for hours.

I started going to Ayvalık frequently. When Ayvalık’s freezing winter cold set in, Fatma had almost regretted returning. Acar burning his palm by pressing it against the coal stove was an accident from which we got off lightly. Although the foreign travel ban had been lifted and I had documentation of this, I was stopped by the passport police on every flight from Istanbul to Stockholm, sometimes taken off the plane. I had many photocopies of the document made and left a copy with the passport police at each departure. I can’t describe what I went through… (I would later learn that a METU faculty member with the same surname as mine was also being dragged off the plane every time he traveled abroad.)

The separation from Fatma and the children had made life in Stockholm unbearable. My mind was on them. What was happening in the homeland also did not match our expectations of the Ecevit government at all. Milliyet newspaper’s editor-in-chief Abdi İpekçi was shot and killed in front of his house on February 1, 1979 by someone named Mehmet Ali Ağca. This event shook us greatly. What kind of country had we decided to return to? When I thought that if I couldn’t find an opportunity to enter a university in Turkey I could do journalism, I would say to myself “If all else fails, I’ll go to Abdi İpekçi and ask him to hire me.” This door had closed.

In the summer of 1979, I simply fell into depression. One day while sitting at home trying to write one of the final chapters of the thesis, suddenly the letters started growing larger and coming toward me. I immediately stopped working. I called Refik Erzan, my military service friend Gündüz Vassaf’s brother-in-law who was then doing a doctorate in the economics department at Stockholm University; I said “I’m having a breakdown, please help me.” Bless him, he immediately came with his car, picked me up and took me to a swimming pool; he calmed me down by chatting. From there, I called Zeynel, who was vacationing on an island in the Stockholm archipelago belonging to his wife Kerstin’s family. Zeynel (Çelikel), who remains one of my closest and most loyal friends to this day, immediately jumped in his car and came; he took me to the island; he brought me back to normal. Only with the help of these friends, to whom I will always be indebted, was I able to pull myself together and continue working.

Writing the doctoral thesis was no small effort. In those years, personal computers hadn’t come out yet; typewriters were used. I was struggling with the F-keyboard typewriter I had brought from Turkey. For statistical analyses, we used the giant (“mainframe”) computers at the university’s computer center. I would leave the cards I punched in the evenings and pick up the outputs in the mornings. A single wrongly punched hole in one card could render the outputs unusable. There’s no way today’s youth, who work with highly capable personal computers, can know what we went through. They may not even understand what I’m talking about. That’s why I must confess that I avoided very sophisticated types of statistical analysis when writing the thesis. After my permanent return to Turkey, when I went to Stockholm for a conference in 1982 and saw that the entire university had switched to personal computers, I would deeply regret this.

At the end of summer 1979, I finished writing the thesis, which I had drafted in English. Tomas Hammar thought it would be good if it were translated into Swedish on the grounds that it could be more widely read. Göran Licke, one of my students from the Turkish courses, took on the translation into Swedish. Tomas and I agreed to publish the English version of my thesis, perhaps the first empirical study in the field of the political consequences of labor migration to Western Europe in the post-World War II period, at the first opportunity. However, due to the difficulties I encountered after returning to the homeland on one hand, and the weariness caused by working on the thesis for a long time on the other, I would unfortunately never be able to fulfill this goal.

At the end of summer 1979, while waiting for the thesis to be translated into Swedish and published by LiberFörlag in Stockholm, I set about moving Fatma and the children to Istanbul. Finding a rental apartment was extremely difficult at that time. There were even days when my temperature rose from stress and I had to stay in bed. Finally, at the end of August, I rented the apartment in the Zerrin Apt. building on Peker Street in Levent, where we would live for 6 years until 1985, for quite a steep rent, and we moved in. We enrolled Elvan in Levent Primary School for her final year. My affairs seemed to be getting on track. The date for my thesis defense was set as November 29, 1980, which coincided with my 15th wedding anniversary with Fatma. After defending the thesis in Stockholm, I would start looking for work in Istanbul. Winter had set in in Istanbul; the heating wasn’t working because there was no fuel, and we could only heat the house somewhat with a wood stove we set up in the living room. The children were constantly getting sick. Fatma also had to take to bed several times that winter with unexplained fatigue and a low fever. These symptoms could have been harbingers of the health problems she would experience later.

Things were getting complicated in the country. We had completely lost hope in the Ecevit government, which we had deluded ourselves into thinking would find solutions to economic and political problems and put an end to polarization and violence. While Ecevit gave long speeches on television every evening, problems continued to grow. Some ministers began resigning from the government. As clashes between right and left groups spread, it was felt that the government’s days were numbered. In the by-elections held on October 14, 1979, CHP’s vote share dropped from 41% to 29%. Ecevit resigned; in his place, a minority government was formed on November 12, 1979 under Süleyman Demirel’s leadership. The economic decisions announced by the new government on January 24, 1980 meant Turkey’s adoption of a growth strategy through an outward-oriented market economy led by the private sector instead of import substitution led by the public sector. Turgut Özal, appointed as undersecretary of the State Planning Organization, was the architect of the new policies. The January 24 decisions brought an immediately perceptible improvement in the economy; however, the right-left clashes, which in the words of a foreign observer resembled a “slow-motion civil war,” had escalated to a point where an average of ten people were being killed every day. Being forced to continue traveling back and forth to Stockholm while leaving my wife and children in Istanbul in this environment was greatly upsetting me.

## No to nuclear energy

I took great interest in the “stop or continue?” referendum on nuclear energy held in Sweden on March 23, 1980. Until that date, the only serious accident recorded at nuclear power plants had occurred in 1979 at the Three Mile Island plant in Harrisburg, USA. After this incident, opposition to nuclear energy was growing in Sweden, which derived a significant portion of its electricity from its existing 6 nuclear plants and had 4 more completed and 2 under construction. When the ruling coalition of right-wing parties couldn’t reach an agreement on what to do with the nuclear plants, they decided to hold a (non-binding, consultative) referendum.

Three options were presented in the vote: The first two options envisioned closing nuclear plants as it became possible to meet electricity needs from other sources, and in any case not building more than 12 plants. The only difference between the second option, supported by the Social Democrats, and the first option, supported by the Conservative party, was that it envisioned prioritizing the safety criterion in closing plants. The third option, supported by the Center party, which had a strong environmental awareness and was the largest party in the coalition government at the time, contained a radical proposal: No more than the existing 6 plants would be put into operation, and the existing ones would be closed within 10 years. In the vote, in which 75% of voters participated, the first option received 19%, the second option 39%, and the third option 38% of the votes. Thereupon, parliament decided to close all 12 plants by 2010. (However, this decision could not be implemented. On July 17, 2010, parliament, violating all three options in the referendum, would decide to build new plants to replace existing ones that had completed their lifespan. According to the decision taken in 2015, four old plants were closed in 2020. Six nuclear plants are currently operating in Sweden.)

In the first referendum in which immigrants with residence permits in Sweden were granted the right to vote, I cast my vote for the third option, that is, the option envisioning the end of nuclear energy. What I learned by following the campaign during the referendum made me a determined opponent of all forms of nuclear energy. After returning to Turkey, I wrote many articles against nuclear energy in newspapers and gave many speeches. (Like many of my writings and speeches, they too would be in vain…)

Since I was close to completing my doctorate, I began searching for a job at one of the universities in Istanbul. We had decided not to return to Ankara even though Fatma had an apartment there, because air pollution had reached incredible levels. Also, I definitely did not want to return to the environment of my “revolutionary” days, which I didn’t even want to remember. My close friend Zafer Toprak introduced me to Prof. Dr. Tarık Zafer Tunaya in the summer of 1980; the late Tunaya had said he would hire me as an assistant at Istanbul University’s Faculty of Political Science, where he was dean, when I completed my doctorate. However, unfortunately, immediately after the September 12 military intervention, Tunaya would be dismissed from the university along with about five thousand faculty members and staff, including many of my acquaintances and friends, under Martial Law Act No. 1402.

I think again on Zafer’s recommendation, I visited Associate Professor Dr. Yaşar Gürbüz, who was then the head of the political science department at Marmara University’s Faculty of Economics and Political Sciences. He received me very positively; he said things like “We need to bring a talent like you to the university.” He asked me to leave a phone number where he could reach me. But apparently someone must have warned him, because not only did he never call, but when we met at a gathering he pretended not to see me. Thereupon, although not very hopeful, I also knocked on Boğaziçi University’s door. I called my classmate from Robert College, Taha Parla, who worked as a faculty member in the Political Science Department. He said there was no open position in the department, but I could discuss this matter with the dean. The dean at that time was Üstün Ergüder, a friend of my late elder brother. He was very frank; he said, “For you to find a job at a university, you’ll need to introduce yourself to society with your new identity.” He was being realistic. I gave up searching for jobs at universities.

## September 12 is coming

After spending the summer of 1980 in Ayvalık, we returned to Istanbul around the time school was starting for Elvan, who had passed the Galatasaray High School entrance exam. It was felt that the country was heading toward a new military coup. Prime Minister Demirel was advocating for elections to be renewed; opposition leader Ecevit was advocating for a national coalition government between the two major parties. When, in utter heedlessness, they failed to compromise, on September 12, 1980, the military once again seized power.

On September 11, Ömer Madra and I had gone to visit Gündüz Vassaf to spend a night at his house on Sedef Island. I was awakened by Gündüz toward dawn. What had been expected had happened. It was understood that for the past year the military had turned a blind eye to the growth of right-left clashes in order to ensure society’s support for the seizure of power. The thought that “this time it was inevitable,” which the military intervention also aroused in me, turned into a great reaction against military rule (in society and in me) following the arrest of hundreds of thousands of people, widespread torture incidents, and the execution of over 50 people shortly after. My anxieties had multiplied: Would I be able to go to Stockholm for my doctoral thesis defense? Would it be possible for me to find any job in Istanbul in this environment? Had we made a mistake by returning to Turkey?

In mid-November 1980, I went to the airport to fly to Stockholm. The relief I felt when I passed through passport control by presenting the document showing that my foreign travel ban had been lifted was no less than what I felt when I managed to escape from the country in 1972. My thesis defense took place as scheduled on November 29, 1980. The task of critiquing my thesis was given to Diane Sainsbury, an American faculty member from Uppsala University. Sainsbury’s not being too hard on me did make me wonder if she was going easy on me… The support from Tomas Hammar and some colleagues, as well as the endorsement I would receive years later from Olof Petersson, one of Sweden’s leading political scientists, would convince me that I had done good work; regarding the thesis, only the regret of having settled for publishing it only in Swedish would remain. At that time, completing doctoral studies at Stockholm University’s Political Science Department took an average of 7 years. I, on the other hand, had completed the doctorate in less than 4 years, a record time, having started in 1976 and finished in 1980. In order to be able to use the full four-year state scholarship I had started receiving in April 1976, I had left one of the doctoral qualifying exams until after the thesis defense. I took the final exam in April 1981 and returned to Istanbul triumphantly with my diploma.

## Detention at the Ayvalık police station

In the last days of December 1980, I went to Ayvalık to see my mother, my elder sister, my father, and my mother-in-law. As I was leaving my father’s house, he now being mostly bedridden, a black police car that had apparently been following me pulled up in front of me. Plainclothes police detained me on the grounds that I was wanted by martial law and locked me in a room in the building left over from the Greeks that had formerly been used as a hospital, then a tax office (now the municipality building), and at that time was being used as martial law headquarters. Toward evening, they took me and handed me over to the police station in the city center. At the station, I was locked in a detention cell 2 x 2 meters wide, with a low ceiling, looking out through a narrow slit. This was the harshest treatment the state had applied to me until that day.

Just about a month before, I had been able to fly to Stockholm without any obstacle. If I were wanted by martial law, they wouldn’t have let me go. There was an unusual situation. I spent that night standing without eating or drinking anything. The next morning, the commissioner took me out and sat me in an armchair, had some food brought, and explained the situation: I was not wanted by martial law. If I were, he would be the first to know in Ayvalık. However, the captain, who was a very strict martial law commander (who raided rich people’s houses in Çamlık and emptied whiskey bottles into toilets), had ordered my detention based on a tip from a teacher who was a hardcore MHP fascist in the town saying “The notorious communist Şahin Alpay is walking around freely.” The commissioner was treating me well. He said he had inquired first from Balıkesir, then from Ankara whether I was wanted, and that this was not the case, that it had originated from the captain. (There was a military-police jurisdictional conflict going on.)

I spent four or five days and nights at the police station, sitting in an armchair. Even my relatives didn’t dare come to see me. On the last day of the year, I learned that the police would come to take me, apparently because the captain insisted on transferring me to the Izmir martial law command. Indeed, toward evening two young plainclothes policemen appeared. My brother-in-law Özbek hired a taxi. Thus we went to Izmir by car, not by bus. The policemen were saying on the way that there might be a mistake, that such mistakes do occur. I was handed over to the First Branch on the top floor of the police center in Basmane. It was apparent from the electrical shock equipment and the bastinado on the floor that the room I was first taken to was a torture chamber. A gray-haired commissioner informed me that he was sure my name was not among those wanted, but that they had to hand me over to martial law; and that this could only be done on Monday. It was Friday. I would spend at least three nights at the first branch. The gray-haired commissioner sat me on a chair in the corridor. The weather was terribly cold. The howling wind entered from one corner of the corridor and exited from the other.

On the last night of 1980, I witnessed scenes that could only be seen in horror films. Near the chair where I was seated, there was a young man lying on the floor, handcuffed to the legs of a bench. Policemen kicked him as they passed by. Nurses in white coats were entering and exiting a nearby room. At one point, about a hundred young people being held in the detention compartments on that floor were lined up under the supervision of plainclothes police and taken to and from the toilet on the lower floor. It was evident from the various limbs of the young people being covered with bandages that they had been tortured, and that the nurses walking around were tending to their wounds. From the television in the room where the gray-haired commissioner sat, belly dance music was rising. That’s how we entered 1981.

The next morning they locked me in the First Branch’s archive and of course handcuffed me by the wrist to metal shelves so I wouldn’t rummage through the files. I had no chance of moving from my spot. The outside was visible through the window, which still meant a positive change of environment. I wasn’t forgotten in the archive; three times a day they gave me a kind of toast sandwich and water, took me to the toilet and back. Spending two days and one night between January 1 and 3, 1981 under these conditions further enriched my experiences of being patient and enduring difficulties.

On Monday, January 3, a new and harsh commissioner came in place of the moderate gray-haired one and ordered me to be thrown immediately into the detention ward. I was taken out of the archive and locked in one of the detention rooms behind iron bars, packed with dozens of people. There was no room to move in the room. For some reason, I didn’t want to talk to anyone. Then a face appeared in the narrow window between the adjacent room and ours. My friend Ahmet Aras, from the TİP days and then Stockholm days, his hair all disheveled and unkempt, was calling out to me in astonishment at seeing me there. I didn’t feel like talking much even with him. During a group bathroom break, I found the opportunity to ask one of the policemen what would happen to me. “We’ll hand you over to Martial Law today,” he said.

## Fatma comes to my rescue

Late in the afternoon they took me and along with several other people put us on a bus and took us to the barracks I would learn was in Narlıdere. During the bus journey, with the joy of seeing daylight after days, I felt like a normal citizen going on an outing. Just like the normality I felt years ago when traveling from Mardin to Gaziantep. I was locked in one of the dormitory wards being used as detention at the barracks in Narlıdere. There were many young people in the ward. Some of the bunks had dirty mattresses on them. Some of the young people, probably because of my age, showed me warmth and I lay down on one of the mattresses. Again I tried to talk to people as little as possible. This must have been a kind of defense mechanism. For a long time I had been in search of saving my own skin. I had no desire to listen to what others had been through. I spent that night, curious about when I could get out of here, sometimes dozing off, sometimes staring at the ceiling. Martial law commands had the authority to hold people in detention for a long time. There were those who remained in detention for years without being brought before a court. I was very worried about my future. For me, life now seemed to have been reduced to a struggle for survival. I was brooding over what Fatma and the children were doing and would do.

On the morning of Tuesday, January 4, the privates took me from the ward and brought me out to the courtyard. A petty officer with some civilians beside him approached me; “Şahin Bey, we’re going to release you today…” he said. I couldn’t believe my ears. Freedom had appeared again. After the soldiers took various photographs of me, they put me in a vehicle and, at my request, dropped me off at Alsancak square. The first thing that came to my mind was to go to the house where Fatma’s niece Aslı and her husband Ali lived. I cannot describe the joy and happiness I felt when the door opened and I saw that Fatma was also inside.

As always, Fatma had come to my rescue again. My release had been made possible as follows: Our Ayvalık friend, the well-known writer and translator Ahmet Yorulmaz, had called Fatma on his own initiative and offered help. His wife Işık’s cousin was serving as a martial law prosecutor in Izmir. After getting the information needed to contact him, Fatma had left the children with relatives and come to Izmir. She had explained my situation to the military prosecutor, and the prosecutor, bless him, had given the necessary orders for my release. I had gotten off very, very lightly. You cannot know how I embraced my Fatma. I am forever grateful also to Ahmet and Işık Yorulmaz, both now deceased. My Fatma, as always, was sad and tired because of the troubles I had brought upon her, but also happy to be reunited with me. We immediately returned to Istanbul, to the children. My little Elvan was 12, my little Acar was 2 years old. Once again I was experiencing the joy of being reunited with my children.

In April I flew to Stockholm, took the final doctoral qualifying exam I needed to pass, and received my diploma. Thus I had become the first research assistant to complete a doctorate from the PRI research project directed by Tomas Hammar. Chief assistant Ko-Chih Tung would complete his doctorate shortly after me. No other doctoral thesis would come out of the project. Hammar was very pleased with me; he would have wanted me to stay in Sweden and at the university; but as he told Nermin Abadan, I was “very nationalistic, very determined to return to the homeland.” I said farewell to Tomas and my friends in Stockholm and returned to Istanbul.

“Classy renegade”

A period in my life had closed. I was returning to the homeland from Sweden with a new paradigm in my mind. What might be the points worth underlining once again regarding the years I had left behind? I could list them as follows:

1) The upbringing I received from my family, the education I received at my schools, and the values instilled in me by my circle of friends and social environment had made me quite distant from the nationalist worldview that was widespread in the society in which I was born and raised and was also instilled by the state. The understanding of “we are human first” instilled by my mother and by teacher Müveddet at Nilüfer Hatun Primary School had deeply influenced me, and this understanding had been increasingly reinforced during the year I spent in the USA on an AFS scholarship. As I explained above, when returning from the USA to Turkey in 1962, the question in my mind was:

Why is the USA so rich and free, why is my country so poor and lacking in freedom? The answer given to this question by the Workers’ Party of Turkey had seemed justified: Poverty was widespread and there was no freedom in Turkey because we were a country that had been left behind, exploited by imperialism, primarily the USA, and their local collaborators.

I had read Karl Marx’s “Communist Manifesto” for the first time in the USA and was influenced by it. The Ankara and especially the Mülkiye environment had surrendered my mind to increasingly radical interpretations of Marxism. Reading Lenin, primarily the books titled State and Revolution and What Is to Be Done?, had opened the door in my mind to the violent and totalitarian interpretations of the left, and I had gradually adopted Mao’s interpretations: For the establishment of socialism, nationalizing the means of production and replacing the market with planning was not enough; a revolution in minds was also needed. This is what the “Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution” was for…

2) During my years studying at Mülkiye, I had gradually become a radical revolutionary, “Marxist, Leninist, even Maoist,” but I had never believed that revolution would be possible “tomorrow” in Turkey, and I had thought that a long and patient preparatory period was needed. I had never been a “man of action.” Because I had received a good education and knew English well, with the opportunities these provided, I was essentially concerned with the “theory” of revolution. Despite this, despite thinking that the revolutionary movement in Turkey was far behind the stage of organization and party formation, I couldn’t refuse to join the TİİKP. Because even though I didn’t believe in the TİİKP at all, even though I thought it was very distant, I believed in revolution.

I hadn’t been able to object to Doğu Perinçek sending me to the Palestinian resistance movement either. This was partly related to being desperate (being wanted by martial law), but it was more related to commitment to the idea of revolution, to the belief that behaving otherwise would be incompatible with honesty. Perhaps my subconscious was saying: I’ll go, I’ll die for the cause, and thus I’ll be freed from this agonizing contradiction between my private and public lives, and find peace. Indeed, with this hope, while at Reşadiye, I had volunteered for the operation to be conducted against Israel.

3) I had two friends (or if you prefer, “comrades”) who were quite influential on my increasingly radical revolutionary activism. The first was Doğu Perinçek (henceforth DP). As I described above, I had initially experienced a great intellectual affinity and friendship with him. Later he had greatly disappointed me, and my trust in him had been completely destroyed. It was clear that DP’s purpose in sending me to the Palestinian Resistance Movement was to rub my nose in it, to remind me that he was the real boss, to strip me of the privileges I had (my family, my status) and to “proletarianize” me. (According to what I heard later, he had said about Atıl, Cengiz, and me, “We sent the loose elements to Palestine so they wouldn’t become a problem for us later…”) Between 1966 and 1971, DP and I had been very close. After that date, I ran into him only once, at a meeting in the 1990s; we merely exchanged greetings. I refrained from sharing my opinions about him publicly. I think he was pleased with this, as he characterized me as a “classy renegade” in one of his writings.

4) The other “comrade” was Halil Berktay. The seeds of Maoism in Turkey had been sown through the joint efforts of the two of us. I had been close to his father Erdoğan Berktay and members of his family. We had common aspects stemming from being of population exchange origin and from studying at Robert College. However, when we parted in 1971, I thought he had “lost his soul” and had become Doğu Perinçek’s “Suslov.” (I should remind you: Mikhail Suslov was the ideologue of the Soviet Communist Party from 1965 until his death in 1982.) Halil’s closeness with Perinçek continued until the end of the 1980s. He later left politics and turned to history. We got together again several times; we remembered that we were friends. What I experienced with these two friends who had roles in my life would lead me to this conclusion: Being of like mind is one thing, friendship is another. What I would experience later would also confirm this.

5) At the end of the approximately 9 months I spent in the Palestinian Resistance Movement, my sympathy and love for the Palestinian people had deepened and become permanent. However, I gradually came to hate weapons and violence. I now believed that violence breeds violence; no one has the right to kill anyone for any reason.

6) Communism, fascism, Islamism, or similar authoritarian-totalitarian ideologies resulted in the enslavement of the individual. The subject of freedom was not class, nation, or religious community, but only and only the human being, the individual.

7) The practice of the left in the world and in Turkey had gone bankrupt. When I understood this, I had become unable to think of anything other than saving myself and being reunited with Fatma and Elvan. I had found no place to take refuge other than my family, my elder brother, and my old close friends. I had not hesitated to risk the safety of my dearly beloved elder brother in order to save myself from the impasse I had thrown myself into. Fatma was right to find this strange and to reproach me for it.

8) Sweden had shown me that it was possible to establish a society as free and as just as possible. In Sweden, I had found the opportunity to put my life back in order with the opportunities provided by civilized society. I couldn’t have found the opportunities offered to me there in any other country. For this reason, I was eternally grateful to the Swedish state and to Swedes. I likened Sweden to “the world’s washing machine”: It took in radicals and revolutionaries from one end, washed them, and liberals and social democrats came out from the other end. (What I would experience in Turkey years later would also strengthen these feelings. My Swedish friends would also play a considerable role in my rescue from the Silivri pit.)

9) I had great admiration for what the Swedish state had achieved; for Swedes’ commitment to human values, their honesty, their industriousness in general. I had made many Swedish friends. I greatly appreciated Swedish politicians. The civilized way they competed and behaved like ordinary citizens had greatly impressed me. Despite all this, I was aware that I didn’t belong there. If Fatma had left me, if no amnesty had been declared and I had been condemned to stay in Sweden for life, I think I would have been miserable and would have withered away. Despite what would happen to me, I never regretted returning to the homeland with the opportunity the amnesty provided. While returning, the thought of applying for Swedish citizenship did cross my mind, but I gave up on it thinking that living in Turkey and obtaining citizenship from Sweden would be morally and legally problematic.

During the process of returning from Sweden to Turkey, a paradigm shift had occurred in my mind. This had not happened all at once, but through a process similar to what Thomas Kuhn described. The roughly Marxist-Leninist paradigm in my mind had developed ever-growing gaps in the face of reality, and eventually collapsed and gave way to a new paradigm that could be called liberal. In this process, the film reel in my mind was rewinding step by step: Mao had taken the place of Chinese emperors… The Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution was nothing but an intra-party power struggle… In Russia, the “revisionists” of the Second International who advocated democracy had been proven right, and Lenin and the revolutionaries had paved the way for Stalin’s personal dictatorship… In reality, the fish was rotting from the head; at the source of totalitarianism was the Marxist paradigm, the idea of the dictatorship of the proletariat… Freedom of expression and criticism, in short political freedom, was the indispensable means of establishing a free and just society… Without establishing a competitive market economy, political freedom could not be achieved in a system where the state, not society, dominated the economy…

In this paradigm shift in my mind, what I had experienced as well as what I had read, but above all one book, had played a great role. Karl R. Popper’s The Open Society and Its Enemies had become my bedside book. (As I mentioned above, when Mete Tunçay suggested in 1967 that I translate the second volume of the book concerning Marx into Turkish, I had felt insulted and immediately refused.) I had started reading all of Popper’s works that I could get my hands on and comprehend. Leszek Kolakowski’s Main Currents of Marxism and Jon Elster’s books An Introduction to Karl Marx and Making Sense of Marx would also help me see the gaps in the “old paradigm.” The articles by Swedish economist Assar Lindbeck that I would translate into Turkish under the title Piyasa Ekonomisi ve Demokrasi (Market Economy and Democracy, Birey ve Toplum Publications, Istanbul 1985) explained very well the differences between the liberal, pro-market interpretations and the statist-centralist interpretations of social democracy. As I read the world and Turkey in line with the new paradigm in my mind, I now defined myself as a liberal social democrat or social liberal.

The weaknesses of the positivism of Auguste Comte, which had long dominated the social sciences, that is, the thesis that science would gradually replace religion with modernization, were also becoming clear in my mind. Religious beliefs that addressed people’s spiritual rather than material needs maintained their power even in the most advanced modernized societies. In the face of life’s uncertainties, pains, and deprivations, people felt the need to believe. My own individual experiences also confirmed this. In my most troubled, most difficult days, I had felt the need to pray in my own language, to beg God to save me. It was not religious beliefs that were retreating in the world, but religious institutions. I now defined my beliefs not with atheism but with a kind of deism. In parallel with this new understanding, my views on religion and secularism had also changed considerably: In Turkey, the authoritarian secularism practice of the state controlling and monopolizing religion was pitting the state against the religious segment of society and leading to the development of Islamist authoritarian political movements. (As I write these lines, I now also have difficulty defining myself as a “deist,” and see myself more as agnostic. Why? This should be the subject of a book called “Religion and Me.”)

# CHAPTER VII / BACK TO ISTANBUL AND CUMHURİYET

In April 1981, I passed my final examination, which I had left until the last day in order to fully utilize the four-year Swedish state scholarship I had received for my doctorate at Stockholm University, received my diploma, and returned home for good. Through my friend Zafer Toprak, who never withheld his support, I found a temporary job and began working as an editor at Yurt Ansiklopedisi (Homeland Encyclopedia). But the time had come to find myself a permanent job. My dear Fatma was saying that finding a job would be difficult in this extraordinary period, and since I loved reading and writing, perhaps starting a bookstore-publishing house would be a good idea. This way, I could both do work I loved and make a living. She was also willing to help me in this endeavor. As always, I did not follow her advice. On the grounds that I had no business acumen and that if we embarked on such a venture we would quickly lose all our capital, I said “no.”

In the autumn of 1981, I had to leave Yurt Ansiklopedisi as well. The general publication director had changed, and a classmate of mine from Robert Lisesi had been appointed in his place. This friend’s first act was to convey through an intermediary the message that I was “working little but receiving much pay; I either needed to work more or accept less money.” Being treated this way by someone I considered a friend and thought would value my work hurt me considerably. I immediately submitted my resignation. The job I had obtained through one friend had been terminated by another friend; I was completely unemployed. When I went to Ayvalık to see Fatma and the children, I felt myself on the verge of depression, also due to the extreme heat.

My father’s health had deteriorated considerably, and he had become quite frail. He could no longer leave his house on Sefa Avenue in Ayvalık, a house left over from the Greeks. I made an arrangement with a family we knew who lived nearby to look after him and meet his needs, including meals. His money was running out. He had leased his olive groves for six years in exchange for an amount to be paid in liras; the inflation that reached 100% in 1980 had rendered the money he received worthless. In the first days of September, I took him to the Kaptan family’s house in Çamlık and gave him a bath; then, with a heavy heart, I took him back to the run-down house where he lived alone. A few days later, the caretaker family informed me that he had passed away in his sleep. On September 9th, we buried him in a solitary grave in the Ayvalık municipal cemetery. A life that had seen happiness in very few moments and was mostly filled with sorrow had come to an end. He was born in 1912 and died in 1981, at the age of 69; he had chosen to be alone for approximately half of his life.

## Toward Cumhuriyet

When I thought that if university did not work out upon returning to Turkey, I could work in the press, Abdi İpekçi, whom I thought I could ask for help, had unfortunately been assassinated. But my friend from Mülkiye, Hasan Cemal, had been appointed as the general publication director of Cumhuriyet newspaper in April 1981, which was a fortunate coincidence for me. Hasan and I had a friendship that continued since the 1960s. In 1968, when the office of Devrim magazine, where he was the managing editor, was across from the office of Aydınlık Sosyalist Dergi, where I was an editorial board member, in an apartment on Adakale Street, we had started seeing each other frequently.

Even during the years I was in Stockholm, we maintained contact with Hasan; when he was the Ankara bureau chief, he had given me a free subscription to the newspaper. I had also sent Cumhuriyet an article under the pen name Mehmet Çağ, about “Swedish imperialism” (!), titled “The Most Advanced Monopolization is in Sweden,” which was published as a full page for two days (October 5-6, 1976), and Hasan had it published. When chief columnist Nadir Nadi read the article criticizing Sweden, he was quite surprised and gave Hasan a mild reprimand. But in the letter Hasan sent to Stockholm, he wrote that the article was well-received and widely read in CHP (Republican People’s Party) circles, and he was awaiting my new contributions.

A more realistic assessment came from Ömer Madra: “Mehmet Çağ’s article was read with considerable interest here. Generally, it was well-liked. There are also some who find it a bit schematic. I also have a criticism: It seemed like some sections were written assuming the reader was more knowledgeable than they actually were. Just one example: Why the ‘reform’ proposal about making workers shareholders in company capital was a crappy thing was not explained but brushed over in one sentence… And so on.” (7.11.1976) What I was trying to convey was this: The project envisioning that funds formed from deductions from workers’ wages would gradually grow and own industrial property had faced harsh criticism on the grounds that it would eliminate competition in the economy. These criticisms, which also seemed very reasonable to me, would eventually lead the social democrats to shelve this proposal. Meanwhile, the truth was that by the end of the 1970s, I no longer saw Sweden as an “imperialist” country.

I decided to go and ask Hasan for a job. One of the newspaper’s writers, Uğur Mumcu, was a friend I had met during my days working at Ankara University. His father had served as the land registry and cadastre director in Ayvalık for a while, and through a housing cooperative formed by employees at the directorate at that time, he had become the owner of a summer house in Armutçuk, on the shore facing Lale Island. Uğur and his wife Güldal spent their summers in this house, and we had good relations with them. During the long walks Uğur and I took, we largely agreed that Turkey’s problems could only be remedied with a Western-style democratic regime. Thinking that Uğur could also support me, I went to Hasan. I said: “As I understand it, you’re trying to turn Cumhuriyet into a ‘reference paper’ similar to Western examples… You know I completed my doctorate in Sweden and returned, but they won’t hire me at universities because of my communist past. With my writing experience, I can help with what you want to do at the newspaper. For example, all serious newspapers in the West have book pages. I could prepare such a page for Cumhuriyet…”

Hasan, after consultations that I believe included Uğur and İlhan Selçuk, invited me to prepare the book page I had proposed at the newspaper starting from the new year. The page began publication on January 28, 1982, under the title “Review and Research in the Publishing World.” I also started working as a staff member at the newspaper from September 1, 1982. Thus, I was taking my first step into journalism within the framework of Hasan Cemal’s project to give Cumhuriyet the identity of a reference newspaper that highly educated people of all political persuasions could read.

When I started working at Cumhuriyet, it seemed inevitable that a conflict would occur between the views I had adopted during my years in Sweden and the nationalist-statist and laicist (in the sense of advocating state control of religion rather than separation of church and state) ideology that dominated the newspaper’s employees in general, but especially the senior writers led by İlhan Selçuk (whom Hasan Cemal would increasingly refer to as “sugar big brothers”), as well as the mentality that saw the armed forces as the guardian of this ideology. This mentality would be best described by Hasan Cemal in his book dedicated to the memory of Doğan Avcıoğlu, published years later. (Let No One Be Angry, I Wrote About Myself, Doğan Kitap 1999.) However, working at Cumhuriyet was the only meaningful job opportunity I had at the time. I needed to be patient. On the other hand, the impression I got from Hasan Cemal gave me hope that views closer to mine, more liberal in orientation, could eventually find ground within Cumhuriyet.

## İlhan Selçuk’s Gulag

From September 1982, I began working at Cumhuriyet newspaper as the Head of the Research Department. Along with me, Aydın Emeç, a close friend of my late elder brother, started as culture editor, and Celal Üster, my maternal uncle Celal’s grandson and from the Aydınlık circle, started as his assistant. My friend from the English High School for Boys, Murat Belge, was preparing a weekly popular culture page for the newspaper, while my friend Osman Ulagay, also from the same school and the Aydınlık circle, began writing economics articles. Of my close friends from the Aydınlık circle, Cengiz Çandar was covering foreign policy, and Kenan Mortan was working as an economics correspondent. In other words, Cumhuriyet presented quite a familiar environment for me. In a short time, I would also make new friends such as foreign policy editor and writer Ergun Balcı, News Director Yalçın Bayer, and back page editor Mehmet Yaşin. From the Ankara bureau, especially the late Ufuk Güldemir, Yalçın Doğan, Sedat Ergin, and Yasemin Çongar would become lifelong friends. Cengiz, with his usual mischievousness, would tease: “So what if you got a doctorate in Sweden? Here we went round and round and ended up meeting here…”

On one hand, I was preparing the (half) page we named “Review and Research in the Publishing World” which came out weekly, and on the other hand, at Hasan Cemal’s (hereafter HC) request, I was attending the morning editorial meetings, voicing the deficiencies and errors I saw in that day’s newspaper and making suggestions. Over time, my functions would diversify to include giving HC reports on possible innovations at the newspaper, editing the newspaper’s yearbooks, preparing the speeches HC would deliver at International Press Institute (IPI) meetings, as well as occasionally conducting interviews for the newspaper and writing for the supplements the newspaper published. One of HC’s suggestions was that I write the history of Cumhuriyet newspaper. Because I could foresee the problems this would cause me, I procrastinated on this task; HC did not insist. As is known, during World War II, Cumhuriyet newspaper had followed a pro-Nazi Germany editorial policy for a while; for this reason, rumors had spread that they had received money from the Germans. In other words, writing an objective history for Cumhuriyet newspaper was not easy. It still has not been written.

Another idea of HC’s was to establish an “Advisory Board” for himself. Its members would consist of the managing editor (my military service friend, SBF graduate) Okay Gönensin, Osman Ulagay, Ergun Balcı, Aydın Emeç, Osman Ulagay, Aydın Emeç, Şükran Ketenci, Cengiz Çandar, and Yalçın Pekşen, and I would serve as secretary. I was recording what was discussed at the Advisory Board’s first meetings held on October 19 and November 2, 1982, as follows:

“It was emphasized that Cumhuriyet, being Turkey’s only opinion newspaper, had this quality as its strongest aspect and that it needed to preserve and develop this quality. It was stated that our newspaper had a great impact and responsibility on the intellectual development of especially the newly emerging intellectual generations. It was said that in the short term, at a time when the struggle to expand and establish democracy would be waged, this responsibility was even heavier.

It was observed that the experiences of the last twenty years in the world and in our country had brought the young intellectual generation to a consciousness of criticizing tested and defeated political stances and learning lessons from them; that the young generations were directed to look at various intellectual currents in the world and at home more democratically and without prejudice.

It was emphasized that in the upcoming period of struggle for democracy, our newspaper, with its line defending pluralism in politics, economy, and culture; fundamental rights and freedoms; national interests against foreign interests; and workers’ interests against the interests of capital, should provide representation opportunities for all intellectual currents within the framework outlined above. It was said that only in this way could it gain readers’ trust and find the opportunity to expand further.

It was discussed that in the upcoming period, while continuing its publication on a pluralist-democratic line domestically and a line defending national interests externally, it was also necessary to establish the understanding that the private sector makes important contributions to our economy, and that not every foreign relation involves malice or enmity. It was said that the newspaper’s ability to sell more and expand further would only be possible by adhering to this correct understanding.

The matter that the participants emphasized importantly and unanimously was related to the newspaper’s ‘image.’ It was stated that the newspaper’s general atmosphere suggested ‘pessimism’; that it left the impression on readers that everything in the world and in the country was going badly and nothing was good. While the generally negative aspects and events of society were persistently dwelt upon (even under today’s conditions, even under much worse conditions), it was said that the perspective that there were and could be many good, positive events in society was being neglected. It was pointed out that everything was viewed with a critical eye ‘for the sake of criticizing,’ and that this had permeated from columnists to the entertainment and Ciddiyet (Seriousness) pages.

It was agreed that the newspaper’s much-complained-about tedious atmosphere came not essentially from layout and printing technique, but from this ‘pessimism.’ It was requested that more space be allocated to positive developments achieved in our country, to positive work done; that a ‘balanced’ approach be provided to the reader.

It was discussed that in cases where Cumhuriyet newspaper’s self-evaluation was concerned, it should not proceed from the assumption that it was right and justified in every period.

The damages caused to the newspaper by the failure to achieve complete objectivity in news, and even by the grave errors made in this regard, were discussed, and it was hoped that the important success achieved in this matter in the last year would be continued, and that complete objectivity would be achieved in news language and presentation.” (For the full text of my report, see Hasan Cemal, I Loved Cumhuriyet So Much, Doğan Kitap, 2005, pp. 75-77.)

I was not sure that these views about the newspaper were fully adopted by the Advisory Board members, except perhaps Osman Ulagay. The report I drafted perhaps more expressed the new direction HC was trying to set for the newspaper, as I understood it. The board, which was planned to meet weekly, dispersed after meeting only a few times. I think İlhan Selçuk (hereafter İS) did not like the emergence of an alternative to the board composed of senior writers. In my first months at the newspaper, during a dinner we had alone during an Istanbul visit, Uğur unexpectedly asked if I wanted to write a column. Honestly, I did not want this yet, because I knew my pen would not be free; I was wary of the senior writers who shared the newspaper’s statist-nationalist-laicist views, especially İS, taking a stance against me; I thought I had to be cautious for a while. It would soon become clear that I was not at all wrong about this.

In October 1983, HC asked me to write a report answering the question “How can Cumhuriyet become a newspaper that resolutely defends libertarian democracy based on human rights and at the same time applies universal journalism rules?” The report dated October 29, 1983, which HC quoted in full in his book titled I Loved Cumhuriyet So Much!, is interesting in that it reflects my excessively optimistic views of those days, quite detached from reality (substituting my wishes for facts), as almost always. I reproduce it below.

## The democracy graft has taken hold

“Why couldn’t a pluralistic democratic order based on political rights and freedoms be established healthily in Turkey? Where should the reasons be sought for its interruption by the 1960, 1971, and 1980 interventions, and for our entering the 1980s with an anti-democratic legal framework like the 1982 Constitution? In light of the answers to these questions, is the establishment of democracy as practiced in Western European countries a pipe dream for Turkey? If not, what are the lessons to be drawn in light of past experiences? What should be done to establish and protect democracy? Before briefly answering these questions, it is necessary to very roughly address some theoretical issues related to social development.

I am of the opinion that theories claiming that social events develop according to certain immutable laws constitute a great obstacle to our understanding and directing social development. I think such theories are related to religious beliefs that explain events through fate and destiny.

Today, science accepts that it is not capable of explaining everything, and teaches that scientific truths constantly change, that is, knowledge considered correct is always falsified, and that science progresses not through the accumulation of correct knowledge but through replacing knowledge understood to be wrong with what appears more correct, and that no knowledge is absolutely correct.

Science, whose primary purpose is said to be seeking certain regularities (laws) in nature as well as in society, today shows that even in nature such regularity occurs very rarely, that it is impossible to establish laws. The understanding that natural and social events are directed by certain laws has remained in the 19th century. In natural sciences, Einstein’s theories replaced Newtonian physics. In social sciences, the positivist understanding that social events (like natural events) are directed by some laws has been largely abandoned. It is generally accepted (except by party ideologues and a very limited circle of scientists) that the theory of historical materialism, which constitutes a positivist interpretation of Marxism, has also been breached in many respects and is inadequate in explaining social developments.

Parliamentary democracy, which had grown and developed in the environment of Western European societies, had been planted in Turkey, which had no such tradition of governance, like a foreign “sapling” by a conscious actor, a political elite that wanted to Westernize Turkey (through a process that began with the Tanzimat and even earlier).

The Ottoman political elite, in constant cultural exchange with the West and influenced by this civilization, introduced the aspects they saw as achievable into Turkish society. Although the structural characteristics of society did not seem at all favorable, they waged a hard struggle against traditionalist forces that wanted to keep society in its traditional structure and gradually brought the institutions of Western civilization to the country. I accept as a secondary explanation that the difficulties we have encountered since the 1950s in establishing parliamentary democracy stem from the difficulties this foreign “sapling” encountered in taking root in our social soil. In my opinion, by the time we reached the 1970s, the graft had essentially taken hold. The sapling had begun to weave its roots in a way that would be difficult to uproot. These roots are democratic institutions to the extent we have been able to establish them, rights and freedoms to the extent they are respected, etc. I reach this conclusion by comparing with “Eastern” and “Southern” societies where the sapling of democracy could not be planted at all, could not find the opportunity to develop.

The democracy graft has taken hold in Turkey. The issue is how it will be developed and protected. Here, the influence of the most general economic and political conditions in the world and in Turkey must be taken into account. But I believe the main knot lies in the stance the Turkish political elite will take. As can be seen, I advocate the thesis that political action and the political elite are of great importance. I agree with those who think the political elite is primarily responsible for the defeats and setbacks democracy has suffered in Turkey.

Although each of the 1960, 1971, and 1980 military interventions had its own specific causes and consequences, the general conditions that gave rise to these interventions lie neither at the economic nor the cultural (structural) level. From the 1950s to the mid-1970s, Turkey was experiencing unprecedented economic development in its history. During the same period, the general and political education of the people was increasing to an unprecedented extent in Turkey’s history.

I see our political elite’s failure to reach a consensus on “pluralistic democracy” as the main culprit for the defeats and setbacks democracy has suffered in our country. Relatedly, our political elite has not been able to unite on the principle that politics should command arms, that the army should be under the command of parliament.

Within our political elite, four fairly strong currents are against democracy, two on the “right” in the conservative sense and two on the “left” in the reformist sense (on the right, fascists and Sharia supporters; on the left, the thousand and one factions of communists and nationalist-revolutionaries). The “populist” wing (DP - AP, the Democrat Party and the Justice Party) of the Westernist-reformists who founded democracy sees democracy as majority dictatorship, while the “elitist” CHP could only accept that the right to govern lies with the majority in the 1970s.
