However, the two democratic parties that could agree on the principle of “parliamentary supremacy” after the March 12, 1971 intervention, with the aim of “being in power at any cost,” committed the folly of portraying each other as outside the constitution and cooperating (at various levels) with anti-democratic currents, one on the right and the other on the left, giving these anti-democratic currents the opportunity to have a say in the country’s fate with a power they never possessed among the people.

“Democratic” parties failed to save the regime by reaching a compromise in an environment where fascist, communist, or Sharia forces ran rampant; they in a sense prepared their own end. Along with the political elite, some of the intellectuals also cut the branch they were sitting on.

Under these conditions, the army, which has always seen itself as having a say in the country’s fate, was “compelled” to intervene in the regime. (I attach no value whatsoever to the theory that the environment created in the second half of the 1970s was a conspiracy to bring the army to power.) And on a foundation of legitimacy and consensus unprecedented in the country’s history… And the army, in accordance with its own traditions and logic, reorganized society in a “barracks” order, in a statist-centralist direction.

A point that should not be forgotten is that the army is aware of the limits of the public support and legitimacy it relies on. That limit is that the majority of the people will not long allow their right to determine political power with their own vote and to change a government they do not like to be taken from them.

In succinct terms, if we want democracy, democracy can exist. (It is of course not possible to protect and develop parliamentary democracy with those who advocate it because it provides a good environment for preparations to destroy it.)

Those who advocate parliamentary democracy based on political freedoms have three tasks ahead:

1. To consider protecting democracy more important than coming to power and to cooperate for this. 2. To draw a clear line between themselves and those who do not believe in democracy on the right and left. 3. Not to accept “the freedom to destroy democracy.” There is indeed a problem in Turkey of limiting the freedoms of enemies of democracy. Is it sufficient to determine this limit by the element of coercion?

This question is a question worth discussing.

I think the main responsibility in achieving these goals falls on the political movement we have now begun to call the social democratic current. Because I believe that true democrats are social democrats. I believe that social democracy in Turkey needs to achieve clarity primarily on the following points:

1. The parliamentary order based on political rights and freedoms, on universal suffrage, is not a bourgeois democracy in the West either, but the work of a workers’ and laborers’ movement led by social democratic parties.

2. Pluralistic political democracy can only be healthy together with a pluralistic economic and cultural structure. Pluralistic democracy requires a cultural structure that is as open to the outside as possible and as decentralized as possible. The polycentric structure in the economy must also be established in culture.

3. The social democratic state’s intervention in society should be for establishing and developing a pluralistic structure. The market economy is the mechanism that most effectively mobilizes the productive power of the people. Humanity is not at a level of maturity to put a stronger motivation in place of personal gain. This means that a fundamental change in mentality is needed in the Turkish social democratic current, which continues a centralist-statist economic mindset.

4. Turkish social democracy must now see that the world economic system is a system of interdependence. Integration with the European Economic Community (EEC) does not conflict with the aim of developing our political and economic relations with Islamic and southern countries.

5. Integration with the EEC is also important in terms of supporting our political democracy with solid external foundations. Turkey should be within the military alliance of Western democracies (NATO). The problems between us and Greece should be resolved as soon as possible.” (For the full report, see: Hasan Cemal, I Loved Cumhuriyet So Much, Doğan Kitap, 2005, pp. 118-122.)

## In Sirmen’s room

At that time, the newspaper’s administrative headquarters was in Cağaloğlu, in a masonry building constructed right next to the wooden building that once housed the headquarters of the Committee of Union and Progress and was now used as a warehouse. In the large room at the end of the top floor was the owner and chief columnist Nadir Nadi, in the room next to him the general publication director Hasan Cemal, and in the following rooms were the offices of senior writers (İlhan Selçuk, Oktay Akbal, Ali Sirmen, in that order) and the “Opinions” page editor Sami Karaören. The room closest to the entrance of the floor belonged to Ali Sirmen, who at that time was in prison, convicted in the Peace Association case. In the first days, Hasan Cemal placed me in Sirmen’s room by having an additional desk put in. (I heard that when Sirmen heard this, he made the joke about me: “The fastest-climbing man in the newspaper’s history.”) However, I would soon descend as quickly as I had climbed. For the books I introduced on the page I prepared and my choices regarding interviews drew reactions not only from senior writers but also from employees who at that time were committed to Cumhuriyet’s traditional line.

In my first days of work, I first visited Nadir Nadi and introduced myself; then I stopped by İlhan Selçuk and paid my respects. I had no prior acquaintance with Selçuk; we knew each other from our writings. Since his views seemed too statist-nationalist-laicist to me, I tried to avoid dealing with him. One day, as he was passing in front of the room where I sat, in an unusual manner, without entering, he poked his head through the door and greeted me; he said it would be beneficial for us to get together and talk from time to time, thus avoiding unwanted disagreements. It was clear that from my first days, he was uncomfortable with my presence at the newspaper. He must have somehow made this felt to HC as well, because after a while HC no longer stopped by or greeted me when passing in front of my room. It was becoming clear that my days in that room were numbered.

## I’m getting on their nerves

Those whose nerves I was getting on with my presence were not limited to the “sugar big brothers.” Okay Gönensin, the managing editor and the newspaper’s second-in-command after HC, who graduated from Mülkiye a few years after me, was also not at all pleased with the criticisms and suggestions I made about the newspaper’s content at morning meetings. (Unfortunately, my relationship with the late Okay, with whom I would later work at Sabah newspaper as well, was never good.) My choices regarding the ten most noteworthy books of the year, which I had made a habit of ranking on the page I managed at year-ends, were also generally not approved of. The absence of Yalçın Küçük’s book Theses on Intellectuals in the 1983 ranking had caused veiled grumbles reflected in the writings of both Oktay Akbal and Yalçın Doğan.

The September 12 military administration had ended, and the Motherland Party (ANAP) founded by Turgut Özal had won the 1983 general elections. I found it very positive that Özal was pursuing a policy of eliminating polarization and reconciling society under the slogan of “uniting four currents” and pioneering steps toward transition to a market economy. For this reason, I wrote a letter expressing my appreciation to him. (Unfortunately, I could not find a copy of this letter in my archive.) I had HC and Cengiz Çandar read the letter. HC said, “Don’t send this, if the sugar big brothers see it they’ll really give us hell…” Cengiz’s reaction was, “Well, well… You’ve gone from Maoism to Özalism…” (Cengiz would resign from Cumhuriyet in 1987 and would become an advisor to Özal some time later.)

Like most of our past (and future) politicians, Turgut Özal also had two faces, positive and negative. I most liked his statements “my mother is Kurdish” and “What if we discussed federalism.” (I would have liked to meet Özal. Taha Akyol, with whom I gradually became close friends, wanted to introduce me to Özal at one point after I left Cumhuriyet in 1992, but it was not meant to be.)

## I’m being relegated to the archive

Finally, I was brought down from the top floor as quickly as I had climbed. First, I was placed in an empty room in the adjacent building where the administrative units were located. Some time later, I was transferred to a narrow, glass-enclosed compartment specially built for me in the newspaper’s archive; in short, I was “relegated to the archive.” Subsequently, my attendance at morning meetings was no longer wanted. This was how HC prevented me from being visible and getting on people’s nerves. He stopped coming by my compartment too. But gradually his nerves were also starting to fray. I had lent him Karl Popper’s book The Open Society and Its Enemies, containing his political philosophy, and then Bryan Magee’s book on Popper’s philosophy of science. He was quite influenced by these, and when Enis Batur mentioned a Popper interview published in a French magazine, he asked him to translate it into Turkish and had it published in the newspaper’s newly launched “Politics ’84” supplement. (December 10, 1984).

Contrary to what HC would write in his book about Cumhuriyet, I had no role whatsoever in the translation and publication of this interview. Indeed, HC would later correct this: “I had begun to know Popper and The Open Society and Its Enemies thanks to Şahin Alpay in the early 1980s. When we devoted two pages to Karl Popper in the politics supplement of Cumhuriyet newspaper, which I was managing at that time, I think it was 1984, there was an uproar within the newspaper, and İlhan Selçuk promptly declared the philosopher a counter-revolutionary in his column…” he wrote. (Milliyet, December 28, 2010.) What was more interesting was that I had notified Enis by letter, after having Seyfettin Gürsel check them since I did not know French, about sentences in the Turkish translation that were incompatible with Popper’s thought; because of this, a rift had developed between Enis and me.

HC would describe what happened following the publication of Enis’s Popper translation as follows: “According to İlhan Selçuk, (Popper) was a ‘counter-revolutionary.’ For this reason, all hell had broken loose between us. There were ‘counter-revolutionary infiltrations’ at Cumhuriyet. He did not name them explicitly, but Şahin Alpay was at the top of these. And I, as general publication director, was not doing my duty properly regarding these ‘infiltrations.’ A few days after the Popper interview in the politics supplement, İlhan Selçuk took up his pen and wrote a piece in his column that slammed Popper, concluding with ‘Despite Popper and his likes, history marches on!’” (I Loved Cumhuriyet So Much, Doğan Kitap, 2005, p. 141.)

“Intellectuals’ hell”

The İS column in question was published on 13.12.1984 under the title “Intellectuals’ Hell.” From that date on, İS and I never reconciled; we did not get together unless necessary. Upon HC’s insistence that it was “indispensable,” I had to include İS in the interviews I conducted during my last year at Cumhuriyet, about how intellectuals, academics, and politicians envisioned the country thirty years into the future. (See “Turkey in the Year 2020”, Cumhuriyet, 26/3 - 13/4 - 1991. The series was published as a book the same year by AFA Yayınları, owned by my old and late friend Atıl Ant.)

I had long since stopped reading İS’s writings. When articles targeting me without naming me came out, friends would immediately call and inform me “he’s writing about you.” That’s how I learned about his article declaring Popper a “counter-revolutionary.” I ignored it, but it did not escape others’ attention. Taha Akyol, who would later become a friend but whom I had not yet met at that time, was criticizing İS as well in his column, while emphasizing the value of Popper’s criticisms directed at totalitarian ideologies, in his usual polite style. (“The Karl Popper debate,” Tercüman, 18.12.1984.) Tahsin Yücel also said in an article, “…starting from a two-page conversation, we had writers who mocked and slammed Karl Popper, one of the most consistent defenders of free thought.” (“Our Cultural and Artistic Life from 1984 to 1985,” Milliyet, 8.1.1985.)

Following the debates that arose, HC came to see me one day in my compartment in the archive. In a very low voice so as not to be heard around, he told me not to pay attention to what İS wrote; that he, just like Doğan Avcıoğlu (1926 - 83), was consuming himself; that the future of the newspaper belonged to our generation, and he left. I too, in those days, mistakenly as always, believed that our generation would fully take over the newspaper after a while. Under HC’s management, the newspaper’s circulation (according to sales department reports) had risen from around 82,000 in 1983 to around 125,000 in 1987; and had reached around 120,000 in 1990. I greatly appreciated the understanding of journalism that HC expressed at morning meetings; I thought “If there is a journalist worthy of the title in Turkey, it is HC after Abdi İpekçi.”

“Conservatives selling progressivism”

Cumhuriyet’s senior columnists who embraced a strange synthesis of Marxism and Kemalism were the main elements preventing HC from making the newspaper he wanted. The late Oktay Akbal (1923 - 2015), who was the representative of views close to pure statist-nationalist-laicist Kemalism, was also one of those writers. The letter that Mete Tunçay sent to Akbal (with a copy to me as well), titled “Not a right-left issue, but a matter of level,” requesting publication in the newspaper, described the common mentality of the “sugar big brothers” very well:

“In your Yes/No piece published in the December 31, 1984 Cumhuriyet, you mentioned me without giving my name. According to you, a study I did (actually together with a friend), published in Tarih ve Toplum magazine last October, made me ‘ridiculous.’ When you say ‘some left-looking ’new right’ researchers, pseudo-scientists,’ you apparently mean to describe me. Dear Mr. Akbal, it is obvious that in your Yes/No, Black/White world, there is no room for ‘maybes,’ for ‘intermediate tones.’ But that world in your head has no relation to the real world woven of contingencies and grays. You are a conservative selling progressivism! I don’t know why you still torment yourself in vain by reading things. Unless you are open-minded, let alone being able to think something new, you cannot even understand and learn what others think! You say ‘I don’t believe in the science called history, I don’t even consider it a science.’ Since you consider yourself (presumably by God) as having been made privy to the secret of everything, you cannot grasp today’s reality just as you cannot grasp yesterday’s reality; you just keep repeating what you knew before.”

I had developed an antipathy, an allergy toward the late İS that seems quite meaningless when I look back from today. However, this was not simply a case of reacting against someone because of their different ideas, which is a typical form of intolerance; it was partly the result of the hostility I received from him. While I was trying to explain that I had purged myself of my past ideology, his persistent characterization of me as a “Maoist” was also getting on my nerves. HC would write about this:

“Ah, those Maoists at Cumhuriyet… I was the one who gathered them. I was the one who brought trouble upon Cumhuriyet… Şahin Alpay, Cengiz Çandar, Kerem Çalışkan, Mehmet Ataberk, Hadi Uluengin, Sabetay Varol, Celal Üster, Alev Er, even Osman Ulagay and many more… I was taking over the newspaper from within with them.” (I Loved Cumhuriyet So Much, p. 199.) The truth is that all these people whose names were listed had long since abandoned Maoism by the time they started working at Cumhuriyet. Cengiz Çandar even claimed he had never been a Maoist. But İS would not stop talking about the “Maoist conspiracy!” against Cumhuriyet. (ibid., p. 252)

While I, helplessly, was consumed by the feeling that I could not make the contribution I wanted to the newspaper, that I could not use my potential, İS continued to be disturbed by my presence and pestered HC. HC would write: “Without naming names, he was criticizing Şahin Alpay and Osman Ulagay; he was saying ‘If you don’t have the courage to say some things, the Editorial Board will say them.’” (p. 374) If HC had happened to let me write a column in those days, the “civil war” at the newspaper, as he called it, might not have broken out much earlier, but I would certainly have found myself out the door long ago.

I came across the following letter in my archive that I wrote to HC, reflecting my feelings about İS. In summary, I was saying: “Dear Hasan Cemal, Recently in your (!) issue dated September 27, 1987, I came across an article by İS titled ‘What is Philosophy?’ It caught my interest and I read it. The authors of the book İS recommended to readers who asked him what to read are Galina Kirilenko and Lydia Korshunova. It was published in Moscow in 1985, and its Turkish translation was printed in Istanbul the same year. It is clear that the book has no value beyond being a philosophy book that the Soviet state deemed appropriate to be taught. It is known by everyone that İS has made a habit of writing on subjects he knows nothing about and does not understand at all. But it is hard to think that he recommended this book without knowing and understanding that it was an official philosophy book of the Soviet state… What can I say, may God grant you ease in your effort to produce a quality and respectable Cumhuriyet newspaper, which I follow with great appreciation. I apologize for troubling you with this small detail among your many intensive and important tasks. Respectfully, A Cumhuriyet reader. October 10, 1987.”

I continued to prepare the book page, which was receiving considerable interest among the newspaper’s readers whose numbers were steadily increasing under HC’s management, and which had no equivalent in the press. This page served a function of establishing a connection between the academic world and the general reading public. My former teacher Şerif Mardin was telling our mutual acquaintances that I was “doing a very important job” with this page. The writings of many well-known academics and intellectuals were published on this page. Among these, I can name Ahmet Arslan, Mübeccel Kıray, Ergun Özbudun, Aptullah Kuran, İlkay Sunar, Feroz Ahmad, Şirin Tekeli, Stefanos Yerasimos, Fahrettin Yağcı, Zafer Toprak, Yeşim Arat, Binnaz Toprak, Asım Erdilek, Oral Sander, Hüseyin Pazarcı, İlhan Tekeli, Selim İlkin, Hilmi Yavuz, Şevket Pamuk, Nora Şeni, Arda Denkel, Taner Berksoy, Ayşe Buğra, Seyfettin Gürsel, and Selim Deringil. The first newspaper articles of people who would later become columnists at newspapers (such as Ertuğrul Özkök, Şükrü Hanioğlu, İlber Ortaylı, Ali Bayramoğlu) would also appear on this page.

Inspired by the interest the book page was receiving, HC had asked me for a report on a “Book Supplement” that the newspaper would publish. The report I submitted on March 11, 1984, which also reflected my views on the publishing world at that time, began as follows:

“In the last ten to twenty years, both the world and our society have gone through very rich experiences. In light of these experiences, questions have arisen in the minds of most intellectuals in our country as in the whole world. Many of the explanations and theories that were previously considered sufficient are now viewed with skepticism. It can be said that an intellectual environment is being experienced in almost all democratic countries where new intellectual currents are being born and ‘old’ ideas are being viewed critically.

Leaving behind the years of turmoil in the late 1970s and the military regime in the early 1980s, we are in a process of transition toward a democratic order. What kinds of wrong views and policies endangered democracy in our country in the past? What are the philosophical, ‘scientific,’ etc. foundations of these wrong views and policies? What can our intellectuals do for democracy to be strengthened, what mistakes can they avoid repeating? Such questions are the main questions in the minds of our intellectuals. A thirst for knowledge, discussion, and intellectual development is observed among our newly emerging intellectuals, the young generations.

This being the situation, universities have been put under barracks control and have been almost prevented from producing intellectual work. The university’s intellectual products, for example its publications, are quite far from responding to the needs of our intellectuals. It is very doubtful that the mostly intellectual journals outside the university, which are published every two or three months and reach at most 2-3 thousand people, respond to these needs.

Under these conditions, there is a dire need in Turkey for a publication that provides information to intellectuals who read books, think and discuss our social problems, about what they can read on the questions that trouble their minds, that addresses different approaches at a popular (but quality) rather than academic level while doing so, and that features articles of reasonable length.

Since 1980, an increasing trend has been observed in the number of books published in our country, especially in the fields of review-research-thought. Demand for books, while far from a satisfactory level, is growing. However, worrying trends are seen in terms of quality in both original and especially translated publications. Frankly, low-quality original/translated books are multiplying. Criticism is the only way to democratically control the quality of books. Due to the absence of a critical tradition, the labor, capital, and time wasted on the production and consumption of extraordinarily worthless books is at a heartbreaking level. Exposing low-quality books is of great importance for consumer protection.

Cumhuriyet, as our country’s oldest and only opinion newspaper, will publish a book supplement aimed at meeting the needs briefly mentioned above, serving the expansion of the pluralistic intellectual environment in our country, similar to examples seen in the West such as* Times Literary Supplement, New York Times Book Review, but surpassing them in some respects…“

## “Sugar big brothers” don’t want it

The “Book Supplement” in question could only be realized six years after my report on this subject, starting from February 1990, under the editorship of Celal Üster. The last of the book pages I prepared was published on January 11, 1990. I was not asked to contribute to the book supplement. My contributions to the newspaper were becoming increasingly sparse because the “sugar big brothers” did not want them. Still, I was happy about some things I could do. In this context, I would like to mention my series of articles, each of which could have been turned into a book, but which I unfortunately could not: I had written the series “Political Parties in the World and Turkey” (January 10-17, 1983); “Liberalism, Conservatism, Social Democracy in the West” (April 26-30, 1983); and “Transition to Democracy in South America” (May 27-30, 1983) as contributions to the process of returning to multi-party life from the September 12 military regime. When I raised the flag of opposition to nuclear energy with the series titled “Nuclear Energy, the World and Turkey” (May 27-31, 1984), the Chernobyl disaster (1986), which would awaken the world to the dangers, had not yet occurred. The “YÖK File” (September 29 - October 5, 1985), which I prepared together with Ömer Madra, who had resigned from his faculty position at Ankara University Faculty of Political Sciences after the YÖK (Council of Higher Education) law was passed (but which was published only under my signature), contained the most comprehensive evaluation up to that date of the turning of universities into barracks.

The series I prepared together with Seyfettin Gürsel, titled “Where Do the SHP and DSP Converge - Where Do They Diverge?” (May 25-31, 1986), on the Social Democratic Populist Party and the Democratic Left Party, was a product of our efforts to graft social democracy onto Kemalism. This series was published as a book under the same title (AFA Yayınları, September 1986). The book ostensibly covered our interview with DSP leader Rahşan Ecevit, but the one speaking was Mr. Bülent himself, who at the time continued to be banned under September 12. On this occasion, we had the opportunity to meet Bülent Ecevit; and we were quite hopeful. The meeting would also result in Gürsel serving as DSP Istanbul provincial chairman, until he became disillusioned and resigned shortly after.

Some of my contributions to Cumhuriyet that I was happy about were the interviews I conducted. Upon the recommendation of my friend Zafer Toprak, after reading his main works, especially “Mentality and Religion: Islam, Sufism and the Economic Ethics of the Dissolution Period,” I developed great admiration for and curiosity about Sabri Ülgener (1911 - 1983) and visited him at his home for an interview (Cumhuriyet, 25.03.1982). Ülgener, one of Turkey’s most brilliant social scientists ever, was both surprised and quite pleased that someone from the Kemalist-oriented Cumhuriyet newspaper had come forward and taken an interest in him. I was very proud when he came to visit me at the newspaper to express this.

## The Ülgener and Mardin discomfort

Because the Marxist paradigm in my mind had collapsed, in my effort to get to know our social scientists in the Max Weber tradition, that is, those who prioritize and research the role of ideas rather than production technology in the development of societies, I also did an interview based on the book titled On Ideology with Şerif Mardin, who was my teacher at SBF, but whom I had considered too right-wing when at school and attended his classes only out of duty. (Cumhuriyet, 29.04.1982) The consecutive Ülgener and Mardin interviews also caused discomfort at the newspaper, leading to a reaction from dear Yalçın Doğan, who was then Ankara bureau chief, directed at me: “this guy is filling the newspaper with right-wingers!”

Some of the other names with whom I conducted noteworthy interviews were: Tarık Zafer Tunaya, İsmail Cem, (my friend philosophy professor Arda Denkel, one of the most brilliant minds I knew, whom we lost at a young age), (Education Minister and my classmate from SBF) Hasan Celal Güzel, (editor-in-chief of Sweden’s best-selling newspaper Dagens Nyheter) Christina Jutterström, (Danish Social Democratic Party leader and prime minister) Svend Auken, (French Prime Minister) Lionel Jospin, (Anna Lindh, who fell victim to a murder while serving as Swedish foreign minister in 2003), (the legendary coach of the Black Eagles, as the Beşiktaş football club is known, who led the team to three consecutive championships) Gordon Milne, (renowned Swedish liberal social democrat economist) Bo Södersten, (director of Spain’s Social Science Research Center) Jose Maravall, (Ottoman historian) Stanford Shaw, (Oxford University Middle East expert) Philip Robins, (Iraqi Kurdish leader) Celal Talabani, and (Gorbachev’s chief economic advisor) Stanislav Shatalin.

During the approximately ten years I worked at Cumhuriyet, some scattered political analyses of mine were also published in the supplements the newspaper put out. However, the feeling that I could not use my potential was increasingly growing, and I was becoming increasingly unhappy. So much so that after a while, I would describe my years at Cumhuriyet as “the unhappiest period of my life.” I was trying to make my existence and views known by writing for magazines and doing translations. I translated Swedish social scientist Ingvar Johansson’s article “Anglo-Saxon Philosophy of Science” (Books 4 and 5, 1982/1983) from Swedish for the Yazko Felsefe Yazıları (Yazko Philosophy Writings) journal prepared by Selahattin Hilav. Mete Tunçay added my translation from Popper, titled “Prediction and Prophecy in the Social Sciences,” to the end of his translation of Bryan Magee’s book, published as Karl Popper’s Philosophy of Science and Political Theory (Remzi Kitabevi, Istanbul 1982). Popper’s article “The Logic of the Social Sciences” was published in Yazko Felsefe Yazıları / Book 7 (Istanbul 1983). A selection from the articles of famous economist Assar Lindbeck, the chief representative of the liberal, i.e., pro-market wing of the social democrats in Sweden, was published under the title “Market Economy and Democracy: A Critique of the New Left’s Economic Views” (Birey ve Toplum Yayınları, Istanbul 1985). With these translations, I was sharing the fundamental ideas of the new, liberal paradigm in my mind with my readers.

## Respect to Kemal Kurdaş

In this context, I also had original publications. The article titled “Views for a Contemporary Social Democracy” published in Banka ve Ekonomik Yorumlar (Bank and Economic Reviews) journal (January 1987, pp. 35-45) was the result of my acquaintance with Prof. Dr. Kemal Kurdaş, former finance minister and founder of METU. My acquaintance with Kurdaş had come about through Asaf Savaş Akat and Seyfettin Gürsel, with whom I shared ideas at the time as liberal-oriented social democrats. Kurdaş, whom I greatly respected, was one of the rare people who shared my political philosophy and quite liked my writings. Not having been able to visit the late Kurdaş (1920 - 2011) in the years after his retirement is something that weighs on my conscience.

Another person who would leave a mark on me like Kurdaş was the late businessman İshak Alaton. Alaton, whom I met during the years I worked at Cumhuriyet, had founded Alarko Holding, one of Turkey’s largest family companies, together with Üzeyir Garih, who fell victim to a dark murder in 2001. I met Alaton in the mid-1980s, at the opening of the architecture office of my friend Dinç Gürs, who had made his permanent return from Sweden a few years after us. Alaton had worked in a factory in Sweden for two years in his youth, and during those two years had learned Swedish better than I had in 9 years. (His Swedish wife, whom he met and married there, certainly had a role in this.) A friendship developed between us because we shared the liberal social democratic understanding in Sweden. Alaton was a cultured capitalist; he had both Marx and Popper in his library. He liked my writings and enthusiastically supported them. One day he came to visit me at the newspaper, and we had lunch together. Then we stopped by to see Emine Uşaklıgil, who was then the Managing Director and one of the newspaper’s partners, and who was married to Asaf Savaş Akat at the time. I think following this visit, there was considerable gossip in the newspaper corridors against me, about my closeness to a big, and moreover Jewish, capitalist.

Alaton, in a letter he sent to İlhan Selçuk in those days, was saying: *“I regularly read* Cumhuriyet and your writings. I try to understand you, mostly I fail. I experienced the same frustration in ‘The Goods of the Sinking Ship.’ You say ‘Don’t let it go cheap, don’t let it go to foreigners’… Millions of Turks have been going cheap, going to foreigners for thirty years, most of them miserable abroad. We accept this exploitation, so why are we opposed to attracting foreign capital here, opening job opportunities, and saving these people from being disgraced abroad, from being humiliated by Neo-Nazis? Which exploitation do you think is less bad? How have you not been able to see this truth for thirty years?… I present my respects with wishes for your success. Attachment: Foreign Capital Phobia.” (22.02.1989) Alaton noted at the end of his letter that he had also sent a copy to me. There was now nothing preventing my promotion in the late Selçuk’s eyes from”Maoist” to “spokesperson of the Istanbul bourgeoisie, of TÜSİAD (the Turkish Industrialists’ and Businessmen’s Association).” My friendship with Alaton would continue until his death while I was imprisoned in Silivri.

## The dream of social democracy in Turkey

One day in my early years at Cumhuriyet, Hüseyin Sönmez, who was then the founder of Hil Yayınları and nowadays Pandora Kitabevi, called and asked, “Brother, I have a text on social democracy in hand. Can you take a look and tell me if it’s worth publishing?” As soon as I read the text he brought, I called Sönmez: “An excellent work. You should publish this immediately… And introduce me to the author Haluk Özdalga right away!..” Özdalga’s book, which I found successful enough to abandon my idea of writing a book on social democracy in Sweden, was published under the title The Formation of Contemporary Social Democracy: Swedish and German Social Democrats (Hil Yayınları, 1984). This is how I met Haluk, who would become one of my close friends. Haluk had convinced me of this: Just as social democracy originating from Marxism was possible in the West, social democracy originating from Kemalism could very well be possible in our country. Our (futile) effort to derive contemporary social democracy from Kemalism began like this, together with Haluk and other friends.

One initiative that I supported thinking it could be effective in the context of this effort was the “Pera Palas Meetings” we started in 1987. I designed this initiative, which would later serve as a model for many similar series of meetings, together with Mehmet Kabasakal and İskender Aruoba, whom I met around that time. Our aim was to bring together SHP-oriented academics, journalists, businessmen, and other professionals to discuss the problems of the left in Turkey and the path it should follow. These meetings would continue until 1994. I continued attending the Pera Palas meetings until 1992, when I went to Ankara as chief advisor to Deniz Baykal, the general chairman of the CHP, which had been reopened in the context of the hope, not yet dashed, of deriving social democracy from Kemalism. (Mehmet Kabasakal compiled information about these meetings in a book: Searching for Solutions to Turkey’s Problems: Selections from Pera Palas Meetings: 1987-1994, [Boyut Yayınları, 1994.]) Another initiative in the same context was the magazine called Sosyal Demokrat (Social Democrat), published by Ercan Karakaş, who had returned from Germany and started doing politics in the SHP ranks in those years. I, along with Asaf Savaş Akat and Seyfettin Gürsel, also made contributions to this magazine, which were frankly not very noteworthy.

“In the manner of a prosecutor”

The article titled “An essay on the ’68 generation” (Issue 41, Spring 1988, pp. 167-185), which contained a kind of reckoning with my radical left past, that I sent to the Toplum ve Bilim (Society and Science) journal published by left-leaning academics, caused an uproar. Some members of the editorial board, especially my friend Ümit Hassan from Robert Lisesi and SBF, had argued that this article should be rejected on the grounds that it was written “in the manner of a prosecutor”; the article was published as a result of Prof. Dr. Sencer Divitçioğlu putting his weight behind it. The late Divitçioğlu told me what had happened one day when he came to visit me at Cumhuriyet and we had lunch together.

The late Divitçioğlu (1927-2014), who at that time was explaining the non-development of capitalism in the Ottoman Empire with the concept of the Asiatic Mode of Production (ATÜT), was an original thinker and social scientist who had a Marxist perspective but behaved very differently from those who, with the “imitative” method I would call it, which was common at the time, proceeded on the assumption that the Ottomans had a feudal structure. I regret not having created the opportunity to meet with Divitçioğlu in the years after this meeting.

My article that caused debates in the Toplum ve Bilim journal editorial board ended as follows: “The elimination of the rights and freedoms of individuals, of those in the minority, for the freedom and liberation of the class, the people, the majority, the nation, etc., is the beginning of the enslavement of the class, the people, the majority, the nation. Because the views, currents, parties that are in the minority today may in fact be the true representatives of the interests of the majority. There is no single, infallible, absolute truth, reality. Things we know to be true today may turn out to be wrong tomorrow. Those we trust today may turn out to be the most untrustworthy people tomorrow. Wrong views, wrong policies, and faulty administrators must be able to be changed. Therefore, the freedom to choose among different views, policies, and administrators cannot be renounced. Freedom of thought for the individual and the freedom to change one’s thought… I think this is the fundamental value that the great majority of the ’68 generation believes in today.” In these lines, one can find a summary of the paradigm that can generally be described as liberal, which I adopted from the 1980s onward. Attributing these thoughts to the majority of the ’68 generation was, as the debate that erupted in the journal showed, a complete pipe dream.

Özal’s Turkey

Excerpts from the text titled “Some observations worth questioning/discussing regarding Özal’s Turkey,” which I wrote at the end of 1988 / beginning of 1989 at HC’s request, are worth conveying in that they reflect my observations about Turkish politics at that time (some of which I would not share later):

“By the end of the 1970s, Turkey:

- Had reached a point of deadlock with the closed and import-substitution industrialization policies that had been in place since the early 1960s.

- The political polarization that had escalated since the mid-1970s had rendered the multi-party democratic order inoperable.

Under these conditions, the September 12 intervention received the approval of the vast majority of society, including civilian politicians. With this intervention, restructuring in the political and economic order came onto the agenda. (The political ambition of the five generals probably does not go beyond being “a drop in the ocean” in explaining September 12.)

With the strength given by the public support behind it, the September 12 regime, unlike the two previous coups: Closed all political parties and subjected the political elite to “pruning.” It renewed the constitution and fundamental laws related to the regime “from head to toe.” Thus, it drew the new framework of politics. It also gave the authority and opportunities for economic restructuring to civilians.

With the 1983 elections, the return to democracy with a step-by-step normalization strategy began with a “surprise” from the start (i.e., under the direction of ANAP instead of MDP, the Nationalist Democracy Party). Turgut Özal, the only link between the last Demirel government and the September 12 regime who was tasked with carrying out economic restructuring in the 1980s, who played the leading role in taking a fairly rapid step toward normalization as the “surprise” winner of the guided 1983 elections, and who finally won the 1987 elections with an electoral system that eliminated parties in conflict with the regime and the possibility of coalition, became, like it or not, the politician who marked Turkey of the 1980s.

Turkey of the 1980s is, like it or not, a very different Turkey from those of the 1960s and 1970s. “New” Turkey is to some extent the result of the September 12 military regime, largely of the ANAP administration, and to a significant extent of the political-economic-ideological climate that dominated the world in the 1980s. (…)

We can also discuss the characteristics of Turkey of the 1980s around the following points. (Each of these propositions can be questioned, of course.)

## In Politics

- Depoliticization: The exclusion of political currents and parties in conflict with the regime, various bans and restrictions brought depoliticization.

- Apoliticization: Especially the segments of society that had become excessively politicized in the previous period (students, workers, etc.) became apoliticized both due to the force of depoliticization measures and the effect of reaction against politicization.

- Depolarization: Alongside the exclusion of currents and parties in conflict with the regime, a tendency toward softening/seeking consensus in relations between different currents/parties (though weak) is observed, partly due to the effect of lessons from the past.

- Significant renewal in the party system has come onto the agenda. The conservative-liberal ANAP has gained the character of the major party in the center-right, and the political cadre of the mainstream on the right has been almost entirely renewed.

- The debate about whether ANAP is here to stay or going has ended. ANAP has gained the position of the major party on the right with a strategy whose basic principles can be summarized as follows: + With the claim of uniting four currents, it has both benefited from the reaction against division and polarization in society, and has pursued a policy of melting the fascist and religious right and/or leaving them outside parliament through electoral system manipulation. + By benefiting from the reaction against old leaders, it has pushed back the AP-DYP cadre; by extending a hand to the left as well, it has secured as much support as possible from those ranks.

- Turkey of the 1980s is an incomparably more optimistic society than Turkey of the 1970s. Part of this optimism has been made possible by breakthroughs achieved in various fields, and part by successfully maintained psychological conditioning.

- ANAP claims to be a brand new party. It has shown that it is not the continuation of AP. It has pioneered some important innovations in the economic field. It has succeeded in building a new discourse for itself by advocating the superiority of an open economy not surrounded by prohibitions, economic rationality, dynamism in doing business, and modernization in material culture with the slogan “leaping an era.” It is successful in giving society an image of being new, even if not actually new.

- The religious right has largely maintained its strength but has not been able to develop as much as feared.

- The fascist right is in a decline that can be called a rout. It has lost a large portion of its voters with a major loss of prestige.

- The democratic left has emerged for the first time with the label “social democrat.” SHP, with the claim of being the continuation of CHP, has rejected the necessity of renewal; Ecevit has emerged with the claim of renewal on the left, but it has been seen that he actually wanted to establish a one-person party/movement. The demand for renewal on the left has remained weak.

- Revolutionary communists have suffered a great loss of prestige. Within the generally declining communist left, Maoism has been almost completely erased due to developments in China, and the Moscow-aligned left has strengthened.

- The nationalist/Kemalist left has almost completely withdrawn from the scene.

- While Armenian terrorism as a destabilization factor has gradually declined, the Kurdish issue has tended to become the fundamental political problem in the 1980s.

- In the 1980s, new and marginal currents such as environmentalist and feminist movements, though weak, have emerged in political life.

## In the Economy

- ANAP pioneered some liberal practices such as changes in the law protecting Turkish currency, abandonment of fixed exchange rate and interest policies, and import liberalization measures. On the other hand, economic decisions became centralized and arbitrary to an unprecedented degree; practices that were diametrically opposed to the requirements of a free market economy became established. How liberal is ANAP in the economy?

- ANAP pioneered opening up to the outside in the economy. Important developments achieved in exports and tourism, Turkish businessmen doing business in other countries occurred during this period. On the other side of the coin, there are problems of fictitious export cases and having reached the limits of exports. On the other hand, fund practices raise the question of to what extent liberalization has occurred in foreign trade.

- The economic stagnation of the second half of the 1970s gave way to growth along with inflation in the 1980s.

- Greater deterioration in income distribution became another characteristic of ANAP’s Turkey.

- It can be said that there has been a revolution in economic mentality. It can be said that economic rationality has begun to dominate society. “Money” has moved to the center of all values.

- An immoral consequence of economic rationality, the development of the philosophy of getting rich quick, the understanding of “Make money, no matter how you make it” has become widespread.

## In Culture

- Collapse occurred in the education system at every level. Science, education, and culture were pushed to the back of the priority order.

- Along with the heavy blows to the freedom of science and art, parallel to money becoming the fundamental value in society, the prestige of science, education, and culture in society’s eyes witnessed a complete collapse.

- Both scientists and teachers became ordinary people as representatives of professions that have no prestige and do not bring money.

- Arabesquization/degradation came to dominate mass culture.

- Intellectuals suffered a loss of prestige.

- Political ideologies largely declined among intellectuals. Being an individual rather than belonging to a current/circle/group gained greater value.

- A television revolution occurred. Print media gradually lost to visual media. Reading newspapers, magazines, and books was replaced by watching television, cinema, and video.

- Due to the state monopoly on TV, there was a revival in the press’s commentary function, in investigative journalism that illuminates what goes on behind the scenes.

- While the space allocated to sex and sensation in newspapers expanded, a development from mission journalism toward professional journalism was also seen.

- Turkey opened up a bit more to the outside, became more internationalized. Western standards seemingly gained the quality of standards to be emulated in every area of society in the 1980s.”

## My search for escape from Cumhuriyet

During the years I worked at Cumhuriyet, I gained two lasting friends: Sedat Ergin, the only Robert Lisesi graduate journalist I knew besides myself (moreover a Beşiktaş supporter like me), and the late Ufuk Güldemir. When Sedat was assigned as Washington D.C. correspondent by Hürriyet newspaper in 1987, Hasan Cemal sent Ufuk with the same assignment so as not to fall behind in the competition. Sedat continues to write at Hürriyet today, in 2022. Ufuk, unfortunately, would leave us in 2007, when he was only 51 years old.

From the mid-1980s, I began to look for opportunities to escape from Cumhuriyet. My close friends like Ömer Madra and Seyfettin Gürsel, who had to leave universities between 1982-85, were working at Milliyet at the invitation of Altan Öymen, who was then the newspaper’s “general publication coordinator.” When I met with Öymen on one occasion, although he seemed to be sounding me out about moving to Milliyet, I was sorry that he did not follow through. In September 1985, Hürgün newspaper began publication under the direction of my old friend from the AFS circle, Haluk Şahin. Although Haluk invited me to join the team, I did not embark on this adventure because the newspaper’s future did not inspire confidence at all. Indeed, Hürgün would close down without even lasting two months.

It must have been 1987: I called Ertuğrul Özkök, who showed considerable interest in what I was doing at Cumhuriyet, who had left the university in 1986 and started working as a publication consultant at Hürriyet, and who would be appointed as the newspaper’s general publication director in 1990, to sound him out about whether there might be a job for me. Perhaps because he was still very new at the newspaper, he was quite cold. A hope was born in February 1989. Famous Cypriot businessman Asil Nadir had brought my classmate and close friend from Mülkiye, Metin Münir, to head Güneş newspaper, which he had purchased. Cengiz Çandar had also left Cumhuriyet and moved to Güneş. Metin called me by phone and said he was thinking of me for Güneş as well. But whatever happened happened; he never mentioned it again. (According to Mehmet Ataberk, who also left Cumhuriyet and moved to Güneş, some in his close circle had said I was “useless.”) In any case, not much later, in October 1990, Metin would also leave the general editorship. In short, no other opportunity appeared in the press; I was bound to Cumhuriyet. During a meeting of ours in those days, HC would say that he was aware of my contacts with both Haluk Şahin and Metin Münir, that I had done well not to embark on these “adventures,” and that I should “be patient.”

## İlhan Selçuk’s Gulag

It’s not that I didn’t also look for opportunities outside the press to escape from Cumhuriyet, which I described (with reference to Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn) as “İlhan Selçuk’s Gulag” (prison camp) in conversations with my friends. Hikmet Özdemir, whom I met because of his successful book titled Yön Movement (1986), was insisting that I apply for the associate professorship examination; he said I could easily pass the exam with my series of articles published in the newspaper. Somehow, perhaps assuming that everything was possible under the YÖK system, I listened to him. This was the only attempt at opportunism I made in my life. After passing YÖK’s foreign language proficiency exam, I took the associate professorship exam at Boğaziçi University, before a jury that did not include my professor friends Binnaz Toprak and İlkay Sunar, who had encouraged me for this. The jury, very rightly, merely recommended, on the grounds that I did not have sufficient publications, that I reapply once my deficiencies were remedied. I was quite embarrassed; I was also very resentful toward Hikmet for directing me to this mistake.

Another “escape from Gulag” attempt of mine occurred in 1988. This time, at the insistence of my late and dear friend Mustafa Gürsel, one of my two classmates from Robert Lisesi who, like me, had joined journalism (the other being Niyazi Dalyancı), I applied for the fellowship of Harvard University’s Niemann Foundation, which he had won and benefited from some time earlier and which provides senior journalists with the opportunity to benefit from the university’s resources for one year. Although I was hopeful, I was disappointed. The reason for not being accepted was probably that I did not have sufficient journalism experience.

My search for escape from Cumhuriyet’s suffocating environment led, again through Mustafa’s mediation, very ironically in the 1987-88 academic year, to my giving a course on “Opinion writing” at Anadolu University’s School of Press and Broadcasting in Eskişehir, even though I was not (able to do) opinion writing. Several well-known journalists would emerge from among my students in that course. One of them, Güven İslamoğlu, would make environmental programs at CNN-Türk for many years.

Mustafa, who at that time was serving as the Turkey representative of an American cigarette company, did not tire in his efforts to help me escape from Cumhuriyet. This time he introduced me to an American woman who was a “head hunter” (that is, someone who recruits executives for various companies). We had a warm conversation at the Hilton hotel that gave me hope, but she must not have liked what she saw, or perhaps found me overqualified for the job, because she would never be heard from again.

As I had done for almost our entire life together, I constantly complained to Fatma about the difficulties I encountered in work life. My Fatma was complaining about becoming a “wailing wall.” She would say, “I told you; when we returned to Turkey and couldn’t get into a university, you should have started your own business.” Since the salary I received from Cumhuriyet could not cover our expenses, I spent all weekends (with an opportunity provided by my friend Zafer Toprak) doing translations for the Britannica encyclopedia. Because of this, I could not adequately attend to my children; the main burden of raising them fell on Fatma. During these years that I worked at Cumhuriyet, our daughter Elvan had finished Levent elementary school and enrolled at Galatasaray High School after passing the entrance exam; our son Acar had also started at Levent Elementary School.

## Fatma falls ill

1986 had been a very unpleasant year for me. With terrible pains from a herniated disc, sometimes with tears flowing from my eyes, I spent a total of five months in bed over three occasions. During these months, Fatma became exhausted from caring for me and began complaining about it in an uncharacteristic manner. The hardships Fatma had endured since almost the time she married me resulted in her health deteriorating in 1987. What the problem was emerged when we went to the doctor with complaints of fatigue. The doctor, a famous internist working at the American hospital, first did not take the complaints seriously, but when she saw the test results and Fatma asked “is there treatment?” didn’t she say “Organ transplants are successful in young people…”???!!! Upon this, we went to four different doctors. Two of them said “a liver biopsy should be done,” while the other two said “an insignificant virus attack.” This time I ran to my classmate from Robert Lisesi, my close friend, the scientist and intellectual I greatly respected, Dr. Hasan Yazıcı.

Hasan recommended that we go to London to see the famous liver specialist Dr. Ian Murray-Lyon and also made an appointment. Murray-Lyon, whom we met at his office on Harley Street, the address of famous doctors, was one of the most gentlemanly and confidence-inspiring doctors I have known. After examining Fatma and also seeing the test results, his saying that there was nothing to worry about, that he could do a biopsy immediately, but that one could wait 6 months given the possibility that it might not be necessary, was very soothing. Fatma and I assessed the situation; we chose to wait and dedicated that week to touring London, which Fatma was visiting for the first time.

Unfortunately, when the test results did not improve, we went to London again 6 months later. My dear Fatma was as cool-headed as ever, but the liver biopsy was a very distressing process; she had to lie on her back for 12 hours without moving to prevent bleeding. Murray-Lyon inserted a needle and took a sample from her liver. After the second biopsy he would do about a year later, he made the diagnosis: cirrhosis was a possibility, not in the liver cells but in the bile ducts. However, three of the four indicators of cirrhosis were present. He recommended a drug that was still in the experimental stage at the time. My dear Fatma would use this drug for the rest of her life.

The very valuable doctors who took over her care in Turkey (first Prof. Dr. Atilla Ökten, and after his retirement Prof. Dr. Sabahattin Kaymakoğlu) determined that the illness was not progressing and told her not to worry about it anymore. Meanwhile, we learned that Fatma’s illness was now defined as cholangitis rather than cirrhosis. I remember both doctors with deep gratitude.

Fatma’s illness upset me extremely. I cannot describe the distress I suffered until we went to London. I couldn’t sleep at night, and every night I prayed to God in my own language and in my own way to protect my wife. In 1987, between the two biopsies, when I went to Japan on an invitation, I tied ribbons to the wishing trees I encountered in parks; I hung the Buddhist amulets I bought at the head of our bed upon my return. I believed that these and my prayers protected my Fatma against cirrhosis. What would take her from me would not be a liver problem.

## Takeda-san

While on the subject, I should describe my first Japan trip in 1987, which is a colorful memory. One of the good things about working at Cumhuriyet was being invited to foreign trips from time to time. Accepting invitations of the kind where the hosts cover the expenses was not correct from the standpoint of journalistic ethics, but I could not resist the allure of trips that I could not make with my own means. In 1985, the American Information Center had invited me on a one-month US tour together with a group of journalists and academics from several countries, the tour, covering several states, had been very educational, and I had written my impressions for the newspaper.

During this time, at his request, I had prepared a report for HC on establishing an “Education - Science Service” at the newspaper. In 1986, the service in question was established; I was also assigned to the editorship of the Education - Science Service instead of the Research Service. After a while, it began publishing an “Education -Technology Supplement” under Orhan Bursalı’s direction, but I was not given a role and was returned to my old position. In those days, a report prepared by the US Department of Education on education reform in Japan had come into my hands. According to the report, which I found extraordinarily interesting, the Japanese education system (just as in our country) encouraged rote learning and hindered creativity. For this reason, no one from Japan was winning Nobel Prizes.

I had met Keisuke Yamanaka (who would become my friend over time), the official responsible for media relations at the Japanese Consulate General, a graduate of Istanbul University Faculty of Letters, who also knew Turkish very well. My audacity got the better of me, and I asked Yamanaka: Would it be possible for me to be invited to Japan to study education reform? Shortly after, I was called to see Consul General Tatsuo Takeda. Takeda was sitting behind his desk with a very serious demeanor. In English, he asked me one by one why I wanted to go to Japan, what I knew about Japan, what work I did at Cumhuriyet newspaper, etc. At one point, when this almost turned into an interrogation, I got annoyed; I showed a sharp reaction along the lines of “Look, Mr. Takeda, yes I would like to go to Japan to research education reform, but this is not indispensable for me…”

Then Takeda asked if I had been to other countries. When I mentioned that I had done my doctorate in Stockholm in the 1970s, his eyes lit up and his attitude changed instantly. When he asked “Talar du Svenska? / Do you know Swedish?” we began speaking in Swedish between us. Our conversation deepened; as he was seeing me off, he said definitively “Of course you will go to Japan.” Takeda had served in Scandinavia, including Sweden, before being assigned to Istanbul. When he was very pleased with the series I wrote after returning from Japan (“The Japanese Miracle in Education,” May 1-4, 1988), he frequently invited Fatma and me to receptions given at the Consulate General, and we had very interesting conversations. The late Takeda would also write a book containing very positive views about Turkey after his retirement.

## The Gorbachev - Ligachev conflict

In the years I joined the newspaper, I thought “If there is a journalist worthy of the title in Turkey, it is HC after Abdi İpekçi,” and I believed that his share in the negative things I encountered in practice was small; that the problems stemmed from the “sugar big brothers.” However, eight years later when 1990 came, this conviction of mine had begun to change, and I had no hope left that HC would eventually take over the newspaper. I had come to think that Hasan was too attached to the “old plus new generation synthesis”; that he had given himself a mission doomed to failure, that of preserving it. Osman Ulagay and I would occasionally discuss the intergenerational tension at the newspaper. On one occasion, I told him that I compared HC at the newspaper to the reformist Gorbachev in Russia, and İS to Ligachev who defended the dominance of the communist party. (HC recorded this as an anecdote in his book on Cumhuriyet. See: p. 387) This was quite a successful analogy; there was also no Yeltsin in sight.

Because I was very far from the newspaper’s management, I was not very aware, but the Gorbachev - Ligachev conflict was escalating. In his book, HC would convey the increasing tension in what he wrote in his diary on January 8, 1991 as follows: “Today İlhan Selçuk and I had a conversation for the first time in a long while. I didn’t think he had so much pent-up resentment toward me. On one hand, he sees me as disloyal, on the other as a ‘scoundrel’ who will unite with capital and purge him from Cumhuriyet. He said: ‘At one point I was so angry at you that I could have done anything.’ But now it seems like he has filed down his negative feelings due to our long history and relationship. During the conversation, he couldn’t contain himself once or twice and spoke almost shouting: ‘You’re mentally ill! You always worked against me, conspired against me, first with Doğan Avcıoğlu, then with Şahin Alpay and Cengiz Çandar, then with Emine.’ I was left astonished.” (p. 401)

When circulation fell below 100,000 after the newspaper’s price was raised from 1200 to 1500 liras (!), HC convened the Advisory Board on February 14, 1991 and asked “What can we do?” In those days, I was quite dejected, hopeless about the newspaper’s future and my future there. Still, according to HC’s notes, I said the following at the meeting:

“Cumhuriyet has certain taboos that we need to overcome. We cannot overcome the deadlock without overcoming these. A chorus and the same ideas being expressed… That is, expanding the range of commentary… Cumhuriyet has lately been run as a ‘one man show’ or ‘two man show’ (a dig at me and Okay). Also, an authority confusion has begun to emerge (a dig at the Editorial Board)…“ (p. 407)

## Hasan Cemal’s vase

Yes, HC wanted to keep Gorbachev and Ligachev together, and thought the newspaper had no other option for survival. I, on the other hand, was of the opinion that the “vase” would inevitably break, and that without breaking it could not become the newspaper HC wanted. Indeed, the “vase” broke; and it was the owners who broke it. It happened like this: they split among themselves and first handed the newspaper over to HC. Upon this, the “sugar big brothers” left the newspaper and, with the outcry of “seized by TÜSİAD,” called on readers to boycott the newspaper. Sales fell to around 45,000. The owners then sent HC away and called back the “sugar big brothers.” However, there was no significant increase in the newspaper’s circulation.

In those days, rightly or wrongly, I was thinking as follows: If the owners had stood behind HC, Cumhuriyet could gradually have become the trusted newspaper of educated people of all political persuasions, and could have made an important contribution to the establishment of libertarian democracy in Turkey. However, from that day on, the Cumhuriyet newspaper evolved ever further away from what HC had envisioned.

What was experienced at Cumhuriyet in the 1980s was, roughly speaking, a fight between the wing led by İlhan Selçuk that advocated a synthesis of Kemalism and a kind of Marxism on one side, and the wing led by Hasan Cemal that saw the need for a libertarian renewal on the left. As is known, this fight did not subside even after the vase broke. About 30 years later, the conflict between the mission newspaper in the “sugar big brothers” tradition and the search for a reliable, quality newspaper this time represented by Can Dündar and his colleagues would lead to the “vase” being broken once again in September 2018.

Hasan Cemal described the first breaking of the “vase” in detail in his book. Everyone who wants to know the story of the press in Turkey should read that book. In any case, in my opinion, HC has three books that shed light on Turkey’s political life and are essential reading: I Wrote About Myself, Let No One Be Angry (1999) describes the March 12, 1971 military intervention; I Loved Cumhuriyet So Much (2005) describes what went on behind the scenes of the fight at the newspaper; Life Just Passes By Like This (2018) is his life story.

Regarding the “breaking of the vase” at Cumhuriyet, it may only be meaningful for me to describe what I experienced. It happened like this: One day in early November 1991, HC called me and invited me to his home in Nişantaşı where he was living with his wife at the time, Necla. I sensed something exciting was happening. He explained that the “sugar big brothers” had decided to leave the newspaper over the dispute that had erupted regarding an article by Osman Ulagay and the increase of his articles from one to three per week. The majority of the owners (that is, Yunus Nadi and his heirs) had left the management of the newspaper to HC; we could now set about making the newspaper we had dreamed of…

Two jobs fell to me in the new Cumhuriyet: I would edit the “Views of the Thinkers” section on the second page and also write a column twice a week. From my first days at the newspaper, HC had thought of having me write a column but had not been able to realize this due to the opposition of the “sugar big brothers.” I was being promoted to column writing for the first time. However, it was felt from the very first days that the new management would not be long-lived. The first of my column pieces at Cumhuriyet was published on November 9, 1991, and the last on February 19, 1992.

On this occasion, I would like to say a few words about my column writing: If you ask me, I wrote noteworthy pieces at Cumhuriyet and later at Sabah, Milliyet, and Zaman where I would work, but not only did I never think of collecting these and turning them into a book in any period, I also could not respond to the invitations I received from publishers in this regard. Despite all of dear Taha Akyol’s insistence, I could not manage to turn my columns and articles published in magazines into a book. Perhaps because it seemed like “too easy” a task to me; perhaps because going back to finished work was difficult… Whatever the reason, I quite regret not being able to do this.

## Earthquake in parliament

Some of the articles that were published twice a week at Cumhuriyet for only about four months are important in that they reflect my intellectual world in those days. In the first of these, while commenting on Leyla Zana’s speech in the Turkish Grand National Assembly, I was saying the following in an article containing my views on the Kurdish issue that would not change much in later years:

“The other day I was watching the swearing-in ceremony in the Turkish Grand National Assembly out of the corner of my eye on television. Meanwhile, I watched the Leyla Zana incident almost entirely. It seemed to me that an earthquake was happening in parliament. It was as if outdated structures were creaking and something new was emerging. I think what was experienced in parliament was the earthquake undergone by the policy expressed by the slogan ‘How happy is the one who says I am a Turk!’ The Republic of Turkey has until now followed a policy of melting its plural ethnic structure in one pot with this slogan. It also largely succeeded in melting in this pot the great majority of large and small ethnic groups coming from the Balkans, the Caucasus, and other places and existing in Anatolia. As long as they did not insist on their ethnic identity, no discrimination for or against any ethnic group in the area of rights was applied in principle. During the single-party period and after the transition to democracy, the main ethnic groups were represented in parliament. The Parliament and political parties of the Republic of Turkey did not exclude any ethnic group. Everyone who said ‘How happy is the one who says I am a Turk’ was given a place at the table.

“Now there is a new demand at this table. The most numerous ethnic group that also shows the greatest resistance to melting in the pot for other reasons, that is, the Kurds, is expressing this new demand for the first time so openly and powerfully. They want to take their place in the Parliament of the Republic of Turkey by freely expressing their ethnic identities. If our political leaders and parliament continue to approach this demand with the view of ‘disgrace, scandal, traitors’ like some of the press, this will be the real separatism. If those who come to parliament saying ‘I defend Turkish and Kurdish brotherhood’ are suppressed from expressing their ethnic identities, they too will be pushed outside the political system, into the arms of chauvinist Kurdish nationalists who are enemies of the unity of the people. Parliament will largely lose its ability to represent the people. Whereas those who defend Turkish and Kurdish brotherhood are in the overwhelming majority. Confusing these with chauvinist nationalists would be ‘murder.’ Our politicians and writers now need to see this:

“In the 1990s, the world and Turkey do not resemble at all the world and Turkey of the 1960s and 70s. In the 2000s, they will resemble even less. Both socialist and liberal thinkers of the 19th century believed that national (and religious) feelings would disappear in the 20th century. This did not happen. National (and religious) feelings maintain their vitality. This is also a fact demonstrated by the earthquake-like changes experienced in the world in recent years. We must learn to live with this fact. Their being able to be expressed through democratic means is an important chance for stability.

“I think we have also come to a fork in the road on the Kurdish issue. From now on, the Republic of Turkey will either solve the Kurdish problem within democracy by recognizing the freedom for Kurds to freely express their ethnic identity as a natural requirement of the libertarian and pluralistic order, or it will not. Choosing the future is in our hands.

Today there is a widespread demand for democracy, freedom, and peace in the world and in our society. Conditions for solving our problems within democracy are more favorable than ever. All societies are in an effort to adapt themselves to new conditions, to renew themselves. In our country, the majority of the people want the suppression of identities and ideas, intolerance of difference to end. Parliament must respond to this demand. In this way, it will also find the opportunity to repair its worn prestige. Here, the greatest duty falls on the political leaders who guide parliament and society. Are our political leaders and parties ready to take on this duty? That is another question.” (“Earthquake in Parliament,” 9.11.1991)

## Internal enemies, external enemies

Another piece of mine that I believe has not lost any of its value was titled “External Enemies, Internal Enemies.” I am quoting it verbatim:

“Sometimes I get the impression that we suffer from a national ‘paranoia,’ that is, a disease of harboring unfounded fears. Those among us who think that almost all of our important problems are created by external enemies who want to divide and fragment Turkey, destroy and scatter our state, or at least want it to remain constantly weak, and their domestic extensions, are so numerous. According to some, all the negatives and evils in Turkey are the work of ‘communists and their local agents.’ (This interpretation is rarely encountered anymore after the collapse of communism in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.) According to some, behind all the evils lie the games of ‘imperialists and their local collaborators’; according to some, these evils are the work of Zionists or Christian missionaries.

“This perspective leads to the most unlikely interpretations: The May 27, 1960 military intervention? It was organized by the Americans who were alarmed that Adnan Menderes, who had decided to go to Moscow, would approach the Soviets… The right-left conflict heading toward a civil war in the 1970s? It was instigated by communists and/or imperialists… The strengthening of religious movements and Sharia advocacy in the 1980s? It is essentially a scheme of Saudi Arabia and Iran… The strengthening of Kurdish currents, Kurdish nationalism? It can only be a result of Western states’ plans to fragment Turkey… In my opinion, the most ‘amazing’ of these interpretations is that Mustafa Kemal himself, the founder of the Republic of Turkey, was a British agent tasked with destroying the Ottoman state…

“According to the perspective I have tried to briefly describe above, Turkey’s fate is determined by conspiracies organized by ‘foreign powers’ who want to dig its grave. There is nothing surprising about those who have obsessions that our path is drawn by ‘fate,’ ‘laws of history,’ ‘laws of the development of societies,’ ‘imperialism that has taken the place of God,’ etc. reaching such interpretations. But the fact that this understanding is sometimes encountered even in our most rational and sensible people makes one think that rationalism has still not been fully established in our intellectual world.

“The fact that rationalism has still not been established also prevents us from making correct diagnoses of our problems. Let us take the religious movements and Kurdish nationalism that have strengthened in recent years. We should be able to see that these developments are essentially a result of the rapid social changes that have been experienced in our country in the last 20-30 years; that they are deep-lying social and economic processes surfacing. Rapid urbanization; the transition from a traditional agricultural society to a modern industrial society has upset the social bonds and sense of identity that millions of people have lived within for centuries. In the effort to adapt to new conditions, some cling to religious feelings and solidarities, some to national feelings and solidarities.

“The ‘roots’ of the problems we face are not outside, but inside. If we cannot make this diagnosis correctly, we may not be able to solve our problems. We live on lands that different peoples and states have wanted to establish dominion over for centuries. Today too, we are surrounded by neighboring countries with which we have various disagreements and conflicts of interest. Many different forces making policy both globally and regionally, each to the extent of their power, are striving to direct developments in our country in ways suited to their interests, some are setting up games, organizing conspiracies. All of this is real.

“But Turkey is not Vanuatu or New Caledonia, that is, one of the United Nations’ many so-called states that have just been freed from colonialism. Turkey has a state tradition stretching back centuries, a population approaching sixty million, a fairly strong economy, and perhaps more importantly than all of these, a democracy that has been standing for 45 years, for better or worse, in a patchy way. Turkey is a considerable power in international politics, a trustworthy actor. Turkey’s fate is not in the hands of foreign powers. We can trust ourselves. Choosing our future is largely in our own hands.” (Cumhuriyet, 27.11.1991)

“Is socialism dead?”

One of my articles summarized well what I was thinking about socialism by the early 1990s:

“After the adoption of the 1961 Constitution, the idea of socialism settled in a central place in our intellectual life. During most of the 1960s and 1970s, as in many other countries, a significant portion of intellectual energy in Turkey was devoted to thinking about and discussing socialism. Could socialism happen in Turkey? By what path could it be realized? Which of the socialism experiments in the world were real socialism, which were not? Was true Marxism being practiced in the Soviet Union, or in China or Cuba? Or had it not been realized anywhere yet? Which of the hundreds of interpretations of Marxism was the ‘correct’ one? For these and similar questions, some gave their minds, some their freedoms, some their lives.

“By the 1980s, the idea of socialism began to rapidly lose its central place in intellectual discourse. Finally, at the end of the 1980s, with the collapse one after another of regimes based on the totalitarian interpretation of socialism in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union, the place of the idea of socialism in intellectual discourse became increasingly marginalized both in the world and in our country. It must be admitted that questions about socialism now interest very few people. Very few intellectuals now find it worth their time to think and write about socialism. The few remaining socialist regimes in the world are now seen as an anachronism, a historical error. There is no doubt that neither infallible laws of history nor coincidence brought us to this point. Behind this point that has been reached are very rich experiences acquired by humanity both in the world and in our country. Experiences acquired at the cost of the painstaking labor, sweat, blood, and lives of millions of people.

“After these experiences, asking the following kinds of questions today seems meaningful. Is socialism dead or does it have a future? Should Marxism be completely abandoned or are there aspects of it that remain valid? Continue with socialism or is it over? It appears that if socialism means ‘proletarian’ dictatorship or any other kind of dictatorship, people will not favor such socialism hereafter. If socialism means the concentration of all economic, political, and cultural power in the hands of the state; the ‘nationalization’ of politics, economics, and culture; the enslavement of the individual and society to the state, it can be expected that it will not be possible to establish such socialisms hereafter.

“If people know how to learn lessons from experience, it can be said that the end has come for totalitarian socialism; and for Marxism to the extent that it is responsible for the totalitarian interpretation of socialism. As a scientific theory, Marxism too will be abandoned to the extent that it has been shown to be wrong. But the idea of socialism neither began with the totalitarian statist interpretation of socialism nor will it end with it. Socialism existed before Marx, and will exist after Marxism.

“The democratic, pluralistic, libertarian interpretations of socialism or social democracy have always maintained their vitality. Totalitarian socialism eventually collapsed, but democratic socialism led giant reforms that made societies freer and more equal in the countries where it came to power. Socialism is, in essence, the ideal of building a society where equality is achieved among people, where peace rather than war, brotherhood rather than enmity, solidarity rather than struggle prevails. Of course, as long as history does not end, this ideal will not disappear. The goal will continue, but the means will change.
