The understanding of socialism based on society and democracy rather than on the state and dictatorship will continue to develop.

“As long as we continue to develop conceptions and theories about what a good society would be like, the idea of socialism representing the search for equality will also live on. Just like liberalism representing the search for freedom and conservatism emphasizing the virtue of traditions distilled from centuries of experience. The ‘continue with socialism or is it over’ meetings held by the Socialist Unity Party last weekend made me think of these things.” (Cumhuriyet, 4.12.1991)

“Oh, that imperialism!”

In the article reflecting the conclusion I reached in the 1990s on the concept of “imperialism,” which tired our minds so much throughout the 1960s and 1970s, I was saying verbatim:

“MÇP (Nationalist Labor Party) leader Alpaslan Türkeş said, ‘The events experienced in our country are monstrous activities organized by imperialism. Terrorists are the servants of imperialism’ (Türkiye newspaper, 8.2.1992). In his new year article for Milliyet newspaper, Türkeş had dwelt on the need to activate the spirit of the National Forces against imperialism that wants to divide and fragment us. In reality, from the most right-wing to the most left-wing, we have become so accustomed to explaining all the negatives and evils in our country with imperialism. Have we fallen behind economically? The reason is imperialist exploitation. Is our democracy limited? Because imperialists do not want democracy in the Third World. Military coups? Imperialists organized all of them. The Kurdish problem? An imperialist game. Terrorism? Imperialist provocation. There have even been those who claim that the War of Independence was the work of British imperialism.

“Behind the understanding of explaining everything with imperialism lies the ‘theory’ that philosopher Karl Popper called the ‘social conspiracy theory.’ According to this theory, which is widely believed in our country and other countries where scientific thought is not well developed, social events are the work of some powerful centers that have an interest in them. According to some, all events are the work of imperialists, according to some capitalists or communists, and according to some Zionists or missionaries.

Hasn’t the time come to set aside these superstitions that are entirely outside of reason and science? Such understandings, which hinder us from investigating the deep-rooted and very diverse economic, social, and political causes of the negatives and evils in our society, and which lead us to look for the main culprits outside our society, prevent our problems from being resolved.

“We also need to now accept some facts about imperialism. The main ones are:

- Borrowing from developed countries, importing capital, doing trade with them does not inevitably result in being exploited, falling behind. On the contrary, countries that cannot manage to benefit from these opportunities or choose self-sufficiency fall behind. Isn’t this why all underdeveloped countries, whatever their political regimes, are now struggling to attract foreign capital, to be able to do trade with the developed ones?

- The poverty of the Third World cannot be explained by the wealth of the First World. Colonialism may be the cause of the West’s wealth. But the only reason for the poverty of underdeveloped countries is not that they were subjected to colonialism. The role of many different factors such as poor management, waste, lack of education, etc. cannot be underestimated. The fact that some underdeveloped countries in the Far East or elsewhere have succeeded in industrializing is perhaps the most important proof that the Third World is not condemned to backwardness.

- Today, a very large portion of both capital flows and trade, around 80-85 percent, takes place among developed countries themselves. The need of developed countries for raw materials is also gradually decreasing as a result of technological developments. This is perhaps the really worrying situation for underdeveloped countries.

- Our world does not consist of “independent” countries on one side and “dependent” countries on the other. We live in a world where interdependence is increasingly strengthening. Economic stagnation in the First World hinders the development of the Third World. Poverty in the Third World does not allow the First World to live in peace and security.

- Does imperialism not exist? Of course it does. But it is not ‘the highest stage of capitalism.’ Imperialism existed before capitalism, and was also seen together with socialism after capitalism. Not only great powers, but almost all countries try to develop and spread their national interests in proportion to their power using various political, economic, cultural, and military means. The US occupation of Vietnam, the USSR’s occupation of Afghanistan were imperialism, so what are Vietnam’s occupation of Cambodia, Iraq’s occupation of Kuwait? Interestingly, none of them succeeded. (Cumhuriyet, 15.2.1992)

## The two faces of Cumhuriyet

Hasan Cemal resigned from the general publication directorship in the last days of February 1992. He called me and explained his reasons. It had become impossible for him to do his job in the face of the “sugar big brothers.” He was right. He said he had no idea what he would do next. (He would start writing at Sabah after a while.) Regarding me, he said “You will probably go back to the university now.” I think he thought there was no place in the rest of the press for the kind of journalism I did at Cumhuriyet. (However, our paths would cross at Sabah in the mid-1990s, and at Milliyet in the late 1990s. I must have reminded him on one occasion of the distinction between news and commentary journalism and that I did the latter, but it was clear that he did not give credence to this distinction.)

Regarding the approximately ten years I worked at Cumhuriyet, I can say that I have two main criticisms of myself: First, I very much regret not listening to HC’s advice in my very first days to “Keep a diary, you will produce many books from these in the future.” Not keeping a diary was a bad habit left over from my communist days, and moreover it was a task I found very boring at the time. My second fundamental mistake was not heeding HC’s warning to “Know your power as a journalist…” The reason for this was probably the cautiousness instilled by being a former communist, and always having preferred (in Nuri Çolakoğlu’s words) to be “the important person in the background / eminence grise.”

I can say that my years at Cumhuriyet had two faces from my perspective, one positive and the other negative. On one hand, it had enabled me to readapt to Turkey, to gain a new identity in the eyes of the literate public; on the other hand, it had quite upset me with the feeling that I could not realize my potential under that roof. On the day Hasan submitted his resignation, I also submitted my resignation and left. Most people from the team that HC had put together, especially Emine Uşaklıgil and Okay Gönensin, inevitably reconciled with the “sugar big brothers,” but they would later have to leave the newspaper one by one.

# CHAPTER VIII / AT TÜSES AND THE CHP

On March 1, 1992, I resigned and left Cumhuriyet. I had no idea what I would do. But shortly after, I received an offer. The government of the DYP (True Path Party) and SHP (Social Democratic Populist Party) under Süleyman Demirel’s leadership had taken office on November 30, 1991, and some time later, Korel Göymen, the president of the Turkish Social Economic Studies Foundation (TÜSES), was appointed undersecretary at the Ministry of Tourism, while the foundation’s director Emre Kongar was appointed undersecretary at the Ministry of Culture. Kongar, having heard that I had left Cumhuriyet, called to say that Prof. Dr. Taner Berksoy had taken over the foundation’s presidency; he asked whether I would be interested in taking over the foundation directorship since he would be starting his new position at the beginning of April. I had been a member of TÜSES’s board of directors since the last general assembly. Since there was no other visible job opportunity at the time, and being idle was depressing me, I accepted the offer (with Fatma’s reluctant approval, as she wasn’t happy about me being unemployed) to work until a better opportunity came along, even though the salary was at the lower limit of what was acceptable. My appointment as foundation director was made at the board meeting on April 8; I would remain in this position until February 1993.

At that time, TÜSES’s headquarters was located in a spacious apartment in Kabataş, Setüstü. Apart from me, there was only Muharrem in the office, a very polite young man who did cleaning and served tea and coffee. Having always worked in crowded workplaces, I found this desolate environment quite strange. But the space was comfortable, and commuting home was easy. Moreover, since I wanted to contribute to discussions about Turkey’s problems, TÜSES was a good platform for this. With this reasoning, I tried to motivate myself for my new job. In the 10 months between April 1992 and February 1993, I organized one local and two international conferences on behalf of TÜSES; I completed two international conferences whose preparations had already begun. President Taner Berksoy and the board members were always supportive of my work.

TÜSES had an established cooperation with Friedrich Ebert Stiftung (FES), Germany’s parliament-supported, social democratic-oriented research foundation. The first conference I attended right after starting was the meeting titled “New Regional Order: Turkey-France Perspectives,” which had been prepared before I took office and was jointly organized by FES and France’s socialist-oriented research institution, the Jean Jaurès Foundation, in Istanbul on June 15-16, 1992. The opening speech was given by SHP General Chairman Erdal İnönü. My only significant memory of the conference was meeting Olivier Roy, the French academician famous for his research on Islamism.

What meaningful thing could I do at TÜSES? Since my return from Sweden in the early 1980s, I had been thinking that for liberal democracy to take root in Turkey, the regime first needed to be compatible with the identity rights of Kurds on one hand, and the religious rights of the Muslim majority on the other. My first initiative was to organize a meeting on the Kurdish question. In the early days of the AP (Justice Party)-SHP coalition government, Prime Minister Süleyman Demirel had gone to Diyarbakır together with his deputy Erdal İnönü and declared from the podium “We recognize the Kurdish reality…” The SHP’s “Southeast Report” aimed at this recognition had been published in May 1990. Hope had emerged for the state to make peace with the Kurds. A civil society initiative called “Peace Initiative for the Kurdish Question” had organized a meeting at the Etap Hotel in Tepebaşı on February 15, 1992; I had attended the meeting where Mehmet Ali Aslan, Murat Belge, Bülent Tanör, Asaf Savaş Akat, Mahmut Alınak, Tarık Ziya Ekinci, Feridun Yazar, and others gave speeches. The atmosphere seemed quite favorable for TÜSES to also organize a meeting aimed at resolving the Kurdish Question.

“The Kurdish Question from a Social Democratic Perspective”

The conference titled “The Kurdish Question from a Social Democratic Perspective” was held on June 19, 1992, in Ankara, at a hotel in Tandoğan. The following speeches were given at the meeting chaired by Prof. Dr. Asaf Savaş Akat: “Social Democratic Parties and the National Minorities Question / Şahin Alpay”; “A Look at Our State Policy Regarding the Kurdish Question / Hikmet Özdemir”; “The Kurdish Question and Democratization / Algan Hacaloğlu”; “Social Democrats and the Kurdish Question / Ercan Karakaş”; “The Kurdish Question and Its Solution / Aydın Güven Gürkan.” The meeting was attended mainly by SHP politicians as well as some Kurdish politicians, among them the late Şerafettin Elçi, whom I greatly valued for his opposition to the use of violence (i.e., to the PKK, the Kurdistan Workers’ Party) and with whom I gradually developed a friendship. The speech texts would be collected in a book titled The Kurdish Question from a Social Democratic Perspective (TÜSES Publications, 1992).

After the usually inactive summer months, we organized a conference titled “Principles of Democracy, Institutions, and the Turkish Experience” in Baku on October 17-18, 1992, with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as the intellectual originator, financial support from the Ministry of Culture, and cooperation from the Azerbaijan Parliament. I remember that among the large delegation attending the meeting were politician Necdet Uğur and academics Binnaz Toprak, Oya Araslı, İlkay Sunar, İlter Turan, and Rona Aybay. This first visit to Azerbaijan was a good opportunity to see firsthand the results of the regime change the country experienced after gaining independence from the Soviet Union. It was predicted that not much might have changed in the regime. Indeed, it would soon be seen that the regime had merely changed its guise under the power of the same person/family, with nationalist autocracy replacing communist autocracy.

“Islam and Democracy”

The international meeting that I was the intellectual originator of as TÜSES foundation director and that I considered important because I hoped it could contribute to distinguishing between relatively liberal/libertarian interpretations of Islamism and radical/authoritarian interpretations was the conference titled “Islam and Democracy” held at The Marmara hotel in Taksim on November 29-30, 1992. In organizing this conference, I worked closely with Dr. Matthes Buhbe, the Istanbul representative of FES with whom I got along quite well. The considerable expenses of the meeting, which included inviting many foreign speakers, were entirely covered by FES. Many renowned social scientists and journalists presented papers at the conference. In addition to Ishtiaq Ahmed (Sweden), Abdullahi Ahmed An-Naim (Sudan), David Barchard (England), Marie Bennigsen Broxup (England), François Burgat (France), Rudolf Chimelli (Germany), John Esposito (USA), Klaus Patzold (Germany), Reinhardt Schulze, Udo Steinbach (Germany), and Marvin Zonis (USA), the local participants were Nilüfer Göle, Fehmi Koru, and Sabri Sayarı.

I agreed with Marie Bennigsen Broxup, the daughter of the famous Central Asia expert Alexandre Bennigsen and herself on the staff of the Society for Central Asian Studies in London, to prepare an English book consisting of papers presented at the conference. She had immediately contacted South Carolina University Press and the publisher had agreed to publish the book without seeing the text in advance. Later, despite Dr. Buhbe also reaching an agreement with Christopher Hill Publishers in London for the book’s publication, unfortunately the project fell through because I left TÜSES shortly after. Following up on the translation and Turkish publication of the book was left to Yurdakul Fincancıoğlu, who was appointed foundation director in my place when I left. The book could only be published exactly ten years later with Taner Berksoy’s foreword (Islam and Democracy, TÜSES Publications, Istanbul 2002).

I had put great effort into organizing this conference; I would have very much liked to undertake the preparation for publication of both the English and Turkish versions of the book, and to write the foreword myself. Publications on Islam and Islamism were gaining new momentum in the world. This book could have opened new horizons for me in the academic world. Unfortunately, this too would become one of my unfinished projects because I didn’t follow through. My habit of always looking forward to new work and being unable to look back was probably the main reason for this. This was why neither the English nor the Turkish version of my doctoral thesis, which was one of the first studies on the political consequences of international migration to Europe after World War II, could be published. This is also why I haven’t produced any book from the thousands of columns and dozens of articles published in various newspapers and magazines over the years. The truly noteworthy report of the research on “Turkey’s Political Culture” that we conducted with Boğaziçi University professors İlkay Sunar and Yılmaz Esmer during the 1992-93 period when I worked at TÜSES also unfortunately couldn’t become a book. Unfinished work is what I regret most about my working life.

“Do You Think This Is Sweden?”

It was time for my CHP adventure. It happened like this: The book Yeni Sol (New Left) that Baykal published together with İsmail Cem in early 1992 was raising hope that Kemalism could gradually become more liberal, or at least it seemed that way to me. At that time, I agreed with Haluk Özdalga: if Marxism could be reinterpreted and transformed into liberal social democracy (as it had in Sweden, for example), then a liberal interpretation of Kemalism could certainly be made. However, it would be understood with time that this was nothing but a pipe dream. (Here I would like to mention my late wife Fatma’s words warning me about my wishful thinking: “Şahin, do you think this is Sweden or England?”)

The reopening congress of the Republican People’s Party (CHP), which had been closed by the September 12 military administration, convened on September 9, 1992, and I had gone to Ankara to observe it. Deniz Baykal’s speech was exciting. The press reported his words as follows: “We will redefine the CHP… The goal is not to make poverty an ideology, but to create a welfare society… From here I address all the people: There is no longer a Kurd-Turk, Alevi-Sunni fight. From now on there is peace. The CHP is coming to realize this great claim. It is coming to reconcile labor and capital. It is coming to reconcile Eastern and Western cultures. We are coming to embrace both the youth who goes to İmam Hatip school and the youth who goes to the disco… The CHP should no longer be understood as a state party, but as a society and people’s party…” It couldn’t get better than this.

Deniz Baykal, the Antalya Deputy elected as CHP General Chairman, resigned from the SHP on September 11. The CHP formed a parliamentary group of 21 deputies with others who left the SHP; the party assembly appointed Ertuğrul Günay as general secretary. Baykal also made hopeful statements about the CHP becoming more liberal in a statement. In summary, he said: “Turkey can no longer be governed only by decisions made from Ankara. Therefore, we propose the creation of a new administrative structure, a system of decentralization (local governance) within a unitary structure… Political parties have become institutions controlled by professional politicians. Delegates also work like political brokers. For this reason, we will move toward a party organization without delegates… We are not against privatization; we will close state enterprises that are losing money… We will put our weight behind having Alevis represented in the Directorate of Religious Affairs…” (Hürriyet, September 28, 1992)

Baykal’s Offer

Encouraged by the hopes that had been awakened, in late 1992 I invited Deniz Baykal to give a speech at the Pera Palas Meetings, of which I was the intellectual originator and among the organizers. Baykal’s speech on December 29 seemed even more liberal in tone than I had expected. After the meeting, I congratulated Baykal and said: “Deniz Abi (Brother Deniz), if you walk this path, you will be Turkey’s prime minister tomorrow… You should establish a team of young and knowledgeable advisors to support you on this path. Look, at least two prime ministers emerged from the brain trust of Sweden’s legendary 1950s Prime Minister Tage Erlander. You too should build a strong political cadre that will serve Turkey for many years…” Despite my objections that I wasn’t young enough for this job, Baykal went ahead and invited me to the CHP to build this cadre…

Of course, my first task was to share Baykal’s offer with Fatma. My dear Fatma, who always listened patiently to my complaints, was well aware that I wasn’t happy with my current job. It was certain that she wanted to see me in more important roles. I think she gave her support immediately, also thinking that this job could open the door to my entering politics and being elected as a member of parliament. But we were still cautious. The children were studying in Istanbul; there was no reason to move home to Ankara without seeing the future. As soon as I accepted Baykal’s offer and agreed to go to Ankara to work at the CHP, I did something I wouldn’t do again until my days at Silivri prison: I started keeping a diary. As you will see below, my memories of the approximately eight months I would spend at the CHP, coming face to face with “normal” (ordinary) politics in Turkey, would become quite detailed.

On January 11, 1993, Baykal called; as if we were discussing the subject for the first time, he asked, “Will you work for us?” I was a bit surprised because I thought we had already agreed on this, but I said “Yes, I’m coming.” On January 14, Besim Üstünel called and said, “Important duties await you in Ankara. I called Baykal and said TÜSES is also important; Şahin should carry out both duties together.” My going to the CHP was being received positively in my circle of acquaintances. Almost all were curious about what path the CHP under Baykal’s leadership would follow. Most thought I could contribute to this path.

## On the Path to the CHP

The TÜSES general assembly was held on January 16; I gave a farewell speech there summarizing my work. Erdal İnönü and the SHP’s top team came to the cocktail reception after the general assembly. I didn’t talk about anything but pleasantries with them. I was now with the CHP. On January 18, I went to Ankara to meet with Baykal. On the plane, I ran into CHP member Mustafa Özyürek; his warning “Baykal’s habit is to approach negatively, don’t let your enthusiasm be dampened…” was interesting.

On January 19, at 1:00 PM, I met with Baykal in the TBMM (Grand National Assembly) group room. He proposed that I take on the CHP Research Center directorship in addition to being advisor to the General Chairman and the parliamentary group. “We should benefit from your experience in creating a think tank for the CHP,” he said. His words excited me greatly. When I said I could also join the CHP’s central executive board, he said, “Of course.” When I returned to Istanbul the next day, I discussed my new job with my close friends Seyfettin Gürsel, İlkay Sunar, Oğuz Öztuzcu, Asaf Savaş Akat, Ömer Madra, Burhan Şenatalar, and of course Korel Göymen. Despite some doubts, Seyfettin and İlkay said I should take advantage of this opportunity. Asaf Savaş, referring to those who shared our understanding of social democracy, said “your taking this position is good for us too.” Burhan said, “This will shake up the SHP.” Seyfettin was cautious; he suggested I get confirmation from Baykal once more. At his warning, I called Baykal by phone. I told him that my family council (meaning Fatma) had approved my decision to work at the CHP, and that I would explain the matter to the TÜSES board tomorrow. There was no problem. “You will add political strength to us,” he said. We agreed that the public announcement would be made when I started work. He asked me to write an “education reform” proposal within fifteen days; he gave extensive directives. When I spoke with Korel, he said “I’m sorry for TÜSES; but now we’ll secure our balanced position between the SHP and CHP…”

The TÜSES board meeting was held on January 21. Taner Berksoy, Asaf Savaş Akat, Gülten Kazgan, Tavit Köletavitoğlu, Meryem Koray, and I attended. Mr. Tavit thanked me for my work with a very complimentary speech. The others also supported my new job. The general opinion was that although my departure would be negative for TÜSES, it would be positive for TÜSES-CHP relations and for social democrats in general. It was decided to find a foundation director to replace me. Yurdakul Fincancıoğlu was mentioned as a possibility.

On January 22, I had lunch with FES representative Buhbe. When I told him I would be leaving TÜSES, he was devastated, for he had established a good working relationship with me and was very pleased with it. He didn’t hide that he was upset.

## Uğur’s Assassination

January 24, 1993, was the first anniversary of my beloved mother’s death. I was in the grip of strange feelings aroused by the year that had passed without her. I went to Ayvalık to commemorate her together with my elder sister and her family. While I was there, Turkey was shaken. The death of Uğur Mumcu from a bomb placed in his car caused a great shock. It was an extraordinarily painful event… Yes, Uğur and I had had intellectual disagreements, we had remained on opposite sides during the Cumhuriyet split, but I had always loved him dearly as a sincere friend, an honest person, and a writer with a very powerful pen. He was one of the most important writers in the Turkish press. Everything aside, we had a friendship of nearly 30 years. Exactly one year earlier, on January 24, 1992, in the middle of the Cumhuriyet dispute, he hadn’t neglected to send a condolence telegram upon my mother’s death.

It hadn’t occurred to me that Uğur’s death would also affect my future. I called Hasan Cemal and Ufuk Güldemir to share my grief. Hasan wrote beautiful pieces about Uğur on two consecutive days after his death. On this occasion, I told him I was going to the CHP and that I saw this as an important duty. “You could do that job with your little finger…” he said. I had lunch with Ahmet Yorulmaz at the Ayvalık City Club. Yorulmaz, whom I called “Ahmet abi,” was the Mumcus’ neighbor in the Kadastro Evleri quarter of Ayvalık and a very close friend of theirs. We were in the grip of the event’s deep shock.

That day Nebil İlseven called by phone; he said Haluk Ülman, with whom he had spoken, was very happy about the news that I was going to the CHP, and had called Baykal to suggest that I stay in Istanbul and continue my position at TÜSES, but Baykal’s response had been “He will come to Ankara and sit in the room next to mine.” Friends who heard I was going to the CHP generally received the news positively. But there were exceptions. According to Hurşit Güneş and Ercan Karakaş, “it won’t work with the CHP…” İshak Alaton said he had “mixed feelings” about this, that he didn’t trust Baykal, and that he would “need to whisper in my ear what to do”; he described my acceptance of working at the CHP as a “great sacrifice.” That day I ran into Osman Kavala. He too said he didn’t trust Baykal, but that I could work with Ertuğrul Günay. On the evening of January 29, after Haluk Özdalga’s speech at Pera Palas, we had dinner together with Seyfettin Gürsel joining us. According to my notes, I said to them: “This is perhaps the last chance for us liberal social democrats… We must do everything we can to enter parliament with the CHP…”

Mete Tunçay’s reaction was interesting. When he came to the TÜSES office on one occasion during my last days there, he said, “I had advised you not to wage war against Marxism, you didn’t listen… I recommend that you not come to the forefront too much in the first few months at the CHP…” He meant that I could face considerable hostility because of my liberal views. (He would be proven right.) Fatma’s maternal uncle Captain Kenan did not receive the idea of my going to the CHP positively at all; “Even you can’t make Baykal fly,” he said. (It would turn out he wasn’t wrong.) I talked to Taha Akyol. He didn’t look at it very positively either. When I brought up the subject with my friend from Mülkiye, Murat Karayalçın, who was SHP General Chairman at the time, I wasn’t surprised when he said “Wasn’t working at TÜSES better?” My friend Rıza Türmen, an ambassador at the time, was pleased that I was going to Ankara; “Looking from Ankara, the future seems to belong to Mesut Yılmaz and Baykal…” he said.

On February 2, Ayşen Gür from Milliyet called, “I learned you’re going to the CHP…” she said. She said she saw this as a very important development; she asked me to fax my resume because she was going to write a story. There must still have been some doubt in me, because I called Baykal and told him Milliyet was going to report on my going to the CHP. In response, he said my room at the General Headquarters was being prepared; I was relieved when he said I would be staying in Ali Dinçer’s deputy residence. The next day, Ayşen’s story appeared in Milliyet at the bottom of page 5 in 3 columns. After the news, my close friends İlkay Sunar, Oğuz Öztuzcu, Dinç Gürs, Asaf Savaş Akat, Haluk Özdalga, Seyfettin Gürsel, and Hasan Cemal called to wish me well in my new job. Hasan Cemal advised me to behave “low-profile” at the CHP. “I did that at Cumhuriyet and did it turn out well…” I said. I talked to Kemal Kurdaş; his positive reception made me happy, because I had great respect for him and valued his opinions greatly. My friend Cem Kozlu, who was an ANAP (Motherland Party) deputy at the time, also pleased me. He both saw a future in Baykal and, as far as I was concerned, said “where there’s movement there’s abundance.” He even said “You never know, we might start a party together…” (But he too wouldn’t stay in politics for very long.)

Yes, I was going to the CHP. I thought I didn’t have a better opportunity at that time to serve a freer and more democratic Turkey. There was doubt within me: Could Baykal be trusted? There was also the distress of being separated from my family inside me. “Everyone goes to Libya, Siberia, etc. for their livelihood, I should also be able to go to Ankara on work days,” I consoled myself. On February 15, 1993, I flew to Ankara. I met with Baykal at the CHP headquarters on Çevre Street. As we had agreed, I started work with great fanfare as advisor to the General Chairman and the TBMM Group, as well as Research Center Director. But as would soon be understood, my job had unfortunately ended before it began. For apparently Baykal, looking at the mass reactions to Uğur Mumcu’s brutal murder on January 24 and the sudden spike in Cumhuriyet newspaper’s sales, had decided that the CHP didn’t need to renew itself and that “inherited” Kemalism still held its validity.

On my first day in Ankara, I visited CHP General Secretary Ertuğrul Günay. He received me very well, “I’m very glad you came,” he said; his adding “I hope you won’t regret it…” was noteworthy. “I won’t regret it, at least I will learn a lot here,” I replied. I spoke with Baykal by phone around 5 PM; we agreed that I would prepare the “administrative decentralization reform” report as a priority. During the approximately 8 months I stayed in Ankara, I traveled to Istanbul every weekend to see Fatma and the children; from Sunday to Thursday nights I stayed at the Mülkiye Association guesthouse in Kızılay. A spacious apartment on Cinnah Avenue was allocated to me as an office; a young high school graduate girl was also assigned as my secretary. Following the signals I received, I changed my manner of addressing Baykal. The “Deniz Abi” of years past was gone, replaced by “Mr. Chairman”; our relationship took on a very formal air. During the eight months I stayed in Ankara, Baykal came to see me a total of three times; I also visited him in his office at headquarters maybe four or five times. Each time we were together for at most 15-20 minutes. At each meeting, almost only he talked. These visits would lead me to think that the esteemed chairman, since he knew everything best himself, didn’t need advisors, and increasingly to question what I was good for at the CHP.

## Notes from My CHP Diary

February 17, 1993 / In the morning at headquarters, I visited Hasan Fehmi Güneş, one of the deputy general chairmen (former interior minister), and explained what I wanted to do at the CHP. His saying “We need to renew ourselves, we’re like paper money that has lost its value…” was encouraging. In the afternoon I met with Baykal. I stated my needs. He said the facilities provided to me were very exceptional, that I should make do with the office and secretary, and that an additional computer wasn’t needed. He implied that I should focus on micro projects that would attract public attention rather than macro projects. He didn’t allocate much time; his tone (discourse) seemed to be changing. I got the impression that he wouldn’t expect initiative from me, and therefore this job of mine couldn’t be very long-lasting. As early as the third evening, I wrote in my notebook: “I hope I won’t regret coming here as Ertuğrul Günay said!”

That evening at Haluk and Elisabeth Özdalga’s house, I met Fuat Atalay and his wife Nevbahar. We agreed on these points: Baykal was one of the country’s most qualified politicians, but his image in society was weak, he needed teamwork. Ideological-intellectual unity needed to be achieved in the CHP. I had also added this note to the diary: “The fundamental political division in Turkey was between center and periphery in the 1950s, between right and left between 1960-80; in the 1990s it will be between change and status quo. Today the main item on the political agenda is the transition to a market economy and establishing liberal democracy. Baykal is a politician of change, but the CHP is a party where the status quo dominates.” Apparently we hadn’t yet given up hope on Baykal.

February 23 / In the morning Taha Akyol called by phone. Baykal, with whom he had spoken, had said very complimentary things about me. He played these to me on tape… “I’m extraordinarily pleased, they appreciate your value,” he said. He said he would write an article about this soon… In the evening I had dinner with Rıza Türmen. He was of the opinion that the CHP had no weight in politics, but Baykal had weight.

February 24 / “Ankara gives me claustrophobia. I hope I’ll overcome this feeling…”

February 26 / Taha Akyol wrote in his column in Milliyet under the title “Producing policy.” “The research center newly created at the CHP and headed by Şahin Alpay will work to base politics on research-examination, information storage and systematization beyond intuition and plain logic. Baykal says ‘Şahin Alpay was the ideal name for this job’ which is true. Alpay has academic training; he conducted political and social research abroad for a long time. Alpay also made important contributions to social democracy in Turkey being purified of Marxism, Third World leftism and Jacobinism. He served as general secretary of the TÜSES Foundation for a while. Alpay’s very close relations with university circles are a great opportunity for the CHP to benefit from scholars… Baykal’s choice of Alpay as the head of the research center and his advisor, we think, gives an idea about the answer to the question ‘Which left?’ Alpay is the liberal left.” Thanks Taha.

In the afternoon I went to visit Yenimahalle Mayor Abdurrahman Oğultürk in Baykal’s official car. “We expect you to bring a lot to the party,” he said. He said they would cover my monthly salary together with Keçiören municipality. I learned how my salary problem would be solved. Apparently the party municipalities were bearing the party’s expenses.

March 2 / I was invited to a seminar at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs by my classmate from Mülkiye, Ambassador Ali Arsın. Sedat Ergin, who was the Ankara representative of Hürriyet newspaper, also invited me to dinner on the evening of March 11 with US Ambassador Morton Abromowitz. Being in Ankara provides the opportunity to get to know political actors.

March 3 / I was pleased by a call from my classmate from Robert College and one of Turkey’s most important bankers, Hüsnü Özyeğin. Bless him, he congratulated me on my new job in a very warm manner and said he would support me in every way he could, that he didn’t want the left to be crushed, and that he was worried about the Welfare Party’s growth… I talked to Haluk and Seyfettin. Both are troubled, both by the state of politics and by the CHP. I said to Haluk again: “The CHP is our last attempt in politics.” (It would be for me and Seyfettin. But Haluk would be elected as an AKP (Justice and Development Party) deputy twice in the 2007 and 2011 elections.) When I went to bed that night I asked myself: Am I really interested in politics?.. I feel like this CHP business will last until summer at most. There should be a place for me in the media…

“Entering Politics”

March 5 / I attended the “Information/Idea Exchange” meeting that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs organized, opening itself to outsiders for the first time. Many acquaintances, mostly from Istanbul, including Osman Kavala, were there. The most noteworthy aspect of the meeting was Özdem Sanberk, Rıza Türmen, and İnal Batu from the ministry saying that Kurds should be granted the freedom to freely express their language and culture. Ambassador Cem Duna said he received my new job, which he described as “entering politics,” very positively. He and Murat Karayalçın had been talking about me the night before…

I also ran into my high school friend Ambassador Ahmet Banguoğlu. “Maybe you’ll become our minister…” he said. Was he serious, or was I being made fun of… Late afternoon Deputy General Chairman İsmail Cem called. He said he was very happy that I had started working at the CHP…

In the evening on the phone I complained to Fatma about my troubles. We bickered a bit… My endless complaints are understandably annoying her. Ankara is suffocating me. I won’t be able to do it…

March 6 / In the afternoon at headquarters we worked with İsmail Cem until 6:30 PM on congress decision drafts. I had never done such “bad” work in my life. We dealt with editing nonsensical texts. The CHP’s condition is terrible; there’s no one who can bring two ideas together! Cem also complained about Baykal’s overly cautious style. He openly expressed concern that “If we can’t present our new identity, we’ll disappear.” He warned “If you don’t push hard, nothing can be done…” He invited me to program commission meetings that he chairs… I shook hands with dozens of people at headquarters. Among them, my friend from the revolutionary period, Gaziantep Mayor Celal Doğan, embraced me very warmly. İstemihan Talay (my fellow executive board member from the SBF [Faculty of Political Science] Student Association), who had transferred from the DSP (Democratic Left Party) to the CHP, also showed friendliness.

March 7 / I attended the meeting of the commission that would prepare the new party program for the first time. Besides Cem, other acquaintances were Algan Hacaloğlu and Haluk Özdalga. The commission reflected how politically cosmopolitan a party the CHP was. The meeting was spent on debates about “supremacy of labor or supremacy of productive labor” and what secularism means. I still got the impression that a radical party program could be written if the leadership supported it… In the afternoon I went to the CHP Youth Branch congress in Keçiören. I got the impression of attending an amateur performance and was quite bored. However, it was pleasant to meet and talk with people in the lobby who questioned the CHP’s Kemalism and found the secularist-Muslim conflict wrong. I thought if the leadership shows the way, a liberal social democratic party could be built… Both Seyfettin and Haluk advise me not to move to Ankara before next March. This reflects their hesitations about the party’s future.

March 8 / Today the CHP Women’s Branch congress convened at Ankara Hilton. Baykal gave a long speech. It was a speech and meeting with a high dose of Kemalism. Baykal saw me as I was leaving the meeting and made an affectionate remark like “Şahin, were you here too?”… Haluk is working hard to get into the Party Assembly (PM). Let’s see if Baykal will put me in the PM?

March 9 / The CHP’s 26th Ordinary Congress convened. At the congress I sat with Hasan Cemal. I described the scene in the party to him as follows: On one side are Kemalists, on the other liberal left elements, in the middle Baykal and his close circle trying to maintain balance. Hasan said “In other words, the situation at our Cumhuriyet…” I hadn’t thought of it. Yes, my position also resembles the one at Cumhuriyet. Again I’m the top man’s advisor and on the liberal left, and I’ll probably experience the troubles I had at the newspaper in the party as well… After the congress I met up with Seyfettin and Haluk. Seyfi had already concluded about the CHP, as about the DSP, that “there’s no democracy, one man rules, it won’t work out…” “The DSP was better; at least there the one man supported us… here that doesn’t exist either…” he said. Maybe he’s tired of politics, wants to get out. Haluk, on the other hand, is trying to get into the PM; he probably wants to be elected to parliament in the next election.

## Repositioning and the CHP

March 10 / This morning I got out of bed with the decision to write about the CHP and took notes. I didn’t go to the congress. I didn’t leave the office either and started writing a piece called “Repositioning in the Turkish political system and the CHP.” (When I joined Cumhuriyet, I had also given Hasan Cemal a piece on “Turkish media and Cumhuriyet”…) In the afternoon Seyfettin came; he complained that there was “more Baykalism than Baykal himself” in the party.

March 11 / I wasn’t elected to PM membership. Haluk and my new friend Fuat Atalay were elected. In the afternoon they came to the office; we discussed the Kemalism-New Left tension within the party and so on. Apparently Sencer Ayata is in favor of criticizing Kemalism; because some Kurds were saying if things continue like this there’s no place for us in this party… It would be good if I recorded my views on the Kurdish issue most clearly. Haluk argues that just as there are no insurmountable walls between Marxism and social democracy, the new left understanding can be built on Kemalism.

March 15 / Baykal made the suggestion “Let our advisor also join the PM”… In the evening I stopped by to see my friend from English High School and Stockholm, Ambassador Müfit Özdeş. He is an extreme—that is, hardcore nationalist—DSP supporter; he claimed Baykal was “pro-American.” It was a bit rude but I couldn’t help saying “That’s a bit thuggish.”

March 16 / Haluk and Fuat came to the office. Haluk suggested some additions to my piece titled “Repositioning in the Turkish political system and the CHP.” I found Fuat pessimistic. Baykal said “I don’t want opposition in the party”! A terrible mentality! Fuat was disappointed at not being elected to the MKYK (Central Executive Committee). They suggested I give the report to Erol Çevikçe and speak openly. I’ll do just that. I had dinner with Timur Ertekin. He said “Şahin’s coming to the CHP is more important than Baykal being elected chairman…”

March 29 / Erol Çevikçe came to the office. I pressed him on the importance of the program issue, that there was no other way to clear up the confusion. He agreed while being a bit on the defensive. As far as I understand, he sees Haluk, Fuat, and me as a kind of “power base” for himself and wants to stand by us. He opened up quite a bit: he said there was confusion in the party, that it wasn’t clear what should be said, that Baykal wasn’t tackling this in the name of being a unifier and was immersed in daily routine, that he had brought me from Istanbul and left me stranded, that he himself now needed to shake off the inertia and get to work, and that the Research Center was attached to him. His suggesting we also invite Bilsay Kuruç to the economics seminar we’re planning for May was surprising. When I said we were looking for “a minimum consensus among speakers” he backed down…

Ertuğrul Günay invited me to lunch. I expressed my concerns about the CHP standing still. He agreed. He said the pressures the party was subjected to after Uğur Mumcu’s assassination had “set the party back.” “There are those among us who are politically hesitant, but you as an outsider should bring up issues related to the program,” he said. I said the leadership couldn’t act according to public opinion trends. He agreed. Günay is someone who generally thinks positively but doesn’t act decisively. Perhaps he too is drowning in daily affairs. During the meal Seyfettin also joined us, then I walked to the office with him. We decided to continue the struggle within the CHP, but also to raise our voices before the public… Taha Akyol called. I told him about my pessimism regarding the CHP. When I said I was giving up going “low profile,” he said Baykal wouldn’t like this. I met Haluk for dinner. He too is of the opinion that we need to ignite the intellectual debate.

March 31 / In the morning I spoke with Prof. Dr. Melih Celasun on the phone. He said he was pleased that I was attempting to establish a research center for the CHP, but that it was also necessary “to be effective.” He was right… In the afternoon I met with Çevikçe, Haluk, and Fuat; we discussed the report to be presented to the PM. Çevikçe had conveyed my complaints to Baykal about not being able to contact him; and he had said something like “I don’t have time, let him work with you.” After Çevikçe left, Haluk, Fuat, and I talked among ourselves. We dwelled on the fact that there was a leadership vacuum in the party and that it was believed one could come to power without saying anything new… Unfortunately, Baykal is not behaving “correctly.” He has withdrawn all his promises regarding the “Research Center.” My PM membership wasn’t mentioned… My observations about the party are as follows: Leadership is weak. It’s assumed that one can come to power without saying anything new. Upper management is incompetent and confused. A crowd of “worn out” politicians who don’t know what to say. They’re taking refuge in the CHP’s old discourse. This includes İsmail Cem; even though he blames Baykal for nothing new being said. What Hasan Fehmi Güneş said very openly about the party is true: “we’ve become as outdated as money out of circulation…” Günay is also right: perhaps only people who come from outside like me can bring up fundamental issues… I’ve started thinking that if things don’t work out, I can stay here until June at most.

April 1 / Ömer (Madra) called. He suggested Baykal give a statement protesting the decision to close private radios. Using this as an opportunity, I called Baykal. After briefly reporting on the work I was doing, I asked if he had found the opportunity to read my March 15 report (titled “Global Trends and Turkey” on the subject of globalization). Contrary to my expectation, he said he had read it and found it good. “I’m very pleased to learn your opinion,” I said. My question “I’m thinking of making a speech on this at the Party Assembly, what do you think?” was answered with “that would be good.” When I asked “I’m thinking of publishing it, do I have your approval?” he said “Yes.” His response to “I’m distressed because I can’t see you” was also “Me too…” My morale naturally suddenly spiked. I went to Istanbul for the weekend with the decision to “keep trying.”

April 4 / It’s understood from Canan Barlas’s article in Milliyet that in his speech at the Mülkiye Association Foundation on the night of April 1, Baykal had taken up the themes from my report.

Complaining About “Lack of Leadership”

April 5 / In the afternoon Denizli deputy Adnan Keskin came to the office. He complained about “lack of leadership” in the party. He doesn’t see things going well. As he was leaving he said “I’ve dampened your spirits too…” Today they were dampened again; tomorrow? I spent the night mostly sleepless with distress.

April 6 / Keskin invited Fuat and me to lunch. He complained about “the absence of someone to manage things” in the party. He said that contrary to what was known publicly, Baykal was very gentle in nature, and couldn’t take charge of things because of his gentlemanly manner. His morale is low. According to the polling firm PİAR, the CHP’s vote is 3.2%.

In the afternoon I discussed the report to be presented to the PM with Gökhan Çapoğlu, Seyfettin Gürsel, and Yahya S. Tezel. We’re a team agreed on liberal social democracy. In the evening I spoke with Merih Celasun on the phone. He was very sincere. For the cause of liberalizing the New Left, he said “Your job is difficult… We’re also trying to contribute in classes.” I ran into Erol Çevikçe at the restaurant where I had dinner. He said tomorrow at the MKYK the Program Commission (PC) members would be determined, and Fuat and I would be included.

April 7 / I spent the day writing the report for the PM. Çevikçe said Haluk, Fuat, and I were admitted to the PC, and the commission would meet on April 19. Let’s see what we’ll do with commission chair İ. Cem who proposes inflated texts?

April 8 / I went to the reception of Milliyet Ankara representative Derya Sazak. CHP notables were there. I just exchanged greetings with Baykal. I ran into Altan Öymen. He was hearing for the first time that I had started working at the CHP. “Why don’t you unite those parties…” he joked. I was quite bored at the cocktail: the feeling of not belonging here engulfed me. I kept asking myself what am I doing here.

April 10-11 / I was in Istanbul with Fatma and the children. For the first time I told Fatma that the possibility of us moving to Ankara was weak; the best thing was to commute this year and see what happens. On the way back to Ankara I ran into my old friend Halil Berktay on the bus. According to him, Baykal is hesitant to express his views…

April 12 / Erol Çevikçe said the introduction of the report to the PM “wasn’t good,” and asked for it to be rewritten. Apparently Baykal wanted it so. Atalay was annoyed; “This party won’t amount to anything,” he said. At dinner I was with Faruk Şen. He and Ercan Karakaş had talked about me. Ercan said about me “He’ll get bored and run away…” He’s a smart man after all…

April 13 / Çevikçe came and spoke openly: Baykal said “These views are correct, but we have a very conservative support base, we can’t say these things…” I couldn’t help saying “If you don’t have the courage to tell the truth, you might stay at 3.5%”… In the afternoon İ. Cem called, he invited me to tomorrow’s PC meeting. Apparently the program draft he wrote (which to me was flowery fluff) would be discussed. At one point I thought of not going, then I decided to go and criticize. It’s clear that, as I said to a friend, “advisory work where you meet for 1 hour in 2 months” won’t produce anything… Should I hang on until June or not?…

April 14 / Çevikçe called around 9:40 in the morning. He said they had reviewed and shortened the report to the PM, and sent it on a diskette. Apparently he and Baykal had worked all night… Baykal also came to the Program Commission meeting. He invited Fuat and me to the empty seats next to him. He gave a substantive speech lasting about an hour and a half. “This commission is the most important body and will do the most important work,” he said. He advised discussing the topics thoroughly. I’m now sure he’s playing us “reformists” against the other “status quo defenders.” We dominated the agenda at the meeting; İstemihan Talay and Algan Hacaloğlu also backed us up. İsmail Cem yielded. He kissed me on both cheeks in front of Baykal. (Did he want to show how close we were?) In the afternoon session of the meeting, Haluk, becoming a “6 Arrows” defender, almost took a stance against me and Fuat. I was surprised.

What to Do with the “6 Arrows”?

After the meeting we went to Çevikçe’s room. When he asked “Did you like the general chairman’s room?” and Atalay said “We liked it but it could be a bit fuller,” Çevikçe said “You mean ideas?” showing he understood the sarcasm. Then together with PM member Adil Özkol we went to my office. We discussed what to do with the “6 arrows.” I argued for renewing the principles as freedom, equality, solidarity, democracy, reformism, secularism. I said let’s consistently defend these principles and leave the ideological burden on the CHP’s back to the SHP. I mentioned Baykal’s two faces: knowledgeable and mature, but lacking courage and a poor manager. He makes good analyses but can’t manage to “run the show” as Çevikçe puts it. I said I couldn’t coexist with the İlhan Selçuks at the CHP either, that I had nothing to lose but my chains, and that I would fight… When I complained to Adil that I couldn’t find the opportunity to write in the press after leaving Cumhuriyet, he explained this as my being “over qualified.” He said he would talk to Zafer Mutlu; maybe I could do a weekly interview at Sabah. He said at the first PM meeting Baykal had proposed that I attend PM and MKYK meetings. But when I said no one had invited me, he said “there’s probably people who don’t want it or it’s an oversight.”

April 15 / I decided to defend the “new six arrows” at the PC: Democracy, Equality, Freedom, Solidarity (or Patriotism), Reformism, Secularism… I called Baykal: “I’m in favor of preserving the 6 principles as historical principles,” he began, but he yielded to my arguments. I said the following: How could the CHP carry the claim of renewing society without renewing itself? The propaganda value of six new principles couldn’t be underestimated. We needed to show we were different from the SHP. “Revolutionism, Nationalism, Statism” were principles incompatible with social democracy… “Okay, bring your proposal, let it be discussed,” he said. I said I had heard he had proposed that I attend MKYK and PM meetings, but no invitation had come to me. “Of course you’ll come, we’ll go together,” he said. At noon, together with his driver, bodyguards, and secretaries, we held a party for the “April-born Baykal supporters,” myself included. It seems the Baykal supporters are a kind of “clan/tribe”…

April 16 / In Istanbul I visited İshak Alaton. He asked if I was getting my money regularly, then he spilled the beans: together with Bülent Eczacıbaşı, Üstün Ergüder, Can Paker, Osman Kavala, Fikret Tokgöz, and others, they were thinking of establishing a new think tank. He had proposed me for the directorship, but the objection was “he has another important position right now.” I asked them to wait for me until June. When I left his office I was flying; an alternative job to the CHP had appeared on the horizon, and in Istanbul no less! Fatma was also very pleased; we agreed not to mention this to anyone. Our decision not to move to Ankara was finalized.

April 17 / It was announced that President Turgut Özal had died. I was sad because market reforms and the Kurdish issue were left without an advocate. I had always valued Özal. I also thought this was an opportunity for Baykal to take the lead on reforms.

April 19 / I attended the PM meeting; it was the scene of debates between conservative Kemalists and reformists. Baykal took a conciliatory stance. He sent word that I shouldn’t speak because I wasn’t a PM member. (This was the first sign that he was beginning to see me as a risk.) İsmail Cem pulled me, Haluk, and Fuat aside and suggested we agree on the flowery program draft he had written. Fuat is uncompromisingly opposed like me, while Haluk has a compromising attitude.

April 20 / My 6 new principles proposal stirred up the PC. There were those who ardently supported it and those who vehemently opposed it. Atilla Sav distinguished himself as the spokesman for the conservatives. He explained that there was nothing in the Six Arrows that was incompatible with today’s needs. An agreement was reached not to leak the debate to the press. İsmail Cem took an ambivalent stance as usual. First he tried to get his own flowery text accepted, then he proposed working together with me to reconcile the two texts.

April 22 / In the afternoon Erol Çevikçe came. “There are three elements in the party. You, the conservatives, and the Baykal supporters. You and we will win, but Baykal is afraid of the conservatives (Ali Topuz etc.) leaving the party and creating a negative atmosphere. Keep doing what you’re doing, but know that there’s such a sensitivity,” he said. Haluk, Fuat, and I decided to write a new program; if it’s accepted fine, if not so be it. Apparently there’s quite a bit of grumbling in the party group. Algan Hacaloğlu, who recently said to me “Maybe a new party is needed,” is now saying “You’re talking like TÜSİAD.”

April 25 / Fatma and Acar came to Ankara for two days; we stayed at Mola Hotel. As Fatma was boarding the bus to return to Istanbul she said: “This time I didn’t find Ankara charming. If I had a home I would probably get used to it, but this isn’t the Ankara I left crying. You’re an intellectual not a politician. I don’t think you’ll succeed in this environment. While we’re still healthy let’s spend this summer together in Ayvalık. We’ll fish, we’ll have a good time together…” These words were very touching to me.

April 26 / Nesrin Baytok (Baykal’s secretary) had spoken with the Keçiören mayor. The mayor said they were “waiting for a tender to be concluded” for my salary to be paid… Falling into such situations nauseates me… Today I told Nur Çekirge, Haluk, and Fuat that “I can’t see myself as permanent in this job”… Apparently unrest is spreading in the party. İstemihan Talay, Veli Aksoy complained to Fuat. I told Fuat, “Baykal can’t provide leadership, it’s time we recognized this.” Still, unless I’m fired, I’ll continue working until the end of June.

## What a State We’ve Come To

April 27 / Baykal cancelled the advisory board meeting I had arranged for today. I felt I was being slighted, that my value wasn’t recognized. The end of this business came into sight… Let’s finish the economic policies conference I arranged for May 11 with our heads held high, let’s see what happens after… If the strategic research foundation general secretaryship Alaton mentioned were guaranteed, maybe I’d quit right away…. Erol Çevikçe said he was working to sort out my salary issue. What a state we’ve come to… Note: According to Sencer Ayata, the CHP needs to determine its mayoral candidates as soon as possible, otherwise “fluidity” between the CHP-DSP-SHP cannot be prevented (!) He’s looking for the reason for fluidity in the wrong place. The CHP couldn’t show its difference from the others; it gives no hope for the future.

April 28 / Fuat said the morale of Çevikçe and Keskin, whom he had talked to, was very low. Apparently our report to the PM had been butchered… I talked to Merih Celasun on the phone. “We’re getting older, we need to speak with courage now. At the seminar I’ll say that wage increases are excessive…” he said.

April 29 / We finally completed the text titled “A proposal for the CHP ‘93 program” and faxed it to İ. Cem. It seems to me this text will be the beginning of my end at the CHP. Before noon I stopped by the Milliyet office to see Derya Sazak. He said he “didn’t see any sparkle in Baykal,” and that maybe the rest of us could do something. In the evening I went to dinner at the Ayatas’. They complained about Baykal. Apparently their relations had been severed for 3-4 months. They said Baykal couldn’t play team games, would avoid bringing young people in, and so on. Late at night Sencer said, in summary,”There isn’t much new to say. There are other parties saying the same new things. If we also lose those who say the Second Republicans killed Uğur Mumcu, we’ll have nothing left, because they’re the ones who bring votes in the provinces.” I said the CHP base wasn’t limited to “Dikili festival-goers”; there was also an innovative base that was pro-secularism and pro-freedom and wanted social justice. We ended the discussion pleasantly with a proposal to brainstorm on these issues.

May 5 / In Istanbul, through the contact Hüsnü (Özyeğin) provided, we met with Satel’s American Entertainment Manager, and he really liked our television program proposal called “Money, Power and Love” that we had prepared together with Refik (Erzan) and Ömer (Madra); he said he would strongly support it. We’ll present the program proposal and budget to him by May 17. Satel was to start test broadcasts on June 15 and regular broadcasts on September 15. (Satel was founded in December 1992 by Sabah newspaper owner Dinç Bilgin, and took its name from combining the words Sabah and Television. It would start broadcasting as ATV in 1993.) I talked to Alaton. Ergüder was insistent on Sabri Sayarı for the directorship of TESEV (the Turkish Economic and Social Studies Foundation). He had lost hope for me. “What will you do if the CHP thing doesn’t work out?” he asked. He suggested the World Bank-funded Zonguldak Development Foundation General Secretaryship!.. What have I come to…

May 10 / After a long absence I’m in Ankara. I talked to Baykal on the phone. He kept it short; he said he was expecting me tomorrow at 9:30, “for half an hour” (!) While I was away Fuat had stirred up the PM. Baykal couldn’t take it and snapped “Are you going to break up the party!” Baykal’s job is difficult; by constantly managing he might end up with nothing. Seyfettin said: in the Istanbul CHP provincial program commission of 18 people, 16 advocated switching to a presidential system (unbelievable!)… Taha Akyol mentioned in his article the seminar titled “Where Is the World Economy Going?” that we prepared as the CHP Research Center, bless him. I told him my position here was the same as at Cumhuriyet, and that Baykal reminded me of Hasan Cemal before the vase broke. He asked if I would consider becoming an ANAP deputy in the future. I said intellectualism and politics don’t mix, and besides Mesut Yılmaz was too conservative for me. He asked what I would do if I left the CHP. I mumbled something like I’d find a job…

My salary seems safe until July. But will I be able to hold out until then? My future depends on the Satel job. I’m thinking: God has made me lucky in everything; despite all the troubles I’ve been through I’ve managed to stay standing. I owe gratitude for this. However, I haven’t been successful in my working life; I admit this at age 49. I don’t have much energy left anymore either…

The “Where Is the Turkish Economy Going?” conference I organized is meeting tomorrow at the Hilton. We’ll see the result of Nur Çekirge’s announcement efforts; if no one comes it’ll be bad…

May 11 / Taha Akyol, unstinting in his support, wrote the following in Milliyet about our conference: “Today in Ankara there is a seminar organized by the CHP Research Center at the Hilton Hotel. The topic: Where Is the Turkish Economy Going? All the speakers except one are names known as advocates of the market economy in Turkey: Prof. Merih Celasun, Assoc. Prof. Gökhan Çapoğlu, Prof. Yahya Sezai Tezel, Dr. Seyfettin Gürsel, economist writer Osman Ulagay, businessman İshak Alaton. The only speaker at the CHP seminar who opposes the market economy is Şemsi Denizer, the famous face of the Zonguldak strike and General Secretary of the Türk-İş trade union confederation…”

Thank God, the seminar was very successful! It started with about 100 people in the morning but the audience quickly rose to 350. Baykal gave the opening speech. The speeches were very high quality and very liberal! Alaton even advocated opening forests to foreign capital!!! Amazingly, no one objected to this except Ankara provincial chairman Nail Gürman (and even he half-heartedly). In Fuat’s words, with this meeting “A major blow was dealt to the conservatives.” Maybe it went a bit too far, but it was good… I left the meeting very happy. Baykal and the speakers also left satisfied. Baykal even said things to Fuat meaning “Except for a few backward-minded people, the party base is with us.” (Osman Ulagay would write the following about the seminar in his article titled “The footsteps of hope” in Sabah: “On a day when politics had become so prominent, a political party finding it worthwhile to discuss the economy, CHP General Chairman Deniz Baykal spending his entire day at this meeting could be considered a ray of hope in my view. However, as we also expressed to the CHP executives, this interest shouldn’t be limited to the period when parties are in opposition.”)

In the evening I talked to Fatma. She had had dental surgery and was in pain. “What am I doing here, I should be by her side. How many more days can we be together anyway…” such thoughts welled up again.

May 12 / I talked to Alaton; Üstün Ergüder asked “Is Şahin happy with his job.” But apparently the new director candidate for TESEV is Orhan Güvenen (head of the DİE, the State Institute of Statistics). In short, I’d better just get on with my own work…

“If You Insist the Party Will Fall Apart”

İsmail Cem’s second program draft arrived. In a word, “hopeless case.” Haluk and I were almost dumbfounded… We decided to tell the commission members to read both our draft and Cem’s and decide. Haluk is worried about a debate that could lead to the party falling apart. He may not be wrong…

May 13 / At the PC meeting Cem’s draft clashed with the Atalay-Özdalga-Alpay draft. Cem brought it to “if you don’t like it that’s all from me.” Hayrettin Uysal and Algan Hacaloğlu hurled the threat at us “if you insist on your draft the party will fall apart.” İstemihan Talay, on the other hand, was positive. “Let’s not say something we’ll be ashamed of,” he said. When I asked what that was, he said “Statism for example.” (Later when we talked privately he said prejudices about Baykal were the problem, and that the party might remain without growing.) At the end of the meeting it was decided that Cem’s draft would be reviewed by Hacaloğlu. Hacaloğlu said the draft was “literary,” but unfortunately Cem was insistent on this text…

I was furious: I’ve been here for three months, Baykal hasn’t even deigned to have a meal with me! I need to leave here as soon as possible… I have no intention of getting into internal party debates and conflicts either. There’s no chance here for those with my views. Ertuğrul Günay is no use either. In the early days he was implying he would give support by saying “We can’t say everything, you say it.” Now he said about the three arrows on the seminar invitation (which we had no intention behind) “I hope there’s no ideological aspect to this”… Çevikçe told Fuat Atalay “Don’t go after Cem but criticize fiercely and bring a new text by the congress.” That’s what we’ll do.

May 19 / No word from Baykal. I wonder how he received Ahmet Taner Kışlalı’s article published in Cumhuriyet on May 16, which contained harsh criticism directed at me? Is he signaling that I should leave now by not calling me? Maybe… I talked to Hasan Cemal. He said İsmail Cem was playing for Baykal’s position. He thinks I need to be patient for a few more months… Adnan Keskin also told Atalay that after the March elections both Günay and Cem would rise up against Baykal. If even Talay can openly tell me that Baykal is a handicap…

May 21-25 / I was in Istanbul. At Taha Akyol’s suggestion I called Yalçın Doğan, Milliyet’s editor-in-chief. “Actually when I heard you had gone to Ankara, I thought this wouldn’t work out… In July we’ll move to the new building. New personnel, new publications will come up. Call me after the holiday,” he said… I stopped by Alaton’s. We reviewed the list of TESEV founders. Only 10 out of 23 people might support me for the general secretaryship… No response yet from the project we submitted to Satel.

May 25 / Baykal called Fuat today, but he didn’t call me… In the evening I had dinner with Rıza Türmen. “I had sensed that this job of yours couldn’t be permanent,” he said… Yet he had received it very positively at the beginning… A heavy defeat is expected for the center-left in the elections… What I want most right now is to somehow make it to Milliyet…

May 26 / The day began with a surprise visit from Ankara provincial chairman Nail Gürman. He started by asking whether the texts from the economics seminar would be printed. He said if the CHP Research Center name would be on it, the CHP’s economic views should be expressed. He said Yahya Tezel’s speech had generated backlash. I said there were also many who spoke in favor, and that I looked at whether the speakers were experts on the subject…

In the afternoon a tall, very attractive woman came from the US Embassy; she asked me to explain the CHP Research Center. She said she couldn’t understand the reasons for the CHP group being against Operation Provide Comfort. I said I shared the same view… Then Fuat came. He had met with Baykal, who had spoken about us as if he supported us. “He might be disappointed if he heard what we think about him,” he said.

May 27 / It was an important day. Baykal came to the Cinnah office at 5:30 PM and stayed for about four hours. Fuat was also there. I told Baykal openly: “The idea that I’m not useful to the CHP, that I’m even harmful, is spreading. The program draft with six new principles generated backlash in the Commission. Cem is trying to impose his own extremely inadequate program draft by saying ‘Şahin Alpay isn’t even a commission member anyway.’ Hayrettin Uysal, Algan Hacaloğlu are hurling threats like ‘Don’t insist too much, you’ll split the party, you’ll scatter the group.’ Do you also think I’m harming the party? This is the first time we’re meeting one-on-one since I came to Ankara. You haven’t commented on almost any of the reports I’ve written. On January 18 we agreed that I would come to the CHP. On January 24 Uğur Mumcu was killed. On April 17 Özal died, Demirel became President. You concluded that the leadership of the opposition would fall to us without us doing anything. I’ve come to think there’s no need for me here…”

Fuat Atalay took the floor. He said a radical program was needed, that Baykal was acting without courage on this matter, that he didn’t want to take risks, that he couldn’t manage the party well, that we had come to a breaking point. Baykal responded as follows: “A radical program would isolate us. We’re playing for the leadership of the left bloc. I share your ideas, but we must proceed step by step. I find your work very useful. Şahin’s coming brought many points to the party. It never crossed my mind that you were harmful; otherwise I would have made it clear.”

“I Don’t Believe in a Radical Move”

I also said: “We should play not for the leadership of the left bloc but of society. Society can only be mobilized around new ideas. A vanguard and cadre to represent new ideas is needed. One man doesn’t provide credibility. A balance policy brings the danger of alienating both conservatives and reformists.” Baykal responded: “I don’t believe in a radical move. I share your ideas, but we can get them accepted over time. Be compromising enough not to put me in a difficult position and support me. Don’t worry, the CHP is receiving great interest from society…”

We agreed that I would report to him once a week; that I would organize meetings with experts and intellectuals; that I would write the local governance report as soon as possible, etc. Meanwhile he asked me to bring Cem Boyner to the party “acting as if the proposal was coming from me”… After Baykal left, Fuat said he wasn’t satisfied, that Baykal thought he could gain support with cosmetic measures like bringing Rüştü Saracoğlu and Cem Boyner to the party, that he even saw me as a cosmetic element, but that given the support he had shown, it wouldn’t be good for me to just leave, and that I needed to stay in the party for at least 6 more months… In the evening I told Fatma on the phone: I’ll continue working at the CHP until I get a better job offer, but I don’t believe I’ll be permanent.

May 28 / I met Hurşit Güneş for lunch. He said: “Until 4-5 months ago Baykal looked like he would succeed, but he didn’t… Despite having a better cadre he won’t be able to pull it off, because he causes an allergic reaction…”

While I was away Erol Çevikçe had come to the office; he told Fuat, “Baykal was very affected by what you said.” But he repeated the impression that things weren’t going well; apparently he doesn’t want to be seen around…

I talked to Ömer: Although the American editors really liked our program proposal, no result came from the meeting with Satel. They said we’ll call you after the holiday… When they hear the fee we’re asking they won’t accept… I told Ömer, “Anyway Fatma also wants me to commit myself to the CHP now, or at least see this attempt through to the end.”

June 14 / After the holiday break and a herniated disc crisis during the holiday, I could only return to Ankara today. At 3 PM we went to Baykal’s room at headquarters. Baykal wanted Sencer Ayata to attend the meeting alongside Haluk, Yahya, and Fuat. Çevikçe was also there. Sencer explained his thesis that the CHP would need to win over former leftists, even revolutionaries in small towns in the coming three months; I explained my thesis that the CHP should work on the liberal social democratic views I proposed. I said the general chairman and the MKYK needed to decide on one of these two theses, otherwise I and those who think like me would break from the CHP. Yahya, Fuat, Haluk all opposed Sencer. Baykal said he didn’t see a contradiction between the two theses…

June 15 / Yalçın Doğan called. Saying we’d talk about “the other matter” (my moving to Milliyet) later, he asked for information on how privatizations were done in Spain. I found texts on this subject at the American Library and sent them.

June 17 / Ömer and Refik this time talked to Satel’s American news editor. He liked our proposal but asked us to turn it into a weekly news program. Our side requested 3,500 dollars per person per month for this. They said they would respond within two weeks.

June 18 / Today I met with Murat Karayalçın. He said he wouldn’t run for SHP chairman without getting 60 percent support, and if he did he would announce a social democratic platform. I said of course that a liberal social democratic platform was needed. He had heard from Hasan Cemal that I was having trouble at the CHP. I said I wanted to return to the press. He said he would tell Yalçın Doğan that he supported me.

June 20 / At Yahya’s house, Haluk, Fuat, and I prepared the critique of the government program. Baykal’s lack of courage, disorganization, irritability came up. None of them finds my idea of leaving unjustified anymore.

“How Do We Raise the Organization’s Morale?”

June 21 / In the morning I talked to Baykal. He was pleased with our preparation on the government program. Meanwhile he had also talked to Fuat; he said “Talk to Şahin too, what can we do to raise the organization’s morale”… Well, let’s hope for the best…

June 24 / Fuat is very upset. Baykal and his colleagues are apparently preparing to oppose Tansu Çiller’s privatizations. We stopped by Ertuğrul Günay’s. I had read in Derya Sazak’s article that morning that he too said they would wage an ideological war against privatization. I told Günay that the CHP couldn’t get anywhere with a schizophrenic identity. In response he said things meaning “The CHP isn’t a new party, we must take Kemalist sensitivities into account…” Meanwhile he criticized my not having CHP spokespersons speak at the economics seminar I organized. I said it would be very wrong if they opposed privatization in principle.

June 25 / I talked to Hasan Cemal on the phone. I said again that I was looking for work; I mentioned the Satel and Milliyet possibilities. I asked if he had any contact with Aydın Doğan. He said he could talk to Altan Öymen. They had offered him the Show TV general manager position at double the salary, but he had turned it down. “Otherwise I would have called you to my side right away…” he said. But he wasn’t going to manage anymore, he was comfortable… “Remind me that you’re looking for work…” he said. Typical HC!

June 26 / Today first the Ayatas then Çevikçe came to the office. There were long debates again. Sencer and Ayşe said Baykal lost by leaning toward liberalism. I said he lost because he didn’t know what he wanted to do. I feel the time has come to leave the CHP… I’ll probably leave as of July 15 even if I can’t find a job. I feel like the happiest person in the world because I’m still Fatma’s beloved. I’ll find a job somehow.

June 27 / I talked on the phone with Refik. When I said “I can’t stand it anymore, I might leave Ankara even if I can’t find a job…” Refik’s response was, “If you panic you’ll end up in a job beneath you; you’ll also upset Ömer and me because of the CHP people and the project we’re waiting for a response on… At least keep quiet until the end of August, get your money, take your vacation…”

June 28 / We delivered the notes to Baykal for his speech in the confidence vote on the government. We also suggested he condemn the US bombing of Baghdad. After dinner I went to Müfit’s (Özdeş). A likeable person despite all his nationalism. İlber (Ortaylı) also came. Tansu Çiller had offered him a history advisor position. For some reason İlber doesn’t like anything or anyone, but he likes and appreciates me…

June 29 / Baykal said he would use the note about the bombing of Baghdad in his group speech.

July 2 / I attended the Program Commission meeting. Now Hacaloğlu is guiding the work instead of Cem… In the late afternoon Fatma and Acar came to Ankara. We stayed at Mola Hotel. At night the news came that the Sivas Madımak Hotel had been burned, 35 people killed… We were deeply shaken!

July 3 / Fuat and I went to the TBMM for the confidence vote debates. Baykal’s speech was generally good. He took a populist stance by defending agricultural subsidies, but it was positive that he said he wasn’t against privatizations and that he advocated local governance as a solution to the Southeast problem. His polemic against Çiller was a bit fierce but well done.

July 5 / Baykal called. He thanked us for the notes we prepared. He said he couldn’t use them much but they helped him find his footing. I also congratulated him on the speech he gave… In the afternoon I stopped by Ahmet Evin’s (my classmate from Robert College who at the time was heading the Ankara office of the American tobacco company Philip Morris). Susan Kemper (headhunter) who had found him his current job was in Istanbul; she wanted to meet with me… I called İlkay Sunar and said I was interested in teaching a course on “Scandinavian Politics” at Boğaziçi… Erdal Yavuz also said I could teach a course on “History of Social Democracy” at METU. Let’s see where my next stop will be?

“This Woman Won’t Be Able to Handle This”

July 6 / The atmosphere in Turkey is changing. The judgment “She turned out hollow… This woman won’t be able to handle this…” is spreading about Tansu Çiller. Yesterday, receiving the generals, she announced that she was delegating the matter to the army by saying “We will stand by the TSK (Turkish Armed Forces) in its struggle against the PKK.” At the Sivas funerals Erdal İnönü was booed along with the ministers accompanying him. The SHP is cracking; its withdrawal from the coalition is on the agenda. The news that SHP Chairman Aydın Güven Gürkan requested a meeting with Baykal led to interpretations that he would run for chairman in September with a “uniting the parties” initiative… I told Haluk I would leave the CHP at the first opportunity.
