July 7 / I didn’t go to the PM meeting. Çevikçe also called the meeting “a waste of time”… My dear Fatma apparently wants me to stay in Ankara… At least until I find a new job. But I’ve completely lost interest now… In the evening I went to the cinema. I don’t want to sit in the Mülkiye Association garden; it’s full of people I don’t want to see.

July 11 / After his meeting with Çiller we talked with Baykal. Çiller’s feeling him out without coming with a concrete proposal had infuriated Baykal. “Either she doesn’t know what she’s going to do or she does whatever the Americans say,” he said. We presented him our five-page ‘Solution to the Kurdish problem’ report. We advocated TRT broadcasting in Kurdish, Kurdish classes being given in state schools. When I said the duty of defending the country’s unity had fallen to him after Özal’s death, Baykal’s response was, “The state shouldn’t have a responsibility like developing Kurdish identity.” He said he opposed Operation Provide Comfort because of “national feelings” (integrity), but he wasn’t opposed to a Kurdish state in Northern Iraq. We revised the report according to his wishes.

July 12 / Taha Akyol talked to Yalçın Doğan about me; “He’s leaving the CHP, Sabah or Hürriyet might grab him, let’s take him,” he said. Yalçın also said “I knew he couldn’t make it at the CHP… We’ll take care of that in August”… In the evening I went to visit İlber; we chatted.

July 13 / Tomorrow I’m going to Ayvalık for fifteen days. I hope these are finally my last days in Ankara. It would be good to end this well… Judging from the news in the papers, it’s clear that Baykal was inspired by our text in his Van speech. I wonder how the bigots in the party are receiving it? The SHP and CHP support Çiller’s proposal for Kurdish classes and broadcasts, but Demirel came out strongly saying “it will lead to division.” Çiller will probably back down.

July 14 / Çevikçe returned from Van. The text we prepared was reworked through the night and given to the press. Today the newspapers wrote that Baykal said “end to the assimilation policy.” Bravo, he spoke quite courageously…

I constantly think about the meaninglessness of living separately from Fatma. If I left without waiting to find a new job, if I spent the summer with Fatma in Ayvalık… I also think about the failures in my life. I’ve reached this age and couldn’t amount to anything… This is perhaps the result of my taking on every task only half-heartedly. Most likely so…

“What Will Be Written on My Tombstone”

August 1 / My elder brother’s daughter Ümit and her fiancé Cem Boyner came to Ayvalık. Cem mentioned his intention to establish a new party that would bring together a sensible left, Kurds, and the religious. He said he was working on this with Zülfü Dicleli, Asaf Savaş, and Hüseyin Ergün. I said our struggles to fix the left hadn’t worked, that this had led us too to the idea of a new party, though we thought this wouldn’t be easy at all, and I congratulated him for showing this courage. He said in fifteen days he would be able to tell me more satisfying things. “What will be written on my tombstone, that’s what matters to me…” he said. He said the success he had achieved in business didn’t satisfy him. He implied that he wanted me to be part of the party they would establish.

August 2 / I’m in Istanbul. Among the important developments of the last twenty days is Satel firing the British editors. Zafer Mutlu and Ercan Arıklı have been brought in their place. In my opinion this is the end of our flirtation with television… Ömer, however, maintains hope because of Arıklı’s admiration for him… Starting tomorrow I’ll launch a job search offensive. I’ve completely broken from the CHP “morally,” especially after hearing about Boyner’s new party idea. Cem and I chatted: While explaining the reasons for his entering politics, he said the trajectory on the Kurdish issue was toward a military regime, in which case the only opposition would be religious opposition, and something needed to be done against this. But he couldn’t help saying that sometimes he thought about spending his life “growing cucumbers”… Last night Aylin Livaneli’s wedding was full of pleasant coincidences: I chatted with Arne Ruth (Dagens Nyheter editor) for a significant portion of the evening. Ataman Onar said Fatma was “as beautiful as Catherine Deneuve.” (In my opinion she’s even more beautiful…) Baykal told Fatma that “they were sharing me among themselves.” Alaton told Fatma that I was more important than both Baykal and Karayalçın… Tuba’s drunken dance with Çetin Altan was a masterpiece.

August 3 / After about 20 days I’m in Ankara again. I talked to Taha Akyol on the phone. Yalçın Doğan really wanted to hire me at Milliyet, but this could only come up after the newspaper moved on August 15. When I called Yalçın and couldn’t reach him I left a note. He didn’t call back. Ömer and I agreed that he would talk directly to Ercan Arıklı about the television program.

August 4 / I spent last night in a nightmare of anxiety about the future. I woke up at 4 in the morning and was lost in thought for a long time… When morning came I consoled myself like this: “You’d better stay at the CHP until the retirement issue is resolved.. What’s important anyway is health, the rest will work out…” It wasn’t ineffective.

Three phone conversations I had today suddenly changed the picture: I called Zülfü (Livaneli); I mentioned the television program Ömer, Refik, and I had prepared. He said after the British editors left, he too was in management alongside Zafer Mutlu and Ercan Arıklı, I should send him the project, he would look into it. When he said he would also be making a program, I said I could be editor for his program. “Look, that’s a good idea!” he responded. He said he would think about these matters and call me…

I called Necla Zarakol. “It must be telepathy, I was going to call you too,” she said. She was also part of the group Boyner mentioned. I said Cem had told me about his preparations too, that I was hesitant about forming a party, and that a manifesto similar to YÖN could be good. She said she was about to leave her current job. We talked about how we could do good work together… Later I talked to Nur Çekirge. She said she was going to Istanbul for the company whose founding she was participating in, and would call soon to give detailed information. These contacts lifted my spirits; I became hopeful that new job opportunities would emerge. I called Fatma in this good mood… I hope one of the emerging options materializes…

August 5 / Yalçın Doğan called and said my Milliyet job unfortunately couldn’t happen… I was quite upset. I’m approaching 50 and facing the anxiety of unemployment. This saddens me greatly… In the afternoon at the CHP Research Center Conferences we organized, Fuat’s friend Osman Coşkunoğlu from the University of Illinois spoke. Then we went together to Baykal’s room. Baykal talked at length. Although he wasn’t opposed to privatization, he said opposing it would put wind in the CHP’s sails… This isn’t a policy I approve of. Not being able to speak openly bothers me. I can carry on this job until September 15 at most.

“I Hear You’re Leaving the CHP…”

August 6 / On the way to Istanbul on Varan I ran into Rıza Türmen; we sat next to each other. “I hear you’re leaving the CHP…” he said; Erol Çevikçe had told Murat Katoğlu… I felt as if boiling water had been poured over my head. Apparently my complaints reached their ears and they wrote me off… Yet yesterday Baykal had shared some information about those who would join the CHP…

In Istanbul, Fatma, Ömer, Oğuz (Öztuzcu), and I assessed the situation. I decided to inform Baykal that I was leaving when I returned to Ankara. I felt relieved… The worst thing is indecision. Besides, nothing can be achieved without taking risks. I told Fatma, “The time to give up the luxury of working for the country and nation and at a job I love, and to get a paying job, has come and is passing.” I announced my decision to Fuat Atalay; he wasn’t surprised at all. Maybe he’s calculating to take my place. I told Haluk my decision too.

August 7 / Elem, the young woman who was my secretary at the Cinnah office, left a letter when she quit. She wrote: “Mr. Şahin, something came up and I had to go to my hometown Gümüşhacıköy tomorrow Sunday. I came here on Saturday to say goodbye to you. But I couldn’t find you. Thank you for everything. When necessary you were my boss, when necessary you were a father to me. You made me love working life. If it weren’t for you I probably would have left this job much earlier. I thank you again for everything. Love and greetings to Mrs. Fatma, Mr. Fuat and his wife.” I was moved…

August 9 / I called Ms. Nesrin (Baytok) and requested an appointment with Baykal. We were able to meet at headquarters between 7:45 and 8:15 PM. I told Baykal: “With my family in Istanbul I’m living a very difficult life. Half of the money I earn goes to travel and hotels…” In response, he said “Move the house; your place is Ankara..” When I said “I can’t decide…” he said “Oh no, I think you have some ideas that aren’t good…” I said:

“The party didn’t receive me well; I came across as too liberal in views. The Research Center couldn’t be properly established. Contacting you wasn’t easy. I personally want to support you but I no longer want to work for the party, because I don’t feel I’m being useful. I can’t establish dialogue with anyone in the party other than you…”

He responded as follows: “You will become a politician. You’re right in your unease; I too encountered the same attitudes when I was an advisor. Despite all the difficulties, liberalizing the left is easier than the right. We will get you into politics. There are developments toward SHP-CHP integration. Now is not the time to leave. Tell me what you need, I’ll try to meet it. I was also at fault. Let’s move your office to headquarters. Go, take a vacation for a while…” In short he didn’t let me go… He spoke so beautifully that there’s no need to rush to leave. He showed such respect and goodwill that I can’t dismiss it out of hand. If a good job opportunity comes up in the meantime, great… For now I continue working. It probably would have been better if he had said goodbye, but he didn’t… I went to dinner at the Özdalgas’. As we discussed there, the CHP needs “revolutionary” (paradigm- changing) politics, but Baykal is a “normal” (even overly normal) politician; too cautious and calculating.

August 10 / Today I told Fuat: We lost the ideological struggle in the Program Commission. Let’s continue by organizing conferences and seminars. Let’s shift our projects from future-oriented to opposition-function oriented. If we did this, I said, we could “coexist” with Baykal. I said I would take the proposal to Baykal that he have equal status with me and receive a professional salary.

August 13-16 / I was in Ayvalık for the long weekend. On the morning of the 14th Cem Boyner called; he praised to the skies my article titled “The need for reform and the left,” a copy of which I had also sent him. “Can I share it with my colleagues?” he asked. He said it had been proposed that they take over the DP (Democrat Party). I wished him well.

August 17 / I talked with Hasan Cemal; I conveyed the negative response from Yalçın Doğan. “Apparently there’s no place for me in the Turkish press,” I said…. Then I talked to Ömer; he too is about to give up hope on the Satel job.

August 18 / Today, a friend of mine who works in the construction industry told me that Çiller was siphoning money into her own pocket from a DYP contractor, and that Demirel, who had noticed the situation, was very angry about it.

August 20 / The appointment with Baykal from two days ago finally happened today. Again he did most of the talking. From now on, the party will cover my travel and hotel expenses. The office will continue. We’ll discuss the cadre issue “later” again. I conveyed my discomfort at appearing to work at two separate full-time jobs. “The Group advisorship is not a problem; don’t mind such things,” he said. We finally delivered the local governance reform project… I need to find a proper job as soon as possible…

August 24 / This morning I returned from Ayvalık where I spent the weekend. According to the poll Hürriyet had conducted, SHP 11%, CHP 10%, DP 7%… There seems to be a shift from SHP to CHP. Hasan Cemal called; apparently Güneri Cıvaoğlu was going to offer me editorship on a television program he would do; he had asked what I was getting from the CHP… I said I wasn’t thinking of being Cıvaoğlu’s assistant; I didn’t like him at all. “You’re right, you can’t work with that man, but still don’t be harsh if an offer comes,” he said. I also said if he made an offer I would politely decline. Shortly after, I was told Cıvaoğlu was calling and Zülfü came on the line and conveyed the offer from Cıvaoğlu who was apparently sitting next to him. I said we were insistent on the program proposal we made to ATV, and that I couldn’t work with Cıvaoğlu… I explained the situation to Fatma. Her reaction was “Zülfü is trying to prepare an opportunity for you, and you’re refusing…” When I said “Leaving my post as Baykal’s advisor to become Cıvaoğlu’s assistant would be a big loss of prestige” she had to agree… When I talked to Zülfü the situation became clear: He had been forced to make this call. While arguing that news needed to be presented accurately and reliably, when he said “For example Şahin used to do this at Cumhuriyet” Cıvaoğlu jumped on it and said he wanted exactly me as editor… I told Zülfü about my recent agreement with Baykal, but said I could still be research editor for a program he would do, and that I could explain the situation to Baykal. “I’ll think about it and call you,” he said.

“The De-personalization of the Turkish Left”

August 25 / Mümtaz Soysal wrote the following lines in his column in Milliyet today, implying me without naming me: “…What has happened is that left parties coming from the Kemalist tradition have, as if all this were a bad dream that should be forgotten, at times come under the influence of a circle called the Second Republicans. This influence, which has seeped into the management of foundations close to the parties, into ministry and general chairmanship advisorships, even into the preparation rooms of leadership races, played an important role in the de-personalization of the Turkish left, in its becoming colorless and integrating with the established order.”

September 1 / I was in Ayvalık between August 28-31. This was the closing of the 1993 season… Today the CHP Kırkpınar district chairman visited me along with his entourage. In summary: He said the CHP executives couldn’t give the party a spirit, and the party could find this spirit in Kemalism. This was supposedly the spirit of national liberation, resistance to Sèvres, revolt against imperialism… The biggest reason for the CHP’s growing in Kırkpınar was MHP (Nationalist Movement Party) youth joining the party; because they had decided that the real nationalist leader was Baykal… Nothing surprising!!!

September 2 / I visited Nur Çekirge at the office of the Alo Bilgi company where she had started working. I met Sedat Örsel, one of the former TRT deputy general managers, who was her boss. The company they founded called Aktif TV was producing contract programs for ATV. He half-heartedly suggested I also make a program… Then I stopped by Ahmet Evin’s (Philip Morris office). “Headhunter” Susan Kemper was coming to Ankara in 15 days. We would have dinner together.

September 3 / Today we suggested to Baykal that he announce before or immediately after the SHP congress, at the merger congress of the two parties, that he wouldn’t run for chairman… I talked to Nebil İlseven: Apparently he’s eager to leave Satel. Meanwhile I talked to Nilüfer Kuyaş; she said she could only stand Satel for two weeks… Cem Boyner called and invited me to the meeting they would hold at The Marmara on September 9 where they would announce a manifesto. He said the Democrat Party founded in November 1992 had made a merger proposal, and they would respond within a week. “You carry great weight, I’m worried it would be squandered in a merger,” I said. “I talked to ANAP and DYP people, you can’t do business with them,” he said. I agreed. His colleagues in the New Democracy Movement had really liked my article; they asked “Did he give this article to that moron?” I said Baykal wasn’t a moron, but unfortunately he was doing “normal politics.”

September 4 / On the occasion of the Sivas Congress anniversary I went to the rally the CHP held in Sivas and to the Party Assembly meeting. If Fuat Atalay and Nur hadn’t come the 6-hour round trip would have been unbearable. Sivas is just another Central Anatolian city; maybe the number of round-bearded men is a bit higher. Baykal was met by a convoy of 500 vehicles also coming from Antep and Istanbul. Çiller was leaving as we were entering the city. Like Çiller’s rally, Baykal’s also gathered at most 2-3 thousand people. When I returned to Ankara at night I had severe diarrhea.

September 7 / Fatma said don’t listen to Seyfettin and Fuat who were against me attending Cem Boyner’s meeting on the grounds that it would cause gossip. I still called Seyfettin. When he advised me to consult, I called Baykal: He said I should attend the meeting and suggest to Boyner that they join the CHP as a team. The conflict between the respect I feel for Baykal’s virtues and my reaction to the CHP’s conservatism is wearing me down… Today Fatma said, “This can’t go on like this, come to Istanbul already.”

“The Need for Reform and the Left”

I was in Istanbul between September 7-13. / On September 9 I attended the meeting at The Marmara of Boyner and his colleagues (Asaf Savaş Akat, Mehmet Altan, Hüseyin Ergün, Cengiz Çandar, etc.). In Cem’s words, they announced a text significantly inspired by my article titled “The need for reform and the left.” Proposals were made to establish an association, foundation, party. İlhan Kesici advocated joining a party. I said the “message” was strong, what mattered was conveying this message most effectively, having it spread through an announcement like the YÖN manifesto, everyone working for the ideas in this text where they were, for example there was a large segment in the CHP too that embraced these ideas. I explained that I was afraid this message would be marginalized and wasted if it became a party. Maybe I didn’t express myself well enough… I couldn’t attend the dinner because I went to the CHP’s 70th anniversary cocktail at Pera Palas. It was a terrible crowd: provincial and old… I was angered when I heard that Ahmet Taner Kışlalı, who had attacked me, was a panelist together with İsmail Cem and Elisabeth Özdalga. Nebil İlseven and I left; we talked about starting a political consulting company. Of course in vain…

September 10 / In the morning I went to the “Chinese House” where Boyner lived in Ortaköy. I said if they established a party, the energy created by the message would go to waste, that even the DYP’s offer of Istanbul Mayor to him seemed more reasonable to me. I mentioned the dangers of setting out with intellectuals. He talked about the difficulty of continuing the battle of ideas with existing parties. When I conveyed Baykal’s proposal that he join the CHP, he said “I’m touched and honored but I haven’t decided what to do yet, when I do I’ll also meet with Baykal.” I said the idea of change still found greater support in left parties. (Really?..) He suggested I join his political movement. I said this wasn’t possible because I worked professionally at the CHP, but I could participate in their intellectual work. We talked about the tension between public and private lives. He said he might not stay in politics for very long. (Interestingly: Indeed, that would be the case.)

September 11 / In the morning I met with Necla Zarakol and we agreed on establishing a political consulting company. If necessary we’ll take a wealthy friend of hers as a partner. The timing looks like it will be around November-December. In the evening it was announced that Murat Karayalçın had won the SHP general chairmanship.

September 12 / Ufuk Güldemir called, and I went to his house in Ulus. He said he had received a general manager offer from Show TV and wanted to know what I thought about it. I enthusiastically supported it. When I said we could work together, he said “that would be amazing.”

September 13 / In Ankara at Yahya’s (Tezel) house we watched the debate on television between Karayalçın and Baykal about uniting the parties. Baykal appeared quite uncompromising. However, the next morning we read in Milliyet that he had proposed merging the parties rather than cooperating in opposition. It seems that, having failed to develop an independent political line or to show any difference from the SHP, he has reached the “throwing in the towel” stage.

September 14 / I conveyed to Baykal what Boyner had said.

“He Made a Mess of It”

September 15 / In his opening speech at the Party Assembly meeting Baykal brushed off the merger issue by saying “under the CHP roof and on an opposition platform.” Then the discussion moved to the program written by Cem and Hacaloğlu, full of repetitions and vague expressions, which lagged behind even the SHP’s. Besim Üstünel gave a speech in favor of making all kinds of concessions for the merger. It seems Baykal has no choice but to merge with the SHP since he couldn’t create a different party. He couldn’t give a clear message either: He tells others “let’s unite in opposition”; but told Milliyet “it could be in government too.” In Sedat Ergin’s words, “he made a mess of it.” It was announced that Ahmet Yücekök and Uğur Alacakaptan would join the party as advisors to the general chairman. I could hand over the job to Yücekök and leave, and indeed I should; but it’s hard without finding a job.

September 16 / In Istanbul I ran into Üstünel at the Japanese Consulate General’s cocktail. He said Alacakaptan was mediating between Baykal and Karayalçın… I talked to Alaton. He said it had been decided that the Strategic Research Foundation would be established under the Boğaziçi University Foundation, that Üstün Ergüder also supported me for the directorship, and that he was waiting for me to return to Istanbul.

September 17 / I visited Ergüder: He said I was always among those mentioned on the list, that he believed I would do this job well, and that we could start as soon as money was collected.

September 19 / I spoke at the joint panel of TÜSES-TDV-SİSAV on “Press and Democracy Culture.” When Taha Akyol didn’t come I was left alone with Altemur Kılıç and Oktay Ekşi… In the evening Yavuz Baydar stopped by; from him I learned that Ufuk Güldemir’s appointment as Show TV editor-in-chief had been finalized. I called, he wasn’t home; I talked to his wife Cumhur. She was very happy.

September 20 / As soon as I returned to Ankara and entered the office Alaton called. I conveyed my conversation with Ergüder. He said he would do his best but there might be obstacles he couldn’t overcome… I called Ufuk and congratulated him. If you think of me, I’m in, I said. “I’m not thinking of anyone else… Let’s bring it up after I start work,” he said. “That would be good, because there are other job possibilities too…” I said. Fuat, Haluk, and I assessed the situation at the CHP. I said: Baykal is under pressure on one hand for merger at any cost, on the other for no merger, that’s why he appears inconsistent.

September 21 / Today Fuat and I prepared a proposal for Baykal that in summary contained a call “The SHP is finished, social democrats to the CHP”… In the afternoon İlter Turan called and suggested I teach a course on “Turkey’s social structure” at the Istanbul University SBF starting October 4. I asked for a day or two to think, but I probably won’t be able to accept. There’s too little time to prepare.

September 23 - October 3 / I stayed nine days in Istanbul with Fatma and the children.

October 1 / Together with Fuat and Seyfettin, I wrote a report for Baykal containing concrete proposals for merger with the SHP. BBC Turkish asked me for commentary on the merger; I didn’t want to speak because I don’t have a political identity… Celal (Üster) said Alp Orçun was preparing an economics newspaper with Aydın Doğan’s support, and he would do the arts pages. Since he didn’t mention me, Alp must not have me in mind… Hadi Uluengin came to breakfast; he said “You’re one of Turkey’s 4-5 intellectuals in the Western sense, decide what you want to do already”… As if there were fifty jobs if I just waved my hand… 9 days in Istanbul did me a lot of good. It would be great if a job came up in Istanbul now and I could finish this Ankara business.

October 4 / Today Karayalçın came to visit Baykal, but it seems he’s not very enthusiastic about the merger. Yet the merger is an opportunity for him.

October 5 / I’ve had it up to here with Ankara now. If I had a little courage, or rather financial strength, I would run away from here tomorrow. But I have to hold on at least until I get my pension from the SGK (Social Security Institution). I called General Manager Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu by phone; he said he would help, bless him.

October 7 / I talked to Baykal on the phone. He had told Karayalçın “Either we’ll establish a new party together or one of us will join the other…” and requested unconditional talks; Karayalçın said he would think it over. The point Baykal has reached is interesting; this is called throwing in the towel… I said I didn’t have much work, I was writing a report on Black Sea Economic Cooperation. “Also look into that water issue…” he said and gave a lecture on the topic. He already knows the subject but I was glad I got a “job.” These two reports, plus preparing a proposal on the election law will keep me busy for a while… Fuat and I went to see Erol Çevikçe: He mentioned the possibility of Ecevit proposing an alliance to Karayalçın; he told Fuat he could propose the chairmanship of the merged party to Aydın Güven Gürkan. Fuat will convey it.

## “Intellectual Perspective” on the Horizon

October 10 / I’m in Istanbul to follow up on my retirement paperwork. Zülfü called; “A page called ‘Intellectual Perspective’ is being prepared at Sabah newspaper, would you take on the editorship?” he asked. “Of course!…” I said. I’m over the moon… Is the opportunity I’ve been waiting for emerging?!.. In the evening I went to Zülfü’s; we exchanged views on details. Initially it was thought that Can Ataklı and Murat Birsel would edit the page, which was to be called “Intellectual.” But Zülfü persuaded Mutlu by saying “Şahin Alpay does this job best, and he’s looking for an opportunity to return to the press. It would also be more appropriate if the page’s name were a bit less pretentious, Intellectual Perspective…” That night when I got home I excitedly put into writing the page proposal I would present to Zafer Mutlu.

October 11 / I met with Mutlu at Sabah; we discussed the proposal I had prepared for the page; he liked it. He offered to pay me the same salary as managing editor Okay Gönensin; I immediately accepted. This was the highest salary I had received up to that point. He also accepted my wish to hire a qualified assistant for the daily page. Was my luck turning?.. I was very happy. Most importantly, Fatma was also pleased with the news.

October 12 / I went to Ankara and met with Baykal. I explained that I was leaving and returning to the press, that I would do a daily opinion page at Sabah. He received it with more understanding than I had ever expected. He probably thought my job would be over if the merger happened. He had me do something I hadn’t done in eight months, asking me to work all night on the proposal document to be given to the SHP. I worked with pleasure. Thus another page in my life, the CHP page, was closing.

As for what I did during the 8 months I worked at the CHP, the main reports, some of which I prepared together with Haluk Özdalga and/or Fuat Atalay and gave to the general chairman, all written with a liberal left understanding, were as follows:

- Global Trends and Turkey

- What Does the CHP Want in Education

- What Is Contemporary Social Democracy?

- The Need for Reform and the Left in Turkey (The text that Boyner, not Baykal, spoke of with praise.)

- Turkish Democracy Toward the 21st Century - Democracy Culture and the Press in Turkey

- Democracies and Political Research Foundations

- Clean Society Project (Alpay - Atalay)

- Local Governance Reform (Alpay - Atalay)

- On the Kurdish Question (Alpay - Atalay)

- CHP - SHP Merger Scenario (Alpay - Atalay)

- The CHP’s Fundamental Goals (Alpay - Özdalga - Atalay)

- Report to the Party Assembly (Alpay - Özdalga - Atalay)

- A Proposal for the CHP Program (Alpay - Özdalga - Atalay)

What happened at the CHP after I left Ankara? The CHP and SHP merged in 1995 under the CHP’s roof and under Baykal’s leadership. The CHP barely passed the 10% national threshold in the 1995 general elections; in the 1999 elections it couldn’t pass the threshold and remained outside parliament. In the 2002 general elections when Ecevit’s DSP was routed with 1% of the vote, the CHP rose to the position of main opposition party with 19% of the vote; in the 2007 elections it also raised its vote share to 21%. Baykal resigned from the CHP general chairmanship in May 2010 following a conspiracy against him (the release of a tape about a secret meeting with his secretary Nesrin Baytok). At the extraordinary congress held after Baykal’s resignation, Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu would be elected general chairman. Despite all Kılıçdaroğlu’s efforts to distance the party from its statist-centralist-laicist (favoring authoritarian secularism) discourse and give it a freedom-oriented discourse, the CHP’s vote remained around 25-26%. I won’t claim that if Baykal had adopted the views I proposed in 1993, the CHP could have become a more influential actor in Turkish politics… But the party’s inability to intellectually renew itself must have played a role in this stagnation.

Was It “Not About the CHP’s ‘Genes’”?

Looking back after so many years have passed, what can I say about my CHP experience? When I couldn’t find the opportunity to continue my academic career after returning from Sweden and started working at Cumhuriyet newspaper, the understanding that gave meaning to my life was that I could contribute to the country’s intellectual life and liberation with my liberal left views. However, the reaction of Cumhuriyet’s older generation of writers who had an authoritarian left understanding resulted in my having to leave the newspaper. The motivation that led me to work first at TÜSES for about a year after Cumhuriyet, and then at the CHP for about eight months, was also the search to inoculate circles that defined themselves as social democratic-democratic left with the modernity of the liberal left views I had acquired in Sweden. However, this search of mine also resulted in a failure similar to what I had experienced at Cumhuriyet newspaper.

In the article I wrote years later titled “It’s Not About the CHP’s ‘Genes’,” I tried to explain the reasons for this failure as follows:

“I met Deniz Baykal at Ankara University SBF in the mid-1960s. I was a student, he was an assistant with a doctorate, then became an associate professor. For me and my friends, although Baykal wasn’t left enough, he was a respected faculty member we found warm and friendly, in short our ‘Deniz Abi.’ About ten years later, I visited Deniz Baykal, who had just left the Ministry of Finance at the time, to ask for his help. I had returned home from Sweden with the political amnesty issued in 1974, and did my military service as a short-term reserve officer in 1975. But because I wasn’t given a passport, I couldn’t return to Stockholm University where I was continuing my doctoral studies. In the end, through his influence I was able to get a passport, return to Stockholm and complete my doctorate. In this regard, I owe him a debt of gratitude I will never forget.

My re-encounter with Baykal was in the late 1980s when he was SHP General Secretary. At that time, while I was working at Cumhuriyet, I was also writing for the magazine called Sosyal Demokrat, which I published together with friends like Ercan Karakaş, Asaf Savaş Akat, and Seyfettin Gürsel. After leaving Cumhuriyet I had also taken on the directorship of the TÜSES Foundation (which I joined at the late Erdal İnönü’s invitation). The question in my mind in those years was this: Could there be a truly social democratic current, a party in Turkey, of the kind I knew in Sweden? When Deniz Baykal and İsmail Cem published the book titled New Left in 1992, I saw this as a ray of hope in that direction.

On September 9, 1992, with some curiosity and some excitement, I went to Ankara to watch the CHP’s reopening congress. At that congress Baykal gave a speech that still seems ‘magnificent’ to me today. He was saying: ‘We will redefine the CHP… The goal is not to make poverty an ideology, but to create a welfare society… From here I address all the people: There is no longer a Kurd-Turk, Alevi-Sunni fight. From now on there is peace. The CHP is coming to realize this great claim. It is coming to reconcile labor and capital. It is coming to reconcile Eastern and Western cultures. We are coming to embrace both the young person who attends İmam Hatip (religious vocational) school and the young person who goes to the disco… The CHP should no longer be understood as a state party, but as a society and people’s party…’

A few days later I called Baykal and invited him to give a speech at the Pera Palas meetings (of which I was among the organizers at the time). The Pera speech seemed even more magnificent… I was saying to myself ‘Here is Turkey’s liberal social democratic leader being born…’ I told him: ‘Deniz Abi, if you walk on this path that Turkey so desperately needs, tomorrow you will be Turkey’s prime minister… You should establish a team of young and knowledgeable advisors to support you on this path. Look, at least two prime ministers emerged from the brain trust of Sweden’s legendary 1950s Prime Minister Tage Erlander. You too should build a strong political cadre that will serve Turkey…’

Despite my objections that I wasn’t young enough for this job, Baykal invited me to the CHP to build this cadre. On February 15, 1993, I started work as advisor to the CHP General Chairman and the Group, and as Research Center director. But my job had ended before it began, for after my late friend Uğur Mumcu’s despicable murder on January 24, 1993, Baykal, looking at the mass reactions to this murder, had decided that the CHP didn’t need to renew itself.

I stayed in Ankara for about eight months. During this time Baykal and I met three or four times, for 15-20 minutes at a time. He didn’t even want to be seen with me. Together with my like-minded friends Haluk Özdalga and Fuat Atalay, I joined the Program Commission. Faced with the reactions our proposals to redefine the six arrows generated, I saw that staying at the CHP was meaningless. I asked Baykal for permission and returned to Istanbul, to the press. After that we never met again.

If Baykal had believed in the power of ideas whose time had come, if he had stuck to his discourse at the 1992 congress, the CHP could long since have been in power, and Turkey could be a completely different place. In my opinion it’s not about the CHP’s ‘genes.’” (Zaman, April 26, 2008)

I am writing these lines in 2022. Looking at the fact that the struggle that broke out at Cumhuriyet newspaper in the 1980s between the left Kemalist (i.e., statist, nationalist, laicist) mentality and the social democratic/liberal left understanding continues within the CHP even today, it is also possible to conclude that the problem does stem from the genes.

# CHAPTER IX / “INTELLECTUAL PERSPECTIVE”

On October 13, 1993, I made my permanent return from Ankara to Istanbul, and my first task was to call Nilüfer Kuyaş to offer her a position working together at Sabah. After graduating from Robert College, Nilüfer had completed her undergraduate degree in philosophy at Wellesley College, one of America’s prestigious universities, and had also earned a master’s degree in social psychology from Boğaziçi University. Between 1982 and 1993, while pursuing her philosophy doctorate at the University of London, she had worked as a programmer at the BBC Turkish Service together with her husband Tayfun Ertan, and that year they had made their permanent return to Turkey. We had known each other since 1982, when she translated Thomas Kuhn’s “The Structure of Scientific Revolutions,” one of the masterworks of the history of philosophy of science, into Turkish, and I had started editing the book page at Cumhuriyet. Her acceptance of my proposal and taking on the assistant editorship of the page that would be published seven days a week was an extraordinary stroke of luck for me; because Nilüfer was not just a friend I loved and admired—I could not have found another work partner with her qualifications.

On October 14, my old friend Nebil İlseven, who was then serving as a consultant to Dinç Bilgin, the owner of the Sabah group, picked me up from home and took me to the newspaper building in İki Telli. The next day Nilüfer also came, spoke with Mutlu, and started work. On October 16, we published the first issue of “Intellectual Perspective.” The page’s headline article was devoted to introducing Huntington’s “Clash of Civilizations” thesis, which had appeared in his article in the Summer 1993 issue of Foreign Affairs magazine and attracted great interest, under the title “Famous American political scientist Huntington claims: Civilizations will clash in the new world.” The rest of the page featured an article introducing the New Democracy Movement under the title “An intellectuals’ initiative against the political class: New world, new Turkey, new democracy,” alongside a piece on British historian Paul Kennedy’s book Preparing for the Twenty-First Century, which was gaining fame at the time.

In the introductory text titled “There is a need for Intellectual Perspective,” I wrote: “Whatever field we work in, we increasingly feel the need to have more and deeper knowledge… Our world and our society are changing at a dizzying pace. To keep up with this change, more or less all of us feel the need for the most important quality of an intellectual—being able to look critically at the society we live in and at ourselves. Different views and different approaches and perspectives now seem more interesting and important to us than before. It can be said that all of us need ‘Intellectual Perspective’ to some degree. For these reasons, on this page called ‘Intellectual Perspective,’ we hope to provide Sabah readers with clues to help them follow developments in the fields of knowledge and thought in the world and in our country, emerging trends, and erupting debates. We plan to spread across a wide area ranging from politics and economics to cultural subjects in the broadest sense, including science, art, music, architecture, environment, and sometimes sports.”

The page was published for a little over six months until April 25, 1994, and we remained committed to this perspective. Nilüfer Kuyaş generally took on the writing and editing of art and culture topics, while I handled politics and social science. Among those who immediately called to congratulate me upon my sudden departure from CHP and appearance at Sabah, I have recorded the names of İshak Alaton, Osman Kavala, Zülfü Dicleli, Hüseyin Ergün, Cem Boyner, Mehmet Kabasakal, Asaf Savaş Akat, Ferai Tınç, Yalçın Bayer, Adil Özkol, Uğur Alacakaptan, and Güngör Mengi from Sabah.

At Sabah, I was reunited with my close and former colleagues Hasan Cemal and Cengiz Çandar.

Hasan was pleased with my arrival. When he saw the first page of Intellectual Perspective (hereafter IP), he said, “This is exactly the page I was expecting!..” Cengiz, with his usual mischievous manner, teased me by referring to what we had experienced at Cumhuriyet in the 1980s: “Oh no, now that you’ve come, it looks like I’m on my way out…” he said. Okay Gönensin (may he rest in peace), who again appeared before me as managing editor, made it clear he was not pleased with my arrival at Sabah. I met Ergun Babahan, Can Ataklı, and Murat Birsel for the first time; they showed neither particular sympathy nor antipathy toward me. However, before my name came up, it had been planned for Ataklı and Birsel to create the page.

My first disappointment at Sabah was that, contrary to my expectations, we were not given an office. We were shown a place at one of the desks lined up in the hall where the reporters worked. My second disappointment was the attitude the owner took toward us. On one of my first days at the newspaper, Mutlu introduced me to Dinç Bilgin, who, as always, was playing backgammon with someone in a room. Bilgin neither asked how I was nor posed a question nor said anything; he just stared blankly. From then on, whenever we crossed paths in the corridors, he pretended not to know me. (Zülfü tried to explain this with Bilgin’s “shy temperament,” but I was not convinced.) Thus I began to get acquainted with the culture of Sabah newspaper.

## The caste system at Sabah

The culture of Sabah was quite different from Cumhuriyet. On the top floor of the newspaper’s modern and ostentatious building was the restaurant where the owner and the “most privileged” writers and managers ate, on one of the middle floors the reporters ate, and on the lowest floor the ordinary employees ate. There was virtually a caste system. Everyone had internalized the rules of which floor they would work on, which restaurant they would eat in, which rooms they could enter and exit; no one made a mistake. The culture of the newspaper, which claimed to represent Turkey’s “rising values” together with ANAP, in my view exactly reflected the mentality of the “nouveau riche,” the new rich. I felt very alien to this “class-based” culture. At Cumhuriyet I had worked with a sense of exclusion; at Sabah I would work with a sense of being out of place.

What made me happy in my new job was Zafer Mutlu’s weekly column published on November 29, 1993. After listing how Sabah was “the best” of the Turkish press in various respects, Mutlu said: “For those interested in the intellectual dimension of events, for those who want to follow our world from a more intellectual perspective alongside current affairs, SABAH is again the unrivaled daily newspaper. Because Çetin Altan, Zülfü Livaneli, and Mehmet Altan are all at SABAH. In addition, Turkey’s only and first (I say first because I’m sure imitations will be made very soon) intellectual page is also at SABAH. The interest shown in this page of incredible quality, edited by Şahin Alpay, makes us very, very happy on behalf of our country. The interest this page has received is extremely encouraging for Turkey.”

At that time in the Turkish media, the Sabah group owned by the Dinç Bilgin family and the Doğan group owned by the Aydın Doğan family were on the one hand forming a cartel among themselves and cooperating against employees, while on the other hand they were in fierce competition for circulation, advertising share, political influence, and obtaining advantages from the government. The Sabah group was close to DYP, and the Doğan group to ANAP. The competition between them had triggered an unprecedented promotion war with a wide variety of products ranging from dishes to dictionaries and encyclopedias given along with the newspaper to increase sales.

Although I was extremely uncomfortable with the culture and environment of Sabah, Nilüfer and I tried to do our job as well as we could. On the other hand, because it was the most prestigious and highest-paying job I had done until then, and because I believed we were providing an important service, I was generally pleased with my job at Sabah. In the IP pages, alongside my and Nilüfer’s writings and interviews, contributions from some of Turkey’s most distinguished signatures also appeared. We were pleased with the work we were doing… Nilüfer expressed it this way: “We like what we’re doing, and that’s enough for us!..” But unfortunately, my Sabah adventure, like my TÜSES and CHP adventures, was not long-lived.

My ATV adventure

The financial crisis that erupted in April 1994 brought the end of IP at Sabah. One day the newspaper went from 40 pages to 20; managing editor Gönensin announced with undisguised satisfaction that it had been decided to close IP. Zafer Mutlu said they had made this decision unwillingly, that I should wait a while, that the crisis would pass, but that they had to say goodbye to Nilüfer Kuyaş. The reason Mutlu suggested I wait was probably that he thought a place could be found for me at Yeni Yüzyıl newspaper, which the Sabah group would start publishing shortly.

At the beginning of May, I decided to resign from Sabah. Since the job I loved doing had ended and Nilüfer had also been let go, there was no point in sitting and waiting at a workplace I found not at all pleasant. I also thought new doors could open. I knew Umur Talu, Milliyet’s editor-in-chief, from Cumhuriyet where he had worked for a time. I had hope that I could find a place there. Ufuk Güldemir had been appointed editor-in-chief at Show TV. We were discussing among ourselves that we could make a program with political-intellectual content where I would edit and he would host. Ufuk had served as Cumhuriyet’s Washington DC correspondent and had returned to the country after his position was terminated following the split at the newspaper. I had strongly supported his acceptance of Show TV’s offer.

Then, at the beginning of June 1994, Sabah’s senior columnist Güneri Cıvaoğlu (hereafter GC) called me on the phone. We met for lunch. In September he would start making a documentary program called “Red File” on ATV; he wanted me to do the research and editing, offering to pay the salary I had received from Sabah. I did not have great respect for Cıvaoğlu’s journalism, but this was the only concrete job offer before me. Fatma was repeating her suggestion that I leave the media and that, after we spent the summer together, we open a bookstore and publishing house. She said she could work with me and that this business could also benefit the children. But when had I ever listened to her… I again went my own stubborn way. I not only accepted GC’s offer but also proposed the topic for the first program: let’s tell the story of the National Outlook movement under the title “Unknown Welfare.” He accepted this proposal and my wish to work together with Tayfun Ertan. However, from our first meeting with him at his villa in Yeniköy, Tayfun and I had deep misgivings: how were we to work with someone who treated us like janitors rather than colleagues? We were right to be worried, but on the other hand the project was attractive and we had no better option at the time.

## The story of the National Outlook

Despite the flare-up of my herniated disc pain that had started in the winter of 1986 and become chronic, I devoted almost all of the summer of 1994 to conducting about 50 interviews, shared between Tayfun and me, telling the story of the National Outlook. When Tayfun’s radio journalism and my print media experience were combined with the knowledge we had gained from watching Western television, in our view a quite high-quality documentary would emerge.

I conducted long interviews on the occasion of this program with the founders of the National Outlook movement Ahmet Tevfik Paksu, Hasan Aksay, Gündüz Sevilgen (one of the leaders of the opposition to Erbakan at the MSP’s 3rd Congress in 1976); Bahri Zengin, who got the RP to adopt the “legal pluralism” view; the RP’s Islamist critics Hasan Mezarcı, Altan Tan, Ercüment Özkan and others. One of the most interesting interviews was with Ahmet Tevfik Paksu. Paksu, who was one of the leading representatives of the Nurcu community and had served as senator from the Justice Party and then as Minister of Labor from the MSP, described the role of Naqshbandi Sheikh Mehmet Zahit Kotku in the founding of the National Order Party, the first political party of the National Outlook movement, as follows:

“Together with Hasan Aksay (also one of the leading representatives of the Nurcu community, a member of parliament from the Justice Party, later deputy chairman and State Minister of the MSP), we were seeking to establish a party that would not look down on Muslims, would not oppress Muslims, and would express its views in its organization and in public squares even if it could not enter Parliament. We presented this idea to Erbakan. At first, Necmettin Bey neither rejected it nor said okay. He said, I have a teacher; the imam of İskenderpaşa Mosque, Mehmed Efendi. Let’s go to him and discuss it, he said. We said okay. Necmettin Bey, Hasan Aksay, the late Arif Hikmet Güner and I got up and went to Hocaefendi. I explained the necessity of establishing a new organization in Turkey to the best of my ability. Arif Hikmet Bey was of a completely opposite opinion. He argued that establishing such an organization would harm Muslims; therefore it was better to work within existing parties. Necmettin Bey, as he had done with us before, stated the positive and negative aspects of this matter. Hasan Bey shared my opinion. In the end, Hocaefendi said to us—I’m saying the sentence exactly as it was, because this is a sentence that will go down in history—‘Follow whatever Hacı Tevfik Bey says.’ That is, he said he approved of our idea. Upon this, together with Necmettin Bey and other friends, we set about establishing this party organization.” (See Şahin Alpay, Milliyet, November 11, 1995.)

The account of Paksu, who had parted ways with Erbakan and left the MSP in the late 1970s due to disagreements, bore witness to the alliance formed between the Naqshbandis and the Nurcus in the founding of the National Order Party. This alliance, which played a role in the MSP receiving 12 percent of the vote in the 1973 elections, broke down when Nurcu candidates were excluded in the 1977 elections, and the MSP’s vote dropped to 8 percent.

“I must have been wrong”

One of the most interesting interviews we conducted for the “National Outlook” documentary in the summer of 1994 was undoubtedly the one I had with Recep Tayyip Erdoğan (future Prime Minister and President), who at the time was completing his third month as Mayor of Istanbul. In this interview, Erdoğan appeared to me as quite a liberal and pragmatic person by RP standards. I had thought that Erdoğan could make the RP a party acceptable to broader segments. The main views that made me think this way were:

“Our concern is not why this person covers her head, why that person goes uncovered. Our concern is neither beards nor beardlessness, neither mustaches nor mustachelessness, neither covering nor not covering… The RP is not a prosecutor or a judge. We have no right to judge anyone. Only God has the authority to judge whether a person is Muslim or infidel… We have no claim that RP equals Islam. Welfare is not a religion. It is a political party established within this system, according to the rules of this system… The RP is libertarian. Islam is the most libertarian religion. Of course there are limits to freedom. That is the freedom of others… We will solve problems with science, not with prayer. Islam does not deny science… Whether the person who comes to my door is Muslim, Christian, or Jewish, they receive equal treatment. My faith commands this…” (For the article where I reported these statements, see Milliyet, July 23, 1996.)

When I read Nilgün Cerrahoğlu’s interview with Erdoğan (Milliyet, July 14, 1996), I would be startled and write the following: “Erdoğan was using the ‘99 percent of us are Muslim’ rhetoric this time with a very different emphasis: ‘There are two types of people in Turkey. This is also our esteemed Teacher’s observation. Those who are Welfare supporters and those who are candidates to become Welfare supporters… We will see Nilgün Hanım in the RP soon.’ This statement was a clear expression of the mentality shared by many RP members that sees democracy only as majority rule (majority dictatorship), that rejects the fundamental rights and freedoms of those not included in the majority that cannot be violated by any majority, that rejects pluralism. So everyone would, willingly or unwillingly, become a Welfare supporter over time, would be forced to become a Welfare supporter.

“Erdoğan was also telling Cerrahoğlu a view he had never expressed before: ‘We say that democracy is not an end but a means…’ For ordinary citizens like me, this statement was the clearest and most concise expression of the understanding in RP ranks that sees democratic competition as merely a process of ‘conquering’ power. I also find Erdoğan’s recent statements about the media alarming. It’s not that the RP doesn’t have media; they have plenty of television stations, radios, newspapers. Why the anger reaching the point of saying ‘The dogs bark but the caravan moves on’ about the media just because the majority of the people prefer the opposition media rather than these?” (Milliyet, July 22, 1996).

In a later article I said: “Wasn’t it that the RP did not equal Islam? Is being against the RP contrary to Islam? Are those who don’t approve of the RP, as Erbakan says, ‘of the potato religion’?.. I had the impression that Tayyip Erdoğan was a representative of the RP’s more democratic face, respectful of freedoms and pluralism. I had thought he could be a leader candidate who could make the RP accepted by much broader segments than Erbakan had been able to achieve. I must have been wrong.” (Milliyet, July 25, 1996)

As I will relate later, I would be wrong about Erdoğan not once but several times…

## The end of the adventure

The documentary we prepared was quite high quality in our view (that is, Tayfun Ertan’s and mine); however, GC did not like the script, which in his words “resembled a doctoral thesis,” and decided that the work needed to pass through the hands of “a professional screenwriter”; for this he made an agreement with writer and former ANAP parliamentarian Yılmaz Karakoyunlu. Karakoyunlu ruined our documentary, which we had designed to be broadcast over two weeks with each part being two hours, by turning it into something to be broadcast in one go in 90 minutes and making various interventions. When GC also devoted most of the time to his interview with Erbakan, the work ceased to be our work. (We had thought that interviewing Erbakan, who spoke every day, wouldn’t be meaningful…) We were greatly disappointed. In September 1994 I left GC, and shortly after Tayfun did too. When I informed him of my decision to leave, GC pretended to be surprised and asked “Why?..” In response, I simply said, “You are intelligent enough to know the answer to that…” (Even while leaving, I still did GC a favor; I recommended my friend Koray Düzgören from the Faculty of Political Science to replace me. He would work with Koray for quite a long time.)

Going to Stockholm for an academic meeting right after leaving ATV did me good. On one of the days I was there, “Unknown Welfare” was broadcast in Karakoyunlu’s version. I was invited to dinner at the home of one of my Turkish friends; I asked them to turn on ATV at broadcast time. The documentary we had put so much work into had become so unrecognizable and meaningless that after watching for a while I asked my friends to turn off the television. Not mentioning our contributions at all was disrespectful to our labor, but fortunately they had done so; because the documentary had become a caricature of what we had designed.

Unfortunately, that was not the end of what happened to the National Outlook documentary. A few months after we left the job, when İkitelli creek overflowed due to heavy rainfall, sewage water flooded the archive section in the basement of the ATV building, and all our work literally went to “shit.” Tayfun and I deeply regretted not having kept copies of the interviews for ourselves. Worse still, while writing these lines I couldn’t even find a copy of the script we wrote for the documentary in my archive. This too must be a reflection of my alaturka ways—my haphazard Turkish-style disorganization.

## Ufuk Güldemir at Milliyet

My hope of finding a place for myself at Milliyet continued. After returning from Stockholm, I made an agreement with Umur Talu and wrote a series about the evolution social democracy had undergone in Sweden, gradually becoming more liberal and starting to view EU membership favorably (Sweden would become a member in 1995). The series was published in Milliyet some time later, somewhat shortened. On the phone, Umur was saying they would soon invite me to work at Milliyet, but I sensed something strange in his voice. The reason became clear some time later. When Ufuk Güldemir called one late afternoon, I thought we would discuss the program we would do together at Show TV, but that wasn’t the topic. He was delivering bombshell news: he had become editor-in-chief of Milliyet. What’s more, he wanted me to bring the “Intellectual Perspective” page to Milliyet. Furthermore, I would be able to bring Nilüfer Kuyaş with me. Furthermore, I would be able to write a column three days a week on the page that would be published six days a week… What more could I ask for?!?!…

I had entered Cumhuriyet through Hasan Cemal, Sabah through Zülfü Livaneli; I was getting into Milliyet thanks to my friendship with Ufuk Güldemir. (My adventure should be considered a good example of how hiring works in the Turkish media.)

Nilüfer and I started doing Intellectual Perspective at Milliyet in the last days of November 1994. Ahmet Altan, Can Dündar, and Nilgün Cerrahoğlu also joined the Milliyet staff around that time. I would receive a salary that couldn’t be compared to the amounts paid to other columnists, but was satisfying for me. Again I didn’t have my own office, but a spacious corner where Nilüfer and I would sit together had been allocated to us; soon we would also have a secretary. Best of all, I would be able to go home and back with the newspaper’s vehicles. Yes, Ufuk hadn’t been able to get the appointment he wanted to introduce us to the owner, but what more could I ask for? For the first time, I held such a privileged position in the media. According to Taha Akyol, who was writing at Milliyet at the time and with whom my friendship would progressively deepen, most writers at newspapers only had a column; I, on the other hand, had a page on top of that, in a way rarely seen in Bab-ı Ali (Istanbul’s old press district)… The page brought us quite a lot of readers and garnered quite a lot of praise. The signatures of many people who later became well-known commentators appeared for the first time on the page I edited at Milliyet, as they had at Cumhuriyet and Sabah.

One, two, or three “l”s?

As at Sabah, a debate arose at Milliyet about how the page’s name should be spelled. I described this debate, which took quite an interesting turn, in a column: “When we started at Sabah, Can Ataklı had conveyed that there was some hesitation about the spelling of ‘Entellektüel,’ that some said it should be written as ‘Entelektüel.’ Then all hell broke loose: The Turkish Language Association dictionary supposedly spelled it ‘entelektüel,’ and the duty of an intellectual was supposedly to show society the truth about everything, and so on… Letters, phone calls, fax messages… Zülfü Livaneli came to the rescue; he wrote ‘The correct form is entellektüel.’ This time the debate was settled amicably with jokes that lightweight intellectuals wrote it with ‘one l’ while heavyweights wrote it with ‘two l’s.’ Hıncal Uluç wrote ‘The number of L’s can even go up to three if necessary.’

We started receiving warnings that it was mandatory to spell it ‘Entelektüel.’ A well-known writer of ours said he didn’t read the page because it was written with two “l”s. One of our readers gave an ultimatum: ‘By such and such date, the two l’s will be reduced to one!’ My dear friend Zülfü Livaneli, with whom by a twist of fate we had reunited under the same roof, again came to our rescue. Again with a fine article he reminded us that the correct form was ‘entellektüel,’ but that the real issue was tied up in the meaning of the word. This time he too started receiving letters full of advice and Zülfü got fed up…” (“Entellektüel,” Milliyet, December 27, 1994)

Since Ufuk wanted me to attend the morning editorial meetings in addition to making the page and, as I had done at Cumhuriyet, to offer suggestions and criticisms, I was staying at the newspaper six days a week from early morning until the late hours when page preparation was completed. Again I couldn’t devote enough time to my family.

Fatma was living her own life as always, but because both my spirits and my earnings were good, perhaps for the first time we were both content with our situation. Our daughter Elvan had married and left home two years earlier, becoming a painter who would gradually gain fame. Our son Acar was attending Işık High School.

At Milliyet, everything went well for the first few months. However, the newspaper’s departure from its traditional seriousness in its headlines was causing discomfort among both readers and the owner. Ufuk thought he could increase circulation by bringing to Milliyet’s headlines the habit of “adding color” to articles that he had acquired at Cumhuriyet. When I mildly criticized this, I remember him saying, “If we don’t put some blood on the front page, how can we connect with the citizen on the street?.. Those looking for seriousness can read your page…” The real crisis erupted in April 1995 over Ahmet Altan’s column titled “Atakürt” (Ata-Kurd), one of his masterpieces. Aydın Doğan, saying he was under intense pressure from readers, demanded that Ahmet Altan leave the newspaper. When Ahmet left, Can Dündar also resigned in solidarity with him. He called me on the phone to probe whether I would join him. I had no doubt that owner interference in a writer’s articles was in no way acceptable, but I didn’t see myself as strong enough to make a heroic gesture by resigning. I now had a job I loved doing, and I was determined to protect this job as long as I could. Unfortunately, after Ahmet and Can, Ufuk also had to resign.

Shortly before Ufuk’s resignation was announced, Aydın Doğan, with Ufuk’s participation, hosted a dinner somewhere on the Bosphorus for the writers Ufuk had brought to Milliyet. His purpose became clear later: Ufuk is leaving but you can stay, he was saying. At the dinner, I was seated (as the most senior writer) across from the owner (whom I was meeting for the first time); on either side of me were Nilüfer and Nilgün Cerrahoğlu. In response to the owner’s words explaining why he had asked Ahmet Altan to leave, I said approximately or exactly the following: “Aydın Bey, while we were struggling for the establishment of freedom of expression in Turkey, you stabbed us in the back by removing Ahmet from the newspaper…” The owner’s response was exactly this: “I have no such cause as defending freedom of expression; I want to publish a social democratic newspaper…” (The owner was indicating that what he meant by “social democracy” was Kemalism.) I’ll never forget, Fatma was surprised at how the owner hadn’t immediately fired me because of these words. Aydın Doğan didn’t fire me immediately after these events in 1995, but (as I will tell the story) he would do so later, and in quite an ugly manner.

After Ufuk’s resignation, Derya Sazak was brought in as Milliyet’s editor-in-chief. Both Nilüfer and I were very happy that Derya was appointed rather than someone else. Derya was Nilüfer’s friend. When he was Ankara bureau chief and I was working at CHP, we had become close. At that time he had mentioned the possibility of being appointed editor-in-chief and had given me hope that perhaps he would also bring me to Milliyet. Derya, bless him, treated us in a friendly manner as long as he remained in the position; under his management we felt secure. Our close friends Edip Öymen and Yavuz Baydar also worked with us for periods.

The political landscape in the mid-1990s

A brand new page was opening in my journalism career. While IP was being published six days a week, I was also writing a column titled “3rd Eye” three days a week on this page. What course should I follow in my columns and in preparing the IP page? My answer to this question was based on the following observations:

1) Liberal democracy (that is, majority rule limited by citizens’ fundamental rights and freedoms), despite its various problems, was the best form of governance that could be found, beneficial both for individuals and for societies. 2) Within a liberal democratic regime, securing both individual freedoms and social justice could only be possible through liberal social democratic policies (that is, the synthesis of market economy and welfare state), not statist ones. 3) If liberal democracy was to take root in Turkey, this could only be possible by integrating Islamists and the Kurdish political movement (their non-radical, non-authoritarian interpretations) into the system.

After I started writing at Cumhuriyet newspaper, I had engaged in an intellectual struggle for the goals I listed above, together with a rather limited number of liberal-minded people like myself. By the time I started writing at Milliyet in the 1990s, the Turkish political landscape in my mind had become quite clear. There were three basic political currents competing to determine the country’s future.

1) Kemalists: They were divided into three main wings: a) Those who were secularist (that is, authoritarian secularism) but also pro-democracy (majority rule) and pro-integration with the West, generally gathered in the CHP. b) Radical Kemalists who were secularist-statist-nationalist, essentially represented in the vein of Cumhuriyet newspaper and its circle. c) Turkish-Islam synthesizers who were proponents of authoritarian identity politics verging on racism (“we are all Turks”) but kept their distance from authoritarian secularism and generally gathered in the MHP.

2) Muslims and Islamists:

It was necessary to distinguish Muslims, who embraced the Islamic faith in its different interpretations, from Islamists, who produced a political ideology from the Islamic religion. Muslims, who constituted the vast majority of Turkey’s population, consisted of orthodox (that is, pure in their beliefs) Sunnis and heterodox (that is, harboring a synthesis of different elements in their beliefs) Alevis. Although the minority Alevis had suffered repression reaching the level of massacre in Tunceli/Dersim through the impositions of Kemalism’s uniform identity policies (saying “we are all of the Diyanet religion”), they mostly supported the Kemalist party CHP out of concern that it would provide them protection against the Sunni majority. Sunnis, on the other hand, were roughly divided into three segments: a) Those attached to State Islam, that is, the “Diyanet religion” represented by the Directorate of Religious Affairs. The political preferences of this majority segment could be directed toward various parties. b) Those attached to Folk Islam, that is, the interpretations of Islam represented by tarikat orders and religious communities.

Although tarikat orders and religious communities had been banned since 1925 due to authoritarian secularism policies (and perhaps encouraged by this), they maintained their vitality. Traditional tarikat orders, whose roots extended to the 12th and 13th centuries, were organized in the form of sheikh-disciple relationships and consisted mainly of the Naqshbandi, Qadiri, Rufai, Halveti, Melami, and (having a special identity) Mevlevi orders. The most dominant segment, the Naqshbandis, were mainly divided into the İskenderpaşa, İsmail Ağa, Menzil, and Erenköy congregations.

Unlike the tarikat orders, the religious communities, which were a product of the 20th century, of the modern era, consisted of a spiritual guide (mürşit) who guided believers and his followers, and were mainly divided into groups known as Nurcus, Süleymancıs, and Işıkçıs (all of Naqshbandi origin). The Nurcus, followers of the teachings of Said Nursi, had over time split into more than 40 branches, the largest being the Fethullah Gülen community.

The Islamists, on the other hand, overwhelmingly consisted of those gathered in the ranks of the National Outlook movement; a segment we could generally call moderate, embracing peaceful, legal struggle rather than violence. (Islamists favoring the use of violence were not making their presence felt.) The İskenderpaşa lodge of the Naqshbandi order, whose sheikh was Mehmet Zahit Kotku, was particularly interested in politics and had played an important role in the emergence of the National Outlook movement. Necmettin Erbakan, Turgut Özal, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, and most famous politicians belonging to the National Outlook movement were of Naqshbandi origin.

3) The Kurdish political movement: The bans imposed on the expression of Kurdish language and identity with the proclamation of the Republic had led to increasingly strong reactions. By the mid-1990s, it was observed that Turkey’s Kurds were roughly divided into a segment that prioritized religious identity and supported Islamist parties, and those who prioritized ethnic identity and supported the Kurdish nationalist movement. The Kurdish nationalist movement was roughly divided into three wings: a) The current represented by the PKK that was based on armed struggle, aiming for autonomy or independence. b) The current represented by legal parties that started with HEP in 1991 and were successively closed down on grounds of separatism, gradually growing to reach HDP today (the third largest party), proposing a peaceful-democratic solution within Turkey’s integrity to the problem arising from policies based on the denial of Kurdish identity. c) Liberal-minded independent Kurdish intellectuals, not very numerous, who thought that the PKK’s armed struggle was playing into the hands of state policies and causing great harm to Kurds.

Of course, there was also a Marxist or Communist current on the scene. Although banned since the first years of the Republic, they had begun to make their presence felt in Turkish politics in the 1960s, splitting among dozens of factions, some of which favored armed struggle. However, the communist current suffered a great defeat after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 and Eastern Europe’s liberation from the Soviet yoke, and had gradually become marginalized. My own political views had moved away from the Kemalism instilled by my family, turning to Marxism in the 1960s when I was at university, and gradually to its Maoist interpretation. However, while doing my doctorate at Stockholm University in Sweden where I had taken refuge in the early 1970s, the Marxist paradigm in my mind gradually eroded and collapsed, and I had begun to see Marxism as the opposite of liberal democracy. Upon returning to the country, inspired especially by Karl Popper’s views, I had written articles criticizing Marxism; I had not hesitated to say that “I was proud of my apostasy.”

In the 1980s, my articles defending liberal social democracy at Cumhuriyet newspaper had met with strong opposition from the secularist-statist-nationalist writers and their supporters who dominated the paper. The split that occurred at the newspaper in the early 1990s, roughly between the wing represented by İlhan Selçuk and the cadre represented by Hasan Cemal, was essentially the product of the conflict between Kemalism’s secularist-tutelary interpretation and its social democratic interpretation. Just as Marxism in history had given rise to communism on the one hand and social democracy on the other, I had thought that social democratic interpretations could also emerge from within the Kemalist current, and with this thought I had briefly pinned my hopes on Ecevit’s (“respectful of religion”) DSP. However, when it was soon seen that the DSP was a personality party with little connection to either democracy or the left, my hopes turned to Deniz Baykal’s CHP; with this hope I had worked at the CHP for a short time, but there too I had been disappointed.

## The path I should follow

When I started writing at Milliyet, the path I should follow as a commentator who idealized the establishment of liberal democracy seemed quite clear to me: I would defend pluralist and liberal democracy, and criticize political views incompatible with liberal democracy. Looking at Turkey’s Islamic geography, it seemed essential to distinguish Islamists from Muslims. Kemalism’s repressive secularism policies had caused justified reactions among Muslims; some of these reactions had fed the Islamist current. However, like believers of all other religious faiths, Muslims could also embrace democracy. Indeed, Turkey’s practice after 1950 seemed to support this.

Islamism, on the other hand, was in principle incompatible with liberal and pluralist democracy. However, it was also necessary to distinguish moderate Islamists who opposed violence from radical Islamists who favored violence. The former could be integrated into the democratic regime; those who really needed to be criticized were the latter. With this fundamental perspective, in my writings and speeches I criticized authoritarian secularism policies; I advocated the lifting of bans on tarikat orders and religious communities, the end of the headscarf ban and other restrictions on religious freedoms, the separation of religion and state, and the transformation of the Directorate of Religious Affairs into an autonomous structure.

The political parties belonging to the National Outlook movement, which represented moderate Islamism, had many elements in their agendas that contradicted liberal democracy: They embraced democratic elections as the path to power, but they did not inspire confidence and raised doubts about whether they would be respectful of the rule of law and pluralism once in power. In my writings, I would call on the moderate Islamists represented in the RP not only to be committed to majority rule but also to be respectful of citizens’ fundamental rights and freedoms. And that is what I would do.

“Religion and politics”

Around this time, also under the influence of what we had learned from the documentary we made for ATV, my understanding of the distinction in Turkey between Official Islam (represented by the Directorate of Religious Affairs), Political Islam (of which the Welfare Party represented a non-violent type), and Folk Islam (divided into tarikat orders and religious communities) had begun to settle firmly into place. I had begun to see that the most important distinction in the context of Folk Islam was between the Naqshbandis and the Nurcus, mainly between the İskenderpaşa lodge and the Fethullah Gülen community (or the Hizmet Movement, as it wished to be called). My article titled “Religion and Politics” published in Milliyet reflected where my understanding of Islam in Turkey had arrived. I was writing:

“A generation of intellectuals, including myself, had difficulty in their youth understanding the place of religion in the lives of individuals and societies. Especially those like me who for a while thought Marxism was the key to building paradise on earth believed that the formula ‘Religion is the opium of the people’ explained everything right there. Everything was determined (even if ‘in the last instance’) by the ‘base,’ that is, production and property relations; the rest was nonsense. First, we began to understand that this was not so; that people’s needs were not limited to eating, drinking, and reproducing; that their needs related to meaning and the world of culture were at least as important; that religion had the function of being a cultural code that held societies together. When we opened our eyes a bit more, we began to understand the impossibility of understanding society without understanding the ‘superstructure’ called culture, including religion.

“Social scientists such as the late Sabri Ülgener and Şerif Mardin, whom I remember with deep respect, made a great contribution to opening our eyes to the world of meaning and culture. Especially Şerif Mardin’s works helped us see the void that single-party rule had created in the cultural world. Then we discovered the impossibility of analyzing politics in Turkey without taking into account the tarikat orders and religious communities that officially did not exist but in reality maintained and developed their vitality. We understood that in Turkey, where modern institutionalization and organization lagged behind, one of the basic forms of social organization continued to be these religious brotherhood and solidarity organizations.

“When we delved a bit deeper, we learned that the National Order Party, founded in 1970, was essentially based on an alliance between the Nurcus, disciples of Bediüzzaman Said Nursi, and the disciples of Naqshbandi Sheikh Mehmet Zahit Kotku; that the foundations of the National Outlook movement were laid in this way. We learned that as a result of the struggles that erupted within the National Salvation Party in the second half of the 1970s, the Naqshbandis had largely purged the Nurcus; that the Nurcus, as they had always done, essentially turned to center-right parties. Also that Kotku died in 1980, at a time when he was very unhappy with the attitude of Necmettin Erbakan and the MSP… Meanwhile, it became understood that Süleyman Demirel’s influence in the DP-AP tradition was significantly based on Nurcu support, and the late Turgut Özal’s power within ANAP was significantly based on Naqshbandi support. Another consequence of our eyes opening was understanding the impossibility of explaining how the CHP-SHP tradition could get votes from society without understanding Alevism in Turkey.

“In the early 1990s, we witnessed the strong opposition of Esad Coşan, the theology professor and son-in-law who succeeded Kotku, against Necmettin Hoca, and his talk of founding a new party. Nowadays, we are witnessing the Nurcu supporters of Fethullah Gülen clustered around Zaman taking, against the interpretation represented by the Welfare Party, a stance that appears more moderate, more ‘tolerant,’ seeming to emphasize cultural Islam rather than the politicization of Islam.

“Religion is one of the most powerful elements of people’s world of meaning and culture. Attempting to abolish religion is, as many experiences have shown, a futile and backfiring endeavor. Religion is not the ‘opium’ of society but perhaps its mortar. Modernization may not eliminate religion but on the contrary may strengthen it. Making religion an instrument of politics is as dangerous as abolishing it. Political religion, in our country political Islam, which divides the people into believers and non-believers, into different belief groups, can plant dynamite at the foundations of society.
