Just as we must treat cultural Islam with respect, opposing the exploitation of the Islamic religion for political purposes should be the duty of all Muslims as much as all democrats.” (Milliyet, February 18, 1995)

Islamic currents were not limited to the National Outlook movement. I had come to the conclusion that the current represented by Fethullah Gülen and his community, which had become increasingly visible in public opinion from the mid-1990s, represented an interpretation of Islam compatible with liberal democracy. Gülen advocated pluralism, secularism respectful of beliefs, mutual tolerance, the separation of religion and politics, EU membership, and the market economy, and opposed the RP’s majoritarian views. In those years, except for radical secularism supporters, there was a positive atmosphere toward the Gülen community in society. Bülent Ecevit, who claimed to be “democratic left” advocating “secularism respectful of religion,” was among those who viewed the Gülen movement positively. The “Tolerance and dialogue awards” ceremony organized by the Journalists and Writers Foundation, of which Gülen was honorary president, at Çırağan Palace on the evening of January 4, 1996, would be attended by Ankara Metropolitan Mayor Melih Gökçek, Istanbul Metropolitan Mayor Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, former Environment Minister Rıza Akçalı, Abdülkadir Aksu, Muhsin Yazıcıoğlu, Mehmet Aydın, Ali Coşkun, and many other politicians.

Among the participants at the meeting were CHP politician Ertuğrul Günay, Journalists’ Association President Nail Güreli, journalists Hasan Cemal, Mehmet Altan, Zeynep Göğüş, and others. That evening, the media/TV programmer award went to Abdurrahman Dilipak and Toktamış Ateş, the columnist award to Cengiz Çandar and Taha Akyol, the sports award to Fatih Terim, the art award to Barış Manço, the nature and environment award to Hayrettin Karaca, and the family award to Perihan Savaş. The award for helping the disabled was shared by Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Müjdat Gezen. Among the many politicians from the right and left to whom the Journalists and Writers Foundation gave awards at various events organized until 1997 were President Süleyman Demirel, Parliament Speaker Hikmet Çetin, Deputy Prime Minister Bülent Ecevit, and (later prime minister) Tansu Çiller, as well as names like Yıldırım Akbulut, Bülent Akarcalı, Cemil Çiçek, Ertuğrul Günay, Işılay Saygın, İlhan Kesici, Mustafa Kalemli, Namık Kemal Zeybek, Nevzat Yalçıntaş, Vehbi Dinçerler, and Muhsin Yazıcıoğlu.

“Respect for Hocaefendi”

The fact that my article titled “Respect for Hocaefendi,” in which I emphasized the importance of the Gülen movement that I saw as a representative of cultural Islam as opposed to political Islam, could be published in Milliyet was an indication of how different the atmosphere was in those days compared to today. As far as I remember, only one columnist among Milliyet employees reacted harshly, claiming that this article was “an attack on the foundations of the newspaper.” The majority either found the article reasonable or remained silent, because it was consistent with the view that was prevalent in public opinion at the time. I was saying:

“It must be acknowledged that even today, the late nineteenth-century Young Turk movement has left a significant mark on how some of our intellectuals view religion in general and Islam in particular. We know that the thinkers and leaders of the Young Turk movement, which later organized as the Committee of Union and Progress, such as Ahmet Rıza and Abdullah Cevdet, held religion in general and Islam in particular responsible for the decline of the Ottoman State. The Young Turk leaders advocated that Ottoman elites adopt the Positivist philosophy that ‘replaced religion with science’ (developed by Auguste Comte and his followers in France) in order for the state to modernize. According to them, for modernization and Westernization to succeed, the people also needed to be educated with a kind of ‘true Islam’ that presented these as Islamic concepts…

“Of course, it is not possible to say that the positivist ideology of the Young Turks is still the dominant ideology among our intellectuals today. But there is no doubt that remnants of this worldview still circulate among us. These remnants, in my view, still manifest themselves in holding religion responsible for our social backwardness, viewing religion and science as rivals, denying the social role of religion and its important place in individuals’ world of meaning, perceiving almost every manifestation of religion, such as the headscarf, as an instance of reaction and a threat to the secular regime, and in other ways.

“With such a perspective, it is certainly not possible to distinguish, analyze, and understand the diversity of Islam in Turkey and the different forms it takes; to put religion and politics in their proper places. Thankfully, with the help of whatever freedom and democracy we have, and with the pressures of society, we are slowly overcoming these shallow understandings. In this context, it is impossible not to see the benefits and contributions of Fethullah Gülen Hocaefendi’s initiatives in recent times. Hocaefendi is the current leading representative of the community founded by Bediüzzaman Said Nursi, a distinctive Islamic thinker and leader of twentieth-century Turkey who was a different kind of Young Turk in his effort to reconcile Islam with modernity and science.

“As far as I can see, Hocaefendi opposes the use of Islam as a political ideology, a party philosophy, and the division of society into two poles of believers and non-believers. He advocates for those with different beliefs and different thoughts to be respectful and tolerant of each other, and for peace and reconciliation in society. In my view, Hocaefendi’s efforts can help us put religion in its proper place… I perceive Hocaefendi as a religious leader who separates religion from politics, opposes the culture of enmity that could divide the people into camps, and contributes to the development of a tolerant understanding of Islam. What Hocaefendi has done should be respected.” (Milliyet, July 29, 1995)

Upon the publication of this article in Milliyet, two representatives from the Journalists and Writers Foundation, which Gülen had initiated, came to visit me at the newspaper with flowers in their hands; they conveyed that they wanted to give me one of the “Tolerance Awards” that the foundation was distributing at the time. I declined the award with thanks, but said that I was curious about the schools the movement had opened in Central Asian countries, and that if they invited me along with a group of journalists to see these schools, I would be very pleased. I made the same suggestion to Hüseyin Gülerce, who was then the editor-in-chief of Zaman.

This suggestion of mine was realized: Together with a group of colleagues including Ali Bayramoğlu, Ali Bulaç, Mustafa Özel, Atılgan Bayar, and others, between October 20-28, 1996, we visited the schools the movement had opened in Uzbekistan’s Tashkent, Jizzakh, Samarkand, and Bukhara; and Turkmenistan’s Ashgabat and Charjew. We spoke with the Turkish, Uzbek, and Turkmen administrators, teachers, and students of the schools.

The series of articles I wrote upon my return from the visit was published in Milliyet under the title “Fethullah Gülen Hoca’s community’s ‘Schools Empire’ spreading around the world - Turkey’s trump card in Central Asia is education” on November 1-5, 1996. My impression of the schools was quite positive. These schools, which constituted one dimension of Turkey’s opening to the world in the post-Cold War era, were providing modern and scientific education in two Central Asian countries governed by authoritarian secular and nationalist regimes, under joint management with local authorities, were among the most prestigious educational institutions in these countries, and were training the leaders of the future.

My impression of the movement’s schools in Central Asia was quite positive. In the Turkey of those days, in an effort to distinguish between interpretations of the Islamic movement that were compatible and incompatible with democracy, I wrote articles that viewed the Gülen movement favorably while looking at the Welfare Party quite critically. Circles favoring radical secularism were furious about my articles on the Gülen community. This was probably the main development that led me to start writing for the community’s newspaper Zaman some time after my job at Milliyet was terminated in 2001. (In 2004, the Journalists and Writers Foundation would compile the articles I had written about the community during my time at Milliyet and my first two years at Zaman in a booklet titled Gülen’s Contribution.)

## Marxism held minds captive

Another result of the publication of my article titled “Respect for Hocaefendi” in Milliyet was that Eyüp Can from the community’s newspaper Zaman conducted an extensive interview with me. In the interview titled “Marxism held minds captive” that I gave to Can, who would later join the Hürriyet group and also serve as editor-in-chief at Radikal, I was saying:

“In my youth, those who read, wrote, and were interested in events were mostly Marxist intellectuals. As such, we found ourselves within the Marxist current. But my ardent Marxist period was short; about 4-5 years. It didn’t take me long to discover the disconnect between what the theory said and reality… Looking back today, I see all of this as experience. I say that perhaps the mistakes we made then were necessary for us to arrive at a more realistic understanding today… Marxist thought unfortunately caused many people’s minds to be held captive in Turkey… Of course, there are still lingering residues. For example, there may be the influence of positivism and the Marxist approach in general on the attitude of some Turkish intellectuals toward religion. There may still be those who think they can explain religion with the opium analogy.

“Yet this way, let alone religion, we cannot even fully understand Marx. It is not possible to explain everything through matter. People have a spiritual world that gives meaning to their lives, and religion responds to needs in this area. A human being is not a machine. There are also moral rules and social values. Answers have always been sought to all of these throughout human history and will continue to be sought; religion is one of the fundamental sources to turn to in this area. This is true both sociologically and philosophically… On the other hand, it is very wrong to see religion and science as rivals. Both have an area that corresponds to something in human beings. One concerns reason, the other concerns faith.” (Milliyet, January 7, 1996)

I think there were not many people in Turkey at that time who came from the Left and arrived at such a liberal understanding on the subject of religion.

“Huntington is talking nonsense”

The person who expressed the views most contrary to my own in the interviews I conducted for Milliyet was certainly the American international relations professor, the world-famous Samuel P. Huntington. My interview with Huntington was published in Milliyet on September 9, 1996, and my column about it came out the very next day. I was saying:

“Huntington is a famous American political scientist. He had long been known in the academic world, but he made the news three years ago. In his article titled ‘The Clash of Civilizations?’ published in the Summer 1993 issue of Foreign Affairs, he was saying: ‘In the post-Cold War world, conflict will primarily occur between Western, Confucian, Japanese, Islamic, Hindu, Slavic, Orthodox, Latin American, and (possibly) African civilizations; it will focus among states belonging to Western, Islamic, and Confucian civilizations.’

Huntington’s thesis drew a storm of criticism. When I asked the famous historian Paul Kennedy, also from Harvard, who was visiting Turkey at the time, what he thought, he said: ‘This article appealed to crude and narrow-minded views about the Islamic and Hindu worlds. I find the article generally negative. The danger it presents is that it becomes self-fulfilling and self-justifying.’ (Sabah, November 24, 1993).

“I listened to Huntington’s speech in Istanbul last week. Afterwards, I conducted an interview with him. As can be seen in the interview published on our page yesterday, Huntington put forward a new thesis in Istanbul: ‘Turkey should become the leader of Islamic civilization!’ When asked how it could achieve this leadership, given that three years ago he wrote that Turkey was a country ‘torn’ between Islamic and Western civilizations, his answer was essentially this: ‘Being a bridge is not a very good thing. You don’t belong to either side and people walk all over you. Since the West doesn’t want you, take the lead of the Islamic world; let the dire leaderlessness there come to an end as well.’ Even if we accept as true that the West doesn’t want Turkey, how realistic is it that Islamic states, almost all of which are at each other’s throats, would want to see Turkey as their leader? About as realistic as Erbakan’s ‘Islamic Union’ dream…

“Huntington’s views that would greatly please our Islamists were not limited to this. His deeming Turkey worthy of a ‘non-secular, Islamic type’ democracy even exceeded the expectations of the Welfare Party. That a political scientist of Huntington’s caliber would consider a democracy ‘respectful of fundamental rights but not secular’ as possible was truly incomprehensible. Especially the connection he drew between liberal democracy and Christianity revealed his terrible prejudices… Huntington also has an idea that some of our Islamists would not like at all (reasonable, but completely inconsistent with his other views): He approves of the ‘Pinochet option,’ that is, the armed forces’ duty to protect the constitution, against governments that do not respect fundamental rights. Listening to Huntington, I concluded that his knowledge about Turkey was quite inadequate and that he was generally talking nonsense.” (“Huntington Is Talking Nonsense,” Milliyet, September 10, 1996.)

## My friendship with Şerafettin Elçi

Starting from my years working at Cumhuriyet, in my articles on the Kurdish issue, while strongly opposing the PKK’s totalitarian ideology and politics of violence, I took a stance in favor of the democratic rights of Kurds and advocated that parties defending these rights find a place in the multi-party system. I wrote that the preservation of the country’s integrity could be achieved not through violence and military methods, but through the recognition of the language and identity rights of Kurdish citizens and meeting demands for regional autonomy. Because of these views, while I encountered hostility from PKK supporters, I earned respect from liberal-minded Kurdish intellectuals. I had a special friendship with the late Şerafettin Elçi (1938-2012), who was foremost among them.

The late Elçi waged a noteworthy struggle for the democratic rights of Kurds. He was elected as a Mardin member of parliament from the Justice Party in 1977; he served as Minister of Public Works (1978-79) in the coalition government that the CHP formed with JP deputies who had resigned to become independents. During his ministry, he was sentenced to 2 years and 3 months in prison by the martial law court for saying “There are Kurds in Turkey, and I am a Kurd”; he was also tried at the Supreme Court on charges of “hiring some Kurds” and was additionally sentenced to 2 years and 4 months in prison; due to these convictions, he spent more than 30 months in prison. In 1992, together with 98 Kurdish intellectuals, he founded the Kurdish Rights and Freedoms Foundation; after a long legal struggle, he managed to register the foundation under the name Kurdish Culture and Research Foundation, thus for the first time in the history of the Republic, an institution gained the opportunity to use the name “Kurdish.” In 1994, together with a group of friends, he pioneered the establishment of the Kurdish Democratic Platform; he assumed the General Chairmanship of the Democratic Mass Party founded in January 1997. When the party was closed down by the Constitutional Court on charges of separatism on February 26, 1999, Elçi spearheaded the establishment of the Participatory Democracy Party in December 2006 and was elected as the party’s general chairman.

I met Elçi in 1992 when he was serving as the founding chairman of the Kurdish Rights and Freedoms Foundation. Our views on the Kurdish issue, which almost completely overlapped, formed the basis of our friendship. On almost every trip I made to Ankara, I would meet with him and exchange views. In the long interview I conducted with him in February 1997, when he was chairman of the Democratic Mass Party, he was saying “I look to the future with hope.” When I asked “What is your proposal for a solution?” he was saying:

“At the founding stage of the Republic, it was promised that the state would be the state of the Kurds as well. In the Amasya protocol, which we can call the social contract upon which the state was founded, it was promised that all kinds of rights of the Kurds would be protected. Kurds participated in the first assembly as Kurdistan deputies. Kurds joined this state with the hope that their rights would be protected. But unfortunately, after things settled down, after Lausanne was signed, all promises were pushed aside. Kurds were assumed not to exist. The destruction of the thousands-of-years-old identity of the Kurds became the fundamental policy. It was not possible for a dignified society to endure this. Rebellions and conflicts arose for this reason. And it has continued until today. That is why we say that the injustices done to the Kurds must be corrected. As Mr. President (Süleyman Demirel) stated in 1992, the ‘Kurdish reality’ must be recognized. The acceptance that Kurds are also one of the essential elements of this society, and its legal guarantee, is necessary. The state must abandon the understanding that everyone living in this country is a Turk…”

Elçi also explained the difference between his party and HADEP as follows: “What is truly important is our ideological difference. We are not inspired by the Marxist tradition. We do not base our politics on class. We are a mass party… We consider intra-party democracy as important as democracy in the country. The party should be of a nature that can act entirely of its own will… Also, style in politics, the method of struggle, is very important. We believe that styles that increase harshness and escalate tension in society will not contribute to solving problems… We need to move politics away from conflict. One of our fundamental principles is respect for the country’s integrity. Since we will solve problems within this country, an atmosphere of friendship and trust must be created among everyone living in this country.” (Milliyet, February 10, 1997)

I would meet with Elçi for the last time, about a year before his death, in Diyarbakır during the 2011 election campaign in which he participated as an independent candidate supported by the BDP. He said that his entering the election on the list of a political movement that he had criticized heavily until that day and viewed as PKK-controlled “should be understood as a sign of how hopeful he was about the resolution of the problem and the guns falling silent, and his desire to contribute to this.” He expressed his belief that the AKP, CHP, and BDP could reach an agreement to solve the problem by negotiating among themselves. He emphasized that this opportunity should not be missed. (“There are Kurds in Turkey too,” Zaman, June 4, 2011) Unfortunately, the opportunities were missed. Another ten years passed. In the last ten years, some steps have been taken toward granting freedom for the expression of Kurdish identity, but a democratic solution to the problem, with the guns falling completely silent, has still not appeared on the horizon at the time these lines are being written.

Elçi passed away on December 25, 2012, while undergoing cancer treatment in Ankara. His body was first taken to Diyarbakır, then he was buried in his hometown Cizre in a ceremony attended by approximately 100,000 people. His name was given to the Şırnak airport, which was inaugurated by Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in July 2013.

## A fair criticism

Throughout my journalism career, I conducted interviews with renowned academics, politicians, and journalists at the newspapers Cumhuriyet, Sabah, and Milliyet. Among those from Turkey, I can mention my interviews with professors Sabri Ülgener, Şerif Mardin, Nur Yalman, Şükrü Hanioğlu, Dani Rodrik, Ayşe Buğra, Bülent Tanör, Asım Erdilek, Ziya Öniş, Gürol Irzık, Ümit Cizre, Kemal Karpat, Ergun Özbudun, politicians Korkut Özal, Rauf Denktaş, Mehmet Ali Talat, and European Court of Human Rights judge Rıza Türmen. These and others were collected in a book titled Turkey’s Witnesses: Those Who Look from Within. (Timaş, Istanbul 2003)

Among the world-renowned social scientists I spoke with, I can primarily mention Paul Kennedy, Ernst Gellner, Dankwart A. Rustow, Abdülkerim Soruş, Martin van Bruinessen, Samuel P. Huntington, Sadık Celal El Azm, Francis Fukuyama, Leonard Binder, Hassan Hanefi, Jeffrey Sachs, Bernard Lewis, Richard Clogg, and Norman Stone. Among others were Danish Social Democratic Party Chairman Svend Auken, French Minister of Education (later prime minister) Lionel R. Jospin, Swedish Foreign Minister Anna Lindh, President of the European Court of Human Rights Luzius Wildhaber, and German Foreign Minister Joschka Fischer. These interviews were also collected in another book titled Turkey’s Witnesses: Those Who Look from Outside. (Timaş, Istanbul 2002)

These books received fair criticism. İlhan Kesici, who would later serve as a member of parliament from ANAP and CHP after serving as undersecretary of the State Planning Organization, said he did not find the interviews satisfying; that it was not good that I included them in the books in their abbreviated forms as published in newspapers rather than in their entirety. He was right. I should mention a serious weakness of mine on this occasion. Yes, in the 1960s and 1970s, during my period when I was intellectually Marxist, communist, even Maoist, I may have refrained from collecting the articles published in magazines and newspapers in books (on the grounds that they no longer represented me). But I regret not turning into books the articles I published during my liberal social democratic period after the 1980s, when I advocated for libertarian and pluralist democracy, despite receiving offers from some publishers. The main reason for this may be my nature that always prefers to look forward. The other reason why there are very few books bearing my signature is that I could not find the time to conduct studies that I would believe were worth publishing.

Among the famous politicians I met, I remember Anna Lindh with great sadness. I conducted two interviews with her: The first was during her first visit to Istanbul when she was still the leader of the Swedish Social Democratic Youth Organization (Cumhuriyet, January 7, 1990), the second was when she came as Swedish Foreign Minister (Milliyet, February 22, 2000). At the time, it was believed that Lindh would be Sweden’s next prime minister, but unfortunately, on September 11, 2003, like Prime Minister Olof Palme in 1986, she fell victim to a senseless assassination. Afterwards, I wrote: “I will not remember Anna Lindh only as one of the brightest politicians Sweden has produced. Anna Lindh had a special interest in and sympathy for Turkey. (Had she not died, she was coming to our country next month for a vacation with her family.) In our last meeting, she had also emphasized that a Turkey meeting the Copenhagen political criteria could not be excluded from the EU, that there was no turning back from the process that began with Helsinki (See Zaman, February 11, 2003)… Prime Minister Göran Persson said the following after Anna Lindh’s death: ‘Social democracy has lost one of its most skillful politicians. The Swedish government has lost one of its most talented ministers and colleagues; Sweden has lost its face to the world.’ Turkey also lost a friend.” (Zaman, September 13, 2003)

“The Martin Luther of Islam”

One of the thinkers who influenced me considerably was Abdülkerim Soruş, the Iranian theologian and philosopher of science who is also known as “the Martin Luther of Islam” and is a leading representative of the reform in Islam or Islamic liberalism movement. My first interview with him was published under the title “Rights come before belief” (Milliyet, August 14, 1995). Eleven years later, in 2006, I had the opportunity to meet with him again and had written the following about him:

“We know that all religions, including Islam, have both fundamentalist and reformist interpretations. It can be said that fundamentalist interpretations adhere to the letter, that is, the word, of sacred texts; while reformist interpretations take the spirit, that is, the meaning, of sacred texts as their basis. Dr. Abdülkerim Soruş, the Iranian theologian and philosopher of Islam and science, rejects the views that he is the ‘intellectual father’ of the ‘reformist’ inclined clergy in his country; but there is no doubt that he is the leading representative of libertarian, liberal Islamic thought.

“It is possible to summarize Soruş’s fundamental ideas in the following points: Islam and democracy are not only compatible, but Islam cannot exist where there is no democracy.

Efforts to produce totalitarian political ideologies from religion are contrary to Islam. Because there is no compulsion in religion; belief based on coercion is not true belief. To be a believer, one must first have the right to believe, have human rights. For an individual to truly believe, they must be free to adopt the faith and, if they wish, to abandon it. For this, religion and state must be separated; neither religion should interfere with the state, nor the state with religion. Secularism in the political sense is not a rival or enemy of religion, but its complement. Sacred texts are divine and unchanging, but their interpretation belongs to human beings and changes. Therefore, there is no interpretation of Islam valid for every place and time; interpretations change over time. Islam does not grant any group, including clergy, the authority to monopolize the interpretation of religion.

“All believers have the right to interpret their beliefs as they wish. Clergy can have no privilege compared to other citizens. In order to free themselves from being spokespersons for official or popular views, they must receive salaries from neither the state nor the people, but earn their living by working. In the West, religion and science clashed, and finally declared a ceasefire; but both benefited from this conflict and learned to be more humble. The interpretations of religion should not contradict science. If a particular interpretation of religion is an obstacle to progress, progress can be encouraged by changing the interpretation. The secret of progress lies in rationalism and the ability to self-criticize.

“Appointed by Khomeini to the Cultural Revolution Council tasked with reorganizing university education programs after the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Soruş resigned from the council in 1983 due to disagreements with the regime and began publishing Kiyan, which became the magazine of religious intellectuals in the 1990s. The magazine was closed by the regime in 1998. Soruş not only lost his job at Tehran University, but his lectures also began to be targeted by attacks from regime supporters.

“In response to the pressures he faced, Soruş said ‘Has this country become a place where a professor must risk his life to teach a class or give a lecture? Do we need Galileos and Brunos?’ and left Iran in 2000. He gave lectures at Harvard, Yale, and Princeton universities in the USA, then at Wissenschaftskolleg in Berlin. He is currently a visiting professor at the University of Amsterdam… According to him: The vast majority of the people are content with their situation because they receive a share of the increased oil revenues in recent years. The regime has complete control in the political, economic, and cultural spheres. The differences among political power holders do not carry significant importance. No change should be expected in the established order in Iran for at least the next twenty years.” (“Abdülkerim Soruş and Islamic liberalism,” Zaman, December 26, 2006.)

“Erbakan should be tried for racism”

In my articles, I advocated that secularism requires the separation of religion and state, and that for Turkey to be a secular country, the Directorate of Religious Affairs (DİB) should be made autonomous even if not abolished. While supporting the understanding of cultural Islam that respects differences, as represented by the Gülen movement, I viewed quite critically the Islamist current represented by Necmettin Erbakan and the Welfare Party (RP), which excluded violence but represented a majoritarian understanding of democracy that could turn into majority dictatorship. In the article titled “Erbakan should be tried for racism,” which contained my first harsh criticism of Erbakan, after first characterizing Erbakan—who some time earlier had had his bodyguards wash his feet at his summer house in Altınoluk—as “a vulgarized would-be Sultan,” I expressed my main criticism as follows:

“His Excellency Necmettin Erbakan, the General Chairman of the Welfare Party, in a propaganda speech he delivered on Tuesday, May 21, on the occasion of the June 2 by-elections, after saying ‘We’ll be in power in a week, ten days,’ decreed: ‘If you vote for a party other than Welfare, you vote for the Jews. The martyrs and saints will strike that person!’… On Thursday evening, May 23, a television channel announced: His Excellency Erbakan, in that day’s speech, this time decreed that ‘those who vote for parties other than RP vote for Armenians, for Israelis.’ If Turkey were a true democracy, a secular rule of law state, prosecutors should have immediately taken action to open an investigation against Erbakan under Article 312 of the Turkish Penal Code; the Grand National Assembly should have lifted Erbakan’s immunity; courts should have convicted Erbakan for racism. But of course Turkey is neither a true democracy nor a true secular rule of law state. How tragic that the probability of Erbakan being tried for racism is zero… Because Turkey is such a country that, although the constitution, the European Convention on Human Rights which we accept as superior to it, and the laws consider it a crime, practicing racism is effectively legitimate and free. The anti-Semitism of RP spokespersons; their anti-Jewish, racist statements have become so blatant that even some Islamists themselves are disturbed by it; but neither an investigation nor a lawsuit has been opened against them…

“The probability of Erbakan and RP spokespersons being tried and convicted for racism is zero, because Turkey is such a country that the best characterization that this country’s emergency governors can find to explain to the people what kind of a calamity the bloody terrorist organization PKK is, is to declare PKK members as ‘Armenian’… Just as His Excellency Erbakan and various spokespersons of his party declare Jews as ‘evil’ as a race, a lineage, at every opportunity, targeting Turkey’s citizens of the Jewish faith as enemies…” (Milliyet, May 25, 1996)

https://i4.hurimg.com/i/hurriyet/75/0x0/55eab4d8f018fbb8f89189c8 Following this article, his lawyers filed a lawsuit against me on the grounds that I had “violated Erbakan’s personal rights.” As a result of the trial, I was sentenced to 3 months in prison in October 1998. The sentence was first converted to a fine of 2 million 900 thousand liras, and was later pardoned by an amnesty law. The interesting aspect of this incident is that this was the only article of mine that was made the subject of a lawsuit throughout my column-writing career that began in 1982 and ended in 2016.

“Erbakan after the truck”

With the Refahyol coalition government established between the Welfare Party and the True Path Party receiving a vote of confidence on July 8, 1996, Erbakan had assumed the prime ministership. On the evening of November 3, 1996, on the Balıkesir-Bursa highway near Susurluk, as a result of a Mercedes automobile crashing into a truck, police chief Hüseyin Kocadağ, organized crime leader and deep state agent Abdullah Çatlı carrying fake identification, and his girlfriend Gonca Us lost their lives; DYP Şanlıurfa member of parliament Sedat Edip Bucak survived with injuries. The accident exposed the dark relationships in the state-politics-mafia triangle. The public demanded that the dark relationships be illuminated through a civil society action called “One Minute of Darkness for Continuous Light” and with the support of the media. Erbakan, however, chose not to pursue the matter, dismissing it as “nonsense.” In my commentary on this subject, I was saying:

“‘After the truck,’ the most important opportunity that Erbakan captured on paper was, of course, to assume the leadership of the ‘clean society, clean politics’ demand rising from society; to open a comprehensive investigation aimed at exposing the criminal gangs nested within the state and those who protect them, with all their connections. By doing so, Erbakan could have gained the support of segments whose votes he could never otherwise obtain, and could have opened the door to a vote share of a height he couldn’t even dream of in an election whose date he would determine himself. However, ‘after the truck,’ Erbakan started off by saying ‘Nonsense.’ Nowadays he is doing everything he can to change the agenda. It is clear that he has no intention of taking advantage of this opportunity that has come before him. He probably sees his main interest in ‘burying’ the matter.” (Milliyet, December 17, 1996)

The public outrage at the deep state’s cooperation with gangs would eventually pave the way to Erbakan’s loss of power and the closure of his party. In light of the facts revealed by the “Susurluk scandal,” in the commentary titled “The state’s gangs” that I would write about two years later, I would write the following:

“Although it is difficult to predict where the ‘Susurluk process’ will lead, we must stop at this point as a society and make an assessment: As it has emerged, the relationship between the state and the gangs was established by assigning certain outlaw bandits to fight ‘communist, ASALA, or Kurdish enemies of the state’ through illegal means, through extrajudicial executions. The bandits who were asked to kill for the state soon began killing for their personal interests (in drug-arms smuggling and other sectors) and eventually reached the point of ‘rebellion against the state’ (in the words of the report given to Prime Minister Mesut Yılmaz by Prime Ministry Inspection Board Chairman Kutlu Savaş)…

“At this point, the state faced the necessity of bringing under control the ‘monster’ it had itself created. Even if we forget for a moment that fighting ‘enemies of the state’ through illegal means is contrary to morality, the rule of law, and democracy, and evaluate this method only by the measure of ‘effectiveness - achieving the goal,’ the result is a disaster: Is it the ‘enemies of the state’ who suffered the most from this method, or is it the state itself, whose reputation, prestige, and credibility have been shaken, stained by ‘the disgrace of our history’? Who will clean this stain, and how?” (Milliyet, August 27, 1998)

## At the European Court of Human Rights

One of the most meaningful things I did at Milliyet was my articles introducing the European Court of Human Rights. During my first visit to Strasbourg in January 1997, the European Commission of Human Rights and the Court had not yet merged—as they would on January 1, 1998, pursuant to Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights—to take the name European Court of Human Rights. Prof. Dr. Şeref Gözübüyük from Ankara University Faculty of Law was a member of the Commission, and Prof. Dr. Feyyaz Gölcüklü from Ankara University Faculty of Political Sciences, who was also my professor, was a member of the Court.

In Strasbourg, I also conducted an interview with Commission Chairman Stephen Trechsel, who was expected to come to Ankara on February 17-18 at the invitation of Welfare Party Justice Minister Şevket Kazan. (During this first visit to Strasbourg, it never crossed my mind that one day I too would have to argue before the European Court of Human Rights that my rights had been violated; but that happened too. You will read the story later.) Trechsel was explaining Turkey’s position before the Commission as follows:

“The countries with the most applications to the Commission are Italy, Poland, and Turkey. Applications from these 3 countries currently constitute approximately half of the total 2500 applications before the Commission. Most applications from Italy are related to the length of trial proceedings. Examinations related to these do not take long. Most applications from Poland are also related to property rights and 80 percent of them are not found admissible… I cannot hide that applications against Turkey have distinctive characteristics. One group of applications belongs to those claiming their relatives were killed by security forces. Some are applications from those claiming they were subjected to ill-treatment or torture by security forces. There are applications related to restrictions on freedom of expression. Of course, there are also complaints of a lighter nature related to non-payment of expropriation compensation.” (Milliyet, January 27, 1997)

In the commentary titled “The rule of law is our cause” published on the last day of the three-day series of articles, I was saying: “The idea that Turkey could withdraw from the human rights oversight mechanism in the face of adverse decisions by the European Court of Human Rights was first put forward by Prof. Dr. Bakır Çağlar, Turkey’s former lawyer at Strasbourg (in the interview Yavuz Baydar conducted with him and published on this page)… It cannot be considered possible that any government could take such a step that would mean Turkey completely giving up EU membership; and, much more importantly, turning its back on the 200-year struggle for modernization and democratization…

“Instead of making threats to withdraw from European human rights oversight, Turkey should aim to conform to the European Convention on Human Rights, which it made part of its domestic law by ratifying it as early as 1954, to the protocols attached to it, and to other human rights conventions signed within the framework of the Council of Europe. For this, it should make the necessary changes in its laws and constitution. The existence of the European human rights oversight mechanism should be seen not as a burden for us, but as a blessing that supports our establishment of the rule of law… What befits Turkey is to make the European Convention on Human Rights, the fundamental document of contemporary democracy, dominant in its law.” (Milliyet, January 29, 1997)

Although Turkey accepted in 1987 the right of its citizens claiming their human rights were violated to apply to the Commission, and in 1990 the jurisdiction of the Court, judicial organs can still act as if ECHR decisions do not exist even in 2021 when these lines are being written; the President can also say that ECHR decisions are not binding. Rıza Türmen, who served as a judge of the European Court of Human Rights from 1998 to 2008, wrote the following exactly 24 years after I penned the series of articles I referred to above: “Those who argue that ECHR decisions are not binding are not only saying they will not comply with the rules of the game, they also want the rules of the game to be adjusted to their views…” (“Are ECHR decisions binding?,” T24, January 1, 2021) These lines are extremely instructive in showing that Turkey is progressively regressing in the field of human rights.

## Post-modern coup

With the Refahyol coalition government established between the Welfare Party and the True Path Party receiving a vote of confidence on July 8, 1996, Necmettin Erbakan had assumed the prime ministership. However, the military-dominated National Security Council soon, with its decisions on February 28, 1997, forced the government to resign on the grounds that it had practices against secularism. The military’s interventions in the political process on May 27, 1960, March 12, 1972, and September 12, 1980 were “modern” in nature, meaning that, albeit in different ways, they overthrew the government in power and installed new ones in its place. The decisions taken by the National Security Council on February 28, 1997, however, were ‘post-modern’ in nature (in Cengiz Çandar’s expression), because they merely forced the government to resign. Prime Minister Erbakan would not be able to withstand the military’s pressure and would submit his resignation on June 18, 1997.

Despite my principled opposition to military interference in politics, following the National Security Council’s February 28 decisions, I was writing the following in the article titled “Erbakan and democracy”:

“Prime Minister Erbakan explained his understanding of democracy at the last RP parliamentary group meeting: ‘What is democracy? First, sovereignty belongs unconditionally and without reservation to the nation. No one can stand before the nation and impose conditions or reservations. They will respect the nation’s decision… Second, the essential thing is the nation, not the state. The state exists to serve the nation. Third, we will believe in the principle that large majorities do not unite in error…’ It is clear that this definition does not conform to the liberal (that is, freedom-oriented and pluralist) understanding of democracy that is valid in contemporary democracies, that is, in countries that are members of the Council of Europe, NATO, and the European Union… In liberal democracies, there are ‘conditions and reservations’ on sovereignty. The right to govern / power belongs to the party or parties that receive the majority vote. On the other hand, individuals / citizens have fundamental rights and freedoms that cannot be violated by any government, by any majority no matter how large. Liberal democracy is majority rule limited by human rights…

“It is clear that Erbakan’s definition of democracy accepts the principle of ‘majority rule’ but excludes the principle of ‘fundamental rights and freedoms that cannot be violated by any majority.’ It is obvious that such a definition is prone to the mentality of ‘majority dictatorship,’ where ‘a government that has the support of the majority can do whatever it wants’… However, we cannot hold only Erbakan and the movement he belongs to responsible for the insufficient development in our country of the awareness that contemporary democracy also has the principle of ‘fundamental rights and freedoms’ equivalent to the principle of ‘majority rule.’ In light of recent events, it is seen that the struggle to establish a contemporary democratic order in Turkey continues not only on the ‘freedoms’ front but also on the ‘majority rule’ front.

“Nevertheless, we can say that a consensus on ‘majority rule’ has been established among Turkey’s civilian-military ruling elites. (Since the transition to the multi-party system, those who lost elections transferred power to those who won; the military, which seized power directly or indirectly three times, transferred governance to civilians after a relatively short period.) Our main problem in the field of democratization (which also prevents the full establishment of the principle of ‘majority rule’) is that the awareness of the individual’s fundamental rights and freedoms has not taken sufficient root… Why could what is called ‘the essence of liberalism,’ that is, the awareness of the individual’s fundamental rights and freedoms, not fully take hold? Probably one important reason… The Turkish Enlightenment movement’s neglect of adopting the doctrine of human rights from the Enlightenment Movement in the West.” (Milliyet, March 4, 1997)

In short, I was not saying an unconditional “no” to the February 28 intervention.

## Is Blair imitating Erbakan

In another article where I attacked Erbakan, I was making the following commentary reflecting my understanding of the religion-politics relationship:

“Prime Minister Erbakan reportedly said: ‘Look at what Blair says: I am committed to religious beliefs… Everything comes from love and faith, never mind leftism… They are imitating RP.’ There is no doubt that RP leader Erbakan has cracked another one of his jokes that make us all laugh. But his words, frankly, also have a serious side. That is Blair’s commitment to religious beliefs. The socialism adopted by the British prime minister is (unlike the Marxists’ understanding of”scientific” socialism) an ethical socialism; one of the sources of this ethics is also religion. Blair, of course, is not the first social democrat to say this. The Socialist International’s Declaration of 1951, about half a century ago, also said this.

“But is Blair imitating Erbakan, or should Erbakan take as an example Blair (who in no way makes his religious beliefs material for political struggle)? This question brings us to one of the topics we have been intensely discussing recently, the religion-politics relationship. It can be said that we have reached clarity that secularism means the separation of religion and state, freedom of belief, and the state being equidistant from all beliefs (and non-believers); and that secularism is a necessary but not sufficient condition for democracy. But there is no clarity on the separation of religion and politics. My view is as follows: A politician should be moral. One of the most important sources of morality (though not the only one) is the values that religion instills, such as respect for creation, for life, ‘sin and merit,’ love, solidarity, acting justly, honesty, not lying… Could there be anything more desirable than politicians being committed to these values?

“But, if a politician declares those who don’t vote for his party as ‘infidels / irreligious’… If he denigrates and demeans citizens of other faiths (for example Jews and Armenians)… If he presents religion as if it were the ‘property’ of his party… If he turns faith into ideology… If his statements are inconsistent with each other… If he does not act honestly… If he uses religious feelings for ‘vote hunting’ and does the exact opposite of what religion instills… That politician is exploiting religion. For these reasons, in the eyes of many of us, Erbakan is an ‘exploiter of religion’; a politician who harms both politics and religion…

“His ‘supplications, ritual prayers, pilgrimages to Mecca’ hold no value in the eyes of many of us beyond being ‘political shows.’ Another point we have not clarified in the context of religion and politics is the claim put forward mostly by those among us who adhere to positivist philosophy, that ‘religious belief, thought, and education lead to an authoritarian mindset’… When we remember that various authoritarian and totalitarian ideologies, primarily communism and racism, were based entirely on secular belief, thought, and education, there is nothing in this claim to be taken seriously.

“To attempt to identify the religion of Islam with Islamism because of the efforts of Islamist currents that strengthened in the 1980s to interpret Islamic faith (just like communism and racism) as an absolutist political ideology is, to put it mildly, nonsense. Marxists and other types of positivists may see religion, including Islam, as ‘the opium of the people’; they may find Islam as religion and culture ‘much more dangerous’ than political Islam (which is ultimately worldly). This view should be met with respect, like all views. However, with such an understanding, it is not possible to explain the contrast between Islam as a religion and political Islam. Nor to understand what is happening in society…” (“Blair and Erbakan,” May 8, 1997)

Closing the RP would be wrong

I was not saying an unconditional “no” to February 28, but I was taking a stance against the closure of RP and listing its “drawbacks” as follows: “1) It could play into the Islamists’ hands. Voters who see that the other parties have made no progress toward solving fundamental problems may, in order to punish them, turn in greater numbers to the party that will replace RP. 2) It will not help voters who put their hopes in it understand RP’s opportunist and demagogic identity and its lack of any solution for Turkey’s problems; the exposure of RP’s true colors will be postponed. 3) Suppression may lead some Islamists who have until now been moderate to radicalization. For these reasons, closing RP would be wrong. RP is actually a moderate party that rejects violence. Like all movements that exclude violence, Islamists should also have freedom of expression and organization. Those within this movement who advocate violence and undemocratic methods should not be left unpunished. However, Islamists should be given the opportunity to ‘democratize by living democracy.’” (Milliyet, December 18, 1997)

In the article I wrote upon the closure of RP by the Constitutional Court on January 18, 1998, I was also making the following commentary: “I have long thought as follows: The political current represented by RP cannot be excluded from democracy. The anti-democratic tendencies of this current can only be remedied through being ‘disciplined’ within democracy, over time. In democracies, freedom of organization is certainly not unlimited. Parties that do not play the game according to the rules can be closed. However, it cannot be said that RP generally ‘does not play the game according to the rules.’ It is clear that RP has members who ‘do not play the game according to the rules.’ The main ones among these are the RP members of parliament whose parliamentary memberships the Constitutional Court decided to revoke. These members, even if they are the party’s general chairman, should be held accountable before the judiciary for their statements and behaviors that violate the rules of the game… The collective punishment of the party is controversial in terms of legal principles and is politically objectionable because it does not benefit the establishment and strengthening of democracy in Turkey.” (Milliyet, January 20, 1998)

“Sèvres Syndrome”

On April 27, 1997, I participated in an international conference at Oxford University’s St. Antony’s College on the topic “Which way Turkey now?” and gave a talk titled “Turkey’s European vocation: Elite and mass perceptions.” In this talk, I focused on a book published by the General Staff with the note “The views contained in this work are entirely the personal views of the author and do not reflect the views of the TAF that published the work,” but with the recommendation that it “be utilized as a reference document and auxiliary source.” The book in question, titled “The Middle East in the Light of International Relations: Lands Sought to Be Partitioned and People Exploited,” written by a colonel, was a sharp example of the belief, quite widespread among Turkey’s military-civilian elites, that Western states are constantly conspiring to divide and partition Turkey, also known as the “Sèvres Syndrome.” In the article I wrote upon returning home from the conference, I was saying:

“I am sure that the views expressed (in this book) do not dominate the TAF. Nevertheless, it is noteworthy that views reflecting deep suspicion and distrust toward Western allies come from within the institution believed to be the most ‘Westernist’ of a country that has been a NATO member for about 50 years. But it is not at all surprising. Because we frequently hear these views or similar ones from various party spokespersons, primarily RP, DSP, and MHP, from ministers, from former presidents and chiefs of general staff, and we frequently read them in newspaper columns. President Süleyman Demirel, whom leftists in the 1960s and 1970s nicknamed ‘Morrison Süleyman’ because they found him too close to the USA, also expressed similar views in May 1995. He said: The West wants to divide Turkey, to bring back Sèvres… (At the conference in Oxford) In my talk on the psychological dimension of Turkey-West relations, I emphasized the above point. My purpose was to remind our Western friends that Turkey cannot be regarded as ‘in the bag.’” (Milliyet, May 9, 1996)

If we look at where Turkey-West relations have arrived today, about a quarter century after this article was published, it can be said that this reminder was quite apt. In January 2021, when these lines were being written, not only had Turkey’s hope for EU membership virtually disappeared, but the USA’s new secretary of state, Blinken, was also referring to Turkey as a “so-called ally.” (Newspapers, January 20, 2021)

## Military solution

One of the most exciting events of my journalism career was the trip I participated in between November 17-20, 1997, at the invitation of the General Staff’s Press-Publication-Public Relations and Promotion Department, covering the bases of soldiers fighting against the PKK in the Southeast. We, the nearly 30 journalists participating in the trip, flew on a military plane from Ankara to Van. From there, by helicopter, we flew to Dağlıca, Köprülü, Mezraa, Gürvil Mountain, Şenoba, Siyahkaya, Çalışkan, Şırnak, Namaz Mountain, Siirt, Doğanköy, Okçular, over Lice to Diyarbakır, and then returned to Ankara by plane. According to information provided by the General Staff, we flew a total of 9 hours and 45 minutes on this trip and covered 2,205 km. I would also express my observations and impressions about the trip in a series of articles.

In the article I sent from Şırnak, I was saying: “As far as I can see, the main message that the commanders conducting the fight against separatist terrorism want conveyed to the public is this: The armed forces have achieved significant success in the fight against terrorism at the cost of great material and moral sacrifice; terrorism has essentially been brought under control. However, for the success to be permanent and for the swamp that breeds terrorism to be drained, it is now time for socio-economic measures that need to be taken without delay. What is meant by this is essentially the provision of job opportunities that will pave the way for the welfare of the region’s people. In short, the soldiers are saying, ‘We have largely implemented what is called the “military solution.” Now it’s time for the civilian solution…’” (Milliyet, November 21, 1997)

In the article I sent from Köprülü near Hakkari, I was also writing the following:

“Brigadier General Fikri Gönültaş, commander of the 1st Commando Brigade stationed in Çukurca, is giving a briefing to journalists participating in the press tour organized by the General Staff about the fight against the PKK. At one point he says: ‘We are aware that whoever wins the people will succeed…’ Here is the most concise expression of what we call the civilian solution: Winning the people… If macroeconomic stability is achieved, if obstacles to investments are removed, if the country becomes attractive for both domestic and foreign investors… If the economic incentives promised to the Southeast and East are fully and expansively implemented… If progress is made in the GAP project… Then we can achieve the development drive that will eliminate the swamp that breeds terrorism, that is, unemployment and poverty. This would be a very important breakthrough toward the civilian solution, that is, winning the people.

“However, economic development is not enough to solve the Kurdish problem underlying the ‘PKK problem,’ that is, to ‘win the people.’ I do not think those governing Turkey have yet grasped that the problem has a psychological dimension in addition to its military and socio-economic dimensions. Because we have been able to go little beyond words in recognizing Kurdish identity, we are unfortunately far from being able to say that the region’s people have been psychologically won. Without resolving the Kurdish problem, that is, without recognizing the right of Kurds to freely develop their language and culture; without opening the opportunity for Kurdish nationalists who reject violence to freely participate in democratic competition, we cannot win the people, we cannot fully solve the PKK problem. The problem is, of course, not one that can be solved immediately tomorrow. It is long-term and multi-faceted. We have come a long way on the military front. It is time for progress on the other fronts as well. This is the task not of the army, but of the civilian administration.” (Milliyet, November 22, 1997)

## Civilian solution

In the general assessment I wrote after returning to Istanbul from the trip, I was drawing attention to the following points: “It was understood that the Southeast Anatolia Press Tour organized by the General Staff had two main purposes: to convey to the public in the most effective way 1) that the security forces, primarily the TAF, have managed to bring separatist terrorism under control to a certain level after a 13-year struggle with a very high moral and material cost; and 2) that military measures alone, the ‘military solution,’ are not sufficient to completely overcome separatist terrorism; that the fight against terrorism also requires a multi-dimensional, multi-fronted ‘civilian solution’… Regardless of what they mean by ‘civilian solution,’ the fact that the military no longer insists on the idea that ‘military solution’ is the sole and sufficient solution is, undoubtedly, a new stage on the way toward solving Turkey’s main problem. Unfortunately, we lack a civilian administration that would take the soldiers’ message and act on it, a strong and stable government…

“The soldiers have largely accomplished the task that fell to them and brought separatist terrorism under control to a certain level. But have the region’s people been won? Or, as some claim, is the PKK retreating militarily while advancing politically? The visible economic revival I encountered when I stopped in Diyarbakır on the way back from the ‘Press Tour’ was hopeful. Learning that MED-TV, the mouthpiece of separatist terrorism, was the most-watched television station in the region was like a cold shower. Why do the state and the region’s people still not have television and radio stations that broadcast in Kurdish and thus can address the entire population of the region? Why can Kurdish music be played on local television channels but Kurdish cannot be spoken? Why does the PKK’s propaganda go unanswered? Is there any way to explain this?” (“Winning the People,” Milliyet, November 27, 1997)

“On Life’s Path”

During the Southeast press tour, I had the opportunity to meet and chat with many officers and soldiers. One of them was an officer who at the time held the rank of Gendarmerie Staff Captain. In the letter he later sent me, he was saying: “Dear professor, I have just returned to Diyarbakır from duty and I am reading your article titled ‘On Life’s Path.’ It is impossible not to agree with you. Hopefully, we will learn to tolerate each other, to discuss like human beings, to look at each other with tolerance. But I think we are slowly learning. Because in this country, there is both a spouse and bread for all of us. We need only one thing: Good administrators who can put the country’s interests ahead of their own interests. My hope is that young people who understand your and Professor Taha’s thoughts will be raised soon. Respectfully, Y.K.”

In my article triggered by this letter that pleased me, I was referring to Taha Akyol’s latest book with the same title (Milliyet Publications, November 1997) and saying: “On Life’s Path is Taha Akyol’s book consisting of articles discussing the experiences he wants to share with young people and the lessons he has drawn from them. With these articles, Akyol, based on his own personal experiences, those of our generation, and those of other domestic and foreign generations, calls on young people who have been captivated by the ‘spell of ideology’ (Islamist, Revolutionary, Idealist, Ummahist, Communist, Turkist, or Kurdist) to break the spell and take the path of critical reason; to live for ideals instead of dying for ideology. He also tries to explain to society and the state the importance of approaching young people ‘with understanding’ and giving them the opportunity to free themselves from the spell (which they have been captivated by partly due to their psychology).

“Akyol and I are two members of the same generation who, after having been at the far extremes of the right and left ideological wings, drew similar conclusions from our experiences. The point where we met after drawing these conclusions was liberal democratic values. Perhaps he remained somewhat attached to local and conservative sensibilities; perhaps I preserved to some extent universal and reformist sensibilities. But we both abandoned dogmas and settled on critical rationalism…

“I completely agree with Akyol. Unfortunately, despite all the local and universal experience; despite the years, lives, generations spent on this path, we have not been able to establish in our country the understanding that human beings are ‘fallible,’ that what we think is right today may turn out to be wrong tomorrow; the questioning, skeptical, critical, rational, that is, scientific mentality. As a society, we still have not understood that perhaps the essential measure of contemporary civilization is being able to criticize oneself; that freedom-oriented democracy is above all ‘the regime that makes it possible to turn back from mistakes, to correct wrongs.’

“Some still prefer ‘dying rather than turning back’ from mistakes; those who consider changing one’s mind as immorality, those who say ‘Shoot those who abandon the Cause!’ can still gain respect. Unfortunately, we have still not been able to establish in Turkey respect for the individual, for the rights and freedoms of the individual. We have not grasped that the subject of freedom can be none other than the individual. We have not transcended the discourse of the ‘freedom’ of the class, the people, the nation, the ummah, the community, identities, etc. The only thing we can take consolation in is that dogmatism and the ‘spell of ideology’ have perhaps retreated a little more today compared to the days when we were young.” (Milliyet, December 27, 1997)

A few weeks after returning from the Southeast Press Tour, a kilim sent as a gift from the Gendarmerie Public Order Command arrived at my address by cargo. With the following note: “Dear Şahin Alpay, the motifs on this kilim woven by the beautiful people of the Southeast are the most original symbols of our unity and integrity woven with love. With our wishes that it reminds you of the region’s beauty that lives on despite everything, and of those who have ‘sworn an oath’ to protect it at the cost of their lives. Respectfully. Lieutenant General Çetin Doğan.” (The same Çetin Doğan was promoted to full General in 1999 and appointed to the Aegean Army Command. Later, while he was the 1st Army Commander, it was claimed that he had prepared the “Sledgehammer coup plan”; he was also retired in 2003. On August 19, 2021, he was arrested as one of 14 officers who received life sentences in the February 28 trial in which he was prosecuted.)

## At Princeton University

When I returned to the country after completing my doctorate at Stockholm University, I had not been able to find an opportunity to continue my academic career and had to take refuge in the press. Continuing an academic career must have remained an unfulfilled aspiration within me, because at the suggestion and encouragement of my late friend Mustafa Gürsel, I taught an elective course on “Opinion Writing” at Anadolu University Faculty of Communication in the fall semester of 1987. When I left Cumhuriyet in 1992, again with Gürsel’s encouragement, I had applied for the one-year fellowship that the Nieman Foundation of Harvard University offers to journalists for their professional renewal, but I was quite disappointed to receive a negative response.

In the spring semester of 1994, at the suggestion and encouragement of Prof. Binnaz Toprak, who was then the department chair, I taught an elective course on “Politics in Scandinavia” at Boğaziçi University’s Department of Political Science. This was a kind of consolation gift that Binnaz offered me to remedy the “defeat” I had suffered in the associate professorship examination that I had entered at Hikmet Özdemir’s encouragement despite being completely unprepared. The most valuable of the opportunities my friends provided for returning to academia was the invitation by Prof. Şükrü Hanioğlu, the chairman of the Department of Near Eastern Studies at Princeton University, one of America’s leading universities, to teach an elective course on politics in Turkey to graduate students in the spring semester of 1998.

I first disclosed the invitation from Hanioğlu to Derya Sazak. Derya said let me raise the matter with the boss (Aydın Doğan); then he told me to see the boss. I called his secretary; after being made to wait for a few days, I was granted an audience. He treated me with his usual distance, but he responded quite positively to the invitation I had received. He even said “We’ll announce with fanfare that you’re going to Princeton.” I was pleased. Indeed, Derya Sazak announced that I was going with a short news item he put on the front page. We agreed with Derya that I would continue writing my column three days a week and leave the editorship of the page to Nilüfer, with Naki Özkan assisting her. At the beginning of February, Fatma and I went to Princeton, and in the spring semester that lasted until June, I taught a course on “Politics in Turkey in the Multi-party Period.”

What made it possible for me to go to Princeton was the financial support provided by the foundation established with the donation made by brothers Ahmet and Nasuhi Ertegün to Princeton University’s Near Eastern Studies Department in order to perpetuate the name of their late father Münir Ertegün (one of the former ambassadors to Washington). The Münir Ertegün Foundation, established in 1994 to encourage Turkey studies, was managed by a committee. At that time, the chairman of the committee was Şükrü Hanioğlu, and its members were the famous historian Bernard Lewis and Abraham Udovitch. The foundation organized conferences and panels each academic year; provided financial support to researchers; and occasionally invited academics or experts to Princeton for one or two semesters to teach.

(A piece of information I want to share about Princeton University is this: With a decision taken in June 2020, the university’s board of trustees removed Woodrow Wilson’s name from one of its faculties because of his “racist views and policies.” Yet Wilson was someone who served as president of Princeton University from 1902 to 1910, as President of the United States from 1912 to 1920, and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1919 for the principles he announced before the USA entered World War I…)

In Princeton, we settled into one of the residences rented to university employees. Although Fatma was a bit bored in the first days, she later got used to the environment; she was quite happy with the visits first of our daughter Elvan and our then one-year-old granddaughter Defne, and later of our relatives including my elder sister Olcay and my brother-in-law Ünal. In Princeton, we formed lasting friendships with Ali and Nazlı Karaosmanoğlu and the couple Heath and Demet Lowry. Lowry, whom I had met during his teaching at Boğaziçi University, was teaching Turkish political life courses at Princeton. Karaosmanoğlu, whom I had met during his teaching at Bilkent, was conducting research at Princeton’s Woodrow Wilson School of Public and International Affairs.

The Near Eastern Studies department where I was a guest was located in Princeton’s building called Jones Hall. The small office assigned to me here had an interesting history: Albert Einstein, one of the pioneers in natural sciences, had used this office for a short time during his faculty position at Princeton in the 1930s.

The six months I spent at Princeton contributed significantly to my getting to know the university, academics, society, and politics in the USA. Only five students, one American and the others Turkish, attended my course, which I gave in the form of seminars lasting several hours once a week. There was nothing surprising about this, because most graduate courses were conducted with a small number of students. This experience would be good preparation for the Turkish Political Life course I would begin teaching at Bahçeşehir University a few years later.

## Meeting Bernard Lewis

During the time I spent at Princeton, I had the opportunity to meet some world-renowned American academics. The most famous of these was certainly the Near Eastern historian Bernard Lewis (1916-2018), who taught at Princeton from 1972 to 1986. Lewis was known in Turkey primarily as the author of the book The Emergence of Modern Turkey, which is the basic reference work for Turkey’s modernization history courses, and as the famous historian who rejected the “Armenian genocide” thesis. The fact that Lewis characterized what happened to Ottoman Armenians in 1915-1916 as “terrible holocaust” in the 1961 and 1968 first editions of his book on Turkey, and as “terrible slaughter” in later editions, had been quite controversial; it was alleged that he engaged in “historical revisionism” for his political and personal interests. Palestinian-American social scientist Edward Said had also characterized Lewis’s works as leading examples of “Orientalism” (that is, Western experts looking at Middle Eastern peoples with a gaze that distorts their reality and others them). Lewis would also be a historian debated internationally as one of the mentors who encouraged US President George W. Bush’s attack on Iraq in 2003.

During the months I was at Princeton, I met with Lewis several times. In one of these meetings, Lewis told me that he had written an article that he never intended to publish in response to the criticisms directed at him by Armenian circles in the USA, and that he wanted to show it to me, but unfortunately he did not keep this promise. In the interview I conducted with him, published in Milliyet under the title “Building democracy is not easy,” he was saying: “Although Turkey has suffered many difficulties, it has established a functioning democracy. It hasn’t solved all its problems yet, but it is quite successful compared to other Muslim countries in the region… I believe Islam is compatible with liberal democracy. But this is a theoretical, not a historical proposition. Today, only one of the 56 members of the Organization of the Islamic Conference, Turkey, is a democracy.” (Milliyet, May 4-5, 1998.) At the time I conducted this interview, Lewis was 82 years old and his mind was working brilliantly. I had also heard that he was living with a woman about 40 years younger than himself. He would live another 20 years until he died at the age of 102.

One of the famous figures I met and became somewhat acquainted with at Princeton was Professor Norman Itzkowitz. Itzkowitz was best known for the book “Immortal Atatürk” (1984) that he co-authored with Vamık Volkan. About the book, he was saying: “Unfortunately, history is written without any reference to psychology. Yet we all know that individual psychology plays a major role in our lives. What we did in this book was to approach Atatürk as a human being…” Itzkowitz and Volkan would later publish another book called Turks and Greeks: Neighbours in Conflict (1994).

Professor Abraham Udovitch, an expert on Near Eastern Jewish history, was one of the department members who showed me warmth and with whom I conversed. I also met his wife Lucette F. Valensi at a dinner. Tunisian-born Valensi was at that time a faculty member at École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales, one of France’s leading schools, and the author of many works on “Islam in the Mediterranean.” Her works “Venice and the Sublime Porte” and “Islam in Revolt” had also been translated into Turkish.

“Greece should advocate for Turkey’s EU membership”

At Princeton, lunch breaks were not wasted; meetings were held during almost every lunch break where a speaker was invited and refreshments were served to participants. The subject of one of the meetings I attended was “US Policy toward Turkey, Greece, and Cyprus,” and the speaker was Monteagle Stearns, one of the USA’s former ambassadors to Athens. Among those who came to attend the meeting was also Mrs. Margarita Papandreou, the American-born former wife of Greece’s late prime minister Andreas Papandreou. I was quite surprised when Mrs. Papandreou took the floor during discussions and said, “For the resolution of the problems between them, Greece should be the leading advocate of Turkey’s EU membership.”

Following the brief chat I had with her after the meeting, I would write as follows: “Mrs. Papandreou complains that Greek politicians cannot see that if Greece takes the lead in Turkey’s accession to the EU, the resolution of Turkish-Greek problems would be facilitated. Mrs. Papandreou, who plays an important role in the Greek women’s movement, is determined to work for Turkish-Greek rapprochement. We may see the first examples of this in the coming days. As is known, Margarita Papandreou is the mother of Greece’s alternate foreign minister George Papandreou.” (Milliyet, February 24, 1998)

I had the opportunity to listen to many famous speakers at conferences organized at Princeton. One of them was the late Prof. Dr. Halil İnalcık, one of the greatest of our Ottoman historians. I would convey an anecdote from his speech as follows: “İnalcık stated that in today’s Turkey it is not possible to write an objective, scientific work on either Fatih (Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror) or Atatürk. I couldn’t help but ask: ‘Why is that?!’ The Professor’s answer was good: ‘As you know, these days it is said that freedom of expression is restricted in Turkey…’ Perhaps the most important of the points the Professor emphasized was this: Turkey suffers greatly from two types of bigotry. The first of these is ‘revolutionary’ bigotry. This bigotry misunderstands Islam and Turkish society. It assumes that the masses attached to their traditions and beliefs do not exist. Because of the mistakes of such bigots, the great mass is being pushed toward the sphere of influence of the second type of bigots, the ‘Sharia advocates.’” (Milliyet, May 17, 1998)

## Visiting the New York Times

Princeton was quite close to New York City; it was possible to reach it in less than an hour by train. Fatma and I made this trip quite frequently. On one of these trips, I visited The New York Times and met two of the newspaper’s unsigned editorial writers, that is, two of its “anonymous heroes.” The subject they were most curious about was how relations between the Islamists and the military, the guardian of the official ideology, would proceed after the closure of RP and its replacement by the Virtue Party. After noting that there were optimists who believed the Islamists had learned their lesson from February 28 and pessimists who did not believe so, I conveyed what I had said in my Milliyet column as follows:

“I find the pessimists too pessimistic and the optimists too optimistic. Virtue’s future will probably be somewhere between the two. But still, we should continue to remind the Islamists of the lessons to be learned from their experiences and their responsibilities. FP can certainly continue to criticize interpretations that turn secularism into ‘hostility to religion,’ as well as ‘imitation of the West’ and policies indexed to the West. It can continue to defend our history and our distinctive identity. But FP should reject RP’s bad legacy. It should bury in history the nonsense of ‘multiple legal systems’ and ‘just economic order.’ It should adopt secularism, which means the state being equidistant from all religions and beliefs and freedom for all beliefs. It should abandon racism and anti-Semitism. It should give up wanting freedom only for itself. It should internalize liberal democracy based on human rights and freedoms, including secularism. It should not harbor those who do not adopt these principles. Then FP can see that it is playing a beneficial role not only in Turkey but in the entire Islamic world.” (Milliyet, March 12, 1998)

## Busy agenda

During my time at Princeton, I was very pleased to receive invitations from many universities to speak on Turkey’s domestic and foreign policy. April was particularly busy. First, I gave two talks to faculty members and students at Princeton’s Near Eastern Studies department. Then I was a guest of the Turkish Student Association at Rutgers University, also in New Jersey. Later I went to the capital Washington DC and spoke successively at the United States Institute of Peace, Johns Hopkins University, George Washington University, and (at the invitation of my friend Prof. Sabri Sayarı) the Foreign Service Institute, the center for training diplomats.

In May, at the invitation of the late Prof. Kemal Karpat, I gave a talk at the University of Wisconsin’s Madison campus. It was a pleasant surprise that our famous surgeon Prof. Münci Kalayoğlu was among the audience. From there I went to Boston and gave a talk at Harvard University’s Kennedy School of Government at the invitation of the renowned Ottoman historian Cemal Kafadar. My last stop was New York. There, I spoke at the Association of Turkish Architects, Engineers, and Scientists. At the meetings I briefly mentioned above, I had very instructive dialogues with both American and Turkish students and faculty members.

## Los Alamos

After the seminar I taught at Princeton ended, Fatma and I set out on an approximately ten-day West Coast trip. At our first stop, we visited my sister Jackie from the Wilson family, in whose home I had spent the 1961-62 academic year as an AFS scholarship student, and her husband Bob MacFarlane at their home in the famous city of Los Alamos in the state of New Mexico. I would write the following about this visit:

“The mystery and secrecy of Los Alamos from the years when the first atomic bombs were made and tested is, of course, gone now. Nevertheless, Jackie’s physicist husband Bob could not obtain the necessary permission for me to tour the laboratories where he had been working for years. Because the work at Los Alamos laboratories is still 60-70 percent ‘for military purposes,’ that is, related to the development of nuclear weapons. (According to what Bob told me, the USA’s signing of the treaty banning tests was creating great ‘distress’ in these circles. Because bomb producers could not find the opportunity to test their products.)…
