“Maybe it seemed so to me, but it was as if Los Alamos was still in a state of ‘remorse.’ In the brochure distributed at the Science Museum in the city, which was frequently the scene of demonstrations by Americans opposed to nuclear weapons, it said, ‘We had to use the atomic bomb because the Japanese were the attacking side; they were not willing to surrender; thousands of people were dying every day as long as the war continued; the bomb saved the lives of many more people than it killed.’ When I browsed through the notebook where museum visitors noted their impressions, I encountered the same arguments. I learned there that the scientists of Jewish origin who developed the atomic bomb were opposed to its use against the Japanese after Germany surrendered.” (Milliyet, May 26, 1998)

From there we flew to California. First we went to Big Bear Lake and spent two nights with Mollie Wilson, the Wilsons’ mother who always showed me great affection. Then we moved to the Los Angeles coast and met with the eldest son Gordon Wilson and his wife Evie, who lived in Newport Beach. It was interesting that Fatma, like me, found Los Angeles and its surroundings to be the most livable place in the USA. Then we flew to Las Vegas. The young American servicewoman I chatted with during the flight inspired me to write the article titled “Women in America.” I was saying:

## Judie and Jackie

“She boarded the plane going from Los Angeles to Las Vegas at 9 pm at the last minute. She was slim, blonde, blue-eyed, quite attractive, and a bit flustered. ‘You were hoping I wouldn’t come, but here I am!…’ she said and sat down next to us, in the window seat. She immediately began to tell her story: When she missed the plane she was supposed to board from Ontario, her friends had rushed her to Los Angeles airport, but they had almost gotten lost on Los Angeles freeways and she had almost missed the plane. When she learned that my wife and I were speaking Turkish between ourselves, she said, ‘I’m learning German, but I wish I were learning Turkish…’ After asking what we were doing in the USA, she told everything about herself: No, she wasn’t going to Las Vegas and had never been there. She would fly to St. Louis on the plane departing from there at midnight; then continue by car, and by dawn arrive at the house where her mother, father, and 5 siblings all younger than her lived; she would spend her fifteen-day leave with them.

“Judie was 18 years old. She belonged to the US Navy’s special forces, the Marines. She had completed her military training and in a month would be sent to the US naval base on Japan’s Okinawa island. No, she didn’t want to spend her life as a marine. She would serve for four years, and during this time would complete the higher education program provided by the Navy through ‘flying professors’ and the internet. This was actually the most important reason for her being a marine. After leaving the Navy, her intention was to find a job at the FBI (the USA’s intelligence organization responsible for internal security). For a woman, being a marine was not difficult at all. Perhaps the hardest part of the job was that there were only 3,000 female marines compared to 176,000 male marines in the Navy…

“The story of the young American woman we met on a plane trip, who came from a small town in the American Midwest and a low-income family, became a marine, and thereby planned to get a higher education and work at the FBI, made one think about the place and role of women in American society. The story of my ‘American sister’ Jackie, whom I visited in Los Alamos, New Mexico, was no less thought-provoking. Jackie grew up in an affluent family in southern California. She studied mathematics at the University of Pittsburgh. In Los Alamos, to which she had become deeply attached after marrying her physicist husband Bob and settling there, she has been teaching mathematics to eighth-grade students for years. In this city at an altitude of about 2,500 meters above sea level, she runs for at least an hour and swims for at least an hour every morning before going to work. In the evenings, she plays the violin in one of the classical music orchestras, as she has done with great pleasure since her youth.

“Jackie has three sons. One is doing a doctorate in philosophy, another in medicine; the youngest is studying economics. All three are competitive swimmers. Jackie doesn’t hide that when they were young, she would get her sons out of bed at 4:30 in the morning and take them to inter-school swimming competitions held at 6:30 in the state capital Albuquerque. Although it may seem like ‘torture’ to some, according to Jackie, this was an important part of her children’s education. And so it must have been… The secret of how the eldest son John, in the years he began studying philosophy at Harvard, could come to Turkey and traverse the Turkish mountains from the Aladağlar to the Kaçkars (by trekking) probably lay here.

“Of course, not all women in the USA are like Judie and Jackie. But one of the most important forces that make the USA what it is, is undoubtedly women like them who contribute to social life in every field. Isn’t one of our greatest hopes for Turkey’s future also the increasing number of women who contribute to social life in every field?” (Milliyet, May 29, 1998)

Like everyone who goes there, we had a good time in Las Vegas. I won’t forget the elderly couple we encountered at a casino, who believed that they owed the money pouring out like rain from the slot machine they were playing to the luck we had brought them when we appeared there, and who cheered for us because of it… The night shows at the MGM hotel where we stayed were also as entertaining as only the USA can offer. We had quite a good time here. Then we flew to San Francisco. We stayed three nights and met with Turkish acquaintances there. The dinners we had at Fisherman’s Wharf were perhaps the most enjoyable part of this trip.

In our last weeks at Princeton, our son Acar, who was studying at Bilkent, came to visit us. Following very poor advice, we went with him to Disneyland in Orlando, Florida, and stayed two nights — an unfortunate visit. Orlando was unfortunately unbearable in the June heat. The New York visit I made with Acar, however, was unforgettable. When we went to the very top of one of the World Trade Center buildings that were destroyed by Al-Qaeda attacks on September 11, 2001, I remember how we trembled inside thinking about what could happen if a plane were to hit these tall buildings.

In my article titled “Farewell to Princeton” that appeared after I returned to Turkey, I was saying: “In the articles I sent from Princeton, I wrote more about what was happening in the USA and the world; trying to draw some lessons for Turkey from them… I believe the time I spent here, the experience I gained, made a great contribution to my getting to know American society and politics, and to my quest for approaching events with a global and comparative perspective. During this time, in both the courses I taught and the talks I gave at various distinguished institutions, I tried to reflect the complex reality of Turkey in various aspects and to contribute as much as I could to the establishment of a balanced perspective on Turkey. I did not only talk about Turkey’s problems; I also emphasized its great achievements.” (Milliyet, June 16, 1998)

The articles I wrote from the USA were worth collecting in a book. Why didn’t I do so? This must be another manifestation of my habit of not being able to look back.

## Milliyet is being sold

We returned home from the USA on June 15, 1998; shortly after, a series of events that would result in the sale of Milliyet began to unfold. At the beginning of August, the tender privatizing the public bank called Türkbank was broadcast live on television. The next day, we learned that someone named Korkmaz Yiğit (hereafter KY) had acquired the bank. I had never heard this name. I went to the newspaper’s economics desk trying to find out who he was.

The economics desk chief Murat Sabuncu (whom I would meet years later in Silivri prison) said, as if saying something very ordinary, “He’s Alaaddin Çakıcı’s partner, bro…” That day and the next, I searched for information about who he was in the newspapers; there wasn’t any. Someone said he was a rich contractor. Then news about Korkmaz Yiğit also buying E-TV, Kanal D, and Genç TV appeared one after another in the press. When I asked Murat Sabuncu, “Hey Murat, why aren’t you doing a story about who this man is?” he said, “Come on bro, maybe ‘those above us’ (meaning the boss) have some business with him; do you want me to create trouble for us?”…

On the evening of September 12, I was invited to dinner at the home of Stephen Kinzer, the Istanbul bureau chief of the New York Times (NYT). I jokingly said to Kinzer, “Why don’t you do a story about who this KY is so we can learn…” When he asked why Milliyet wasn’t doing it, I conveyed what I had heard from Sabuncu. A few days later, curious about what reaction I would get, I told Derya Sazak about what I had discussed with Kinzer. He merely said, “Well said, bro!” (!)

Then it was announced that Yiğit had also acquired the newspaper Yeni Yüzyıl; rumors spread that he would also buy Radikal. I called İsmet Berkan, the Ankara representative who was my friend from Cumhuriyet. Berkan said “it would be more reasonable for him to buy Milliyet instead of Radikal which has no printing press or building”… Then word began to spread that KY was holding talks to buy Milliyet. Derya was confirming the rumor but insistently saying he didn’t think it would happen. When I returned from an overseas trip I made between September 16-27, 1998, I would learn that the sale of Milliyet to KY had been formalized in a protocol and that the transfer of the newspaper would take place on October 8. Fatma told me that Güneri Cıvaoğlu had called while I was abroad, but I hadn’t paid attention. As I later learned, Cıvaoğlu had been calling Milliyet writers saying things like “Don’t worry, everything is under my control…” The general atmosphere among newspaper employees was that they were trying to get used to the new boss. This is how they were talking: KY was said to have a relationship with Alaaddin Çakıcı, but what was wrong with that? He was a rich man… He was giving tremendous raises to salaries… Besides, breaking the cartel wouldn’t be so bad…

The announcement that appeared in the newspaper on October 8, 1998, stated that the process of “transferring the shares of Milliyet Gazetecilik A.Ş. and AD Yayıncılık A.Ş., which publishes the magazines of the Milliyet Group, to the Korkmaz Yiğit Group” would be completed soon; it was stated that “the total shares of the companies in question were valued at 310 million US dollars and that a preliminary agreement had been reached on the sale of the majority shares based on this price.” On the same day, Aydın Doğan’s farewell article to the effect that “I sold the newspaper because of cartel accusations” was also published in the newspaper. In the following days, Güneri Cıvaoğlu’s column where he wrote “Korkmaz Yiğit used to sell newspapers when he was little” would be followed by articles themed “Welcome Korkmaz Yiğit” by Hasan Pulur, Doğan Heper, Derya Sazak, Yalçın Doğan, and Umur Talu.

On the evening of October 8, the handover ceremony of the newspaper was held. I learned that such a ceremony would be held from the drivers when I was leaving the newspaper in the afternoon. Thinking that I had no business there since I had not been invited, I went home. Yet the ceremony had been held open to all employees on the floor where the restaurants were… As I later learned from Osman Ulagay, who was present at the ceremony, Aydın Doğan had looked sad; KY was so excited that he couldn’t read the text in his hand properly. According to the rumors I heard, after the ceremony, celebrations were held on the top floor occupied by the bosses, with managers and writers attending and champagne corks popping. Cıvaoğlu had played the leading role in the celebrations. When the waiters recounted to him what had happened, Aydın Doğan was terribly resentful…

## Milliyet is not being sold

Due to my work, I went to Ayvalık between October 11-13. When I returned to Istanbul on the evening of October 13, something inside nudged me, and instead of going straight home, I stopped by the newspaper to pick up incoming mail. I encountered people with sullen faces in the newsroom and around it. That day, CHP deputy Fikri Sağlar had released at a press conference in the Grand National Assembly the recording of the telephone conversation (sent to him by mail) between mafia leader Alaaddin Çakıcı and Korkmaz Yiğit. According to the recording, Yiğit, who said he wanted to acquire Türkbank, was asking Çakıcı to eliminate the other bidders from the process… KY’s relationship with the mafia had been clearly exposed. What would happen now?.. I immediately went to see Derya Sazak. Derya said, “Of course we will publish the news; tomorrow we’ll also get together as writers and decide what to do.”

On the morning of October 14, Derya called the newspaper’s writers to a meeting in Aydın Doğan’s office. I went together with Nilüfer Kuyaş. Also there was a person named Yaşar Eroğul, who was said to have brokered the sale of Milliyet from Aydın Doğan to Korkmaz Yiğit, just as he had previously brokered the sale of Hürriyet from Erol Simavi to Aydın Doğan. Taha Akyol immediately sidled up to me and advised me not to open my mouth because Aydın Doğan was going to take the newspaper back. I was happy about this news, for after hearing Fikri Sağlar’s disclosure, I had decided not to work at a Milliyet whose boss was KY.

At the writers’ meeting, Derya conveyed that they had gathered to discuss what should be done following Fikri Sağlar’s disclosures, that he had met with Aydın Doğan that morning, and that the boss had asked for two days to make a decision. Hasan Pulur and Meral Tamer thanked Derya for publishing the phone recording news as a headline in the newspaper; they asked what Yaşar Eroğul, who had left the room at that moment, was doing at the meeting. Eroğul returned shortly; he said that KY had no concern other than Milliyet’s prestige and that he was ready to return the newspaper to Doğan if terms were agreed upon. When Nilüfer asked, “If the newspaper is taken back, are we going to continue as if nothing happened?!”, Abbas Güçlü said, “What, are you tired of Aydın Doğan?” The meeting dispersed to wait for the two-day period.

I spoke with Zülfü, who was in Germany. “I’ve submitted my resignation,” he said. He had agreed with Zafer Mutlu to return to Sabah. Nilüfer Kuyaş and Nilgün Cerrahoğlu were inclined to resign; I told them I was in favor of waiting. Meanwhile, it was learned that Ali Sirmen and Oktay Akbal would return to Cumhuriyet. According to the gossip that reached Derya’s ear, Sirmen had said at a meeting that Milliyet writers ‘wiped their behinds with dollars.’ Derya was very angry about this: he spoke of how Sirmen was one of those who drew the most money from the newspaper and spent a significant part of the year in Paris.

Finally, on October 20, it was announced that an agreement had been reached between AD and KY for the return of the newspaper to AD. When Hugh Pope in the Wall Street Journal wrote that part of the 310 million dollar sale price had not been returned, AD denied this; Pope then corrected the story. Doğan returned to the newspaper on October 21 with a grand welcome. Almost all employees had gathered at the door. I contented myself with watching the event from my office window. On the evening of October 23, AD gave a “hello again” dinner for the writers. I was in Antalya with the late Sami Kohen for an EU-Turkey journalists’ meeting; Sami Bey immediately returned to Istanbul, while I stayed.

A week after the announcement that Milliyet would be sold, I had published an article expressing my reaction to this. In the article titled “Milliyet is important,” which summarized my views on the function of media in democracies and the state of media in Turkey, I was saying:

“Freedom of the press and independent and respected media organizations and institutions that exercise this freedom are one of the ‘sine qua non’ conditions of democracy. Because: Citizens receive news about national and world events and the commentary that enables them to make sense of these from the media. It is natural that a democracy can only function well to the extent that citizens are informed, knowledgeable, and have the opportunity to see the truth behind events.

“The media’s ability to properly fulfill the democratic functions mentioned above depends on three main conditions: 1) The constitution and laws must guarantee freedom of the press. 2) The press business is not just any economic enterprise, any money-making pursuit. Media owners are responsible not only for ensuring that their organizations are financially healthy, but also for fulfilling the functions they assume in a democratic society. For journalists, acting in accordance with professional principles carries perhaps even greater importance than it does for other professional groups. The main task of professional organizations is to defend these principles. 3) The media must have institutions that are independent from the state, strong, competing with each other, and have traditions built on professional principles…

“It is clear as day that various practices in Turkish media are incompatible with a pluralist and competitive structure; that not all journalists in Turkey act in accordance with professional principles and ethics. However, despite all these limitations, we know that the media in Turkey plays an even greater role than parliament in monitoring whether political and economic power holders are acting in accordance with laws and ethics, and that the media is perhaps the most important force of democracy in Turkey. The media’s ability to fulfill its functions is the most important guarantee for the future of democracy in our country. The media’s ability to fulfill its democratic functions is possible with strong, reliable, respected media organizations and institutions. Milliyet newspaper, as old as our democracy, is undoubtedly one of the foremost of these organizations and institutions. To protect and develop these qualities of Milliyet is perhaps the duty of us, its employees, more than of anyone else.” (Milliyet, October 15, 1998)

I have thought that the above article of mine played a role in my employment at Milliyet being terminated in a rather ugly manner, in less than three years.

“The Türkbank Scandal”

What would come to be known as the “Türkbank scandal”—a series of events that exposed the “politics-business-media-mafia” relationships in Turkey—would eventually result in former Prime Minister Mesut Yılmaz and former State Minister Güneş Taner being tried before the Supreme Court (Yüce Divan, the Constitutional Court sitting as a high tribunal for trying ministers). The indictment would allege that the defendants “carried out all the arrangements to establish a media order under their control by committing fraud in the conduct and price formation of the Türkbank tender” and would seek a prison sentence of no less than 10 years.

When I arrived at the newspaper on the morning of December 19, 1998, I learned that Derya Sazak had resigned from his position as editor-in-chief and that Yalçın Doğan had been appointed in his place; Umur Talu would become the publication coordinator. I went to Yalçın and said, “If you want, let’s close ‘Intellectual Perspective.’” His response—“No, Intellectual Perspective is this newspaper’s pride”—both surprised and pleased me. Two days later, he gave a wonderful speech to the newspaper staff: “We will set the bar high; we will make Milliyet a quality newspaper committed to professional principles,” he said. My relationship with Yalçın had completely improved…

However, a few days later, one morning when I saw that Intellectual Perspective had been replaced by Süleyman Demirel’s draft constitutional amendment, the blood rushed to my head. I went to Yalçın in anger and asked what this meant. He said it was just a one-day intervention, but that he might occasionally want to use the page. A few days later, I also saw that the headline I had put on the page had been changed without my knowledge. It was clear that Yalçın wanted to remind me that he was the one running the newspaper; that I didn’t have a feudal fiefdom within the paper. I would either herd this camel or leave this land… Where could I go anyway? I chose the former.

## My “Brilliant” Year in Journalism: 1999

1999 was a year full of events both for Turkey and for me personally. The year began with Fatma and me going to the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus from January 19-22. We met with my old friend Ahmet Aker and his new wife Şule in Kyrenia. Ahmet was serving as Denktaş’s advisor at the time. Through an appointment he arranged, on January 21 Fatma and I were invited to lunch with President Rauf Denktaş and his wife. According to Ahmet, this was “a great honor” shown to me. It truly was; until that day, no important politician had ever invited me to a meal. At the lunch, where Ahmet and Şule were also present, Denktaş shared a Demirel anecdote on condition it wouldn’t be written. (I think there’s no harm in writing it now; neither of them is alive.) Demirel had once told him, “There are people working for the CIA even in our Foreign Ministry, even in the General Staff. So don’t believe anything unless you hear it from me…” This was an anecdote consistent with Denktaş’s staunch nationalist stance.

My interview with Denktaş was published on January 25-26 with the headline “TRNC President Rauf Denktaş ready for EU membership on condition of confederation.” In the interview, Denktaş said: “We are ready to negotiate EU membership on the condition that we enter as a confederation and that they accept us on equal terms with the Greek Cypriots. At the very least, they must acknowledge that the Greek Cypriots do not represent all of Cyprus… Turkey does not need to be an EU member for the TRNC to join the EU.”

My interview was also covered in the Wall Street Journal, but unfortunately opportunities continued to be missed in Cyprus. UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan’s unification plan for the island was rejected by the Greek Cypriot side in a referendum held in April 2004. The Greek Cypriot Administration, which rejected unification, was made an EU member on May 1, 2004, representing the entire island no less; Greece’s threat to veto EU enlargement if Cyprus was not included paved the way for the island’s permanent division.

## At the Peak of My Reporting Career

At the suggestion of German Ambassador Joachim Vergau, who served in Ankara from 1995 to 2000, I went to Germany as an invited guest in the first week of February 1999. The necessary appointments had been arranged for me to conduct various interviews. The most important of these was with Foreign Minister Joschka Fischer. In the interview published in Milliyet with the headline “For us, Turkey is a candidate,” Fischer said: “Turkey is a very important partner for Europe. From our perspective, it is a candidate for EU membership. However, we have problems. We want to develop relations, and a positive approach from Turkey would make us very happy.”

The interview with Fischer was one of my most successful works in the context of “news journalism.” Indeed, Yağmur Atsız, who was living in Germany at the time, would write in his column in Milliyet: “Şahin Alpay’s interview with German Foreign Minister Joschka Fischer in Milliyet dated February 3, 1999 unfortunately did not receive the attention it deserved from the public. Yet this was a text carrying important messages beyond any ordinary exclusive interview, one that needed to be carefully analyzed… Germany’s first ‘Green’ Foreign Minister Fischer’s interview should be evaluated in connection with the following sentence he said during a speech in parliament shortly before: Germany has acted wrongly in EU-Turkey relations!” (Milliyet, February 10, 1999)

Fischer’s words were truly important; they signaled the process that would begin at the end of that year with Turkey being declared an EU candidate at the EU’s Helsinki summit in December 1999. Meeting him had been a happy occasion for me. I would write the following about Fischer, who belonged to the same generation as me (the ’68 generation):

“One of the foreign ministry officials I spoke with in Bonn interpreted the results of the 1998 elections as ‘Germany catching up with the 1989 revolution.’ One-third of the federal parliament had been renewed; a new and young generation of politicians had taken over the country’s governance. National interests hadn’t changed, but new ideas about how to serve them had come into play. As the official was explaining these things (as you might guess), I couldn’t help thinking about how desperately we needed such changes as Turkey: A young generation of politicians with new ideas that would enable us to adapt to the post-Cold War world; that would better serve our unchanging national interests. Unfortunately, it seems we will have to wait quite a while longer for these innovations to arrive.” (Milliyet, February 4, 1999)

On February 10, German Ambassador Vergau called; he said Fischer was very pleased with the interview I had conducted. Fischer had also agreed with my view that “conditions are always imposed on Turkey, but there is never any encouragement.” I was pleased.

When I returned from Germany, I learned that Nilüfer had left Milliyet and would start making programs at NTV. I was naturally upset; she was a colleague I had worked with at Sabah and then at Milliyet, above all an old friend. I immediately called her. “I’m sorry, I couldn’t wait for you. The new management was treating me very badly, I couldn’t take it anymore…” she said. She was right too. My morale was shattered. How would I continue?.. I thought about giving up my page. My friends I consulted—Ayşe Buğra, Şirin Tekeli, Güven Nil, Meral Tamer—said “don’t you dare”… Taha Akyol insisted, “Don’t close the page; that’s where your power comes from. You’re the only writer in the press who has not just a column but a whole page. Leaving would also be a blow to Yalçın Doğan…” I decided to continue. But I complained to Yalçın Doğan about my low salary. He confirmed that I was one of the lowest-paid writers (probably the lowest-paid writer); he promised to add a bonus. He said I had done good work in Germany, but added that he couldn’t see any “local colour” (?!) in my writings.

“Abdullah Öcalan Is in Turkey”

The first major event of 1999 was the capture of PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan in Kenya with US assistance and his extradition to Turkey. Prime Minister Bülent Ecevit announced this on February 16 with his statement “Abdullah Öcalan is in Turkey.” Öcalan, who was sentenced to death on June 29, 1999 for “founding and leading an armed terrorist organization,” had his sentence commuted to aggravated life imprisonment in accordance with EU harmonization laws. He has been imprisoned in İmralı Prison since that day. In my article titled “Historic Opportunity” that I wrote upon Öcalan’s capture, summarizing my views on the PKK and the Kurdish issue, I said the following:

“The capture and neutralization of Öcalan undoubtedly dealt the heaviest blow to the gang that sought to establish a so-called Marxist dictatorship over part of Turkey’s territory. However, Turkey should also see this success as an opportunity for resolving the issue that this armed gang—which has spared no effort for years to incite fraternal strife in the country—has exploited and manipulated: namely the Kurdish issue, and for establishing democracy with all its rules and institutions. Otherwise, our country cannot escape the damage caused by Kurdish racist nationalism that obstructs progress toward development and democratization, and the Turkish racist nationalism it has provoked. Great progress has been made in resolving the PKK problem. Now it’s time to solve the Kurdish issue. Let us determine the content of the ‘political solution’ ourselves. Without being subjected to the increasing pressure from Western allies in this area, as a country ‘determined to take its rightful place in European integration,’ let us take the steps we should have taken long ago.

“President (at that time Prime Minister) Süleyman Demirel declared 8 years ago, in 1991, that we recognized Kurdish identity. It’s time to act on this: Let us grant our citizens of Kurdish origin who so wish the right to freely use their language and culture. If they have certain demands different from the rest of society, let us open opportunities for them to freely express these and to engage in political struggle for them on legal, peaceful, democratic grounds. At the same time, let us accelerate the economic incentives necessary for the development of the Southeast.

If we are to progress on the path of modernization, civilization, and democratization, if we are to base our national unity on voluntary foundations, if we are to become a truly free country rather than partially free, taking these steps is inevitable. The earlier we take them, the more we gain. This truth doesn’t change.” (Milliyet, February 18, 1999)

## At the European Court of Human Rights

I went to Ankara on February 22 after being invited to Nazlı Ilıcak’s program “The Essence of the Matter” on a television channel. Among the participants were Abdullah Gül and Cemil Çiçek, heavyweights of the Virtue Party. Both showered my writings with compliments. Their saying “Continue to criticize us” was noteworthy; it seemed like a harbinger of a split in the FP.

1999 would also be a year when I “saw the stork in flight” [a Turkish idiom: seeing the stork on the wing augurs a year full of travel]. I spent the first week of March in Strasbourg, France. My friend Rıza Türmen, whose path had crossed mine at various periods of my life, had been elected as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in 1998 and would serve in this position for ten years. Taking advantage of this, I convinced Yalçın Doğan that a visit to Strasbourg would be beneficial. Turkey had accepted its citizens’ right to individual application to the ECHR in 1987 and compulsory jurisdiction in 1990. (Of course, it never crossed my mind that about 20 years later, I would be one of the Turkish citizens exercising the right of individual application in a case where I was tried on charges of being a member of “FETÖ, the Fethullahist Terrorist Organization,” and would be the subject of an ECHR ruling ordering the termination of my detention on the grounds that my rights had been violated.)

The best work I did in Strasbourg was an interview with the ECHR’s new Swiss president Luzius Wildhaber. In the interview published with the headline “Don’t leave matters to Strasbourg,” Wildhaber said: “If Turkish courts apply the Convention [the European Convention on Human Rights] on their own initiative, there would be no need for these cases to come to Strasbourg. It would also prevent the impression that the Court in Strasbourg is interfering in Turkey’s affairs…” (March 9, 1999)

The Constitutional Court would express the legal changes that occurred after this interview was published on its website in 2012 as follows: “The Republic of Turkey became a party to the European Convention on Human Rights in 1954; it accepted the right of individual application to the European Court of Human Rights in 1987 and compulsory jurisdiction in 1990. With the constitutional amendment made in 2004, international conventions on fundamental rights and freedoms to which Turkey is a party, particularly the European Convention on Human Rights, were given a value above laws. The final link in the amendments referring to ‘universal standards’ regarding fundamental rights was the opening of the individual application path to the Constitutional Court with the constitutional amendment made in 2010. With the implementation of individual application, constitutional judicial review against violations of rights caused by persons and institutions exercising public power was initiated as of September 23, 2012. Accordingly, as of September 23, 2012, everyone can apply to the Constitutional Court claiming that any of the fundamental rights and freedoms guaranteed in our Constitution and within the scope of the European Convention on Human Rights has been violated by public power.”

Unfortunately, despite all the legal changes made, today, in 2022, the Turkish government still does not implement the ECHR rulings regarding Osman Kavala and Selahattin Demirtaş that call for their “immediate and unconditional release.”

## A Night in Jerusalem

At the beginning of March 1999, I received a surprise invitation from Israel’s Consulate General in Istanbul to visit Israel. I had seen Israel from the outside in the summer of 1971, looking from the camp of the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine in the village of Jaba near Syria’s occupied city of Quneitra. In those years, I viewed Israel as an occupying state that should be thrown into the sea. Much time had passed, and my view of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict had changed. It had become more or less understood that throwing Israel into the sea was neither possible nor right. The 1993-1995 Oslo peace accords had resulted in Israel’s recognition of the Palestine Liberation Organization; hope for a two-state solution had emerged. Turkey-Israel relations were experiencing a honeymoon. (Unfortunately, in 2022, as I write these lines, the two-state solution has never been so far away.)

In that environment, I saw no moral problem in going to Israel with a group that included Culture Minister İstemihan Talay (my colleague on the SBF Student Association Board that I chaired in the 1966-67 academic year) and journalist colleagues Doğan Hızlan and Murat Bardakçı among others, and spending two nights and three days there. Our hosts showed us around Jerusalem, Tel Aviv, the Dead Sea shore, and other places. Our Ambassador at the time, Ahmet Üzümcü, also hosted us for a dinner at the embassy in Tel Aviv. In the article I sent to the newspaper from Jerusalem, I wrote the following:

“The night of my first and only day in the holy city of Jerusalem. We’re exhausted from rushing from visit to visit. I’m hoping to at least get to bed by midnight before waking at 4 a.m. to start the return journey. Just as I’m about to go up to my room, I notice: the sounds of a very cheerful celebration are rising from the hotel’s ballroom floor. When I look down from the terrace and see the young girls in their long black skirts and white blouses and the young men with their hair in ringlets, I begin to understand…

“Then I run into Luiz Salgırtay, the charming Istanbul director of the Israeli airline El Al, one of our hosts. ‘Yes, this is a Hasidic celebration,’ she says, ‘Come, let’s go take a look. They’ll probably let us in…’ When we enter somewhat hesitantly, I’m faced with an incredible scene: The hall is divided in the middle by a wooden partition about 2 meters high; on this side of the partition the girls, on the other side the young men, are dancing the hora in ecstasy.

“I go to bed with the sweet happiness of having seen something the other journalists in the group didn’t see. In the morning I learn that the devoutly religious Hasidic young men took our friends Culture Minister İstemihan Talay and Doğan Hızlan by the arms right into the celebration area and danced the hora together. Murat Bardakçı also recorded this historic moment with his video camera…”

I also added this to the article: “Foreign Minister Ariel Sharon received Talay and those accompanying him… We had the opportunity to ask Sharon a few questions. On questions about the PKK, Sharon said, in summary: ‘As a country that has suffered greatly from terrorism, we view terrorism as a great danger and are determined to fight all forms of it. It is well known that we have traditionally good relations with the Kurds in Iraq, especially the Barzanis, but we have no relationship with the PKK…’

“Israeli officials, following their statements that they had no role in the capture of PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan, also categorically denied reports that they had indirect relations with the PKK. However, to date, no Israeli official has characterized the PKK as a terrorist organization. Apparently, Turkey is not insisting on this either.” (Milliyet, March 18, 1999)

## New China

The summer of 1999 also witnessed a visit that was meaningful for my autobiography. One day in early June, editor-in-chief Yalçın Doğan called. Our mutual friend Ambassador Daryal Batıbay (my friend from both Robert College and the Political Science Faculty) had called saying that the Chinese News Agency (Xinhua) wanted to invite a journalist from Turkey to China. Naturally, I—as a former Maoist—was the first to come to Yalçın’s mind… When he asked me “Would you like to go to China?”, I nearly jumped to the ceiling with joy.

I immediately contacted Daryal and our ambassador to Mongolia, Nuri Yıldırım (also my friend from both Robert College and the Political Science Faculty). Fatma and I agreed to make this trip together. That’s how the journey to China and then Mongolia began that month. Our trip covered Beijing, Shanghai, and Xi’an in China, then we flew to Ulaanbaatar. From June 8 to 22, 1999, I never missed my column. The four-day series titled “New China” that I wrote upon returning home was also published over four days from June 29 to July 2.

What the “Maoist” Şahin Alpay of the late 1960s and early 1970s wrote from and about China in 1999 could naturally be of interest to my friends and readers who knew me. In this context, I wrote the following:

“My first day in Beijing was a special day in terms of my life story. About 30 years ago, for 2-3 years I had fallen under the illusion that Mao Zedong’s interpretation of socialism could be a remedy for Turkey’s troubles. It was impossible not to reflect on the changes that I and of course China had undergone in the intervening time. I remembered those years, frankly, with pain. How I could have been swept up in such impossible ideas—even though I wasn’t alone, even though I had conformed to the ‘intellectual climate’ of the day—was a painful question. My awakening from the fantasy, or rather the nightmare, had been relatively quick. My sorrow for those who couldn’t wake up for a long time never subsided. My only consolation for myself and my generation is that perhaps without living through this experience, it would not have been possible to understand the value of freedom to our very bones. From this, I can also draw consolation for Turkey’s present: Looking at our experiences, we have still come a long way as a society. Without painful experiences, the value of freedom and democracy cannot be appreciated. Thirty years ago, no one around me believed in democracy. Today, that is the fundamental belief.”

About China I said: “China too has left the Mao Zedong era far behind. With the reforms initiated in 1978 by the ‘Second Man’ Deng Xiaoping, who fell from power and returned several times, China is now a completely different country. The symbolic expression of this is that nothing remains of Mao except his portrait hanging in Tiananmen Square. It is very striking that the single party he founded, which still governs the country, has reached the judgment that the ‘worshipped man’ of about 20 years ago ‘did 40 percent right and 60 percent wrong.’ Beijing, where 74 five-star hotels have risen, clearly shows in every way that China has made considerable progress in establishing a competitive market economy—or in their own terms, ‘socialism with Chinese characteristics’—under Communist Party rule.

“With the reforms initiated by Deng, in the last 20 years incomes in rural China have increased 3-fold and in cities 5-fold. China’s GNP increased 20-fold, from 44 billion dollars to 904 billion dollars. The average growth rate for the period was 10 percent! (The world average was 3.3%). Foreign trade volume jumped 15-fold from 20 billion dollars to 325 billion dollars. China rose from 27th to 10th place in world trade. Today, China is the world’s 2nd largest economy after the US based on purchasing power parity calculations…” (Milliyet, June 8, 1999)

## Tonyukuk and Bayınmunk

Our visit to Mongolia, which came about because my friend Nuri Yıldırım, from both Robert College and the Political Science Faculty, was our ambassador there, was also extremely interesting. In the column I sent to the newspaper from Ulaanbaatar, I wrote: “Mongolia, which until just ten years ago was one of the most closed countries in the world, is now not only a Central Asian country considered fully ‘free’ (according to the New York-based organization Freedom House), but is also rapidly opening up to the world… Nambaryn Enkhbayar, the leader of the Revolutionary People’s Party (former communists), who is very likely to assume the prime ministership after the next elections, said they were pleased with the cultural enrichment brought by opening up, but that the missionary activities of Christian sects were an exception to this…

“I want to immediately share a very interesting memory of Enkhbayar’s: As the general secretary of the Mongolian Writers’ Union at the time, he had hosted the late Aziz Nesin who visited Ulaanbaatar in 1980, and personally took him to the Tonyukuk inscriptions. The master became very emotional when he reached the inscriptions left by our Göktürk ancestors, and he hugged them and wept. I couldn’t help saying, ‘The late Aziz Bey was never known as a Turkish ethnic nationalist!’

“We too were fortunate to see the Tonyukuk inscriptions. What excited me more than the inscriptions was the boundless Mongolian steppes on which they stood, lush green in June. ‘Our ancestors must have gained the horizon (vision) that took them to the gates of Vienna from these steppes,’ I thought. The Mongolian government has surrounded the inscriptions—erected between 720 and 725 in the name of Tonyukuk, who was the vizier and father-in-law of the Göktürk Khagan Bilge Kagan, and which are among the first written examples of Turkish—with a 1-meter-high iron fence to protect them. The Turkish government has also built a dig house (newly completed construction, still empty inside) to be used in future archaeological work. The Tonyukuk inscriptions also have a guard paid for by the Turkish government. His name is Bayınmunk. Bayınmunk is a very likeable 23-year-old Mongolian youth living in his ger (Mongolian tent) set up in the middle of the steppe with his motorcycle, bicycle, and his dog Harszık.” (Milliyet, June 12, 1999)

“Gülen’s Cassettes”

At the beginning of the “February 28 process” that led to Erbakan’s resignation and the dissolution of the Refahyol government, the Ankara Police Directorate had prepared a report on Fethullah Gülen and his community. According to the report, Gülen was an organization leader and the organization’s members were infiltrating police units. Three days after this report reached the General Directorate of Security, on March 21, 1999, Gülen flew to the United States citing health reasons and began residing in Pennsylvania. When I returned from the China-Mongolia trip, I learned that during the days I was out of the country, some video cassettes had been broadcast on television channels leading to accusations that Gülen was “inciting his followers to infiltrate the state in order to overthrow the secular order and establish a sharia state.” Thereupon, I made the following comment in my article titled “Gülen’s Cassettes”:

“I have no way of knowing whether the claims that Fethullah Gülen established relations with the Taliban ‘to seize the state and establish a sharia state,’ that he worked in the service of both the KGB and the CIA, that he has 3,000 suicide commandos and 2,000 teachers with US diplomatic passports, are true or not. However, I imagine my readers are curious about how I, as a writer who has expressed positive views about him, interpret Gülen’s ‘cassettes.’

“Gülen came before the public in 1995 with a call for tolerance and dialogue. As someone who thought that various polarizations were hindering Turkey’s efforts to become a strong market democracy, I found what he said very noteworthy: ‘There will be no return from democracy. Bigotry, intolerance must be abandoned. Turks have developed a tolerant, non-bigoted understanding of Islam. Religion cannot be made a subject of politics. Unfortunately, we are experiencing the harms of this in Turkey. The broadest freedom of worship for Muslims exists in Turkey because there is democracy. Faith is not in the headscarf but in the heart. Belief must be based on reason, on science. We cannot neglect reason, rationalism, because it is the foundation of science…’ These were extraordinarily positive views for Turkey, especially coming from a religious leader of a community. While some politicians, even official voices, made statements inciting hatred and animosity against citizens belonging to minority religions, Gülen’s words and actions promoting brotherhood among religions were highly commendable.

“At the invitation of the Journalists and Writers Foundation, in the autumn of 1996 I toured the community’s schools in Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan along with other colleagues. The schools operated under the support and supervision of the governments in these countries (which were even more strictly secular than Turkey’s). They were doing important work in bringing Turkish, and even world culture to these places. Their activities were not outside the knowledge and supervision of the Turkish state. The hosts were pleased with the schools. (I heard the same satisfaction from Mongolian state officials two weeks ago.) I came to the conclusion that through the schools, media organizations, companies, etc. he had established, Gülen was transforming his religious tradition-based ‘community’ into ‘society’; that is, into modern-based relationships. I listened to Gülen himself twice along with other colleagues; I did not sense any falseness in what he said. I attributed the community’s eagerness to involve others in their activities and the meaningless awards they distributed to a concern for ‘protection’ in a country where religious orders and communities are legally banned.

“As for the cassettes: There is no doubt that they will spread the conviction that Gülen acted hypocritically, that he practiced ‘taqiyya’; that they will shake the value of his words. But I don’t think they are enough to prove that he was preparing an uprising to establish a religious state. Why were they held back and released now? Why were they delivered to the media rather than to the authorities authorized to initiate prosecution? Is the ‘reactionary threat’ being exploited? These are not questions I can answer… The aspect of the campaign against Gülen that targets almost the entire political class, including the President who received an award from him and the Prime Minister and former Prime Minister who accorded him respect, is extremely worrying for civilian governance.” (June 24, 1999)

After the videos were broadcast, in August 2000 the Ankara State Security Court Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office filed a case against Gülen claiming he planned to “use the youth whose brains he washed in his schools and the society he would form with them to end the Republic of Turkey, which is a secular, democratic, and social state of law, and to establish in its place an Islamic state ruled by sharia law.” Gülen defended himself against the charges by saying: “A member of a nation does not infiltrate the institutions that exist for his nation; it is his right to enter there; he enters the civil administration, enters the judiciary, enters intelligence, enters foreign affairs…” In March 2007, the Ankara 11th Heavy Penal Court concluded that no crime had been committed in light of the Anti-Terror Law and acquitted Gülen; the General Assembly of the Court of Cassation unanimously upheld the decision in June 2008.

## Earthquake Grandpa

The 7.5 Richter scale earthquake centered in Kocaeli/Gölcük that occurred around 3 a.m. on the morning of August 17, 1999 shook the country. According to official data, around 17,500 citizens lost their lives and nearly 24,000 were injured; according to unofficial data, the number of dead reached 50,000 and the number of injured 100,000. The fact that the earthquake occurred in one of the important industrial regions also dealt a major blow to the country’s economy.

Following the tragedy, I toured the Kocaeli/Gölcük region that was hit hardest by the earthquake. What surprised me most was that buildings that remained standing solid were right next to buildings that had been reduced to rubble. What I saw was like concrete proof of the saying that has now become a proverb: “It’s not the earthquake that kills, it’s the building”… I conducted two interviews about the earthquake. The first was with the late Prof. Dr. Ahmet Mete Işıkara (1941-2013), director of the Boğaziçi University Kandilli Observatory and Earthquake Research Institute, who would frequently appear in the media after that date and earn the nickname “Earthquake Grandpa.” The words of Işıkara that I made into a headline were: “The big earthquake has passed; a new one may come after many years.”

Işıkara gave the following answer to my question “Could there be another big earthquake soon?”: “A very long process is needed for another earthquake of this intensity, that is, magnitude 7.4, to occur. No, the big earthquake happened, it’s done… Such a 7.4 magnitude earthquake doesn’t just happen. It prepares itself. And it takes a very long time to be ready.” (Milliyet, August 19, 1999) Considering that the expected big earthquake in Istanbul was still being awaited in 2021, Işıkara was not wrong.

I conducted the second interview with ITU’s world-renowned geologist, member of the European Academy, Prof. Dr. Celal Şengör. In the interview published with the headline “You can’t escape an earthquake, but you can take precautions,” Şengör said that the next earthquake could occur when the fault line south of the Istanbul islands ruptures, that it could be 6-plus on the Richter scale, and that it should be expected “within 10-12 years maximum.” According to Şengör, his professor from ITU, Prof. Dr. İhsan Ketin, had submitted a report to the authorities advising against building the TÜPRAŞ refinery in İzmit, but it had been ignored. When I asked “Why?”, Şengör’s answer was: “Our esteemed Speaker of Parliament reflects the same mentality when he says ‘Kurdish is a dialect.’ The mentality of ‘Science is outside us, we live differently.’” (Milliyet, August 20, 1999)

The parliament speaker Şengör was referring to was Yıldırım Akbulut. Ten days earlier, Akbulut had announced to journalists that “henceforth, some deputies will not be allowed to write Kurdish in the foreign language section of the parliament album,” saying: “We are learning the languages that deputies know in order to use them in inter-state relations. Kurdish is not a language, it’s a dialect. Let this no longer be dragged into different dimensions…” (Newspapers, August 10, 1999)

The interview occasioned by a very sad event led to my meeting Şengör and becoming friends with him for a while. We agreed that Karl Popper was a great philosopher of science. (I think for this reason Şengör even told me that I was “Turkey’s greatest social scientist.”) However, I could not understand how Şengör could reconcile Popper’s political philosophy with the militarist views he himself advocated (the kind that holds ‘soldiers know best’). Nevertheless, we could still have enjoyable discussions. In this context, I would like to share my article summarizing my conclusions about the relationship between religion and science, inspired by my discussions with Şengör:

“Professor Celal Şengör, in Greenland where he went last August to study the oldest known section of the earth’s crust, found himself without food and fuel for about a week. A storm had blocked the supply routes. He became anxious that he might not see his beloved wife and son again. In this mental state, he discovered that in addition to religion’s ‘explanatory’ and ‘regulatory’ functions, it also has a ‘psychological’ function: ‘Religious belief is a support against humanity’s sense of loneliness,’ he thought.

“When he told me these things, I reminded Şengör of religion’s ‘sociological’ function, the role of religious teachings in shaping people’s values and behaviors. He asked this question: Without falling into relativism on one hand (not in the physics sense, but in the philosophical sense—that is, without denying that there is objective truth and rules binding for everyone), and without falling into scientism on the other hand (that is, the fallacy that science is a body of eternally proven, infallible truths and is omnipotent), how can religion and science be compatible?”

In response, I said: “The answer to this difficult question that can fit in this short article might be this: Religious explanations that contradict the findings of science are invalid. For example, the theory of evolution does not invalidate the doctrine of creation; but a religious teaching that insists humans were created in their present maturity cannot be credible. The claims of religious teachings such as ‘Jesus Christ is the son of God’ or ‘Israel was promised to the Jews by God’ and similar ones are of course incompatible with reason. Religious law loses its validity to the extent that it contradicts human rights and freedoms, which are the common heritage of humanity. Religious obligations that prescribe treating women as ‘second-class humans’ or recommend ‘killing non-believers’ are unacceptable. A religious teaching that insists on these will lose its credibility.

“Science, which appeals to reason, can never (except perhaps for a very small minority) eliminate humanity’s sense of loneliness, uncertainty, and meaninglessness in the universe, the need to ‘take refuge in God.’ Only religious teachings that appeal to emotions can respond to this psychological need of humans. Science can never answer the question of whether there is a creator. The massacres caused by doctrines like ‘scientific’ socialism, which set out to create paradise on earth supposedly ‘using science,’ or ‘national’ socialism, which aimed to create a superior race, have surpassed the murders committed, for example, by the Inquisition in the name of protecting religion (actually the church). The sociological functions of religion cannot be ignored. The precepts about what is a good deed and what is a sin have extremely important effects—preventing crime, providing social solidarity and integration, hindering or encouraging socio-economic development, and others.” (Milliyet, December 28, 2000)

Interestingly, Şengör, with whom we had interesting discussions and socialized as families, would completely cut off relations with me after I was arrested and thrown into Silivri prison in the days following the July 15 coup attempt (just like another professor friend of mine, Şükrü Hanioğlu).

“The Earthquake Was No Coincidence”

The earthquake of August 17, 1999, which had the most devastating consequences in our recent history, had also given rise to religiously-flavored interpretations. Regarding these interpretations, I wrote the following:

“Recently a guest from England came to visit Milliyet. While discussing what was happening in Turkey, I conveyed one of the most heated debate topics of recent days.

One of the headscarved students who was not admitted to university had unfurled a banner saying ‘7.4 wasn’t enough?!’; then a religious community leader had stepped forward and said ‘The earthquake was no coincidence, it was God’s punishment for those who made the February 28 decisions’; similar interpretations were frequently made in the Islamist press. My professor friend also told me this: About ten years ago, lightning struck the cathedral in York, England, starting a fire. Thereupon some Christian fundamentalists claimed that God had sent the lightning as punishment for the York bishop, known for his liberal views…

“Yes, attributing natural events to supernatural forces, to God, is not peculiar to Turkey and some Muslims, but is a universally observed tendency. Perhaps what is peculiar to us about this tendency—which grants no autonomy (will) to nature or humanity, which are God’s creations; which bypasses the question of why humans were created with reason and will; and which reflects an extremely primitive understanding of religion—is the exploitation of religious beliefs for political purposes. My readers know that I am not in favor of immediately seizing and imprisoning those who exploit religious beliefs for political purposes, and that I see benefit in all views being freely expressed except calls to violence and racism. I think the best attitude to adopt toward these people is to expose their nonsense and drivel.

“I don’t find the exploitation of religion in Islamist newspapers surprising, but that Mehmet Kutlular—a community leader who had opposed Islamists’ exploitation of religion—was engaging in religious exploitation himself truly astonished me. The response of another Nurcu community leader, Fethullah Gülen, to Kutlular was also interesting from a theological standpoint: ‘If a religious reason is to be sought for such disasters, it should be considered that it may be related to general errors, and everyone should first examine themselves…’ Apparently Gülen also shared the view that ‘the earthquake was a divine warning,’ but was saying that ‘we are all targets of the warning.’

“All of this surprised me, because I thought Said-i Nursi argued that ‘Islamic faith can only be strengthened through interpretations compatible with political freedom and modern science; that religion and science occupy separate domains.’ Of course, I (as an outsider) may be mistaken about Said-i Nursi’s message. But another serious (and more grave) possibility is that both Kutlular and Gülen are badly mistaken in their understanding of Said-i Nursi’s message. Fortunately, the sensible majority of society knows how to separate the domains of religion and science.” (Milliyet, October 19, 1999)

I had met Mehmet Kutlular (1938-2021) mentioned in the article. The followers of Said Nursi, known as the “Nur community,” were divided into ten branches; one of the main ones was the community gathered around the Yeni Asya newspaper and known as the Yeni Asya group. Kutlular, the owner and editor-in-chief of Yeni Asya, while making detailed statements that the earthquake was a “divine warning,” was saying that this warning “could be related to the oppression during the February 28 process,” and that it could not be a coincidence that the earthquake’s epicenter was the Gölcük Naval Base where the February 28 plans were made.

The same Kutlular, impressed by my articles defending freedom of belief, had called me and invited me to his newspaper. During our meeting, Kutlular said they were greatly disappointed by Şerif Mardin’s book titled The Bediüzzaman Said Nursi Phenomenon (İletişim Publishers, 1989). He added that they would be very pleased if I wrote a book on Nursi and his thought; that they were ready to provide any sources I might need on this subject. Frankly, the topic was quite appealing to me in terms of efforts to understand religion in Turkey; however, I was managing the opinion page at Milliyet six days a week and writing a column three days a week; unfortunately I didn’t have the time to do this work properly.

“CNN Türk Desk”

In September 1999, it was announced that the Doğan media group had reached an agreement with CNN, that a news channel called CNN-Türk was being established, and that Taha Akyol would manage the channel. Some time later, Akyol called me and said they wanted me to do a talk show on the new channel. Of course, I received this with pleasure but also with some hesitation, as I had no screen experience until then. According to the concrete proposal, I would host “CNN Türk Desk,” to be broadcast in the 9-10 PM slot, every Tuesday evening with a guest. Mehmet Ali Birand, who took on the position of programs director, said he was surprised when he learned I would be among the presenters, that I was “a person whose opinion should be sought, not one who conducts interviews.” But then, perhaps to mollify me, I remember him coming during the test recordings and calling out “A local Larry King is being born!”

Birand was advising me to invite guests from almost every field, from politics and economics to sports, cinema, and entertainment, on the program I would do. Unfortunately, the right to select guests was left to me, and by choosing them only from the worlds of politics and academia, I perhaps caused the program to fall out of favor shortly after. CNN-Türk began broadcasting on October 11, 1999; the first program I did was also broadcast on October 12. My first guest was our famous novelist Orhan Pamuk. The announcement that appeared in Milliyet that day said: “The famous writer, who until now has been in the spotlight with his novels and is a favorite of literary circles, will for the first time discuss and comment on politics in this program.” That evening Pamuk was at least as excited as I was. Indeed, I remember him trying to calm down in the makeup room by drinking whiskey from a small bottle he took out of his pocket.

My program on CNN Türk Desk was short-lived. The interviews I conducted began to be broadcast once a week at noon under the name “Intellectual Perspective” starting from January 2000. Among those I hosted in this program, which lasted about a year and a half, were: Academics Sami Selçuk, Ayşe Buğra, Ergun Özbudun, Ersin Kalaycıoğlu, Nevra Necipoğlu, Ali Yaşar Sarıbay, Celal Şengör, Kemal Kirişçi, Fahrettin Yağcı, Burhan Şenatalar, Faruk Birtek, Çağlar Keyder, İzzettin Doğan, Seyfettin Gürsel, İlter Turan, Emin Yaşar Demirci; novelist Nedim Gürsel; writers Ali Bulaç and Mustafa Çalık; BJK President Serdar Bilgili; businessman İshak Alaton; journalist Hasan Cemal; Istanbul Bar Association President Yücel Sayman; politicians Sami Uslu, Sema Pişkinsüt, Mehmet Ali Talat, Bülent Arınç.

The program, whose viewership remained limited outside academic circles, was ended in April 2002. A bad memory related to my CNN Türk days was this: In some programs, I had to strain to keep myself from yawning, to keep my eyes from closing. Meanwhile, Fatma was also becoming alarmed noticing that I frequently stopped breathing while sleeping at night. When I went to my high school classmate and friend Sedat Tavşanoğlu, who was then a cardiology professor at Cerrahpaşa Medical Faculty, with complaints of high blood pressure, he suspected I might be suffering from sleep apnea. I spent two nights in Cerrahpaşa’s sleep laboratory; the severity of my apnea (my breath-skipping affliction) was measured with the primitive equipment of those days. As a result, I started using a device called CPAP that pumps air into my nose, and I will use it until I die. If I hadn’t been diagnosed and started CPAP, I might have long since died like many others who lack the necessary precaution. CPAP became a device that extended the lives of many people I know as well.

## Helsinki in Thessaloniki

During the days of the Helsinki Summit (December 10-11, 1999), where Turkey’s candidacy for the European Union (EU) was declared, I was in Thessaloniki. Haluk Şahin, one of my senior friends, had arranged for me to be invited to the Balkan Journalists Conference to be held in Thessaloniki, of which he was one of the organizers. It was my first opportunity to visit Greece. Thessaloniki, where my maternal grandfather Halit Remzi Bey, originally from Skopje, had lived for many years, was only 80 km from Serres, where my paternal ancestors originated. On this short visit, touring Thessaloniki’s “Turkish quarter” and listening to Rebetika songs of Izmir origin in the tavernas at night made me very happy. The main reason for my happiness in Thessaloniki, however, was the news that broke that day of Turkey being declared an EU candidate. For years, I had ardently advocated Turkey’s EU membership, believing it would help purify the pluralist democratic regime of its deficiencies and flaws and “anchor it firmly.” In my commentary on the Helsinki decisions that I wrote upon returning to Istanbul, I said:

“During the Helsinki days, I was in Thessaloniki for a conference. Along with the announcement of the decisions, the first news from the Greek agencies was government spokesman Dimitris Reppas’s statement: ‘We got three out of three!’ Reppas was saying that all three of Greece’s conditions had been adopted when Turkey’s candidacy was accepted. The point that the Greek colleagues I spoke with emphasized, however, was that Athens had opened the EU path for Turkey by not using its veto right.

“We reached a consensus on this point: A unity of will had emerged between the two countries for resolving disputes within the EU framework. The Helsinki decisions had been given a form that (so to speak) both sides could ‘sell’ to their publics. Reppas’s ‘three out of three’ could be read very differently. Namely: 1) The solution of the Cyprus problem would not be a precondition for the Greek Cypriot Administration’s EU membership, but the EU Council would decide whether the GCA could become an EU member, taking into account ‘all relevant factors.’

“2) If all candidates cannot resolve their disputes through peaceful means, they are expected to take them to the International Court of Justice ‘within a reasonable time.’ The EU Council will review unresolved issues by the end of 2004. However, there is no time constraint for going to the Court. (How can this be made a condition for Turkey when France does not accept the Court’s jurisdiction?) On the other hand, didn’t Turkey just confirm last week that it could go to the Court if necessary? Greece says it can only discuss the continental shelf issue. Yet the Helsinki decisions speak of ‘problems.’

“3) The letter from Finnish President Lipponen, holder of the term presidency, confirms that no condition other than fulfilling the Copenhagen political criteria has been imposed on Turkey for starting membership negotiations. Since Turkey has already accepted this, the condition that Athens had inserted into the Helsinki decisions regarding progress in democracy and human rights has almost no meaning.

“The Greek opposition’s reaction to the Helsinki decisions indicates that it is even possible to read Reppas’s ‘three out of three’ as ‘zero out of three’: According to New Democracy Party leader Kostas Karamanlis, the Simitis government’s stance was ‘A very dangerous departure from traditional foreign policy…’ According to the conservative newspaper Eleftheros Typos: ‘The Simitis government shared the responsibility of issuing Turkey an EU ticket. Turkey’s demands from Greece became official; it erased its aggressive and expansionist past from the records.’ According to Greek Communist Party leader Aleka Papariga: ‘Greece made new concessions from its sovereign rights…’

“However, the Greek people in general (just like the Turkish people) are pleased with the Helsinki decisions. Perhaps the most direct expression of this is that the Athens stock exchange index recorded a 2.4 percent increase following the announcement of the decisions. (The increase in the ISE index was historic: 14.2 percent!) Commentators agree that Simitis has increased his chances of winning the elections expected to be held on March 26. In short, those who are not pleased with Helsinki are a minority who, by virtue of their ideologies, positions, and interests, favor Turkey remaining outside the EU and Turkish-Greek disputes continuing forever.” (Milliyet, December 14, 1999)

Unfortunately, the Helsinki Summit could not open the EU path for Turkey; more than twenty years later, Turkey’s EU membership today remains nothing but a dream.

## “Turkish Occupation” in Athens

I also participated in and gave a speech at the Turkish-Greek media conference held in Athens on February 5-6, 2000, at the initiative of the Press Council of which I was a member, or officially the “1st Mass Communication Conference.” Regarding this speech, I wrote the following in my column in the newspaper:

“In the words of the Kathimerini newspaper, last week the Greek capital witnessed giant steps toward the desired Greece in the Greeks’ three greatest obsessions: politics, relations with Turkey, and Athens traffic. The Athens metro went into service. The Turkish foreign minister officially visited Athens for the first time in 40 years. Prime Minister Simitis announced early elections on April 9. Another important event of the week was the Turkish-Greek Media Conference held on February 5-6. On this occasion, the arrival of about 40 Turkish journalists and media executives in Athens was announced by the weekly English newspaper The Hellenic Star (humorously) with the headline ‘Turkish occupation.’

“Prime Minister Simitis’s statement at the reception held for Turkish journalists at his residence on February 4—that journalists bear as much responsibility as politicians in resolving problems—attracted great interest. I think this was also the most important question discussed at the conference: Can journalists play as important a role as politicians in improving relations and resolving problems? Some colleagues objected to Simitis. According to some, his words reflected an attitude of ‘dumping responsibility on journalists.’ According to others, the journalist’s duty was limited to reporting news and criticizing policies. I completely agree with the Greek Prime Minister. In the speech I gave at the conference, I essentially tried to explain why Simitis was right.

“Yes, journalists’ responsibility in improving Turkish-Greek relations is no less than that of politicians. Why? The media, with its provocative attitude and broadcasts during the Kardak-Imia crisis in the winter of 1996, nearly dragged the two countries into war. In the summer of 1999, the same media used the earthquake disasters as an occasion to pave the way for politicians’ efforts to improve relations. Yes, if it does its job properly, the media can make a great contribution to realizing the peace that both peoples desire. The media doing its job properly means, of course, above all presenting news as accurately and objectively/impartially as possible (that is, without filtering and distorting it through prejudices).

“Of course, journalism is not limited to reporting news; interpreting events from different angles is as much the journalist’s duty as reporting news accurately. Today, the media is perhaps a more important factor than family and school in acquiring political attitudes and values. The greatest influence on the formation of public opinion is again the media’s. Of course, any commentator will interpret events as they wish. However, if issues are interpreted freely and independently rather than through the eyes of Ankara or Athens; if interpretations oriented toward resolving problems find as much space as interpretations that would prevent this, the peace that both peoples desire can be realized much more easily.

“At the media conference, it appeared that a fairly strong unity of will had formed on both sides regarding eliminating their deep ignorance about each other; reporting news accurately and without distortion; avoiding hostile provocations; and not tagging along behind state policies. The issue is to implement this will and make it permanent. That’s no small matter either, but one has to start somewhere, I suppose.” (Milliyet, February 8, 2000)

## Yannis Atmazoğlu

This was my second visit to Greece and my first to Athens. I wrote about my Athens impressions as follows: “On the occasion of the Turkish-Greek Media Conference, I went to Athens for the first time last weekend. At the first opportunity I found from the program prepared by the Greek colleagues who showed warm hospitality, I wanted to go to the seaside. I asked the hotel receptionist: Where should I go? ‘To Pashalimani…’ I asked him to write down on a piece of paper where I should go so I could tell the taxi driver.

When the taxi driver looked at the paper and muttered to himself in Turkish ‘What is this?!’, I thought he was someone who knew Turkish well, perhaps of Istanbul origin. No, he wasn’t. His parents from Isparta, who had migrated to Greece with the 1923 population exchange, had spoken only Turkish between themselves until they died.

“Yannis was born in Athens and had managed to learn a little Turkish in his childhood. We mostly communicated in English. He told me he would be going to Turkey and Isparta for the first time in his life in the coming summer months. He would definitely join the trip organized by the Isparta Immigrants Association headquartered in Athens. As soon as we set off, he put on a cassette. He had transferred the Turkish Rumelian folk songs from his father’s old ‘stone’ records to cassette and always listened to them. Listening to these songs whose words he didn’t fully understand was ‘something else’: ‘I’m being swept away, to the wind of my fate. Oh horizons, I say…’ I couldn’t help thinking about what Yannis’s mother and father must have felt when they left Isparta. Just as I thought about what my grandfather might have felt when he left Serres.

“When I asked what he thought about recent developments in Turkish-Greek relations, Yannis’s answer was: ‘Let the hostility end; we’re fed up…’ Did everyone want that? ‘No, but I think the majority does,’ he said. Of course, he would vote for Simitis. Partly for Turkish friendship. When parting, he gave me his card. He explained that his surname was actually Atmazoğlu, but he had changed it to a more native name. ‘But we’re still different,’ he said; ‘We’re unique.’

“The exchangees, their children, and grandchildren certainly have a different, unique identity of their own. Even though they are perhaps the ones who have suffered the most pain and endured the most torment from the hostilities, it is also certain that the ‘exchangees’ are one of the bridges of friendship between the two countries. The meeting organized last month in Istanbul by the Lausanne Exchangees Association that those who migrated from Greece to Turkey wanted to establish, which brought together exchangees from both sides, was perhaps the most concrete expression of this.

“Turkish-Greek peace won’t happen tomorrow. The difficulties are great. The two peoples defined their national identities in war against each other. Cyprus only knows its own story. There are tough issues in the Aegean. However, there are also elements that can make peace possible. Common interests are greater than national interests. Common geography, history, and culture unite. There have always been groups on both sides who sincerely believe in friendship. Since the earthquakes, there is a new mentality on both sides. But most importantly, Greek governments have abandoned policies of excluding Turkey. The more Athens opens Turkey’s EU path, the easier the resolution of problems will become. Of course, if Turkey is willing to progress on this path.” (Milliyet, February 10, 2000)

“Here Is the President!”

In May 2000, Süleyman Demirel’s seven-year term was coming to an end. A new president would be elected. With a joint motion from deputies belonging to the parties included in the ruling coalition government of the time (the Democratic Left Party, the Nationalist Movement Party, and the Motherland Party), as well as the Virtue Party and the True Path Party, Constitutional Court President Ahmet Necdet Sezer was nominated for the presidency on April 25, 2000, and was elected the 10th President by securing the necessary majority in the final round of voting held on May 5; he assumed office from Demirel on May 16.

During his presidency of the Constitutional Court, Sezer was leaving a positive impression on the public with his views defending fundamental rights and freedoms and the rule of law, and with his modest persona. I also carried the same impression. I kept telling my friend Rıza Türmen, who was then a judge at the European Court of Human Rights, that it would be very appropriate for him to meet with Sezer when he came to Turkey. Indeed, Türmen had visited Sezer and he too had gained very positive impressions.

In the article I wrote upon Sezer’s nomination for the presidency, titled “Here Is the President!”, I said:

“… Both Prime Minister Bülent Ecevit and the other coalition leaders deserve congratulations; they found the unifying candidate. The Virtue Party leadership’s unhesitating support for the candidacy of Sezer, who had signed the decision to close the Welfare Party, is enough to show the prestige this name carries. Mr. Sezer, in his speeches on the occasion of the Constitutional Court’s founding anniversaries both last year and this year (even after it was announced that he would be nominated for the Presidency), emphasized the importance of human rights, fundamental rights and freedoms, and the rule of law, and repeated his call for a new, freedom-oriented, and pluralist constitution. Sezer’s election would mean both that a person respected by the great majority would ascend to Çankaya; and that the demand shared by the great majority for ‘an end to lawlessness and the rule of law to prevail’ would be carried to the highest office.” (Milliyet, April 27, 2000)

Shortly after being elected President, Sezer called me by phone and thanked me for the support I had given. Of course, I was extremely pleased; for the first time, I was being acknowledged by a president. For the first and last time in my entire professional life, I was invited to Çankaya that year for the October 29 Republic Day. My darling Fatma was also quite pleased about this. We would shake a president’s hand for the first time and see what the Çankaya mansion was like. But it was not to be. On October 28, Fatma couldn’t get out of bed due to severe pain in her joints. One of my closest and most loyal friends, my high school classmate Prof. Dr. Hasan Yazıcı, diagnosed Fatma with acute joint rheumatism. With the treatment Hasan recommended, Fatma was able to get back on her feet before long, but we couldn’t go to Çankaya. After I left Milliyet some time later, Sezer never invited me again, so we never had the opportunity to see Çankaya.

“The Two Faces of the FP”

The congress of the Virtue Party, established to replace the Welfare Party after its closure by the Constitutional Court, held on May 14, 2000, became the scene of competition between the “Traditionalist” (pro-Erbakan) and “Reformist” (anti-Erbakan)

wings. In the days leading up to the congress, I was writing the following about this competition:

“I looked at my archive: My first article in Milliyet on the two different ‘faces’ of the Islamist movement in Turkey appeared on November 25, 1995, with the title ‘The Two Faces of Welfare.’ In that article, I wrote, in summary: On one face, the WP is an important element, a success of our democracy.
