If Turkey is the ‘star of Islam,’ one reason is its success in making the Islamist opposition part of the democratic process rather than pushing it underground. The WP’s other face is the doubts about its commitment to fundamental rights and freedoms. The WP’s division of society into Muslims and non-Muslims; its exploitation of religious feelings; its anti-Semitism and racism under the guise of anti-Zionism were worrying tendencies.

“Since I wrote those lines, much water has flowed under the bridge. The National View Movement today is, in no sense, at the point where it stood at the end of 1995. The principle that the only thing that doesn’t change is change naturally applied to this movement as well as others. The National View Movement has undergone continuous change over time. The NSP was different from the NOP; the WP from the NSP… But the biggest change in this political line undoubtedly occurred while it was sharing government responsibility during the Refahyol period. That experience benefited the WP greatly. The nonsense about the Just Economic Order and the freedom to choose one’s law was abandoned. No one talked anymore about leaving NATO or tearing up the Customs Union. In short, the WP moved toward a reasonable line.

“According to some: If the WP hadn’t been closed, if Erbakan hadn’t been banned, the leap the National View Movement made with the FP couldn’t have happened; the new discourse emphasizing the need for compromise and dialogue, human rights, and fundamental freedoms adopted under Recai Kutan’s leadership couldn’t have developed easily. I don’t know. But what is certain is that the FP doesn’t resemble the WP either. Perhaps the most important indicator of this dissimilarity is that the ‘two faces’ of the moderate Islamist movement in Turkey are openly competing for power within the FP for the first time. In my view, if the Reformist wing, which appears to have adopted the goal of making the FP a party ‘as committed to the fundamental principles of freedom-oriented and pluralist democracy as it is to Islamic values,’ wins this competition, not only the FP but all of Turkey will benefit.

“The Reformist wing can make the FP the Muslim Democrat Party that Turkey yearns for. In that case, the FP could assume a prominent role in favor of liberalization and democratization in Turkey’s political life. It seems to me that even if the Reformist wing cannot win this first congress to be held on May 14, it can win the next congress. Some friends remind me that today’s ‘reformists’ in the FP were yesterday’s ‘radicals.’ I tell them this: It is normal for yesterday’s ‘radicals’ to become today’s ‘advocates of freedom’ who have learned the value of freedom through experience, by living.” (Milliyet, May 11, 2000)

The Hürriyet newspaper reported the FP’s congress result as follows: “Kutan, who entered the election with Necmettin Erbakan’s support behind him, could only get 633 votes out of the FP’s 1,238 delegates. Abdullah Gül, the Reformist wing’s candidate, caused a big surprise by receiving 521 votes, while 43 delegates did not participate in the voting… The result Gül achieved, which Erbakan tried with all his might to prevent, was interpreted in FP circles as: Kutan was re-elected General Chairman, but looking at the result, the winner was Gül; and the only loser of the congress was Erbakan.” (May 15, 2000)

For some time I had been following the statements of the leading spokespeople of the “Reformist” wing, especially Abdullah Gül, and I had become hopeful that the Islamist movement could gradually embrace fundamental rights and freedoms. Following his success at the congress, I called Gül and conveyed that I wanted to meet with him. When he invited me to lunch, I went to Ankara. This first and last private meeting between us was very sincere. I was quite pleased when Gül said that my articles in Milliyet criticizing both the authoritarian secularism practices inherited from the single-party era and the majoritarian understanding of democracy disrespectful of fundamental rights and freedoms prevalent in the Islamist movement had been very influential; that he and his “Reformist” friends had reproduced these articles and discussed them among themselves. I fell under the illusion that my commentaries were having an impact. From that date on, I also began to expect Gül to become more influential in Turkish politics.

“Thank You, Alpay”

It was becoming clear that my criticisms of authoritarian secularism practices were not only influencing the “Reformists” of the Islamist movement. The radical Islamists’ newspaper Akit, in its November 26, 2000 issue, under the headline “Hypocritical EU,” referenced my article published the day before and said “The EU’s hypocritical attitude was raised for the first time yesterday by Şahin Alpay, a former Marxist.” The eight-column headline of Akit’s “Mediacritique” page was also “Thank You, Alpay.” Below it said:

“… But he is now a liberal. He rejects both Marxism and Marxist terror. He works in the cartel. He both writes and makes television programs. In doing so, he doesn’t share some people’s nature. He doesn’t join in ‘reactionary hysteria’ just to protect his position. He doesn’t send ‘I’m one of you’ messages to power centers by insidiously attacking Muslims and their sacred values. The article below, like many before it, is proof of this. Moreover, it’s a document defending the rights of the oppressed on an issue that many Muslims either couldn’t notice or couldn’t reconcile noticing with their ‘EU advocacy.’ Thank you, Şahin Alpay…”

And Akit quoted my article titled “Religious freedom” in full without any abridgement: “The EU Commission’s ‘Progress Report 2000’ on Turkey’s candidacy, announced on November 8, says in the section on religious freedom: ‘No change is seen in the official attitude toward Alevis. The compulsory religion classes in schools and their textbooks not including Alevi identity, and the state providing financial support only to Sunni mosques and foundations are the main complaints of Alevis.’ In the first ‘Progress Report’ on Turkey two years ago, the Commission noted that ‘officially recognized religious minorities are free to practice their religion…’ but that ‘beliefs other than (Sunni) Islam face many bureaucratic obstacles,’ after which it was underlined that the clergy of Alevis, ‘whose numbers are estimated to be at least around 12 million,’ did not receive salaries from the state.

“Considering that they were not mentioned at all in the 1999 Report, it can be said that Alevis’ problems found the widest coverage in the latest report… This may partly be due to some Alevi community leaders having conveyed their complaints to the Commission’s Ankara Representation. The latest ‘Progress Report,’ while referring to the problems of Alevis, also notes that ‘some signs are seen that tolerance toward non-Muslim minorities has increased.’ However, the noteworthy point is that not a single word is mentioned about the continuing bans and pressures on religious orders and communities, which are folk interpretations of Sunni Islam.

“It is not at all a harsh judgment to interpret this as a result of the EU Commission’s deep ignorance and prejudices regarding Islam. The fact that EU reports never in any way mention the headscarf ban in universities, which means not only the restriction of freedom of belief but also of educational freedom and discrimination against women, makes this interpretation even more justified. Whether the EU Commission sees it or not, ending the headscarf ban for university students is one of Turkey’s democracy issues. Members of religious orders and communities and headscarved students must respect the rule of law based on human rights. Those who don’t will of course face bans and penalties. But for those who do show respect to also face bans and penalties is incompatible with democracy. Presumably someone needs to explain this to the EU Commission as well.” (Milliyet, November 25, 2000)

It was understandable that this article of mine would increase my prestige in religious circles. In secular, especially secularist (pro-authoritarian secularism) circles, however, my prestige was gradually decreasing.

## Virtue Is Also Being Closed

On May 7, 1999, the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office applied to the Constitutional Court for the closure of the Virtue Party (FP), on the grounds that, just like the previous NOP, NSP, and WP, it had become “a center of activities contrary to secularism.” I expressed my view on this in an article titled “The Venice Commission”:

“From the perspective of European and Turkish political party law principles, the closure of the FP would be very surprising. Of course, if Turkey is a state of law that has been a member of the Council of Europe for about half a century and is an EU candidate… When looking at the issue from a political angle, the question that always nags at my mind is this: Would it have been very good if the NOP-NSP-WP-FP had never been allowed, if all those representing the political views and demands of Islamist and religious circles had been forced (to go underground and multiply there, just like the religious orders)? I am surprised that some ‘responsible’ persons appear to be unaware of this question.” (Milliyet, January 29, 2000)

The Constitutional Court decided to close the FP on June 22, 2001. The FP applied to the European Court of Human Rights against the closure decision. However, it later withdrew its application on the grounds that the Court “applied double standards to Muslims.” The deputies of the FP called “Traditionalists” joined the Felicity Party under Recai Kutan’s leadership, while those called “Reformists” would gather in the yet-to-be-established Justice and Development Party, which would elect Recep Tayyip Erdoğan as its leader.

## The Partnership of Radicals

In the days when the decision to close the Virtue Party had not yet been announced, a topic that was becoming increasingly clear in my mind was the common aspects of Kemalist and Islamist radicals. I addressed this topic in an article titled “Kemalism 2000”: “Britain’s weekly politics and economics magazine The Economist, read all over the world, in its first issue right after the EU’s Helsinki Summit (December 18, 1999), quoted the words of a European diplomat stationed in Ankara: ‘Many Turks see EU candidacy as an end in itself. But few are aware of what will come after candidacy, what complying with golf club rules might mean.’ The magazine then turned to Daniel Cohn-Bendit, the head of the European wing of the Turkey-EU Joint Parliamentary Commission: Following one of his visits to Ankara, Cohn-Bendit had argued that EU membership would ‘mean the end of Kemalism in Turkey.’

“In this article titled ‘Farewell to Atatürk?’, The Economist, proceeding from Cohn-Bendit’s words, wrote that EU membership posed a dilemma even for ‘the most pro-Western Turks’ and added this comment: ‘Even the most pro-Western Turks, while on the one hand thinking that EU membership would prevent radical Islamists from coming to power, on the other hand question whether giving up the guarantee the army provides in this regard is a wise thing to do…’

“Let’s start with Cohn-Bendit. Frankly, I couldn’t understand why EU membership would mean ‘the end of Kemalism (and farewell to Atatürk).’ If Kemalism meant, as some try to load onto it, ‘Turkish ethnic nationalism, rigid secularism, statism in the economy and politics, authoritarian centralism, militarism, anti-Westernism, etc.,’ Turkey could never have become what it is today: a market economy that, despite all its constraints, has 50 years of democracy experience and is increasingly opening up and integrating with the EU. The intellectual legacy of the founder of the Republic of Turkey rests on two fundamental principles: 1) Catching up with contemporary civilization. 2) And for this, remaining committed to Enlightenment Thought (symbolized by the saying ‘My spiritual legacy is science and reason’), that is, to critical rationalism. These are the Atatürk principles that Kemalists should embrace in the year 2000.

“Viewed this way, Turkey’s EU membership would mean nothing other than Kemalism’s reaching its ultimate victory, and when this happens, the value of Kemalism as an intellectual force contributing to Europe’s integration on the basis of universal values can be fully understood. Because the EU is the idea of Europe’s integration on precisely these principles (Enlightenment Thought, not Christianity). A type of ‘Kemalism’ that obstructs Turkey’s catching up with contemporary civilization, meaning freedom-oriented and pluralist democracy based on human rights, is surely contrary to the essence of Kemalism. As for some ‘most pro-Western Turks’: The Economist’s correspondent probably hasn’t lived in Turkey long enough to know these people. Otherwise, he could have added to his commentary that these people are no less intolerant of difference than radical Islamists; that they cannot seem to grasp that the more authoritarian the regime, the greater the radical Islamist threat will grow.” (Milliyet, April 25, 2000)

As can be seen, this must be the column where I looked at Kemalism with the most benevolent eye.

“Earthquake in the Cartel”

The political crisis that began when President Ahmet Necdet Sezer threw the constitution booklet in Prime Minister Bülent Ecevit’s face at the meeting held on February 19, 2001 (“Black Wednesday”) had turned into an economic crisis. Large-scale layoffs began in the media, especially in the Doğan and Sabah groups, which were referred to as the “cartel” because they both competed for influence and circulation and showed solidarity against their employees. I didn’t expect to be one of the victims of the “earthquake” that the Akit newspaper announced with the headline “Earthquake in the Cartel,” but I was.

I had joined Milliyet in 1994 when Ufuk Güldemir became editor-in-chief. After his departure in 1996, Derya Sazak continued in the position until 1999, then the duo of Umur Talu and Yalçın Doğan took over. I had worked in harmony with all these managers. In December 2000, Mehmet Y. Yılmaz, who had until then been editor-in-chief of Radikal, was brought in to manage. For the first time, someone I wasn’t friends with would be running the newspaper. Naturally, I became a bit uneasy. I did what I had to do; I went and wished Yılmaz success. I even noted that I said, “I see your appointment as an opportunity for Milliyet to return to the Abdi İpekçi tradition.” In response, Yılmaz said, “The boss wants us to make the newspaper more popular. There’s no longer a possibility of being a reference newspaper, but we will continue the tradition of being a newspaper of ideas. We will expand your page to two pages by adding other writers…”

Before long, the first crisis arose between me and Yılmaz; the interview I did with painter İpek Aksüğür-Duben disappeared from the page. After waiting two days, I asked Yılmaz why. His answer was, “There was a communication failure… I didn’t know it was your interview.” A few days later, Melda Türker’s piece on “F-Type prisons” flew off the page. There was no longer any need to talk to him… A few days later, the page secretary also conveyed that Yılmaz found my column pieces (2,700-2,800 characters) too long. When I ran into him in the corridor, I asked the reason for his complaint. He actually said, “Şahin Bey, I used to write 1,400 characters at Radikal… If you get down to 1,500 characters, you’ll be Turkey’s best writer!..”

A few days later, the page’s name became “Entelektüel Bakış” (spelled with a single “l”). And finally, on January 4, the page completely disappeared without my knowledge. It had become quite clear that Yılmaz didn’t want me. I went and told him I could also stop writing the column. In response, he said the page had been temporarily closed due to the economic crisis and would be published again in the future. It wasn’t convincing at all. I began to think I might be on my way out.

The Death of Güven Nil

In this troubled environment, I was shaken by the death of one of my closest friends, Güven Nil, at the age of 57 from a heart attack while playing basketball. I wrote the following in my column: “The Turkish business community has lost one of its most distinguished members. Güven Nil, co-chairman of the TÜSİAD Agriculture Working Group and member of the Foreign Relations Commission, passed away on Sunday, February 18. I met Güven Nil exactly 40 years ago, on a journey. He was a student at the Austrian High School, I was at Robert College. We were going to study in the USA for a year on a scholarship. On our return, he transferred to our school to complete his senior year. Throughout that year, we were inseparable. Many from our generation will remember the folk music trio he formed with Münir and Mürüvvet. We were together in the theater club. When Shakespeare’s ‘Julius Caesar’ was staged, he was Caesar, I was Brutus.

“Then our paths diverged. I decided to go to the Political Science Faculty intending to become a diplomat, he continued to the upper division of the College to become an engineer… He worked as an engineer and administrator for a while, but he wanted to do bigger things. He found his real excitement in trade, opening up abroad, investment, and globalization. He started from scratch in business and was very successful. We always ran on different paths in life, but even when long years came between us, our friendship continued where we left off. For the last 20 years, we were always in a close and intense relationship.

“We looked at life from very different positions. Partly because of this, I learned a lot from him. His most distinctive characteristics were his brilliant intelligence, his determination to create from nothing, his foresight, and his unshakeable optimism. Even in our last phone conversation a few days before his death, he was advising me not to fall into pessimism looking at today’s temporary troubles, that Turkey was a society strong enough to overcome all difficulties, to look at events with a long-term rather than short-term view, to try to see the forest rather than the trees. I will follow this advice.

“I had mentioned him in an article published in August 1999. I had written: ‘Three friends who shared the same room while boarding at the College met in Çanakkale 36 years later. Ahmet (Kutman), if left to his own devices, might have become a famous theoretical physicist. He studied chemistry, took over the family business, and became one of Turkey’s leading wine producers. Güven, if left to his own devices, might have become a great musician. But life made him one of Turkey’s most creative, most entrepreneurial businessmen. His great curiosity about the history of the Gallipoli War eventually led him to buy the Sarafin Farm and to produce some of the country’s highest quality wines together with Ahmet.’

“Güven did what very few people in Turkey do: He invested the money he earned in agriculture. Books never left his hand. There was no place left he hadn’t gone to see. He bought his last guitar a few days ago. He was one of the founding partners of Açık Radyo. He prepared and presented ‘Wine Conversations with Music.’ His heart stopped while playing basketball, as he did every Sunday. He had much more to do.” (Milliyet, February 20, 2001)

Güven used to say he was ready to invest quite a bit of money in a film that would tell my life story. Unfortunately, he would not be able to see what I experienced after that day.

“Sweeping Operation”

Then news began to appear on internet platforms that a “sweeping operation” would be conducted at Milliyet and that I would be among those to be fired. I asked Hasan Cemal, who had transferred from Sabah to Milliyet two years earlier and who was also close to the boss, to investigate whether the news was true. The fact that there was no word from Hasan despite considerable time passing was not a good sign.

My last article in Milliyet was published on February 27, 2001. I was fired the next day. I was at CNN-Türk to do a program. My friend Naki Özkan, who had taken over as my assistant on the page after Nilüfer Kuyaş transferred to NTV about two years earlier and who started working in the editorial department when the page closed, called. He informed me that at the editorial meeting he attended, it was announced that about ten writers had been terminated, and I was one of them. The others whose employment was terminated were Doğan Heper, Yalçın Doğan, Umur Talu, Nilgün Cerrahoğlu, Yalım Eralp, Zeynep Oral, Duygu Asena, Turhan Selçuk, and Bedri Koraman. Among these, the ones I was most surprised to see let go were the last two names, two monuments of Turkish cartooning. (That summer I ran into Bedri Koraman on the Bandırma-Istanbul ferry. When the new editor-in-chief took office, he had told Aydın Doğan, “I can leave now if you want”; the boss’s answer had been “Don’t even think about it.”)

Despite everything, and strangely enough, I was surprised to be suddenly fired. Apparently, I didn’t expect such an ugly end to a job I believed I was doing well and for which I received praise. It couldn’t have been my generally liberal views that criticized Kemalist, authoritarian secularism practices and looked favorably on the Gülen movement and the “Reformist” wing of the Virtue Party that caused this. Because my views on these issues were not much different from those of Taha Akyol, who was also writing at Milliyet at the time like me. This must have been the decision not of the boss but of Mehmet Y. Yılmaz, who apparently wanted to renew the newspaper, I thought. I called Taha and asked if I would continue with the CNN-Türk program. “I haven’t received any notification to the contrary,” he said. After congratulating me on my last interview with Yeşim Arat some time later, he confirmed that my job at CNN-Türk would continue; he added that he would do whatever he could if he could help in any other way. (Taha Akyol would always show that he was a true friend.)

Of course, I first informed Fatma that I had been fired. My dear immediately consoled me, saying “Don’t worry, you’ll find a job anyway…” When the news of my dismissal from the newspaper was heard, many people, especially close friends, called to express their sorrow. Among those who called, I noted the names of retired ambassadors İlter Türkmen, Şükrü Elekdağ, Oktay İşcen; politicians Ertuğrul Günay, Abdullah Gül, Mehmet Ali İrtemçelik, Sema Pişkinsüt, Salim Uslu; businessmen İshak Alaton, Murtaza Çelikel; (Court of Cassation President) Sami Selçuk; from the press Mehmet Ali Birand, Ahmet Sever, Güneri Cıvaoğlu, Nazlı Ilıcak, Ali Bulaç, as well as diplomats Swedish Ambassador Henrik Liljegren and Istanbul Consul General Sture Theolin and EU Representative Karen Fogg. I was both surprised and pleased that TBMM Speaker Ömer İzgi, of MHP origin, called and spoke in praise of my writings and expressed his sorrow. I would also be surprised by the commiseration calls from Hasan Pulur and (my friend from the Ankara years) Melih Aşık, Milliyet colleagues with whom my views seldom coincided.

When Orhan Pamuk called, he said, “I used to buy Milliyet because you wrote there, I won’t buy it anymore.” Retired Ambassador Ümit Pamir called and said “I was reading all your articles. This country has no gratitude…” Social scientists Andrew Mango, Philip Robins, and Jan Erik Zürcher from abroad showed the kindness of calling. A message that made me happy was an unsigned note that one of our neighbors wrote on a mail envelope addressed to me: “My dear, can a valuable writer like you be fired? This is the state of our country!..” I was also pleased in the following days when Güler Sabancı, whom I met at my daughter Elvan’s art exhibition, said “I can’t say ‘my commiserations,’ because it’s a disgrace…”

Messages expressing solidarity continued for a while. I was pleased by the message from Bülent Gültekin, one of the former governors of the Central Bank, who was then a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School: “Dear Şahin Alpay, I am sorry that you have left Milliyet newspaper, or rather that you have been fired. I am not surprised. And I think this is the right outcome. It was not right for you to remain in these now completely corrupted institutions. You were giving them unnecessary legitimacy. I hope this unjust action spurs you on and provides an occasion for you to use your talents in better places. May you be together with your readers in more pleasant environments. If there is anything I can do during this transition period, please don’t hesitate to call. I can be considered experienced in resignations and departures. Much love.” (March 30, 2001)

My friend Zülfü Livaneli would also write the following in his column: “Şahin Alpay is my friend of 30 years. Recently we met for dinner with our esteemed history professor at Princeton University, Şükrü Hanioğlu. Şahin had also taught at Princeton as a visiting professor for a period. The conversation turned to the media and Hanioğlu told an interesting thing: The professors at Princeton occasionally ask what Şahin Alpay is doing. I tell them that he had to leave the newspaper he was working for, that is, he was fired. Then they are astonished and say ‘So the level of journalism in Turkey must be very high, even Princeton professors are not considered worthy of writing in newspapers’…” (Sabah, April 29, 2001)

“The Fish Rots from the Head”

A few months after I was dismissed from Milliyet, I ran into İsmet Berkan, my friend from Cumhuriyet who had taken over as editor-in-chief of Radikal in place of Mehmet Y. Yılmaz, on an Ankara flight. İsmet described the “sweeping operation” at Milliyet as follows: One day Aydın Doğan, Mehmet Yılmaz, and İsmet gathered. Yılmaz said he wanted to change the newspaper’s columnists, but that the boss needed to decide who would go. Thereupon Doğan, without thinking much, wrote the names he saw fit to send off one by one on a piece of paper… The proverb “The fish rots from the head” was apt; I had been wrong to hold Mehmet Y. Yılmaz responsible for my dismissal. Moreover, I knew that Doğan didn’t like me at all. I was also aware that one of my last articles at Milliyet, titled “Quality in the Media,” would not please him at all if he read it. In the article, I said:

“What has been happening in the media recently has been a good occasion for remembering the profession, principles, ethics, and ideals of journalism. I can touch on the main ones as follows: Under today’s conditions, media owners cannot be expected to invest only in this sector. But we can hope that during the membership process, we will bring the principles that media owners will follow when entering public tenders, and the standards regarding the shares newspaper owners can have in other media, into line with EU norms.

“The problems of the media sector other than those related to ownership can only be solved by establishing professional principles and ethics. The foremost of these principles is that media owners and journalists avoid ‘conflict of interest.’ Today, with its increasing importance as a source of news, commentary, and information, the media has assumed a function even more significant than family and school in shaping citizens’ values and behaviors, that is, their general and political culture. It has become all the more important for media owners to act with awareness that the media is not just any investment field.

“Media bosses should be meticulous about leaving the journalistic activities of the organizations they own entirely to journalists and not interfering with the journalistic aspect of the work. The prestige that media organizations operating according to professional principles will bring to their owners is too valuable to be measured by financial gain. The situation of those who don’t think this way is instructive. As for journalists: Using one’s profession as a tool for personal gain is both the greatest immorality and a crime. But there are other things journalists must avoid. A journalist cannot undertake work incompatible with the profession: cannot be both a journalist and a parliamentarian, politician, or member of intelligence organizations. They avoid establishing cozy relationships with political and economic power holders. There are drawbacks to being a journalist on one hand and a financial-administrative manager on the other, because the interests of the workplace can conflict with the interests of journalism (and thus the public).

“The distinction between news and commentary in journalism is as important as the separation of religion and state in politics. This does not only command that commentary not be made in news. It requires that the executives responsible for news and those responsible for commentary be different people. It is natural for journalists’ salaries to be proportional to their skills and their contribution to the organization they work for: Some will earn less; some will earn more. However, if some journalists’ salaries are higher than those of their colleagues in similar positions in the richest countries, the existence of a ‘media aristocracy’ attached to their high salaries rather than professional principles will be suspected.

“As journalists, we have a responsibility to keep quality high. A quality newspaper is not, as was claimed in Turkey until very recently, ‘a newspaper printed with the newest equipment, on the best paper, with the best ink,’ but a newspaper that strictly applies professional principles. In a country without quality media, neither press freedom nor democracy can function fully.” (October 31, 2000)

Interestingly, on the morning this article was published, Hakkı Devrim, a writer for Radikal newspaper who was one of the columnists Aydın Doğan respected most, called me by phone and congratulated me on this “courageous” article, greatly surprising me. The late Devrim also called when he learned I had been dismissed from Milliyet, said he was sorry; he described what was done as “rudeness.” I think he was right.

## Looking for Work Again

When it was heard that I had been dismissed from Milliyet, the most valuable job offer I received came from “Açık Radyo.” Dear Meral (Madra) called and said, half-jokingly, that Açık Radyo could also pay me what I was getting from Milliyet, that they could support me for at least a year, and therefore not to rush to find a job. It was wonderful that Ömer also called and said, “Don’t you dare find a new job and leave Açık Radyo out.” In the mid-1990s, Ömer had said “Enough of being at the mercy of media bosses!” and decided to establish a free and independent radio station. I was, of course, one of the first people he shared this idea with. Açık Radyo (now 95.0) began broadcasting on November 13, 1995; Ömer had achieved the independent media he longed for.

From the early days of Açık Radyo (1995-1996; then between 1999-2004), I was a guest on Ömer’s “Açık Gazete” program and made political commentary. I have an interesting memory related to this (in the context of the power of radio in general and Açık Radyo in particular): One day in the late 1990s, I was traveling by bus from Ayvalık to Bandırma to catch the Istanbul ferry. The young man sitting next to me and I hadn’t talked at all during the trip. As we approached Bandırma, I happened to ask him something. When he heard me, his eyes lit up; “Are you Şahin Alpay?!” he asked. He had recognized me by my voice. He lived in Germany. He had never read any of my articles, had never seen me on screen, but he constantly listened to Açık Radyo… (You can imagine how happy Ömer was when I told him this anecdote.)

I would once again not listen to my wife Fatma, who had long been suggesting I start a publishing house and choose freedom, and would continue to be at the mercy of media bosses… One day, Ali Bulaç, one of the writers I had traveled to Central Asia with, called and invited me to write at Zaman newspaper. I didn’t give an immediate positive answer, because it hadn’t yet occurred to me that I would be left without options, and I wasn’t thinking of writing at a newspaper supported by a religious community… A job offer also came from Swedish Consul General Sture Theolin. After telling me that his wife Marit was very upset by my being fired from Milliyet, that her eyes had teared up, he suggested I work as a consultant for him. I was very touched, but I said I would primarily look for work in the media or universities. I was also pleased that Arne Ruth, one of Sweden’s well-known journalists and now retired editor-in-chief of Dagens Nyheter, called to offer his commiserations. My late friend Ufuk (Güldemir) also called and suggested I write for Habertürk newspaper, of which he was editor-in-chief. I said I would think about it.

NTV was on my mind. I gathered the courage and called Cem Aydın (a former “Aydınlıkçı”), who was then Editor-in-Chief. “Brother, we need you, come let’s meet one day…” he said. When I called a few days later to make an appointment, he said, “Unfortunately, we can’t do anything in the next month or two; if you’re in a tight spot, you can do a radio program for us.” It was apparent that he couldn’t get approval from his boss regarding me…

Then Nebil İlseven, whom I had known since childhood and who was at the time on the Board of Trustees of Bilgi University, conveyed that the university’s founder Oğuz Özerden wanted to meet with me. When we met, Özerden, who pleased me by saying he constantly followed my newspaper articles and my commentary on Açık Radyo, had in mind that I would turn “Medyakronik,” a publication of the university, into what he called an outlet “that intellectuals follow,” and also that I would manage the university’s EU Studies Institute. When I said I would prefer to teach, he said he would need to discuss that matter with rector İlter Turan, who was abroad. Later he would convey that Turan had told him “they didn’t need Şahin Alpay,” and that he was very sorry about this.

# CHAPTER X / AT BAHÇEŞEHİR UNIVERSITY

At the beginning of the 21st century, I was living through a very happy period in my family life. There was no deterioration in the health of my beloved wife Fatma. The liver failure diagnosed in 1987 generally left her tired and weak, but it did not pose a life-threatening danger. Our daughter Elvan, who graduated from the Fine Arts Faculty of Marmara University after finishing Galatasaray Lycée, was rapidly advancing toward becoming a painter whose original works garnered admiration. From her 1994 marriage to businessman Altan Güler, a daughter — my beloved granddaughter Defne — was born in 1997. (Sadly, this marriage, which did not bring happiness, would end about ten years later.) Our son Acar would go on to study graphic design at the Fine Arts Faculty of Bilkent University after graduating from Işık Lycée. After completing his short-term military service in Sivas in 2004, he began working in his profession. The arrival of our second grandchild Leyla, born in 2014 from his marriage in 2009 to our much-loved daughter-in-law Gökçe (Özkaya), would be the pinnacle of our family happiness. I want to emphasize that not being able to devote enough time to my grandchildren, just as with my children, due to my demanding professional life, has remained a lasting regret.

Before long, a period of stability would open up in my professional life as well. An important pillar of this would be Bahçeşehir University (henceforth by its abbreviated name, BAU), where I would work full-time for fourteen years. One day in early March 2001, Prof. Dr. Süheyl Batum — whom I had met in the days of TÜSES (the Turkish Social, Economic and Political Research Foundation) and who had transferred from Galatasaray University to BAU to assume the deanship of the Law Faculty — called me.

He suggested I teach at BAU, “at least until you find another job in the media…” In truth, I had not even been aware of BAU’s existence until Dr. Ahmet Sözen (now a professor at Eastern Mediterranean University in Cyprus), who was teaching there and had taken an interest in my writings, came to visit me at Milliyet to make my acquaintance. I hesitated. The person who convinced me to work at BAU was Prof. Dr. Eser Karakaş, whom I had met at New Democracy Movement gatherings and who was then the dean of BAU’s Business Faculty. Karakaş — whom I ran into at a conference on March 16 and who would gradually become one of my closest friends — said, “Şahin Bey, we want you to work for us full-time.” When Rector Halil Güven, whom he introduced me to at the same meeting, repeated the same proposal, my future was settled.

Karakaş and I agreed and shook hands on my going to Bahçeşehir three days a week to give a total of nine hours of political science lectures, as well as on the salary and other matters. However, when I pointed out that I did not even have a driver’s license, let alone a car, and asked how I would get back and forth from Akatlar where I lived to Bahçeşehir, Eser’s face fell completely. “From now on, the first thing I’ll ask the people I offer jobs to is whether they have a driver’s license,” he exclaimed! We burst out laughing… (Poor Eser would pick me up from my home and drive me to Bahçeşehir and back for months, sometimes with a driver, sometimes without.)

A few days later, I met the university’s founder, Enver Yücel. After graduating from the Mathematics Department of İstanbul Atatürk Education Institute, Yücel had taught for a while in his hometown of Giresun, then entered the business world and over time established the Uğur Preparatory Schools, then the Bahçeşehir Colleges, and finally BAU (reportedly “so his daughter could study there”). As would become clearer with time, he was a very energetic, intelligent, and shrewd businessman. After obtaining his approval as well, I started work at BAU as a lecturer on April 1, 2001; I taught for approximately fourteen years until February 2015 (with the status of Assistant Professor between 2005 and 2011).

In the days when I joined the faculty, BAU was operating out of an old high school building in the Bahçeşehir neighborhood from which it took its name, along with a few villas nearby. There was talk of building a campus on a large plot of land in the vicinity. But the institution grew rapidly and in 2004 would move to its current buildings in Beşiktaş, gradually spreading into the surrounding area. This move was a great blessing for me, living as I did in Akatlar. More importantly, the university’s teaching staff kept expanding and became a circle of friends for me. My senior colleagues Seyfettin Gürsel from Galatasaray University and İlkay Sunar and Binnaz Toprak from Boğaziçi University, along with economist Nuri Yıldırım (my friend from the Ideas Club at SBF, the Faculty of Political Sciences), joined us at my urging. First İlkay, then Binnaz served as chair of the Political Science and International Relations department. I would also become friends there with Murat Çizakça, who joined us shortly after me. Among us, Gürsel would be the most enduring presence at BAU. As of 2022, when these lines were written, he was continuing his professorship while also serving as director of BETAM (Bahçeşehir University Center for Economic and Social Research), which he had steadily developed.

Over fourteen years, I taught various courses in undergraduate and graduate programs. The principal ones were required courses such as Introduction to Political Science, Introduction to Turkish Political Life, Comparative Politics, and Turkish Foreign Policy, along with an elective course on Religion and Politics. I must confess that I prepared seriously for every course I taught, and I reaped great benefit from this in terms of expanding my knowledge. In particular, the reading I did in preparation for the Religion and Politics course — which I would teach from 2003 until my departure in 2015 —would profoundly influence my thinking on the place of religion in society and politics. Both the rise to power of the AKP (Justice and Development Party), a party with Islamist roots, in 2002, and my beginning to write for the newspaper Zaman — published by a religious community — around the same time had certainly been strong incentives for me to take on the Religion and Politics course, which I knew was widely taught at Western universities.

I was happy working at BAU. The boss, Enver Yücel, treated me with particular respect during the 2002–2011 period when my columns took a favorable view of the AKP government. The esteem I enjoyed from him during this period would peak at a meeting attended by nearly all the faculty, when he declared, “Wherever Şahin Hoca is, that’s where I’ll be…” My standing would last until November 2013. Enver Bey would call to congratulate me on the column I wrote (titled “No tolerance for civil society”) about the AKP government’s decision to shut down preparatory schools, saying, “You’ve captured the essence of the matter.” Yet from that point on, as I began writing increasingly harsh columns critical of the AKP government, our relationship would gradually cool, and — as I will recount later — in February 2015 he would decline to renew my contract (while implying that he did so unwillingly).

At BAU, the rectors, the deans, and the department chairs — most of whom were my friends — all treated me well. Unlike the media world, I was happy to be among highly educated colleagues. It was very gratifying to be ranked among the most popular professors in student evaluations. The fact that young women made up the large majority of my successful students was one of the things that made me optimistic about Turkey’s future.

This may not be the place, but I cannot help touching on a subject that I never addressed in any column during my time at BAU. My command of English had also played a role in my finding a job at BAU, since BAU was one of the institutions of higher education where the language of instruction was English. I have no objection to the opening of private universities — provided they do not compromise on quality — nor to instruction in a foreign language in higher education. However, while everyone knows that foreign language education at the secondary level is virtually nonexistent (excluding foreign schools), it is equally certain that one year of intensive language instruction in higher education cannot suffice. For this reason, English-medium instruction at BAU —as at other English-medium institutions of higher education — sadly remained largely nominal. My conviction, therefore, is that instruction in a foreign language has become one of the obstacles to receiving a proper higher education in Turkey! To overcome the problem, like many other faculty members, I limited the English requirement to the assigned readings for courses, and conducted both lectures and examinations in Turkish. No one was in a position to object.

## My eye still on the media

When I began working at BAU in April 2001, I was still doing the “Intellectual Perspective” program on CNN Türk. One day, at the Hürriyet / CNN Türk building in İkitelli where I had gone to record the program, I ran into Hasan Cemal. He asked how I was. I told him I was content with my life, that although I missed newspaper writing, I was not too unhappy with my situation since I was freed from the stress of producing columns on deadline. I also asked the question I had been wanting to ask: “Did it never occur to you to ask the boss why he fired Şahin from Milliyet?” He said it hadn’t, because being let go was a perfectly ordinary thing in the Turkish press… “So Hasan Cemal saw nothing unusual about my being fired!” I thought, and felt somewhat resentful. But I reminded myself of what I often said to him: “Nobody’s perfect…”

Then something interesting happened. While trying to call my Mülkiye friend Prof. Dr. Nuri Yıldırım, I accidentally dialed Nuri Çolakoğlu, one of my oldest friends. When Çolakoğlu asked what I was up to, I told him I was working as a lecturer at BAU and that I “hadn’t been fired yet” from CNN Türk. Nuri surprised me by saying, “Why would they fire you? You lend them prestige…” A few days later, in early October, when it was announced that Taha Akyol had handed over the post of editor-in-chief of CNN Türk to Nuri Çolakoğlu, I called to congratulate him and naturally asked whether the program I was doing could continue; I asked him to tell me personally if the boss should want my employment ended. “The program will of course continue, but let’s think about a new format together,” he said, and asked me to consult him about which guests I would have on. He cautioned me that “a global February 28 had begun” and that I should steer clear of names like Şerafettin Elçi or Mehmet Şevket Eygi.

Naturally, I continued doing the program as I saw fit. (As is well known, I was committed in principle to “editorial independence”…) I don’t know whether it was for this reason, but some time later, in March 2002 — just as at Milliyet in February 2001 — my employment at CNN Türk was terminated one day abruptly and rather shabbily. When I went to the channel for a recording, a third-tier manager informed me that the program had been cancelled and there would be no taping. I was forced to call and apologize to that day’s scheduled guest, the late Professor Dr. Nur Vergin.

Being fired from CNN Türk in such a similar fashion after Milliyet had been quite hard to take. Unfortunately, this was the “culture” of the media owned by Aydın Doğan. (How could I have known that the group would later pass into far “worse” hands?!) Because of this incident, I was deeply resentful toward Nuri and cut off all contact. Yet when he called Fatma following my imprisonment in the summer of 2016, and then called me after my release, our old friendship was revived. He would tell me that he had no hand in the cancellation of my program at CNN Türk, that it had been done without his knowledge.

I was content with my job at BAU, but partly because I wanted to share my ideas by writing in newspapers as I had grown accustomed to over the years, and partly because I needed supplementary income, I began searching for a writing position. When my program at CNN Türk was cancelled in March 2002, my search became more urgent. Shortly after I had started working at BAU, the late Kürşat Bumin had called and told me that, from what he had heard, the newspaper Zaman wanted to add me to its staff, and that Ali Bulaç had even gone to the United States to discuss the matter personally with Fethullah Gülen. Kürşat would call again a few days later to say that word had reached him that Zaman’s management would offer Etyen Mahçupyan and me positions writing columns five days a week.

Sure enough, Bulaç called and asked whether I would agree in principle to write for Zaman. I merely said, “Let’s talk…” since it was certain that Fatma would not approve. Word must have gotten out that Zaman was interested in me, because at a dinner that EU Representative Karen Fogg hosted for Istanbul journalists, Cüneyt Ülsever — then a columnist at Hürriyet — while heaping praise on my writing, spoke warmly in support of my writing for Zaman… Yet for a long time, no concrete offer would come from Zaman.

## A journey to origins

In October 2001, I was in Athens for the Turkish-Greek-Cypriot journalists’ forum that the German Friedrich Ebert Foundation (FES) had been organizing for years. On October 20, my Greek colleague Michalis Moronis did me the kindness of driving me to Serres, where my father was born. I saw that only two mosques from the Ottoman-Turkish era remained in Serres — one restored, the other under restoration — and that a surviving bedesten building had been converted into a Greek historical museum. I was overjoyed to find in a bookshop a photographic history of Serres. The photographs bore witness to the classical Ottoman architecture (based on wooden buildings) and the hundreds of minarets rising across a city that, until the Balkan Wars (1910–1912), had been predominantly Muslim — two-thirds of the population, according to Mark Mazower. I could not help reflecting on how ruthlessly both sides had turned their backs on their histories.

After returning from Serres, when I visited my paternal relative Yahya Alantar in Adapazarı, he told me something I had never heard before: my paternal grandmother’s (Mukaddes Hanım’s) maternal great-grandfather was “the conqueror of Crimea, Ömer Lütfi Pasha, of Hungarian origin,” and his wife was Maria, the daughter of a Serbian prince. I found the story of Ömer Lütfi Pasha (1806–1871) in the Encyclopedia of Islam. He was described as being of Hungarian origin, but was born in Croatia. In pursuit of the family tree, I visited Zehra Abla, the daughter of my father’s maternal aunt. She told me that Kadı Osman Bey — the father of my father’s maternal grandmother Güllü Hanım and the son of Ömer Lütfi Pasha — had come from Crimea and settled in Serres. Could Agâh Efendi, the Mevlevi Sheikh of Serres, have been Osman Bey’s son? I was unable to confirm it. If everything I learned was true, our origins and lineage were quite mixed; apparently there was Croatian, Serbian, and Crimean (Tatar?) ancestry as well.

Karen Fogg’s “secret organization”

The magazine Aydınlık, whose editor-in-chief was Workers’ Party Chairman Doğu Perinçek, proclaimed on the cover of its February 10, 2002 issue: “We have obtained Karen Fogg’s secret correspondence: How to bring the Turkish state to heel…” The internet correspondence that Aydınlık had “managed to obtain” proved (!) that Fogg, the EU’s representative in Ankara, was scheming to “bring the Turkish state to heel.”

The cover story was remarkable in two respects: it showed how deep-seated hostility toward the EU and the West in general was in Turkey, and what conspiracy theories —in other words, the invention of theories bearing no relation whatsoever to the facts —were capable of. The article stated the following: EU Representative Karen Fogg had established a special organization. This Special Organization operated under EU Commissioner for Enlargement Verheugen… Fogg’s Special Organization in Turkey included government officials, top-level state administrators, certain trade union leaders, “civil society” leaders, certain retired generals linked to the Çevik Bir junta, certain academics, and certain agent-journalists… In her correspondence, Fogg explicitly stated the aim of bringing the Turkish state to heel… On this basis, the magazine demanded that Fogg be “immediately expelled from the country.”

Yes, you guessed it: according to Aydınlık, I was one of the “agent-journalists” who belonged to Fogg’s “organization” and corresponded with her by email (along with Mehmet Ali Birand, Sami Kohen, Semih İdiz, Cengiz Çandar, Lale Sarıibrahimoğlu, Metin Münir, Ferai Tınç, and Zeynep Göğüş). After reproducing the brief message I had sent Fogg saying I wanted to introduce her to Eser Karakaş, Aydınlık included these amusing lines about me: “We leave it to our magazine’s expert on turncoats, Hasan Yalçın, to evaluate the meaning of the warmth in the correspondence that begins with the salutations ‘Dear Karen’ and ‘Dear Şahin’ and in which they even share their sleeping hours, and to assess the state of mind of Fogg’s ‘chat buddy’ Şahin Alpay, who once championed proletarian revolution against the Karen Foggs of the world and now, together with her, tries to rouse ‘sleeping beauties’ against the Turkish nation-state…”

As can be seen, the magazine’s claims extended from the fact that we addressed each other as “Dear” in a few email exchanges — as is customary in English — all the way to the insinuation that Fogg and I had a “warm relationship.” The reality was this: EU Representative Fogg would come to Istanbul on several occasions and host columnists who took an interest in Turkey-EU relations for an exchange of views. I was one of those invited. My being among those whom Aydınlık magazine accused of being “agent-journalists” was interesting in the following respect: Aydınlık’s editor-in-chief Doğu Perinçek, who had been my “comrade in the cause” between 1968 and 1971, and I had parted ways never to cross paths again. Over time, we had both abandoned communism; he chose an increasingly hardline Turkish ethnic nationalism, while I chose liberal social democracy. (Perinçek would say in 2021, the year these lines were written, “It is an honor to lead the MHP [Nationalist Movement Party].”) Just as I had completely cut off contact with him after our last meeting in 1971 and avoided so much as uttering his name, I did not see the need to respond to his declaring me an “EU agent”; I left it to the public’s judgment. I mention the incident here because the Doğu Perinçek / Şahin Alpay comparison must be a striking example of how members of the ’68 generation could diverge onto such different paths.

Following the interception and publication of Fogg’s emails, European Commission President Romano Prodi called Prime Minister Bülent Ecevit to express his displeasure at the incident and requested that the communication security of EU representatives be ensured. The Commission spokesperson denied claims that Fogg would be recalled and said there had been no such demand from Turkey either. (NTVMSNBC, February 20, 2002) Nevertheless, Fogg — perhaps at Brussels’ urging — left her position at the Commission. In July 2002, shortly before departing Turkey where she had served for four years, she would answer the questions of A Haber magazine as follows:

“Are you angry about the uproar over the emails? — I’m not, but the reaction of the Turkish authorities was disappointing. I was surprised that an injunction could not be issued against the illegal distribution… It was a great misfortune, because it was grossly misinterpreted, distorted, and exploited by people with questionable political ideologies. Turkey was harmed by this at least as much as I was.

“What was the biggest distortion? — I don’t waste my time with what Perinçek thinks I said, but the most ridiculous distortion was about HOR. Incredible! Even after I denied it, there were those who insisted that by HOR I meant the President of the Republic (Head of the Republic) and that I was attacking him. Anyone with even the slightest knowledge of the EU Commission would have understood that HOR stood for Head of Representation — that is, me!”

## Toward Zaman

Autumn 2002 had arrived and I had begun my second academic year at BAU. One day, Eyüp Can (Sağlık) — who had also conducted interviews with me for Zaman — came to visit me and conveyed Zaman’s offer of a column. None of my searches at other newspapers had borne fruit; I said I could consider writing for Zaman. Some time later he called again and informed me that a meeting had been arranged for me with the editor-in-chief Ekrem Dumanlı. At the time, familiar figures such as Hilmi Yavuz, Etyen Mahçupyan, Nuriye Akman, and even Cem Behar from Boğaziçi University were writing columns for Zaman. Even the late Sami Kohen — my office neighbor who had come to my room on the day I was fired from Milliyet to express his regret — had said, “You could write for Zaman… It’s a serious newspaper, it would suit you…”

On the day and at the time Eyüp Can had indicated, I went to Zaman’s old administrative headquarters in Yeni Bosna. Mehmet Gündem and Zafer Özcan, newspaper staff whom I had known for some time, greeted me. Eyüp unfortunately had not been able to come because something had come up. Dumanlı and I were introduced. After some pleasantries, I told him I could write a column three days a week for Zaman. In response, he actually said they had no need for a new writer!!! I could not believe my ears… What had I been reduced to!.. I was furious at Eyüp Can, and even more so at myself…

A few days passed; Eyüp Can came again. He apologized profusely for what had happened, implying that Dumanlı had not known what he was doing. He said they wanted me to start writing two days a week, and that in time I could write three times a week like the other columnists… It was plainly obvious that there was an authority above Dumanlı at the newspaper Zaman, and that this authority was none other than Fethullah Gülen himself. I told Eyüp Can that to give him a positive answer, I needed to obtain approval from BAU’s administration. The proposal made sense to me, but how was I going to convince Fatma?!

I first broached the subject with Eser Karakaş. Eser was positive; he said that if the boss gave permission, he too would like to write once a week for Zaman. The next day, he came with the news that Enver Bey had said “that would be fine” for both of us. The boss had said, “They want to use you, but you can use them too…” The boss had probably caught the scent that the Justice and Development Party, which Zaman was close to at the time, would soon come to power.

Now came the main issue: obtaining Fatma’s approval. She was telling me to focus on the university, that we had no need for me to wear myself out for extra income… İshak Alaton came to my rescue. When I mentioned in a phone conversation that I had received an offer to write for Zaman, he gave his enthusiastic support. When I told him that Fatma viewed it negatively, he took the phone and explained to her at length that Zaman was a very important newspaper, both for its Muslim identity and its affinity for liberal (freedom-loving and pluralist) views, and yes, he convinced Fatma. Thus Sami Kohen, the distinguished representative of the Jewish minority in the media, had convinced me, while İshak Alaton, the distinguished representative in the business world, had convinced my wife to accept my writing for Zaman… I called Eyüp Can and gave him my positive answer. I said they could also invite Eser Karakaş to write. And so, from November 2002 onward, I began writing twice a week, soon three times a week, and Eser once a week for Zaman. (May he rest in peace, Alaton passed away in 2017, while I was imprisoned in Silivri. When he heard of my arrest, he had told someone close to him that he deeply regretted having encouraged me to write for Zaman; “We got the boy into trouble…” he had said.)

When I went this time to discuss the details, Dumanlı was somewhat sheepish. Etyen Mahçupyan — whom I had known since the 1990s and who had contributed to “Intellectual Perspective” at both Sabah and Milliyet — was also in his office. When we left the newspaper together, Etyen told me that it was he who had suggested they invite me to write for the paper. Bless him, years later (while I was residing in Silivri prison), he would write the following about my relationship with Zaman:

“I wrote a column for Zaman newspaper for nearly ten years, leaving aside the intervening Agos and Taraf period. I was probably the first writer to come from the secular camp… After a while they wanted to bring on Şahin Alpay as well, and Editor-in-Chief Ekrem Dumanlı asked me to speak with him. Şahin thought about it for a long time, remained undecided, and resisted this transition, which in his world meant a ‘major’ change. His entire family, friends, and companions were secular leftists… But after a while he moved away from viewing the Islamic sector through a secularist lens and began writing for Zaman newspaper. Those were the years when there was a nearly organic closeness between the AK Party and the Gülen community, and when the secularist/statist status quo was trying by every means to halt the wave of Islamic conservative power coming from the periphery. Şahin, insofar as he was someone who could channel his militant left-wing past into a freedom-loving mold and increasingly embraced pure liberalism, supported the positive work the Gülen community was doing at the societal level. He found the criticisms directed at the community’s political aims to be speculative. But he was never part of the Gülen movement or a political sympathizer.” (“What had Şahin Alpay done?”, Karar, October 29, 2017)

“In my youth I was an atheist, now I’m an inconsistent deist”

Two days before my first column appeared in Zaman, on November 3, 2002, Nuriye Akman’s interview introducing me to the newspaper’s readers was published. I reproduce below in its entirety the interview, which ran under the headline “Şahin Alpay: I am philosophically a turncoat, and I am proud of it.”

Dear Şahin Alpay, welcome to our newspaper. I am extremely pleased to meet with you here. I think the most straightforward way to introduce you to our readers is for you to tell your life story. Because this story will also give us all the opportunity to do a media analysis. If you like, let’s begin from February 2001, when you were ‘fired’ from Milliyet, where you had worked for nearly seven years.

Ten writers and cartoonists were let go along with me. Although this purge was explained by the economic crisis, many new writers were hired shortly afterward. Clearly a staff change was what they wanted. No one can object to that, of course. What offended me was that our dismissal from the newspaper was not even communicated to us personally by the paper’s owner or editor-in-chief. We had deserved at least a letter or phone call of thanks.

It’s a pattern of gracelessness. For instance, I left Sabah without even being able to collect my retirement bonus. They still haven’t paid it. When I ran into Zafer Mutlu by chance at the airport and asked, he said to me, “I’ve built a wall, nobody can get past that wall.” I understand very well how your heart was broken…

Last July, it fell to Nuri Çolakoğlu — my friend of forty years, with whom I had spent ten years of my life — to end my program at CNN Türk. He too ended my employment in the manner of Milliyet Editor-in-Chief Mehmet Yılmaz, someone I barely knew. He did not even deign to make a phone call. I think these are not things that befit colleagues.

Perhaps there was no need for the kind of program you were doing.

Perhaps, but my objection is to colleagues not treating each other as colleagues. Only journalists themselves can protect the principles, ethics, and freedom of the press. If we don’t stand up for the dignity of our own profession and our colleagues, if we allow the owners to push us around, things get completely out of hand, as they have in Turkey.

Why did it turn out this way?

The owners used the media as an instrument for their non-media interests and made undeservedly vast sums of money. By paying certain executives and columnists salaries and providing perks unseen anywhere else in the world, they created a media aristocracy. Because these people owed their income levels to the owners, they became “their masters’ voice.” Whether professional principles were being trampled or not was no longer their concern. During the debates over the RTÜK (Radio and Television Supreme Council) Law, the media aristocracy was so blatantly exposed… Even writers who presented themselves as paragons of democracy either defended this law — which was contrary to the constitutional amendments and the EU’s Copenhagen criteria, and which trampled on press freedom — or fell silent, because their owners wanted them to. The owners also eliminated unionization in the press. The disorganization and fragmentation among journalists, as a serious obstacle to press freedom, even made it into EU progress reports.

Why couldn’t you become part of the media aristocracy?

I always earned less than I deserved in the media. Some of my colleagues, upon hearing my salary, could not restrain themselves from saying “that’s a disgrace”… I received a good upbringing. Just as I always knew my place, I never groveled before anyone for the sake of money.

If Aydın Doğan were to invite you back, despite everything, wouldn’t you go?

No, never… The money they earned thoroughly spoiled the media aristocracy. They committed every manner of vulgarity. At a panel on quality in the press, some editors-in-chief of major newspapers said: “Our newspapers are very high quality. Because they use the finest ink, the best quality paper, and are printed on the most modern presses…” I remember the audience bursting into laughter.

What did you see that was different at Zaman that made you come?

As soon as I left Milliyet, they said “Come right away” from Zaman. But I had started teaching political science courses at Bahçeşehir University… As you know, I am primarily a political scientist. I did my doctorate in Sweden, at Stockholm University. Because of the September 12 coup, I had been unable to return to academia… On the other hand, I had decided to continue with the program at CNN Türk. I thought you can’t carry three watermelons under one arm. But once my job at CNN Türk ended, I knocked on the doors of the newspapers.

Including Cumhuriyet and Star?

Not quite. Cumhuriyet was out of the question, because I had resigned from there in 1992. Honestly, I never even considered Star. There was no response from the other papers. Zaman, on the other hand, renewed its invitation. I owe Zaman a sincere debt of gratitude for giving me the opportunity to write again. For now, I’ll write two days a week. We may increase it to three later on. Of course, having received an invitation was not the only reason I accepted Zaman’s offer.

I think the real reason is your desire to strengthen the existence of a “gray” area in this polarized, “black or white” media.

Correct… I received a good education. I have had rich experiences in life. I want to share my knowledge and accumulated insight. For me to find fulfillment as an intellectual, I need to be able to say what I think and to make my analysis heard. Unfortunately, the prevailing view in our country equates journalism with news reporting. Perhaps partly because of this, nearly all columns have become news-writing spaces, while news stories are filled with commentary. Yet journalism has two branches: commentary and reporting. Unfortunately, in our country they are conflated, whether consciously or not.

Ah! You’ve come to just the right place. Zaman is perhaps the only newspaper that is aware of this distinction.

Yes, that’s right. So first of all, I’m at Zaman because they wanted me. Second, for the past year there has been an effort at Zaman toward professionalization — toward putting out a serious newspaper that applies professional principles. A serious newspaper where everyone can read accurate news and different, high-quality commentary…

There was a similar situation at Cumhuriyet in the early 1980s, I believe.

You can think of Cumhuriyet in those days as a secular, left-wing community. In those days, I was part of a young cadre who were themselves leftists but had renewed their views and begun to value freedom, and who believed Turkey needed a serious newspaper that applied professional standards. The community’s mostly elderly leaders reacted strongly against this cadre’s effort to professionalize the paper. They panicked: “We are defending an ideology that’s a mix of Kemalism and Marxism here… These people are going to turn this newspaper into a liberal paper that anyone can read…”

And they won, not you.

Yes, after ten years of wrangling it became clear this marriage could not work. We, the younger generation, left Cumhuriyet and scattered across the entire media. Now at Zaman there is also a young cadre. They too say, “We are journalists, and we should make Zaman a real newspaper.” I don’t know how the people running the paper will take this. But the young ones tell me, “We’re only getting encouragement.”

And from what I understand, you are saying, “If there’s a group trying to liberalize, I’ll put my shoulder to the wheel.”

I too want to lend my support to this effort. There is yet another reason I write for Zaman: the polarization you just mentioned… I know that the overwhelming majority of Turkish society does not approve of the religionist-secularist polarization. I see that the middle ground — which opposes both kinds of bigotry — needs to be strengthened. I am as much against the suppression of religion and belief in the name of secularism as I am against the suppression of freedoms in the name of religion, and I will never compromise on this stance in any way. As long as Zaman newspaper continues to publish my columns, I will write them. One reason I was let go from Milliyet may well have been my opposition to secularist bigotries.

Have you come to terms with your Maoist past?

In the 1960s I was a leftist who became progressively radicalized. It began with sympathy for Mehmet A. Aybar’s Workers’ Party of Turkey. It went as far as believing that the truest path was the one shown by Mao… Actually, it started like this: in 1961–62, on an AFS (American Field Service) scholarship, I went to attend senior year at one of California’s most famous high schools. When I returned, the question in my mind was, “Why is Turkey so poor and why are these Americans so rich?”

And the Workers’ Party of Turkey offered you an answer: Because of imperialism…

Yes, I got caught in that chain. And my search ultimately led me to Mao. Let’s not forget that in those years, the West was experiencing the ’68 Revolution and the East the Cultural Revolution. It was a period when critiques of capitalism had become very radical. My ideas radicalized to a degree that exceeded even my own nature. In truth, I am a thoroughly conventional person, deeply devoted to family life. But intellectually I was a revolutionary. Intellectual inquiry and experience eventually showed me that the things done in the name of leftism were producing results exactly opposite to what was intended. I began to be horrified by the things we had done. But for a while, of course, it was not possible to — how shall I put it — tarnish one’s own valor. In the end, though, God helped me and I freed myself from those errors.

Really? Are you a religious person?

I am definitely not devout. But I am culturally Muslim. I think a creator may exist. In my youth I was an atheist. My current position could be defined as deism. Over time, I came to appreciate the meaning and importance that religion holds for people. I reached the conclusion that religious beliefs must be respected and that religious faith is as valuable as intellectual conviction.

So how did God help?

After the March 12 intervention, I was a wanted man. The reason was the articles I had written in left-wing magazines. I fled Turkey. I spent nine months in the ranks of the Palestine Liberation Organization. Then I returned to Turkey. The movement fell apart. With the help of my family — especially my late older brother — I escaped to Sweden. I put my life in order. I began doctoral studies at Stockholm University. But I was never involved in any armed action.

In those days you were together with Doğu Perinçek. What is your relationship like today?

After 1971, I think we met only once. He keeps having things written about me in his magazines calling me a “turncoat.” But I am philosophically a turncoat, and I am proud of it. If a person decides he is intellectually on the wrong path, he should correct himself. The greatest virtue of democracy, after all, is that it gives both societies and individuals the opportunity to turn back from their mistakes. Democracy is an educator. It makes radicals moderate.

You also taught for a period at Princeton University, didn’t you?

During the years 1982–2001, when I was primarily working as a journalist, I also found opportunities to make use of my academic side. While at Cumhuriyet, I taught opinion writing at Anadolu University’s Faculty of Communication; in the 1994–95 academic year, I gave courses on Scandinavian Political Life at Boğaziçi University. At Princeton University, I taught a seminar on Turkish Political Life in the spring semester of 1998.

Have you ever given thought to metaphysical questions?

No. Definitely don’t look for a spiritualist side in me. I grew up in a secular family. My mother’s father was an atheist member of the Committee of Union and Progress, while my maternal grandmother was an extremely devout lady. But they were so in love with each other that a year after my grandfather’s death, my grandmother too died of grief. On both my father’s maternal and paternal sides, they were Mevlevi sheikhs. They came from Serres, which was a Muslim city until 1913. My mother’s side, on the other hand, was from Midilli (Lesbos). In the family I grew up in, religion had become an entirely personal matter. No one interfered with anyone else’s beliefs. My late mother, between her own mother and father, took a somewhat agnostic, skeptical stance. My father never discussed religious matters. Both of them, like all immigrants from Rumelia, were deeply devoted to Mustafa Kemal.

So there is a very strong secular vein in your upbringing.

Yes. But we need to distinguish between secularism and secularist ideology. Secularism also entails full respect for religion. It does not mean the suppression of religion. I believe that social problems stem not from a conflict between believers and non-believers, but from the contradiction between the poor and the destitute, between those who can exercise their rights and those whose rights are denied. I used to think that Proudhon’s famous dictum — that property is theft — was the absolute truth. But the conclusion I reached over time was this: Property is liberty…

Let’s talk a bit about your family too…

I have a very happy marriage. My wife Fatma is my youthful sweetheart… She was studying pedagogy at Istanbul University. She dropped out of her studies and came to Ankara because I was going to finish Mülkiye and join the Foreign Service… We were separated between 1971 and 1974. She played a great part in my finding the path of reason… I am proud of the achievements of my daughter Elvan, who is a painter. My son Acar is a graphic designer, a recent graduate of Bilkent University. That our children became artists is a great source of happiness for us.”

Perhaps the most notable question in this interview was the one about my religious beliefs. In my youth, I had been an atheist until my thirties; when I felt the need to pray during the very difficult times I lived through (even if in my mother tongue), I began, out of honesty, to describe myself as a deist. I may have been the first person in Turkey to openly describe himself as a deist. I should note on this occasion that there was a serious inconsistency in my deism. For deists — the most famous of whom were America’s founding fathers — believe that a creator, having created the universe, does not intervene in its workings. I, on the other hand, was the kind of deist who prayed and thereby invited the creator to intervene in my fate — an inconsistent deist, in other words. I would become increasingly conscious of this inconsistency.

# CHAPTER XI / 14 YEARS AT ZAMAN

Zaman was the newspaper I wrote for the longest. For approximately 14 years, I wrote a column three days a week for Zaman. My first article was published on November 5, 2002; my last on February 27, 2016. I also wrote a weekly column for Today’s Zaman, the English-language newspaper that the Zaman group began publishing in November 2007. On March 4, 2016, both newspapers were seized by court order and a trustee was appointed. Following this, some Zaman employees started publishing two newspapers on March 6. I wrote for one of them, Yarina Bakis (Looking to Tomorrow). My last article opposing calls for military intervention against the AKP government was published on July 14, 2016, one day before the coup attempt of July 15. The weekly commentary program called “Akil Defteri” (Notebook of Reason), which I did together with Mehmet Altan and Eser Karakas on Mehtap TV, one of the Zaman group’s television channels, and which attracted considerable attention, would also be broadcast for ten years between 2006 and 2016.

When I started writing for Zaman in 2002, I certainly knew that it was the media organ of the religious community led by Fethullah Gulen, or as they called themselves, the Hizmet (Service) Movement. I saw no problem in writing there. My view of religion had changed over time. People had not only material but also spiritual needs; religious beliefs maintained their power in almost all societies. On the other hand, if the liberal and pluralist democracy I advocated was to take root in Turkey, there was a great need for an interpretation of Islam compatible with it. I thought Gulen represented such an interpretation of Islam. By writing for Zaman, I could continue to defend liberal democracy as I had done before at Cumhuriyet, Sabah, and Milliyet, and in this way I could also influence the views of Gulen community members. As an intellectual, I was burning with the desire to write for newspapers and share my ideas with society as I had been doing since the 1980s. Moreover, my monthly salary from the university was insufficient for my living expenses; I also needed additional income. Only Zaman in the Turkish press was giving me the opportunity to write.

What Kind of Community?

By writing for their newspapers, speaking on their television channels, and visiting the schools they opened both domestically and abroad, I had the opportunity to get to know the Gulen community, or as they called themselves, the Hizmet Movement, to some extent. To some extent, because my views and impressions about the community were limited in several ways: First of all, I was working full-time at the university. I knew the community primarily through my contacts with media organizations, mainly with Zaman employees. My contact with the newspaper was also limited to writer meetings held a few times a year, and largely to my dialogue with opinion page editors. In short, I was looking at the community “from the outside”; I was not familiar with its non-transparent aspects or internal workings.

As I explained above, I viewed the Community positively, with “benevolence,” on the grounds that it represented a liberal interpretation of Islam. The modern building in Yeni Bosna, where the newspaper would move shortly after I started writing, resembled a beehive. A quiet but intense work routine was in place that I had not seen in any other newspaper I had worked for. I explained this with the work ethic expressed by the concept of “Hizmet” (Service), working for the benefit of society with religious motivation. I would see the same work routine and ethics in other workplaces of the Community. Yes, I was aware that there was a “closed” or, as its opponents put it, “non-transparent” quality in the Community’s operations. However, I did not find the criticisms in this direction important, considering that all of the community’s activities directed at society were in public view. I attributed this introversion, this lack of transparency, essentially to the pressures that the Kemalist state imposed on religious movements making it necessary. In 2004, in the second year of my writing for Zaman, I would explain my views about the Community as follows:

“About ten years ago, I wrote in an article titled ‘Respect for Hocaefendi’ published in Milliyet newspaper: ‘As far as I can see, Hocaefendi opposes the use of Islam as a political ideology, as a party philosophy; the division of society into two poles as believers and non-believers.
