He advocates that those who believe differently and think differently should be respectful and tolerant of each other; peace and reconciliation in society… I perceive Hocaefendi as a religious figure who separates religion and politics, opposes the culture of enmity that could divide people into camps, and contributes to the development of a tolerant understanding of Islam. Hocaefendi’s work should be respected.’ (Milliyet, July 29, 1995) In the ten years that have passed, my conviction about Gulen’s contribution has not changed, it has grown stronger.

“Today too, I think Gulen represents an interpretation of Islam suited to the requirements of our age, of a world that is increasingly modernizing, individualizing, democratizing, and globalizing. I believe that Gulen’s contribution has value and meaning on a global scale: If the many and very different interpretations of Islam existing in the world today can be compared, it can be said that Wahhabism is at one end and Gulen’s interpretation is at the other.

“If, since the 1980s, the idea has taken root to some extent in Turkish society that problems can be solved not through fighting and violence, but only by respecting different beliefs, views, and understandings; through dialogue, talking, and reconciliation, I have no doubt that Gulen’s advice has made an important contribution to this. I also think that Gulen’s advice has had an indirect but important share in the fact that the political cadre that emerged from the Milli Gorus (National Vision) Movement, Turkey’s own unique Islamist movement, founded the Justice and Development Party in 2001, came to power in 2002, and over time reached a consensus on European-standard democracy and secularism for Turkey. The fact that a significant portion of society is still unaware of this is an important deficiency of ours.” (Sahin Alpay, Gulen’s Contribution, Journalists and Writers Foundation, Istanbul, June 2004.)

Except for the last 4-5 months of the approximately 14 years I was a columnist at Zaman, the newspaper’s constant editor-in-chief was Ekrem Dumanli. Dumanli graduated from Istanbul University’s Faculty of Literature in 1987, started working as a reporter at Zaman in 1993, went to the US in 1997 to pursue a master’s degree at Emerson College in Boston, and upon his return to the country in 2001, took over as Zaman’s editor-in-chief. Reportedly, he was one of a group of young people sent to the US for education at Gulen’s instruction.

I first met him briefly in 1998 on the occasion of a speech I gave at Harvard University at the invitation of Cemal Kafadar. Our first proper meeting, as I described above, was during a visit when I went to meet him with the expectation of writing for Zaman, but received a negative response. After I started writing for Zaman, our relationship always continued within a framework of mutual respect. I think our good relationship peaked in July 2006. During a visit to the newspaper, he said that they greatly appreciated me, that they would do everything they could to make me happy, that if I had to leave the university I could do additional work for the newspaper, and thus compensate for my income loss.

## Censorship at Zaman

My articles at Zaman were very rarely interfered with. In this respect, I was perhaps the writer who was “given the most latitude” at the newspaper. As a general form of censorship, at the beginning of my time writing for the newspaper, I was asked not to write critical articles about Central Asian dictators. Concerns were expressed that the Hizmet schools in these countries could face the risk of being closed. I received this with understanding, decided not to touch on those subjects, and did not. At a time when the intensity of my criticism of the AKP government was increasing, I had to change the last paragraph of an article titled “The Prime Minister Must Change.”

The original version of the paragraph was: “If the Prime Minister cannot be persuaded to change, then it can be concluded that he has become extremely tired as a result of the intense work he has carried out for approximately eleven years, or that his health condition does not allow him to continue at this pace, and the mechanism of the parliamentary system that enables the renewal of the executive when necessary can come into play. The AKP group, if necessary alone, can vote no confidence in the current government and ensure continuation with a new prime minister. This is in the interest of Turkey, the AKP, and its members of parliament.”

Dumanli called me on the phone and said, “I agree with you, but they will assume that we made you write these lines and will create an incident…” and asked me to soften the paragraph. I did my best and revised the paragraph as follows: “If the Prime Minister cannot be persuaded to change, then I personally will conclude that he has become extremely tired after the intense work he has carried out for approximately eleven years, or that his health condition does not allow him to continue in office. Then the responsibility to find a solution will fall to the people.” (Zaman, June 6, 2013)

Dumanli was not satisfied with this version of the article either, but he did not push further. Some time later, he told another Zaman writer what had happened: Prime Minister Erdogan, having read the softened version of the article, had called him furiously, saying “Throw this man out of the newspaper…”; Dumanli’s response had been “We don’t have a practice of removing writers.” When I learned this, I was truly startled. Even though I had always given due credit for his services, the Prime Minister’s intolerance toward me had surprised me.

My article titled “Why Hagia Sophia Should Remain a Museum,” which was supposed to be published on December 7, 2013, was censored and completely eliminated. The page editor called me on the phone to say that the newspaper management agreed with the content of my article, but that, due to the increasing tension between the community and the government, there was concern it could cause conflict among Muslims and demonstrations in front of the newspaper. Sometime later, another Zaman writer would explain to me exactly where the concern originated: Said Nursi had sent a letter to Prime Minister Adnan Menderes requesting “the opening of Hagia Sophia for worship.” In other words, the Community could have no objection to opening Hagia Sophia for worship (!)

## The Huseyin Gulerce Case

One of the first people I met at Zaman was Huseyin Gulerce, the institutional director who had served as the newspaper’s editor-in-chief until Dumanli was appointed. Gulerce, who also served as president of the Journalists and Writers Foundation established by the Community for a time, showed me great warmth. I was a guest on his weekly program on the Samanyolu television channel several times. I had formed a very positive impression of him. I can say that he was one of the people under the Zaman umbrella with whom my views most aligned.

Gulerce ended his columns at Zaman and his program on Samanyolu channel some time after the judicial investigations launched against some ministers on December 17/25, 2013. I would hear that when leaving Samanyolu, he had warned employees there, “they will lock all of you up.” Gulerce, who was said to be one of Gulen’s closest associates, and was even known for a time as “the spokesperson of the Community,” would surprise everyone by making statements against the “Fethullahist Terror Organization, FETO” after cutting ties with the Community.

(In its decision overturning the 8-year 9-month prison sentence given by Istanbul 13th Heavy Penal Court in July 2018 on the grounds that “I was a member of the Fethullahist Terror Organization,” the Court of Cassation requested that Huseyin Gulerce be heard as a witness about me. At the hearing held on January 11, 2022, Gulerce said the following: “I know Sahin Alpay closely. I don’t think he has any connection with FETO at all. He was writing for the newspaper. He wasn’t even someone who came to the newspaper often. I think Mr. Sahin made a choice between the government and the community through his articles, but I don’t think he was affiliated with FETO or that he received instructions. What I said about Mr. Sahin also applies to the other four friends (tried in this case). I knew these friends as people who did not abandon the honor of the pen. I don’t think they wrote articles on instructions. Because they are people who are closed to suggestion. I haven’t even heard rumors of such a thing.”)

## Bilici: The AKP Government Proved the Kemalists Right

Abdulhamit Bilici, a graduate of Bogazici University’s Political Science and International Relations Department who took over this position following Dumanli’s resignation as editor-in-chief in October 2015, was also one of the people with whom I had the closest dialogue at the newspaper. What Bilici, who continued as editor-in-chief until March 4, 2016, when the newspaper’s management was transferred to a trustee by court order, said in our last meeting was very striking: The AKP government’s practices had proven the Kemalists right. The practices of Islamists in Muslim-majority countries had caused great disappointment in him. He no longer found my objections convincing that authoritarian secularism policies had made Islamists a problem everywhere, including Turkey. As far as I know, Bilici settled in the US some time after the newspaper was transferred to a trustee.

I also had good relations with Bulent Kenes, the editor-in-chief of the English-language Today’s Zaman newspaper, published between 2007 and 2015, to which I contributed by writing a weekly column. Kenes, who like Bilici was a graduate of Bogazici University’s Political Science and International Relations Department, and who had previously served as editorial coordinator of Turkish Daily News and bureau chief of Anadolu Agency in New York, also left the country after the newspaper was transferred to a trustee; he sought asylum in Sweden. As far as I know, in 2019 he made an announcement that he had left the “Hizmet Movement.”

The Zaman employees with whom I had the closest contact were, of course, the page editors responsible for the columns I sent three times a week. (In order: Ahmet Turan Ayhan, who left the newspaper in 2007 to become an advisor to a ministry and then a program maker at TRT; Levent Kenez, Yavuz Altun, and Buket Davulcu, all of whom emigrated abroad after July 15.) The writers with whom I became friendly during my time writing for Zaman, and with whom I grew closer as pressures on the newspaper increased, were Ali Bulac, Ahmet Turan Alkan, Mumtaz’er Turkone, Nuriye Akman, and Lale Kemal. After July 15, we would meet with them in detention, in prison, and in courtrooms.

My view of the AKP government in my columns at Zaman can be roughly divided into three periods. The first period covers the time from their coming to power in 2002 until 2011, during which I generally viewed them positively. The second is the period extending from 2011 to the end of 2013, when I called on the AKP government to return to its early days. The third period is from early 2014 to March 2016, when my articles ended with the appointment of a trustee to the newspaper, during which I harshly criticized the AKP government. My harsh criticisms would continue in the daily newspaper called Yarina Bakis (Looking to Tomorrow), which Zaman employees began publishing on March 6, 2016, and which was shut down by the government after the July 15 coup attempt.

Nowadays, it is not possible to access my articles published in both Zaman and Yarina Bakis between 2002 and 2016. This is because, similar to how the communist regime that was in power in Russia between 1917 and 1992 erased facts it wanted forgotten from historical records, the AKP government has also completely erased from the internet the archives of Zaman, Yarina Bakis, and all publications belonging to the Gulen community. For this reason, I will include some short and some long excerpts from articles I consider important below.

“Victory of Democracy”

In 2001-2002, three events that would deeply affect my intellectual world came roughly one after another: I had started teaching political science full-time at BAU. This was followed by my starting to write a column three days a week for Zaman newspaper, published by a religious community. And in the days when I started writing for Zaman, the Justice and Development Party, which had its roots in Turkey’s own unique Islamist movement and now declared itself “Conservative Democrat,” came to power. My first article in Zaman was published two days after the election with the title “Victory of Democracy.” I wrote:

“The election resulted in a victory for democracy. In several respects. First of all, the election was held in great calm, with fairly high participation and with almost no incidents. (…) Second, despite perhaps the world’s worst electoral system (neither providing stable government nor ensuring fair representation), democracy worked. The coalition parties that had dragged the country into crisis were removed from power, suffering a heavy defeat at the ballot box. (…) Third, partly perhaps thanks to the world’s worst electoral system, Turkey purged a political cadre whose failures had been proven time and again, who were deeply involved in corruption, and whose time had long passed. (…)

“Unfortunately, this victory for democracy is overshadowed by perhaps the world’s worst electoral system. A very large portion of voters, approximately 45 percent, will not be represented in parliament. Despite all the warnings made over the years, the election law was not changed; even the 10 percent threshold was not reduced to a normal level. In the end, those who did not do this fell into the pit they dug for others. So much so that no one may have the nerve to argue about legitimacy.

“The great winners of the elections are undoubtedly Recep Tayyip Erdogan and the AKP. There are many factors that explain this success. First, the AKP is undoubtedly not a ‘fifteen-month-old party.’ It is the heir to a great political movement that has been organized step by step since the early 1990s, the movement that makes the AKP Turkey’s own unique and only mass party. Second, AKP leaders carried out a great ideological transformation from Islamist discourse toward a discourse of human rights, freedom, European-standard democracy and economy. Seeing that the overwhelming majority of the Turkish people are as committed to secularism and democracy as they are to religious values, they pulled the party to the center. On this path, they did not miss the opportunity to shake off the burden of Erbakan and the cadre around him whose time had long passed. With its current discourse, the AKP can only be characterized as a Muslim democratic or conservative party. Now it has the opportunity to show those who have doubts about this whether its essence matches its words.

“Actually, the AKP is also a victory for Turkish democracy. A young cadre that entered the political scene with a radical Islamist stance, under the conditions forced by democratic competition and gradually understanding that freedom is necessary for everyone, adopted a moderate and reasonable center-right line. The greatest virtue of democracy is that it gives political movements, as well as societies and individuals, the opportunity to correct their mistakes. Democracy educates; it makes radicals moderate. We can be proud of our democracy, even as it is.

“There is also a message to the world from these elections: Islam absolutely does not mean terrorism, fundamentalism, bigotry, or backwardness. Islam, like all religions, is open to all kinds of interpretation. In a Muslim country, both secularism and democracy can function perfectly. Turkey has shown this once again with its recent election. The AKP is undertaking a very difficult task. To succeed, it must gain everyone’s support. And everyone should help. Because success is in all our interest.” (Zaman, November 5, 2002)

(This article was an expression of how much goodwill I viewed the AKP and its government with in 2002, and how much credit I extended to them. Unfortunately, the hopes that the AKP raised in me and many others for Turkey and the world would not be realized; before ten years had passed, it would be seen that AKP leader Erdogan’s “essence and words” were gradually moving apart from each other; the attributed title of “Muslim Democrat” would gradually give way to “Islamist populist.”)

Just as I characterized the AKP coming to power on its own as a victory for democracy, I also advocated that its leader Erdogan, who could not run for parliament because his political ban was still in effect, should assume the prime ministership. I wrote: “The President has tasked AKP deputy chairman Abdullah Gul with forming the 58th government. We wish Mr. Gul success. Gul is the AKP’s second man, Tayyip Erdogan’s closest associate; with his always reasonable and moderate line, he is also an acceptable figure among those who did not vote for the AKP. But he is not the AKP’s chairman. For this reason, Gul’s prime ministership can only be for a temporary period. It would be beneficial for this period to be as short as possible.” Indeed, with the support of the CHP under Deniz Baykal’s leadership, the TBMM lifted Erdogan’s political ban. Erdogan entered parliament as a deputy for Siirt following the by-election held on March 9, 2003, and with Gul submitting his resignation, he assumed the prime ministership on March 14, 2003.

“We Have No Business in Iraq?”

In early 2003, Turkey witnessed one of the most important foreign policy crises of its recent history. US President George W. Bush decided to intervene militarily in Iraq on the grounds that Saddam Hussein’s regime had developed nuclear and biological weapons and had ties to Al Qaeda, thus becoming a major threat to the US and the world. He asked Ankara for permission to station 62,000 troops in Turkey for 6 months in preparation for an invasion from the north. The prime ministry motion submitted to the TBMM on February 25 by the AKP government to be authorized on this matter caused controversy. When the AKP group split, the motion was rejected in the vote held in the general assembly on March 1, 2003, with the votes of the CHP and AKP dissidents. The rejection of the motion caused great disappointment in the US administration.

The invasion, which all NATO allies except Britain opposed, resulted in the overthrow of Saddam Hussein’s regime. The intervention, which resulted in the deaths of nearly three hundred thousand people, both civilian and military, caused great destruction in the country. Perhaps the most important consequence for Turkey was that the Kurdistan region in northern Iraq, neighboring Turkey, gained an autonomy close to independence. After the war, it would emerge that both of the justifications used by the Bush administration for the invasion were inconsistent with reality.

Perhaps for the first time in my writing career, I hesitated on whether to say “yes” or “no” to the motion. This hesitation was expressed in my article titled “Between ‘Yes’ and ‘No’”: “Washington is expecting the 59th government, to be formed under the leadership of AKP General Chairman Recep T. Erdogan, who was elected deputy from Siirt, to resubmit the motion rejected on March 1 to the TBMM. During this waiting period, Turkey continues to debate whether to say ‘yes’ or ‘no’ to the motion. (…) The scenario that the ‘yes’ camp hopes for is that the Bush administration will be proven right, that is, that the intervention will be successful in a very short time and without much harm to the people. That the Americans will immediately establish order and bring democracy to Iraq whose integrity is preserved, then turn to resolving the Palestinian issue, opening an era of peace and democracy in the region.

“The scenario that the ‘no’ camp fears is exactly the opposite: The US wins the war but cannot win the peace; the state collapses in Iraq, civil war breaks out between ethnic groups, Turkey, along with other neighboring countries, is drawn into this war, the region begins to burn. It is because they are caught between the logic of ‘yes’ and ‘no’ that the calendar of those governing Turkey does not match Bush’s calendar. (…) If Ankara finally says ‘yes,’ it should still act according to the logic of ‘no’: Above all, it should definitely avoid standing in the way of the democratic aspirations of the people of Northern Iraq, the ethnic kin of our brothers…” (March 11, 2003)

Shortly after, I changed my view and took a determined stance against getting involved in Iraq in my subsequent articles. In the article titled “Address to the TBMM,” I called on the parliament to stand by the March 1 decision and wrote: “Distinguished deputies seated in the TBMM… Regardless of which party you belong to, stand up for the authority and dignity of the TBMM, which achieved Turkey’s independence, founded the Republic of Turkey, and is the main pillar of our democracy. No other authority besides the TBMM can decide on the stationing of foreign soldiers in Turkey or the sending of Turkish soldiers to foreign countries…” (March 15, 2003)

I explained why I was against intervention in Iraq in an article titled “We Have No Business in Iraq”: “… If we think long-term rather than short-term, we did the right thing by staying as far away and outside as possible from the war that the US started in accordance with the Bush-Sharon doctrine. Maintaining this position is a requirement of our national interests. This is so in several respects. Let’s start with the Kurdish separatism issue: There can be no doubt that the division of Turkey would be a disaster. But how will we preserve national unity?

“If we think long-term, this cannot be achieved through pressure, bans, or force of ‘arms.’ We can only preserve national unity by ensuring and reinforcing the voluntary loyalty of our Kurdish-origin citizens to Turkey. For this, we must remove without further delay the obstacles to their freely expressing their culture and identity, and seeking solutions to their troubles and problems within the democratic system. As long as Turkey’s Kurds can benefit from the blessings of Turkish democracy, as long as Turkey is a strong democracy and economy advancing on the path to EU membership, our unity will not be harmed.

“Preserving Iraq’s integrity is certainly our fundamental preference in terms of preventing the region from being dragged into great instability. But preserving Iraq’s integrity is not the task of the TSK (Turkish Armed Forces). If we had passed the motion and sent 40,000 of our soldiers to Iraq along with the Americans, even the smallest provocation could have put the TSK in the position of Israel in Palestinian territories, of the US in Iraqi territories, that is, in the position of occupier. We must be extremely vigilant because this danger is still at our doorstep. (…)

“The Republic of Turkey is not a racial state. All of our people from different origins are first-class citizens. We are related to all neighboring peoples. We must certainly use all our means to defend the rights of Arabs, Kurds, and Turkmens in Iraq, and support them in healing the wounds caused by Saddam’s dictatorship and the war. But the Turkish army should not become a force that occupies its neighbor. We must preserve our reputation in the eyes of all the people of Iraq. In the long run, this is our greatest capital.

“Let us also know this: In the end, the people of Iraq will decide Iraq’s future. If Iraqi Kurds want to be autonomous within Iraq or to be independent, Turkey should not be the one standing in their way. Iraqi Kurds are the ethnic kin of our brothers. We have all kinds of means and reasons to win their friendship and trust. We can continue the policy of friendship we have pursued since 1991, and we can act together against the PKK and the like. The closest friend of Iraqi Kurds should not be the US, but Turkey.” (Zaman, April 15, 2003)

This article also reflected the essence of my views on what Turkey’s Kurdish policy should be; how we should view our own Kurds and Kurds in neighboring countries.

“Gulen and Secularization”

One of the fundamental views I advocated with my new “social liberal or social democratic” identity after returning to the country from Sweden in the early 1980s was this: Turkey’s problems can only be solved through liberal, that is, libertarian and pluralist democracy. The establishment of liberal democracy can only be possible through this regime’s reconciliation with Islam, the belief of the majority, through secularism gaining a democratic interpretation, that is, through the separation of religion and state. The Justice and Development Party government with its “Muslim Democrat”

identity could provide this interpretation, and thus reconciliation. The Gulen community, or as they called themselves, the “Hizmet movement,” could also contribute to this.

This was also one of the reasons I agreed to write for Zaman newspaper. The first of my articles about the community in Zaman was published with the title “Gulen and Secularization.” In this article, I was referring to the articles of a sociologist, METU faculty member Elisabeth Ozdalga, who supported my expectation that the community would contribute to secularization.

” ‘One of the most powerful–and controversial–Islamic movements in Turkey is the Gulen community, gathered around the charismatic leader Fethullah Gulen. There is no other religious figure against whom circles strictly committed to secularism have shown such a reaction. Considering that Gulen’s supporters are modest people who avoid coming to the fore, this becomes even more difficult to understand. Gulen’s opponents attribute to him great, secret powers that could even challenge political authority. This fantasy is fed by a fear of ’reaction’ reaching panic proportions and ignorance about the Gulen community. This ignorance stems partly from the community’s attitude and partly from indifference to reaching a healthy understanding about this movement. The result is the development of the darkest kind of prejudices about the community.’

“Elisabeth Ozdalga’s article titled ‘Secularizing Trends in Fethullah Gulen’s Movement’ published in the Spring 2003 issue of the academic journal Critique: Critical Middle Eastern Studies begins with the observation I quoted above. In her first article on the Gulen community, titled ‘Worldly Asceticism in Islamic Casting’ published in the Autumn 2000 issue of the same journal, Ozdalga had analyzed Fethullah Gulen’s worldview. In that article, she concluded that rather than pursuing political ambitions, Gulen was trying to develop an ethical understanding directed toward the rationalization of social relations (very close to Max Weber’s concept of ‘worldly asceticism’ that he developed while studying Protestant ethics), that is, basing them on reason.

“In her newly published article, Ozdalga goes a step further, arguing that despite its strong religious appeal, the Gulen movement is actually leading the community toward secularization. According to Ozdalga, there are striking similarities between the activities of the Gulen community and Christian missionaries, especially 19th-century Protestant missionaries. The Gulen community carries an educational mission just like the 19th-century Protestant missionaries. Robert College, which is today a national, secular, expensive, and prestigious high school in Istanbul, was founded in the 19th century by Protestant missionaries who came from the US and dedicated their lives to this work. All schools established by Protestant organizations in the US and abroad in the 19th century, while initially strongly committed to Christian values, gradually transformed into truly secular institutions over time. Schools opened by Protestant missionaries initially devoted great space to religious subjects and practices. This was not the case in Gulen schools. Although teachers embraced their work with religious faith, the curricula under the supervision of the Ministry of National Education never focused on religious education.

“According to Ozdalga, there are the following similarities between the behaviors of the Gulen community and Protestant missionaries: Although the driving force in the work of both movements is religious faith, their mission or cause is not to spread religion. They are guided by more general or universal values than those belonging to a particular faith. Members of both movements share these characteristics: Leading a pious and self-sacrificing life; a deep interest in acquiring knowledge, especially in natural sciences; the desire to convey acquired knowledge to others through various educational institutions; an entrepreneurial spirit; providing useful services to society and the desire to transcend national boundaries and reach other countries of the world.

“Ozdalga’s conclusion is this: Community members may be highly devout people, but their formulating their mission as a humanitarian project weakens their religious foundations. The sociological paradox here is that even the most vibrant Islamic renewal movements can be carriers of modernization… What if the MGK (National Security Council) also read and examined Elisabeth Ozdalga’s (and of course other academics’) ‘reports’ about the Gulen community?” (Zaman, April 29, 2003)

“Where Are We in ‘Taqiyya’?”

The first of the commentaries I would write in Zaman about the nature of the AKP was titled “Where Are We in ‘Taqiyya’?” I wrote: “How the AKP, which has its roots in Turkey’s own unique Islamist movement, and the political cadre at its head, which was not distinguished by liberal qualities, has come to bear the standard for the country becoming a democracy at EU standards today, may not be easy to understand for many inside and outside the country. (…) Two main (non-mutually exclusive) ‘theories’ are being put forward to explain the change in the AKP. According to the ‘stick’ theory, we owe this change to the ‘state’s,’ that is, the military-civilian bureaucracy embodied as the MGK and the Constitutional Court’s, non-liberal interventions in the democratic process.

“According to the other, ‘carrot’ theory, we owe this change to Turkey having adopted the process of democratic political competition since the 1950s. That a political movement that does not respect the people’s fundamental preferences (democratic and secular order as well as Islamic values) can neither come to power nor maintain power was gradually understood, step by step, from the MNP to the AKP. According to this second theory, which I most fervently advocate, what happened in Turkey’s own unique Islamist movement is meaningful evidence on a global scale of democracy’s educating, democratizing quality.

“There are also those who take the change in the AKP too far. According to them, the AKP is on the way to rapidly ‘assimilating’ into the system, that is, fully conforming to the status quo, becoming indistinguishable from other parties; its only concern is actually ‘rent-seeking.’ My theory is that the AKP is in ‘cohabitation,’ living together with the system, and that its ammunition to reform the system in the direction supported by the majority has not yet run out.” (Zaman, May 24, 2003)

AKP or “Ak Party”

In all my articles, I referred to the Justice and Development Party by the abbreviation AKP; I refused to use the “Ak Party” abbreviation that the party itself preferred. I explained my reasoning as follows, when the AKP government was still in its tenth month:

“The other day I watched almost from start to finish the speech Prime Minister Recep T. Erdogan gave at an AKP provincial congress. The Prime Minister again devoted a large portion of his speech to the subject that the abbreviated name of the Justice and Development Party is not AKP but ‘Ak Parti.’ He also explained his reasoning as follows: 1) The party’s abbreviated name is registered that way. Just as the Motherland Party is called ANAP by its registered short name rather than AP, the Justice and Development Party should also be called ‘Ak Parti.’ 2) Just as the concept of ‘Justice’ in the party’s name represents the party’s ideal of ensuring justice in the country, and the concept of ‘Development’ represents achieving development, its abbreviated name also symbolizes this party’s goal of ending corruption in the country.

“I find both the Prime Minister and other Justice and Development Party officials who devote their valuable time to this claim rather strange. For the following reasons: 1) The reason the Motherland Party is commonly referred to as ANAP in the media and public opinion is presumably not because the party’s registered short name is so, but to avoid confusion with AP, the abbreviated name of the Justice Party. Moreover, the ANAP abbreviation is not loaded with meaning like the ‘Ak Parti’ (meaning ‘White/Clean Party’) abbreviation. 2) Everyone can see that there is a somewhat crude ‘image game’ behind the ‘Ak Parti’ abbreviation. This is why very few people outside party members have adopted this abbreviation. 3) Although the Justice and Development Party’s claims that it will end corruption and that it itself will first be a ‘clean party’ are as noble and commendable as its promise to achieve justice and development, they are doomed to remain mere words unless proven over time. For this reason, instead of preemptively declaring itself ‘Ak’ (‘Clean’), it would be much more convincing if the AKP waited for the people to give it this title.” (Zaman, July 17, 2003)

Let me confess that when I was writing the lines I quoted above, it did not occur to me how much my arguments in the article would be vindicated over time. But now, the reality that is clearly evident in 2021, when these lines are being written, is that the AKP represents not only the most unjust, most oppressive, but also the most degenerate, most corruption-tainted government in Turkey’s multi-party history; the gains it has made in the area of development are also rapidly declining; as the regime becomes increasingly authoritarian, the country is becoming increasingly impoverished.

“The Future of Political Islam”

My beginning to think that political Islam could become increasingly liberal was largely based on the impressions and hopes raised by the Gulen movement and the AKP government in Turkey. What made me think that similar developments could occur in the rest of the Islamic world were the analyses put forward in books and articles by Graham E Fuller, an American political scientist who had held important positions in the US intelligence agency CIA for a time. I wrote the following about Fuller’s book The Future of Political Islam (Palgrave, 2003):

“Let me say at the beginning what should perhaps be said at the end: I cannot claim to be familiar with the entire literature on political Islam, but as far as I know, Fuller’s latest work is perhaps the book most worth reading on this subject. What is political Islam or Islamism? What is its relationship to the religion of Islam? What kind of ideology is it? What forms does it take? What kind of evolution is it going through? What should the West’s attitude toward Islamism be? I hope that this newest book in this field, which in my opinion gives the most satisfying answers to these and similar questions, will be translated into Turkish without delay… Fuller’s advantage is combining his academic personality with the knowledge and experiences he gained during his tenure as deputy chairman of the CIA’s National Intelligence Council in the 1980s and during the fourteen years he spent in Islamic countries (including Turkey).

“Fuller’s most important theses are these: The religion of Islam, like all other religions, is concerned with spiritual and moral issues. Islamism is the result of efforts to produce a political ideology from the religion of Islam; it is a product not of the religion of Islam, but of the troubles experienced by Muslim societies. Islam will live on as a spiritual and moral force, but the fate of Islamism is uncertain. To understand Islamism, one must examine not the religion of Islam but the problems of Muslim societies, the demands and needs of Muslims. (Isn’t this the fundamental truth that some in Turkey cannot or do not want to understand?) Islamism should be understood not as a rigid ideology, but as a political program for expressing the social and political needs of Muslims. Islamism, which is rapidly growing, evolving, and diversifying, is today the most

powerful movement aimed at political change in the Islamic world.

“Muslim societies had previously tried secular nationalism and socialism to find a cure for their troubles, and Islamism rose as a result of the disappointments caused by these experiments. Islamism takes on many different forms ranging from Radical Islamism at one end, which wants to establish a totalitarian regime based on so-called religious principles using violence, to Liberal Islamism at the other end, which makes a synthesis of Islamic values with libertarian principles and institutions. Radical Islamism has been tried so far in three countries (Iran, Sudan, and Afghanistan) with very different practices, and has failed in each. Liberal Islamism is not the dominant trend today, but it is a rising trend, also thanks to the failures of radical Islamism and the reactions it has aroused. Radical forms of Islamism should be fought, but the way should be opened for the diversification of other interpretations; the development of liberal and pluralist Islamism should be encouraged.

“According to Fuller, the country where Liberal Islamism has gone furthest is Turkey… ‘A candidate to be the first country to succeed in making a true synthesis of Islamist and Western liberal democratic traditions.’ One disagreement I have with Fuller is whether the AKP can be characterized as liberal Islamist. I am of the opinion that because it has broken from its Islamist roots and characterizes itself as ‘Conservative Democrat,’ the AKP cannot be called Islamist. Fuller, on the other hand, finds it correct to characterize the AKP as Islamist, as a successful example of the liberal interpretation.

“Fuller also writes this about himself:”The years I spent as a CIA member, especially in the developing world, lead many people to think about me, even though I left official duty fifteen years ago, that once an intelligence officer, always

an intelligence officer.” Moreover, many foreigners believe that my views represent the CIA or the US government. I wish they did.” (Zaman, August 12, 2003)

“In Memory of Anna Lindh”

I certainly have a special affinity for Sweden, which opened its arms to me during the most difficult period of my life; which I see as the world’s relatively most civilized, most just, and freest society; whose state and society stood by me when I was accused of terrorism and would be imprisoned in Silivri. Throughout my life, I have known many Swedes from all professions. Among them, one of those who impressed me most was Foreign Minister Anna Lindh, who fell victim to murder. Lindh appeared to me as a summary of Sweden’s virtues. In the article I wrote upon her death, which I quote in full below, I tried to explain this.

“I was acquainted with Swedish Foreign Minister Anna Lindh, who died as a result of a stabbing attack. I first met her in Istanbul in January 1990, when she came to participate in a conference on social democracy. At that time, she was still the president of the Swedish Social Democratic Workers’ Party’s youth organization, SSU. On this occasion, I had a long interview with her about the ‘Swedish Model’ and social democratic youth

organizations (Cumhuriyet,

January 7, 1990).

“After she became Foreign Minister in 1998, I had the opportunity to meet with her every time she came to Turkey as well

. As a knowledgeable, intelligent, skilled, and moreover charming and humble politician, she always impressed me. The last time we had a chance to chat, although briefly, was at the beginning of February this year during the conference on ‘Women in Turkey and Sweden’ organized by the Swedish consulate general. When she was leaving the consulate building in her official car, with Turkish police guards in front and behind, she saw me and waved warmly. That scene will probably never

leave my memory.

“Unfortunately, because Anna Lindh could not be protected in her own country, she was stabbed to death one September day, in broad daylight, in the center of Stockholm, in the middle of Sweden’s most prestigious store. Very similar to the way Prime Minister Olof Palme was killed seventeen years ago… I will not remember Anna Lindh only as one of the most brilliant politicians Sweden has produced. Lindh had a special interest in and sympathy for Turkey. If she had not died, she had been due to come to our country next month for a holiday with her family. She had also emphasized in our last meeting that a Turkey that meets the Copenhagen Political Criteria cannot be excluded from the EU, and that there can be no turning back from the process that began with Helsinki. (Zaman, February 11, 2003).

“There is nothing to take seriously in the claims of some of Turkey’s filthy newspapers and filthy writers: Anna Lindh was a person who sympathized with neither separatism nor

terrorism in Turkey. During an interview, she had answered my question on this subject as follows: ’We believe it is very important to grant everyone the right to speak their mother

tongues and develop their own cultures as individual rights or minority rights. However, we also very clearly state that the Kurdish problem must be solved within Turkey’s existing borders. We have never been on the side of separatism anywhere in Europe up to now. We have always explicitly condemned terrorism, including the PKK.’ (Milliyet, February 22, 2000)

“Anna Lindh was of the opinion that whatever rights those of Kurdish origin in Sweden have,

those of Kurdish origin in Turkey should also have the same rights. Just like democrats who believe in freedom everywhere in the world… Prime Minister Goran Persson said the following after Anna Lindh’s death: ‘Social democracy has lost one of its most masterful politicians. The Swedish government has lost one of its most talented ministers and colleagues; Sweden has lost its face to the world…’ Turkey too has lost a friend.” (Zaman, September 13, 2003)

“The Impasse of Turkish-Style Secularism”

One of the topics I frequently addressed in my columns at Zaman was the critique of Turkey’s own unique, authoritarian secularism practices. In these articles, I advocated the need for ‘secularization of secularism’ in Turkey; that is, for state control over religion to give way to separation of religion and state, for restrictions on religious beliefs that are incompatible with the democratic order to be lifted. The lines I quote below reflected the essence of this view of mine:

“…It is certain that Turkish-style (alaturka) secularism is in crisis. This crisis stems, at its most fundamental level, from the conflicting aims of official identity and secularism policies. While undergoing changes over time, the identity policies of the Republic of Turkey essentially aimed to create from the Muslim population of the Ottoman Empire, which spoke many different languages and was attached to very different interpretations of Islam, a homogeneous Turkish nation that spoke Turkish, shared Turkish culture, and was attached to the state-approved (Sunni-Hanafi) interpretation of Islam. The religion of Islam was accepted as an inseparable part of Turkish identity. This is why non-Muslim citizens were never seen as part of the national community; most state positions, especially military officership, were kept closed to them.

“The secularism policy pursued by the Republic of Turkey charged the state with secularizing society, that is, with religious institutions and ideas losing their influence, with religion being removed from social life and limited to people’s inner worlds and mosques, to belief and worship. This policy was the product of the positivist philosophy that deeply influenced Ottoman-Turkish reformers: For social progress and development to be achieved, religious thought had to give way to scientific-rational thought. For this reason, Turkish-style secularism (which we can characterize as positive, militant, radical secularism or laicism) was based not on the separation of religion and state but on the state keeping religion under control. While the state supported the official interpretation of Islam with all its means through the Directorate of Religious Affairs established based on the Byzantine-Ottoman tradition, it imposed various bans and restrictions on other beliefs, on Alevism, on the Islamic interpretations of religious orders and communities, and on non-Muslim religious groups. Secularism remained limited to secular laws.

“It can be said that the Turkish-style secularism regime is caught between promoting a certain interpretation of Islamic faith on the one hand as a requirement of identity policies, and practices aimed at excluding religion from social life on the other. No one is satisfied with this type of secularism: Right-wingers and left-wingers, conservatives and liberals,

## Islamists and Kemalists, Alevis and Sunnis, Muslims and Christians,

everyone is complaining. Neither policies that define national identity with Islamic faith nor policies based on the state controlling religion and restricting religious freedoms are compatible with the requirements of liberal and pluralist democracy. As long as identity policies that define Turkishness not by language, culture, or belief but by citizenship are not adopted; as long as a genuinely secular order is not established in which religion is left to society, the state stands at equal distance from all beliefs, and all restrictions on freedom of belief are lifted, complaints will not end. It is certain that we need reform not in religion but in secularism.

“However, we are still very far from this point, because clearly Turkish-style secularism serves the interests of both parties to today’s conflicts to some extent: One side believes that with this method the state somehow controls religion, and the other side believes that with this method their religion somehow uses the state. That is why the headscarf ban,

the admission of imam-hatip high school graduates to university is being discussed, but why non-Muslim communities cannot open seminaries, why they cannot build places of worship, why changing religion is seen as a threat, etc. is not being discussed. And of course the fundamental question is not being asked: In a regime that separates religion and state, can there be

a Directorate of Religious Affairs, mosques, religious officials, imam-hatip high schools, and mandatory religion classes financed by all citizens’ taxes?” (Zaman, October 28, 2003)

I don’t think I need to explain how much further we have moved away from genuine secularism as I advocated by 2022. Under AKP rule, we have witnessed the state gradually moving away from controlling religion, and religion increasingly deeply penetrating the state.

“Goodbye Ecevit”

Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit had been one of the leaders at the focal point of my interest in politics. From the 1960s onwards, I had closely followed his discourse and behavior; for a brief period I had hoped (or deluded myself) that the DSP he founded in the 1980s would contribute to the liberalization and democratization of the country. The vote share of his party, which had carried Ecevit to the prime ministership by collecting 22.19% of the vote in the 1999 general elections, dropped to 1.22% in the general elections held three years later in 2002. Thereupon, at the DSP’s 6th Ordinary Congress held on July 25, 2004, Ecevit bid farewell to the party he founded and to politics. In the article commenting on his farewell to politics, I wrote:

“At the DSP’s 6th Ordinary Congress, Bulent Ecevit implemented a rather delayed decision: He bid farewell to the party chairmanship and to a fifty-year political life, together with his closest colleague and wife, Mrs. Rahsan. I wish Mr. Ecevit health and wellness in his years outside politics. Ecevit has a special place in the lives of my generation, to which I also belong, who attended university in the mid-1960s. The main reason for this is that no other leader has been

on the stage, part of our lives, for this long. Those of my generation who share similar

perspectives with me see three separate periods of Ecevit.

“In the first period extending to the March 12, 1971 military intervention, Turkey

‘s Workers’ Party sympathizers like me, who adopted increasingly radical forms of socialism, saw Ecevit as a bourgeois politician trying to keep

a dying collaborationist capitalism alive by making some improvements in favor of the working masses. Still, on the grounds that he represented a more democratic

form of capitalism and that it would be easier to spread socialism in a more democratic capitalism, we preferred him to other “bourgeois politicians” and trusted that he would end military rule. And so it happened.

“The period extending from the 1973 elections when the CHP became the first party to 1979 when Ecevit resigned from the prime ministership is the 2nd Ecevit period. In this period, for those who had gradually moved away from radical interpretations of socialism and reached a consensus that the issue was not overthrowing democracy and capitalism but establishing a more democratic and just society, now ‘Ecevit is our hope.’ He promised a Turkey as prosperous, just, and independent as the Scandinavian countries

. He would end the war between the extreme right and

extreme left armed gangs that caused the country to bleed internally, he would bring peace and tranquility to the country…

“These hopes peaked in the 1977 elections when the CHP succeeded in getting more than 41 percent of the vote for the first time in its history

. However, shortly after, hopes gave way to disappointment. The government that Ecevit formed in 1978 together with independents

and that could not cure any ill, I remember together with the prime minister’s increasingly prolonged and increasingly distressing empty speeches, and when he resigned

with the “Ohhh…” our whole family breathed. This period is the first experience of the Turkish people placing great hopes in Ecevit and very soon being deeply disappointed.

“For those like me who, from the 1980s onwards, came to the increasingly firm conviction that a Western-type social democratic party was Turkey’s greatest need, Ecevit’s third period began with the DSP (founded in 1985). We were thinking: Was Ecevit, when founding the DSP, aiming to purge himself of the mistakes of the pre-1980 CHP? Would the DSP become the longed-for modern social democratic party in its ideology and organization? Was it bringing a liberal nationalism respectful of our cultural differences, a”secularism respectful of religion”? Hopes flared up and died out like a straw fire.

“It was soon understood that the DSP was neither democratic, nor left-wing, nor a party; it could best be characterized as a one-person or ‘husband and wife’ party. The DSP, while representing an ethnic nationalism competing with the MHP and undiluted laicism, became the number one example of the phenomenon called ‘leader’s dominance’ in Turkish politics. If the DSP succeeded in becoming the first party with 22 percent of the vote in the 1999 elections, it was due to the Turkish people’s reaction to corruption and decay in politics and their delusion that Ecevit had captured Abdullah Ocalan. However, with the financial crisis of February 2001, the Turkish people woke up to the realities of Ecevit and his party and gave him the vote he deserved in the November 2002 elections. The fact that the CHP leader has taken Bulent Ecevit as his ‘model’ shows that even if Ecevit leaves politics and the DSP closes, the style of politics he represented will continue to live for some time.” (Zaman, July 29, 2004)

## Farewell to Ecevit

I bid farewell to Ecevit with the article I wrote upon his death on November 6, 2006:

“Bulent Ecevit, one of the figures who left his mark on Turkey’s political life for the last 40 years, has passed away. Among adults living today, those who did not at some point in their lives place hope in Ecevit are, I think,

in the minority. For those like me who opened their eyes to politics in the 1960s, Ecevit has meant something different in every period. One reason for this is that my generation’s values and views have changed over time, and of course the other

reason is the changes in Ecevit’s attitudes and behaviors. Since we’re talking about at least 40 years, what could be more natural?

“Throughout my entire journalism career, I met with Ecevit twice. Once, together with my friend Seyfettin Gursel, for the long interview we conducted at his home in Oran (which we later included in a book). (This interview appeared in the book as if it was done with Rahsan Ecevit, who was then the DSP’s proxy founding president. But as everyone understood, it was Bulent Ecevit who was speaking.) Another time, at the request of my friend Haluk Ozdalga, who was then DSP Deputy Chairman, we met at the Istanbul Provincial Chairmanship. The problems of

Turkish immigrants in Europe were to be discussed. I too was invited as someone knowledgeable. But no one asked my opinion.

“As will be understood, I had no close relationship with Ecevit. I always stayed away from political or other power holders anyway. This was partly because of my nature that does not enjoy power holders, and partly because I believed excessively that keeping distance between oneself and power holders is a principle of the profession that journalists, especially commentators, must observe.

“I had no close relationship with Ecevit, but I have intense memories of him. When Ecevit was beginning to emerge on the political scene, I was a university student deeply sympathetic to the TIP. I saw the ‘Left of Center’ movement he led as an operation to block the rise of

the TIP, which I thought was destined to rise. The March 12

memorandum being given against him was a claim I could not make sense of at the time, but later I understood that this was Ecevit’s message of commitment to civilian rule and of his candidacy for the CHP General Chairmanship. When he became CHP General Chairman in 1972 despite Inonu, I remember being very happy about it.

“Now ‘Ecevit was our hope.’ When he, as Prime Minister, paved the way for the 1974 political amnesty, opening before me the possibility of ceasing to be a political refugee in Sweden and returning to the country

, as a now convinced social liberal, I felt great affinity with Ecevit’s democratic left discourse. I could not vote in the 1977 elections; but I was among those who wholeheartedly celebrated the victory in front of the CHP’s general headquarters. ‘Karaoglan’ was going to take us to ‘Bright Days’… That day, my wife and I decided to return to the country from Sweden, and we returned the following year.

“In the period before September 12, I remember Ecevit as a Prime Minister who gave long and empty speeches. I too, like everyone else, saw that together with Demirel they were fueling political polarization and leading the country toward a military coup. And I was very resentful of Ecevit. His resignation from the General Chairmanship of the CHP, which had been closed by the September 12 administration, initially seemed rather meaningless to me. Later I would come to believe that ‘this could be a message to start an alternative political movement to the CHP, which could not put a wall between itself and the communist left.’

“I looked positively at the DSP initiative. I became hopeful about him again, thinking perhaps Ecevit had become a sincere social democrat just like me. I found Ecevit’s discourse of ‘secularism respectful of religion’ particularly apt. (The Merve Kavakci incident would cast a very heavy shadow on his sincerity on this matter.) Close friends like Ozdalga and Gursel decided to enter politics in DSP ranks. But unfortunately

it soon became apparent in all its nakedness that the DSP was neither left-wing, nor democratic, nor a party. A good assessment of Bulent Ecevit’s political legacy can be found

in Haluk Ozdalga’s book titled ‘Badly Governed Turkey: The DSP Example.’ I offer my condolences to all who loved him. May God have mercy on him. (Zaman, November 7, 2006)

“The EU Is Not a ‘Christian Club’”

I saw Turkey’s gradually approaching and eventually becoming a member of the EU as the greatest hope for the establishment of liberal and pluralist democracy in Turkey. The EU’s decision in December 2004 to begin membership negotiations, after declaring Turkey a candidate for membership at the Helsinki summit in December 1999, had strengthened this hope. However, I was also aware of the obstacles to its realization. I wrote:

“What does the decision taken by the EU Council on December 17 to begin accession negotiations with Turkey on October 3, 2005 mean? In my view, it means above all this: The EU is not a ‘Christian club’ but a project of lasting peace and democracy in Europe. This project cannot be completed without Turkey joining the EU; Turkey cannot be without the EU. Nor can the EU without Turkey. The second meaning of the December 17 decision is this: Turkey’s march toward catching up with ‘contemporary civilization,’ the modern civilization pointed out by Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, the founder of our Republic, has entered a new phase. The EU leaders on December 17, in the words of the Dutch Prime Minister Jan Peter Balkenende, truly ‘made history.’

“Turkey’s membership in the EU will take at least ten years, yes. Because due to public opinions that do not look favorably on it, the EU is subjectively not yet ready for Turkey. Turkey, objectively, is not yet ready for the EU because it is far from fulfilling all the Copenhagen Criteria. But if Turkey shows in fulfilling the political criteria

the same determination in fulfilling all the Copenhagen Criteria, what Giscard d’Estaing fears could happen: In 2015, Turkey could very well become the EU’s largest and therefore most influential country. We should never lose sight of this goal.

s.alpayf3zaman.com.tr “Yes, the decision taken by the EU Council envisages an accession process for Turkey that includes conditions different from those applied to other candidate states. However,

we must also accept that Turkey is in a different category from the states that have been (and will be) candidates for the EU to date: Almost as populous as the total of the 10 countries that joined the EU last May, with a per capita income level reaching only one-third of the EU average, with agriculture still having a considerable share in the economy

, with great income imbalance between regions, and moreover a country whose membership EU public opinions have not yet accepted. For these reasons, while it may not be desirable that the accession conditions foreseen for Turkey are different, it should be considered reasonable.

“It is stated that the negotiations will be ‘an open-ended process whose outcome cannot be guaranteed in advance’

. Yes, after the negotiations are completed, just as any member country can say ‘no’ to Turkey’s membership, Turkey, having brought its democracy

and economy into line with EU norms, can very well give up being a member in the end. Just as Norway did… Turkey’s being

strongly tied to EU structures is foreseen in case it cannot fulfill all the obligations of membership. Whether to fulfill the obligations

or not is in its own hands, so it definitely cannot be said that there is a cause for concern here regarding the future of Turkey-EU relations. The provision for suspending negotiations in case of serious and continuous violation of the principles of freedom and democracy is a provision in Turkey’s favor that ensures the continuation of the reform process

. Unlike the method followed until now, it is not sufficient for the acquis to be accepted by the candidate country on paper

, but also requiring its implementation, which can help Turkey’s economy achieve EU norms.

“Everyone knows that the expressions in the decision about ‘permanent restrictions being conceivable’ are aimed at calming European public opinions where unemployment is widespread.

Finally, for negotiations to begin, Turkey is required to sign the protocol regarding the adaptation of the 1963 Ankara Agreement with the ten new members. Ankara recorded during the summit that signing this protocol, which would bring Turkey into a customs union with the 10 new members, would not mean officially recognizing the Greek Cypriot Administration; it will also record this with a reservation when it signs the protocol. Therefore, signing the protocol is not an issue. (See Prof. Ali Karaosmanoglu’s commentary in yesterday’s Zaman.) The issue is the reality that Turkey cannot become a member of the EU without the Cyprus problem being solved. Therefore, it is inevitable that new initiatives will be launched to solve the problem.” (Zaman, December 21, 2004)

Yes, these were my hopes in 2004. Unfortunately, in 2021 when these lines are being written, almost no one is left who believes that Turkey could one day become an EU member. This is partly the result of developments in the EU that have distanced the union from digesting Turkey, but more so the result of Turkey, especially since 2011, coming under an authoritarian one-man rule and moving away from the goal of membership.

“Presidential System Does Not Suit Us”

The proposal for Turkey to abandon the parliamentary system and switch to a type of presidential system was seriously brought to the agenda for the first time by President Turgut Ozal. The proposal came up again in the early years of the AKP government. I took a stance against this idea from the days it was first proposed. In the article I wrote on the occasion of the AKP government beginning to flirt with this idea, I wrote:

“…Since the late President Ozal, proposals for Turkey to abandon the parliamentary system, which is its traditional regime, and adopt a type of presidential system instead have come up from time to time. Now the AKP is also seen to want to open this proposal for discussion. I do not know whether what the AKP administration has in mind is an American-style presidential system or a French-style semi-presidential system (which is a mixture of presidential and parliamentary systems). However, neither from the first

nor from the second am I certain that any good will come to Turkey.

“The drawbacks of the presidential system are well known. The first of these is: In case the president and the majority in parliament are from different parties, there is a danger of the system locking up or becoming paralyzed. Because in this case there is no institutional method to resolve the disagreement between the two organs. (In the semi-

presidential system, the difficulty known as cohabitation arises in case the president and prime minister belong to different parties.) Whereas the vote of confidence mechanism in the parliamentary system easily resolves disagreements between the two organs.

“The second important drawback of the presidential system is that in this system politics tends toward polarization because a single candidate and a single party win and all other candidates and parties lose. (In the semi-presidential system, this drawback is mitigated.) Presidential and semi-presidential systems may suit societies where the tendency of the leader who holds executive power to slide into authoritarianism (sultanism) is weak and the culture of compromise among politicians is strong, due to the basic drawbacks listed above, but they do not suit us.

“As far as I can see, the two basic justifications behind proposing a presidential or semi-presidential system for Turkey are: 1) Resolving the elected-appointed conflict in governance and fully establishing the authority of the former over the latter. 2) Giving long-term stability to the executive. Presidential or semi-presidential systems that tend to create polarization in politics one does not need to be a political scientist to foresee that they could yield results completely opposite to these goals in a country with Turkey’s conditions.

“On the other hand, to achieve these goals, there is no need to change the parliamentary system to which Turkey has adhered for about a hundred years. What really needs to be done is: 1) Removing the powers granted to the president by the 1982 Constitution that are incompatible with the parliamentary system and thus ending the

dual leadership in the executive, that is, establishing a pure parliamentary system. 2) Abandoning the proportional representation system that leads to unstable coalition governments and

adopting a two-round, single-member constituency majority system of the type applied in France. On this matter, we can finally say this: Since the probability of obtaining a majority in parliament sufficient for switching to a presidential or semi-presidential system is remote, it will be difficult for Turkey to be dragged into such an adventure.

“I am of the opinion that Recep Tayyip Erdogan ascending to Cankaya in 2007 within the existing system would not be auspicious for either his party or the country. The damage that Ozal’s and Demirel’s ascent to Cankaya caused to ANAP and DYP due to the leadership struggle that erupted should not be overlooked.” (Zaman, December 23, 2004)

The above article was one of the signs that I was rowing against the current in my commentary on Turkish politics. As is known, a presidential system of the “alaturka” type was accepted by referendum on April 16, 2017 (in which I, imprisoned in Silivri prison, voted “no”) and began to be implemented as of July 9, 2018. Turkey’s regime turned toward “sultanism.” It has become apparent that the drawbacks of the “alaturka” presidential system are even worse than the general drawbacks of presidential systems. Today, in 2023, opposition parties are busy with preparations to return to the parliamentary system.

“Long Live Turkey on the Path to the EU!”

I welcomed with great happiness the EU Council’s decision on October 3, 2005 to begin membership negotiations with Turkey. I wrote: “Zaman’s headline summed up the situation well: ‘Turkey’s European march continues…’ I agree with Prime Minister Erdogan’s words: Every negotiation is open-ended. The goal is full membership. Whether it will reach this goal and how long it will take is now largely in Turkey’s own hands. Perhaps any government in Turkey would have made this effort; but the determination and success the AKP government has shown on the EU path is commendable…” (Zaman, October 6, 2005)

Now, looking back from 2021, the excessive optimism I see in these lines reminds me once again how far I could be from foresight when commenting on politics.

“Re-establishing Turkish-Armenian Friendship”

A product of the AKP government’s and especially Foreign Minister Abdullah Gul’s search for normalizing relations with Armenia was the conference “Ottoman Armenians in the Final Period of the Empire: Issues of Scholarly Responsibility and Democracy.” I also participated in the conference, which was planned to be held at Bogazici University in May but after various obstacles were overcome could only take place on September 24-25, 2005 at Bilgi University under the shadow of protests, at the invitation of Halil Berktay on behalf of the organizing committee. On the second day of the conference, at a panel chaired by Murat Belge, I spoke alongside Ali Bayramoglu, Etyen Mancupyan, Ahmet Insel, Murat Paker, and (may he rest in peace) Hrant Dink. The column summarizing my speech, titled “Re-establishing Turkish-Armenian Friendship,” reflected my view on the Armenian issue. I wrote:

“I am not a historian. As a political scientist and commentator, I am primarily concerned with the current problems of Turkish political life. I find the overcoming of what we call the ‘Armenian Question’ necessary for the establishment of liberal and pluralist democracy in Turkey and for a culture of peace to prevail. Therefore, I am concerned with the future rather than the past. My question is: What can be done for the re-establishment of Turkish-Armenian friendship?

“There are certainly those among both Turks and Armenians who want to reach a reconciliation and overcome the problem. Reconciliation advocates are in the minority today, but tomorrow they could constitute the large majority. For this, solution advocates must reach consensus on some

fundamental findings. The event is this: What happened at the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century is the story of the multi-religious, multi-ethnic Ottoman Empire falling apart through the conflict of ethnic and religious nationalisms supported by imperialist European states. Ethnic-religious

cleansing, expulsion from homelands, massacre of millions - this is their story.

“Almost all ethnic and religious groups that constituted the Ottoman Empire have taken their share from this tragedy to one degree or another. The Committee of Union and Progress decided to have absolute dominance over Anatolia and to purge it of religious and ethnic elements whose loyalty it did not trust. In 1915-16, the Unionists, with the aim of

punishing the separatists who collaborated with the Russians and sought to establish an independent Armenia, subjected Armenians from almost everywhere in the country to forced migration to Syria (the province of Zor), and as a result, Armenians endured the worst of the suffering experienced during the dissolution of the Ottoman Empire.

“Not only Armenians in the war zone but Armenians from everywhere in the country except Istanbul and Izmir were subjected to the Deportation; during the forced migration, hundreds of thousands were killed or perished from hunger and disease. Some escaped the deportation by adopting Islam, some were saved by Muslims and then managed to survive by converting. Some of those who could reach Syria without dying settled there, many

migrated to France and the USA. The Turkish people have very little information about this tragedy experienced by Ottoman Armenians, and without having sufficient information

, there is absolutely no possibility of overcoming the problem. On the other hand, reaching a consensus on the claim that Armenians were subjected to genocide is out of the question. Some will insist on this claim; some will never accept it.

“But it is an indisputable fact that this claim prevents Turkey from freely discussing what happened in history. Holding all Turks of yesterday and today responsible for the crimes committed by the Unionist administration, using the genocide claim to generally

incite racist hatred and enmity against Turks is unacceptable. If a consensus can be reached on these fundamental findings, progress can be made toward a solution. As reconciliation and solution advocates in Turkey

, our duties are clear: First, we must work for our Armenian citizens to enjoy equal citizenship rights and for minority rights to be secured. Historians should, with courage and determination, accelerate research that will shed light on what happened and who was responsible. We must build public opinion for the establishment of diplomatic relations between Turkey and Armenia and the opening of borders between the two countries.

“Ankara can thereby also contribute to peace between Azerbaijan and Armenia. We must multiply and strengthen contacts

and dialogue between the civil societies of Turkey and Armenia. If we can do all this, the day will come when it will be possible to erect a monument

in Anatolia in memory of the great suffering of Ottoman Armenians.” (Zaman, September 29, 2005)

Unfortunately, hopes for Turkish-Armenian, Turkey-Armenia reconciliation could not advance. Only 17 years after the publication of the above article, in early 2022, a new step (with uncertain outcome) toward Turkish-Armenian reconciliation could come on the agenda: On January 14, 2022, representatives of Turkey and Armenia meeting in Moscow announced that negotiations had begun aimed at achieving unconditional normalization between the two countries, without bringing the Armenian Genocide and Nagorno-Karabakh issues to the table.

“Not the Parliamentary System But the Electoral System Should Change”

One of the views I advocated throughout my column-writing career and which largely failed in foreseeing the direction the country would take was that we needed to change the electoral system, not the parliamentary system. In an article on this subject, I wrote:

“There is no doubt that Suleyman Demirel, who served as prime minister seven times between 1965 and 1993, was removed from his seat twice through military interventions during this time, and served as president between 1993 and 2000, is Turkey’s most experienced politician. It is also well known that the most experienced politician is distinguished by frequently changing his views without seeing the need to explain his reasons, with his famous logic of ‘yesterday is yesterday, today is today.’ However, Mr. Demirel has been advocating, without changing his mind on this matter for at least ten years, the transition to a presidential system. In his statement to Murat Yetkin from Radikal newspaper the other day, he also said that a system should be adopted where the President is elected by the people in a two-round election (May 15). He said very confidently, ‘Eventually, both Europe and Turkey will switch to the presidential system!’…

“I have long been one of those who think that changing the parliamentary system, which is Turkey’s traditional regime, will not only be of no benefit but will create new and bigger problems. There is a very rich political science literature on the political deadlocks and polarizations that arise in presidential systems when different parties dominate the executive and legislature, and in semi-presidential systems when the president and prime minister come from different parties. Moreover, it is known that these systems can function effectively only in environments where there is a strong culture of compromise (which we do not have). What needs to be done in Turkey is to make the parliamentary system a true parliamentary system…

“However, I have long wholeheartedly supported Mr. Demirel’s proposals that the electoral system should be fundamentally changed from proportional representation to a majority system, and that candidates should be determined by primaries rather than by party leaders. The current system turns elections into a gamble. It can lead to great injustice in representation due to the 10 percent threshold. The unfair distribution of electoral districts does not give equal weight to every citizen’s vote. Because it leaves the door open for candidates to be determined by central nomination, it alienates deputies from voters and reinforces leader dominance in parties.

“In my opinion, the best solution was proposed by Prof. Dr. Seyfettin Gursel in research he did for TUSIAD years ago: A proportionally supplemented, single-member district, two-round majority system (See Milliyet, Intellectual View, November 14, 1998). A TBMM consisting of 450 (in my opinion 550 or 650) deputies elected in two rounds from small districts and 100 deputies elected through a proportional representation system with a maximum 1% threshold could provide an effective answer to our search for stability in government and justice in representation.” (Zaman, May 18, 2006)

“Freedom of Expression, the Essence of Civilization”

There were also views I advocated throughout my column-writing career that I never thought I was wrong about. One of them was my belief that freedom of expression is the essence of civilization. This was the view I held firmly after abandoning Marxism, one that never wavered. Unfortunately, under AKP rule, Turkey would increasingly move away from civilization. According to the European Court of Human Rights report, Turkey was the European country where freedom of expression and thought was most violated in 2020 as in 2019. Signals that this would be the case began to come in the early years of AKP rule. In 2006 I wrote:

“The fact that in Turkey, which is a member of the Council of Europe, NATO, OSCE and has begun membership negotiations with the EU, in the year 2006, people who neither praise nor call for the use of violence are still being tried in courts and sentenced to prison is, in my opinion, the clearest indication of how far the Republic of Turkey still is from the ‘contemporary civilization’ it is trying to achieve. Because ‘contemporary civilization’ is essentially nothing other than an environment in which ideas, thoughts, views, and theories can be freely expressed, respectfully listened to, freely debated, and criticized.

“The only thought that should be banned and punished is the call for and praise of suppressing thought, expression, that is, violence, that is, barbarism. It has been said and written I don’t know how many times before and will be said and written I don’t know how many more times: Human beings’ needs do not consist only of material needs, that is, needs like eating, drinking, shelter, and reproduction. Human beings also have spiritual needs. If human beings do not have the opportunity to freely express their ideas, beliefs, and identity without any sanction, they cannot be happy.

“The spiritual needs of human beings are sometimes stronger than their material needs. That is why many people can face all kinds of difficulties and even give up their lives for the sake of expressing their ideas, beliefs, and identity. Societies where people do not have the freedom to freely express their ideas, beliefs, and identities, that is, their personalities, cannot overcome the problems they face. That is why societies that did not allow freedom of expression withered and collapsed, while societies where freedom of expression existed advanced. That is why the fundamental struggle being waged everywhere in the world today is between those who advocate the free expression of ideas, beliefs, and identities and those who want to suppress this, that is, between those for and against civilization.

“Turkey is a society with many problems but also with tremendous potential. Turkey’s progress and rise in every respect can only be possible if it succeeds in freely discussing its problems and producing civilized solutions. It is not possible for Turkey to become a country that develops and progresses in peace unless both its appointed and elected officials fully realize this. This is the essential issue. Whether the European Union grows or falls apart, whether Turkey is admitted to the European Union or not, this truth does not change.” (Zaman, June 8, 2006)

“Why Is the World More Religious?”

One of the views reinforced by the readings I did for the “Religion and Politics” course I began teaching at Bahcesehir University was the invalidity of the theory, generally advocated by positivist thinkers, that societies would move away from religion with modernization.
