In one of my articles, I explained this view based on the theses of American sociologist of religion Peter L. Berger, whose work I was considerably influenced by:

“Nineteenth-century social scientists, especially August Comte, Karl Marx, Emile Durkheim, and Max Weber, argued that religious beliefs would gradually weaken with industrialization and modernization; that religious thought would give way to ‘rational and scientific’ thought. This was also the dominant approach in social scientists’ view of religion until the late 20th century: It was believed that as modernization progressed, societies would move away from religion, religious beliefs would have no social role, and religion would at best be confined to individuals’ private worlds.

“Those who understood secularism in Turkey not as the separation of religion and state, the state keeping equal distance from all beliefs, a political arrangement where freedom of belief including non-belief is secure, but rather as scientific thought replacing religious thought, religion being excluded from social life and confined to individuals’ consciences, the state helping this by controlling religion and restricting religious freedoms, that is, ‘secularists,’ must have thought that science was on their side. However, faced with the rise of Evangelical Protestantism in the USA, Latin America, South Korea, and elsewhere, new types of religious movements developing in Western Europe, the revival in Islamist movements, and similar developments, social scientists abandoned the theory that modernization would bring secularization in the sense of moving away from religion from the mid-1990s onward. That is, science is no longer on the side of ‘secularists.’

“It can be said that the person who best reflects the changing views of contemporary social scientists on modernization and secularization is American sociologist of religion Peter L. Berger. According to Berger, who completely abandoned his old views, the theory that rational scientific thought would become dominant with modernization (Weber), that religion would lose its social function (Durkheim), and that its influence would gradually be confined to individuals’ consciences, does not fit the realities of the world we live in; because ‘Today the world is as religious as it has been at any time in the past and in some places more intensely religious than ever in history.’ The understanding currently dominant among contemporary sociologists of religion is that as long as humans exist (even if religious institutions decline or take on new forms), religious beliefs will continue to exist. Berger expresses this view as follows: ‘The religious impulse, the quest for meaning that transcends the restricted space of empirical existence in this world, has been a perennial feature of humanity… To extinguish this impulse would require something like a mutation of the species.’ (Secularism in Retreat, 1996.)” (Zaman, October 24, 2006)

“Religious Orders from a Scientific Perspective”

In addition to Berger, the questioning by some contemporary sociologists of religion like Thomas Luckmann and Grace Davie of positivist theories that modernization would lead to societies moving away from religion also shed light, in my view, on the question of why religion, religious orders, and communities in Turkey maintained their vitality. I wrote:

“President Ahmet Necdet Sezer touched on the subject of religious orders in his press statement on the occasion of Republic Day on October 29. He said they were ‘formations that should be closed down’ and characterized ‘their presentation as civil society organizations as initiatives lacking good faith.’ The President’s statements made me think quite a bit as someone involved in social sciences. As follows: Religious orders are Sufi, mystical interpretations of Islam whose roots go back at least a thousand years. Their main purpose is the spiritual and moral training of believers (disciples) under the guidance of a sheikh (teacher). They were banned in 1925 because they were seen as a threat to Republican rule, and the ban continues today. Religious orders, which display great plurality, maintain their existence and vitality despite the ban. In 20th-century Turkey, religious communities and groups that gathered around charismatic religious figures (different from religious orders because there is no sheikh-disciple relationship) also emerged and spread.

“What is the reason for religious groups such as religious orders and communities maintaining their vitality despite prohibition and pressure? People’s needs are not limited to eating, drinking, sheltering, and reproducing; they also have spiritual needs belonging to their inner worlds. Religious groups respond to these needs as well as taking on social and economic functions. Organizations aimed at social solidarity that rush to help citizens in the grip of poverty and unemployment are organized to a very large extent by religious groups. Schools opened by religious groups have made a great contribution to meeting educational needs. A concept that greatly helps us understand the importance of religious groups for society is the concept of ‘social capital’ developed by social scientists. Social capital can be defined most simply as people cooperating on the basis of mutual trust developed in the context of face-to-face relationships.

“Since the 1980s, religious leaders’ encouraging teachings to their members to work, earn, and transform earnings into investments have played an important role behind the economic development experienced especially in Anatolian cities, behind the ‘Anatolian Tigers.’ This is what lies behind the entrepreneurial groups that some local politicians call ‘Green Capital’ and some foreign researchers call ‘Islamic Calvinists.’ The social capital provided by religious groups has had a considerable share in Turkey’s development.

“It cannot be ignored that religious groups have played a notable role in preserving social unity in an environment where the democratic rule of law has not developed, and in softening ethnic conflicts. It has also been seen that these groups have pioneered the establishment of legitimate political parties to expand the rights and freedoms of believers. It is certainly possible to characterize religious groups, as voluntary associations independent of the state, as part of civil society in Turkey as everywhere in the world.

“However, all this does not mean that there are no opportunists, moral degenerates, and religion exploiters in Turkey who exploit religious order and community solidarity and gain economic and political advantage from it. There have certainly been swindlers who, by collecting the savings of religious people who consider interest forbidden with promises of ‘profit partnership / profit share’ payments, established pyramid schemes as in the examples of the 1980s ‘bankers’ and the 2000s ‘Titans.’ Just as there have been those who derived political terror organizations from religious groups. The effective way to prevent the exploitation and misuse of religious beliefs in various ways is not prohibition and pressure policies, but transparency and the democratic oversight mechanisms it will make possible. The continued validity of bans placed on religious orders eighty years ago, in accordance with the needs of that day, in 21st-century Turkey, which is moving toward liberal and pluralist democracy, is literally anachronistic.” (Zaman, November 21, 2006)

## AKP as a Sunni Party

While taking a stance against all forms of bigotry, religious dogmatism, and the exploitation of religious beliefs for various purposes in my articles at Zaman, I also advocated for respect for religious beliefs. In this context, I harshly criticized the AKP government’s attitude toward the Alevis, the country’s largest religious minority. I wrote:

“The Istanbul 5th Administrative Court, in its decision dated October 12 and reported in the press on November 23, ruled that compulsory religion courses were contrary to freedom of belief. In the case filed by Alevi Bektashi Federation Vice President Ali Kenanoglu, the court concluded that children of parents who think that the content of the religious culture and ethics course is not compatible with their religious and philosophical beliefs should be exempted from this course…

“The decision of the 5th Administrative Court, from one perspective, in Turkey’s primary and secondary education

means the certification that compulsory religion courses are implemented in the form of teaching students the official, state-approved interpretation of Sunnism. From another perspective, it means the determination that in Turkey, which claims to have a secular regime, religious education is kept under state monopoly contrary to secularism in the sense of separation of religion and state, and that the beliefs and worship of a particular sect are being compulsorily taught to all students in public schools financed by all citizens’ taxes.

“One of the conditions for the secularization of Turkish-style secularism, that is, for the transition to a system where neither the state interferes with religion nor religion interferes with the state, is certainly the removal of religious education from being a duty of the state. Since we are far from the necessary consensus for this, shouldn’t the minimum conditions of religious freedom, one of the basic conditions of democracy, be ensured? Wouldn’t the path shown by the 5th Administrative Court be appropriate for this, that is, exempting children from compulsory religion courses if their families so wish? This

exemption, which was previously possible, is also possible within the framework of the 1982 Constitution…

“Alevi parents’ request for their children to be exempted from compulsory religion courses does not make Alevis a ‘minority’ according to either Lausanne or any other legal acquis. That Alevis are the largest religious minority in Turkey in the sociological sense is also scientifically indisputable. As for the debate about whether Alevism is a part of Islam, a sect: The head of the Directorate of Religious Affairs, the representative of the official interpretation of Sunnism, saying ‘Discussing whether Alevis are Muslim or not is an insult to Islam,’ and the Minister of National Education’s statement that ‘No one has the luxury of saying I am not taking this course’

alongside some leading representatives of the Alevi community themselves accusing those Alevis who view Alevism as outside Islam of ‘divisiveness, reducing Alevis to minority status, atheism, communism, etc.,’ are worrying examples of religious intolerance in Turkey.

“Are these statements not contrary to freedom of religion as well as to the Islamic belief that says ‘There is no compulsion in religion’? In democracies, citizens are free to choose their beliefs, including unbelief, and to interpret them as they wish. Only Alevis themselves can answer the question ‘Are Alevis Muslim or not?’ It is true that the vast majority of Alevis see themselves within Islam. But the claim that those who do not think so cannot be considered Alevi is not reasonable.

The insensitivity of AKP spokespersons, who rightly complain about restrictions on the religious freedoms of the Sunni majority, regarding the freedoms of Alevis is certainly the most obvious example of this party’s double standard in defending religious freedoms. The attitude of AKP spokespersons, who claim to represent the entire nation, reducing Alevism to ‘a culture within Islam’ and the AKP’s doors being kept closed to Alevi citizens is, unfortunately, the clearest indication that this party discriminates among citizens based on religion, that it is a Sunni party.” (Zaman, December 7, 2006)

“The Gold Medal of the Literary Olympics”

One of the events that made me happiest during the years I wrote for Zaman was Orhan Pamuk winning the Nobel Prize in Literature. On the occasion of the award ceremony, I went to Stockholm, where I had lived for nearly ten years in the 1970s, and sent the following article from there, mixed with my Swedish memories:

“Stockholm, the city where I lived the longest after Istanbul, has an important place in my life. Every place is full of memories. Since my permanent return to the homeland twenty-five years ago, I come to Stockholm once a year, sometimes once every 2-3 years. For the first time, I came with such great happiness and excitement. After settling into the hotel, I immediately headed to Stockholm University to see an old friend. When I entered the metro station, I encountered a huge sign. It said: ‘Dear Orhan Pamuk, we wish you a good time in Stockholm! Since you’ve come this far, wouldn’t you consider a more permanent solution? As an expression of our respect for you, we have opened a page at www.pamukforpresident.se. Was that too much? Then what do you say to <www.iwonthenobelprize.se>? In any case, we would be very pleased to host you.’ The city of Stockholm was advertising itself in this way with Orhan Pamuk, who had arrived here the day before.

“On my way back, I stopped by the university’s bookstore. A special corner had been prepared for the 2006 Nobel Prize in Literature. All of Orhan’s novels stood before me with their Swedish and English translations… When I arrived at the hotel, I reviewed the newspapers dated December 6. Sweden’s number one newspaper Dagens Nyheter, in its news with the headline ‘Nobel Prize in Literature winner arrives in Stockholm,’ wrote that Swedish Academy Secretary General Horace Engdahl greeted Orhan at the door of the plane and took him to the city in a limousine. When I turned on the television before going to bed at night, with the magnificent views of Istanbul in the background, I listened to what Orhan had said to the world media at the press conference he held that morning.

“When I picked up Dagens Nyheter the next morning, I saw that the editorial was devoted to Orhan Pamuk. The editorial, which began ‘This year’s Nobel Prize in Literature winner Orhan Pamuk strongly supports Turkey’s EU membership. Pamuk has as multifaceted an authorship as the European integration project…’ was about the importance of Turkey’s EU membership for Europe and the world. It seemed to me that Stockholm and the world through Stockholm went to sleep and woke up with Orhan Pamuk.

“I attended the luncheon given by our Stockholm Ambassador Mr. Necip Eguz and his wife Mrs. Senay in honor of Orhan Pamuk. After he won the Nobel, I found the opportunity to embrace Orhan there for the first time to congratulate him, and to thank him for the joy and pride he gave us. At this age, I have not experienced another event that made me as happy as a Turk as Orhan Pamuk winning the Nobel. I asked the Ambassador what Orhan’s success meant for Turkey’s image and prestige. Raising his hand toward the ceiling, he said in a single word, ‘Tremendous!’ He told how Swedes who recognized him from photographs in newspapers stopped him on the street and said, ‘You are the Turkish ambassador, aren’t you? I heartily congratulate you on the Nobel Prize.’

“December 7, 2006, Thursday, the biggest event in Stockholm was, of course, Orhan Pamuk’s Nobel Prize acceptance speech at the Swedish Academy’s historic and magnificent building in the old city. Although it was announced that he would give his speech in Turkish, tickets had sold out days in advance, and the hall was packed full. The large majority in the hall would follow the speech from the distributed Swedish and English texts. When Orhan entered the hall together with Engdahl

hundreds of people stood up and applauded our great writer for minutes. The whole world listened in ‘Turkish.’ His speech titled ‘My Father’s Suitcase’ was about the story of Orhan Pamuk’s authorship and his father’s role in this story. He told how his late father, when he read his first novel, embraced Orhan and said, ‘My son, you will win the Nobel one day.’

“When he ended his emotional speech, listened to in complete silence, with ‘Distinguished members of the Swedish Academy who gave me this great award, this honor, distinguished guests, I very much wish my father were among us today…’ many of our eyes had welled up with tears… After leaving the Swedish Academy, I returned to the hotel with a long walk. Along the way, I thought about how much I envied Orhan, and how I had never envied anyone else in life. Years ago I had told him too: How much I envied him for giving his entire life only to literature and for never doing anything other than writing…

“My early youth ideal was also to become a literary figure, to write novels; but my path was drawn more by fate than by myself. Yet that evening my heart was laden not with envy, but with pride… Yes, Orhan Pamuk received the gold medal of the literary Olympics; he brought great reputation and prestige to Turkey. He succeeded in reaching humanity in 49 languages, including most recently Vietnamese, Bengali, and Basque, which only a few hundred thousand people can read and write. He alone carried Turkey to the world. No matter how much we take pride in him, it is not enough.” (Zaman, December 9, 2006)

Is Islamic Liberalism Possible?

During the years I wrote for Zaman, I had the belief that not only dogmatic-totalitarian but also liberal, libertarian interpretations of Islam and Islamism were possible, and the expectation that such interpretations would gradually become dominant. One source of encouragement for this was certainly the Iranian Islamic (not Islamist) thinker Abdulkerim Sorush, whom I met in Istanbul in the mid-1990s and whose writings I continuously followed afterward. I wrote the following about Sorush and political liberalism:

“We know that all religions, including Islam, have both fundamentalist and reformist interpretations. It can be said that fundamentalist interpretations adhere to the letter, that is, the word of sacred texts; while reformist interpretations take as their basis the spirit, that is, the meaning of sacred texts. Iranian theologian, philosopher of Islam and science Dr. Abdulkerim Sorush rejects views that he is the ‘father of ideas’ for ‘reformist’-inclined clerics in his country; but there is no doubt that he is a leading representative of libertarian, liberal Islamic thought. It is possible to summarize Sorush’s basic ideas as follows:

“Islam is not only compatible with democracy, but Islam cannot exist where there is no democracy. Efforts to produce totalitarian political ideologies from religion are contrary to Islam. Because there is no compulsion in religion; belief based on coercion is not real belief. To be a believer, one must first have the right to believe, human rights. For an individual to truly believe, they must be free to adopt faith and to abandon it if they wish. For this, religion and state must be separated, neither religion should interfere with the state nor the state with religion. Secularism in the political sense is not the rival or

enemy of religion, but its complement.

“Sacred texts are divine and do not change, but their interpretation belongs to humans and changes. Therefore, there is no interpretation of Islam valid for every place and time; interpretations change over time. Islam does not grant any group, including clerics, the authority to monopolize the interpretation of religion. All believers have the right to interpret their beliefs as they wish. Clerics can have no privileges over other citizens. In order to free themselves from being spokespersons for official or popular views, they should receive salaries from neither the state nor the people, and should earn their

living by working. In the West, religion and science clashed, and finally declared a ceasefire; but both benefited from this conflict and learned to be more humble. The interpretations of religion should not conflict with science. If a particular interpretation of religion is an obstacle to progress, progress can be encouraged by changing the interpretation. The secret of progress lies in rationalism and the ability to criticize oneself.

“Sorush, who was appointed by Khomeini to the Cultural Revolution Council tasked with reorganizing university education programs after the 1979 Islamic Revolution, resigned from the council in 1983 due to disagreements. In the 1990s, his relationship with the regime grew increasingly strained; he began publishing”Kiyan,” which became a magazine for religious intellectuals. The magazine was closed by the regime in 1998. Sorush not only lost his job at Tehran University, but his lectures also began to be targeted by attacks from regime supporters. Saying in response to the pressures he faced, “Has this country become a place where a professor must risk his life to give a lecture or conference? Do we need Galileos and Brunos?” Sorush left Iran in 2000. He gave lectures at Harvard, Yale, and Princeton universities in the USA, then at the Wissenschaftskolleg in Berlin. He is currently a visiting professor at the University of Amsterdam.

“The interview I conducted with him (Milliyet, August 14, 1995) had contributed to Sorush becoming known in Turkey as well. After an approximately 11-year hiatus, I found the opportunity to be together again and chat with Sorush, who visited Turkey last week. Naturally, we also talked about what the results of the local council and Assembly of Experts elections held on December 15 in Iran meant. Sorush does not see the election results, which Nesrin Alavi characterized as the end of Mahmoud Ahmadinejad’s rise (Open Democracy, December 19), as harbingers of major political changes in Iran. According to him: The vast majority of the people are satisfied with their situation because they are receiving a share of the increased oil revenues in recent years. The regime has complete control in the political, economic, and cultural spheres. The differences among the holders of political power do not carry significant importance. No change should be expected in Iran’s established order for at least the next twenty years.” (“Abdulkerim Sorush and Islamic Liberalism,” Zaman, December 26, 2006)

Today, as I write my memoirs in 2021, I can say that there is no trace left in my mind of the expectation that liberal interpretations of Islam could gradually become dominant, and that I am completely disappointed on this matter. It was also understood that Sorush was not wrong in his pessimism regarding Iran.

## In Memory of Hrant Dink

Agos, the newspaper of the Armenian community in Turkey, published mainly in Turkish and Armenian, began publication in 1996. I appreciated the efforts of Hrant Dink, the newspaper’s editor-in-chief and writer, both to have Turkish society face the great catastrophe that befell Ottoman Armenians and to bring about rapprochement between Turkey and Armenia. When I visited the Agos office, which was then in Beyoglu, to meet him in the early 2000s, the warmth he showed me made me very happy. We had come together on various occasions and had spoken on the same panel at the Ottoman Armenians conference held at Bilgi University in 2005.

Hrant’s falling victim to a shadowy assassination in front of the Agos office in Osmanbey on January 19, 2007 had deeply shaken me. In the article I wrote in great sorrow upon the sad news and sent to the newspaper, after making references to Hrant’s last article published on January 10, I wrote:

“Hrant Dink was a friend of mine. He was a person with a warm heart and a lion-like character. His conscience was free, his mind was free. He was a first-class intellectual who did not hesitate to say what he believed was right. He was as much a Turk as he was an Armenian. He had put his life on the line to re-establish Turkish-Armenian friendship and gave his life for this cause. I feel great shame and great pain in the name of Turkey, Turkishness, and humanity…

“Those who killed Hrant dealt a very heavy blow to Turkey, Turkishness, and humanity. Those who killed Hrant truly degraded Turkey and Turkishness… There could be no greater insult to Turkey and Turkishness… No heavier blow could be dealt to Turkish democracy and Turkey’s prestige and reputation in the world… Unfortunately, the cost of this crime committed by the real enemies of Turkishness will be very heavy for Turkey. Hrant Dink died physically. But he will live forever with the great contribution he made to Turkey’s cause of freedom and democracy.” (“Hrant Dink (1954 - 2007): Here is your price…,” Zaman, January 20, 2007)

I would also write the following after Hrant’s funeral:

“The great reaction shown to the savage and treacherous murder of Hrant Dink, who was targeted through a hate campaign conducted by racist circles, was a strong sign that humanity and civilization will sooner or later prevail over barbarism and brutality in Turkey. Tens of thousands of Istanbulites marching behind Hrant Dink’s coffin with slogans of ‘We are all Hrant… We are all Armenian’ were only saying ‘We are all human!’… More than a hundred thousand Istanbulites from all walks of life and all origins marching in silent rebellion behind Hrant’s coffin gave a lesson in humanity. But the real lesson in humanity was given by his wife Rakel Dink with her dignified stance that day. In her speech that touched hearts, she said, ‘Whatever their age, 17 or 27, whoever the killer is, I know they were once babies. Nothing can be done without questioning the darkness that creates a killer from a baby, my brothers…’” (“Lessons in Humanity,” Zaman, February 15, 2007)

## The 367 Crisis

As the term of the 10th President Ahmet N. Sezer approached its end in May 2007, the debate over who would replace him had become one of the main items on the political agenda. Representatives of the authoritarian secularism understanding that restricted religious freedoms launched a campaign against the possibility of Prime Minister Erdogan being elected President. Cumhuriyet newspaper came out with the headline “Are you aware of the danger?” CHP chairman Deniz Baykal threatened Erdogan, “Don’t you dare be a candidate!” In this environment, after intra-party negotiations, Erdogan announced (even though perhaps he himself actually wanted the position) that the AKP’s presidential candidate was Foreign Minister Abdullah Gul.

Threats aimed at preventing Gul’s election peaked with the statement published by the General Staff at midnight on April 27. However, the AKP government, trusting the strong voter support behind it, reacted harshly to the General Staff’s memorandum for the first time in Turkish history. Government spokesman Cemil Cicek made a statement emphasizing that the TSK was attached to the Prime Ministry and responsible to the Prime Minister. Following this, Chief Public Prosecutor of the Court of Cassation Sabih Kanadoglu distorted the rule that according to the constitution, two-thirds of TBMM members, that is, 367 deputies, must vote for the President to be elected in the first round, with a scandalous interpretation, putting forward the condition that 367 deputies must be present in the General Assembly in the first round for the election. When none of the opposition parties participated in the first round, the Constitutional Court (following Kanadoglu) annulled the election. Thereupon Gul withdrew his candidacy; the AKP decided to hold early elections on July 22.

In the articles I wrote during the 2007 presidential election process, I advocated that Erdogan continue as prime minister, Gul as foreign minister, and that an AKP member who the opposition could also support be elected to the Presidency. I first explained my opinion on this matter in an article titled “Erdogan should remain prime minister” as follows:

“Last week I met with the 9th President Suleyman Demirel in a television program. Of course, we asked him what he thought about the presidential debates. Mr. Demirel implied that Prime Minister Erdogan’s election as President was inevitable, saying that the answer to this question was given on November 3, 2002… However, I have not yet lost hope: I think Erdogan has services to render to Turkey as Prime Minister and I am expecting an announcement that another respected AKP member is a candidate for the Presidency.” (Zaman, April 17, 2007)

The television program I mentioned above had been the occasion for my first and last meeting with the late Demirel. At that time, I was one of the regular guests of “High Politics,” the program of my friend from the AFS years Haluk Sahin, broadcast on TV8. Meeting Demirel through the program would be a valuable opportunity for me. When Mr. Demirel came to the studio, Haluk and I greeted him together. Thinking that he might not know me, I introduced myself somewhat embarrassed, saying “Mr. President, I am Sahin Alpay. I am a faculty member at Bahcesehir University, and I also write a column for Zaman newspaper…” Demirel looked at me with a mocking air and said, “I was prime minister seven times and president for seven years in this country; I know who Sahin Alpay is…” I had wanted to sink into the ground… It was known that Demirel had an extraordinary memory. Certainly, during the years he was in office, MIT files about me must have come before him, he must have come across my newspaper columns and the television programs I participated in. The late Demirel (1924 - 2015), whose policies often saddened me and sometimes gave me hope, had left me no choice but to apologize.

# CHAPTER XII / BOTH SUPPORT AND OPPOSITION TO THE AKP

In its early years, I viewed the AKP government quite positively and with hope. However, starting from 2007, I began to voice my objections to their policies while maintaining what I considered a balanced perspective—supporting them on one hand while not withholding criticism on the other. In one of the first articles I wrote from this angle, I said:

“First of all, I must state that I greatly appreciate the role played by the AKP under the leadership of Recep T. Erdoğan, Abdullah Gül, and (yes) Bülent Arınç in transcending the National Vision Movement and in committing Turkey’s distinctive Islamist movement to democratic and secular principles. The AKP’s performance in power was even more successful than I expected. The AKP government made a very important contribution to raising democratic standards in Turkey, especially in the context of EU reforms,

and by ensuring macroeconomic stability, it achieved a significant development push.

“Our not getting entangled in the Iraq quagmire until now was perhaps a matter of luck. But with its foreign policy bearing the signatures of Abdullah Gül and Ahmet Davutoğlu, which was based on diplomacy and dialogue, Ankara increased its prestige across almost the entire world—from the USA to Israel, from the EU to the Islamic world, from Africa to India and China. The AKP became synonymous with change and progress in Turkey. In the upcoming elections, the Turkish people will appreciate these services.

“What we have experienced since the April 27 memorandum shows that the gains Turkey achieved under AKP rule are unfortunately at risk due to the AKP administration’s own mistakes. I hope Turkey succeeds in overcoming the crisis we are going through and continues and strengthens the democratic process. But if the AKP leadership is to continue leading change in Turkey, it must once again succeed in learning from its mistakes and purging itself of errors. To help with this, I want to list what I consider the AKP’s most important mistakes and errors.

“It is quite obvious that the AKP made a complete mess of the presidential election. The AKP administration, by treating this issue as an internal party matter, as ‘capturing another position while the opportunity arose,’ paved the way for the April 27 military intervention. However, an AKP member whom the opposition could also accept could have been elected president, and this crisis might not have occurred. The elimination of the bureaucratic tutelage regime established through military interventions requires a patient, long-term struggle to be won step by step. I hope the AKP administration immediately abandons its enthusiasm for transitioning to a semi-presidential system ‘while taking advantage of the opportunity’ and aims to strengthen the parliamentary system.

“The AKP must take seriously the widespread doubts and fears about its commitment to secularism and its respect for different lifestyles and beliefs, and do what is necessary to address them. Those who want respect for their own lifestyles and beliefs must be respectful of others’ lifestyles and beliefs. This principle applies to everyone. The AKP must use every opportunity to show the nation that it is committed to this principle. In this context, the primary problem it must immediately overcome is to cease being a ‘Sunni party’ and to ensure that Alevi and non-Muslim citizens are represented at all levels of the party. Without achieving this, the AKP can neither convince society of its commitment to secularism nor become a center party, a party of the entire nation, as it claims. The most justified objection directed at AKP rule is the criticism of ‘cadre-building.’ The impression has taken hold that loyalty, not merit, is the basis for almost every appointment. In its second term in power, the AKP must completely erase this impression. Autonomous boards must be ‘autonomous in substance, not just in name.’ It must be understood that this is in the interest of all governments and the country.

“The claim of being ‘Ak (meaning Clean) Party’ requires proof. Unfortunately, the experiences of 4.5 years of AKP rule (despite the main taps being turned off) are not of a nature to convince anyone that corruption is behind us. The impression that corruption has grown along with the economy is widespread. Finally, the AKP should devote its greatest effort to making the Copenhagen Criteria the Ankara Criteria, to fulfilling these standards. The most crucial task here is establishing the rule of law. The rule of law cannot be established unless political murders are fully brought to light. Those who do not do everything possible to establish the rule of law will themselves become victims of lawlessness.” (“My Objections to the AKP,” Zaman, 24.5.2007)

“Abdullah Gül should remain as foreign minister”

In the general election held on July 22, 2007, the AKP received 47% of the vote and maintained power much more strongly; the MHP, which had remained outside parliament in the 2002 elections, also passed the threshold and entered parliament. When the AKP won 341 and the MHP won 70 parliamentary seats, the 367 requirement was easily surpassed, and Gül was elected the 11th President on August 28, 2007. Despite the great electoral victory it won, I insisted on the idea that the AKP should elect the new president by reaching consensus with the opposition, because I believed it would be the right thing to do, even though I did not think it likely. I wrote:

“Judging by the interview he gave to Hasan Cemal, Foreign Minister Abdullah Gül appears to have decided to run for President again. (Milliyet, July 26) I have not been warm to this idea since the day his candidacy was mentioned. The July 22 election results did not change my mind either… My final word on this matter is: I see it as being in the country’s interest for Mr. Erdoğan to continue as prime minister and Mr. Gül to continue as foreign minister for at least one more term.” In the same article, I said I would consider Gül’s presidency a “waste of talent.” (Zaman, 28.7.2007)

However, in light of the electoral victory it achieved despite the April 27 memorandum, the AKP administration did not give up on Gül’s candidacy, and Gül was elected the 11th President of the Republic of Turkey on August 28, 2007, receiving 339 votes in the third round of the presidential election held in the Grand National Assembly. Upon it becoming clear that he would be elected, I wrote the following:

“As a commentator who believes that Foreign Minister Abdullah Gül assuming the presidency is a waste of talent, I must first state this: I wish Mr. Gül success in his new position. Everyone must show absolute respect for the decision of the Grand National Assembly, the most fundamental institution of our democracy. However, there is benefit in examining what Gül’s presidency means for Turkish political life. The fundamental goal is for Turkey to be a free and prosperous country in every sense. For reforms toward the establishment of democracy and modernization of the economy to continue, bureaucratic tutelage must end. There is complete consensus on these matters among those who believe in freedom and democracy. However, opinions differ on how the bureaucratic tutelage regime can be liquidated.

“The view that dominated the AKP leadership until last April was this: Erdoğan would ascend to Çankaya, thus the Presidency, the fortress of the tutelage regime, would also pass to the AKP. After the general election, the constitution would be changed and a semi-presidential system would be established. Erdoğan and Gül would govern the country together. However, this scenario was abandoned at the last moment partly due to strong objections from the tutelage front to Erdoğan’s ascent to Çankaya, and partly due to concerns that power could be lost if he left the party leadership; Gül was declared as a candidate instead of Erdoğan.

“When the Constitutional Court’s invention of ‘367’ made the presidential election impossible, an early election became necessary. In light of the discussions conducted in public opinion and the experiences gained, Erdoğan changed his view on two important matters: 1) He saw that breaking bureaucratic tutelage could be possible through patient, step-by-step struggle, and decided that at this stage it would be more appropriate for a low-profile AKP member to ascend to Çankaya. 2) He abandoned the semi-presidential system. He tasked an expert committee headed by Prof. Dr. Ergun Özbudun with preparing a democratic constitution draft that would strengthen the parliamentary system and grant only symbolic powers to the president.

“The elections resulted in AKP’s victory. Bülent Arınç, saying that the architect of this was Erdoğan and therefore everyone should accept the positions he deemed appropriate, did not run again for Speaker of the Grand National Assembly. A low-profile AKP member, Köksal Toptan, was elected to this position with very broad consensus. Erdoğan emphasized that he wanted ‘work, not crisis’ in the new term; he said he would go to the opposition parties with a candidate list; he gave all the signs that he preferred Gül to withdraw his candidacy. But he also emphasized that ‘the decision and responsibility’ belonged to Gül. When Gül insisted on his candidacy, Erdoğan had nothing left to say. Since the MHP announced that it would take the victimhood card from the AKP’s hands, Gül’s ascent to Çankaya as the 11th President on August 28 was certain. (…)

“So, what does Gül’s ascent to Çankaya bring? It is clear from day one that a suitable ground for the opposition’s tactics of putting the government in conflict with the military and civilian bureaucracy will emerge. How will this affect the political and economic stability that we have greatly benefited from? Will the AKP government be strengthened or weakened in dealing with the tough domestic and foreign problems before it? Will we face a ‘two-headed’ AKP in the coming period? Will the constitution that would grant only symbolic powers to the president

be shelved? It is certain that uncertainties have increased.” (“Everyone Must Respect the Decision of the Grand National Assembly,” Zaman, 16.8.2007)

“Congratulations”

It quickly became apparent that my suggestion on who should be president, like my suggestions on other matters, was extremely idealistic. When it became clear that Erdoğan would remain prime minister and Foreign Minister Abdullah Gül would be brought to the presidency, I found myself having to say “Congratulations”:

“Because of his conciliatory and reconciling character, it is understood that Mr. Gül’s presidency is approved even by segments that are not fanatically opposed to the AKP. There is no reason why Mr. Gül should not show the same success in the presidency that he showed in the Foreign Ministry. Perhaps most importantly, Mr. Gül’s words about what kind of president he would be if elected: ‘I know Turkey’s sensitivities. I am also aware of the problems Turkey faces. From today, I am determined to work in harmony with all institutions and civil society. I will try to put myself in everyone’s place and think that way. I will embrace everyone.’ If Gül remains true to these words, the presidency can become an office that solves problems rather than creates them. Congratulations on the presidential election.” (Zaman, 26.4.2007)

Interestingly, my advocacy for Abdullah Gül to remain as foreign minister would also have a ‘cost’ for me. During the presidency of Gül, who had made me happy in 2001 when we met by saying that my writings had contributed to the formation of the ‘Reformist’ movement that brought the AKP to power, I was not invited to any reception at Çankaya. Whether not having been invited to Çankaya throughout my column-writing career can be considered a deficiency from my standpoint, I do not know.

## My AKP optimism at its peak

In the days leading up to the July 22, 2007 elections, Haluk Özdalga called: Prime Minister Erdoğan had proposed parliamentary candidacy to two former CHP members, himself and Ertuğrul Günay; he was asking how I would react to his becoming a candidate from the AKP. I told him to definitely accept. This would be a contribution to keeping the AKP on the right track. When he asked “what would you do if you received such an offer,” I got the impression he was sounding me out. I replied, “I’m not thinking about politics; I’m happy with what I’m doing, I want to maintain my independence…” When their candidacies were announced, I called both to congratulate them. Günay said, “The boss had mentioned that he would also propose candidacy to you, but for some reason he changed his mind…” If I had received such an offer from Erdoğan, would I have accepted? I don’t think so.

I interpreted the great success the AKP achieved in the 2007 general elections as a new victory for democracy. I wrote: “My first column in Zaman newspaper, published two days after the November 3, 2002 elections, was titled ‘Victory of Democracy.’ The July 22, 2007 elections also resulted in a new victory for democracy. Mainly for these reasons: The Turkish people conducted the 15th general elections since the transition to a multi-party system with great maturity, with high turnout (around 85%), and without any noteworthy incident. The efforts of gangs to sabotage democracy, the speculations that some excuse would be found to prevent the elections, proved futile, and the bomb plots in this direction failed.

“The Turkish people gave clear and explicit support to the single-party rule of the last five years; they said ‘continue on the path’ to the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government. Despite perhaps the world’s worst electoral system (proportional representation with a 10% threshold), the situation that emerged in the last election was not repeated, no ‘shadow’ fell on democracy: The proportion of votes that would not be represented in parliament fell to an acceptable level (around 13%). The ruling party will have fewer seats in parliament, but will form a stronger government with much greater legitimacy and authority (because no ‘shadow’ of inadequate representation fell on parliament). At the same time, it will be monitored by a stronger opposition consisting of at least three parties. It is hoped that, as indicated by the signals given in the Prime Minister’s thank-you speech, greater attention will be paid to the need for consensus with both parliamentary and extra-parliamentary opposition on fundamental decisions.

“The biggest message these elections gave is that voters definitely do not approve of polarizing attitudes. As a reformist party in favor of open society and competitive economy, the AKP was registered as the dominant, center party of the system. Despite perhaps the world’s worst electoral system, the political party that claims to represent primarily the concerns and demands of our citizens of Kurdish origin, the DTP, entered parliament through independent candidates. This is a very important opportunity to exclude violence and weapons from Turkish politics, if all politicians act responsibly. That this opportunity not be wasted is perhaps the greatest hope born of these elections.

“With the July 22 elections, the AKP received the authority to govern the country alone for another five years. Approximately half of the voters from every background, belief, and class and from all regions of the country said ‘Yes!’ to the AKP. The AKP became the party that increased its vote share the most while in power in the history of Turkish democracy. How can this great electoral victory be explained? The main reasons can be listed as follows: The AKP government (following the ‘roadmap’ drawn by the EU) stabilized the economy in Turkey, average income increased by more than double; a relative improvement in income distribution was achieved. Despite ongoing problems with fundamental rights (thanks to EU reforms), Turkey became a country where freedoms expanded compared to pre-2002, where fundamental rights were more respected, and where improvements in the human rights field were experienced. The vast majority of voters did not give credence to claims that secularism was in danger or that the ruling party was responsible for the surge in terrorism.

“The fact that the opposition parties were run by a tested cadre whose failures were established, who lacked credibility, and who were quarrelsome worked very much in the AKP’s favor. Another factor explaining the AKP’s electoral victory is undoubtedly Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s having support even higher than his party. ‘Charismatic authority’ is effective on a significant portion of Turkish voters. On the other hand, it is clear that many CHP voters either voted for another party or did not go to the polls because of the party’s ‘repellent’ leader. It is difficult to estimate what contribution the anti-democratic interventions by the military and civilian bureaucracy in the presidential election process made to the support given to the AKP. According to KONDA researchers who successfully predicted the election results, the AKP’s vote appeared to be above 45% since September 2006. Certainly today Turkey looks to its tomorrow with greater confidence and optimism.” (“The New Victory of Turkish Democracy,” Zaman, 24.7.2007)

## Problems cannot be solved if ideas are not free

In my articles in Zaman, I explained the most fundamental principle I adhered to:

“I have forty years of experience in expressing my thoughts in writing and orally in public. During these forty years, my ideas have changed and evolved considerably depending on what I learned by reading, living, and discussing. During these forty years, while expressing my thoughts, I had to struggle on the one hand with the restrictions and bans imposed by the state, and on the other hand with the prejudices of the society and environment I was in (if you will, ‘neighborhood pressure’), and I still struggle. Looking at the fact that the limits of freedom of expression are gradually expanding and that ‘neighborhood pressure’ on those who think differently is gradually easing, I still maintain my optimism for the future.

“When faced with a question like ‘What is the most fundamental lesson given by forty years of experience?’ my unhesitating answer is this: There can be nothing that gives greater happiness to a thinking person than saying what they think, and nothing that causes greater torment than not being able to say what they think… For a society to overcome the problems it faces, there is no more effective way than acquiring all the information it can reach about the facts that give rise to the problems and conducting the broadest discussion about how they can be solved… The advancement of science is also only possible where there is freedom to question and criticize… For this reason, no limit should be placed on expression other than calls for and praise of violence, incitement of hatred and enmity, and insult, and people should be encouraged to say what they think… This is the strongest, the most indispensable of the ideas and principles I adhere to.

“Because this idea and principle, unfortunately, is still far from being established in our society, like others I often feel the need to voice it. These days we are living through times when the negatives arising from Turkey’s two fundamental problems, the ‘Kurdish problem’ and the ‘Armenian problem,’ not having been overcome are piling up. It is certain that both problems have very complex aspects and that there are no easy solutions. But the fundamental truth behind these problems with about a century of history still occupying and distressing us today is that Turkish society has been prevented from acquiring all the available information about the facts that gave rise to them and from conducting the broadest discussion about how they can be overcome. The primary instrument of this prevention is, no doubt, the cover called ‘official history’

that the state has been trying to spread over historical facts for years using laws, the education system, the media, and other means, and which has only begun to be torn in recent years.

“Perhaps the best indicator of this dire situation is the point reached in the ‘Armenian problem.’ This problem is essentially the inability to freely discuss the questions of ‘What happened to the Ottoman Armenians in 1915-16?.. Are there responsibilities that these events impose on the Republic of Turkey?..’ The imposition of ‘official history,’ that is, the state’s view on this matter, on society, the punishment of those who think differently, and their exposure to the harshest insults and the harshest ‘neighborhood pressure.’ Was not our valued colleague Hrant Dink, who made great efforts to achieve Turkish-Armenian reconciliation and to free relations from being a subject of confrontation fueled by ethnic nationalists on both sides, made the target of a campaign of hatred and enmity for expressing his ideas?

“Was he not, in a great injustice, sentenced to prison under Article 301 of the Turkish Penal Code for allegedly ‘insulting Turkishness’? Did it not become plainly clear that despite reports that he would be killed, the necessary measures for his protection were not taken? Even after he was killed, was his trial not continued, and this time was not his son Arat Dink also convicted? Are not those who (rightly) oppose the criminalization of saying ‘there was no genocide’ in Switzerland and France also defending the criminalization of saying ‘there was genocide’ in Turkey? Is not this the fundamental reason behind the resistance to changing or abolishing Article 301 of the Turkish Penal Code? Is the number of those prosecuted under Article 301 not increasing every day? As long as we cannot fully establish freedom of expression, as long as a ‘culture of fear’ dominates even our universities, we cannot overcome any problem.” (Zaman, 18.10.2007)

## Opportunity in the Kurdish problem

I thought that the AKP’s emerging from the July 22, 2007 elections with its power strengthened created an opportunity for the Kurdish problem to enter a path to solution:

“After the July 22 elections, an opportunity arose to solve the Kurdish problem and end PKK terrorism. Not only the domestic but also the external conjuncture became perhaps more favorable than ever. Why? It is certain that after entering the EU accession process, the world’s perception of Turkey changed. Because after the 2001-2004 EU reforms with the de facto recognition of Kurdish identity, some steps being taken to remove the obstacles to citizens who consider themselves Kurdish freely living their language and culture, and the expansion of freedom of expression, there remained no justifiable aspect to the armed uprising.

“Even those who saw the PKK as ‘freedom fighters’ began to understand that it was a genuinely terrorist organization that applied the harshest terror mainly to Kurds and its own members. Perhaps the clearest sign that the external conjuncture had changed was both the USA and the EU placing the PKK on their lists of terrorist organizations in 2002. The PKK, which serves an unclear purpose and unclear masters, panicked about losing its influence among Turkey’s Kurds after the July 22 elections. It escalated provocative attacks aimed at drawing Ankara into

a Turkish-Kurdish war encompassing the entire region by occupying Northern Iraq. The EU strongly condemned the attacks and stood by Turkey. The US administration also finally understood that the PKK was also seeking to destabilize Northern Iraq… At the point reached today, it can be seen that both the USA and the KRG want the liquidation of the PKK, which is a festering sore that damages their relations with Turkey.

“In light of the experiences since 1984 when the PKK launched its armed uprising, what needs to be done is clear: First of all, the obstacles to citizens who consider themselves Kurdish freely living their language and culture and freely expressing their particular concerns should be removed step by step. The government should determine the steps to be taken in this direction through dialogue with Kurdish politicians inside and outside parliament who are against violence. Amnesty is an indispensable tool in the fight against terrorism. For the PKK to be neutralized, its ordinary militants must be pardoned with an appropriate formula and the way must be opened for them to return to normal life. For the amnesty to produce results, thought must also be given to how the young people who escape from the PKK’s grip will earn their living.

“If Ankara truly wants the PKK to be finished, it should also not object to PKK ringleaders seeking asylum in third countries on condition that they abandon terrorism. One of the most important tools in solving the problem is, without doubt, the elimination of unemployment and poverty in the Kurdish-majority region. Finally, dialogue must definitely be established with the Kurdish Regional Government in Iraq. Ankara should respect the KRG’s autonomy in return for it never allowing its territory to be used by the terrorist organization and pursuing a policy of friendship, and should deepen economic interdependence with the region…” (“What needs to be done on the Kurdish problem is clear,” Zaman, 12.1.2008)

“Is the AKP abandoning the EU?”

Starting from early 2008, I began to question the AKP government’s foreign policy. In this context, one of my first articles was titled “Is the AKP abandoning the EU?” In those years when I was careful to distinguish between the positive and negative aspects of AKP rule, I wrote:

“It is certain that AKP rule has brought positive innovations to Turkish foreign policy. Looking at the statements of foreign policy advisor Prof. Dr. Ahmet Davutoğlu and the declarations and practices of the government, I had been convinced that, at least until the end of 2005, the AKP’s foreign policy was essentially guided by the following principles: The fundamental foreign policy goal is EU membership. However, multidimensionality will be given to foreign relations. The multidimensional foreign policy to be conducted with self-confident diplomacy will not only reduce problems with neighbors to zero, but will also make Turkey

a ‘central country’ with a say in both regional and world politics (including international organizations).

“Post-September 11 world conditions give Muslim-majority Turkey the opportunity to be not just a bridge between the West and Islamic countries, but a ‘model’ for the Islamic world with the strong economy and democracy it will build. There is not conflict but rather complementarity between EU membership and multidimensional foreign policy goals. Because gaining effectiveness and prestige in its region and especially over Islamic countries will increase Turkey’s value to the EU. How can recent foreign policy developments be evaluated from the perspective of the above paradigm?

“Kostas Karamanlis being the first Greek Prime Minister to come to Turkey in 49 years is, no doubt, a result of the AKP government’s policy of improving relations with neighbors. The disputes between Turkey and Greece have not been resolved, but there is visible rapprochement in relations between societies and even between armed forces. The probability of a war breaking out between Turkey and Greece is close to zero. The AKP government did not damage relations with Israel, but rather developed them. But Prime Minister Erdoğan is just as right in showing a strong reaction to the policy of collectively punishing the Palestinians in Gaza by blockading and bombarding them today as he was right in accusing Israel of being a ‘terrorist state’ yesterday.

“The AKP government was also doing the right thing by inviting Hamas representative Khaled Meshaal to Ankara in February 2006. Israeli-Palestinian peace can never be achieved by excluding Hamas. However, neither can Sudan be equated with Palestine, nor can Hassan al-Bashir be equated with Khaled Meshaal. Hamas, which Khaled Meshaal represents, is the legitimate, elected representative of a people under occupation and subjugation, the Palestinians; Hassan al-Bashir is a dictator who seized power through a military coup and oppresses the religious and ethnic minorities in his country. How can the crimes against humanity committed by the al-Bashir government against non-Arab Muslims in Darfur, which caused the deaths of more than 200,000 and made more than 2 million refugees, and which outraged the civilized world including the UN, be ignored?

“Prime Minister Erdoğan’s participation in the Arab League meeting in Khartoum in April 2006 and his claim that ‘assimilation and genocide’ could not happen in Darfur because Islam rejected ‘tribalism and racism’ had nothing humane about it. Looking at the increasingly frequent visits and closer relations with Sudan, what can you say to those who say Ankara is now pursuing a policy of ‘Islamic, Sunni solidarity’? Turkey will of course establish and develop relations with countries with different regimes in line with national interests. But there is certainly a moral limit to this. It was absolutely unnecessary to invite someone like al-Bashir to Ankara.

“I wonder: How can a Turkey that is close to Sudan, which has not signed the UN’s Kyoto Protocol, is not a party to the UN International Criminal Court, and does not implement UN decisions, contemplate being elected to the Security Council, how can it be considered European? I ask: Is the AKP abandoning EU membership? How else can the fact that relations with the EU are not mentioned with a single word in the 60th Government Action Plan be explained?

Is the meeting with Sarkozy and Merkel a move to trip up Turkey’s supporters in the EU, a preparation for ‘privileged partnership’?” (“Is the AKP abandoning the EU?” Zaman, 26.1.2008)

“Why I am not just a ‘democrat’”

Yes, I was advocating liberal democracy. But was there not a tension between citizens’ fundamental rights and freedoms and democracy in the narrow sense, that is, majority rule? I often felt the need to explain this. As follows:

“In an article I wrote recently, I referred to my political identity as ‘liberal social democrat.’ Some of my readers said they knew me as a ‘social democrat’ and asked why I felt the need to add the adjective ‘liberal.’ The reason is this: As I have stated in many of my articles, I am not just a ‘democrat,’ but both a ‘liberal’ and a ‘social’ democrat. I am a ‘liberal democrat’ because I believe in democracy limited by individuals’ fundamental rights and freedoms as much as in government by the consent of the people, in a libertarian and pluralist society. I am a ‘social democrat’ because the market economy based on private property, which has great superiority in creating wealth, when left to itself both produces great injustices and causes great damage to the natural environment.

“That is why I am in favor of a ‘social market’ economy of the kind where equality of opportunity and social justice are ensured and nature is protected through laws enacted by parliament. Undoubtedly, one reason for calling myself a ‘liberal social democrat’ is also that the term ‘social democrat’ has been ruined in Turkey, that is, it has come to be used as a label also by those holding Kemalist, secularist-nationalist, and nationalist (national) socialist ideas.

“Some of my friends also ask why I did not sign the statement of academics supporting the constitutional amendment proposal that would allow headscarves at universities. The reason is definitely not that the statement was prepared by ‘those close to the AKP.’ The removal of other legislation restricting freedoms is of course as important to me as the removal of the headscarf ban at universities. But it is not realistic to expect all steps toward freedom to be taken at the same time. Yes, this constitutional amendment may be a legitimate source of concern in terms of delaying a new and civilian constitution, but there may also be benefit in discussing the new constitution independently of the ‘turban issue.’ I do not understand at all what harm there could be in the MHP also supporting the constitutional amendment. Every step toward freedom can be taken with different alliances in parliament.

“I did not sign the statement, because my views are not unknown. For years, both in my writings and in the television programs I participate in, I have been saying that the headscarf ban as implemented in Turkey is compatible with neither human rights nor secularism. Secondly, I am not in complete agreement with the text of the statement, because I do not advocate unlimited ‘dress freedom’ at universities. I do not accept the headscarf-turban distinction; I do not believe that either ‘under the chin’ or ‘GATA bow’ is a solution. But it cannot be reasonable to allow attending classes in a black chador that leaves only the eyes visible, or in a ‘burqa’ that also covers the eyes, or in a bikini or shorts.

“I am neither the kind of ‘democrat’ who advocates that covering should be unconditionally free (because the majority wants it so), nor do I approve of the ‘secularists’ who want covering to be unconditionally banned on the claim that it is contrary to gender equality. Just as I am against the headscarf ban being applied to university students, I also do not approve of it being applied to people’s representatives in parliament and to those receiving public services in public buildings. But I believe that public officials representing the secular state, which does not discriminate between beliefs, and those providing public services wearing religious symbols is incompatible with secularism.

“I approve of the headscarf ban being applied to minor students attending publicly owned primary and secondary schools financed by the taxes of all citizens. However, I have no objection to the ban being lifted from private schools in terms of recognizing freedom of choice. Finally, the protection of the freedom of female students who do not consider covering a religious obligation is as valuable to me as the freedom of those who consider it a religious obligation. In short: I am not just a ‘democrat,’ because ‘democracy’ alone can turn into a dictatorship of the majority; it can result in the stifling of both freedom and secularism.” (Zaman, 07.02.2008)

## The headscarf ban is a human rights issue

From when I began writing in newspapers, I opposed the headscarf ban applied in schools and public service as a requirement of the Kemalist authoritarian secularism regime. By 2008, I was writing:

“Radikal newspaper headlined the result of a TESEV study: ‘If the goal is girls’ education, the turban is really trivial’ (February 7). According to the study, among the factors preventing female students from continuing to university, the headscarf ban comes last and concerned only 1%. That is: If the headscarf ban violates girls’ right to education, this is true for only 1% of them, therefore it is not worth dwelling on… Then Zaman newspaper headlined the result of a survey conducted by the Ankethane Research Company: ‘80 percent of society wants the ban lifted’ (February 9). That is: If 80% wants the ban lifted, it should be lifted…

“The message from both headlines misses the essence of the debate about the headscarf ban. Neither supporting the continuation of the headscarf ban because it takes away the right to education of only 1%, nor advocating its lifting because 80% wants it, is compatible with the logic of the libertarian order we want to establish. The question to be asked of those who think like Radikal’s headline is: The penal articles that restrict freedom of thought and expression in Turkey in a way that touches the essence of the right, primarily Article 301 of the Turkish Penal Code, do not concern more than 1% of society. So should these bans continue? The question to be asked of those who think like Zaman’s headline is: The vast majority of society is in favor of the death penalty. Should the death penalty, which violates the most fundamental right, the right to life, be reinstated just because that is the case? Even if the headscarf ban at universities concerns only 1%, even if 80% is in favor of the ban continuing, it should be lifted, because it violates the fundamental right to education and the fundamental freedom of expression. This ban must end, because it is contrary to human rights.

“Much can be said about the way the lifting of the ban, which has been a major subject of debate for at least ten years, came onto the agenda. It can be said that because the AKP government did not see the strength in itself to lift the headscarf ban in its first term, it had said through Deputy Prime Minister Mehmet Ali Şahin: ‘The number of those who consider it a problem is 1.5 percent. We as the government focused on the problems that the people want to be solved first… Our priority is not the turban but unemployment.’ (NTV, May 23, 2006) For the same reason, Prime Minister Tayyip Erdoğan had also made this comment on a question about Şahin’s statement: ’Let us think of the forest, not a few trees there. If we act based on a few trees, we will make a mistake. Indeed, the results of public opinion surveys are very clear and evident. That is, if we make evaluations looking at these, Turkey will win, not lose…

“It can also be said that the AKP government, which emerged considerably strengthened from the July 22 elections, was preparing to bring the issue onto the agenda with a new constitution. However, the process that began with the Prime Minister’s answer (without thinking where it would lead) to a journalist’s question in Madrid, ‘Even if it were a political symbol…’, gave the MHP the opportunity to wear down the government and do ‘vote harvesting’ in its own way. It can also be said that the poor management of the issue made its resolution difficult; baseless concerns that the AKP government is leading Turkey toward a religious state are being made subjects of political exploitation; the Prime Minister, instead of answering criticisms coolly, is shouting and yelling and thus abetting this exploitation…

“All of this may be true. But just because all of this is true, can the continuation of the ban

be defended? What falls to those who are in favor of freedom is to support the implementation of the constitutional amendment and leaving the ban behind. Encouraging the AKP government to make other reforms in the direction of expanding freedoms and deepening democracy; advancing the struggle for the rights of religious and ethnic minorities and other minority rights (which do not concern more than 1 percent of society) can only be possible in this way. The logic of either all freedoms immediately or none is not logical.” (“The headscarf ban is a human rights issue,” Zaman, 16.2.2008)

Fortunately, as a result of libertarian writers preparing public opinion, the CHP also gradually abandoning its strict secularist stance, but above all the AKP government’s determination on this issue, the headscarf ban was gradually lifted. First in 2007 at universities with the instruction sent by the Presidency of YÖK (the Council of Higher Education) to rectorates; it ended in public workplaces in 2013 with the change of the dress code regulation in the public sector. Shortly after this, female AKP deputies began entering the Grand National Assembly with their headscarves. Thankfully, such a ban does not exist today.

“Liberals” and the AKP

In late 2007 and early 2008, commentaries began appearing in the media about the alliance between the AKP and liberal-minded intellectuals breaking down. In those years when I had not yet lost my hope that AKP rule would serve liberalization in Turkey, I explained my view on this matter:

“Haluk Şahin first put forward these views: Liberals in Turkey helped the neo-Islamist AKP express its actually ‘reactionary and archaic’ goals in terms of concepts like democracy, freedom, human rights. They ‘entered into ideological struggle with segments sensitive about secularism and battered them’ and paved the way for the AKP. Thus they gave the AKP, which they enabled to be known in a very different way than it actually is, ‘legitimacy and modernity’ in domestic and foreign public opinion (Radikal, September 22-23, 2007). Then, in a long interview based on these theses, he developed his analyses on Turkey’s intellectual and political climate and collected them in a book worth reading and thinking about titled ‘Liberals, Nationalists, Islamists and Others’ (Istanbul: Say Publications, 2008).

“What both this book and recent discussions themed around ‘Liberal-AKP alliance and its breakdown’ made me think can be listed as follows: Some intellectuals who were in authoritarian or totalitarian socialist, nationalist, Islamist, etc. movements in the period between 1960-80, drawing lessons from what was experienced in Turkey and the world, reached the following conclusions: Turkey is an illiberal type of democracy under bureaucratic tutelage. There is no separation of state and religion; secularism is limited to secular laws. Political freedoms, particularly freedom of expression and association, are restricted.

“The state’s official ideology, referred to as ‘Kemalism,’ covers up the country’s historical realities and cultural differences. State-dominated economic policies closed to competition are preventing the country from becoming prosperous. It is not possible for Turkey to cope with its differences and become a rich and just society without establishing a libertarian and pluralist democracy and transitioning to a competition-based market economy. Intellectuals (‘Liberals’) who adopted to some degree the liberal-critical discourse I have briefly summarized from the 1990s onwards, ardently advocated the EU accession process, which they saw as strong external support for liberalization and democratization.

“The said discourse that emerged from the accounting of painful events that have been and are being experienced affected almost all political currents in Turkey to some degree. Turkey’s distinctive Islamist movement, the National Vision Movement, was no exception to this. The influence of liberal-critical discourse also played a major role among the various factors that led to the transition from RP to FP and then the transformation into AKP. So much so that the AKP, while culturally its ‘conservative’ qualities predominated, signed on to a program and practice that was liberal and libertarian in both political and economic terms (at least to a degree Turkey had not seen until now). Not to see the evolution that the Islamist movement has undergone in Turkey, to declare the AKP ‘Islamist with a hidden agenda,’ one must either be blind or (like the CHP) hope to reap political gain from it.

“‘Liberals’ supported all the steps the AKP took toward liberalization, democratization, and prosperity in the context of EU reforms (while also criticizing their inadequacies and contradictions). The bureaucratic, secularist-nationalist, nationalist, and Islamist opposition that rose in parallel with the decline in societal support for the EU, which began to wane with the negative signals coming from the EU from 2005 onwards, undoubtedly weakened the AKP’s reformist will and strengthened its tendency to compromise with the established order. As the AKP distances itself from reforms and thus from the EU agenda, it becomes a target of some ‘liberals’’ critical discourse.

## “After the EU largely lost its ‘soft power’ over Turkey,

and after the political opposition increasingly lost its credibility, the only force that can (unfortunately) encourage the AKP toward reforms is these ‘liberals.’ But, of course, ‘liberals’ can have very different perspectives among themselves (on various issues, including the AKP). So much so that some ‘liberals’ (somehow) equate liberalism with secularism, uniformity, monoculturalism, in short Kemalism, and can declare themselves only ‘democrat.’” (“In my view ‘Liberals’ and the AKP,” Zaman, 23.2.2008)

## Islamism and the AKP

Whether the AKP’s ideology was Islamist, and whether it would be more accurate to characterize it as “conservative democrat,” was also a subject of debate among political scientists. In an article I wrote directly on this subject, I said:

“We know that circles who want democracy to be destroyed and Turkey to sever its ties with the EU characterize the AKP as ‘Islamist,’ even ‘Islamofascist,’ and we laugh it off. However, even in the Western media, which could be expected to be more faithful to reality, those who speak of the AKP as ‘Islamist’ (even if the adjectives ‘moderate, modernist and liberal’ are put before it) are still widespread. So what does ‘Islamism’ mean? Can the AKP be called Islamist? There is benefit in addressing these questions.

“Political Islam or Islamism, by its academic definition, is a modern political ideology produced from Islamic belief that claims to be an alternative to capitalism, communism, and socialism. For example, according to the well-known French expert Olivier Roy, Islamism is ‘a political ideology that envisages Islam dominating every aspect of society (politics, law, economy, social justice, foreign policy, etc.).’ According to him, the minimum common point of Islamist movements is their desire for religious rules to dominate at least in the field of private law. American expert Graham E. Fuller, in his book titled ‘The Future of Political Islam,’ has made the broadest definition of Islamism. According to him, Islamists are ‘those in the contemporary Islamic world who believe that Islam as a faith has something important to say about how politics and society should be ordered and who seek to implement this idea in some form.’

“If we look from the perspective of definitions, it can be said that the Welfare Party, which was closed in 1998, was a ‘moderate Islamist’ party because, at least until the Refahyol government was formed, it advocated the ‘Just Economic Order’ supposedly as a system different from ‘capitalism and socialism’; freedom to be subject to Islamic law (at least in the private sphere) for those who wish; and Islamic unity. The closure of the RP, despite having no connection to violence except for the statements of a few members, was not a situation that could be explained by democratic standards. But RP members did not resort to other means against the decision about them; they appealed to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR). The ECHR, with a highly debatable decision, approved the party’s closure.

“It is quite clear that the AKP cannot be considered Islamist even by the broadest definition. The party program closest to liberal views in Turkey is the AKP’s program. Being devout also never means being Islamist. The AKP has both devout and non-devout members. The AKP receives votes from every region of the country and every segment of society. It has never proposed the adoption of Islamic law, even in the private sphere. The AKP has not imposed a covering requirement on anyone; it made the constitutional amendment toward lifting the headscarf ban in universities that was contrary to human rights, with the encouragement and support of the MHP. It wants an end to discrimination not only against graduates of imam-hatip schools (opened and supervised by the state) but against all vocational high school graduates in university admission. Although not always consistent on this matter, it advocates that the state treat all religious beliefs equally.

“AKP governments have been in favor of close political and economic relations not only with Islamic countries but with all countries, specifically with Western countries, including the USA and Israel, and have made reforms that opened the way for Turkey to join the EU. The points that those who claim the AKP is ‘Islamist’ fail to understand are these: The cadres who founded the AKP abandoned Islamism, because they saw that Islamism would never be adopted by the majority of the Turkish people and that it was not a way out for Turkey either.

“The pressures they were subjected to taught them not to hide their agenda, but the importance of political freedom. That is why the AKP, compared to other parties, has a more libertarian, more democratic, and more secular identity. Turkey’s flawed democracy has made it possible for the Islamist movement to gradually moderate and finally transcend Islamism. Turkey is the star of the Islamic world essentially in this sense. It is not possible to understand Turkey without understanding these things.” (Zaman, 5.4.2008)

After the years that have passed, when I ask whether this assessment still holds, my answer is roughly this: By Olivier Roy’s narrow definition, calling the AKP Islamist still does not capture reality in my opinion. But if we define Islamism very broadly like Graham E. Fuller, calling the AKP Islamist is possible. My preferred characterization for the AKP today would be ‘Islamic populist.’

“What is being done to the AKP fits neither law nor ethics”

Court of Cassation Chief Public Prosecutor Abdurrahman Yalçınkaya applied to the Constitutional Court on March 14, 2008, requesting the closure of the AKP on the grounds that it had “become a center of actions contrary to secularism” and a 5-year ban from politics for 71 party members including Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and President Abdullah Gül. The Constitutional Court accepted the said indictment on March 31, 2008. Turkey was referred to as a “graveyard of parties” due to the multitude of closed parties, but this was the first time a closure case was opened against a party in power, one that had received approximately half of the voters’ votes. I strongly opposed the attempt to close the AKP. The article I will quote below, after listing the practices of AKP rule that I found positive and negative, reflected my view that the former considerably outweighed the latter.

“I did not vote for the Justice and Development Party (AKP) in either the 2002 or 2007 elections.
