I will not call it ‘AK Party’ without being convinced that it is truly a ‘clean party’ and not tainted by corruption. There are many aspects of AKP rule that I do not approve of and criticize. I see its inability to escape its identity as a ‘Sunni Party’ as its biggest mistake. I find its constant zigzagging on the Kurdish issue, its taking a stance sometimes for freedom, sometimes for bans and oppression, grave.

I find its almost complete lack of sensitivity on environmental issues shameful. I see the AKP as tending to capture the established order rather than change it. In this context, I think it is doing very wrong by bringing its own members or close associates to important public positions (including the Presidency) instead of people the whole society can trust. (…)

“However, despite all my criticisms, I see the AKP as a great success of our flawed democracy. The AKP is an example that where political competition is legitimate, an Islamist movement can transform into a center party committed to democracy and secularism. The AKP’s leading cadre, by drawing lessons from experiences and seeing that Islamism was not a way out, succeeded in renewing itself. That is why I have great admiration for this cadre (to whom I personally have no closeness). AKP rule, by adhering to the IMF-supported economic stability program and the route drawn by the EU accession process, achieved a ‘silent revolution’ in both the economy and democracy, at least until 2005.

“I have not the slightest doubt that today’s Turkey is a more prosperous and freer country than pre-AKP. That is why the AKP managed to increase its vote from 34% in 2002 to 40% in 2004 and to 47% in 2007. Today the AKP is the center party that has the trust of the vast majority of the Turkish people including Kurds and is the guarantor of the country’s integrity. What is being done to this AKP fits neither law nor political ethics. The clique at the head of the CHP, by spreading delusions that secularism is being lost, is calculating to come to power at the cost of crushing democracy. (…)

“In 2003 and 2004, two military coup attempts were made. In 2006, they tried to place the responsibility for the Council of State attack in which a judge was killed on the government. Last April, the people were provoked against the government with rallies organized by coup supporters. On April 27, 2007, the Constitutional Court was put under pressure by posting a statement on the General Staff’s website meaning ‘If Gül’s election as President is not prevented, there will be a military coup.’ Now, with an indictment that has no legal merit, they want to close the AKP… The only hope is that the Constitutional Court, saving its own and the country’s reputation, puts a stop to this.” (Zaman, 15.4.2008)

As is known, the Constitutional Court, in its decision announced on July 30, 2008, reached by a margin of one vote, would rule not for the closure of the AKP but for halving the treasury aid it would receive.

“The ’68 generation forty years later”

The 40th anniversary of the ’68 events had also been an occasion for me to look back at my own past. I wrote:

“It was not easy in Turkey’s busy agenda, but from what was written and said about the ‘68 generation, from television series and debates, I finally realized that exactly forty years have passed since 1968, the year of ’youth uprisings’ all over the world… I am also from the ’68 generation. I contributed more to the discourse than to the actions of that generation. I either knew or was friends with almost all of the youth leaders belonging to the ’68 generation. I always remember with respect and sorrow those who are no longer among us because they were killed.

“Were there not among us police agents from the beginning or later, mentally ill people

or those lacking character? Today we can identify them better… But the overwhelming majority of us, with great moral idealism, had committed to a political ideal: We believed that we could turn Turkey into paradise with a ‘revolution’ that would happen one way or another. Unfortunately, we were not aware that the authoritarian and totalitarian ideologies that set us against each other, the paths we took, those who wanted to use us in the power struggle, were taking us in the exact opposite direction of the ideals of equality and freedom we shared. Unfortunately, the power holders of the established order were also too bigoted and ruthless to see that we were young and in need of understanding.

“The vast majority of those from the ’68 generation who managed to survive and look critically at what happened, some after a short time, some after a long time but definitely, saw the wrongness of the ideas they had committed to and the paths they had taken. If I can find time from my work and my life allows, I want to write the view of the ’68 generation from my own window… To be honest, until now, few of those who should really write have written about the experiences of the period that ended with the 1971 military intervention. The most important of what has been written is undoubtedly Hasan Cemal’s book, which tells the story of the March 9 junta attempt (for some reason ignored in March 12 documentaries and in television series about March 12) by those seeking to bring Turkey a Baath

(Iraq, Syria)-type regime. I Wrote Myself, Let No One Be Angry (1999) also sheds light on understanding the anti-democracy putschist tradition that has made itself felt again in recent years.

“One of my contributions to understanding the ‘youth uprising’ that occurred in Turkey in 1968 is the article titled ‘An Essay on the ’68 Generation’ published in issue 41 of Toplum ve Bilim journal twenty years ago, on the twentieth anniversary. When I read this article today, twenty years later, which I later learned caused a storm in the journal’s editorial board between those who wanted it published and those who wanted it rejected, I see that some of the findings here no longer have much validity. My main concern when writing this article in 1988 was, as someone who (unfortunately) contributed to the spread of these views in Turkey 20 years ago, to settle accounts with Marxism and Marxism-Leninism and to explain why I completely abandoned these views. Since what happened in both the world and Turkey in the years after this article was written has made both Marxism-Leninism and Marxism museum pieces, what I said in this context may no longer have much value.

“But there are findings in the article that I think are still meaningful. The conclusion reached in this context is noteworthy: ‘In my opinion, what has been experienced in the last twenty years has taught the ’68 generation the indispensable value of fundamental rights and freedoms, individual rights, especially freedom of thought. The ’68 generation had turned its back on pluralist democracy that guarantees the individual’s fundamental rights and freedoms in 1968. Today, however, those most wholeheartedly committed to fundamental rights and freedoms are in my opinion largely them.’ Looking at what happened in China governed by Deng Xiaoping, in the Soviet Union led by Mikhail Gorbachev, and throughout the world, the article may also be found noteworthy in terms of predicting the dissolution and collapse of ‘real socialism’ that would begin just one year later, in 1989.” (Zaman, 12.4.2008)

“Kemalism must be reinterpreted”

One of the themes I frequently addressed in my writings and speeches was that Kemalism needed to be reinterpreted. I grounded this claim as follows:

“(…) It must now be understood: The oppressive understanding of secularism developed approximately a hundred years ago, under an authoritarian single-party rule, in accordance with the understanding of modernity of that time, definitely contradicts the needs of Turkey at the beginning of the 21st century, which is socio-economically much more developed, much more differentiated, has nearly 60 years of democratic experience behind it (albeit frequently interrupted by military interventions, incomplete and flawed), and is conducting EU accession negotiations.

“The oppressive understanding of secularism aimed at imprisoning religious beliefs in consciences cannot be sustained in today’s Turkey, let alone within democracy, even under a military dictatorship. Religious beliefs do not disappear with modernization; they continue to exist in harmony with modernity. Therefore, the liberalization of oppressive secularism; the removal of restrictions on the freedom of belief of Sunnis, Alevis, non-Muslims, those who believe in no religion, everyone, is now on Turkey’s agenda. Those who cannot see this and insist on the oppressive understanding of secularism are causing very, very great harm to Turkey by leading society toward polarization.

“The Islamist movement in Turkey succeeded in leaving Islamism behind and reconciling with both democracy and secularism. For democracy to be established in Turkey, radical secularists must also reinterpret Kemalism according to Atatürk’s legacy pointing to contemporary civilization and the needs of contemporary Turkey, thus reconciling with democracy and tearing down the walls between them and the people.” (Zaman, 17.6.2008)

“Why shouldn’t the military interfere in politics?”

From the late 1990s onwards, the existence of a secret armed organization called Ergenekon was claimed in Turkey. Prosecutors alleged that this organization (the “deep state”), organized within the state’s security forces and consisting of soldiers, police, journalists, and academics, made plans to overthrow the AKP government in 2003-2004; that it organized the Council of State attack in 2006 in which a high judge was killed, and the Zirve Publishing House attack in Malatya in 2007 in which three Christians were killed. However, in the Ergenekon case with 235 defendants, all defendants were acquitted of charges of ‘establishing an armed organization, managing it, membership, aiding and abetting’ by the Court of Cassation’s decision on April 21, 2016… In the early days when the Ergenekon investigations first came to the agenda, I interpreted the subject as follows:

“What we have experienced in recent weeks—reports leaked to the press about how the military would shape politics in Turkey and other matters, court decisions, some trampling the rule of law and others raising hope for its establishment, progress made in the Ergenekon gang investigation, and other signs—raise this question in our minds: Is there perhaps a struggle within state institutions in Turkey between those who support democracy and the rule of law and those who oppose it? I do not possess information to answer this question. But if this is the case, I certainly hope that democracy and the rule of law emerge victorious from this struggle.

“What I know is this: Since April 27, 2007, we have entered a very concerning political struggle. In this process, the Turkish Armed Forces, the guarantor of Turkey’s internal and external security, unfortunately appears as a party to the political struggle, almost like a political party. In the 8th year of the 21st century, unfortunately there is no consensus in Turkey—neither among elites nor in public opinion—that problems can only be solved within a democratic order based on the rule of law, and that keeping the military out of politics is one of the most fundamental conditions of this order. In this environment, we must persistently continue to explain that secularism and national unity can only be secured in a state based on human rights and the rule of law, and that military involvement in politics, even for these purposes, carries great dangers.

“All human experience shows that only countries with liberal democratic regimes can succeed in diagnosing and solving their problems; can earn the loyalty of their citizens; can have stronger economies and therefore stronger armies and security. Is the Soviet Union not the greatest example of this? Did it not turn out that the USSR, considered a superpower throughout the Cold War, was ultimately a ‘paper tiger’? Because there was no freedom, it could neither develop economically nor escape disintegration despite its enormous military power.

“Strong armies, like strong societies and economies, can only exist in democratic regimes… One of the most fundamental principles of democratic societies is the separation of the military from politics… Armies are built on principles of hierarchy, discipline, and absolute obedience due to the nature of their duties—that is, on principles that are the exact opposite of democracy. The principles and requirements of military service are incompatible with the principles and requirements of democratic society… If the army becomes a party to politics, it cannot properly fulfill its duties, and the country’s internal and external security weakens… If it takes sides in politics, it becomes inevitable that the army will be used by politicians against each other, that its reputation and prestige in the eyes of the people will be eroded, and much worse, that it will become a scene of internal divisions and conflicts… We are one of the societies that has best seen and experienced the consequences of this for national security.

“For soldiers to properly fulfill their duties in democratic societies: 1) The army must be subject to the authority of civilian administrators who are democratically elected and accountable to the people. 2) Even defense policies must be determined by civilians. The authority of soldiers even in this area is limited to making recommendations and taking responsibility for implementation. 3) Regardless of which party is in power, the army must be loyally bound to the government that comes to power through elections, by the people’s vote. 4) Like all citizens, soldiers must also receive education in liberal and pluralist democracy in their schools. We must establish these fundamental principles of democratic society irreversibly.” (Zaman, 3.7.2008)

“Is the AKP government at the beginning of the end?”

It was in late 2008 that I first began questioning in my own mind where the AKP government was taking Turkey. After examining how Turkey-EU relations had evolved in recent years, I was trying to answer the question ‘Is the AKP government at the beginning of the end?’:

“Is the AKP government at the beginning of the end?.. Recently I have been frequently confronted with this question, especially from foreign colleagues. I tell them that to answer this question, one must compare the conjuncture of the 2002-2004 period, when the AKP government led reforms referred to as a ‘Silent Revolution,’ with what came after. In the 2002-2004 period, the main opposition party CHP was saying ‘yes’ to EU harmonization laws. The majority of the media, including the Doğan Group, and the educated classes approved of the reforms. Public support for EU membership was reaching 75 percent. The Chief of General Staff was Hilmi Özkök, who viewed the reforms favorably. Those seeking a coup could not find the support they sought in the army. The PKK was maintaining the ceasefire it declared in 1999. The EU, including France and Germany, was encouraging the reforms.

“In May 2004, ten new members join the EU, including the Greek Cypriot Administration (which had said ‘no’ to the Annan Plan for a solution on the island a month earlier). In the summer months, the PKK ends the ceasefire. During the referendums on the EU constitution draft in the summer of 2005, voices begin to rise in Europe against enlargement in general and Turkey’s membership in particular. Angela Merkel, who will assume the German chancellorship in November, is proposing ‘privileged partnership’ to Turkey. Nicolas Sarkozy, who will be elected president in France in May 2007, is saying ‘there is no place for Turkey in the EU.’ Nevertheless, in October 2005, the decision to begin accession negotiations comes from the EU. However, the adopted Negotiating Framework does not guarantee membership even if negotiations are successfully completed. The AKP government’s enthusiasm is dampened.

“From the beginning of 2006, public support for EU membership in Turkey begins to decline and gradually falls below 50 percent. After the Council of State attack in May 2006, the political atmosphere becomes murky. The struggle for the presidential election has begun. In April 2007, ‘Republic rallies’ are organized against Abdullah Gül’s candidacy (by defendants in the Ergenekon case). The CHP virtually declares the AKP an ‘enemy,’ opposing Gül’s election and all reforms. The General Staff publishes a ‘memorandum’ against Gül’s candidacy on its website. The Constitutional Court blocks Gül’s election. The AKP calls early general elections, wins by a wide margin, and elects Gül as President. Tension between state elites and the AKP continues.

“The Doğan Group goes into opposition, claiming that secularism is being violated (or for other reasons). The MHP begins to apply tactics to pit the government against state elites. The PKK escalates its attacks. The DTP increasingly follows in the PKK’s footsteps. The Bush administration does not lift a finger against the PKK until November 2007. The neoconservative gang in Washington intensifies its campaign against the AKP. Sarkozy adds 4 more chapters to the 8 chapters suspended due to Ankara’s not including Southern Cyprus in the customs union. Negotiations proceed at a snail’s pace. The Ergenekon gang’s preparations for a coup against the government in 2009 are revealed. The Chief Prosecutor files a closure case against the AKP. The AKP narrowly escapes being closed, but the Constitutional Court declares juristocracy (rule by judges). The CHP expands corruption allegations against the AKP. Economic crisis is at the door.

“The AKP has received the votes of half of the electorate, but it is besieged from within and without. Under these conditions, there are essentially two paths it can take: to embrace reforms by trusting the voters and its supporters in the EU, or to surrender to the status quo and continue to benefit from the advantages of power. Because the first is very risky, it chooses the second. This time, it also alienates the circles that supported the AKP as long as it was making reforms. Let’s say this much is understandable… But how can we explain AKP spokespeople, especially Erdoğan, increasingly embracing MHP rhetoric? Perhaps with the calculation that this will win votes… In my view, a wrong calculation. If it persists in this attitude, if it avoids reforms, the AKP government may be at the beginning of the end.” (Zaman, 18.11.2008)

Yes, a political observer can only be this wrong!.. Fifteen years after these lines were written, the AKP was still in power and when it would leave was still unknown.

“Why am I ‘apologizing’?”

In mid-December 2008, a declaration stating “My conscience does not accept the insensitivity to the Great Catastrophe that Ottoman Armenians were subjected to in 1915, or its denial. I reject this injustice, and for my part, I share the feelings and pain of my Armenian brothers and sisters, and I apologize to them” was announced to the public with numerous signatures. I was one of the first to sign the declaration. I explained my reasoning as follows:

“I avoid signing texts written by others, because as a commentator, I have the opportunity to express my views on subjects I consider myself competent in. But I signed this text without deliberating over its wording. Why? Why am I apologizing to our Armenian brothers and sisters? During the dissolution of the Ottoman Empire, all the peoples involved faced great tragedies. Among these, what happened to the Armenians has a special place. I do not think that the catastrophe that befell the Ottoman Armenians in 1915 was a genocide of the kind claimed by some Armenian nationalists, comparable to what Jews were subjected to in Germany. Armenian nationalists collaborated with Russia to separate from the Ottoman Empire and establish an independent Armenian state, engaged in terrorist acts, and killed many Turks and Muslims. In response, the Ottoman government, or rather an inner clique within it led by Talat Pasha, decided and implemented the deportation of all Armenians living mainly outside Istanbul and Izmir to the Syrian desert, that is, their forced migration.

“Approximately half of the roughly 1.5 million Ottoman Armenians subjected to deportation lost their lives during the migration—some from attacks by members of security forces and bandits who coveted their property, some from epidemic diseases and starvation. Some survived by being protected by Turks and Muslims and converting to Islam. The rest migrated to the West, primarily to France and the USA. Armenians who served in the Ottoman army found upon returning from the war that no one from their families and communities remained, and that their property had been confiscated.

“Armenian nationalists claim that the Ottoman government’s intention with the deportation was the wholesale destruction of Armenians, similar to what the Nazis did to the Jews. This claim has not been proven. Respected non-Turkish Ottoman historians do not support this claim either. However, there is no debate about the fact that the Ottoman government collectively punished all Armenians for the crimes committed by Armenian nationalists. Today in Turkey, we have knowledge about all the tragedies that occurred during the dissolution of the Ottoman Empire. The catastrophes that befell Turks and Muslims who were expelled from the Balkans and massacred, who were killed by Armenian insurgents in the northeastern provinces, and Muslims who were expelled from Russia in the mid-19th century are all known and freely discussed. But the tragedy that befell the Ottoman Armenians is covered up and cannot be freely discussed. The responsibility for this tragedy lies neither with the Turks nor with the governments of the Turkish Republic; it lies with the Committee of Union and Progress dictators who led the Ottoman state to ruin.

“Of course, I have no personal responsibility for what happened to the Ottoman Armenians. But as a human being and a Turk, I feel great sorrow for a tragedy that occurred in my homeland and has been covered up and made taboo by the state. The primary reason for signing the declaration is a moral obligation arising from this. Secondly, I want Turkey to strengthen its democracy, and for no subject to remain undiscussed and unilluminated so that evils are not repeated. Thirdly, as Turks and Armenians who lived in friendship for centuries until the age of nationalisms, I value the re-establishment of friendship between Turkey and Armenia. I believe that as Turkey confronts its history, Armenia and the Armenian diaspora will also confront theirs. The signs are already visible: voices are rising saying ‘We cannot debate as freely as Turkey… We too should apologize for the killed Turks and Muslims… Let Armenian archives be opened…’” (Zaman, 23.12.2008)

“Science is science, and faith is faith”

In the days following UNESCO’s declaration of 2009 as Darwin Year, the “turmoil” that occurred at the TÜBİTAK magazine provided an occasion to express my views on the relationship between science and religion. I wrote as follows:

“Reports in some newspapers about the March issue of the ‘Science and Technology’ magazine published by the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkey (TÜBİTAK) were as follows: Because 2009 was declared ‘Darwin Year’ by UNESCO, the magazine first made Charles Darwin and the theory of evolution its cover story. But at the last moment, with an intervention from senior management, the cover story was changed, a 16-page dossier was removed from the magazine, and editor Dr. Çiğdem Atakuman was dismissed. State Minister Prof. Dr. Mehmet Aydın, responsible for TÜBİTAK, said the following in response to these reports: ‘TÜBİTAK exists to open all doors to science, not to censor science… No one’s purpose can be to approach science from an ideological perspective or to approach science from a religious perspective. Science is science, faith is faith. As long as these proceed in their own lanes, they are beneficial to each other.’ (…)

“Minister Mehmet Aydın has essentially said what needed to be said about the incident. Nevertheless, there are two aspects of the incident that need to be addressed. The first is that disrespect and intolerance toward different ideas, understandings, and beliefs—regardless of the justification (except for those advocating violence)—is in no way acceptable. The second is the importance of the incident in terms of properly understanding the relationship between religion and science, and criticizing the bigotries that view religion as hostile to science and science as hostile to religion. On this occasion, both religious bigots and science bigots should be reminded of the following:

“The domains of religion and science are different. Religion is a body of beliefs that responds to the spiritual and moral needs of human beings. Science, on the other hand, is the effort to understand and explain oneself and the universe one lives in, based on human reason and logic. Viewing religion and science as rivals, and efforts to substitute one for the other, have caused great disasters for humanity. The Inquisition, Communism, and Nazism are just the best-known examples of this. Civilization, on the other hand, has developed through religion and science showing respect to each other.

According to the understanding of science that prevails among scientists today, science consists of theories that are valid until proven otherwise; it advances by replacing theories shown to be wrong with new theories; and as science advances, it becomes apparent how little we know about the universe.

“Ideas that science is capable of explaining everything, that science will replace religion, are not accepted. On the other hand, dogmatic interpretations claiming that religion is capable of explaining everything are also becoming increasingly marginalized. Interpretations of religions that are at peace with values and institutions developed and adopted as a product of humanity’s centuries of experience (human rights, democracy, separation of religion and state, rule of law, science) and compatible with modern life maintain their vitality; fundamentalist interpretations are increasingly standing against civilization. It is also certain that the majority of scientists do not see a contradiction between religion and science; they both pray and continue their research. Just like other people who both pray and do not neglect to go to the doctor when fighting disease.” (Zaman, 14.3.2009)

“Time to abandon weapons”

By 2009, I thought an opportunity had been seized to solve the Kurdish problem. That this was another of my errors would soon become apparent, but the arguments I relied on were as follows:

“In some of my writings and speeches, I put forward this view: If the PKK had not appeared on the scene or if the path of armed struggle had not been taken, Turkey’s Kurdish problem could have been solved without so much bloodshed and without so much suffering. The two basic assumptions underlying this view are as follows:

Firstly, despite all its deficiencies and flaws and being under bureaucratic tutelage, the existing democracy in Turkey would have made it possible to seek rights without resorting to violence. Indeed, during periods when PKK attacks stopped, democratic openings on the Kurdish issue became possible. Secondly, the PKK’s policy of violence laid the groundwork for demands related to Kurdish identity to be identified with violence and suppressed with violence. This is the main reason why many Kurdish politicians and intellectuals believe that the PKK was used by the state to delegitimize the Kurds’ rightful struggle, and even that the PKK is a curse brought upon us by the ‘deep state.’

“The opposing view, as is known, is that the PKK put the Kurdish problem on Turkey’s agenda, and that without the PKK, there would have been no awareness of the problem. Then the question to ask becomes this: To advocate that Kurds also live in Turkey and have the right to freely live their language and culture, one would certainly have had to take some risks, but would the bloodshed and suffering have been this great? Such a debate may have no meaning in retrospect. But it has meaning for the future. Namely:

“At the point reached today, neither the PKK nor the state is in the position it was at the beginning of the 1980s. The PKK has moved far from its original goal when it emerged—an independent Marxist-Leninist Kurdish state that would gather all Kurds under a single flag. It has abandoned Marxism-Leninism as well as the goal of an independent state. Unlike some other Kurdish parties, it is not pursuing federalism either. It is quite clear that the PKK has become aware that there can be no solution through arms. What Murat Karayılan told Hasan Cemal is very clear: Kurds freely living their language and culture, and strengthening local governments not only for the Kurdish-majority region but nationwide. For this to happen, weapons must first be silenced and then abandoned. For this, the government must talk with the DTP, or if not, with ‘wise men.’ Turkey is also not the Turkey of September 12.

“Despite many obstacles and restrictions in practice, the ban on Kurdish was lifted in 1991. Kurdish newspapers, magazines, and books became free. Between 2002-2004, Kurdish names, learning Kurdish, and radio-television broadcasting in Kurdish became free. Since 1991, parties began to be established that put the Kurdish issue at the center of their program. Although they were closed one by one, they began to come to power in local governments from 1999 and entered parliament in 2007. Even the military is declaring that it is not against identity rights at the individual level and is giving the green light to amnesty for PKK militants.

“What has essentially changed is the world: In the world and Turkey of the 1960s and 70s, the idea that Marxism-Leninism was the guide to building a free and just world, and that armed revolution was the only method, was widespread. Since then, it was first understood that Marxism-Leninism promised nothing but a totalitarian dictatorship. Then it was gradually understood that violence is barbarism; that it breeds violence; that it is impossible to get anywhere with violence; and the ideals of freedom, human rights, democracy, and peace became dominant.

“For all these reasons, there is a real opportunity to remove violence from Turkey’s agenda. To do this, one must of course talk with the legitimate representatives of Turkey’s Kurds, with Kurdish MPs from the DTP and other parties in parliament. All democratic countries that have had to deal with separatist movements resorting to terrorism—Spain, Britain, France—have succeeded in at least marginalizing separatism and violence by expanding democracy and freedoms. Turkey can succeed too. Because it is time to abandon weapons.” (Zaman, 14.5.2009)

“Action Plan to Combat Reactionism”

The Taraf newspaper, in its headline story on June 12, 2009, wrote that a “briefing document” allegedly prepared by the Information Support Department of the Turkish Armed Forces General Staff, signed by Colonel Dursun Çiçek, contained plans aimed at destroying the AKP and the Fethullah Gülen community. For this purpose, an “Anti-Reactionism Unit” had been established within the General Staff. Following Taraf’s report, the General Staff ordered an investigation of the matter. The military prosecutor’s office, in the investigation it launched the same day, announced that “when the evidence obtained so far is evaluated, an opinion has been reached that the document alleged to have been seized was not prepared in any unit of the General Staff” and decided there were no grounds for prosecution.

However, a debate had begun about whether there was an organization within the TAF referred to as the “Ergenekon Terror Organization” preparing a coup against the elected government. When writing about this in 2009, in light of what I knew about the history of civil-military relations in Turkey, I said:

“With the legislative changes adopted by the Grand National Assembly and approved by President Abdullah Gül, Turkey accepted the principle that civilians be tried in civilian courts under all circumstances, and that soldiers who commit civilian crimes also be tried in civilian courts.

Thus, another step was taken toward normalizing civil-military relations.

The CHP, which is becoming increasingly determined in favor of the continuation of bureaucratic-military tutelage over democracy, is taking the legislative changes to the Constitutional Court. It is likely that the Constitutional Court will annul the legislative changes, finding them contrary to Article 145 of the Constitution. On the other hand, it is certain that the legal changes needed to establish civilian democratic oversight of the military do not end here, and that a fundamental change in mentality is needed among both soldiers and civilians to make the military subordinate to civilian authority.

“Nevertheless, with the ongoing Ergenekon Terror Organization case, in which those accused of creating conditions for a military coup against the legitimate government have reached the 3rd indictment stage regarding coup plots, with more than a dozen active-duty officers detained within the scope of this case, and with civilian prosecutors continuing to investigate the ‘Action Plan to Combat Reactionism,’ it can be said that expectations for democratic principles to prevail in civil-military relations in Turkey are strengthening.

“In the summer of 2009, it can be said that there are two basic theories about the future of civil-military relations in Turkey. According to the pessimistic theory, as long as the mentality that the soldier is the owner of the state and the country remains widespread among bureaucratic elites and a considerable portion of voters share this view, the political role of the military will continue. Indeed, according to a recent public opinion survey, the proportion of voters who agree with the view that ‘country problems should sometimes be solved by a military regime instead of elected politicians’ is not less than about a quarter. (See: Understanding the New Turkey, Konda, November 2007).

“According to the optimistic theory, the idea that the military’s involvement in politics has resulted in neglecting its primary duties and that problems have become completely intractable is spreading not only among civilians but also among soldiers. The Ergenekon case indicates that the TAF will no longer turn a blind eye to coup plotters within its ranks. Chief of General Staff İlker Başbuğ’s statements on various occasions that ‘personnel who are not committed to the principles of democracy and the rule of law cannot remain in the TAF’ is also an expression of this.

“One of the main references for those closer to the second theory is certainly the words of General Hilmi Özkök, one of the former Chiefs of General Staff, who is also known to have supported EU reforms in the 2003-2004 period and prevented coup attempts: ‘The intellectual level achieved by TAF personnel, the evolution in communication technology, the stage reached in democracy, developments in political, economic, and other national power elements, the Republic of Turkey’s increasing participation in international institutions and organizations, the increase and development in civil society organizations and other civilian power elements, and developments in techniques for drawing lessons from previous events have closed the era of coups. In the near future, Turkey will be a country where every job is done by those who should do it. In my opinion, the people have proven their maturity.’ (Hürriyet, March 21, 2009)

“It can be said that the truth lies somewhere between these two theories. The era of interventions of the 1960, 1971, 1980, or even 1997 type may have ended. The TAF may henceforth purge ‘personnel who are not committed to the principles of democracy and the rule of law’ from its ranks. It may even be that only Chiefs of General Staff can serve as the military’s spokesperson from now on. But as long as the military believes it represents the national interest and continues to protect its privileges, the end of the military’s political role should not be expected.” (“Coups and the military’s political role,” Zaman, July 14, 2009)

## What the AKP is and is not

In the debates over whether the AKP—in its eighth year since its founding and seventh year in power—was Islamist, conservative democrat, or what kind of party it was, the view that I also shared at the time (quoted above) was most competently presented in the book titled Islamism, Democracy and Liberalism in Turkey: The Case of the AKP (Routledge, 2009), co-authored by the distinguished constitutional law scholar Ergun Özbudun and William Hale, one of the leading political historians of Turkey. (Turkish translation: Türkiye’de İslamcılık, Demokrasi ve Liberalizm: AKP Olayı / Doğan Kitap, 2010) I made the following assessment about the book, which I had the opportunity to read before its publication:

“The Justice and Development Party (AKP) celebrated its 8th founding anniversary on August 14. In terms of coming to power the year after its founding and spending seven of its eight years in power, the AKP is probably a party with a world record. In one sense, the AKP is of course not just eight years old; as one of the parties born of the National Vision Movement, it has a history of about 40 years. But in another sense, the AKP is really eight years old, because it has little resemblance to the National Vision parties that came before it.

“There is various hearsay about the nature of the AKP. It defines itself as ‘Conservative Democrat.’ But if you ask not only authoritarian secularists in Turkey, but also analysts working at research institutions closely connected with neocons in the US (and therefore the Israel lobby), and even Northern European ‘Kemalists,’ the AKP is an Islamist party that is Iranizing or Malaysianizing Turkey. According to AKP opponents who find this excessive and want to appear more reasonable, Erdoğan is the ‘Turkish Putin’ and the AKP is taking Turkey toward a Russia-type democracy. Of course, there are also those who think the exact opposite. According to them, Erdoğan is the greatest reformer after Atatürk and Özal; the AKP is taking Turkey toward a European-standard democracy and economy, even if it is not ultimately admitted to the EU.

“Academic studies as well as junk and propaganda books about the AKP are proliferating. The most noteworthy of these studies, in my opinion, is being published on September 17 by Britain’s Routledge Publishers. Its authors are two professors well known to the public. One is Ergun Özbudun, the dean of Turkey’s constitutional law and political science fields. The other is William Hale, known for his publications on the military and foreign policy in Turkey. I think the identity of the authors is sufficient guarantee of the book’s quality. The main conclusions of the book, whose writing was completed at the beginning of the year and which I had the privilege of reading before publication, are as follows:

“‘It is possible to characterize the AKP as the Muslim equivalent of conservative parties in Western democracies. While adopting faith-based values on social, cultural, and perhaps economic issues, it rejects the idea of establishing an Islamic state whose laws and processes are incompatible with basic democratic values… In his approach to the Kurdish issue, Tayyip Erdoğan made some important goodwill gestures that went far beyond previous governments in officially recognizing Kurdish identity. However, the AKP failed to produce and pursue a consistent policy that would protect the country’s territorial integrity while meeting the legitimate demands of the Kurds. Similarly, in its stance toward the modest demands of Turkish Alevis, the AKP government preferred to implement an ’avoidance policy’ rather than taking concrete measures…

“The AKP made other mistakes in public policy, but none of them have anything to do with Islamism… The claim that the AKP government has a secret plan to destroy democratic governance and establish an Islamic state in its place is not convincing… Far from undermining democracy, the AKP has worked harder to expand fundamental rights and freedoms than all the governments established since 1960… It is observed that economic factors are much more important than religious factors in explaining the votes it receives…

“At the beginning of 2009, after 6 years in power, it appears that the AKP is being forced to choose between continuing to act as a liberal and reformist force and making peace with conservative state elites. Although concerns that it will turn Turkey into an Islamist autocracy are still widespread among members of the CHP, the TAF, and the judiciary, the possibility that the AKP, by reaching a compromise with its opponents to avoid being subjected to a closure case again, like the center-right parties before it, will not slide toward authoritarianism and inward-looking nationalist attitudes seems more realistic.’ Don’t the developments since Özbudun and Hale put the finishing touches on their book give the impression that the AKP has not exhausted its reformist energy?” (Zaman, 25.08.2009)

It is clearly visible that when I wrote these lines I was unfortunately badly mistaken, and had no concern that the AKP government could slide into Islamist populist authoritarianism.

“Conspiracy theories are poisoning minds”

Since the years when I started writing for Cumhuriyet, one topic I occasionally had to address in my writings was the prevalence of conspiracy theories that poison people’s minds in Turkey. The National Unity and Brotherhood Project that the AKP government launched in 2009 to solve the Kurdish problem was also met with conspiracy theories. I, on the other hand, saw this as an opportunity to end the Kurdish rebellion. As follows:

“The leaders of the MHP and CHP say that the ‘democratization/Kurdish opening’ that the government says it will lead and has been making contacts about is an evil that will lead the people to division and the country to partition, and that behind this evil (‘treason plan’) is the US and the EU. According to the leader of the closed RP, Necmettin Erbakan, the initiative is part of the ‘Haim Nahum Doctrine,’ that is, the Zionists’ plan to ‘make Turkey a province of Israel.’ MHP Deputy Group Chairman Mehmet Şandır also wholeheartedly agrees with this interpretation. There is common ground that brings together the CHP, MHP, and former RP leaders. This ground is that their minds operate not from the analysis of objective facts, but from conspiracy theories, which Karl Popper described as ‘secularized forms of religious superstition.’ The diagnosis and exposure of conspiracy theories is of vital importance for establishing scientific thinking habits in our country.

“Seventeen years ago, based on MÇP leader Alparslan Türkeş’s statement that ‘The events happening in our homeland are monstrous activities organized by imperialism. Terrorists are the lackeys of imperialism…,’ I wrote: ‘Behind the understanding that explains everything with imperialism lies the ’theory’ that philosopher Karl Popper called ‘the conspiracy theory of society.’ According to this theory, widely believed in our country and other countries where scientific thought is not well developed, social events are the work of some powerful centers that benefit from them… According to some, it is the work of imperialists or communists, according to others, Zionists or missionaries. Hasn’t the time come to set aside these superstitions that are completely irrational and unscientific?’ (Cumhuriyet, 15.02.1992)

“Apparently not… Today the same minds are trying to present the government’s search for a solution to the Kurdish problem as the US’s, EU’s, Israel’s plan/conspiracy to divide and partition Turkey. Let us no longer deceive ourselves: The Kurdish problem was not created by imperialists, Zionists, or others; we created it ourselves by ignoring the Kurds with an outdated understanding of modernity and attempting to Turkify them. Because we insisted on this wrong policy, some Kurds rebelled; the PKK rebellion is the latest of these. And yes, now there is an opportunity to end this rebellion.

“Because: 1) The militarists on both sides have understood that they cannot solve the problem with violence. 2) The government in Ankara has grasped that identity policies that ignore the Kurds are unsustainable. 3) Iraqi Kurds no longer see Turkey as a threat, they see that they need rapprochement with Turkey more than ever, and they want to help eliminate the PKK, which is the main obstacle to this. 4) The EU has been repeating for more than a decade that a civilian and political solution to the Kurdish problem must be found for Turkey to meet the membership conditions.

“The US, since the beginning of the Cold War, and especially in the post-9/11 world, places great importance on stability in Turkey, its most reliable ally and partner in the Islamic world. The US under the presidency of Barack Obama is giving great support to the establishment of democracy in Turkey to a degree that no other American administration has done. The Kurdish opening is not an evil imposed by some foreign power to divide the people and partition the country; on the contrary, it is a necessity dictated by reason and conscience to preserve the integrity of the country and the unity of the people, which Turkey has become aware of through debates made possible by its flawed democracy after immeasurably great moral and material losses caused by an internal conflict lasting 25 years. If vote calculations prevent what reason and conscience dictate from being done, one’s eyes must be blinded by superstition not to see that the danger of division-partition will only then become serious.” (Zaman, 5.09.2009)

“Prime Minister Erdoğan should receive the Nobel Peace Prize”

One of the most important reasons for my positive view of the AKP government was the “zero problems with neighbors” policy whose architect was Foreign Minister Ahmet Davutoğlu. My nomination of Prime Minister Erdoğan for the Nobel Peace Prize due to the policies pursued in this context probably constituted the peak of my support for the AKP government in my writings. I wrote as follows:

“In recent weeks, we are witnessing extraordinary activity in foreign policy. Last month, a High-Level Strategic Cooperation Agreement was signed with Syria; the visa requirement between the two countries was mutually lifted. The rapprochement with Syria, with which we have various problems and from which we were on the brink of war just ten years ago because it harbored PKK leader Öcalan, is undoubtedly one of the most important achievements in the AKP government’s ‘zero problems with neighbors’ policy.

“Last weekend, President Gül made an official visit to Paris on the occasion of Turkey-France Year events. French President Sarkozy did not mention ‘privileged partnership’ to Gül; he emphasized that differences of opinion on EU membership should not affect bilateral relations and did not refrain from showing his interest in tenders in Turkey. Of course, the most noteworthy thing in the context of France is that French officials declared to Chief Negotiator Egemen Bağış during his visit last month that they were in favor of continuing negotiations with Turkey.

“Something unexpected also happened last weekend. Greece’s brand-new Prime Minister Yorgo Papandreou made his first foreign visit to Turkey on his fifth day in power. While Papandreou was in Istanbul, I also went to Athens for a meeting and had the opportunity to talk with Greek colleagues about the meaning of this visit. According to the general opinion, Papandreou’s coming to Istanbul to meet with Prime Minister Erdoğan and Foreign Minister Davutoğlu before his visit to Cyprus on October 19, despite the strong reactions in Greek public opinion to Turkish warplanes flying over inhabited Greek islands, is a sign that the coming months are pregnant with new initiatives in Turkish-Greek relations.

“Perhaps the most important foreign policy development not only of the past weekend but of recent years is, of course, Turkey and Armenia officially signing on October 10 in the Swiss city of Zurich the protocols providing for the normalization of relations between them, which they had previously agreed upon. It appears that Ankara is making rapprochement with Armenia contingent on Azerbaijan-Armenia normalization. Prime Minister Erdoğan is repeating that without progress on this second front, there is no question of the protocols passing through parliament and the borders opening. There is no doubt that this is a requirement for achieving peace and stability in the South Caucasus. Ankara is doing the right thing.

“Another very noteworthy foreign policy development of the past week was the cancellation of the joint air exercise in Konya that Israeli warplanes were also to participate in. It appears that the policies pursued by Israel are causing great disappointment not only to the government but also to the TAF. What is disturbing Ankara is apparently not only Israel’s Gaza attack earlier this year, but perhaps even more so, the new Israeli government under Netanyahu setting aside all commitments and continuing to expand Jewish settlements on Palestinian territories, thereby derailing peace negotiations with the Palestinians.

“I came across the most meaningful commentary of recent days in the editorial of Israel’s Haaretz newspaper: ‘Turkish Prime Minister Erdoğan, showing impressive wisdom, is leading reconciliation with Armenia while also working on a solution in Cyprus by improving relations with Greece… The peace agreement between Turkey and Armenia is also a fascinating lesson for Israel and the Palestinians… The Turks, whose ancestors were the Ottomans who ruled our region for centuries, have opened a door of hope for us too.’ (October 12)

“The AKP government is pursuing a policy, of which Mr. Davutoğlu is the architect, that is exemplary for the whole world (including Obama) in solving problems through diplomacy and negotiation. I hope Prime Minister Erdoğan succeeds in all his domestic and foreign policy openings and wins the Nobel Peace Prize.” (Zaman, 13.10.2009)

Considering the points mentioned in the above article, it must be admitted that by late 2009 there were valid reasons to think that the AKP government was pursuing a peaceful foreign policy (one compatible with Turkey’s interests).

## The Sledgehammer mentality is doomed to defeat

The Taraf newspaper, in its headline story on January 20, 2010, wrote that at a plan seminar held at the 1st Army headquarters on March 5-7, 2003 under the leadership of Gen. Çetin Doğan, a military coup plan called “Sledgehammer” was made with the aim of overthrowing the Turkish government. My comment on Taraf’s report was as follows:

“When I read the ‘Sledgehammer coup plan’ news published in Taraf on Wednesday morning, January 20, I had not the slightest doubt about its accuracy. Because for almost as long as I can remember, that is, for about the last fifty years, I have been living in a country where military coup

plots are made and carried out. However, some of the people I encountered throughout the day viewed the news with suspicion, saying it could be ‘disinformation.’ At first I was surprised… Then, once again, I thought about how dependent our perceptions are on the values and ideas in our minds. I do not know what these people think after the details of the coup plan published in Taraf, and after the General Staff’s statement essentially confirming the report. But their skeptical approach to news of the various exposed coup attempts and to the Ergenekon case must be related to their concern about the end of the bureaucratic tutelage regime prevailing in Turkey.

“For a moment, let us assume that there is a serious side to these concerns. Let us say that if the bureaucratic tutelage over it ends, democracy in Turkey will face the danger of turning into a majority dictatorship. Because what has provided balance in the regime and prevented power from being concentrated in one hand until now has been

bureaucratic tutelage. Well, how valid is this claim? Certainly, liberal, in other words libertarian and pluralist democracy, is not just about power being determined by election, that is, majority rule.

The fundamental rights and freedoms of citizens (primarily freedom of expression, organization, and belief) being under constitutional guarantee; the legislature and executive being subject to judicial

oversight; the existence of a strong civil society composed of voluntary organizations independent of the state, a competitive market economy—these are the other indispensable elements of democracy.

“However, the problem Turkey faces today has not the slightest connection with the elimination of fundamental rights and freedoms, with democracy turning into a majority dictatorship. Today in Turkey, neither the principle of majority rule

is valid, nor are fundamental rights and freedoms secure… The administration that comes to power through the people’s vote is under the tutelage of bureaucratic elites who are committed not to liberal democratic principles but to an authoritarian interpretation of Kemalism (or nationalism and secularism)

as it is under tutelage; fundamental rights and freedoms are also restricted by this interpretation. In Turkey today, on one hand the struggle to establish popular sovereignty, on the other hand the struggle to remove the restrictions on fundamental rights and freedoms

is being waged. Turkey today is going through a transition from a kind of democracy that is under the tutelage of a bureaucracy committed to the authoritarian interpretation of Kemalism to a liberal, that is, European-standard democracy.

“This process can succeed, because the ‘Sledgehammer mentality’ is a retreating mentality doomed to defeat. Not only in parliament but in almost every segment, the preference for democracy prevails. It is for this reason that military coup plans are being exposed and failing. The Ergenekon investigation and case became possible because of this. In both the judiciary and the media, the ranks of liberal democracy are getting stronger. Among businessmen as well… On January 21, the election of Ümit Boyner, who comes from the New Democracy Movement, to the TÜSİAD Presidency—

isn’t it a sign of this?

“It is certain that we need external support to establish liberal democracy. Yes, Western allies, especially the US, do not ignore the nature of the regime in Turkey as long as it remains committed to the alliance, as in the Cold War years. But the greatest opportunity we have is the EU membership perspective. The AKP government should once again show the determination and energy of the 2002-2005 period to overcome all the obstacles and make all the reforms necessary for EU membership. If it cannot completely renew the constitution, it should make changes in the constitution and basic laws in the direction of democratization and civilianization without delay. All forces in favor of democracy should also mobilize to give support.” (Zaman, 23.1.2010)

The ‘Sledgehammer coup plan’ disclosed by the Taraf newspaper became the subject of a judicial investigation. The case opened as a result of the investigation began on June 19, 2010 at the Istanbul 10th High Criminal Court. On September 21, 2012, the court sentenced 325 of the 365 defendants, including retired generals Çetin Doğan, Özden Örnek, and İbrahim Fırtına, to aggravated life imprisonment for ‘overthrowing the council of ministers of the Republic of Turkey or forcibly preventing it from performing its duties’; however, it applied various sentence reductions due to “incomplete attempt.”

In the continuation of the case, the Istanbul 4th High Criminal Court on June 19, 2014 unanimously ruled that 234 officers be released and retried and that all arrest warrants at the prosecutor’s office be lifted. In the “Sledgehammer Plan” case, which was retried following the Constitutional Court’s decision of “rights violation,” the Anadolu 4th High Criminal Court on March 31, 2015 decided to acquit 236 defendants as it was not established that they committed the crime charged. However, the prosecution appealed to the Court of Cassation against the acquittal decision regarding defendants Çetin Doğan and 6 other defendants. The 16th Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation on June 14, 2021 unanimously ruled that the crime of “conspiracy to commit a crime” had been committed and overturned the acquittal decision regarding 7 defendants. The case will be retried.

Was the “Sledgehammer coup plan” real, or was it a plot against the military?.. When I wrote the article I quoted above, I had no doubt that the “Sledgehammer coup plan” was real. Years later, writing these lines, I can dwell on two points: 1) As seen in other examples in our history, many years must pass and governments must change for questions related to military coup attempts to be fully clarified. 2) The AKP government experience should have shown that military tutelage does not provide a guarantee against authoritarian civilian rule, and that this can only be achieved by embedding liberal democratic institutions in people’s consciousness and strengthening them.

“Baykal’s resignation should not have been like this”

In the news announced by the Hürriyet newspaper on May 8, 2010 with the headline “Tape blow to Baykal,” it was said that “the hidden camera footage placed on internet sites, allegedly belonging to CHP leader Baykal and CHP MP Nesrin Baytok, created an earthquake effect in politics…” Following this news, Baykal resigned from the CHP leadership. My comment on the incident was as follows:

“When I read the news, I thought the tape was a ‘product of montage’ and an instrument of a vile conspiracy. It is not certain whether the tape is a ‘product of montage’ or not, but there really is a vile conspiracy at hand. Baykal’s resignation should not have been like this. My acquaintance with him goes back a long way… Had Mr. Baykal remained faithful to the libertarian discourse he adopted when the CHP, which the September 12 coup had closed, was reopened in September 1992, he would have become prime minister and could have gone down in Turkish history as a leader who served democracy. But, unfortunately, he headed in the opposite direction; he increasingly settled on guarding the bureaucratic tutelage order, and even worse, on serving as a lawyer for those who attack democracy.

“For these reasons, as someone who voted for the CHP in almost every general election except 2007, I was against the ideas Mr. Baykal defended and the political attitude he adopted, especially from 2005 onward. But I was saddened that Baykal was forced to resign through such a vile conspiracy. I would have wanted him to be held accountable for his wrong policies at the ballot box. Being forced to resign in this way, I’m afraid, will not help the CHP correct itself and review its policies.

“Baykal, while resigning, claims he was subjected to a conspiracy orchestrated by the ruling party, the government. I find this not at all convincing. I don’t think it will be found convincing in public opinion either. Because from the AKP’s perspective, there could not have been a more acceptable chief opposition leader than Baykal. While there were clearly many aspects of the AKP government to criticize, by taking on the role of advocate for those who opposed the government through illegitimate means and those who damaged democratic principles and institutions, he distanced the CHP from being an alternative to power in the eyes of the people. He was supported only ‘reluctantly’ even by die-hard CHP voters.

“For this reason, I find the Taraf newspaper’s headline diagnosis of ‘His supporters struck…’ (May 9) apt. Indeed, the fact that those who thought he could no longer successfully serve their cause were fervently calling on Baykal to resign also pointed to this. That circles which failed to remove the AKP from power through illegitimate means are seeking to equip the CHP with a leader who could block the constitutional changes in the upcoming referendum and win the next elections seems to me to be the strongest ‘theory’ explaining the tape.

“There are also points about the ‘tape blow to Baykal’ that need to be dwelt upon from a media perspective. The first of these is this: Of course, newspapers may have different understandings about to what extent this carries news value. They can view the event as ‘big’ or ‘small’ if they wish. But there could not be the slightest hesitation that the event carried news value and deserved to be commented upon. The second point is this: The secret recording of the tape and giving it to the media is of course a crime; those who did this must definitely be found and punished. The Prime Minister’s instruction to the National Intelligence Organization (MİT) to find the culprits is very appropriate in this regard.

“However, once the ‘tape’ reached the media, it was out of the question not to make it a subject of news and commentary. It should not be forgotten that in democracies, the most important (fourth estate) function of the media is to monitor whether holders of political, administrative, economic, and cultural power are acting contrary not only to democracy and laws but also to moral principles. Holders of power are not ordinary citizens; what they say and do concerns not only themselves but the whole society. Therefore, they do not have ‘private lives’ like ordinary citizens.” (Zaman, 11.05.2010)

## The two faces of the CHP

While commenting on the arguments in the article titled “Sex tape opens the door to a bright future for Turkey” by New York Times Istanbul bureau chief Stephen Kinzer, I also wrote:

“For years, I have been arguing that the other face of the CHP tradition should not be neglected. Yes, on one face, the CHP is the state party, the guardian of the bureaucratic tutelage order. But the same CHP, on its other face, is also the heir of a tradition that opened the door to democratization, even if under tutelage, in the 1940s, that brought the concepts of fundamental rights and freedoms to this country in the 1950s, social rights in the 1960s and 1970s, and cultural rights in the 1980s and 1990s. If the CHP had been able to rebuild itself along the lines of this tradition when it was reopened in 1992, democracy would have long been established in Turkey.

“The National Vision tradition, by learning from mistakes, succeeded in abandoning Islamism and rebuilding itself as ‘Conservative Democracy.’ With a determined leadership cadre, the CHP could very well have abandoned an authoritarian understanding of Kemalism and rebuilt itself as a social democratic party in the European sense. This was the (unfortunately unfulfilled) expectation of myself and many of my friends when the CHP was reopened. Is the door to rebirth now opening for the CHP? I am not optimistic about this. But I agree with Kinzer on this point: Behind Turkey’s successes has always been its ability to renew itself.” (Zaman, 15.05.2010)

After Baykal’s resignation, I welcomed Kılıçdaroğlu’s announcement of his candidacy for the CHP leadership. I wrote as follows:

“Kılıçdaroğlu can pull the CHP onto the democracy mat, that is, he can turn it into a serious opposition party that opposes through legitimate means, directs legitimate criticisms at the government, and therefore an alternative to power, instead of hoping for help from military and judicial coups and playing ‘Ergenekon lawyer.’ He can make a civilized political style that appeals to minds prevail instead of a shouting, polarizing style. Both our democracy and the CHP would greatly benefit from this. I think this is the hope that Kılıçdaroğlu has aroused in public opinion.” (“The hope aroused by Kılıçdaroğlu,” Zaman, 20.05.2010)

More than ten years have passed since then. Despite the great difficulties Kılıçdaroğlu faces, I believe he has played an important role in steering the CHP, which during the Baykal era was dominated by an authoritarian understanding of Kemalism, toward a liberal understanding of democracy.

## Militarism befits neither Ortaylı nor the MHP

As the first decade of the 21st century was coming to a close, as intellectuals who had embraced liberal views since the 1980s, we believed that the main reason Turkey could not establish liberal democracy was the military-bureaucratic tutelage over democracy (majority rule), upon which the frequently recurring military interventions were based. It never occurred to us that majority rule unconstrained by fundamental rights and freedoms could lead to majority dictatorship—to one-man rule, as would be seen under the Erdoğan government. In an article where I criticized militarism, I wrote:

“Prof. Dr. İlber Ortaylı has been a friend I’ve known since our years studying at Ankara University’s Faculty of Political Science. He graduated two years after me, in 1969. He stayed away from the student movements of those days and devoted himself to his education. He learned many languages and became a good historian of the late Ottoman period. I believe the first articles he published in the press appeared on the book page I edited in Cumhuriyet in the 1980s. His book titled The Longest Century of the Empire is a valuable work. It is perhaps the book that best explains that the Tanzimat reforms were a turning point in Turkey’s modernization, not in its semi-colonization. Through this book and other works, he has gained increasing prestige.

“As far as I know, İlber has developed a habit as he ages of viewing almost every notable idea and person negatively, of not approving of anyone. (According to some friends, when this habit combined with the increasing attention he received from society, it led him to a kind of megalomania.) As far as I can follow, in recent years İlber has shown particular hostility toward ideas and people who approach late Ottoman and Republican history with a humane and libertarian perspective. The views he expressed at a Nationalist Movement Party meeting on February 6 are the latest manifestations (perhaps excessive) of this reaction.

“With a charitable reading, some valid points can be found in Ortaylı’s views. Mümtaz’er Türköne addressed some of these on this page (February 9). However, the proper response must surely be given to Ortaylı presenting the scourge called militarism—one of the primary characteristics of fascism—as if it were a virtue. Based on the claim that ‘the primary characteristic of Turks is being a soldier nation,’ Ortaylı argues that ‘in recent years in Turkey a feeling of shame about one’s nationality and a drift toward an anti-militarist, soldier-hating society have been stoked’… He asks what harm Europe could suffer from ‘Turkish society being militarist.’

“Ortaylı cannot be speaking without knowing what militarism means. Militarism means arguing that political problems can best be solved by military methods, that is, by force of arms; wanting the principle of absolute obedience peculiar to armies to dominate all of society; believing that the country can best be governed not by those who come to power through elections but by soldiers, and supporting this. Militarism is not synonymous with soldiering, and it is definitely not a mentality or ideology peculiar to soldiers. Today in Turkey, militarism is unfortunately more prevalent among civilians than soldiers, and we are having great difficulty freeing ourselves from it. Opposing militarism is definitely not being hostile to soldiers. As long as there is a need for defense, there will be armies, soldiers, and weapons. And Turkey also needs an army that does its job properly.

“Turkey has suffered greatly from militarism. The damage inflicted on the country over the last quarter century by the mindset of violent, forceful solutions prevalent among both Turks and Kurds is evident. Ortaylı complains about ‘not having become France in the last 30 years’… If we haven’t, the main culprit is militarism. The militarist mentality is doing great harm to both the army and soldiers in Turkey. Because involvement in politics has resulted in the TAF’s inability to perform its duties properly, and unfortunately is also eroding its prestige.

“Europeans also suffered greatly from militarism. To escape from it, they founded the European Union; they turned to solving problems by talking rather than fighting, to establishing democracy, that is, to making civilization dominant. As Turkey, with our great majority, we also want to be part of the EU for this reason. Yes, joining the EU would for this reason be ‘bliss’ (which Ortaylı doesn’t like)… If European states are inciting us against militarism, good for them… There is much to say about Ortaylı’s other claims too. But let me conclude like this: Militarism befits neither İlber Ortaylı nor the MHP that hosted him.” (Zaman, February 13, 2010)

Upon the publication of this article, the congratulatory messages I received from some of Ortaylı’s historian colleagues were surprisingly numerous. I should also note that İlber, a very old friend of mine, received this criticism of mine with maturity.

Hey soldier, don’t meddle in politics!

The article I wrote about Hasan Cemal’s book titled Turkey’s Soldier Problem also well reflected the view, shared by many liberal-minded intellectuals, that the main problem of democracy in Turkey stemmed from being under military tutelage. I said:

“… It can be said that the ‘soldier problem’ is Turkey’s number one problem today, because the insolubility of all other problems stems from it. Well, why does Turkey have a ‘soldier problem’? Because the role soldiers play in Turkey is incompatible with the liberal democratic order we want to establish. In liberal democracies, there is a clear distinction between the roles of politicians and soldiers. This distinction rests on three pillars. First, soldiers do not interfere in politics and are absolutely subordinate to the elected government. Second, even in matters related to military affairs and defense, it is the elected officials who determine policies. Soldiers may offer advice on these matters, but they are obligated to implement the policies determined by the government. Third, soldiers are absolutely impartial politically; that is, regardless of which party is in power, they must faithfully implement the policies pursued by governments. Turkey has a soldier problem because since the transition to the multi-party system, soldiers have intervened in politics through direct and indirect means, have interfered in the affairs of elected officials on every matter, and have not been politically impartial.

“Well, where does the ‘soldier problem’ originate? It can be said that at the source of the problem is the fact that a significant portion of officers, due to the political culture they acquire in military schools, are committed not to liberal democracy (which makes the West the West and constitutes the fundamental philosophy of the European Union) but to the ‘Atatürkist Thought System’ or to the prohibitionist and authoritarian interpretation of Kemalism. The fact that politicians in Turkey have not been able to reach an agreement among themselves to establish civilian authority over the military (what Hasan Cemal calls the ‘civilian problem’) is also the second, auxiliary reason why the soldier problem still cannot be solved. Hasan Cemal’s latest book is a great service to the struggle to establish democracy because it tells the story of the soldier (and civilian) problem experienced since the 1980s and what this has cost Turkey, with all its important details.

“On the one hand, signs that commitment to the democratic rule of law is increasing among soldiers, and on the other hand, that the Republican People’s Party may henceforth throw its weight behind ending the political role of the military, are giving rise to hope that in the coming years we may achieve, in the words of former Chief of General Staff General Hilmi Özkök, ‘a Turkey where everyone does their own job.’” (Zaman, May 22, 2010)

The experiences we gained in the years after these lines were written revealed that to establish liberal democracy, not only soldiers but also civilians must show loyalty to the fundamental principles of this regime. The AKP government gradually ended military tutelage and built in its place a one-man regime that we can characterize as a majority dictatorship. We will only see over time whether our lived experiences have helped establish the principles that liberal democracy includes not only majority rule but also respect for the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals, no matter how much they remain in the minority.

“We solve by talking, not by fighting”

In July 2010, upon Prime Minister Erdoğan’s announcement during his contacts with opposition leaders that preparations were nearing completion for a professional security unit whose sole task would be to combat the PKK, and that it had not yet been decided whether the unit would be attached to the TAF or to the Police, I wrote the following:

“… It is not possible to underestimate or belittle the necessity and importance of military measures in the fight against the PKK. However, on condition that we do not forget even for a moment that the fight against the PKK cannot be won through military methods alone… It cannot be forgotten for a moment that to win this fight, what essentially needs to be done is to solve the Kurdish problem by resolutely continuing the ‘democratic opening.’ To solve the Kurdish problem, as we have repeatedly stated without tiring, means first of all removing all obstacles to the free expression of Kurdish identity in Turkey, ensuring that Kurdish citizens can freely express their unique concerns, in short, fulfilling the democratic demands of Turkey’s Kurds. Solving the Kurdish problem also means making Turkey a democratic country that all Kurds respect and trust, no matter what country or continent they live in. Only when full respect is shown to Kurdish identity can the environment that feeds the PKK insurgency and drives Kurdish youth to the mountains come to an end. And Turkey can achieve this.

“To solve the PKK problem, which is a product of the Kurdish problem and which has gained aspects independent of the Kurdish problem after a 26-year struggle, what needs to be done above all is to talk with whoever needs to be talked to (the Peace and Democracy Party represented in the parliament, or failing that the PKK leaders in Kandil, or failing that Abdullah Öcalan in İmralı), through whatever direct or indirect channel is necessary; to open the way for PKK militants to engage in politics through legitimate means rather than with weapons.

“If the special units to be deployed on the borders cause even the slightest neglect of the political measures that must be taken as the primary focus, causing attention to once again focus on military methods doomed to fail, let us recognize from now that this will not serve in the slightest the outcome desired by the overwhelming majority of the Turkish and Kurdish people, namely peace and stability prevailing in the country, the ideal of a Turkey growing freer and more prosperous together.” (Zaman, July 17, 2010)

## A thousand times yes

The constitutional amendments proposed by the AKP government to break bureaucratic tutelage over governments based on majority vote were announced to the public on May 12, 2010; the referendum on them was held on September 12, 2010. I had explained in an article dated July 10 that I would say “Not enough but yes” to the constitutional amendments. In my article that came out a few days before the vote, I said:

“Now I feel the need to say ‘A thousand times yes!’ because what was said and seen during the referendum campaign allows me to see better that the acceptance of this package is of vital importance for the normalization of democracy in Turkey; and that if ‘no’ comes out of the ballot box, the forces struggling for bureaucratic tutelage over democracy to continue and for the coup plotters to be acquitted could seize the initiative.

“As I have written before: Of course, I have respect for those who will say ‘no’ to the constitutional amendments or those who will boycott the vote (for one reason or another). After all, democracy means freedom of expression as much as majority rule. However, there is a very fundamental disagreement between those who will say ‘yes’ and the others. Those who will say ‘yes’ prefer Turkey to achieve a democracy at EU standards, while the others prefer it to remain under bureaucratic-military tutelage. According to the others, secularism in its current form (meaning the state controlling religion and restricting religious freedoms) is more important than democracy. For them, the principles to be followed are not those of liberal democracy but of an authoritarian interpretation of Kemalism. Unfortunately, in Turkey there is no consensus on the liberal and pluralist democratic regime that generally prevails in EU countries.

“I say ‘A thousand times yes!’ I can list the basic reasons for this as follows: A ‘yes’ result from the referendum will show that there is a majority in Turkey in favor of a new, civilian, and democratic constitution; from the morning of September 13, a campaign will begin for a new constitution that will secure the free expression and practice of religious and ethnic identities alongside individual freedoms. I believe that the adoption of the constitutional amendments will also help the main opposition party CHP to get its act together and break its ties with the tutelage system. In that case, Turkey will have a stronger will to solve its fundamental problems, primarily the Kurdish problem and subordinating the military to civilian authority. (…) I say ‘A thousand times yes!’ because if the constitutional amendments are adopted, the pressure from society on the ruling AKP government to solve the Kurdish problem by negotiating with the Peace and Democracy Party, to end PKK violence, and thus to make Turkey a free, prosperous country that is an example to its entire region, will increase greatly.” (Zaman, August 31, 2010)

Looking back from today, from 2021, what is now patently obvious is how naively optimistic I was in those days; that it never even occurred to me that ending military tutelage could open the door to majority dictatorship.

## Presidentialism is bad, the parliamentary system is good

Prime Minister Erdoğan, immediately after the referendum held on September 12, 2010, repeated the view he had first touched upon in April of that year; he spoke of abandoning the parliamentary system and switching to a presidential system with new constitutional amendments to be made. Upon this, I wrote the following:

“… As is known, there can be essentially three types of government systems in democracies: The parliamentary system (cradle: Britain), the presidential system (cradle: USA), and the semi-presidential system, which is a hybrid of the two (cradle: France).
