Therefore, a claim that presidential or semi-presidential systems are incompatible with democracy certainly cannot be made. However, like the great majority of our political scientists, I also think that presidential systems are particularly unsuitable for Turkey. I can list the main reasons for this as follows:

“I see great benefit in the head of state (that is, the President) only representing the state and nation, being in a supra-partisan position that all citizens can trust. In the parliamentary system, the President, who is generally elected by parliament through inter-party consensus, can easily play the role of a supra-partisan, unifying statesman. However, in both the presidential and semi-presidential systems, because the president is also the head of the executive branch, it becomes impossible for them to play this supra-partisan, unifying statesman role.

“Turkey needs reforms and therefore a strong executive branch. Only a parliamentary system can provide this. In a parliamentary system, because the Prime Minister, who is the head of the executive branch, comes from parliament, there is no incompatibility between the executive and legislative branches. However, in presidential systems, if the president and the legislature are from different parties, there are major problems in governance. And problems can only be overcome with a culture of compromise (which we don’t really have). The difficulties experienced by the AKP government and Prime Minister Erdoğan during President Ahmet Necdet Sezer’s term were definitely not caused by the parliamentary system, but by the powers granted to the presidency as a tutelage institution by the 1982 constitution, which were incompatible with the parliamentary system and resembled those in semi-presidential systems. In other words, Turkey in a sense experienced the disadvantages of the semi-presidential system.

“Turkey’s need for decentralized restructuring of the state in no way necessitates a switch to a presidential or semi-presidential system. The parliamentary government system is compatible with a federal state structure (as in India); with a structure based on devolution or transfer of powers to regions (as in Britain and Spain); with a unitary structure where all powers except those related to the state’s basic functions (namely defense, security, economy, foreign policy, justice) are transferred to municipalities and local governments (as in Sweden); and even with a unitary structure where governors are elected by general vote (as in Japan).

“The (in my opinion) problematic and therefore undesirable aspect of the parliamentary system is related to its also leaving the door open to coalition governments. But the parliamentary system definitely does not necessitate coalition governments. What leads to incompatible, internally quarreling coalition governments is the proportional representation electoral system. We have learned from experience that even a 10% threshold in the proportional representation system is not enough to prevent coalitions. Coalition governments are (in my opinion) bad, but the remedy is definitely not presidential systems, but the majoritarian electoral system.” (Zaman, October 7, 2010)

In light of the experiences we have gained over the years, I should note that my views on coalition governments and the proportional representation electoral system have changed: Today, I think not that the majoritarian electoral system is more democratic than the proportional representation system, or that single-party governments are more democratic than coalition governments, but quite the opposite…

## The two faces of enlightenment

Enlightenment, light, intellectual… These were concepts frequently used in Turkey’s left (both Kemalist and communist) tradition, drawing their source from the intellectual movement that emerged in Western countries in the 17th and 18th centuries, from positivist philosophy. In one of my articles, I was trying to draw attention to the shallowness and superficiality in the use of these concepts in Turkey:

“Yesterday we celebrated the 87th founding anniversary of the Republic of Turkey. If, like me, you live within the boundaries of a municipality governed by the CHP, you frequently encountered posters containing slogans like ‘The Republic enlightens… Toward brighter tomorrows…’ and similar ones on this occasion. Especially if you are a reader of the Cumhuriyet newspaper, ‘Enlightenment’ will perhaps be one of the concepts you encounter most often. I thought it might be a good idea to write about this concept on the occasion of Republic Day.

“In the history of Western thought, the 18th century is referred to as the Age of Enlightenment. In this era, a series of thinkers, in light of the findings of developing science, subjected traditional institutions, traditions, and morality, and in this context religious beliefs and the authority of the church (in short, the status quo), to critical questioning. The values related to using the findings of reason and science to question the established order, the status quo, the dominant institutions and ideas (ideology) (if you will, critical rationalism), are certainly a legacy of the Age of Enlightenment.

“But this is not the only legacy of ‘Enlightenment.’ The Age of Enlightenment is also the source of the idea that humanity, using its reason, science accepted as a body of absolute and indisputable truths, and the technologies that are its products, can make the world an increasingly better, more advanced, more civilized place by shaping nature and society according to its own preferences (let us call it social engineering). It can be said that what characterized the Modern Age, extending from the Middle Ages to the 20th century, was essentially these two legacies of the Age of Enlightenment.

“The ‘wholesale’ (if you will, revolutionary) interpretations of what we might roughly call ‘social engineering,’ the second legacy of the Age of Enlightenment, yielded disastrous results. Some of these are the disasters caused by the totalitarian regimes (communism) established under the leadership of Marxist-Leninist parties that claimed to be ‘midwifing history’ based on the idea that Karl Marx discovered the laws of society’s development. Another part consists of the disasters caused by Nazism, fascism, and similar totalitarian and authoritarian regimes based on the idea, again using science, of making the superior race/nation dominant. It can be said that the ambition to dominate nature and exploit it for its own purposes using science-technology has also come to threaten life on earth in the 21st century with global warming and climate change.

“The leaving behind of the disasters that Enlightenment’s second legacy (wholesale social engineering) brought upon humanity was made possible largely thanks to Enlightenment’s first legacy (critical rationalism). Critical rationalism not only enabled the mistakes made to be seen; by questioning the idea that all societies would necessarily follow the same path, it opened the door to the transition to the Postmodern, or Post-Modernity, Age. If the dominant ideology of the traditional (pre-modern) age extending to the 17th century was religion, the dominant ideology of the modern age extending to the 20th century was science. Just as in the 18th century religion and religious institutions were subjected to critical questioning, in the 20th century the established (positivist, absolute, infallible) understanding of science was also subjected to critical questioning. As a result of this questioning, it was understood that science consists only of theories valid until proven otherwise, and that as our knowledge of the universe advances, it becomes apparent how little we actually know. The Postmodern Age thus entered suggests that religion and science have separate domains; that religion must approach science with respect, and science must approach religion with respect.

“I am aware of the problems that come with reducing complex matters to simplicity. But at the very least, one must be conscious that ‘Enlightenment’ does not have a single legacy, that it has at least two faces. The legacy of ‘Enlightenment’ that must be embraced is critical rationalism. But unfortunately, the circles in our country that constantly trumpet ‘Enlightenment’ are turning their backs on critical and questioning reason.” (Zaman, October 30, 2010)

## The two different faces of the ’68 generation

At the end of 2010, when Prof. Dr. Burhan Kuzu, Chairman of the Constitutional Commission of the Turkish Grand National Assembly, was pelted with eggs at Ankara University’s Faculty of Political Science and not allowed to speak, his statement that “The ’68 generation has been a curse on this country…” inflamed debates about the ’68 generation. While following these debates, I concluded that there were still some reminders I could make in addition to what I had previously written and said. And I wrote the following:

“First: What do we mean by ‘the ’68 generation’? We are talking about young people who, while studying at universities in Ankara and Istanbul in the late 1960s, engaged in intense questioning and debate about the fundamental political problems of the world and Turkey, and who eventually took action with a great sense of social responsibility and idealism, guided by certain ideas, to fundamentally change the country. When evaluating the ’68 generation, as with almost every subject, it is necessary to consider it in light of the conditions of its time, with its different aspects and the evolution it has undergone.

“Those were Cold War years. The Western and Eastern blocs were competing for influence over Turkey. The young people were under the influence of the world: they were under a bombardment of ideas from the West about criticisms of capitalist democracies and from the East about criticisms of established communist regimes. On the other hand, internally, they were under the influence of the political environment determined by the May 27, 1960 military coup and the 1961 constitution adopted afterwards. The most influential intellectual movement on the ‘68 generation was undoubtedly Marxist socialism with its different interpretations (which has also become quite marginalized in the world today). The answer to the question of why there was such an oppressive regime and such an unjust social order in Turkey was quickly found: The culprits were imperialism and capitalism; the remedy was revolution and socialism. There were different prescriptions for how the revolution would take place: Some were convinced of top-down approaches (coup-making) for the revolution, while others adopted armed revolution models from Latin America or China learned from books. With increasing fanaticism, a race over ’who is more revolutionary’ began.

“These were years when development policies based on import substitution were still producing quite successful results, when the economy was growing, real wages were rising, and villagers were getting richer. The young people received no support from society; the state, for its part, approached them with its usual unsympathetic, merciless attitude of punishing in the harshest manner. Some of the young people were executed, some were killed extrajudicially; the great majority served years in prison. This treatment they received encouraged many to persist in the path they had taken. While many over time gave up socialism and turned to nationalism, some became outright fascists.

“But among the members of the ’68 generation, most of those who were able to find the opportunity to reflect on what was happening in the world and in Turkey reached a different conclusion: They understood (some at an earlier stage, some later) that freedom of expression, individual autonomy, human rights, the rule of law, and democracy are indispensable for a society’s liberation and attainment of prosperity and justice. (This understanding also applied to a significant portion of those among the young people studying at universities in the late 1960s who were captivated not only by Marxist ideology but also by other authoritarian and totalitarian ideologies of a nationalist or Islamist nature.)

“Consequently, a portion of the ’68 generation, coming from painful but rich experiences, today ranks among the leading advocates of freedom and pluralist democracy in Turkey. (I have never doubted that most of those who were executed or killed extrajudicially would also be in the democracy camp today if they had survived.) If Turkey is today progressing from democracy under tutelage toward a normal democracy (in this context, if the party to which Burhan Kuzu belongs has been able to take off the National Vision shirt), this has been made possible to some extent thanks to the effective criticisms that intellectuals belonging to the ’68 generation directed at the tutelage order and the national security state established in the 1980s…” (Zaman, December 16, 2010)

Years later, now reading these lines, I say: What great naivety it was to think in those days that Turkey was progressing “from democracy under tutelage toward a normal democracy”… Indeed, the signals that I would begin to awaken from this dream would not be delayed…

# CHAPTER XIII / DOES ERDOĞAN WANT TO BE PUTIN?

It could be said that the first sign that my commentary on the AKP government, and specifically on Prime Minister Erdoğan, would shift from a benevolent to a critical perspective was the article I wrote in early 2011, expressing my own suspicions that Erdoğan wanted to become Putin. Some opponents were saying that the AKP wanted to turn Turkey not into Iran but into Russia, and I agreed with this diagnosis. Here it is:

“The opposition has for some time abandoned the claim that the AKP would turn Turkey into Iran, instead saying it would turn it into Russia, that Erdoğan wants to be Putin… I have difficulty understanding the Prime Minister’s citing France and (yes!) Russia (the semi-presidential system where almost all powers are concentrated in the president’s hands) as examples. Because as we head to elections in June, polarizing the country, alienating some AKP supporters, and reducing the government’s votes is highly likely; I don’t find it compatible with reason and logic to bring up a proposal that has very little chance of being adopted.

“When it doesn’t accord with reason and logic, psychological explanations come to mind. It is claimed that the Prime Minister wants to be the next President and then to be as powerful a president as possible. It’s also difficult to explain how Erdoğan, who when addressing the Egyptian dictator Mubarak could say ‘We are mortal, we are not permanent. As Muslims, the place we will all end up is a pit two meters deep…’, who surely knows that democracy is the rule of rules not persons, could think this way, but I don’t see any other acceptable explanation…

“It’s very clear that presidential or semi-presidential government systems are not suited to Turkey’s makeup. Because unfortunately, both consensus on democracy and the culture of compromise are quite weak in our country. If we take the last referendum as a measure, at least 42% of the people are in favor of continuing the bureaucratic tutelage system. Almost every issue can become an occasion for polarization. In our society, besides political differences of opinion, there are divisions along religious-secular, Sunni-Alevi, Turkish-Kurdish axes. What we really need is to save both the government and the electoral system from being a monstrosity…” (Zaman, 8.2.2011)

Unfortunately, developments went in exactly the opposite direction of my hopes and expectations. Prime Minister Erdoğan gradually achieved his goal of “becoming Putin.”

The 2007 referendum established the rule that the President would be elected by popular vote; Erdoğan became President on August 28, 2014. With the referendum held on April 16, 2017, Turkey moved from its own peculiar parliamentary system to its own peculiar presidential system; Erdoğan’s one-man rule as both AKP leader and President became institutionalized.

“We are learning the value of the rule of law”

However, I maintained my optimism about the future of democracy in Turkey. The European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) prepared a report titled “What does Turkey think?” after similar reports on China and Russia. In the study conducted jointly with the Centre for Economics and Foreign Policy Studies (EDAM), ECFR-affiliated researchers held a roundtable meeting with academics and journalists from Turkey in Istanbul at the end of February 2011. In my speech at this meeting, I said that Turkey was learning democracy and the rule of law through experience. I explained my view as follows:

“The history of the Republic in the first half of the 20th century is a period of building a secular Turkish nation under authoritarian single-party rule. The second period roughly covers the second half of the 20th century. During this period, Turkey experienced the establishment and operation of a type of democracy under the tutelage of the military-civilian bureaucracy (state elites), where democratic rights and freedoms were quite restricted. Since roughly the beginning of the 21st century, we have been in a struggle to establish a normal democracy. By normal democracy, I mean a democracy in which the country is governed by the party or parties that win elections, but where the rights and freedoms of minorities (in every sense—political, religious, ethnic) are guaranteed by the rule of law (that is, laws and practices that respect human rights).

“We hope that this struggle will be completed after this year’s elections with the discussion and adoption of a new, civilian, and democratic constitution. There are both major obstacles ahead of this struggle and factors that could secure its success. The most important obstacle is that a significant portion of political, bureaucratic, economic, and cultural elites and civil society take a stance in favor of the continuation of the ‘old regime,’ that is, bureaucratic tutelage. The front opposing the transition to normal democracy is also quite broad: it includes not only the kind of Kemalists who yearn for 1930s Turkey but also (for different reasons) portions of Islamists, Turkish and Kurdish nationalists, extending into the ruling party and the government itself.

“Among the factors that give hope that the struggle can succeed is that the great majority of the people, as well as Western allies after the Cold War, take a stance in favor of a normal democracy in Turkey. The factor I particularly want to emphasize is that Turkey is learning through experience that democracy does not just mean majority rule, but also a state of law that respects individual and minority rights.

“In recent days, Turkey is seeing and learning that rights and law are valuable not just for themselves but for everyone. Until recently, the common understanding among officers was that democracy could be destroyed and the law trampled underfoot for the state’s interests. Active and retired soldiers being tried in the Sledgehammer and Ergenekon cases have seen the value of the rule of law and begun speaking of rights and law in their defenses. Some civilians who until yesterday worked for Turkey to come under military rule are now speaking of rights and law.” (Zaman, 5.3.2011)

Ten years later, what I said in the above article seems noteworthy to me in this respect: how I had substituted my expectations and hopes for reality when I said “Turkey is learning through experience that democracy does not just mean majority rule, but also means a state of law that respects individual and minority rights…”

“The Imam’s Army”

At this time, allegations that the Gülen community had taken over the police, prosecutors, and judiciary in Turkey had spread everywhere. Regarding these allegations, I wrote the following:

“You can guess that I was also confronted with questions about the Fethullah Gülen movement from EU parliamentarians and officials I met in Brussels last week: ‘What did I think about the allegations that the Gülen movement had taken over the police, prosecutors, and judiciary in Turkey? Was the Ergenekon case a fabricated case by Gülen supporters in the police and judiciary to silence opposition to the AKP government? Was Ahmet Şık arrested because he wrote the book The Imam’s Army revealing these truths, and was the book banned before printing for this reason?’ I want to share with readers the answers I gave to these questions.

“One: I have been writing for Zaman for more than eight years. This newspaper is published with the support of the Gülen movement. Since I am not in the habit of hiding my views, I first expressed my opinion about Gülen in 1995, in an article titled ‘Respect for Hocaefendi’ published in Milliyet newspaper. My views have not changed; they have strengthened.

“Two: Islamophobia (fear of Islam) may not be as widespread in Turkey as in Europe, but it is quite strong in certain segments. According to the understanding that has dominated a segment of the elites since the founding of the Republic, especially the military and civilian bureaucracy, if Islam is not kept under state monopoly and control, if religious freedoms are not restricted, if religious movements are not kept under pressure, Turkey could become like Saudi Arabia or Iran. For this reason, Sufi orders, which are popular interpretations of Islam, have been banned since 1925; Alevism is not officially recognized; religious communities are not allowed to gain legal personality. Yet Turkey is predominantly a religious society. Despite all prohibitions and pressures, Sufi orders, the communities deriving from them, and faith-based social movements, most adapting to modernization, maintain their vitality. The prevalence of the Gülen movement, a faith-based social movement, frightens positivist and Islamophobic elites.

“Three: In Turkey, where scientific thinking has not developed, conspiracy theories—the belief that behind every event there is an omnipotent actor—are very common. This actor can be imperialism, communists, Zionists, and so on. Turkey today is experiencing the pains of transition from a kind of democracy under military-bureaucratic tutelage to a democracy at European standards. Society is polarized between those who want democracy and the tutelage advocates. Among the former, there is a widespread tendency to see the ‘deep state’ or the Ergenekon organization under every rock; among the latter, there is a tendency to see the Gülen movement, which they try to demean, as they imagine, by calling its members ‘Fethullahists.’

“Four: Gülen is a religious scholar who supports modernization, meaning democracy, secularism in the sense of freedom of belief, fundamental rights and freedoms, respect for different beliefs and lifestyles, and development based on a market economy; who sees religion and science as complementary to each other; who emphasizes the spiritual and social aspects of Islam. He encourages his followers to serve the people and humanity by organizing companies, schools, hospitals, and aid organizations. He has always advocated adherence to laws and legitimacy. These are the reasons why he has gained great respect in Turkish society during the modernization process. But positivist and Islamophobic minds, because they can never accept that religion can play a positive role, hold the Gülen movement responsible for almost every evil.

“Five: The Ergenekon case is absolutely not a case fabricated to silence opposition to the AKP government. The emergence of practices contradicting the rule of law in its conduct does not even slightly overshadow the fact that this case is of great importance as it is the first time in the country’s history that coup instigators and perpetrators are being held accountable. As in every segment of society, there may be those who respect Gülen among the police, prosecutors, and judges involved in this investigation. But the claim that all of them take orders from Gülen or his movement neither accords with logic nor serves any purpose other than sabotaging the case.” (7.4.2011)

As can be understood from the above article, I was explaining the allegations about the Gülen community essentially as conspiracy theories arising from secularist, positivist prejudices. My extremely well-intentioned, naive perspective toward this community would unfortunately continue until the coup attempt on July 15, 2016—that is, until it became clear that community members in the armed forces played an important role in this attempt.

“A solution is possible, the opportunity should not be missed”

Yes, by 2011, I maintained views that I now, looking back, characterize as completely disconnected from reality—that Turkey would gradually establish liberal democracy over time and achieve a regime respectful of freedom of belief and ethnic identities. I was not at all alone in these views. After a visit to Diyarbakır in June 2011, I reflected the views expressed in the region as follows:

“The two days I spent in Diyarbakır reinforced my belief: Turkey, having left denial behind, can advance toward recognizing Kurdish identity. There is an opportunity that must not be missed. The cornerstones of this opportunity are these: The overwhelming majority of Kurds are committed to the country’s unity. The ruling party AKP, despite its vacillations, retains the trust of at least half of the Kurds. It is aware that, in order not to lose this trust, the new constitution must respond to Kurds’ common demands. That’s why the Prime Minister, in Diyarbakır, which gave him a great morale boost, did not content himself with emphasizing unity of faith and history; he promised ‘a constitution that both the person from Diyarbakır and the person from Istanbul can call my constitution.’ An extremely important intellectual transformation is taking place in the main opposition CHP. Chairman Kılıçdaroğlu is aware that not only the country’s but also the party’s interests require winning the trust of the Kurds. That’s why after 9 years he goes to Diyarbakır and says: ‘Yes, there is a Kurdish problem and your brother Kemal will solve it… Whatever the cost, we will bring peace…’

“Well, what does the BDP say? Since undoubtedly the KCK/PKK cannot speak with a single voice, the BDP also does not speak with a single voice. I think one of the most noteworthy voices rising from the BDP is Abdullah Demirbaş, mayor of Diyarbakır’s Sur district, who opened the door for municipalities in the Southeast to provide multilingual services and who is being tried in more cases than he can count. The main points of what Mr. Demirbaş, who could say about my criticisms of the BDP ‘Everyone needs criticism…’, told me are as follows:

“Don’t look at the increasingly tense atmosphere between parties during the election campaign. On June 13, the atmosphere will normalize, Turkey will seek the path of reconciliation. 75 percent of Kurds are in favor of the country’s unity. A constitution reconciling Turkish sensitivities with Kurdish demands can be made. There have been three great alliances between Turks and Kurds until today. The first was the joint conquest of Anatolia in 1071, the second was the war of liberation between 1919-1925. Now it’s time for the third alliance; the constitution that will democratize the Republic. We have two basic expectations from this constitution: Either it should make no reference to ethnic identities, or it should stipulate that all ethnic and religious groups are equal, free citizens. It should restructure the administration in 20-25 regions in a way that makes the principle of bottom-up local governance dominant. A statement from the Prime Minister on June 13 that such a constitution will be made will, I am sure, start the process of silencing the guns once and for all.

“In Diyarbakır, I also met with Mr. Şerafettin Elçi, one of the BDP-supported independent candidates. He said that his being an independent candidate from the BDP, which he had criticized much until now, should be understood as a sign of how hopeful he was about the resolution of the problem and the silencing of guns, and his desire to contribute to this. He expressed his belief that AKP, CHP, and BDP could reach a consensus to solve the problem by negotiating among themselves. He emphasized that this opportunity should not be missed. (…)

“Let us hope that his commitment to the vision of Turkey in 2023 as one of the world’s strongest, most respected countries, receiving the respect of all Kurds and being the guarantor of stability in its region, will push Prime Minister Erdoğan to act decisively on the path to resolution.” (Zaman, 4.6.2011)

Why is my vote going to the Has Party?

I explained whom I would vote for in the general elections held on June 12, 2011 as follows:

“Since 1994, when I started regular column writing, I have written in every election which party I would vote for. As columnists, we comment on almost every political issue and share our opinions with readers. I consider declaring whom I will vote for as a requirement of commentary. I had mentioned recently the reasons why I was undecided for the first time in this election. But in the end, I decided to vote for Has Party. Why?

“I have not the slightest doubt that the Justice and Development Party government is Turkey’s most successful government since the transition to the multi-party system. For this reason, the AKP is coming to power for a third term in the June 12 elections. It doesn’t need my vote for that. But the Prime Minister, who has turned the government and the AKP into a party of ‘yes-men,’ will need warnings and criticisms very much in the coming period. One of the issues the AKP government most needs to be warned and criticized about is its view of development as an end rather than a means. With the mentality of ‘development at any cost,’ we should not allow the destruction and plunder of our country’s nature, its most precious asset, or the disregard of human health.

“Turkey’s need for a strong Green Party that above all defends nature and wildlife is growing. The Turkey Greens Party, founded in 2008, co-chaired by Ümit Şahin and Yüksel Selek, unfortunately cannot participate in the election because it has not yet managed to organize in enough provinces. Among the parties participating in the election, the party whose views are close to mine on environmental issues as well as many other issues is the People’s Voice Party (Has Party), founded last November under the chairmanship of Mr. Numan Kurtulmuş. While ruling party spokespersons, despite the Fukushima disaster, speak like lobbyists for the nuclear industry with great obliviousness and indifference, what Has Party says seems particularly commendable to me. Has Party says exactly this in its June 12, 2011 Election Manifesto:

“‘The depletion of oil and natural gas reserves and the gradual increase in their prices, as well as the allocation of water resources for human use, has directed the whole world toward nuclear energy. However, the magnitude of the risks is causing people to hesitate. Today, many countries in the world, especially developed countries, meet their energy needs with nuclear power plants. We know that the history of nuclear power plants is full of accidents threatening the existence of humans and even all living beings. Most recently, the radioactive danger spreading from the Fukushima nuclear power plant damaged by the earthquake in Japan still threatens a large part of the world. Not only accidents but also the dangerous radioactive wastes produced by nuclear power plants continue to pose a threat to living beings. Has Party is a political party that puts humans and humanity first. Our party is against nuclear power plants, which pose a great threat to humanity. Because the essence of nuclear technology is not peaceful but warlike. A technology whose “margin of error” is mass deaths and permanent diseases is unacceptable. No nuclear power plant will be built in Turkey during our government. In addition, our party will show solidarity with nuclear energy opponents around the world and work for the closure of nuclear power plants and the elimination of nuclear weapons numbering in the tens of thousands.’ (p. 49)

“This is why my vote goes to Has Party…” (Zaman, 7.6.2011)

“I take back my vote”

My announcement and act of voting for HAS Party in the 2011 general elections was rightfully regarded as “comical” by some friends and, worse, by my wife Fatma Alpay. No positive (or negative) reaction had come from HAS Party members either. The People’s Voice Party, HAS Party, founded on November 1, 2010, dissolved itself on September 19, 2012 and joined the AKP with most of its members; thus completely abandoning its criticisms of the government. Numan Kurtulmuş, who entered politics with the Virtue Party, joined the Felicity Party during the process in which the Virtue Party split into the Felicity Party and the AKP, and then left the Felicity Party to found HAS Party, interpreted the invitation they received to join the AKP by saying “it is because of the value of HAS Party’s word, the reputation of its word.” It cannot be said that Kurtulmuş, who continued as AKP Deputy Chairman in 2023 and became one of Erdoğan’s closest supporters in the process of moving toward authoritarian one-man rule, has had an unusual political career by Turkish standards. About a year later, I would feel the need to take back my vote for Has Party and write as follows:

“In the first election I participated in after my final return in 1981 from Sweden, where I had taken refuge as a victim of the March 12 coup, I voted for the Motherland Party newly founded by Turgut Özal, believing he would civilianize the administration. I never regretted it. But from 1987 to 2002, I voted for CHP in all general elections (not for any other reason but lack of alternatives). I regretted most of them. In the 2007 elections, I voted for my friend Baskın Oran, who was an independent candidate from my electoral district. Baskın was not elected, but he said what needed to be said. Well done…

”In last year’s elections, I voted for HAS Party led by Numan Kurtulmuş. The parting of ways of Kurtulmuş and his friends with the Felicity Party had made a positive impression on me. But the reason for my voting for HAS Party was single and simple: It was the one and only party whose program opposed the construction of nuclear power plants. To underline how much I valued this stance against the AKP government, which with complete obliviousness had set out to bring the curse of nuclear energy upon the country regardless of the majority of the people being against it, I voted for HAS Party. You can guess the thoughts aroused in me by the same HAS Party now deciding to join the AKP… What can I say to not say something harsher?.. I take back my vote.

“Kurtulmuş, who accused Erdoğan of ‘becoming a pharaoh’ and the AKP of ‘becoming like Croesus,’ who left nothing unsaid about the AKP including that it was ‘a friend of Israel’ and ‘a political structure at the IMF’s service,’ has now decided to join the AKP, probably providing the freshest example of doing politics for seats rather than ideas and ideals in Turkey. I don’t know what the participation of Kurtulmuş and his party, whose reputation has been severely damaged, will bring to the AKP, but the purpose of Erdoğan’s invitation and the tactic he follows is very clear: To make the AKP the only alternative for voters in the same lane…” (Zaman, 21.07.2012)

“Liberal and pluralist democracy is being established”

In the general elections held on June 12, 2011, the AKP won 50% of the votes and 327 seats in parliament. I saw the election result as positive for the future of democracy and commented as follows:

“The June 12 election results are a new victory for democracy in Turkey. The first democratic victory on the path to liberation from military-bureaucratic tutelage occurred on November 3, 2002. In my first article titled ‘Victory of Democracy’ published in this newspaper (November 5, 2002), I said in summary: Despite perhaps the world’s worst electoral system, Turkey wiped from parliament the coalition parties that had dragged the country into the worst economic crisis in its history; it gave power to the cadre that had achieved a great intellectual transformation from the anti-EU National View to the pro-EU Conservative Democracy. In my article titled ‘New Victory of Turkish Democracy’ published after the July 22 elections (July 24, 2007), I expressed in summary: The achievements in both economy and democracy were rewarded; Turkey said ‘continue on’ to the AKP government under Prime Minister Erdoğan’s leadership.

“The June 12 elections also confirm Turkey’s progress toward establishing liberal and pluralist democracy. No record was broken in voter turnout, but the highest rate of recent years was reached. The rate rose from 79% in 2002 to 85% in 2007, and to 87% now. Voting took place with great maturity; no serious incident was encountered. Voters showed great care in concentrating their votes on parties or independent candidates they believed could enter parliament: Despite the 10% threshold, the rate of wasted votes dropped from 45% in 2002 to 15% in 2007, and to 5% this time. The 24th Term Turkish Grand National Assembly has no representation weakness; 95% of the votes are represented. The number of female deputies rose from 50 to 77; nearly one-third of the target has been reached.

“The AKP government received the reward for its services to the country in economy, democracy, and foreign policy. It raised its vote share from 34% in 2002 to 47% in 2007, and to 50% this time. It was seen that those who work in democracy win. This is a great success that should be celebrated for the AKP, especially for Prime Minister Erdoğan, its architect. The AKP not only received one out of every two votes but also strengthened its standing as the party of all of Turkey, of all regions. With this democratic victory, Turkey shines a light on the entire region, on the entire world. The people of Turkey gave the AKP government strong authority to govern the country for another 4 years, but did not give it the authority to draft alone the new, civilian, and democratic constitution it expected. The AKP’s number of deputies dropped (from 341) to 326. All political and civil society will prepare the new constitution through dialogue and consensus.

“The CHP received only half as many votes as the AKP, but increased its vote share from 20% in 2007 to 26%, and its number of deputies from 112 to 135. It became the party that increased its vote share and number of deputies the most. Kılıçdaroğlu’s policy of removing the CHP from being the party of the military-bureaucratic tutelage regime found serious support. The CHP could have been even more successful if it had not included Sledgehammer and Ergenekon defendants, some hardened representatives of the tutelage order, in its candidate lists. The MHP, despite all the efforts Prime Minister Erdoğan made to push it below the threshold, despite the ugly tape scandals (it is still unclear who orchestrated them), did not fall below the threshold. I attribute the decrease of its vote share by only one point (from 14% to 13%) to its having become a victim and thus winning the votes of some voters who would not normally vote for the MHP.

“With its ‘Labor, Democracy, Freedom Bloc’ policy, the BDP, which nominated socialist Turks as well as conservative, religious Kurds, managed to increase its number of representatives in the Turkish Grand National Assembly from 20 in 2007 to 31. The Kurdish-majority region strongly showed its support for democratic struggle, not violence. Let us hope that the BDP taking an important role in drafting a constitution that will also respond to Kurds’ demands will be a major step toward defeating the war lobbies and Turkey solving its problems in a civilized manner, through dialogue and consensus. The overwhelming majority of Turkey approves of Prime Minister Erdoğan’s ‘balcony speech’ on the evening of June 12 and expects him to remain committed to the promises made there.” (Zaman, 14.6.2011)

## Erdoğan can achieve peace and go down in history

It could be said that after the June 12, 2011 elections, my suspicions that Erdoğan “might want to be Putin” had dissipated, and my optimism about our future as a country had peaked. I wrote:

“The Justice and Development Party under Prime Minister Erdoğan’s leadership won a historic electoral victory on June 12. It became the first party in the history of our multi-party system to win an election by increasing its votes for the third time. The Prime Minister built his election campaign on the slogan ‘Turkey is ready, target 2023.’ He set himself the goal of making Turkey one of the world’s most advanced democracies and one of the ten most developed economies on the Republic’s 100th anniversary. This goal can definitely be achieved, but unfortunately Turkey is not yet ready for it, because its fundamental problem, the Kurdish problem, awaits a solution. Yes, the denial of Kurds has ended; but neither have the democratic demands of Kurds been met, nor has the PKK laid down arms. Without achieving these, Turkey can never reach the goals Mr. Prime Minister has set his heart on.

”On June 12, the people of Turkey from almost every segment gave Prime Minister Erdoğan and the AKP government very strong support—seldom given to any government in democracies—to achieve the 2023 goals. Now they expect something in return. There is a historic opportunity before the Prime Minister: The people of Turkey in this election said ‘Absolutely no!’ to the military-bureaucratic tutelage that would tie the government’s hands and trip it up, to authoritarian Kemalism. But the overwhelming majority is ready to support a new Republic faithful to what Mr. Prime Minister said in his ‘balcony speech’ on the night of June 12—the ‘founding philosophy of the Republic’ followed by ‘Gazi Mustafa Kemal and his friends’ between 1919-1923. As clearly seen in this election, both Turkish nationalists who reject coexistence and want to forcibly impose Turkish identity on Kurds, and Kurdish nationalists who seek a separate state, are only a very small portion of Turkey’s society. The overwhelming majority of the people of Turkey are in favor of becoming free and prosperous in peace.

“The cadre under Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu’s leadership is working for the main opposition party CHP to be freed from military-bureaucratic tutelage and to commit to the principles of liberal and pluralist democracy. Mr. Kılıçdaroğlu said in Diyarbakır, ‘There is a Kurdish problem and your brother Kemal will solve this problem… Whatever the cost, we will bring peace…’ He even mentioned the declaration of a general political amnesty in exchange for the PKK laying down arms. He proposed the establishment of a commission in the new Turkish Grand National Assembly composed of wise men from all parties who would not make the issue a matter of political contention, and that this commission should talk with Abdullah Öcalan if needed. Despite making such a great intellectual renewal, the CHP under Kılıçdaroğlu’s leadership received approval from voters and increased its votes. Kılıçdaroğlu is ready for ‘reconciliation’ after the election; he tells the Prime Minister ‘my door is open.’ Had he not made the mistake of nominating Ergenekon defendants, perhaps he would have received even more votes.

”Former BDP chairman Selahattin Demirtaş said the following on June 13: ‘Now we can open the paths to peace. For this, in all constitutional discussions, in all solutions, we are the interlocutors, the elected politicians… For this war to stop, negotiations with Mr. Öcalan must continue, direct talks must be held with the PKK, which is one side of this war. The government should not avoid this. We politicians are also ready to support this.’ (Zaman, June 14) PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan attributes the Kurdish problem to ‘departing from the founding philosophy at the beginning of the Republic.’ ‘The constitution of the Republic of Turkey accepts the democratic existence and expression of all cultures… Let them put this sentence in the constitution, and within two months the PKK will lay down arms,’ he says. (See Yıldıray Oğur, Taraf, June 14.)

“There is a historic opportunity before Prime Minister Erdoğan: By talking and reaching consensus with all parties, by making the constitution of ‘Turk, Kurd, Zaza, Arab, Circassian, Roma, Alevi, Sunni, minorities, that is, 74 million’ that he promised from the balcony on June 12, he can go down in history as the leader who brought Turkey to peace and tranquility.” (Zaman, 16.6.2011)

What is happening in Turkish foreign policy?

By 2011, I also maintained optimism about the foreign policy pursued by the AKP, whose architect was Ahmet Davutoğlu. With these arguments:

“Recently I’ve been inundated with foreign visitors. Just last week, the common question of academics, analysts, and diplomats from Spain, the USA, Greece, Japan, and even Australia was: What is happening in Turkish foreign policy? My readers might be curious about my answer to them. In summary: Throughout the Cold War, Turkey’s foreign policy was almost entirely indexed to the West; it was based on the principles of commitment to the NATO alliance and the goal of integration with Europe. With the end of the Cold War, the perception that its value to the Western alliance had diminished, the beginning of questioning its human rights and democracy performance by allies, and falling far behind in the queue for EU membership led to a period of confusion in Ankara that would last about ten years. This was overcome with the AKP government. The ‘zero problems with neighbors’ policy, designed by Ahmet Davutoğlu and envisaging adaptation to post-Cold War regional and global conditions, was adopted.

”The ‘zero problems’ policy, based on the liberal principles of solving problems through dialogue and increasing mutual economic dependence, had two main goals: to support growth by increasing political and economic relations with regional countries, and to strengthen democracy at home and national security abroad. With these two main objectives, Ankara either resolved or put on the negotiating table its problems with all its neighbors; on the other hand, it tried to help dialogue between problematic parties to reduce the risk of conflict and war in the region. This policy was also inspired by the EU’s ‘neighborhood policy’ and helped Turkey get closer to the EU in every respect: The economy grew, democracy advanced, Turkey became a source of inspiration for its region.

“The ‘zero problems’ policy included rapprochement not only between governments but also between peoples. Through trade, tourism, cultural exchange, television series, and so on, societies drew closer to each other. Everywhere, but especially in the Arab World, Turkey’s image changed fundamentally. The image of a Turkey whose economy and democracy were strengthening under a Muslim Democrat government, which did not turn its back on the Islamic world, which started accession negotiations with the EU, which could say no to the USA, which had the courage to remind Israel of its mistakes, turned positive in the Arab street. Turkey as a source of inspiration has a ‘contribution’ to the Arab Spring.

”However, the Arab Spring (the collapse of authoritarian regimes in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya, and the appearance that others’ turn would come) is reshuffling the cards in the region. It could be said that the Arab Spring is causing as fundamental a change in environment/context for Turkish foreign policy as the end of the Cold War. In this new period, Ankara is turning to emphasize the role of ‘Turkey as a focus of democracy and secularism in the Middle East,’ which Prime Minister Erdoğan signaled in his visits to Arab Spring countries. However, to play this role, it must solve the Kurdish-PKK problem; it must implement the state that stands equidistant from all beliefs, including atheists, which it proposes to Arab Spring countries.

“I don’t think Ankara’s foreign policy disturbs sensible Western governments. Is Ankara doing wrong as the only member of the Western alliance keeping dialogue channels with Tehran open? Do you think Washington is not in some way pleased that it is the only member of the Western alliance that finds the courage to remind the Israeli government of its mistakes? Would you prefer the Arab Street to respect Tehran or Ankara? If Muammar Gaddafi and Bashar Assad didn’t listen, was it wrong for Ankara to invite them to reason? If Turkey establishes a ‘democracy axis’ with emerging Arab democracies, will this be to the detriment of Western allies? Finally, if there is a deadlock in Turkey-EU relations today, is Ankara mainly responsible for this, or is it Mr. Sarkozy, Ms. Merkel, and the Southern Cyprus governments who rely on them?” (Zaman, 3.11.2011)

Should the government return to its ‘apprenticeship’ period?

It could be said that during roughly the first ten years of its rule, I had given substantial support to the AKP government with the hope that it would lead Turkey to liberal and pluralist democracy and eventually EU membership, and my criticisms had been limited to its policies on issues such as media, environment, and energy. From the end of 2011, however, I began to criticize the AKP government in my writings with increasing intensity, out of concern that it was taking the country toward one-man rule. In the article titled “Should the government return to its apprenticeship period,” I said:

“Politicians not keeping their word, displaying inconsistencies, falling short of expectations is probably not a situation unique to Turkey. Of course, they cannot be expected to act like intellectuals, to follow the rule of saying and doing what they believe to be right. Politicians have vote calculations to come to power and stay there. This is also in the nature of democracy. All this is true, but in Turkey, politicians’ failure to keep their word, their inconsistencies, their falling short of expectations are exceeding reasonable limits. This, unfortunately, casts a shadow over the respectability of the institution of politics (which actually increased with the AKP government). What has happened since the June 12 elections is in this direction.

“The most striking example is the AKP government’s attitude of leaving the new constitution to ‘another spring’ after entering the last elections with the promise of a civilian and democratic constitution and receiving half of the votes. Another example is the parliament’s inertia on issues concerning the majority of society, especially democratization reforms, while achieving unanimity around common interests (such as changing the match-fixing law, doubling retired deputies’ salaries).

“In his speech on behalf of the government at the end of the budget discussions last week, Deputy Prime Minister Bülent Arınç made a hopeful statement for those who want liberal and pluralist democracy. He said, ‘The existence of Kurds has been a fact for at least a thousand years. You cannot deny this. We will give to a person who says I am Kurdish all the rights to life, knowledge, education, language, culture, identity—as much as all of us, at least as much as all of us in this country…’ However, unfortunately, this statement was perceived by many not as a sign of the government’s serious intention, but as Arınç’s announcement of his candidacy for the party leadership once Erdoğan was elected president. The MHP spokespersons’ remarks accusing Arınç of ‘negligence and treason’ reminded us how empty the claim of making a constitution with full consensus is.

“Last week, Deputy Prime Minister Beşir Atalay also made a hopeful statement for those who want liberal and pluralist democracy. While answering the press’s questions before the Counter-Terrorism session organized at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, he said the government was working on legal changes that would ensure the free expression of non-violent views. Before the ‘ink of Atalay’s words had dried,’ Interior Minister İdris Naim Şahin came out and, as if the breadth of the terror definition in the laws were not the most important problem of freedom of expression in Turkey, brought a definition of terror so broad that it could lead to any view and even activity being accused of terrorism, the kind of breadth seen only in police states: ‘There is psychological terror, there is scientific terror, there is a backyard feeding terror… How does one give (support to terror)? Perhaps by painting, reflecting it on canvas; by writing poetry, reflecting it in their poetry; by writing daily articles, columns, writing and drawing things there…’ And more such appalling words. (Please see: Radikal, December 26) I wonder how much longer a person who can say these words will be kept in that position.

“The most noteworthy development of last week was the statements of Ayhan Çarkın, convicted in the Susurluk case. Çarkın, who had been making statements for some time about murders committed by the gang within the state, said in his meeting with Hüseyin Aygün, the CHP member of the Turkish Grand National Assembly Human Rights Commission (who said Dersim was ‘not a rebellion but a massacre’), that ‘prime ministers, high-ranking figures’ whose names he gave were aware of the Susurluk gang’s extrajudicial executions; that a team of 150 people is still on duty in the Police Special Operations Branch, not just carrying out executions. (Taraf, December 28) Prime Minister Erdoğan promised on various occasions that the fight against gangs within the state would be carried out to the end. For this promise and the ones related to reforms to be fulfilled, should Erdoğan and the AKP government perhaps abandon mastery and return to the apprenticeship period? This is the question being asked more and more.” (Zaman, 29.12.2011)

## Party of the arrogant, not the aggrieved

On the night of December 28, 2011, in the village of Ortasu (Kurdish: Roboski) in the Uludere district of Şırnak, 34 civilians, 28 from the same family, were killed as a result of bombardment by the Turkish Air Force. Official authorities announced that the dead were a smuggler convoy of Kurdish citizens bringing diesel and cigarettes from Iraq to Turkey. The General Staff announced after the incident that it had been decided to strike the identified group because it was using routes used by the PKK. In the article I wrote about the incident, I said:

“It is true that the tragedy in Uludere unfortunately divided the country in terms of mood. Not a trace of the solidarity shown in the Van earthquake was seen. If this were a civilized country or a country with emotional unity between its west and east, where Kurds were not discriminated against, mourning could have been declared. Not only was that not the case, but the government did not even apologize to the families of the dead, let alone the people. Most of the media (presumably in light of instructions given from the Prime Minister to the ‘shop owners’) delayed reporting the incident and tried to minimize it. The (absolutely inexcusable) attack on the district governor was found almost more important than 35 young people being killed by bombing. The MHP leader went so far as to say, ‘The state did what was necessary…’

”You might say that the PKK on one hand, and the state on the other, disregarding human life for years; killing by shooting, by bombing, has numbed feelings against killing. You might say that the bombing of smuggler villagers, mistaken for PKK militants preparing to attack soldiers, was seen as somewhat forgivable. But as a society, will we surrender to re-escalating violence, will we again forget humanity? If those who died had been PKK militants rather than villagers, would there have been celebrations? If bandits kill one, must the state kill five? Is the main thing for a democratic government not to ensure that people live? Wasn’t the state supposedly no longer killing ruthlessly, approaching even militants with compassion? Morally, what is the difference between PKK terrorists saying ‘we thought they were police’ after shooting young girls and the state saying ‘we thought they were terrorists’ after bombing young men?

“Perhaps the most serious aspect of the Uludere tragedy is the deep shaking of trust in the Prime Minister and government among citizens committed to liberal and humane values, who had hoped they would go down in history by solving the Kurdish problem and ending violence. When AKP Diyarbakır Deputy Galip Ensarioğlu said, ‘We have responsibility for every drop of blood shed here. If this is not stopping, it is because of our incompetence… The Prime Minister cannot go up to the Presidential Palace and be at peace before this is finished. Going to the Palace will have no meaning either…’ (Taraf, January 2), is he not expressing the crisis of confidence the Prime Minister and government have created in their own party? Do the words of some AKP members, ‘we have become the party of the arrogant, not the aggrieved…,’ not reflect the same crisis of confidence?

”Look at what Ümit Fırat, a Kurdish intellectual committed to liberal and humane values, says: ‘It would be bad if this incident is blamed on the AK Party. People will say, what is the difference from Tansu Çiller’s government in 1993. They must not cover up the incident, but find those responsible and ensure they are punished. This is now a test. They must take actions that will make amends to society. Even if they cannot completely erase the traces of this incident, at least they can convince society that today is not like the past. Otherwise, it would be a pity. Because there is no other party in Turkey that gives hope to people, to society…’ (Star, January 2) Don’t Fırat’s words reflect the great disappointment experienced in society?

“Prime Minister Tayyip Erdoğan is a leader to whom at least half of society, both Turkish and Kurdish, pins its hopes. This hope must not be broken. A ‘Blair syndrome’ should not be experienced. Prof. Dr. Erhun Kula, faculty member at Bahçeşehir University, recalled the possibility of it happening in an article (Taraf, December 19) as follows: ‘I liken Prime Minister Erdoğan to former British Prime Minister Tony Blair. Both are highly eloquent, religious, and charismatic figures. Both rendered great services to their countries. Blair modernized the Labour Party, which had become a dinosaur. For the first time in the party’s history, he won elections three times in a row. The economy grew unprecedentedly. Unemployment decreased greatly. Perhaps most importantly, Blair resolved the Northern Ireland problem. But Blair made one mistake: following George W. Bush, he dragged Britain into the Iraq war and eventually had to leave both the prime ministership and politics with a great loss of reputation.’ Yes, is there anyone left today who remembers Blair’s achievements?” (“Let there not be a Blair syndrome,” Zaman, 5.1.2012)

Are only soldiers responsible for coups?

Since 2008, cases have been opened against hundreds of officers on charges of attempted coups. In an article I wrote on this subject, I felt the need to remind readers that not only soldiers but also their civilian supporters were responsible for coup attempts, and that none of us had a clean record in terms of commitment to liberal democracy:

“Since 2008, hundreds of active and retired officers, including a former chief of general staff and two former force commanders, are being tried in cases opened on charges of coup attempts, primarily Ergenekon, Sledgehammer, and Internet Memorandum. Last week, those who actually carried out a coup were added to these—retired generals Kenan Evren and Tahsin Şahinkaya, the main responsible parties for the September 12 coup. If cases are soon opened against retired generals responsible for the February 28, 1997 post-modern coup and the April 27, 2007 e-memorandum, no one will be surprised.

“That soldiers who carried out coups or allegedly attempted coups by violating the constitution and laws are finally being held accountable is certainly an important stage in the liquidation of the military tutelage system. In this context, we often repeat that the military tutelage system can only end with the liquidation of tutelage powers granted to soldiers in the constitution and laws, and with the restructuring of the regime on the foundations of liberal and pluralist democracy instead of the principles of Kemalism, which means authoritarian secular nationalism. There is no doubt that for these crimes not to be repeated, coup makers and soldiers alleged to have attempted coups must be tried and, if found guilty, sentenced to the punishments they deserve. However, while these trials continue, there are some facts that must not be forgotten. I can list the main ones as follows:

“First, yes, soldiers planned the coups that were successful or remained at the attempt stage until today; therefore, soldiers are primarily responsible for these. However, almost all of them received encouragement and support from civilians. Soldiers were not solely responsible for the coups. Second, both the soldiers who planned coups and coup attempts and the civilians who provided encouragement and support for them did this (yes, partly to protect and develop their privileges, but) essentially for ideological reasons, because of their commitment to Kemalism and militarism.

“Kemalism is essentially based on the belief that the people do not have the maturity for self-governance; that a modern society can only be a mono-cultural society (speaking the same language, attached to the same culture, sharing the same religious beliefs) where religion is confined to consciences. Militarism believes that the country can best be governed by soldiers and that problems can only be solved by force. It is certain that Kemalist militarists (whose numbers we hope are now decreasing) are as prevalent among civilians as among soldiers in Turkey. Until secularist-nationalist militarism is marginalized (as hoped) especially among soldiers, but also among civilians, Turkey cannot be a normal democracy. (I think it is also clear enough that the PKK represents secularist-nationalist militarism among Kurds.)

“Third, until they got slapped by September 12, until the Cold War ended, the great majority of intellectuals in Turkey believed not in liberal and pluralist democracy but in various authoritarian and totalitarian ideologies, in top-down coups or bottom-up revolutions (force and violence). Politicians representing society against the state represented by the military-civilian bureaucracy also essentially understood democracy as ‘national will,’ that is, majority rule. Politicians who believed that democracy means not only majority rule but also that citizens (of all political, ethnic, and religious identities) have fundamental rights and freedoms that cannot be violated by any majority were few enough to count on one’s fingers. In short, perhaps until the 21st century, Turkey was a democracy with very few democrats. In light of what I have listed above, the fourth fact that must not be forgotten is this: As people of Turkey [Türkiyeliler], we are a society that has been learning liberal and pluralist democracy through experience over the last 60 years. When looked at from the perspective of commitment to liberal and pluralist democracy, almost none of us has a clean record.” (Zaman, January 21, 2012)

Is the AKP ‘Islamic Kemalist’?

In articles I wrote in early 2012, while I continued to support the AKP government because of practices I found positive, on the other hand, my criticisms of its increasing negative practices were growing more intense:

“I received the following message from one of my foreign readers who follows my English commentary in Today’s Zaman from abroad: ‘I am still trying to understand why the situation in Turkey has come to this. Can you understand why the AKP is acting so slowly in changing Kemalist laws and structures? Yet it has been in power long enough to do this. Should we conclude that AKP members are ’Islamic Kemalists’; that because their brains were washed by the ‘strong state’ for a long time, they don’t know how to govern any other way?’

“The answers I gave are briefly as follows: The AKP is a mass party that brings together people of quite different mindsets. But of course, it can be said that the party’s founding and leading cadre has a common mindset. Looking from this cadre’s perspective, the AKP certainly has Islamic sensitivities. Well, can the AKP be called ‘Kemalist’? In most respects no, in some respects yes. From a cultural perspective: The AKP is definitely not Kemalist. Kemalists think religion is an obstacle to development and therefore should be confined to consciences. AKP members, on the other hand, are religious Sunnis and represent some victims of the authoritarian secularist order. However, although Prime Minister Erdoğan defined secularism as the state standing equidistant from all beliefs including atheists during his North Africa trip last September, the AKP government has been able to make very few changes to the Kemalist authoritarian secularist order.

“From an economic perspective: Although Kemalists have moved away from this understanding somewhat, they are essentially statist. The AKP government, however, represents the most liberal economic policies Turkey has seen. In addition, it has also taken some social welfare measures in health and education. This is the main explanation for the AKP’s electoral victories. From a political perspective: Kemalists in principle do not believe in democracy. Forced by circumstances, they at most accepted democracy under military-bureaucratic tutelage. It is certain that the AKP, like all peripheral parties before it, is committed to democracy in the sense of ‘national will,’ that is, majority rule. It cannot be denied that the AKP government has made some improvements in both the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals and the rights of minorities (Kurds and non-Muslims) within the framework of the EU accession process. It can also be said that a significant portion of society (also influenced by opposition parties not inspiring any confidence) still sees the AKP as the only hope for democratization.

“On the other hand, despite ten years of AKP rule, the fact that ‘Kemalist laws and structures’ largely remain in place can indeed be explained to some extent by ‘not knowing how to govern any other way because their brains were washed by the ’strong state’ for a long time.’ If we start with the Unionists who dominated the late Ottoman period, Turkey underwent nearly a hundred years of statist-secularist-nationalist indoctrination, brainwashing. As a result, Unionist-Kemalist values left deep marks on Turkey’s elites. It is possible to see these marks in Turkey’s socialists, liberals, Islamists, even Kurdish nationalists, alongside the AKP members I characterize as Muslim Democrats. While it cannot be said that the AKP is statist or secularist, it is true that it has an (Islamic, with a drop of liberalism) nationalist identity.

“Of course, there are also other reasons why ‘Kemalist laws and structures’ largely remain in place. In this context, rather than the weakening resistance of the bureaucratic tutelage order, what can be underlined is that the AKP has come to believe it has sufficiently adapted the old order to itself to maintain its power—in other words, that it has fallen into the complacency of power. However, I don’t think society in Turkey will accept this complacency. If the AKP cannot respond to the quite strong expectation of democratization in society, it will gradually lose power. I don’t think an AKP that is becoming Kemalist, that is, becoming authoritarian, can stay in power.” (Zaman, January 26, 2012)

When I read this article ten years later, it did cross my mind that I might have been right.

## Religious freedom and the “transparency” issue

In my article commenting on the US Congress report stating that religious freedoms were being systematically and visibly violated in Turkey, I drew attention to how authoritarian secularism practices and restrictions on freedom of belief were driving religious communities to avoid transparency. This article was an indirect response to the criticism of “lacking transparency” directed at the Gülen community, which published the Zaman newspaper. I said:

“The United States Commission on International Religious Freedom counted Turkey among the 16 ‘countries of particular concern’ in its 2012 report on the grounds that it violated religious freedoms ‘systematically and visibly.’ Yet in the Commission’s 2008 report, Turkey was in the ‘under review’ category, and in 2009 in the ‘monitored’ category. Yet Turkey had been praised in the US State Department’s religious freedom report published last year ‘for the steps it took to develop an environment of religious tolerance.’ The Turkish Foreign Ministry reacted harshly to the report: ‘This report, which deliberately ignores the steps taken forward in recent times and the political will that forms the basis of the reforms made… is null and void for us,’ it said. Meanwhile, it also emerged that although 5 of the Commission’s 9 members voted against, and Turkey should have been removed from the ‘countries of particular concern’ category when one of them changed their opinion, the report was published in its original form.

“Does Turkey have a place among the 16 ‘countries of particular concern’; frankly, I don’t have the comparative knowledge to decide on this. It is true that there have been some improvements in the rights granted to non-Muslims in the last few years. However, like everyone else, I know that restrictions on religious freedoms that are absolutely incompatible with democratic order continue in Turkey. If you like, let me remind you again of just the main ones. According to Kemalism’s authoritarian understanding of secularism, which considers religion, especially Islam, as ‘reactionism,’ there is no separation of religion and state in Turkey; there is a state monopoly and control over religion.

“Citizens of all faiths must finance the Directorate of Religious Affairs, which represents official Sunni-Hanafi Islam, with the taxes they pay. Advocating taking the Directorate outside the administration is grounds for closure for political parties. The Directorate controls all mosques; it sends Friday sermons from the center. Other belief groups receive not a penny of help from the state. Alevis have only been able to open their places of worship, the cemevis, for the last twenty years; however, their ability to obtain permits is still subject to municipalities’ arbitrary permission. Like Alevis, Apostolic, Catholic and Protestant Armenian, Greek Orthodox, Syriac, Catholic and Protestant churches, Jews, Bahai, Yazidi, Shia, Jafari and other religious groups also have no legal guarantees; they are all subject to arbitrary practices of the state and politics.

“Although the vast majority of Sunnis believe in Sufi Islam and belong to Sufi orders and the communities that evolved from them over time and new religious movements, Sufi orders have been legally banned since 1925; threats and pressures on believers continue. The headscarf is banned not only in all public buildings including parliament but in all schools; it has only been effectively free in universities for a year or two. According to the ‘Unification of Education’ Law, religious education (including of clergy) is a state monopoly. Contrary to the European Convention on Human Rights, families are not granted the right to ensure their children receive the kind of religious education they wish. The justification for almost all the military coups carried out or attempted since 1960 has been the fight against ‘separatism’ (meaning the expression of Kurdish identity) and ‘reactionism’ (meaning the expression of Islamic identity). Parties with no connection to violence and racism but with Islamic sensitivities were closed; in this context, even the ruling party AKP, which received half of the people’s votes, was left under threat of closure.

“Just as religious freedoms are restricted, due to pressures and threats, citizens still hesitate to reveal their religious identities. Alevis hid their beliefs until the last twenty years. Those who discover they are originally Armenian are only recently showing the courage to be baptized and join a church. Forget Alevis and non-Muslims, there are Sunnis who feel the need to hide which religious community they belong to. Setting aside that religious freedom is not secure, I just laugh at the secularists who keep demanding ‘be transparent!’ of religious communities.” (March 29, 2012)

It is certain that the AKP government took some steps toward removing restrictions on religious freedoms. Fortunately, in 2022 when these lines are being written, such an absurdity as the “headscarf ban” in schools and parliament no longer exists in majority Sunni Muslim Turkey. Alevis have also made some progress in opening their cemevis. But there is still a long way to go for religious freedom to be established and for the regime to become secular.

Democracy is not just “national will”

The AKP government’s democracy report card was getting worse and worse. How could this be explained? On this subject, I wrote the following:

“… I expressed in many articles the AKP government’s contributions to the economy, democracy, and the country’s respectability. These services were possible thanks to a single-party government that could be established after the coalition governments of the 1990s that had sunk the country in every field by squabbling with each other, and a prime minister at its head who had more support than even his party. However, in its tenth year, the reforms that brought the AKP government its successes almost completely stopped, and its democracy report card began to deteriorate.

”How can this be explained? According to one theory, Prime Minister Erdoğan focused on the goal of being elected President in 2014; for this, he built his game plan on maintaining the balances as they were. According to another theory, because the AKP government could not manage to bring the military-civilian bureaucracy under its control, it turned to reconciling with it (without taking into account that the tutelage advocates’ audacity could increase); it gradually ‘became Kemalist.’ According to yet another theory, the weaknesses in the AKP government’s understanding of democracy began to show themselves.

“The last of these theories, all of which could be valid together, is worth dwelling on. The cornerstone of the weaknesses in the AKP government’s understanding of democracy is the mentality that sees democracy as identical only to ‘national will,’ to majority rule—a mentality also seen in all previous ruling parties (DP, AP, ANAP) that claimed to represent popular sovereignty against the bureaucracy’s tutelage. Yet democracy is the regime in which the right to govern belongs to the party or parties that have the majority’s vote, but also in which governments are checked and balanced by the opposition so they don’t make mistakes; in which citizens have fundamental rights and freedoms that cannot be violated by any majority.

”One of the recent examples displaying the weakness in the AKP’s understanding of democracy is the education reform proposal. A reform of this scale should have been brought to Parliament after consulting all relevant parties, and it should have been possible for the opposition to criticize it using all means in Parliament. Another example is the destruction caused by the insistence that Newroz celebrations must be held on March 21.

“Democracy cannot function without a media that reports and comments freely. One of the AKP government’s most fundamental mistakes is its policy of bringing the media under control through ‘shop owners’ instead of passing laws that would secure the independence of journalism from the state, government, and bosses. Yes, like people from all professions, journalists can also commit crimes, and there may be journalists in Turkey who have become involved with terrorist organizations and coup attempts. But if laws that provide for the prosecution and punishment of individuals as if they were members of illegal organizations even though they are not remain in place, one cannot speak of the rule of law. This government rendered a very great service to this country by ending the denial of Kurdish identity. But reforms toward recognizing Kurdish identity stopped; it started negotiations with the PKK to ensure it lays down arms, but signals that it was again leaning toward a ‘military solution’ intensified.

”Yes, even in its strongest period, the AKP government’s mistakes are increasing. Hopes now rest on what Amberin Zaman reminded us of: ‘Still, I keep my hope. Because one of the characteristics that makes Prime Minister Erdoğan and the AK Party strong is their ability to turn around very quickly and make radical decisions. They took steps that no government dared; they can take them again. They must. After all, everyone with reason and conscience knows that Turkey can neither achieve real democracy nor peace without solving the Kurdish problem.’ ” (Zaman, 22.3.2012)

## Prolonged power exhausts, wears down

Following Prime Minister Erdoğan’s launch of the “Let’s switch to a presidential system” campaign, I had started writing articles reminding readers of the problems this could cause for the country. In an article that ended with “Prime Minister Erdoğan has rendered very great services to this country. But apparently, prolonged power exhausts, wears down leaders…,” I said:

“The ‘Let’s switch to a presidential system’ campaign that started with Prime Minister Erdoğan’s encouragement is spreading. Deputy Prime Minister Bekir Bozdağ, who took over the standard-bearing from Constitutional Commission Chairman Burhan Kuzu, has already declared that Turkey will ‘inevitably’ switch to an (American-type) presidential system… However, opposition parties are against the presidential system. Since it is certain that a significant portion of the AKP group will also oppose this in a secret ballot, this campaign may be, as CHP chairman Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu said, an ‘artificial agenda.’ But since the Prime Minister wants it, of course it should be discussed.

“There are essentially three types of government system: the parliamentary system that developed in Britain through an evolution whose roots go back to the Magna Carta of 1215; the presidential system established by the USA, which gained independence from Britain in 1776; and the semi-presidential system invented by France in 1958 (which is a mixture of the first two). It is quite possible to access information on the principles, advantages, and disadvantages of these systems. Undoubtedly, every country adopts a system according to its needs; if it doesn’t work, it changes it. What must not be forgotten is that the governance system is determined not only by the government system but also by the electoral system (proportional representation, majority system, or mixed).
