“In our country, a truly ‘monstrous’ system that mixes the parliamentary system with the semi-presidential system—brought by the September 12 military administration with the aim of reinforcing the military-bureaucratic tutelage order—and on top of that places a proportional representation system with a 10 percent threshold, has been in effect since 1982. With the AKP government’s constitutional amendment in 2007 introducing the principle of electing the president by popular vote, the system became even more monstrous. However, switching to a semi-presidential or presidential system on the grounds that the system should be freed from monstrousness probably cannot be meaningful.

“What is meaningful is not Prime Minister Erdoğan’s remaining in power until 2024 with a new constitution, but diagnosing and establishing the government and electoral system that will secure democracy in Turkey. My view, which I have expressed in countless articles regarding this debate that has been going on for at least thirty years, is clear: The system suitable for Turkey, where the culture of compromise is weak and political, religious, and ethnic divisions are numerous, is the parliamentary system where the executive emerges from the legislature. In presidential systems, if the popularly elected president and the parliamentary majority belong to different parties, governance can face serious deadlocks, it can become unable to make decisions. (Just imagine what could happen to us in an environment where the president is from the AKP and parliament has an opposition majority…) Another drawback of presidential systems that we cannot ignore is the tendency to divide society in two and polarize it.

“Yes, there is a need for a strong executive in Turkey. For the reasons mentioned above, a strong executive exists not in presidential systems but in the parliamentary system. (The solution of the Kurdish problem also depends not on the government system but on whether there is political will on this matter.) Yes, besides political stability, achieving justice in representation and freeing parties from leader domination are important needs of ours. The way to this is to adopt a two-round majority system where a single candidate is elected from each single-member district. We have really suffered much from proportional representation that gives birth to coalition governments.

“Presidential systems do not serve our democratization. Don’t Prime Minister Erdoğan’s recent attitudes also show this? The Prime Minister has begun to see the people of Turkey as a flock in need of herding and himself as their shepherd. For this, he has begun to intervene in every issue that doesn’t concern him, from art to sports, from theater to abortion, to what the media should or shouldn’t write. Finally, his saying that Turkey faces international conspiracies from Uludere to births has come to resemble ‘old Turkey’s’ discourse of blaming ‘internal-external enemies’ for problems. Prime Minister Erdoğan has rendered very great services to this country. But apparently, prolonged power exhausts, wears down leaders.” (“Why presidentialism doesn’t suit us,” Zaman, 22.03.2012)

The partnership between Kemalists and Islamists

As the AKP’s authoritarian tendency advanced, I was finding common aspects uniting Kemalists and Islamists that were much more interesting and in need of explanation than the well-known ‘tension’ between them.

“… Former NSC Secretary General and Ergenekon case defendant retired Gen. Tuncer Kılınç was saying: ‘May God have abundant mercy on him, Erbakan was a nationalist leader. We couldn’t understand him correctly, soldiers didn’t understand Erbakan correctly.’ (Yeni Akit, April 1) Retired Maj. Gen. Osman Özbek, who had openly cursed Prime Minister Erbakan, repented and spoke thus: ‘If only we had understood the National View. If only those days had never happened. I really value the National View’s fight against imperialism and its upright stance.’ (Samanyolu Haber, March 23)

“… The most important indicator of the partnership between positivist and secularist Kemalists and a certain understanding of Islam is undoubtedly that the Republic, which claims to have separated religion and state, actually has an unofficial religion, and this is represented by the Directorate of Religious Affairs, which monopolizes and controls Islam with the task of ‘ensuring national unity.’ The question of why most religious Muslims in Turkey are nationalist and statist, why they share with Kemalists the view on the Kurdish issue, the Armenian issue, and other matters, may have roots extending to Ottoman and even pre-Islamic Turkish history. It is possible to find the analysis of this in the extraordinarily important study of our teacher Prof. Dr. Şerif Mardin, who sheds light on many issues related to religion in Turkey, titled ‘Turkish Islamic Exceptionalism Yesterday and Today: Continuity, Rupture and Reconstruction in Operational Codes’ (Turkish Studies, Vol. 6, No. 2, June 2005, pp. 145-165)…

“Mardin says that the characteristics of Islam in Turkey derive from the interaction between the positivist modernism of the Ottoman-Republican bureaucracy and the innovative Islamic interpretation of the Naqshbandi order. In an interview he gave on this analysis, he underlines the following points: Throughout its history, the Ottoman Empire was careful not to keep religion away from the state. For Arabs, religion comes before the state. For Turks, however, the state has been more important than religion since the pre-Islamic period. ‘When I say the Turkish exception, this is what I mean.’ (Asharq Alawsat, December 12, 2007)

“It can be said that the transformation of the tension between Kemalists and religious Muslims in Turkey into a partnership in statism and nationalism finds its best expression in the Turkish-Islamic synthesis ideology, which is also the ideology of the September 12 regime…” (“Where are the roots of Islamic Kemalism?” Zaman, 19.4.2012)

“Where is the AKP government going?”

By the middle of 2012, I no longer had any doubt that the AKP government was taking Turkey toward authoritarian one-man rule. However, I maintained my optimism and thought Erdoğan would not succeed in realizing his ambitions. I wrote:

“The Justice and Development Party (AKP) government is the most successful of the governments established in the multi-party period. It performed great services in ten years. It at least doubled the average income. It pushed back military-bureaucratic tutelage. It ended the denial of Kurdish identity. It sought to end PKK violence through dialogue. It started membership negotiations with the EU. It made Turkey a country cited as an example in many respects in the international community. The two most important factors that brought these successes were: The ‘Reformist’ cadre within the Welfare Party (RP), headed by Tayyip Erdoğan, learned from criticisms. When founding the AKP, they took off their ‘Islamist shirt’ and acquired a Conservative Democrat identity (similar to Christian Democrats). They listened to the people’s demands for freedom and democracy; they charted their course accordingly. Thus, they came to power with 34%, gradually climbing to 50%.

“Their military-bureaucratic tutelage-supporting opponents resorted to every means to bring down the AKP from power. They claimed it would turn Turkey into Iran, and when that wasn’t convincing, into Russia. They attempted coups. When that failed, they tried to have the party closed by the Constitutional Court. When Turkey-Israel relations deteriorated after the Mavi Marmara, the Israel lobby also threw its weight everywhere behind efforts to distort the reality of the AKP. Despite all these attempts to trip it up, the support it received from freedom and democracy supporters played a major role in the AKP government’s success. The exposure and bringing to trial of coup attempts was possible thanks to the media with editorial independence, primarily the Taraf newspaper.

“However, since the last general elections held last June, since the announcement that it had entered the ‘Mastery’ period, the AKP government step by step took on an unrecognizable identity. Prime Minister Erdoğan’s discourse roughly became: ‘The national will, the nation is me… The people don’t know their interest, I know. I decide who gets contracts, what the media writes… I know football, art, theater, religion, abortion, cesarean section best… Criticizing a government that received half the people’s votes means not wanting Turkey’s development, falling for foreigners’ game, it is treason…’ With this discourse, expected reforms toward democratization completely stopped. It began to be said, ‘Denial is over, assimilation is also over. There is no Kurdish problem, there is a PKK problem…’ Instead of ending PKK violence through dialogue, there began to be talk of ‘minimizing’ it. Journalists writing critical articles began to be fired through Erdoğan’s ‘shop owners.’ The Interior Minister, speaking like the MHP, declared the victims of the Uludere bombing guilty. The question of whether Erdoğan wanted a new constitution that wouldn’t bring some kind of presidential system made it doubtful whether a democratic constitution would be made.

“Where might this reversal, this authoritarian tendency observed in Prime Minister Erdoğan and the AKP government stem from? Various theories are being put forward in this context: 1) Erdoğan now says ‘I am the state… Anyone who criticizes me is Turkey’s enemy…’ because he dominates the military-civilian bureaucracy and has consolidated his power. 2) He absolutely wants to be elected president. For this, he wants to win MHP votes with a nationalist-conservative cooperation strategy. 3) He abandoned his democratism and embraced conservatism; he is returning to RP Islamism. 4) Inflated self-confidence, insistence on one-man rule, the sycophants around him have gone to his head. 5) His physical and mental health is not in order.

“Well, where does this course take the AKP? In my opinion, if Erdoğan doesn’t learn from criticisms and put himself and his circle in order, this course will sooner or later bring down the AKP from power. Even Erdoğan’s election as president would be endangered. Well, where does Turkey go? With its economy and civil society growing stronger through Erdoğan’s achievements; with its media that doesn’t hold back from criticism; with its people who increasingly know the world and demand freedom and democracy, Turkey will not tolerate authoritarianism. Even a portion of the AKP will not accept this.” (Zaman, June 5, 2012)

What an illusion I was living in… At least until 2022, when these lines are being written, society in Turkey tolerated authoritarianism perfectly well: The majority of society didn’t care about authoritarianism as long as the economic situation was going well. It was seen that if the AKP were to lose power, it would lose because of bankrupt economic policies that raised inflation to at least 70% in 2022.

Government - Community fight?

In my first commentary written on allegations that there was a fight between the AKP government and the Gülen Community, I said:

“Let me come to the claims that the Specially Authorized Courts (ÖYM) debate reflects ‘the latest stage of the fight between the government and the community’—claims adopted even by people whose logic I trusted until recently. The claim is in summary: The ‘Fethullah Gülen community’ has taken over the police and judiciary. All or most of the ÖYM prosecutors and judges belong to this community and act on instructions they receive, with evidence produced by police belonging to the community. The Ergenekon and Sledgehammer prosecutions are based on fake evidence fabricated by community members. The government has also begun to be disturbed by the ÖYMs. Even the MIT Undersecretary, whom it trusted greatly, being summoned to testify as a suspect increased the Prime Minister’s anger.

“When those who say the evidence in the Ergenekon and Sledgehammer cases is fabricated are asked for evidence for their claims about the community, their answer is: Well, the ‘community media’ defends the ÖYMs… Well, is it only the ‘community media’ that finds these cases credible? Is it only the ‘community media’ that opposes the abolition of the ÖYMs? Can’t those who write in the ‘community media’ be concerned that the abolition of ÖYMs could lead to coup attempters escaping justice? Does the claim that all or most of the ÖYM prosecutors and judges belong to the ‘community’ and act on instructions accord with reason and logic? Isn’t this disrespect for the personalities of the said prosecutors and judges? Isn’t it logical to look for the source of the justified complaints caused by ÖYMs in the authoritarian judicial culture that prioritizes the state’s interests over citizens’ fundamental rights?

“When I ask these questions, I conclude that the claims of ‘government - community fight’ carry no meaning beyond being another manifestation of the secularist mentality. I am not a legal scholar, but I am a social scientist. I have been following the Gülen movement, a faith-based civil society movement, for years. I am committed to the values of freedom and democracy. This is the conclusion I have reached.” (Zaman, 14.06.2012)

As can be understood from this commentary, I was striving to defend the Community against any and all criticism, on the grounds that it was being unjustly accused by “secularists.” After years have passed, after what has befallen us, I must confess today that I had fallen quite far from objectivity on this matter. Probably for this reason: I thought that if there really was a Government - Community fight, I should take the Community’s side. Because the AKP government was taking the country toward an authoritarian regime; if the Community was opposing it, it was playing a positive role.

## Erdoğan and Gül should switch places

How could Prime Minister Erdoğan’s taking the country toward an authoritarian regime be prevented?.. I had a proposal completely detached from reality: I was proposing that Erdoğan become President and leave the prime ministership to Abdullah Gül. As follows:

“Ankara seems focused on the presidential election to be held two years from now. According to what I hear from my Ankara friends, in the AKP it is viewed as certain that the Prime Minister will be elected president in two years. When he goes up to Çankaya, the question of who will head the AKP, who will be prime minister, who will go where in the new administration has become a more important issue than all of Turkey’s other problems. And while urgent reforms are needed in every field, Turkey is wasting precious time. The Prime Minister may think he will secure his ascent to Çankaya by preserving the status quo as is. Yet wasn’t it being the leader who changed the status quo and pioneered renewal that got him the votes of half the people, including Kurds? If he loses this identity and holds back from reforms, as I have written before, he may not be elected President in two years. Don’t trust polls. This people can change its preference quickly…

”I’m thinking, the Constitutional Court, by interpreting Abdullah Gül’s term as 7 years, made a decision that was wrong legally and negative politically. If it had made the correct interpretation, we would have elected a new President this summer. Erdoğan and Gül could have agreed between themselves; Erdoğan could have gone up to Çankaya, Gül could have been elected deputy in a by-election and become prime minister. This opportunity was missed. What a pity. Gül’s election as president was in a way a waste of talent; the government weakened. But Gül won the trust of people from all segments at Çankaya. Finding a way for Erdoğan and Gül to switch places, and without delay, would be very auspicious.” (13.9.2012)

Looking back, I think that yes, I fell very far from reality, but I wasn’t wrong at all. If Gül had become Prime Minister while Erdoğan went up to Çankaya, what befell us might not have happened.

Does Putinism fit Turkey?

In the face of Erdoğan’s increasing turn toward Putinism, I was asking ‘Does Putinism fit Turkey?’

“Domestic and foreign opponents put forward the claim that when Erdoğan and the AKP first came to power, they were practicing ‘taqiyya,’ that they were secret Islamists who wanted to make Turkey like Iran. When the absurdity of this claim became apparent, they developed a different claim: Erdoğan wanted to be Putin, to take Turkey toward an authoritarian regime similar to Russia’s. When I encountered these claims at home and abroad, I stated that the first was too wrong to be taken seriously, and that I was not at all convinced by the second. However, about two years ago, doubt began to gnaw at me. I expressed this in my article titled ‘Does Erdoğan want to be Putin?’ (February 8, 2011).

“But when Prime Minister Erdoğan’s conservative populist discourse that has been rising since last May—‘Let abortion be banned… Let the death penalty return… I will build a mosque in Çamlıca, in Taksim… I will close prep schools… This Süleyman doesn’t represent my ancestors…’ and so on—was added to the ‘Turkish-style presidential’ system proposal the AKP submitted to the Turkish Grand National Assembly Constitutional Reconciliation Commission, I no longer had any doubt: I don’t think the AKP wants to take Turkey to an authoritarian regime; but Prime Minister Erdoğan wants to be Turkey’s Putin.

“The essentials of the ‘Turkish-type presidential system’ produced by Constitutional Commission Chairman Burhan Kuzu at the Prime Minister’s directive are as follows: There will be a single chamber; the president will be responsible only to the people, not to the assembly; there will be no vote of confidence or motion of censure for the president; the president will choose his cabinet from outside parliament; senior state officials will be appointed by the president without requiring the assembly’s approval; the president will issue decrees with the force of law when needed (not subject to assembly oversight); the president will dissolve parliament when deemed necessary, and so on. Our leading constitutional law scholar Prof. Dr. Ergun Özbudun is of course quite right in saying that this system is called ‘decretismo’ (rule by decree) in Latin America and means ‘the concentration of power in a single person.’ (Akşam, November 29, 2012)

“‘Turkish-type presidentialism’ may be inspired by Latin America. But, (according to its inventor Burhan Kuzu) the rule-by-decree system that will save the president from ‘crying day and night, begging parliament’ is also applied in Russia. The regime in Russia is called not liberal democracy but ‘managed democracy,’ ‘sovereign democracy,’ or in short ‘Putinism.’ It can be said that Erdoğan finds his role model in Putinism, in the sense of the regime being shaped by a single person’s personality and political power. A Russia expert defines Putinism briefly as follows: ‘The concentration of political and economic power in one center, the emasculation of parliament, the silencing of the media, a return to Great Russian nationalist rhetoric, and bullying interference in the affairs of neighboring countries…’ (Daniel Beer,”Russia’s Managed Democracy,” History Today, Volume: 59, Issue: 5, 2009.) Putin’s supporters value the strong state, economic growth, and security much more than human rights or democracy.

“The resemblance between Erdoğan and Putin must be so palpable that even Fehmi Koru recently wrote that Erdoğan is ‘a stern father who sees the people as his children whom he tries to make good people’ (Star, December 2). I had previously written that the Prime Minister ‘has begun to see the people of Turkey as a flock in need of herding and himself as their shepherd.’ (Zaman, May 29) Will Putinism take hold in Turkey? Yes, Erdoğan may want to become a Putin, but I don’t think the people of Turkey, the Turkish Grand National Assembly, or above all the AKP will allow this. Why? The subject of another article.” (4.12.2012)

I explained why Putinism would not take hold in Turkey, or so I imagined, as follows:

## Putinism won’t take hold in Turkey

“…Still, I don’t think ‘Putinism’ can be implemented in Turkey. First of all, because Turkey is not Russia. Turkey has at least 60 years of democratic experience, however deficient and flawed. The people of Turkey have a democratic maturity; it has been seen that they know how to reward politicians for their successes and punish them for their mistakes. Turkey is a long-standing member of the Western alliance. Its frame of reference is Western democracies. The underground (oil, natural gas) riches that enable Putin to maintain his authoritarian regime do not exist in Turkey. Many Russian intellectuals go abroad, but the intellectuals of Turkey cannot be expected to flee the struggle for democracy. It is not possible for an administration that antagonizes intellectuals to stay standing for long. On the other hand, it should not be forgotten that popular opposition to Putinism in Russia is growing step by step.

“It has become clear that Erdoğan’s ‘Turkish-type presidential’ system proposal, which would mean governing the country by decree, cannot be accepted by the Turkish Grand National Assembly; finding the three-fifths majority to take it to referendum also seems very difficult. In a secret vote, the AKP group cannot be expected to act like a herd. Let’s say the Prime Minister managed to take the proposal to referendum. In this case too, its rejection by the people is very likely. Because it takes no prophet to say that a significant portion of the electorate that has supported the AKP government until now—primarily the religious segment demanding a democratic constitution and rejecting arbitrary rule, and Kurds—will not approve one-person rule. In my opinion, if Erdoğan continues the Putin-like line he has held since the last elections, he faces the risk of losing the presidential election to be held by popular vote in 2014, for the reasons I listed above, and being left out of politics.

“If my assumptions are correct, the auspicious choice for himself, his party, and certainly Turkey is for Mr. Prime Minister to correct his line and accept the presidency with its existing powers; to hand over the prime ministership to Abdullah Gül, who seems to be the only person who can hold the party together.” (20.12.2012)

I think an observer of politics in Turkey could only be as wrong as I was in the articles above… Developments would go in exactly the opposite direction of what I thought, and Erdoğan would succeed perfectly well in becoming Turkey’s Putin and remaining so for a long time.

## Unity cannot be preserved by dying, by killing

I was once again grounding the claim that Turkey “cannot preserve its unity by dying, by killing” as follows:

“Last week the Turkish Grand National Assembly Human Rights Investigation Commission announced: The TSK has lost 818 martyrs in the fight against the PKK in the last ten years, while 934 privates and noncommissioned officers under arms have committed suicide. I couldn’t believe my eyes when I read it! I knew suicides were common in the army; I also knew that suspicions that some of them were actually killed by their superiors were widespread. But I didn’t think the numbers could be this high. Could there be stronger evidence than this for the claims that the TSK doesn’t value the lives of our young people doing mandatory military service? The commission chairman says, ‘This is unacceptable…’ Then do what is necessary as the Turkish Grand National Assembly!

“The event of last week that completely darkened my soul was some media announcing, as if a great victory had been won, that 1,176 PKK militants had been killed in the first 11 months of this year. As if even Kurdish citizens who don’t embrace the PKK in the slightest don’t have their attachment to this country and this state diminish a little more with every Kurdish youth killed! According to the media, the number of young martyrs we lost in the first 6 months of this year is 117. At this rate, 2012 is heading toward being the year we lost the most martyrs in the last ten years. It’s very clear: The party mainly responsible for the deaths that distance us from each other is the political power. The truth cannot be covered up forever. It must be accepted that two peoples with different languages and cultures live in this country, and the government must finish what it started. The legitimate, democratic demands of our Kurdish citizens must be met; by negotiating with the PKK, their leaders should go to other countries, and their ordinary militants should return to their homes with a general amnesty. We cannot preserve our unity by dying, by killing. Listen to what Lawyer Muhammed Akar, from one of Diyarbakır’s prominent families and an AKP supreme board delegate, said in his letter:” after which I left the rest of the article to Akar:

“Military operations, detentions and arrests, the dead bodies of young people and mothers’ tears have replaced the democratic opening that led everyone to great hope. While soldier funerals in western provinces feed social anger, militant funerals in eastern provinces bring people to the streets. The greatest danger for a country is the formation of two separate worlds blind and deaf to each other. The extinction of the sense of empathy. The loss of a common moral and conscientious stance. More importantly, the shaking of trust in justice.

“Unfortunately, we have sacrificed the principle of justice to nationalist reflexes. Kurdish society demands justice, law, freedom, and equality from the state. Can an understanding that discriminates between the languages its citizens speak, that finds mother-tongue education dangerous, that has children say ‘How happy is the one who says I am a Turk’ every morning be just? People are happy if they are free, if their stomachs are full, if they can look to tomorrow with hope. Not because they are Turkish or Kurdish. In the provinces where Kurds live, a quarter of the people are at the hunger line, half at the poverty line.

“Now we are also tense with the lifting of immunities of BDP deputies. A few years ago, we had brought those with weapons down from the mountains and entered political negotiations. Now we are showing politicians the path to the mountains. The more the BDP is targeted, the more its votes increase. Its mistakes become invisible. Even conservative Kurds who vote for the AK Party have begun to turn to the BDP. Because the current perception is ‘The AK Party is arrogant, the BDP is aggrieved…’ In this region, the aggrieved always wins. Military operations, detentions, arrests, road checks, highland bans have always won the PKK a base. For 87 years, names, parties, governments change but the Kurdish problem continues to grow. It depletes our resources, impoverishes us. More importantly, it takes our children from us never to return.” (7.12.2012)

Lawyer Muhammed Akar, whose words I quoted above, would continue as AKP Diyarbakır Provincial Chairman until November 2017.

# CHAPTER XIV / FROM ERDOGAN I TO II

How could the difference between Erdogan’s first term, defined by policies aimed at establishing democracy, and his second term oriented toward establishing authoritarianism, be explained?.. I wrote:

“The other day I was chatting with a young academic friend. The conversation kept circling back to how Prime Minister Erdogan’s political profile had changed so fundamentally since the last general elections. How is it that Erdogan I, who contributed so greatly not only to the country’s prosperity but also to its democratization, was replaced by Erdogan II, who puts the brakes on democratization reforms and increasingly shows clear signs of arbitrariness and Putinization. In short: How can the transition from Erdogan I to II be explained?

“In response to this question, my friend put forward a ‘theory’ I had not heard before. According to this, Prime Minister Erdogan does not feel secure and therefore increasingly compromises with the status quo / established order, ‘becoming one with the state.’ After listing various signs of this, my friend drew attention to the Prime Minister’s statement in a television interview the other day that ‘the deep structure in the state has not been completely cleaned,’ and to his sharing with the public, for the first time, the bugs planted in his offices.

“Interestingly, the Prime Minister elaborated on this last topic at his press conference the other day: ‘We completely erased, finished, destroyed this—it’s impossible for me to make such a claim. Because as a politician, I don’t believe that any country or state in the world has finished or cleaned out its deep state. Every country has its deep state within it; they cannot reach a point of scraping it out and cleaning it. It’s like a virus. The moment it finds the right opportunity, the right ground, that virus emerges and tries to do what it wants to do.’

“The theory my young academic friend put forward was the exact opposite of the theory I had credited until now—that the 180-degree change in the Prime Minister stemmed from excessive, inflated self-confidence; that after believing he had established his authority, he fell under the delusion that he could turn to arbitrariness: in other words, the issue is not ‘self-confidence’ but ‘insecurity.’ I objected to my friend with the following reasoning: Let’s say the Prime Minister doesn’t feel secure (against ‘deep structures’); shouldn’t he rationally work to expand his social support as much as possible? But it appears that, following a line completely contrary to expectations, he is polarizing society and alienating at least some of the conservative-religious segments, Kurds, and freedom-loving intellectuals who had strongly supported him until now. (…)

“In the end, my friend and I agreed that the line the Prime Minister had been following since the last general elections was not rational. I concluded the conversation as follows: I now better understand why the U.S. Constitution allows presidents to be elected only twice at most. And why Tony Blair, who rendered great services to his party and country in Britain, had to resign before completing his third term as prime minister… Carrying such heavy responsibilities is not easy and is exhausting. I understand this, but we don’t have to bear the consequences.” (Zaman, 27.12.2012)

No to the AKP’s presidential proposal!

In opposing Erdogan’s proposal for transitioning to a presidential system, I put forward the following arguments:

“The judicial arrangements of the Erdogan-style presidential system proposal that the Justice and Development Party submitted to the Constitutional Reconciliation Commission have also been revealed. Thus, the government system proposed by the AKP has become somewhat more concrete. This system gives the President: 1) authority to dissolve Parliament, 2) authority to rule the country by decree, 3) authority to appoint high-level public officials, ambassadors, and some judges without parliamentary approval.

“According to the judiciary-related arrangements, the President will: 1) appoint one-quarter of the members of the Court of Appeals to be established (the rest to be chosen by the HSYK, the High Council of Judges and Prosecutors), 2) appoint 7 members of the HSYK (only 6 of the total 22 members will be elected by judges), 3) appoint 8 members of the Constitutional Court (the rest of the 17 members will also be elected by the parliamentary majority). That is, the Constitutional Court will not be able to review presidential decrees. Annulment cases at the Constitutional Court can only be filed by the President or 110 deputies, and most members of judicial bodies will be determined not by judicial members but by the political authority.

“It is quite obvious that this presidential system, which in the words of Prof. Dr. Ergun Ozbudun is ‘a peculiar absurdity of our own,’ responds to the needs not of Turkey but of Prime Minister Erdogan. It may be argued that this system is a reaction to the bureaucratic tutelage system over democracy that came with the 1961 Constitution and was reinforced by the 1982 Constitution. However, if adopted, it is inevitable that this system will bring the domination of the elected majority instead of the tutelage of the appointed. Liberal democracy in the sense of libertarian and pluralist democracy may not be a perfect regime, but it is certainly the best form of government found so far.

“The regime that came to Turkey with the 1961 and 1982 constitutions and placed ‘national will’ under the tutelage of the military-civilian bureaucracy loyal to Kemalist ideology was one of the main obstacles to establishing democracy. But liberal democracy is not just ‘national will’ or majority rule. It is equally a regime where ‘national will’ is limited by citizens’ fundamental rights and freedoms; checked and balanced by the rule of law, separation of powers, independent judiciary, freedom of the press, and civil society organizations. Democracy can only be established on these two legs. The Erdogan-style presidential system proposal, which contradicts both the parliamentary system envisioned in the AKP’s 2007 election manifesto and the constitutional amendments made by referendum in 2010, will not bring stability; on the contrary, it is inevitable that it will be a source of instability by reinforcing personal rule, and therefore must be rejected.

“It seems impossible for the AKP’s constitutional draft to pass through Parliament today. However, Prime Minister Erdogan, who says ‘We don’t have the numbers to make constitutional changes with the BDP (Peace and Democracy Party). But if we can agree on a referendum, we can take joint steps with them…,’ is apparently calculating to win the BDP’s support by adding articles they would accept to this draft; to take it to a referendum with this support and have it approved by the people. We will see whether he succeeds in this calculation.

“I find it difficult to understand how Prime Minister Erdogan, who has truly rendered great services to this country in various fields, can so set aside the fact that democracy is governance by rules not persons, and that Turkey will be governed after him as well. I do not find his obsession that Turkey can only be best governed by himself, with unlimited power, compatible with the Islamic moral principles he claims to follow, such as staying away from arrogance and not abandoning humility.” (Zaman, 9.2.2013)

## The meaning of being liberal in Turkey

While writing in the Zaman newspaper published by the religious community formed under the guidance of Fethullah Gulen, a cleric, and as a commentator defending liberal democracy, I occasionally felt the need to explain what I meant by being liberal in Turkey, and wrote as follows:

“What does it mean to be ‘liberal’ in today’s Turkey? In my view, it essentially means adopting the following ideas: People are of equal worth from birth. For this reason, all citizens should be equal in rights and before the law, regardless of gender, race, ethnic identity, or religious belief. However, people being of equal worth does not mean they do not have different abilities. The effort to make people equal in economic conditions rather than in rights has resulted in the suffocation of freedoms, as shown by totalitarian socialist practices.

“Like people, the identities, nations, religions, and cultures they belong to are also of equal worth and deserve equal respect; no hierarchy of superiority can be made among them. Conflicts can only be resolved through dialogue and compromise, not through violence and imposition. Authority in society should be based on voluntary acceptance, relationships between people on agreement, and governance on the consent of the governed.

“In the 19th century, liberals believed in governance limited by fundamental rights and freedoms, but they did not believe in governance by elected governments, that is, in political democracy. But over time they adopted the principle of ‘one person, one vote’; this principle was established in the West through the joint struggles of liberal and democratic socialist parties. Today, anyone who does not believe in political democracy and governance limited by human rights is not a liberal. Political democracy requires strong checks and balances to prevent the abuse of power, regardless of the form of government. A judiciary and media independent of the government, and academic freedom in universities, are among the indispensable conditions of political democracy.

“State and religion should be separated, and the state should maintain equal distance from all beliefs and non-believers. Until the second half of the last century, liberals argued that only individuals could be subjects of rights, and that the state should be ‘blind’ to ethnic-religious identity differences among citizens. But although the debate continues between monocultural and contemporary multicultural interpretations of liberalism, it is the latter that is increasingly prevailing through international group rights conventions.

“A free society can be pluralistic not only politically but also economically and culturally, meaning a society where decisions are made from multiple centers. A market economy based on private property is not a sufficient but a necessary condition of a democratic society.

“Through science based on reason, people can gain knowledge about the workings of nature and society. Through reforms based on this knowledge, they can build a freer, more just, and prosperous society. However, science consists only of theories that are valid until proven otherwise; it advances by replacing theories shown to be wrong with new ones. As science advances, it becomes clear how little we know. Therefore, science has its limits. At the source of moral values is not science but religions and philosophy. There is no single, absolute, infallible, unchanging truth or correctness. The domains of religion and science are separate; they should respect each other. All kinds of fanaticism, whether religious or scientific in origin, should be opposed.”

The final paragraph of the article can only be meaningful in showing how idealistic I was about Turkey’s political culture, substituting what I wanted to see for reality:

“Although those who adopt the label ‘liberal’ in Turkey today are limited to a rather narrow circle, the idea of governance by elected governments limited by citizens’ fundamental rights and freedoms, especially freedom of expression, organization, and belief—political liberalism—constitutes the common denominator of society. ‘Human Rights,’ which almost every segment wants to be respected, is a concept derived from liberalism.” (Zaman, 06.04.2013)

Why is Fethullah Gulen so influential?

The article I will quote below well reflected that I valued Fethullah Gulen more than he deserved, and that perhaps I only considered the aspects of reality I wanted to see regarding his expressed views and the religious community he led.

“Time magazine in its April 29 - May 6, 2013 issue introduced, according to its own assessment, ‘The 100 Most Influential People in the World.’ One of them was Islamic scholar Fethullah Gulen. The short piece about Hocaefendi was written by Stephen Kinzer, bureau chief of The New York Times in Istanbul from 1996-2000 and author of the book ‘Crescent and Star: Turkey Between Two Worlds’ (2002).

“Kinzer wrote: ‘From his secluded corner in Pennsylvania, his message of tolerance and respect for difference has won him admirers spread across the world. Schools opened by his followers have spread to about 140 countries… In his home country Turkey, through graduates of the schools he opened who have risen to high positions in government, judiciary, and police, he has enormous influence. This makes him look like a puppeteer operating in the shadows, and he has almost as many detractors as admirers. However, as the most powerful advocate of moderation in the Islamic world, he is waging a very urgent and important campaign.’

“After reading Kinzer’s article, I thought. What makes Gulen one of the world’s most influential thinkers? And why in Turkey does he have ‘almost as many detractors as admirers’? For me, the answers to these questions are very clear. In Turkey and everywhere in the world, there are millions of Muslims who do not give credence to fundamentalist, fanatical interpretations of Islam, to efforts to produce a totalitarian ideology from Islam. These millions want to remain attached to the spiritual and social values their faith instills, while also living in a world where freedom of thought, belief, and enterprise is established; where different identities and beliefs are respected; where education replaces ignorance; where science is respected as much as religion; where working and earning is encouraged and appreciated. This is the primary factor that has made Gulen one of the world’s most influential thinkers with his messages ‘from his remote corner in Pennsylvania.’

“Another important factor, without doubt, is that Gulen is a thinker coming from within Turkey’s Sufi, folk Islam tradition. In this tradition, if Said Nursi is the name who carried Sufi Islam to the modern age, Fethullah Gulen is the person who interprets it in light of today’s increasingly liberalizing and globalizing world. If Nursi is the leader of a religious community, Gulen is the inspiration for a faith-based civil society movement, the ‘Hizmet movement.’ Today, the Hizmet movement, in line with the values Gulen instills, not only enables Turkey to build ‘bridges of peace’ with the world through schools spread across 140 countries that have earned societies’ respect with the quality of education they provide. It also contributes to the establishment of a modern economy in Turkey and, with the values it represents, supports the establishment of libertarian and pluralist democracy.

“The secret behind the Hizmet movement’s successes is not Gulen’s orders from Pennsylvania or its centralized and hierarchical structure, but quite the opposite—its being based on principles of decentralization and voluntarism. Yes, among Turkey’s administrators, judicial members, and police today, there certainly are those who graduated from the Hizmet movement’s schools and respect Gulen’s guidance. But to assume that these people act on orders, to attribute Gulen’s influence to this, is nothing but a conspiracy theory.

“Yes, Gulen has ‘detractors’ who have forced him to live far from his homeland. These are essentially proponents of authoritarian secularism in its various shades, who see Islam as the chief enemy of modernization and believe it should be confined to consciences and completely excluded from social life. It is certain that Kemalism is still strong.” (Zaman, 07.05.2013)

## Erdogan should return to pre-2011

In June 2013, with an understanding that substituted my own liberal preferences for society’s choices, I invited Prime Minister Erdogan to abandon the policies he had begun following after 2011 and return to the previous period. As follows:

“Turkey is a society with a plural structure in many respects—ethnic, religious, linguistic, cultural, ideological—with delicate balances. It contains many divisions within it, primarily Turkish and Kurdish, Sunni and Alevi, religious and non-religious, Muslim and non-Muslim, democrat and tutelage supporter, secular and secularist, libertarian and authoritarian. The government must take into account these divisions in society and the delicate balances between them. A society with a plural structure can never be governed with a majoritarian understanding (whoever has the majority’s support can do whatever they want). On the contrary, it requires a pluralist governance (seeing differences as richness, establishing mutual respect).

“Prime Minister Erdogan’s performance in the period up to the 2011 general elections followed a line that took into account the structure and delicate balances of society. This was one of the most important factors in his party collecting half of the votes. However, after receiving this 50 percent and succeeding in pushing back military tutelage, the Prime Minister adopted an attitude incompatible with libertarian democracy, assuming with inflated self-confidence that he could do whatever he wanted, didn’t have to listen to anyone, and only had to account from election to election. The point this attitude has brought him to (even if it is unclear with what purpose he said this) is the place Education Minister Nabi Avci described: succeeding in doing what the opposition could not have done in years of trying—uniting against the government groups that could not otherwise be imagined coming together…

“Finally, President Gul had to raise his voice: ‘Democracy is not just elections. The message has been received. What is necessary will be done…’ he said. The Prime Minister may not know or understand ‘what is behind this statement,’ but society understood very well what the President meant. Society hopes and expects that the President will not repeat mistakes like ‘Yavuz Sultan Selim’; that he will remain faithful to the pluralist, participatory democracy he says he supports. If the message was received, what needs to be done first is for Istanbul’s urban development to be taken out of the Prime Minister’s hands and left to its municipality and people. The second is for the imposition of a presidential regime, ‘Turkish-style’ or not, to end.

“The fact that the President felt the need to intervene in the situation showed how vitally important a parliamentary system functioning with all its institutions and rules, not under tutelage, is for Turkey. I hope everyone saw that the distinction between the head of state representing the nation and the prime minister representing the majority in a parliamentary system is one of the safeguards against abuse of power. What I see is this: The Prime Minister must now change. He must be the Erdogan of before 2011. He must re-adopt an attitude respectful of the sensitivities of all segments of society. The President, taking with him the founders and prominent figures of the AKP who can see the gravity of the situation, should seriously warn the Prime Minister on this matter. For those who want to bring back military tutelage, revive the Turkish-Kurdish conflict, and destroy the good image the country has built with great difficulty and effort are right behind the door!

“If the Prime Minister cannot be persuaded to change, then I personally will conclude that he is extremely exhausted after the intense work he has been doing for about eleven years, or that his health condition does not allow him to continue in office. Then the responsibility for finding a remedy will fall to the people.” (“The Prime Minister must change,” 6.6.2013)

“Throw this man out of the newspaper”

While writing for Zaman, I very rarely encountered censorship. One example is this: I had to change the last paragraph of my article titled “The Prime Minister must change” that I quoted above. The original form of the paragraph was: “If the Prime Minister cannot be persuaded to change, then it may be concluded that he is extremely exhausted after the intense work he has been doing for about eleven years, or that his health condition does not allow him to continue at this pace, and the mechanism of the parliamentary system that allows for renewing the executive branch when necessary can come into play. The AKP group, if necessary on its own, can provide for continuing with a new prime minister by casting a vote of no confidence against the current government. This is in the interest of Turkey, the AKP, and its deputies.”

When Editor-in-Chief Ekrem Dumanli saw this version of the article, he called and said, “I agree with you, but they will judge that we made you write these lines and will cause an incident…” and asked me to soften the last paragraph. Although I believed that no one had the power to make me write any line, I did my best and put the paragraph into the form I quoted above. Dumanli was not satisfied, but did not press the matter. Some time later he told another Zaman writer what had happened: Prime Minister Erdogan, reading the softened version of the article, had fumed and called Dumanli saying about me “Throw this man out of the newspaper…”; Dumanli’s answer had been “We don’t have a practice of dismissing writers.” When I learned these things, I was truly startled. Although I had always given him due credit for the services he had rendered, I was surprised that the Prime Minister was so intolerant of me.

Another and more serious example in the context of censorship at Zaman was this: My article titled “Why Hagia Sophia should remain a museum,” which was supposed to be published on December 7, 2013, was censored and completely disappeared. The page editor called me and said that the newspaper management agreed with the content of my article, but that due to the increasing tension between the community and the government, the article raised concerns that it might cause conflict among Muslims and demonstrations in front of the newspaper. Some time later, another Zaman writer would explain to me where the concern actually stemmed from: Apparently, in Said Nursi’s time, he had sent a letter to Prime Minister Adnan Menderes requesting “the opening of Hagia Sophia for worship”…

## Gezi Park: Democratic consciousness is strengthening

Following the forcible dispersal by security forces of the sit-in protest that began on May 28, 2013 to oppose the AKP government’s plan to reconstruct the historic barracks building in place of Istanbul’s Taksim Gezi Park, approximately 3.5 million people participated in mass demonstrations that spread across the country to protest the government’s increasing authoritarianism and continued until late August. During the demonstrations, which were of a scale rarely seen in Turkish history, 11 people died, 8,000 were injured, and 3,000 were detained. I interpreted the Gezi Park demonstrations in the articles I will quote below as follows:

“About two years ago, in an article I wrote for a booklet titled ‘What does Turkey think?’ published by the European Council on Foreign Relations, I answered the editors’ question ‘Will Turkey without an EU anchor turn toward authoritarianism?’; I explained why the claim that ‘the alliance between the AKP and various religious movements is taking Turkey toward elected authoritarianism…’ which was ardently defended by authoritarian secularists at the time, was not at all convincing. (…) In Turkey, where under AKP rule the economy has strengthened, prosperity has increased, the middle class has expanded, it has opened to the world, pushed back military tutelage, broken taboos with expanding freedom of debate, ended the denial of Kurds, and started the peace process with the PKK, I have argued in various articles and speeches that the people will not accept or tolerate an authoritarian government. In my view, the main message of the demonstrations that began in Taksim Gezi Park on May 31 and have spread across Turkey is that democratic consciousness in Turkey is gradually strengthening.

“As for those who try to explain the protest movements that united very different segments against Prime Minister Erdogan’s increasingly unacceptable imposition as the work of ‘internal and external enemies’: This is, as always, nothing but self-deception. These protests are the unintended consequences of the great services Erdogan and his government have rendered to Turkey. The AKP government made Turkey relatively richer and freer. In Turkey, which is richer and freer than yesterday, young generations have increasingly embraced the ideals of democracy and freedom, human rights and environmental sensitivity more deeply. (Emphases added later.)

“Today’s young generations are the products of the ‘new Turkey’ that AKP governments paved the way for; their values are fundamentally different from those of the generations of 30-40 years ago who pursued various authoritarian and totalitarian visions. The burning and destruction by ‘old Turkey’ remnants who use the nonviolent and creative reactions of these generations to the government’s authoritarianism, imposition, and police violence as an excuse to attack left and right should not prevent seeing the main character of the Gezi Park protest movement. (…)

“For many years Turkey struggled with the authoritarian secularist and monoculturalist military-bureaucratic tutelage over democracy; in the coming period it appears it will be the scene of struggles against the arbitrariness and authoritarianism of the elected government. In the end, we are learning democracy by living it, gradually maturing and establishing it.” (“Democratic consciousness is strengthening,” Zaman, 8.6.2013)

## Lessons from Gezi Park

As can be seen, while interpreting the Gezi Park protests as signs of the strengthening of democratic consciousness in Turkey and the birth of “New Turkey,” I was also arguing that there were those who wanted to use the resistance to revive “Old Turkey” under military tutelage:

“The resistance movement against the construction of ‘Topcu Barracks’ in Taksim Gezi Park is full of lessons to be drawn for Turkey’s political life. As almost everyone, including the Prime Minister, acknowledges, the resistance began as a peaceful and democratic protest movement in which young people of very different political views participated. However, the movement took on a character that spread to all of Istanbul, and from there to all of Turkey, opposing the arbitrary and authoritarian governance style the Prime Minister has pursued since the 2011 elections, uniting very different segments who could not otherwise have come together.

“The pioneers of the movement were the young generations of New Turkey, largely the work of Prime Minister Erdogan and his government, who respect democracy, human rights, diversity, and the environment. Unfortunately, Old Turkey remnants who wanted to revive military tutelage, sabotage the peace process, and create chaos tried to hijack the movement. Militants who burned and destroyed businesses and attacked police with Molotov cocktails appeared on the scene.

“The Gezi Park resistance showed the Prime Minister that New Turkey will not accept arbitrary and authoritarian governance, whether military or civilian. The Prime Minister, who had previously given messages that ‘he wouldn’t listen to any supreme council,’ declared that he accepted the most fundamental requirement of the rule of law and would wait for the outcome of the judicial process for Gezi Park. By proposing a referendum, he also had to accept that the decision on whether to build Topcu Barracks should be left to Istanbulites.

“The Gezi Park resistance once again showed how centralized Turkey’s administrative structure is, and that this centralization is now concentrated in the hands of almost a single person (the prime minister). Mayor Kadir Topbas, who had rendered great services to Istanbul, was almost erased from the scene. (In my opinion, he should have resigned to express his objection to the prime minister who ignored him.) Our need to strengthen local governments and local administration was once again seen.

“The Gezi Park resistance showed that ‘New Turkey’ will not accept a governance style that attempts to arrange everyone’s lifestyle according to its own preferences. But unfortunately, the Prime Minister continues to divide society into ‘those who are with us and those who are not’; to accuse ‘those who are not’ of treachery and baseness; to strain and polarize society by organizing rallies to intimidate those who don’t think like him. Instead of seeking the causes of what has happened in his own mistakes, he tries to explain it with the ostrich method of Old Turkey, with ‘conspiracies of internal and external enemies.’ He is practically inviting the destruction, within a few weeks, of the international reputation he personally earned for Turkey over ten years with great effort. Turkey’s identity that reconciles Islam with democracy and serves as an inspiration to all Islamic countries is suffering great damage. Perhaps worst of all, he is endangering the steps taken toward solving the Kurdish problem that has been bleeding Turkey for 30 years.

“There are also lessons to be underlined from the perspective of society. We must make public institutions respectable and strong. Of course we will criticize when the police use excessive force and act contrary to human rights, but as a society we can never forget that our security depends on the police force. Yes, democracy is not just elections. There is no democracy where there is no freedom of expression and organization. National will is not just the majority. Yes, we will criticize the elected government in the harshest terms when necessary for its practices incompatible with democracy, human rights, and the rule of law, but we cannot forget even for a moment that democracy means government by election.” (Zaman, 20.6.2013)

## A sincere appeal to Prime Minister Erdogan

In 2010-2011, that is, in the early years of his turn toward authoritarianism, I was approaching Prime Minister Erdogan with more goodwill than he deserved; while directing my criticisms on one hand, on the other hand I was reiterating my appreciation for the services he rendered in the first half of his rule, calling on him to abandon the turn toward authoritarianism; as in the article I quote below:

“(…) The Prime Minister should be able to see that the New Turkey, which will never accept arbitrary and authoritarian governance, is largely the product of reforms that he himself pioneered, which made Turkey a richer, more democratic, and more open society. Brazil’s rulers say that the mass demonstrations that erupted over transportation fare increases and spread to 100 cities showed the whole world how democratic a society Brazil is, and that they are proud of these demonstrations. Surely, Turkey’s rulers, especially Prime Minister Erdogan, can see that the Gezi Park protests are not the results of ‘conspiracies of internal and external enemies’ but of the ideals of freedom and democracy taking root in society, and they can be proud of this.

“The opportunity has not been missed to reverse the negativities caused by the Gezi Park protests that harmed our democracy, economy, and international reputation; to show the whole world that first-class democracy can be established in a Muslim-majority country. To seize this opportunity, it is enough for the Prime Minister to return to the attitude he followed for about ten years until the 2011 elections, which enabled him to overcome the great troubles he faced and elevate Turkey, which was respectful of the sensitivities of various segments of the people of Turkey, which united rather than polarized society, and to embrace the policy of governing the country in consultation with his government and people.

“As his past political career shows, the Prime Minister is a pragmatic, not ideological leader; one who knows how to learn from mistakes rather than insisting on them. These were the qualities that brought him his successes. His insistence on these qualities will save Turkey from increasing tension and polarization, and serve its progress on the path of democratization and peace. His insistence on these qualities will serve to emphasize—something we as the people of Turkey desperately need, and what will truly make us strong as Turkey—that we are one whole with all our differences, as Turks and Kurds, Sunnis and Alevis, Muslims and non-Muslims, religious and non-religious, and to establish mutual respect for each other’s opinions, language and culture, and way of life.

“There are great opportunities ahead of us. We have effectively left behind the era of military tutelage that made Turkey a semi-democracy. The Turkish Grand National Assembly can certainly find the necessary majority to make a constitution that will establish libertarian and pluralist democracy. We have the opportunity to end the armed uprising that has been bleeding and weakening our country for 30 years, that has crippled democracy and made our people unhappy. Prime Minister, you have largely created these opportunities; do not let these opportunities be wasted by straining and polarizing the country.

“With your encouragement as well, the PKK has embarked on the path of pursuing a responsible policy toward all of Turkey and all Kurds. It has finally seen that armed struggle has been harming the cause of equal citizenship for Kurds. It is giving signals that it will no longer resort to arms and will focus on political struggle. The time has come to advance to the second phase of the peace process. We must meet the common, legitimate, democratic demands of our Kurdish citizens. Democracy must now be established, violence must come to an end.” (Zaman, 22.6.2013)

Yes! But not enough…

In those years, a perspective that I would later almost completely abandon dominated my writings. I defined this perspective, which I called “strategic optimism,” as follows:

“I have an understanding that looks optimistically at the future of humanity and, as a part of it, Turkey in a strategic (long-term) sense. At the foundation of this optimism is my trust in critical reason, that is, in people’s ability to correct their mistakes using their minds. Looking at history, we see that it has never been easy for societies to reach conditions where critical (self-questioning) reason prevails. Establishing libertarian and pluralist democracy, the political order produced by critical reason, has required tough struggles everywhere; in much of the world it still awaits establishment.

“Even in countries with long histories in this field, various problems are experienced.

Although there is still a very long road ahead and sometimes setbacks occur, humanity is progressing toward a freer and more just future. Great disasters have been overcome. Humanity defeated Nazism, which stifled critical reason, and liquidated many fascist regimes. Communism was also defeated. The communist party itself led this in Russia and China. Yes, in Russia an authoritarian one-man regime replaced it, but Russians are freer today than yesterday and can look to the future with hope. Yes, in China the communist party monopoly continues, but the hope for prosperity and liberation is much further ahead today than yesterday.

“Yes, today humanity also faces great dangers, especially climate change. But it is not impossible for it to overcome this threat using critical reason. Yes, acts of violence have become much more visible today due to globalized communication, but statistics show that violence and the destructiveness of wars have decreased compared to the past. I believe that Turkey is also progressing toward a freer and more just society by using critical reason and learning from mistakes. In my youth, believers in critical reason and libertarian and pluralist democracy among intellectuals in Turkey were a very small minority; today, believers in dictatorship are a small minority. Today’s Turkey is much freer and more prosperous than the Turkey of my youth.

“It cannot be denied that Turkey, which set out on the path of the rule of law with the Tanzimat reforms and people-based governance with the Second Constitutional Era, is progressing toward establishing democracy that increasingly includes individual freedoms and group rights. No one can deny that through the efforts of both secular and Islamic modernization advocates, Turkey today holds an exceptional place among Muslim-majority countries in terms of democratization experience. In the process that began with the transition to a multi-party system in 1950 after an authoritarian modernization experience, Turkey witnessed the gradual expansion of freedoms despite all the setbacks brought by coups and efforts at violent suppression. Even today we are far from establishing libertarian and pluralist democracy, but as long as criticism is met with respect and lessons are learned from criticisms, we can look to the future with optimism.

“While listening to the Prime Minister yesterday, I was essentially thinking about these things. Definitely ‘Yes!’ to the democratization package he announced, but far from sufficient for Turkey to be a democracy by EU standards. The Prime Minister’s acknowledgment of this; his emphasis that progress cannot be achieved without strong support from society, despite the current opposition’s resistance, are the points I agreed with most in his speech. The Prime Minister’s return to a discourse embracing all of society is, in my opinion, the most gratifying aspect of the speech.” (Zaman, 1.10.2013)

## The goal is to control civil society too

In one of the articles where I increased the dose of criticism against the increasingly evident authoritarianism of the Erdogan government, I said:

“(…) There is no field the Prime Minister has not touched in his effort to shape society according to his own preferences. First comes the media that shapes public opinion. Through large media owners who are dependent on him due to their commercial dealings, he has critical journalists fired. He holds decisions on which companies will benefit from which state opportunities and which tenders will be awarded to whom. He unleashes finance inspectors on companies whose attitude he doesn’t like. He violently suppresses demonstrations organized by opponents. Pointing to the attempt by opponents of democracy to hijack them, he explains the Gezi Park demonstrations, which were essentially led by those who want freedom and democracy to be established, as conspiracies of internal and external enemies who don’t want Turkey’s development. He threatens civil society saying ‘you’re either with me or against me… Those who are neutral will be eliminated…’ When a critical voice comes from the ranks of his party, he immediately warns ‘Don’t serve the enemy!’ and expels them.

“The latest link in Erdogan’s effort to bring civil society under control is the closure of private tutoring centers under the guise of ‘transforming them into private schools.’ The Prime Minister wants to suppress by law the demand for educational support that will continue to exist as long as the supply and quality of education are not increased. At this point, the Hizmet Movement, which represents not the entire sector but about a quarter of it, is rightfully reacting to the ‘closure by law’ effort that will also result in most of those working in their tutoring centers becoming unemployed, that is, to the initiative that disregards both society’s need for educational support and freedom of enterprise and contract. If there are problems in the tutoring sector and improvements are needed, reforms should be made in consultation with stakeholders, as in almost all matters. Imposition is not a method proper to democracy.” (Zaman, 23.11.2013)

This article of mine received unexpected but quite understandable support. Enver Yucel, founder of Bahcesehir University and one of the pioneers of tutoring centers preparing students for university entrance exams, who in this context was also a competitor of the Gulen movement, called and warmly congratulated me.

## The partnership between the Kemalists and the AKP

The antipathy Kemalists and the AKP felt toward each other often hid their common aspects from view. In an article where I pointed out these commonalities, I said the following:

“(…) It is certain that there are some fundamental understandings that the Kemalists and the ‘conservative democrat’ AKP administration share. The foremost of these is that one represents authoritarianism of the top-down and minority-based kind, while the other represents authoritarianism of the elected and majority-based kind (not totalitarianism, of course). For this reason, both harbor vast intolerance toward voluntary organizations independent of the state, that is, toward civil society; for this reason they strive to keep civil society under tight control.

“Another common aspect of the mentality dominating both the Kemalists and the AKP administration is that both believe in keeping religion under state monopoly and that the state should decide which religious beliefs are correct/acceptable and which are wrong/ unacceptable. Their complete agreement on the indispensability of the Directorate of Religious Affairs is of course the clearest indicator of this. Kemalists cling tightly to the Directorate so that it doesn’t bring Islamic interpretations contrary to their secularist (that is, understanding secularism as a lifestyle distant from religion) views and makes society homogeneous in terms of religion as well, not allowing differences. The AKP administration, on the other hand, holds the Directorate dear so that it serves their Sunni-Naqshbandi understanding of Islam. For this reason, neither of them has any liking for the understanding of Islam that embraces pluralist democracy, human rights, rule of law, respect for different ethnic and religious identities, and a competitive market economy that Fethullah Gulen represents today; they see it as a threat to themselves.

“Another common aspect of the mentality dominating both Kemalists and the AKP finds expression in the understanding of nation. According to both, the nation in Turkey consists of Turks and Muslims. What had the AKP’s well-known Defense Minister Vecdi Gonul—on whose acceptability as a politician both sides displayed complete agreement—said on a national day like November 10 in 2008? ‘If the deportation and population exchange had not happened, we would not have the national state we have today!’

“The Kemalists’ understanding of nation has sometimes emphasized Turkishness in an ethnic (Central Asian origin) sense, sometimes in a cultural (‘Happy is he who says I am a Turk’) sense. The AKP’s understanding of nation has almost always been based on the understanding of ‘Islamic nation’ consisting of Turks, Kurds, Laz, Circassians, and other ‘anasir-i Islam,’ that is, Muslim elements… Kemalists represent the secularist, the AKP administration represents the religious, but both largely agree both on statism (in the sense of ‘the state is not at the service of the nation, the nation is at the service of the state’) and on nationalism (based on the understanding of nation consisting of Turks and Muslims).

This is why neither can confront the deportation during World War I and the human tragedy it caused… This is why the Hrant Dink murder can never be solved.” (Zaman, 30.11.2013)

Why the attitude against Hizmet?

The common aspects of Kemalists, the AKP, and Islamists in general also manifested themselves in the hostility both adopted toward the Gulen movement. However, the anti-Hizmet front was not limited to these two. I examined the anti-Hizmet front in the following article:

“The alliance formed against Fethullah Gulen Hocaefendi and the Hizmet Movement, a faith-based civil society movement formed under his guidance, which has been gradually expanding in recent days, interests me greatly. The locomotive of this front is certainly the hardline Kemalists who have not the slightest tolerance for civil society; for example, the generals who declared the Hizmet Movement very dangerous at the National Security Council (NSC) in 2004, wanted it placed under strict surveillance, and started the profiling. Ardent supporters of authoritarian secularism and military tutelage (or Nationalists) naturally follow these generals.

“Right beside them are intellectuals some of whom are referred to in public as ‘worried moderns’ and writers who can be characterized as ‘secularist democrats.’ At one end of this segment are those who believe that religious beliefs, especially Islam, can never be compatible with modernization and are considerably influenced by positivism and Orientalism. At the other end are those who accuse some members of the Hizmet Movement of being a hidden power nested within the state, an ‘autonomous power.’

“The ‘worried ones’ extend all the way to the USA. Those at this end long spread the theory that the Gulen Movement was on its way to making Turkey a Sunni Iran hand in hand with the AKP. These days they are working the claim that the ‘real big danger’ for Turkey is not the authoritarian AKP but the Gulen Movement. Those who harbor an animosity toward the Hizmet Movement bordering on enmity are the supporters of the KCK (Kurdistan Communities Union). Their concern is that Hizmet is taking Kurdish youth away from them by providing opportunities for education and social advancement.

“Recently, the anti-Hizmet front has been joined by the Prime Minister and his close circle, who are no less eager than the Kemalists in their quest to bring all of civil society under control; they speak of Hizmet as a ‘gang’ or ‘organization’ that has infiltrated the state. We have not been able to see evidence that they committed crimes, but public servants who are profiled on the allegation that they belong to Hizmet are being subjected to purges.

“Finally, in recent days some pure Islamists have also joined the front. When the AKP government attempted to close tutoring centers, some of which are operated by Hizmet, they too seized the opportunity and began raising their voices. According to one, for example, Hocaefendi represents the understanding of ‘moderate/light Islam without sharia, without fiqh, without jihad… that the USA, Israel, Evangelists, Crusaders, global capitalism and liberalism desire.’ Another recently wrote: ‘The movement actually resembles the headquarters of the “moderate Islam” project. It wants to advance not by confronting the USA, EU and Israel, but by having them alongside or behind it. Actually the project doesn’t concern only Turkey. Turkey is a pilot region. There is an effort to expand the workshop conducted here gradually toward other Islamic countries through education and media, business relations, in a way that will not pose a threat to Western values and interests, to the international order…’

“As you can see, the stance against Hizmet has now spread to quite a wide front. All the elements in this front have their own justifications, of course. Well, what could their common denominator be? In my view, all of them are very disturbed by Hocaefendi representing an alternative understanding of Islamic modernity that also appeals to the religious; that advocates democracy, rule of law, human rights, respect for differences, and integration with the EU; that encourages education and science; that embraces the whole world and all of humanity; that is libertarian and pluralist; and by his being a source of inspiration for alternative elites who are both religious and modernist.” (Zaman, 17.12.2013)

My benevolent view of the Gulen movement, which was shattered when its participation in the July 15 coup attempt was revealed, was perhaps best expressed in the article above.

Something is very rotten

The investigations initiated with a series of reports in September 2012 and February 2013, in which public officials including four ministers were accused of misconduct and bribery, became public on December 17, 2013 with the implementation of Public Prosecutor Celal Kara’s detention orders and the related courts’ search warrants. In the operation carried out by the Istanbul Police Department’s Organized Crime and Financial Crimes units, an investigation was opened against persons including businessmen, bureaucrats, a bank manager, public officials of various levels, and four ministers and three ministers’ children, on charges of “bribery, misconduct in office, bid rigging, and smuggling.”

Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan claimed the investigation was a conspiracy set up by the Gulen Movement against the government. However, following the public disclosure of the investigations, Egemen Bagis was removed from his position as Minister for EU Affairs; Interior Minister Muammer Guler, Economy Minister Zafer Caglayan, and Environment and Urban Planning Minister Erdogan Bayraktar resigned from their positions; Bayraktar also resigned from his parliamentary seat. In the vote held in the Turkish Grand National Assembly on January 5, 2015, it would be decided not to send the former ministers to the Supreme Tribunal (Yuce Divan). I interpreted the investigations, which would be referred to in the media as the ‘December 17-25, 2013 Corruption and Bribery Operation,’ in the articles I will quote below as follows:

“One of the famous lines from William Shakespeare’s play ‘Hamlet’ is, as you know: ‘Something is rotten in the state of Denmark…’ The operation called ‘Big bribery,’ initiated by the order of the Istanbul deputy chief prosecutor about which the public has very little information, and in which 52 people including ministers’ sons, bureaucrats, and businessmen have been detained as of yesterday, unfortunately creates the impression that there is something very rotten in the Republic of Turkey. Those close to the government first of all, and generally the anti-Hizmet writers in the media, did not hesitate to cling to the cliche that this operation was a manifestation of the ‘power struggle between the Government and the Community.’ Some, after starting by admitting they knew nothing about the subject, were even able to claim that the operation was started by the Community on the instructions of the USA.

“I am not as certain as these people about how the operation should be interpreted. Moreover, I continue to be ‘naive’ enough to believe that there are still prosecutors and police officers in Turkey who are primarily committed to democracy, rule of law, and their duties, regardless of their political views or religious beliefs. What concerns me is that, whoever started it and for whatever motive, some rotten things in the Republic of Turkey are being uncovered through this and other investigations and the filth is being cleaned. What concerns me is what the government will do about the investigations that concern 3 ministers through their sons, and one minister directly.

“There appear to be different views within the ruling AKP party on this matter. AKP Deputy Chairman and party spokesman Huseyin Celik says, ‘As the AK Party, we want everything that needs to be done for the truth to be revealed to be done completely…’

Isn’t the foremost requirement for this that the relevant ministers step down? After all, didn’t Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek say ‘If such a thing happened to me, my choice would be to resign’?

However, it is sensed that the Prime Minister interprets the investigations as a ‘trap’ set by ‘dirty alliances… gangs…’ for the government and is determined not to give way.

“The Deputy Prime Minister also speaks of psychological warfare against the government, attempts to wear down the government, organizations nested within the state. After all, didn’t one of the ministers the investigation concerned declare: ‘Nothing will come of this investigation…’ The appointment of new prosecutors to the investigation, the removal of some police branch directors from their duties on the allegation that they ‘abused their office,’ raises the suspicion that the government will try to interfere with the investigation. Will it succeed? I don’t know. But I hope not. (…)” (Zaman, 19.12.2013)

## Old – New Turkey struggle
