“Whenever a crisis occurs, I devote more time to commentaries in the foreign press. Because some of them are illuminating, and most are entertaining.

The title of an article commenting on the bribery and corruption investigation involving 4 ministers of the so-called ‘AK’ Party government, a public bank general manager, and a mayor is ‘Religious War…’ Many people in Turkey think so too. But is it so?

“In my view, what is happening is this: All the struggles Turkey has witnessed in the 21st century are fundamentally the pains of the transition from the authoritarian modernization defined by Kemalism to liberal modernization that can be roughly defined by EU criteria. On one side there is Old Turkey with its regime that started as single-party rule and turned into military tutelage, with authoritarian secularism and single-identity policies imposed on society. On the other side there is New Turkey trying to establish democracy, human rights, rule of law, and respect for minorities.

“In roughly the first decade of the 21st century, the AKP government headed by Prime Minister Erdogan took the lead of New Turkey by placing EU accession at the center of its program and made considerable progress. Very different (political, economic, cultural) forces, primarily the victims of Old Turkey, each with their own characteristics and expectations, supported the struggle of Erdogan and his party. The New Turkey alliance found its broadest expression in the 2010 referendum (58% yes). This alliance extended from capital groups pleased not with the AKP’s religiosity but with the liberalization of the economy, to soldiers who realized that their political role benefited neither the country nor the military.

“In the second decade of the 21st century, the agenda of not the entire AKP but of the Prime Minister ceased to be New Turkey. Erdogan, having received nearly 50% of the vote in the 2011 elections, and assuming that he had fended off coup attempts and that military tutelage had effectively ended, set about implementing his own agenda: to ‘make Turkey one of the world’s ten largest economies by 2023’ he had to gather all power in his own hands and be as powerful as Putin. The ‘Turkish-style presidential’ system that would not be hindered by separation of powers was the most concise expression of this quest. He began to think that he could be an authoritarian reformer in the tradition of Abdulhamid II and Ataturk, to say that democracy is only about elections. He tried to silence critical voices in the media. He set about repairing his ties with Old Turkey. He began to pretend to be solving the Kurdish problem. While taking on an Islamic Kemalist appearance on one face, on the other face he revived the National Vision Erdogan image; he increased the dose of Islamic populism.

“Erdogan’s third term as prime minister increasingly came to resemble Lord Acton’s words ‘Power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely…’ In the end, it came to his close associates, who believed their power was unlimited, being neck-deep in corruption, as the latest scandal revealed. Erdogan’s performance caused divisions in almost every segment and polarization in society. Even his own party could no longer maintain its unity. The increasingly apparent differences of opinion with President Abdullah Gul, resignations from his party, and rising objections are signs of this.

“The first big sign that the longing for New Turkey would not surrender to Erdogan was last summer’s Gezi Park demonstrations. The second big signal is the current major bribery and corruption investigation initiated by duty-bound prosecutors and police. These developments are leading to the repositioning of the Old and New Turkey alliances and the sharpening of the struggle between the two. In other words, what is happening is not a religious war, but a struggle between Old and New Turkey.” (Zaman, 21.12.2013)

## The ‘parallel state’ issue

I did not find the claims that the Gulen community had formed a “parallel state,” that is, a state within a state, convincing. For the following reasons:

“First, those convicted in the Balyoz and Ergenekon trials claimed that the accusations against them were based on evidence fabricated by a ‘Fethullahist, F-type’ (that is, related to the ‘community,’ to the Hizmet Movement) ‘secret organization, gang, junta, autonomous power, parallel state’ nested within the judiciary and police. Now the Prime Minister, whose four ministers are under suspicion in the ‘Big bribery and corruption’ investigation, is repeating the same claim. Most recently, the Fenerbahce club president convicted of match-fixing also demanded a retrial of his case with the same claim. It is also observed that there is a widening consensus in public opinion about the existence of a ‘Fethullahist parallel state.’

“I, probably with the information and perspective provided by being a political scientist who has been writing for 11 years in the Zaman newspaper founded by the ‘Community,’ who knows the ‘Community’ well through its media and schools, and who advocates libertarian and pluralist democracy, think that the ‘Parallel State’ claim has turned into a perfect conspiracy theory (in the sense Karl R. Popper explained) that people involved in various types of crimes use to clear themselves. It is also seen that those who harbor hostility toward the Hizmet Movement, of which the cleric Fethullah Gulen is the inspiration (due to their authoritarian secularist or Islamist ideologies), wholeheartedly adopt and spread this conspiracy theory.

“The main thesis on which the perfect conspiracy theory is built is this: Students who studied (some on scholarship) at the Hizmet Movement’s tutoring centers and schools have gained important positions within the state’s judiciary and security apparatus. On instructions received not from their superiors but from Fethullah Gulen or the leaders of the Hizmet Movement, they trap those they consider enemies of the movement with fabricated evidence and send them to prison.

“This thesis has never seemed logical to me since it was put forward, and therefore not credible. Because: Yes, there are certainly people in the police and judiciary who have affinity with the Hizmet Movement. Turkey is a fairly plural society in terms of political views and religious beliefs, and it is highly likely that people of almost all these views and beliefs exist to one degree or another among police and judicial members. Therefore, it is incompatible with reason and judgment that all police and all judicial staff (including those who gave conviction verdicts in the Balyoz and Ergenekon trials) who played a role at key points of the relevant investigations and trials are ‘F-type.’ Moreover, for the thesis to be acceptable, it must be proven that all the police and judicial members who played a role at key points of the investigations and trials in question are ‘F-type,’ and also that they acted according to instructions received not from their superiors but from Fethullah Gulen and the Hizmet Movement administrators.

“No sane person can argue that there cannot be police and judicial members at the key points of the investigations and trials in question who are primarily loyal to the rule of law, regardless of their political views or religious beliefs. The claim that the investigations and trials in question are conducted by ‘F-type’ people unfortunately also damages the healthy conduct of the judicial process by casting suspicion on police and judicial members.

“It is now well known that pursuant to the decision taken at the NSC in 2004, public servants were profiled according to their religious beliefs and wave after wave of purges were carried out based on this profiling. Now too the Prime Minister is threatening ‘We will go into their dens… we will expose them… we will root them out’; hundreds of police officers are being removed from their duties. As the dismissals resemble a witch hunt, the suspicion in public opinion that the aim is to cover up the ‘Big bribery and corruption’ investigation is gradually strengthening. So much so that even those who have not the slightest sympathy for the Hizmet Movement have begun to say ‘Thank goodness there is a parallel state… They are the only element of checks and balances against authoritarianism and corruption…’

“In my view, if there is a real ‘parallel state’ in Turkey, it is the KCK-PKK with its hierarchy (whose reasons for existence are understandable), chain of command, armed forces, organization that collects taxes, dispenses justice, and tries to put Kurds under tutelage. Isn’t the ultimate aim of the solution, the peace process, to eliminate the reasons for that parallel state’s existence?” (Zaman, 26.12.2013)

The conflict between the AKP government and the Gulen Community or Hizmet Movement, as I mentioned above, started with the closure of the tutoring centers operated by Hizmet and escalated with the December 17-25, 2013 “Corruption and Bribery Operation.” Zaman newspaper editor-in-chief Ekrem Dumanli and Samanyolu broadcast group chairman Hidayet Karaca were detained on December 14, 2014. Karaca was arrested on charges of founding and running a terrorist organization (still in prison); Ekrem Dumanli was released with a travel ban. (It would later be understood that he had sought asylum in the USA.) In my last meeting with him in January 2015, Dumanli would tell me that Erdogan had wanted to make me an AKP parliamentary candidate in 2007; and that in 2013 he had said about me “Why are you still keeping this infidel in the newspaper.”

## Conspiracy theory peaked

The claim that the “parallel state” formed by the Gulen Community or Hizmet Movement was responsible for all negative developments in society was spreading rapidly. Against this claim, which I found not at all convincing, I wrote a series of articles starting with the title “Conspiracy theory peaked.”

“In another article titled ‘Conspiracy theory and what we suffer from history,’ referring to Karl R. Popper, I tried to explain what conspiracy theory is as follows: ‘Conspiracy theories are a product of the secularization of religious beliefs. People first explained social events with God. Then natural laws took the place of God, then the laws of history. The most primitive form of secularization of religious beliefs is also conspiracy theories… Capitalists, imperialists, communists, fascists, masons, Zionists, etc. thus appeared on the scene as creators of social events. Yet the subject of social sciences, which try to understand and explain social events, is to examine the “unintended consequences of the intended actions” of the millions who are the actors of social actions. It’s not that conspiracies don’t happen, but conspiracies can only very rarely succeed.’ (Sabah, 6.12.1993)

“Frankly, it had never crossed my mind that after more than 30 years, I would witness a perfect conspiracy theory capturing not only everyone in Turkey from the most Islamist to the most secularist, but even people you would normally expect to think soundly. According to the ‘Fethullahist conspiracy, plot’ theory we go to bed and wake up with today: The ‘Fethullahists’ fabricated the Balyoz and Ergenekon trials… They had those tried for KCK-PKK membership imprisoned… They wanted to have the undersecretary of MIT (the National Intelligence Organization) arrested… They wiretapped tens of thousands of people’s phones… They exposed politicians with sex tapes… The club president convicted of match-fixing fell into their trap… The ‘Big bribery and corruption’ investigation is a trap against the AKP government, devised by the USA and Israel and implemented by them… They also killed the three PKK female activists murdered in Paris, they also wanted to search the truck bringing aid to Syrian Turkmens… They even committed the Uludere massacre!

“Many adopt this ‘theory’ with their secularist or Islamist prejudices. The aim of those marketing this is certainly to cover up the wrongdoings and crimes committed.” (Zaman, 7.1.2014)

It was supposedly a power struggle…

I answered the questions of readers writing from abroad about what I thought about the fight between the government and the Community as follows:

“… I give no credence to the claim of a ‘power struggle’ between the government and the community. On one side there is a government that is increasingly becoming authoritarian by integrating with the ‘state’; on the other side is a civil society movement that has no claim to power but supports the establishment of democracy… In my view, the ‘Fethullahist parallel state’ claim is a perfect conspiracy theory exploited by both secularists and Islamists, especially by the AKP government which once again confirms the maxim ‘power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely.’

“As in other places, there are certainly people in the judiciary and police who respect Gulen. This is their democratic right. But if there are among them those who violate laws, who commit crimes, they should of course be tried and punished. (Italics added later.) Is the ‘Big bribery and corruption’ investigation a ‘Fethullahist conspiracy’ as Erdogan claims? I don’t think so. I tend to believe that the investigation was initiated by judicial and police members committed to the law.

“I understand the Gulen movement as a faith-based civil society movement that supports the establishment of democracy and thus the securing of religious freedoms that the Kemalist state kept under pressure. The Gulen movement did not feel affinity for Necmettin Erbakan, who had Islamist tendencies; it supported Erdogan as long as he served democratization; but it adopted a critical stance when he turned toward authoritarianism. Erdogan, as he became more authoritarian, set about suppressing the Gulen movement that he could not control.

“Finally, as for the claim that the Gulen movement is a more dangerous Islamist force than the AKP: The proponents of this claim are perhaps not aware that Turkey is already Muslim enough not to need Islamization. Due to their secularist prejudices, they may not be able to see that Gulen’s libertarian interpretation of Islam in the Sufi tradition is the most effective interpretation against Islamism.” (“It was supposedly a power struggle…” Zaman, 16.1.2014)

## You can’t fool everyone all the time

I interpreted Prime Minister Erdogan’s claims that the corruption and bribery investigation against members of the government was “slander” as follows:

“As someone who has visited Hizmet’s schools in many countries for about twenty years and seen their cultural and commercial activities on the ground, I believe that the movement, in interaction with both Turkish society and the world, has now acquired a quality of serving not only our country but all of humanity. I find what some members say about Hizmet noteworthy in terms of showing the point the panic in the government has reached. The Prime Minister is instructing ambassadors: ‘Tell the world that the corruption investigation is slander, an attempted coup! Expose the organization! Ambassadors are responsible!..’ I do not think that either sensible ambassadors or the governments they are addressing will pay attention to this fairy tale. What this government is doing brings to my mind an American saying: ‘You can fool some of the people some of the time, but you can never fool all of the people all of the time.’” (Zaman, 18.1.2014)

The statements of some AKP spokespeople indicated that they too did not believe the claim that the corruption and bribery investigation was a conspiracy set up by the “Fethullahist parallel state” against the government. Upon this I wrote the following:

“The AKP administration is trying to suppress and cover up the biggest bribery and corruption investigation in the history of the Republic with the claim that it is a plot, a coup attempt, designed by the USA and Israel against the government and implemented by the ‘Fethullahist parallel state,’ that is, by judicial and police members who receive instructions from Fethullah Gulen. The effort is being continued on the one hand with the ugliest conceivable insults against Hocaefendi and the Hizmet movement, and on the other hand with the effort to put the judiciary under the command of the Minister of Justice.

“However, it is becoming increasingly clear that the ‘parallel state’ fairy tale is an excuse that everyone from bribers to real coup plotters, almost everyone convicted of various crimes, takes refuge in to be cleared. First it emerged that in a three-page report prepared on April 18, 2013, 8 months before the operation launched within the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office on December 17, MIT, which the Prime Minister trusts greatly, focused on the relationship of the arrested businessman Reza Zarrab with some ministers, and in the conclusion section of the report, warned the Prime Minister personally that ‘if the ministers’ relationship with Zarrab is revealed, this situation could be used against the government.’ (See: Arzu Yildiz, T24, January 5, 2014) (…)

“It appears that even government members themselves have difficulty believing the ‘parallel state’ fairy tale. Indeed, Customs and Trade Minister Hayati Yazici said that he ‘did not find the parallel state claims very realistic… the claims need to be substantiated with evidence and documents.’ I have the impression that Deputy Prime Minister Bulent Arinc is also not convinced by the ‘parallel state’ claim. Speaking to a local television station in Bursa, Arinc first said: ‘We have nothing to say about the respected person said to be at the head of the community. We cannot even flick a finger at one of the people who have embraced the whole world…’

“If we are to believe these words, we must first judge that Arinc does not adopt the Prime Minister’s words about Hocaefendi: ‘False prophet, fake saint, hollow travesty of a scholar…’ Arinc then implies that not the community but some of its members are trying to stage a coup against the government and addresses whoever they are: ‘They should say we have no problem with this government. They haven’t said so until now. We have no intention of overthrowing the government, wearing it down, or bringing someone else in its place. If you say we are cutting ties with those among us who do wrong, this problem will end in a day…’ (Zaman, January 26, 2014)

“I don’t understand. According to the Prime Minister, aren’t these people ‘parallel state, crazed Hashashins, organization, gang…’? Didn’t the Prime Minister say ‘we will go into their dens, we will root them out, we will extinguish their hearths’? If there is such a ‘parallel state,’ isn’t it imperative that they be caught and tried? How can the ‘problem end in a day’ if they say ‘we have no problem with the government’? But I understand Mr. Arinc, in reality you too don’t believe this hogwash. Yet I thought you had ‘specific weight’; that you were your party’s ‘conscience.’ I was wrong.” (Zaman, 30.1.2014)

## Yes, crime and punishment are personal

I wrote about the claim that the December 17-25 “corruption and bribery” investigation was a coup attempt by the Community against the AKP government as follows:

“Prime Minister Erdogan, in Germany, in response to the question ‘Can the corruption investigation shake confidence in the economy?’ said that there could be corruption by individuals, but the claim that the administration committed corruption was not true. The Prime Minister is right. In countries where the rule of law based on human rights applies, both crime and punishment are personal; that is, people can neither be collectively accused nor collectively punished.

“Furthermore, a person is presumed innocent until found guilty at the end of a trial. It is not the AKP government that is alleged to have committed corruption, but the members of this government against whom summaries of proceedings have been prepared. They are considered innocent until their crimes are established by a court. However, at the Prime Minister’s request, they have resigned from their positions to make it possible for them to be tried fairly. Their immunity needs to be lifted.

“Yes, the Prime Minister is right. But it is quite clear that he does not believe even a bit of what he says. In the angry speeches he gives almost every day, he does not refrain from collectively accusing Fethullah Gulen Hocaefendi and the Hizmet Movement that he inspires, the ‘community,’ of being a ‘parallel state, gang, organization, crazed Hashashins…’ preparing a ‘coup’ against the AKP government with the bribery and corruption investigation.

“These collective accusations are unjust and unlawful. Among judicial and police members, there may be and certainly are those who feel affinity with the Hizmet Movement, the ‘community.’ Feeling affinity with the Hizmet Movement is not a crime and cannot be. However, if among these people there are those who act on instructions received not from their superiors but from the Hizmet Movement, as claimed, they should of course be brought before the judiciary with evidence and documents; they should be removed from duty for a fair trial; and if the judiciary decides they are guilty, they should be sentenced to the punishments prescribed by law. (Italics added later.)

“There is not the slightest hesitation about all this, but the Prime Minister and his close circle’s collective accusation of the Hizmet Movement, launching a witch hunt based on this accusation, displacing 5,000 police officers and hundreds of prosecutors is compatible neither with democratic morality nor with the concept of rule of law. In this context, on the one hand some circles (rightfully) demanding that ministers subject to corruption allegations be held accountable, and on the other hand the Prime Minister and his close circle constantly making the ‘parallel state’ accusation against the Hizmet Movement, virtually screaming ‘Death to the Community!’ is compatible neither with democratic morality, nor with secularism, nor with the concept of rule of law.” (Zaman, 8.2.2014)

## The essence of the matter is the struggle for freedom

In my article that came out two days after the article I quoted above, I also analyzed what had happened since the AKP came to power in 2002:

“The fact is that the Justice and Development Party (AKP), which came to power in 2002, took important steps toward adopting the Copenhagen criteria through constitutional and legal amendments, drawing on the support of Turkey’s European Union accession process that began when it was accepted as a candidate for membership in 1999. These steps were reciprocated by the EU with the launch of accession negotiations. (One should doubt the intelligence of those who characterize intellectuals who supported the AKP government’s reforms in this direction as ‘useful idiots.’)

“Supporters of military tutelage made direct military coup attempts to sabotage the reforms they found contrary to their authoritarian Kemalist principles and threatening to their privileges; they tried to have the AKP shut down through a judicial coup. The AKP government neutralized these threats with the support of the great majority who were in favor of establishing democracy, including soldiers who believed that the political role it played was damaging to the prestige and professional responsibilities of the Turkish Armed Forces. On one hand, the improvement in the average citizen’s standard of living through economic growth, on the other hand, the de facto if not legal end of military tutelage, won the AKP approximately half the votes in the 2011 elections. The significance of the 2011 elections for democracy in Turkey was that it indicated that one of the two fundamental principles of libertarian and pluralist democracy, as expressed in EU criteria, namely the principle of governance by elected governments, was being established.

“However, the elected government quickly entered into a trend of arbitrariness and authoritarianism, the signs of which began to appear just before the 2011 elections. The top-down arbitrary and authoritarian governance based on the justification of defending ‘Ataturk’s principles and revolutions’ was replaced by a form based on the ‘national will.’ Prime Minister Erdogan said, with the claim that he would ‘make Turkey one of the world’s 10 largest economies’ by 2023, ‘I want a Turkish-style presidential system where the legislature and executive don’t get in my way.’ He began to emulate Putin. (My article titled ‘Does Erdogan Want to Be Putin?’ was published in Zaman three years ago on February 8, 2011.)

“TRT became the government’s mouthpiece. Part of the private media came under the Prime Minister’s command through owners dependent on government contracts. Critical writers began to be fired from their jobs. The Prime Minister monopolized all decisions from what would or wouldn’t be written in media loyal to him to who would get which public contract. Court of Accounts audits were restricted. Finance inspectors began to be sent after businessmen who angered the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister increasingly adopted an attitude of seeing himself as a shepherd, the people as a flock, identifying himself with the state. Every day he would interfere in citizens’ lifestyles, including how many children they should have, scolding and threatening opponents.

“In the summer of 2013, mass demonstrations that began in Istanbul’s Taksim Gezi Park and spread across the country gave the first signs of rising opposition against the increasingly arbitrary and authoritarian AKP administration. The attempt to close prep schools was a sign of the AKP government’s search to suppress civil society as well. The major bribery and corruption investigation that began on December 17, 2013, containing allegations about at least 5 ministers, businessmen and bureaucrats close to the government, and the Prime Minister’s family members, revealed that the AKP government was not only becoming authoritarian but was also the government facing the most serious corruption charges in the history of the Republic.

“Since December 17, we have been witnessing the administrative and legal measures taken by the AKP government to cover up the corruption investigation, using the ‘parallel state’ lie as a pretext: These measures ranged from the transfer of hundreds of prosecutors, judges, and police officers from their posts to the Judicial Police Regulation, from changes to the HSYK Law to changes in internet legislation. These steps came to threaten not only to wipe out Turkey’s gains in the area of freedoms and rights over the past decade, but also democracy itself in the sense of governance by elected governments.

“The essence of the matter is this: Just as Turkey was beginning to believe that it had left behind the military-bureaucratic tutelage regime and established democracy in the sense of governance by elected governments, it is faced with the elected government moving to stifle freedoms. (Italics added later.) Now a struggle for freedom and rule of law is being waged against an increasingly arbitrary and authoritarian prime minister and a clique around him who have tied their political careers to him. Turkey cannot solve any fundamental problem, neither secularism nor the Kurdish issue, without establishing libertarian and pluralist democracy through this struggle. It is time for responsible members of the AKP to see this reality too, because the course is not good for the party any more than it is for the country.” (Zaman, 11.2.2014)

## Disappointments: Gul and Arinc

I believed that Abdullah Gul and Bulent Arinc did not approve of the path Erdogan was taking. In time, this would also become apparent. However, I was also hoping that they would oppose Erdogan. I expressed my disappointment on this matter as follows:

“In the late 1990s, I found an opportunity to have a private conversation with each of Tayyip Erdogan, Abdullah Gul, and Bulent Arinc, who would later form the top leadership of the AKP, only once. (In my effort to stay away from political, economic, administrative, and other power holders, the role of my personality that does not enjoy unequal relationships was greater than the journalism principle of not getting too close to news sources.) … I opposed Gul’s ascent to Cankaya on the grounds that it would be a waste of talent, but I respectfully accepted it when the Grand National Assembly deemed it appropriate. I generally appreciated Gul’s performance at Cankaya. Arinc, whom I believed played an important role in overcoming the mentality widespread in the Welfare Party that saw democracy as a ‘Greek deception,’ became a politician who succeeded in presenting himself to society as the voice of common sense and conscience in the AKP, despite his occasionally unbecoming statements.

“It appears that the arbitrary and authoritarian leadership that the Prime Minister has been pursuing since the last general elections has disturbed both of them. They expressed in various ways that they did not adopt Erdogan’s harsh response to the Gezi Park demonstrations. Gul stated several times that democracy is not just about elections. It was heard that Arinc came to the brink of resignation in the face of Erdogan’s bluster. He openly asked Erdogan to respect his ‘specific gravity.’ The attitudes of both toward the December 17 bribery and corruption investigation were also different from Erdogan’s. It is obvious that they did not approve of the ‘parallel state, gang, organization, crazed Hashashin’ rhetoric that Erdogan used to cover up the investigation. Nor the hate speech directed at Fethullah Gulen Hocaefendi in the form of ‘false prophet, fake saint, sham scholar’…

“Neither of them can fail to see that the Prime Minister is declaring almost everyone who does not think like him a traitor; polarizing society in a very dangerous way; destroying the rule of law to cover up corruption; in short, following a line incompatible with reason, prudence, and logic. It is plainly obvious that where the Prime Minister is leading will cause great harm to the country. The majority of society believes that these two leading politicians’ loyalty to the country’s interests is much stronger than what they feel for the Prime Minister; they expect them to put a stop to this course that will cause great harm to both the country and the party. President Gul should veto the laws that trample on freedoms and the rule of law that come before him. Otherwise, his respectability will be damaged.” (“What is expected from Abdullah Gul and Bulent Arinc,” Zaman, 13.2.2014)

When it became clear that neither Gul nor Arinc would do what was expected of them, I would write: “Unfortunately, Gul chose the path of being satisfied with partially correcting the laws leading the country to a police state, acting not as a president but as the former prime minister of the AKP. By acting this way, sadly, he continues to be worn down. As for Arinc, who is preparing to retire, it is obvious that he does not see in himself the ‘specific gravity’ to stop the disastrous course. Are there no AKP deputies with reason, prudence, and morality who are worried about the future of both the country and their party? Perhaps there are. Ultimately, the matter is left to the people. Fortunately, there are three elections ahead of us.” (Zaman, 27.2.2014)

Unfortunately, the number of AKP deputies who were worried about the country’s future did not exceed the fingers of one hand. Unfortunately, when the matter was left to the people, the AKP would win the elections.

The ultimate goal of the Hizmet Movement

In forming my conviction that the Gulen Community supported libertarian and pluralist democracy and the economy in Turkey, in addition to people I knew at the Zaman newspaper and what I saw in schools it opened domestically and abroad, the comments of some observers whose views I valued also played a role. One of the publications that supported this conviction was the articles in the book Toward an Islamic Enlightenment: The Gulen Movement (Oxford University Press, 2012) by Hakan Yavuz, a professor of political science at the University of Utah in the USA. I had written the following about the book:

“It certainly cannot be said that this study has the last word on both Gulen’s views and the examination of the Hizmet Movement’s evolution over time, that it is satisfying in every respect, and it has aspects open to criticism. It can be said that the author having made critical statements about the Gulen movement from time to time makes his study even more noteworthy. (…)

“I can summarize the most noteworthy argument, which also gives the book its title, as follows: There is no single interpretation of Islam. Like all other religions, the history of Islam is a history of different interpretations. The processes of modernization and globalization have essentially led to two different interpretations. Fundamentalists who reject modernization advocate a pure Islam based on the Quran and what the Prophet Muhammad said and did. Those who advocate Islam’s compatibility with modernity (democracy, human rights, secularism as freedom of belief, respect for different identities, economic development, and science) have rescued Islam from its rigid and bigoted interpretations and reinterpreted it to meet the spiritual and material needs of Muslims. Enlightenment, in essence, is not the rejection of religion (as claimed by the prevalent shallow understanding in Turkey), but the use of critical reason and science in understanding society and the universe. In Turkey, Said Nursi and Fethullah Gulen are Islamic thinkers who apply reason and science to the interpretation of religion for social and cultural reforms aimed at building a more humane society.

“A question that is emphasized both in Turkey and in the outside world is what the ‘ultimate goal’ of Gulen and his movement is. Yavuz’s answers are as follows: ‘As this research reveals, the goal of the Gulen movement is neither to establish hegemony over society nor to seize control of the Turkish state. The goal is to reshape society and politics by strengthening the sense of morality and virtue among believers, in society, in the state, and in humanity… The movement’s main political goal is to transform society by raising individuals’ moral consciousness. By raising moral consciousness, the movement aims to cleanse the bureaucracy of widespread corruption, increase the effectiveness and transparency of state institutions, revive public work ethics to strengthen the state’s legitimacy, and create areas of opportunity for the marginalized segments of the Anatolian people.’ (Italics added later.)” (Zaman, 22.2.2014)

After so many years and so much that has happened since then, I can say today that I have deep doubts about the judgment that “The movement’s main political goal is to transform society by raising individuals’ moral consciousness…”

How will this filth be cleaned up?

I thought that the “theory” that almost everyone who does wrong or commits a crime clings to, that unites secularists and Islamists, that all evils originate from the “parallel state, parallel structure, Fethullahist gang” was heading toward bankruptcy. However, in time the exact opposite would prove true, that is, the “theory” would unite secularists and Islamists. But I was writing that the steps of the “theory’s” bankruptcy were listed in the eleven questions that the leader of the main opposition party CHP, Kemal Kilicdaroglu, asked Tayyip Erdogan:

“Did the parallel state give the 700,000 lira watch to a minister? Did the parallel state put the 4.5 million dollars in the shoe box? Did the parallel state place seven safes, at least as tall as you, in the ministers’ children’s bedrooms? Did the parallel state place the millions of dollars, Euros, Turkish Liras in those safes? Did the parallel state place the money counting machines in the bedrooms? Did the parallel state take you as a family on Sarraf’s private plane to umrah? Four ministers resigned when their names were tainted by corruption. Did the parallel state make those four ministers resign?..

“You created a 630 million dollar pool, starting from 100 million dollars each, to create a partisan media for yourself. Did the parallel state create this pool? Your son Bilal Erdogan founded a foundation called TURGEV. Those who received contracts from the state paid bribes to that foundation. Did the parallel state have your son establish that foundation? When four ministers were resigning, did the parallel state ask you to have a declaration signed in your favor? You sold a governor for two villas. Did the parallel state advise you to sell a governor for two villas? And Kilicdaroglu asked the 12th and final question at the last CHP group meeting, in essence: On the morning of December 17, did the parallel state tell you to have your son Bilal immediately distribute the money in his house? (…)

“The main opposition leader says of the audio recording, ‘As real as Mount Ararat, as Mount Erciyes…’ Anyway, it is plainly obvious that the claim that the recording was ‘doctored’ has no meaning other than an effort to cover up the scandal. The real question that needs to be asked is this: How will this unbelievable corruption, this filth be cleaned up? The truth is, of course, as Kilicdaroglu said, that Erdogan should either resign or leave the country. I don’t consider these impossible. However, unfortunately the greater probability is that Erdogan, with an attitude incompatible with reason, prudence, and morality, will try to hold on tightly to power, not hesitating to drag the country into great turmoil for this purpose.” (Zaman, 27.2.2014)

In the time that has passed until the day these lines were written, the following was seen: Kilicdaroglu not only failed to get answers to the above questions but also gave up asking them. Erdogan not only did not resign or leave the country but also succeeded in gathering all power in his own hands. But I was not wrong on one point: This success of his was leading the country toward a major economic and political crisis.

This nation is not ‘blockheaded’

In those days, I was asking myself this question: “Can Erdogan and his clique stay in power, can they turn Turkey into a police state?” I was answering as follows:

“My answer is clear and open. No, never! Erdogan and his clique are covering up the biggest corruption investigation in history step by step, erasing its traces, making up lie after lie every day, and thus may think they will eventually escape being tried. But they have long been convicted in the conscience of the nation. A growing majority of the nation, (in Erdogan’s definition, the ‘national will’) is no longer behind this clique.

“The opposition parties, whose votes are steadily rising, have rendered their verdict on Erdogan and his clique. After the filth that has emerged, they are demanding that he resign and be tried. The CHP leader said, ‘A thief cannot be prime minister…’ The MHP chairman said, ‘The Prime Minister must account for his shamelessness in denying the theft…’ The BDP leader said, ‘Walking with this government has become impossible…’ It is becoming increasingly clear that this clique is also an obstacle to the resolution process. Increasingly broader segments of civil society want Erdogan and his clique to resign and be tried. The US administration is exposing the corruption scandal in Turkey and the human rights violations committed to cover it up. The EU has never come so close to suspending membership negotiations. Erdogan and his clique, unfortunately, are destroying our reputation in the eyes of the world.

“I’m sure the majority of the AKP group in Parliament, who don’t see their political fate tied to the clique, are anxiously thinking about how their party will survive this ordeal. A growing segment of our citizens who voted for the AKP is distancing themselves from Erdogan and his clique. An increasing portion of believing citizens are saying, ‘Islam is incompatible with corruption and lying…’

“A visible village needs no guide: Whatever he does, the end of Erdogan and his clique’s power is in sight. The people of Turkey, this nation is not ‘blockheaded’! The people of Turkey no longer want to be ruled by the military stick or the police stick; they are standing up for their rights and law. This people did not bring the AKP to power because they were ‘blockheaded’; because they are not ‘blockheaded,’ they will know how to end the power of Erdogan and his clique, and will not allow them to ‘screw the nation over.’” (Zaman, 01.03.2014)

After so much time has passed, perhaps I can say that this has been understood: A large segment of the people in Turkey may not have a demand for the establishment of freedom and democracy; they can only change their preferences when livelihood concerns come knocking at the door.

“Why should I criticize the Community”

In early 2014, I had begun to face questions about why I was not criticizing the Community. My answer to these questions summarized what I thought about the Community at that time:

“Some of my readers ask: ‘Why don’t you criticize the Community?!..’ Some are also surprised: ‘Why aren’t you neutral in the dispute between the government and the Community?!’ It is possible to find the answer to these questions in my writings over the past approximately 20 years. But, apparently, it is useful to give a collective answer to these questions in these days when Erdogan and his clique are showering Fethullah Gulen and the Hizmet Movement he inspires with baseless accusations, insults, and threats. Actually, my answer is essentially another question: Why should I criticize the Community?

“I call Gulen ‘Hocaefendi’ because he is a cleric I respect. Yes, I am not a religious person at all. But I am not at all someone (like Marxists and Kemalists) who wants religion to be excluded from the public sphere; who sees religious beliefs as an obstacle to modernization in the contemporary, liberal sense. Religious beliefs are as indispensable a need for people as bread and water. Religions have both bigoted, fundamentalist interpretations that reject modernization in the liberal sense, and interpretations that support and embrace it. In my view, Gulen is a religious scholar of worldwide value with his interpretation that reconciles liberal modernity with Islamic faith.

“I refer to the ‘Community’ as the Hizmet Movement, because I believe that characterizing it as a faith-based civil society movement is more accurate. I am not one of those who, like secularists (that is, authoritarian Kemalists or Marxists), adopt the claim that there cannot be a religion-based civil society movement. My view of religion is based on liberal principles that prioritize freedom of expression. There can certainly be a civil society movement based on religious belief that is independent of the state and advocates freedoms, and there are many examples of this in the world. The strongest example in Turkey is undoubtedly the Hizmet Movement. I see the Hizmet Movement as one of the most influential civil society forces providing unique support to Turkey’s development, solidarity, democratization, and integration with the world. Why should I criticize the Community?

“I give no credence whatsoever to the ‘Fethullahist state, structure, gang’ claims that almost everyone who commits crimes, most recently those caught in the largest bribery and corruption investigation in the history of the Republic, takes refuge in and uses to clear themselves. I see these claims as a full-blown conspiracy theory diametrically opposed to reason, logic, prudence, and scientific thought. Gulen is a human being, therefore of course he is not infallible. The Hizmet Movement, consisting of institutions spread around the world in the fields of education, media, commerce, industry, and social solidarity, perhaps encompasses hundreds of thousands. Of course, wrongdoers and lawbreakers can emerge from within this movement. But it is unacceptable to portray Gulen and the Hizmet Movement as ‘the gang at the source of all evil.’

“Let’s not get into the others. I was not convinced in the slightest that the Sledgehammer, Ergenekon, and KCK cases, based on allegations of coup attempts and attempts to establish a real ‘parallel state,’ were ‘conspiracies produced to throw innocent people in prison.’ But I always wrote and said that unjust, unnecessary detentions were made in these cases, that detention was turned into punishment, that defense rights were violated, and that these wrongs needed to be corrected. I also argued that the release of those convicted in these cases through a general amnesty was a social necessity. (Italics added later.) I have always defended all fundamental rights and freedoms of citizens, including the right to a fair trial, and the democratic group rights of Kurds (including secession by referendum). I have always opposed the provisions of the Anti-Terror Law that are incompatible with freedom of expression. But I am equally opposed to the armed impositions of both military tutelage supporters and the PKK. It is certain that, due to my profession and expertise, I focused on the political rather than legal aspects of the above-mentioned cases.

“It is inconceivable that among police and judiciary members in Turkey there are not those who feel intellectual affinity with various parties, political and ethnic groups, sects, religious orders and communities, including the Hizmet Movement which provides great support for young people from poor families in Anatolia to study and acquire professions. If this is a more or less democracy rather than a Kemalist or Islamist dictatorship, it is the right of all these people to serve within the state bureaucracy; to act according to their knowledge, beliefs, and consciences. If among these there are those who violate laws, who receive orders from outside rather than from their superiors, who do not comply with the requirements of the rule of law, they should of course be caught, brought before the judiciary, and punished. Within the Hizmet Movement, which encompasses hundreds of thousands, there may be lawbreakers as well as agents, informers, and turncoat witnesses (who, in line with Kemalist practices, kept files on and monitored religious citizens). (Italics added later.)

“Both Gulen and the Journalists and Writers Foundation, which is the spokesperson for the Hizmet Movement, have repeatedly called for them to be caught and tried. If this is a state of law (if Soviet law does not apply here), it is probably not the movement’s responsibility to prove that it is not ‘a gang that sets traps for innocent people and throws them in prison.’ It is also out of the question for me to criticize them by saying ‘Why don’t you prove to society that you did not set up a conspiracy…’

“It is said, ‘The Community has transformed from a religious community into a political organization… Let them establish a party…’ Truly, there cannot be a claim so contrary to the democratic order. In democracies, politics is never just the business of politicians and political parties. Politics is also the business of workers’ and employers’ organizations, associations, foundations, all civil society organizations, of course the media, and individual citizens.

“It may be said, ‘Why don’t you criticize this or that particular view of the Community?’ What we are talking about is a very broad civil society movement. There are people with very different views and preferences within it. Very different ideas are also put forward in media close to the Community. In my commentaries, I defend libertarian and pluralist democracy and mainly criticize the statements and behaviors of politicians that contradict this ideal. When we speak of the Community’s view, probably only the statements made by Gulen himself and the Journalists and Writers Foundation can be taken as a basis. If I have not encountered in these statements a matter that contradicts the libertarian and pluralist democracy I defend and that must be addressed and criticized, why should I criticize?

“It is said that it is not ‘transparent’… I don’t know how much more transparent and visible a social movement that spearheads the establishment of schools, universities, media organizations, foundations, associations, and companies can be in Turkey’s current conditions. Let’s say you want movement members to carry membership cards, to hang signs saying ‘This is a Hizmet Movement organization’ on their institutions. Then first, (as I and all freedom advocates do), advocate secularism in the true sense, that is, where the state maintains equal distance from all beliefs. Then fight for the establishment of a regime where freedom of religion and conscience is fully established and respected, where belief groups including non-believers can have legal personality, where they are not discriminated against in any way, where they are not kept under threat and pressure. How far we are from a true secular order is evident, isn’t it, from the uninterrupted profiling carried out for years on the orders of the National Security Council; from ‘plans to finish off the Community’ that envisage ‘secretly planting weapons and drugs in Community dormitories and trying their members on terrorist organization charges’?

“In short: The unjust, baseless accusations directed at the Community by radical secularists and Islamists; the heavy insults and threats showered upon it, deeply wound my sense of fairness. How can I be expected to remain neutral in the dispute between a government whose legitimacy has become questionable as the subject of the largest bribery and corruption investigation in the history of the Republic and the ‘Community’? In Turkey’s suffocating media environment, under pressure first from the military and bosses, then from the government and bosses, struggling with censorship and self-censorship, the media supported by the ‘Community’ gives a say to me and writers like me who defend libertarian and pluralist democracy (without touching a hair). Why should I criticize the Community?” (Zaman, 4.3.2014)

“Even the AKP cannot tolerate this Erdogan”

One of my subsequent articles also carried the errors I fell into in my observations and comments on Turkish politics to their peak. I wrote:

“Where did we start, where have we come? The AKP, headed by Tayyip Erdogan, came to power with the promise of saving Turkey from corruption and prohibitions. An increasing portion of our people supported this promise. In its first two terms, the AKP rendered great services to the country. However, at the point we have reached 12 years later, (thinking of those with sense, honesty, and conscience within it, I cannot bring myself to say AKP government), Erdogan and the clique consisting of certain ministers, bureaucrats, and businessmen gathered around him have shown what the pinnacle of corruption and the epitome of prohibitionism are.

“Some of my friends think that our situation at the point we have reached resembles the Sisyphus legend in ancient Greek mythology. Sisyphus is the king who was eternally condemned by the gods for his crimes of deceit to push a huge rock up to the top of the mountain, only to push it up again when it immediately rolls back down. According to some of my friends, like Sisyphus, we will never succeed in placing the rock at the top, that is, in establishing libertarian and pluralist democracy.

“I don’t think like them. As a member of a generation that in its youth (that is, in the 1960s and 70s) believed that democracy was identical to the dictatorship of the proletariat, I look differently at where we started and where we have come. In my view, we are learning by living and experiencing what libertarian and pluralist democracy is and is not, and progressing step by step toward establishing it. We need to be patient, thinking that what Western countries achieved through centuries of struggle cannot be expected to fit into our 60-70 years.

“Let’s take a look at the adventure of our democratization process that began with the transition to a multi-party system. We spent the second half of the 20th century with a kind of democracy under military tutelage. Soldiers, whose brains were washed in their schools in line with the Republic’s founding philosophy that they were the owners of the homeland and the nation, disrupted the functioning of the democratic process by staging coups four times and attempting coups. In the end, it was seen that military interventions created bigger problems than they solved; we made considerable progress toward establishing the principle of governance by elected, representative governments, one of the two fundamental principles of democracy. It was seen that military tutelage had ended de facto, if not in the constitution and laws. Among soldiers, the awareness spread that the political role they played was shaking the prestige of the Turkish Armed Forces and preventing them from fulfilling their professional duties.

“Then, we witnessed the elected government, which played a major role in ending military tutelage, emboldened by receiving nearly 50 percent of the vote in the last elections, escalate an authoritarianism and corruption that reduces democracy to elections. For the past three years, we have been learning by experience that democracy does not permit the shelving of the rule of law, the trampling of rights and freedoms underfoot. No matter what percentage of votes Erdogan and his clique receive in these elections, their end is in sight. Even the AKP cannot tolerate this Erdogan.” (Zaman, 22.3.2014)

“There is no room for pessimism”

With an understanding bordering on naivety in my effort to understand the ongoing process, I could even claim that there was no room for pessimism:

“According to documents published by the Radikal newspaper, the head of the Anti-Terror Department of the General Directorate of Security requested in a ‘secret’ letter sent to the security directorates of 30 provinces that it be determined ‘whether the Fethullah Gulen community has an armed force’… He was not satisfied with this; he also requested that the community’s ‘connection’ with the Aziz Santoro, Hrant Dink, Council of State, Zirve Publishing House, Necip Hablemitoglu, and Uzeyir Garih murders be investigated… (July 6)

“The Taraf newspaper, with its headline ‘Witch hunt dropped below age 18,’ reported that the same ‘secret’ letter gave instructions to ‘keep files on millions of students who attended Community prep schools and schools and stayed in their dormitories’ over the past ten years. (July 7) It announced that the ‘Cosmic Working Group’ formed within the General Directorate of Security kept files on 100,000 businesses large and small in 81 provinces, saying they ‘may be related to the Community,’ down to their customer profiles. (July 9)

“When I read these news reports that documented with evidence that the government, on Prime Minister Erdogan’s orders, had embarked on an effort to portray the Hizmet Movement as an armed organization, a terrorist organization trying to overthrow the government, and had launched an unprecedented witch hunt for this purpose; then that Erdogan had said at the previous day’s AKP group meeting that he would ‘hold accountable those who remain silent and unresponsive’ against the Hizmet Movement, I thought we were facing a surreal scene in Turkish politics that was impossible to explain with reason and logic, hard to believe was real. Taraf was absolutely right in its headline diagnosis of ‘The government has gone mad.’ (…)

“There is no room for pessimism. Turkey is not a society primitive enough to tolerate such an abnormality, such an absurdity for long, to put up with the injustices and evils being done. Sooner or later, but without fail, an accounting will be demanded for these lawless acts.” (“The government has really gone mad,” Zaman, 10.7.2014)

## Toward a mukhabarat state

Yes, my prediction that Turkish society, including AKP members, would not tolerate Erdogan’s rule was unrealistic to the point of naivety. However, I was not very wrong in my observations about where the ongoing process was taking us:

“It is now clearly seen that the goal of the initiative launched by Prime Minister Erdogan with the claim that the major bribery and corruption investigation was a ‘coup attempt orchestrated by the USA and Israel and implemented by the Pennsylvania organization – parallel state’ was not limited to suppressing the investigation, but that the aim was to take the entire state and society under his control with this pretext. The handcuffed detentions of security personnel who conducted the bribery and corruption investigation on the morning of July 22 were the new step in the implementation of the mukhabarat state. The architect of the mukhabarat state had said, ‘We are developing a project. When it is finished, the process will accelerate. We will open thousands of cases…’ On July 22, in response to a question ‘Could the operation spread to other areas?’, he did not hesitate to express that he was personally running the ‘process’ by saying, ‘Of course, of course…’

“The concept of ‘mukhabarat state,’ which we will apparently use frequently in the coming period, can be defined as follows: The type of regime in which the state’s intelligence organization (including the armed forces) penetrates and controls all social institutions; is not accountable to anyone; holds very broad police powers; and becomes impossible to separate from the government. The concept entered our language because of the Assad dictatorship in Syria, but various examples of the regime in question, with its varying types, can be counted from the totalitarian Soviet Union to the authoritarian Russian Federation. Starting from the definition and examples, it can be said that the end of the road has not yet been reached in the construction of the mukhabarat state in Turkey.

“The Prime Minister, who is a presidential candidate, is justifying the move toward a mukhabarat state with national security threatened by Western allies. Most recently, in his speech at the iftar of Alevi associations in Ankara, he said, ‘Many countries in the Western world are doing everything to set us against each other…’

“Where did we start, where have we come? At least until the 2010 constitutional referendum, we believed that Turkey under AKP rule was progressing toward establishing democracy with reforms made in the EU accession process. Now, under the same government, we are witnessing progress toward a mukhabarat state with the ‘internal and external enemies’ rhetoric frequently used during the military tutelage period, declaring Western allies as enemies.

“Can we stop this course? Absolutely yes! Yes, we gained rich experience in the struggle against army-based authoritarianism, but our accumulated experience against authoritarianism that comes through elections is weak. In the coming period, as democrats who believe in freedom, we must develop this ability. The first step is to do everything we can to prevent Tayyip Erdogan from being elected president.” (Zaman, 24.7.2014)

No to Erdogan!

As Turkey was heading toward the presidential election on August 10, 2014, I was saying “No to Erdogan!” with all my might. As follows:

“With the operation launched on July 22, 115 security officers were detained, 31 of whom were arrested. On August 5, with the operation spreading to 14 provinces, 33 more security officers were detained. There is not the slightest doubt that these operations are links in the AKP government’s, primarily Prime Minister Erdogan’s, effort to take revenge on judicial and security personnel who served in the December 17-25 investigation, the largest bribery and corruption investigation in the history of the Republic.

“CHP leader Kilicdaroglu said, ‘This is a revenge operation against the police who exposed the bribery and corruption…’ MHP leader Devlet Bahceli said of the operation, ‘It is nothing but the thieves’ action to cover up the theft…’ HDP leader and presidential candidate Selahattin Demirtas said the operation was conducted ‘with a feeling of vengeance and revenge,’ and that ‘the order was given by the Prime Minister.’ The fact that the main opposition leaders are in full agreement on this matter gives sufficient idea of what the truth is.

“It is very clear that the law was trampled underfoot in the revenge operation. (See ‘9 articles of the European Convention on Human Rights were violated 11 times.’ Zaman, August 4, 2014.) The facts that emerged due to the operation showed that the prosecuted security officers, contrary to the claim that they constituted a ‘Fethullahist parallel state,’ had very different identities; that they acted on orders given by their superiors. (…)

“What Tayyip Erdogan said on the NTV - Star TV broadcast on the evening of August 5 gave a very noteworthy clue as to what kind of person we were about to elect as president. Erdogan, while explaining his words at a rally, ‘Kilicdaroglu, you are Alevi, I am Sunni. Say this. Demirtas, you are Zaza. Don’t be afraid to say this…’, uttered these shameful words implying a dark racist mentality: ‘What’s wrong with that? Either appear as you are or be as you appear. The things they said about me. One came out, the same mentality, and said he’s ’Georgian.’ Another came out and, excuse me, said with much uglier things that he’s Armenian…’

“What Devlet Bahceli said in his speech in Izmir on July 30 contained perhaps the most striking depiction of under what conditions the presidential election was being held: ‘Can a man who was caught while emptying the Treasury, while embezzling the state’s coffers, become president? Can someone who paves the way for bribe-takers, who shelters thieves, who stocks robbery money in villas become president? Can someone who releases the immoral people who hid millions of dollars in shoe boxes and bedrooms become president? Someone who calls a money launderer and gold smuggler charlatan a philanthropist, calls a box banker naive, calls pool businessmen the pride of Turkey, and brands those who pursue theft as traitors – he can be anything but one thing he will not be is president…’

“I fear he can be, and in that case very great troubles await Turkey. If you don’t want this, act with civic consciousness, go to the ballot box, and say ‘No to Erdogan!’” (Zaman, 7.8.2014)

The above lines also remind us how MHP Chairman Devlet Bahceli could transform from a harsh opponent of Erdogan to an uncompromising ally.

“Supreme leader Erdogan”

As expected, Erdogan won the presidential election held on August 10, 2014. But I persisted in my errors, not giving up the idea that not just Turkey, but even the AKP would not be able to tolerate Erdogan for long. I wrote:

“(…) I absolutely do not share the pessimistic views that the establishment of a kind of ‘one party, one man’ regime, an autocracy, could be possible in Turkey. As I have always written and said, the gains provided by the services the AKP itself rendered to the country in its first two terms of power, the spread of awareness of freedom and respect for difference, the globalization of the economy, the increasing integration with the democratic world do not allow for the revival of the ‘old old Turkey.’ Yes, even the AKP cannot tolerate this course for long.

“Are the signs of this not already visible? Are not some of its founders crying out that the path being followed will drag the country into troubles? Is the conflict within the party between the ‘newcomers’ and the ‘elders-veterans’ not an expression of this? Are not all the tricks to prevent Abdullah Gul from returning to politics, the smear campaign against him, signs of this? Is there not an expectation of ‘when will the uprising of the Guls come’?

“A question I wonder about is this: How is it that Tayyip Erdogan, who is certainly quite an intelligent person, cannot see the following? What made Erdogan successful were the liberating, democratizing reforms he pursued in his first two terms of power, the style that embraced the whole of society and aimed at adopting universal values. Mustafa Kemal Pasha also succeeded in liberating Turkey from occupation and subjugation and rebuilding it with his style and practices that embraced the whole society, respected all identities, and were liberating and democratizing. ‘Supreme leader Ataturk,’ who is identified with one-party, one-man rule, however, laid the foundations of the deep-rooted problems we still cannot leave behind today, namely authoritarianism, commandism, worship of power, militarism, intolerance of civil society, disrespect for difference, identities, and beliefs. ‘Supreme leader Erdogan’ can only cook up new troubles for us.” (Zaman, 30.8.2014)

## Time to stand against authoritarianism

I was calling on society to resist the increasingly darkening one-man rule, authoritarianism:

“We are living in an international conjuncture where storms are blowing in our region, in both our northern and southern neighbors. We are in a period when there is the greatest need to protect domestic peace and stability by strengthening democracy, rule of law, human rights, and respect for minorities. Yet a narrow clique that has entrenched itself at the head of the ruling Justice and Development Party is leading the country toward a corrupt, arbitrary, and authoritarian one-man rule.

“The country’s fault lines are cracking. Mistakes that provoke Turkish-Kurdish, Sunni-Alevi, and all other social divisions are being persisted in, and even Sunnis and Kurds are being set against each other. Attempts are being made to suppress criticism. Attempts are being made to silence the opposition, which is indispensable to the democratic regime, with accusations of ‘Traitors, scoundrels, ingrates…’ and openly with the words ‘Shut up, we don’t need your ideas…’ What we are experiencing presents an almost surreal scene that evokes a feeling incompatible with Turkey’s level of development… We cannot allow the country to be taken back to the old days, to the painful days of the 1990s, with the nonsense of a New Turkey. Against the worrying course, we must voice our criticisms without bowing to pressure and threats…” (Zaman, 16.10.2014)

Due to my identity as an academic and commentator, I was one of those whose views foreign observers frequently consulted in those years. A conference I attended at the University of Macedonia in Thessaloniki, in neighboring Greece, in November 2014 provided a good example of what kind of questions I generally faced and the answers I gave to them. I leave it to readers to judge how accurate or inaccurate I was in my answers.

“Where is the ‘resolution process’ going? It is very clear that Turkey cannot find peace or maintain its integrity without making peace with the Kurds at home and abroad. The AKP administration’s main concern is to protect power; for this, not to lose half of the Kurdish votes. With this calculation, it is conducting the ‘resolution process’ with the logic of ‘the process is everything, the result is nothing…’ The PKK, on the other hand, is benefiting from the process to consolidate its forces. What the result will be is impossible to predict.

“Is the AKP Islamist-Sunni? The AKP government did not promise sharia, did not advocate turning its back on the West, and also made many reforms for EU membership. Its ideology is not Islamism but at most religious nationalism, but its main compass is to hold on to power and continue to benefit from its fruits; to do whatever is necessary for this. It engages in Islamic populism domestically, addressing the Sunni majority, but in foreign policy its dialogue with Shiite-majority Iran is good, whereas there is no dialogue left with Sunni-majority Egypt; now an enemy, but before 2011 it was hand in glove with Alawite Bashar al-Assad. (…)

“How do you see the future of the AKP government? As everywhere in the world, the economy is decisive in Turkey too. However, Turkey is not as primitive a society as the AKP administration thinks. In a country where the opposition and civil society are quite strong, the people cannot tolerate an arbitrary, authoritarian government tainted by corruption for long. The AKP may win the upcoming elections, but Erdogan’s ‘Turkish-style’ presidency is now a pipe dream.

“‘What happened to the AKP-Gulen community alliance?’ We call the faith-based civil society movement formed by the counsel of religious scholar Fethullah Gulen the Hizmet Movement. Hizmet is not a politically-aimed movement, but it has an indirect influence on domestic and foreign policy through the foundations it established, media organizations, and schools spread around the world. Like everyone who wanted military tutelage to end in Turkey and libertarian democracy to be established, Hizmet also supported the AKP government in its first two terms of power when it acted in this direction. Many civil society organizations did the same. But there was no ‘political alliance’ between the AKP and Hizmet. If there were, presumably a considerable portion of the AKP’s parliamentary group would consist of people close to Hizmet; these people would vote no confidence in the government when they deemed necessary. Nothing like this was seen. The AKP government is trampling the rule of law underfoot with the nonsense that a ‘conspiracy’ was set up against it through the December 17-25 corruption investigation, conducting a witch hunt against Hizmet.” (Zaman, 25.11.2014)

## The December 14 operation

On December 14, 2014, Zaman’s editor-in-chief Ekrem Dumanli and Samanyolu Broadcasting Group General Manager Hidayet Karaca were detained. Three days later, the court they were brought before decided on the arrest of Karaca along with three security officers, and on Dumanli’s trial without detention. In the article I wrote in response, titled “Zaman is the bastion of the free press,” I defended the Community media that opened its pages and screens to me as follows:

“The mere fact that this case, built on an absurd claim like ‘establishing an armed terrorist organization to seize the sovereignty of the state’ based on two columns and one news report, was even opened is perhaps the most striking expression to date that judicial independence and the rule of law are increasingly disappearing in Turkey, that the country is increasingly coming under an arbitrary and authoritarian one-man rule.

“It is certainly no coincidence that the one-man rule targets Zaman and STV first in the media. The truth indicated by the December 14 operation is that Zaman and STV are the leading bastions of the free press in Turkey. No one can deny that both Zaman and STV have been the media organizations that have shown the most determined stance against both the military tutelage regime and the one-man rule (which has now taken the tutelage supporters in tow) in Turkey. That Zaman and STV are bastions of the free press in Turkey certainly stems from the Hizmet Movement, which they receive support from, being one of the most important forces of civil society in Turkey.

“The December 14 operation may perhaps also help in understanding the following points, like the saying ‘there is good in every evil’: The editors and writers of Zaman, the editors and commentators of STV, do not write or speak on instructions received from Fethullah Gulen Hocaefendi, from the ‘Community’ as some claim. What guides them and the entire Hizmet Movement is yes, the understanding of Islam and worldview pioneered by Hocaefendi. The understanding they share is one where commitment to democracy, secularism as freedom of belief, the rule of law, universal human rights, and the principle of respect for difference, summarized in the principle of ‘accepting everyone as they are,’ is being internalized ever more deeply. Zaman Newspaper and Samanyolu Broadcasting Group are not, as some claim, only and solely the spokesperson of the Hizmet Movement. These media organizations have been open to all views that defend democracy, fundamental rights and freedoms, and human rights.

“Another result emerging from the December 14 operation is that the one-man rule is seeking to maintain its dominance by polarizing press members as well as the whole society through the ‘pool media’ it has established, using the state radio and television financed by all our taxes as its own mouthpiece. The fact that some media members almost celebrated their colleagues being detained on absurd claims reminded once again that democracy cannot be established in Turkey without professional ethics and principles being established in the media. The only consolation that can be felt in this context is that professional organizations and self-respecting names in the media have taken a determined stance against the operation.

“We are learning by living that rights and law are necessary for everyone. The December 14 operation also provided the occasion for Zaman’s managers and writers to show the virtue of self-criticism by accepting certain mistakes made in the past struggle against the military tutelage regime. None of us learned the value of democracy and the rule of law in our mother’s womb. We learn democracy by living it. The freedom struggle, just as it brought down the military tutelage regime, will also bring about the end of the one-man rule.” (Zaman, 20.12.2014)

My above article was met by some of my friends with the comment that I was “more Community-ist than the Community.” Subsequent developments showed they were right. However, in those days I saw defending the Community as a requirement of defending freedoms and democracy against authoritarianism.

What is the AKP, what is it not?

In my first article of 2015, I explained my view on where the AKP had come from and where it had arrived. As follows:

“The AKP defines itself as ‘conservative democrat.’ The most common definition among its opponents is that it is ‘Islamist.’ (Including so-called political scientists who use the concepts of devout Muslim and Islamist identically.) There are types of the Islamist definition. Those I have encountered: Secret, soft, radical, dissimulating Islamist, neo-Islamist, post-Islamist, Islamofascist, Muslim Brotherhood branch… There are also those like me who refer to the AKP as religious nationalist, Sunni nationalist, Islamic-Kemalist. And of course, there are the recently raised claims that the AKP is an ‘American or Israeli project.’ Thank goodness, there are more than enough people in our country looking for an ‘American, Zionist, mastermind’ finger under every stone. We can set aside such claims by those whose minds are poisoned by conspiracy theories. So, how can the AKP be defined at the point it has reached today? First, the following observations need to be made.

“The AKP is a product of the more or less multi-party system that has existed in Turkey for approximately 70 years, of the deficient-flawed democracy. It takes its roots from the National Outlook Movement (MGH) that emerged on the scene from the 1970s onward. The parties born of the MGH, up to the Welfare Party, deserve the Islamist characterization because they are against integration with the West, advocate Islamic unity, and at one point also took up the idea of ‘freedom to choose law, legal pluralism.’

“However, the MGH underwent a transformation that began with the traditionalists-innovators split that started in its ranks in the 1990s, continued with the U-turns during the Refahyol government, and became fully apparent with the Virtue Party experience. At the basis of this transformation lies the politicians belonging to the innovator wing seeing the impossibility of coming to power with an Islamist agenda in a country where the people demand freedom and prosperity and where the reins of power are in the hands of the Kemalist military-civilian bureaucracy. For this reason, the AKP declared it had ‘taken off its Islamist shirt’ and entered the political scene with the most liberal program in Turkish history, both politically and economically, with EU membership at its center.

“The AKP succeeded in coming to power as a result of tutelage parties dragging the country into the most severe financial crisis in its history. In its first term in power, it clung to the EU’s rope, embraced broad segments of society, and doubled its vote share. In its second term, it repelled military and judicial coup attempts with society’s support. When it collected half the votes in the 2011 elections, Tayyip Erdogan at the head of the party, judging that he had neutralized military tutelage and won the people behind him, decided together with the clique around him (who had tied their entire political careers to him) that he could govern the country as he wished; the Erdogan II period opened.

“How was the transition from Erdogan I to II made? Theories vary: According to Kemalist tutelage supporters, this was the inevitable result of the Islamist hidden agenda. According to freedom advocates, what is in question is the ‘power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely’ syndrome. There are also those who resort to psychological analyses. (See Hadi Uluengin, ‘Erdogan: A case of hubris,’ Taraf, 18.10.2014.) What is certain is that, like every organism, the AKP also underwent an evolution. At the point it has reached today as a result of this evolution, it has become difficult to speak of the AKP’s ideology, its ideas.

“If an ideology must be attributed, it can be said that the AKP carries Kemalist tendencies in the sense of authoritarianism, intolerance of civil society and opposition; that it resorts to Islamic populism (demagoguery) to maintain its power; and that it emulates Putinism with its desire to establish one-man, one-party rule. But what essentially defines the AKP now is that it has no aim, ideal, or quality left other than maintaining the power of a political and economic interest group; that it is an opportunist party of one person (Erdogan).” (Zaman, 6.1.2015)

Is the AKP cracking?

In February 2015, there were signs that some cracks had appeared in the AKP. I drew attention to these signs, which would lead nowhere, as follows:

“It appears that the differences of opinion in the AKP have gone beyond the party summit and spread to the ranks. The first sign of this was given by Davutoglu’s chief advisor Etyen Mahcupyan: ‘The corruption is not nonsense… Half of the AKP voters are not happy about this.’ (November 23, 2014) A more distinct sign emerged when around 50 AKP deputies voted in favor of sending the 4 ministers who resigned over corruption allegations to the Supreme Tribunal. (January 20) The Prime Minister had asked the relevant ministers to go to the Supreme Tribunal on their own, but President Tayyip Erdogan had not allowed it.

“The rest of the signs were lined up as follows: Following Erdogan’s warning that ‘If you lower asset declaration to the level of provincial and district chairmen, you won’t find anyone to take on duties…’, Davutoglu withdrew the ‘transparency’ bill he said he attached great importance to. HDP Co-Chair Selahattin Demirtas said, ‘Mr. Davutoglu would do well not to make such statements again without asking the President.’ (February 6)

“None other than one of the founding fathers of the AKP and Deputy Prime Minister Bulent Arinc’s words were heavy: ‘Trust must be in its rightful place.
