It absolutely cannot be near this or that person, on their side, here or there. This is what destroyed ANAP, this is what destroyed DYP… We get 50 percent of the vote. But in the remaining 50 percent, it is turning into hate speech. We used to go out on the street, our supporters loved us very much. The opponents on the other side also showed respect. Now I sense a look of hatred. There is ossification, polarization. This won’t prevent our 50 percent vote. But Turkey may cease to be a governable country.’ (February 7)

“MIT Undersecretary Hakan Fidan resigned from his position to become an MP from the AKP, not complying with President Erdogan’s wishes. (February 7) Erdogan said, ‘he may have been made promises.’ Davutoglu broke his silence on the ‘Turkish-style’ presidential system that Erdogan wanted; ‘The issue is not concentrating power in one person’s hands within a non-libertarian constitutional system. Neither our President wants this, nor do I want it, nor does any sensible politician in Turkey envision something only for their own future…’ he said. (February 5)

“However, the great majority in society agree that ‘our President wants to concentrate power in one person’s hands.’ It is understood that most AKP members are not convinced about the presidential system. (Taraf, February 14) Deputy Prime Minister responsible for the economy Ali Babacan’s response to Erdogan, who was pressuring the Central Bank to lower interest rates and questioning the bank’s independence, was clear: ‘The sole authority lies with the Central Bank. This should not be a daily matter of debate from the government’s perspective… (Otherwise) the risk premium and interest rates will rise.’ (February 14)

“Perhaps TBMM Speaker Cemil Cicek’s statements can also be seen as a crack coming from the AKP: ‘Due to our party’s decision, I will not be able to be a deputy candidate this term. Turkey’s perhaps biggest difficulty is here: In advanced democracies, maximum benefit is derived from those who have performed certain duties…’ (February 15) It is certain that the real cracking will break out in the context of the candidate lists to be announced on April 24. As you know, whoever determines the candidates is also the owner of the party. It was reflected in the press that Erdogan said to Davutoglu, ‘Let’s give you Konya…’ (Taraf, February 5)

“There is no room left for other signs of ‘discord’ in the AKP… I keep writing and saying: Turkey is not as primitive a society as Erdogan thinks; even the AKP cannot tolerate one-man rule… Perhaps I will be proven right.” (Zaman, 17.2.2015)

In 2022 when I am writing these lines, that is, seven years after my above article, the probability of being proven right was increasing; the crack had grown, both Ahmet Davutoglu and Ali Babacan had long since left the AKP and established separate parties and were opposing with all their might.

## Why ‘Hizmet’ is enduring

In early 2015, I grounded my view that the Hizmet Movement, whose founder is Fethullah Gulen, would be enduring in arguments inspired by the sociology of religion, as follows:

“As a reminder: All the founding fathers of social sciences who lived in the 19th and early 20th centuries shared the view that societies would move away from religion with modernization and that science would replace religion. Beginning from the end of the last century, social scientists saw that this theory did not accord with facts, that the world today is as religious as ever, if not more so. Some embarked on an effort to save the secularization theory; others turned to the social scientific explanation of why modernization did not result in moving away from religion. (…)

“In the context of the latter, one of the analyses that recently came to my attention was the article titled ‘Beyond beliefs: Religions bind individuals into moral communities’ by two social scientists from the renowned University of Virginia in the USA, named Jesse Graham and Jonathan Haidt. (Personality and Social Psychology Review, Vol. 14: 1, 2010, pp. 140-150.) In this article, the authors explain (in their own words) ‘three puzzles’ based on research findings, namely why most people are religious, why religious people are happier than others, and why they are more charitable than others. The findings can be summarized as follows:

“The claim put forward by some (radical secularists almost everywhere) that religiosity is based on belief in God or the prophet and that people can abandon these beliefs if the scientific invalidity of religious beliefs is demonstrated, is not valid. Most people are religious because religious beliefs integrate people with spiritual-moral communities. Religious people are happier than others. There is truth in the view that religious beliefs protect people against the threats and uncertainties they are exposed to. But happiness among the religious stems not from a sense of protection, but essentially from the spirit of unity and solidarity provided by being part of a religious community. There is a strong relationship between religiosity and engaging in charitable works regardless of education, age, gender, income, and political preferences. Having common ideals appears to be the strongest explanation of why the religious are more charitable than others.

“The scientific findings I conveyed above may help those who have difficulty understanding how Hizmet, a faith-based civil society movement formed by the counsel of Fethullah Gulen Hocaefendi, was able to motivate thousands of volunteers to work selflessly in distant lands; its ability to create financial resources from the contributions of volunteers.

“How is it that Hizmet has been able to provide scholarships enabling many young people to study and acquire professions, to open schools throughout Turkey and in around 160 countries? How is it that the ‘Kimse Yok Mu’ (Is Anybody There) association has been able to deliver humanitarian aid throughout the country and to three continents? How is it that the Journalists and Writers Foundation has organized so many conferences and meetings domestically and abroad? How is it that Zaman has nearly a million paid subscribers? How is it that those devoted to Hizmet have stood by Bank Asya, the participation bank that the AKP government wanted to sink, by selling their goods and properties and forming long queues to deposit their money? And how is it that Hizmet not only remained standing despite the pressures and prosecutions of the 1980 and 1997 military coups, but found the opportunity to grow stronger?

“In its mortar there are certainly religious beliefs, respect for Hocaefendi’s interpretation of Islam that reconciles Islam with modernity. But this mortar does not stem solely from belief. Commitment to the spiritual and moral values that Hizmet has developed, the interpersonal mutual trust and solidarity it provides also have an important share in this mortar. That is why, whatever those who try to eliminate it do, Hizmet is enduring.” (Zaman, 21.2.2015)

In 2022 when I am writing these lines, the claim I put forward in the above article appeared quite open to debate. Namely, while pressures and arrests against the Community / Hizmet Movement continued domestically, it was seen that there were cracks in its organization abroad, and dissidents were emerging from within the movement.

## Presidential system would be a disaster

One of the rare subjects I was not wrong about in my political commentaries was that a presidential system, especially the kind that Erdogan wanted to bring, would be a disaster for Turkey. I explained this view as follows:

“Yes, the proposal to transition to some kind of presidential system was raised from time to time from the late 1970s onward. Prime Minister Turgut Ozal mentioned it in the late 1980s, and President Suleyman Demirel in the late 1990s. However, the proposal never came to the agenda as a government bill or election manifesto. Erdogan says he has been advocating this since his Istanbul mayorship, but such a proposal was not included in the AKP program. The AKP government he headed promised in its 2007 general election manifesto to establish the parliamentary system with all its institutions and rules through the new constitution to be drafted. The constitutional draft prepared by Professor Ergun Ozbudun and his team at Erdogan’s invitation, announced in September 2007, was based on this promise.

“However, Erdogan immediately shelved the draft. It can be said that from that date onward he turned to concentrating all power in his hands. In October 2007, he had the constitutional amendment providing for the president to be elected by the people for five-year terms, up to two times, adopted through a referendum. Thus, the unaccountable but empowered president envisaged by the 1982 military tutelage constitution came to be elected by the people. In December 2012, the AKP, knowing that opposition parties would oppose, ensured the dissolution of the parliamentary Constitutional Conciliation Commission by proposing a ‘Turkish-style presidential’ system to the commission. President Erdogan, who has taken an oath of impartiality according to the Constitution, is currently (judging by his latest statement) continuing a campaign to ask for votes for the AKP for a ‘Mexican-style’ presidency.

“The Mexican-style presidency that Erdogan apparently discovered during his Latin America visit really suits him. Because it gives unlimited power to a president who can be elected only once for 6 years, this system is called a ‘6-year monarchy.’ The president is at once head of state, head of government, and commander-in-chief (but not ‘head of the legislative body’ as Erdogan claims). He fully commands both the state and the party he is a member of. He has no deputy. He can appoint and dismiss ministers and the entire bureaucracy alone. There is a bicameral parliament, but it convenes only between November 1 - December 15 and April 15 - July 15; for the rest of the year, a mixed committee of 31 people from both chambers represents the parliament. Legislative, law-making authority is essentially in the hands of the president. The president even determines whom his party will nominate for the presidency after him. As you can understand, it has come close to Erdogan’s ideal presidential system.

“So, how does Erdogan defend the transition to a presidential system? As follows: While it is a fact that almost all developed countries are governed by a parliamentary system, he claims the opposite; (of Britain, which is the cradle of the parliamentary system) he says ‘Even England is semi-presidential. The dominant element is the queen…’ He says that the USA, the cradle of the presidential system, ‘tried the parliamentary system for 20, 30, 40 years and then got stuck and transitioned to the presidential system.’ To these incredible, inconceivable words, the other day was added ‘actually the presidential system is in our genes.’ What he means is clear: We Turks were created to be ruled by a sultanate!

“In the presidential system debate, we are literally at the point where words fail. A presidential system can work in places where a high culture of consensus prevails among politicians. Even if copied from the USA, a presidential system would be a disaster for Turkey. Erdogan’s performance is more than enough to prove this: He brazenly tramples on the Constitution; he acts as the president not of all the people but of those who voted for him; he accuses all opposition of treason; he is polarizing society in an increasingly worrying manner. If tomorrow Erdogan (or someone else) confronts us with a presidential system of any kind, I don’t even want to imagine what could happen to us.” (Zaman, 26.2.2015)

“Alliance of thieves and coup plotters”

In early 2015, I assessed the political landscape in the country as follows:

“Why was Mehmet Baransu arrested and put in prison? Let me also explain: In March 2003, at the 1st Army Command located in Istanbul, under the guise of a ‘plan seminar,’ a coup aiming to overthrow the AKP government that had come to power a few months earlier was planned. Senkal Atasagun, who was the MIT undersecretary at the time, told Cumhuriyet newspaper executives Ilhan Selcuk, Ibrahim Yildiz, and Mustafa Balbay in May 2003, ‘Tip-off letters are coming from Istanbul and they are important. Everything is ready in the First Army, they are preparing for a coup…’ and suggested they meet with Chief of General Staff Hilmi Ozkok, who opposed the coup. This information was included in Mustafa Balbay’s (now CHP deputy) diaries.

“In the speeches recorded at the ‘plan seminar,’ what would be done if the coup succeeded was described as follows: ‘Units are ready. We are descending on Istanbul. We are seizing the administration. Mayors, public institution employees will be changed. They will be arrested. There will be harsh intervention. No mercy or anything, there is crushing…’ The coup attempt failed. In the following years, Chief of General Staff Hilmi Ozkok and the Land Forces Commander of the time Aytac Yalman quarreled over which of them had prevented the coup.

“Documents leaked from the TSK regarding the ‘Sledgehammer’ coup attempt were reported by Mehmet Baransu in the Taraf newspaper in January 2010. Copies of the documents submitted to the prosecutor’s office by Baransu were found in a secret compartment at the Golcuk Naval Command during a search conducted as part of another investigation in January 2011. The case that was opened concluded in September 2012. 361 defendants, primarily Cetin Dogan, were tried for ‘incomplete attempt to overthrow the government of the Republic of Turkey.’ 325 retired and active-duty officers found guilty were sentenced to prison terms ranging from 6 to 20 years. The Court of Cassation, finding sufficient the evidence deemed serious by the European Court of Human Rights, confirmed the convictions of 237 defendants in September 2013.

“The Sledgehammer case defendants, their lawyers, and the front of military tutelage supporters claimed the evidence was fabricated. The case was subject to criticism due to the arrest of many relevant and irrelevant defendants, the conversion of long detention periods into punishment, and the violation of defense rights. Upon the defendants’ application, the Constitutional Court decided on retrial in June 2014; the convicts were released.

“Immediately after the major bribery and corruption investigation of December 17-25 (2013) became public, then Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan’s Chief Advisor and AKP deputy Yalcin Akdogan, just like military tutelage supporters, raised the claim that a ‘conspiracy against the national army’ was set up through the Sledgehammer case. From that day to this, this claim has become the common discourse of the ruling party and military tutelage supporters. After the cover-up of the December 17-25 corruption investigation was completed, Mehmet Baransu was arrested for ‘disclosing state secrets’ by doing what journalism requires and reporting the Sledgehammer coup plan documents. Moreover, even though a decision of non-prosecution had been made in the investigation with the same accusation 5 years ago…

“So what is the meaning of all this? Ahmet Altan explained it best: ‘Since when are coup plans characterized as ’documents related to state security’ and ‘information that the state must keep secret’? Since when? Since thieves and coup plotters linked arms to escape the law… (Italics added later.) A government caught while stealing, when it started committing crimes greater than theft to save its skin, decided to go and take refuge with the coup plotters. The coup plotters, caught with their plans in hand, with their knees trembling from fear, shamelessly hid behind the men they clearly knew were thieves… Together they are trying to declare those who exposed their crimes as criminals.’ (Cumhuriyet, 03.03.2015)” (“Alliance of thieves and coup plotters,” 5.3.2015)

In 2022 when these lines are being written, Mehmet Baransu is unfortunately still in prison. Upon the Court of Cassation’s reversal decision regarding seven of the Sledgehammer coup plan defendants who were acquitted in June 2014, including former 1st Army Commander Gen. Cetin Dogan, the case began to be heard again on October 22, 2021. Meanwhile, on August 18, 2021, the Ankara 5th Heavy Penal Court issued an arrest warrant for 14 defendants, including Cevik Bir and Cetin Dogan, whose life sentences in the February 28 case in 2018 were confirmed by the Court of Cassation on July 9, 2021. In the face of these events, what else could be said but to ask, “has the alliance between thieves and coup plotters ended?”

# CHAPTER XV / A DARK PERIOD

Upon the prosecutor’s invitation, on February 4, 2015, Ali Bulaç and I went to the Courthouse in Çağlayan. The subject of the invitation was the article dated November 23, 2014 by Etyen Mahçupyan, who had left Zaman and started writing for the Akşam newspaper in June 2014. Mahçupyan had written the following about a meeting he attended earlier that year:

“The date is January 8, 2014, the place is Mabeyin Restaurant. The Journalists and Writers Foundation is holding its quarterly evaluation meeting. Along with me are Zaman newspaper writers Ali Bulaç, Mümtazer Türköne, and Şahin Alpay. Besides the foundation’s administrators, there are some guests I don’t know, as well as Ergun Özbudun, Fatih University Rector Şerif Ali Tekalan, and the newspaper’s former administrator Alaattin Kaya. We are roughly twenty people. Everyone has in mind what has been happening since December 17 and how events will develop. Before even getting into the topic, one of our journalist colleagues simply asks one of the Hizmet members ‘what’s happening?’ The answer is exactly this: ‘Nothing has changed for us… We’ll get results within a month.’ Since the conversation occurred during a quiet moment, everyone would have heard it. The moment of silence after the answer must be an indication that the audience understood very well what this answer meant.”

In response to this article, the Journalists and Writers Foundation had also made this statement: “If Mr. Mahçupyan had asked for confirmation from any of those he mentioned in his article who attended the meeting—Ali Bulaç, Mümtazer Türköne, Şahin Alpay, Ergun Özbudun, Şerif Ali Tekalan, Alaattin Kaya, or the Foundation administrators—before writing his article about this meeting that took place 10 months ago, he could have easily learned that such a conversation did not occur and would have understood that his memory had deceived him. Furthermore, Mr. Mahçupyan should clearly and explicitly state from whom he heard this statement. We call upon Mr. Mahçupyan, who has participated in such meetings of the Journalists and Writers Foundation for years, to prove his claim or apologize.”

The prosecutor, who treated Bulaç and me quite courteously, was asking whether the words “Nothing has changed for us… We’ll get results within a month…” quoted in this article were actually spoken. I had not heard such a thing. Neither had Bulaç. (Ergun Özbudun and Mümtazer Türköne, whom I had called and spoken with before going to the prosecutor’s office, had also said they hadn’t heard it.) We left after signing our statements. At that time, it hadn’t occurred to us that this would be only the first of our visits to Çağlayan, but we had become uneasy.

My last day at Bahçeşehir University—A sign that my future was darkening also came from the workplace where I had worked the longest in my career. I quote from my notes: “On January 22, 2015, around noon, when I received the news from Zekeriya (Tüzen, my student and later my assistant) that the make-up exam schedule was set, I went to school. Near the entrance, I encountered the owner Enver Yücel and his companions. We exchanged brief pleasantries. As he was leaving, he stroked my cheek. At that moment, I couldn’t make sense of it. I went up to my room; I wrote my article that would be published two days later. Then I prepared the syllabus for the Media and Democracy course I would teach again in the spring semester. I ran into Seyfettin (Gürsel) in the corridor; I told him we would go to Ayvalık on the 27th; ‘Maybe we’ll come too,’ he said. Then I stopped by Dean Necip Çakır; I told him I would go to Ayvalık for about ten days. He said okay.

I started preparing the questions for the make-up exams in my room. Then the phone rang. The assistant Hülya was saying that the rector wanted to have coffee with me. I immediately understood… I called Seyfettin and Necip to say ‘the day of parting has arrived.’ Neither of them was at their desks. I went up to the rector’s floor. Hülya asked what she could offer me. I asked for plain coffee. Rector Şenay Yalçın, as if nothing extraordinary was happening, perhaps a bit nervous, first talked about BAU opening branches in Djibouti, Georgia, and Casablanca. I said I enthusiastically supported it. She asked about my health; she expressed her sorrow saying ‘Look at what condition Yaşar Kemal is in…’ She said she greatly admired me for standing firm against the government; ‘The country needs intellectuals like you,’ she said. I asked her to read my article that came out that day, in which I said ‘Don’t be surprised if Davutoğlu is also declared parallel…’ She read it and said she liked it very much. Then she got to the point: a letter had come from YÖK (Council of Higher Education); apparently a certain maximum number of teaching staff was required for each department. Also, there was the budget issue, of course. Therefore, it was time to ‘part ways’ with me (unfortunately, although I was a lecturer, I was receiving a faculty member’s salary).

I wasn’t surprised at all. I said I owed gratitude to BAU; that I had worked here with pleasure for 14 years and was now leaving happily; that I would always consider myself a part of BAU; that I would be ready if there was any service I could provide in the future; and that I would donate some of my books to the university. ‘You were already talking about leaving anyway…’ she said. (Yes, it had occurred to me that my job might be terminated.) ‘Am I leaving immediately from February 1?’ I asked. She confirmed. She said my severance would be calculated and paid immediately after my approval. ‘Please give my regards to Enver bey,’ I said, and took my leave. ‘He probably wants to have coffee with you too… We would also like to organize a farewell dinner for you,’ she said. As I was leaving, her secretary Hülya said, ‘Şahin bey, you didn’t remember me; I was Zülfü Livaneli’s assistant at Milliyet.’ I had forgotten.

I thought: The owner had given me the first signal that my job would be terminated at a reception on the terrace at the end of that summer, early fall. On the day BAU received permission to open a branch in Washington DC, he had said ‘Well professor, if you need to flee, you now know where to go…’ He had given the real signal in October during a group dinner with department members: ‘Professor Şahin, the other day I had dinner with your Ekrem Bey, and I told him to tell Professor Şahin to write a bit less harshly…’ (When I asked Dumanlı months later, he confirmed this and said he had replied ‘But Enver Bey, having Professor Şahin teach at your institution is a matter of prestige for you…’)

I went to Dean Necip Çakır to say goodbye. He had heard that my job would be terminated. After the rector met with me, she had called and informed him. ‘There is political pressure,’ he said. He said my articles against military tutelage had created discomfort in the administration. They had been thinking about terminating my contract for some time. They had asked Eser to explain this to me; he had refused. ‘We will organize a farewell party,’ he said. (Indeed, on the afternoon of February 13, a farewell cocktail was held that almost all faculty members attended. It was a nice farewell.) I stopped by Seyfettin’s. He said he was sorry that we wouldn’t be able to see each other as frequently anymore. While returning home after buying fish from Beşiktaş market, I decided it would be good to postpone the Ayvalık trip.

When I told my Fatma, who had been dealing with repair work at home with workers all day, that my job had been terminated, she said with her usual composure that she was very happy, that now we could stay in Ayvalık as long as we wanted, that we could do what we wanted, and that I would be less tired. She was genuinely pleased. She reminded me that we wouldn’t have financial problems. I informed my daughter Elvan and my son Acar about the development. They just said congratulations. We postponed going to Ayvalık. I asked Fatma, ‘I wonder if I should ask Zaman for a room and go there 2-3 days a week?’ ‘Don’t rush; let’s get through the summer and see what happens…’ she said.

The next day I went to school and signed the contract termination document. I started sorting through books. I called the opinion page editor Abdullah Yavuz Altun from the newspaper. ‘Talk to Ekrem bey. Maybe they’ll give me a room; I’ll put my books there and have my meetings there,’ I said. I wasn’t very sure it would be a good idea. Indeed, I gave up on this.

“Ten days that shook the AKP”

I had no job left other than Zaman. In one of my first articles to be published, I wrote that the alliance formed between the AKP government and its supporters and the military tutelage proponents—what Ahmet Altan aptly called “the alliance of thieves and coup plotters”—had the aim of “reversing Turkey’s democratization history”:

“The cover-up of the December 17/25, 2013 investigation—containing the largest bribery and corruption allegations in Republican history—by the AKP government not only initiated the process of destroying the rule of law in Turkey and dragging the country toward one-man, one-party rule, but also reversed the process of dismantling the military-bureaucratic tutelage system.

“The bribery and corruption allegations revealed in the investigation, which Istanbul prosecutors had conducted with great meticulousness since September 2012, not only covered four ministers, three of their sons, public officials, and businessmen, but also extended to the Prime Minister himself and his family members. Celal Kara, one of the prosecutors conducting the investigation, would express his opinion as follows: ‘It is impossible and improbable that these affairs were conducted without the Prime Minister’s knowledge, awareness, and permission. Looking at the phone conversations and the dialogues between them, you definitely say that it is the Prime Minister who allowed and permitted these affairs from behind the scenes.’

“The government headed by the Prime Minister of the time immediately took action to cover up the investigation. The fallacy was put forward that the evidence was ‘doctored, dubbed, staged’; that the investigation was a ‘plot’ set up by ‘foreign powers that cannot tolerate Turkey’s strengthening and the Fethullah Gülen community’ to overthrow the government. The detained suspects were released. A ‘witch hunt’ declared by the Prime Minister of the time was launched. Thousands of police officers and hundreds of prosecutors and judges were reassigned; hundreds of police personnel were detained, some were arrested.

“In short, the ‘witch hunt’ was used to ensure the subordination of the entire state apparatus to one-man, one-party rule. By changing the HSYK (High Council of Judges and Prosecutors) law, the judiciary was tied to the executive. Not only was a decision of non-prosecution made for the four ministers who were forced to resign due to the gravity of the allegations, but the AKP majority in Parliament also prevented them from going to the Supreme Tribunal. Thus, the referral of the grave allegations to the judiciary was prevented (certainly for now).

“The other important result of suppressing the December 17/25 investigation was that the AKP government also put forward the fallacy that the Sledgehammer and Ergenekon cases were ‘plots against the national army’ set up by foreign powers that cannot tolerate Turkey’s strengthening through the ‘community,’ thus paving the way for covering up the coup attempt cases as well. Today we are facing an alliance between the AKP government and its supporters and military tutelage proponents, seemingly established with the aim of reversing the history of democratization in Turkey.” (Zaman, March 21, 2015)

“We will not let you become president”

In an article challenging Erdoğan’s leadership and his ambition to be elected president, I said:

“Last Saturday, while watching on screen the hundreds of thousands gathered at the Newroz celebrations in Diyarbakır to listen to the conditional peace message of Abdullah Öcalan, the natural leader of the PKK, my mind went back to old times. I remembered the first column article I had the opportunity to write in the press; I opened it and read it. In the article titled ‘Earthquake in Parliament’ I had written: ‘The other day I was casually watching the oath ceremony at the Turkish Grand National Assembly on television. Meanwhile, I followed the Leyla Zana incident almost entirely. It seemed to me that an earthquake was happening in parliament. It was as if old structures were creaking and new ones were emerging… Now there is a new demand at this “table”… The Kurds are voicing the new demand this clearly and strongly for the first time. They want to take their place in the Turkish Republic’s parliament by freely expressing their ethnic identity.’ (Cumhuriyet, November 9, 1991.)

“In the 34 years that have passed, unfortunately much blood was shed, much suffering was endured, but progress was also made in resolving the Kurdish issue. President Erdoğan is right: Denial policies have ended; most of the bans on the expression of Kurdish identity have been lifted; a search for a peaceful solution has begun… But the Kurdish issue has not disappeared. The truth, which even the State Security Courts accepted in the 1990s, is this: There are two peoples in Turkey. As long as this is not reflected in the Constitution, as long as the Kurdish mother tongue is not recognized as a regional official language, as long as the Kurdish-majority region does not gain a status of self-governance, the Kurdish issue will not end. So why is Erdoğan—the leader who ended the denial of Kurdish identity, lifted the bans on its expression, and initiated the search for a peaceful solution—now saying again ‘There is no Kurdish issue…’?

“Because now we are facing a completely different Erdoğan than in the first two terms of power. Erdoğan, now consumed by the ambition to establish his ‘unchecked—unrestrained’ personal rule, needs to win the votes of Turkish nationalists and consolidate the alliance he has formed with the Turkish Armed Forces. Isn’t his statement the other day at the War Academies about the Sledgehammer and Ergenekon cases, of which he was once the ‘prosecutor’: ‘Through these operations, myself first and foremost, the entire country was misled, deceived…’ a clear expression of this? However, Erdoğan’s risk of ‘losing the bulgur at home while going to Damietta for rice’ is increasing. The possibility of Turkish nationalists’ votes that he has managed to win so far shifting to the MHP, and Kurdish nationalists’ votes shifting to the HDP is growing.

“I have always written: Turkey is not as primitive a society as Erdoğan thinks. No matter what he does, no matter what he says, the people will not follow him. Even the AKP cannot tolerate Erdoğan’s arbitrariness and authoritarianism. Indeed, the signs of this are increasing. Abdullah Gül says, ‘Democracy is not just about elections, Turkish-style presidency won’t work…’ Bülent Arınç warned that if Erdoğan continues to polarize society, the country will become ‘ungovernable’; he was forced to say ‘don’t forget, there is a government in this country…’ Ali Babacan constantly feels the need to say ‘There can be no development in a country without law…’ Even Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoğlu, who owes his seat and entire career to Erdoğan, didn’t he want to send the ministers accused of corruption and bribery to the Supreme Tribunal; didn’t he try to include Erdoğan’s ‘secret keeper’ in the government? He was even able to say ‘It is dangerous for a statesman to become arrogant…’

“At least half of society cannot tolerate Erdoğan, how can the Kurds tolerate him? Aren’t these reassuring words of HDP co-chair Selahattin Demirtaş an expression of the fact that an increasing portion of Kurds have also become unable to tolerate him?: ‘We are not a bargaining movement, a bargaining party. There was no dirty bargain between us and the AKP, there never will be… Mr. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, as long as HDP members breathe on this land, you will not become president. We will not let you become president, we will not let you become president, we will not let you become president…’” (Zaman, March 24, 2015)

## There is no alternative but HDP

In an article published as we were heading to the general elections to be held on June 7, 2015, after saying “I had written that I would unhesitatingly vote for CHP in this election too, but I no longer think so,” I listed the reasons why there was no alternative but to vote for HDP as follows:

“(…) One cannot vote for a CHP from whose candidate lists true social democrats—not demagogic ones—have been almost completely erased, and which has been filled with military tutelage supporters. The main reason is this: It has become completely clear, along with the candidate lists, that President Tayyip Erdoğan—who brazenly declared that he has put the Constitution in the waiting room and who already sees himself as president—has fully established his hegemony over the AKP, and that almost no one from within the party will object to this in the foreseeable future. Restraining Erdoğan’s ambition to destroy democracy and the rule of law under the name of ‘Turkish-style presidency’ has become Turkey’s undisputed number one issue.

“Turkey went through very bad days during military coup periods. In those periods, we at least knew that military rule was temporary and that we could return to some form of democracy, however deficient and flawed, after a while. I don’t even want to think about the damage Erdoğan—who, even now in a position where he has no authority, can declare everyone who opposes him as ‘parallel, agent, traitor,’ and who considers the nation as a flock and himself as the nation’s shepherd—could do to the country if he somehow manages to become president. As Seyfettin Gürsel’s analysis shows very convincingly, the only way to stop Erdoğan, the only solution, is for HDP to pass the threshold and be represented in Parliament. (‘General election scenarios’, Zaman, April 9.) In that case, even if AKP maintains power alone, it will become impossible for it to win the minimum 330 seats required to change the constitution.

“This will have other benefits too: First of all, a situation that would fundamentally wound representative democracy—such as HDP remaining outside Parliament—and push the Kurdish political movement to act outside Turkish politics will be prevented. The Kurdish nationalist movement will find the opportunity to abandon arms within Turkey and focus on political-democratic struggle. It will even benefit the AKP; even if it maintains power alone, it will not feel obligated to Erdoğan. Erdoğan, whose morale will inevitably drop, will be left face to face with the obligation to act within the framework of the current constitution.

“With HDP’s candidate list aimed at winning the votes of conservative Kurds as well, it has become clear that the intention of the Kurdish political movement is not to remain outside Parliament. Yes, despite HDP Co-Chair Selahattin Demirtaş’s repeated promise ‘We will not let you become president!’, there are those who think he might be forced to change his tune tomorrow, and that there is an implicit give-and-take agreement between the Palace and İmralı. The only way to test whether such an agreement really exists is for HDP to pass the threshold and enter Parliament. Let’s say there is such an agreement. Even then, since HDP will have the ability to impose its own conditions, even if there is a presidency, it will not be the ‘Turkish-style presidency’ that Erdoğan wants.

“For all the above reasons, if you want to restrain Erdoğan’s ambition, even if this doesn’t sit well with you at all, the only solution is to vote for HDP. Yes, tactical votes may not be enough for HDP to pass the threshold; HDP mainly needs to win votes from Kurds who are AKP voters. For those who defend democracy, there is no alternative but HDP.” (Zaman, April 11, 2015)

Why this hostility toward Hizmet?

In an effort to understand the AKP government’s increasingly growing hostility toward the Gülen community or Hizmet movement, I wrote the following:

“If you asked what could be the reason for the Erdoğan government’s hostility toward the Hizmet movement, I think the average citizen in Turkey would answer as follows: ‘He believes that the December 17/25 investigation—the largest bribery and corruption investigation in Republican history—was conducted by judiciary and police members who feel close to Hizmet; that’s why he approaches Hizmet with great anger and a feeling of revenge.’ The questions that should be asked of the average citizen are these: Hasn’t it sufficiently emerged that the judiciary and police members who conducted the December 17/25 investigation had very different identities?

“Even if there are those among them who feel close to Hizmet, isn’t their common denominator being people who do what the law and morality dictate? Let us accept for a moment the fallacy, that is, that the December 17/25 investigation was conducted solely by judiciary and police members close to Hizmet, and moreover by the instruction of Fethullah Gülen Hocaefendi… Can this make it justified and logical to accuse the entire Hizmet movement collectively of being an ‘illegal terrorist organization’? It absolutely cannot.

“Then what is the logic behind the AKP government declaring the Hizmet movement an ‘illegal terrorist organization’? It is this: Democracy is not just elections. It also means the rule of law and that the fundamental rights and freedoms of citizens are secure. For this, courts independent of the government, independent media, and perhaps most importantly, a strong civil society composed of independent voluntary associations are needed. The common characteristic of power holders in authoritarian regimes is intolerance of strong civil society.

“Perhaps the strongest element of civil society in Turkey, with its scope extending to education, media, and social welfare institutions and economic enterprises, is the Hizmet movement. Hizmet not only took its roots from the tarikat (Sufi order) and community tradition, which are undoubtedly the most important civil society elements of our society; it evolved beyond the religious community shell toward a faith-based civil society movement; and from there, it has been moving toward acquiring the character of a global civil society movement addressing all humanity, based on universal values that all humanity shares.

“Religious or secular fundamentalists, authoritarian Islamists, Kemalists, and Marxists may not see this, may not comprehend it. This is why the Erdoğan government had no difficulty in gaining the support of all these circles in the war it waged against Hizmet, or at least in ensuring their silence. The real truth that those seeking an answer to the question of why Hizmet was left so alone cannot see, which will be understood in time, perhaps is already beginning to be understood, is this.”

The article ended with a self-criticism: I attributed my not being sufficiently critical of the AKP government until 2011 to my focus on defending fundamental rights and freedoms against military tutelage:

“Yes, the (insufficiently critical) support that the media, whose establishment Hizmet pioneered, gave to the AKP in the first two terms of power with the expectation that it would ‘defeat military tutelage, establish democracy and the rule of law, secure fundamental rights and freedoms, and end the mistreatment of the religious’ may have played a role in Hizmet being left alone. But didn’t almost everyone who was committed to fundamental rights and freedoms in the struggle against military tutelage make this mistake?” (Zaman, May 26, 2015)

No to Erdoğan, yes to Demirtaş!

As we were heading to the June 7, 2015 elections, as had become my custom, I declared who I would vote for as follows:

“Next Sunday, the most vital election of multi-party life will be held in Turkey; the future of the regime will be determined. The proportional representation electoral system with a 10 percent threshold—the gift of the September 12 military dictatorship to the country—continues to make the country gamble. That is, if HDP passes the threshold and wins around 60 deputies as expected, President Erdoğan will have to bid farewell to his ambition to change the constitution and be elected president, to rule the country like a company (that is, his own property); there is a possibility that the AKP will not be able to govern alone. On the other hand, if HDP cannot pass the threshold, especially if Erdoğan’s party AKP gets at least 330 seats in Parliament with the parliamentary seats it will steal from HDP, I don’t even want to think about what could happen to the country.

“If you don’t want the country to go in the direction President Erdoğan wants to take it, that is, you don’t want press freedom—like the rule of law before it—and increasingly the opposition (already declared ‘legal in appearance’), and therefore democracy, to be reduced to nothing; in short, if you say ‘No to Erdoğan!’, there is no alternative but to say ‘Yes to Demirtaş!’ The apparent truth is this: the biggest fear of Erdoğan and his supporters is HDP passing the threshold.

“That’s why Erdoğan (as if his own government wasn’t conducting peace negotiations with the PKK) says of HDP, which promises ‘We will not stray from the path of peace!’: ‘The party backed by the terrorist organization is after blood and lives…’ Even more interesting, Erdoğan and his supporters fear the strengthening of Demirtaş’s position within the Kurdish political movement. For this reason, Bülent Arınç attacks Demirtaş saying ‘You want to discredit Öcalan!..’; for this reason, Yalçın Akdoğan accuses Demirtaş of being ‘a Brutus against İmralı…’ (that is, a backstabber).

“Yes, if you want Erdoğan to retreat to his constitutional limits, the only solution is to vote for HDP. It is said, ‘Yes, Demirtaş says “We will not let you become president; we will not support the AKP in any way…”, but what if he doesn’t keep his word? What if Öcalan or Kandil pushes him in another direction?..’ We cannot know the answers to these questions without HDP entering Parliament. On the other hand, the cost to the country of acting on the assumption that Demirtaş will not keep his word is very great. It is also certain that the cost to Demirtaş of not keeping his word will be very great. Some say, ‘Since it’s a Kurdish party, let the Kurds vote for HDP…’ Although HDP is a party supported by some Kurds, it is Turkey’s party. Turks, Kurds, citizens of all identities, we are all in the same boat. The issue is Turkey’s issue.

“It is also certain that the reasons for saying ‘yes to Demirtaş’ are not limited to saying ‘no to Erdoğan’. HDP is striving to transcend the boundaries of the Kurdish political movement; to be a ‘Turkey party’ firmly committed to peace, democracy, and the rule of law. Shouldn’t those who want Turkey’s integrity to be preserved and politics to be cleansed of weapons support and encourage HDP, which emphasizes not Kurdishness but humanity, even if only for this reason? (Italics added later.) Yalçın Akdoğan says ‘If HDP enters Parliament, AKP will lose power, the solution process will end…’, but the truth is the exact opposite! Peace cannot come to Turkey precisely in an environment where HDP is not represented in Parliament. On the other hand, the truth is that Selahattin Demirtaş, with his election manifesto, his peaceful and pro-freedom discourse, and his trust-inspiring personality, has succeeded in giving HDP a new identity; votes are rising because of this.

“HDP passing the threshold is to the benefit not only of Turkey but also of the AKP. Thus, the AKP can be freed from one-man rule and find the opportunity to repair its increasingly worsening image, and perhaps even return to inclusive policies. HDP entering Parliament is also to the benefit of President Erdoğan. He can be saved from being destroyed by the ambition to become president and rule the country like a company, and at least complete his term in peace. He has been running around too much for years, sweating; he needs rest. (Italics added later)” (Zaman, June 2, 2015)

The nightmare is over!

In the general elections held on June 7, 2015 to determine the 550 new members of the Turkish Grand National Assembly, no political party reached the 276 seats required for single-party government. The AKP, which had been in power since 2002, lost its parliamentary majority but emerged as the first party from the elections with 40.9% of the vote and 258 seats. The Republican People’s Party (CHP) obtained 132 seats with 25% of the vote and became the second party, but both its vote share and number of deputies declined compared to the 2011 general elections. The Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) won 80 deputies with 16.3% of the vote and increased its vote share by 3.28% and its number of deputies by 27 seats compared to the previous elections. The Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) won 80 parliamentary seats with 13.1% of the vote. I welcomed the AKP’s being reduced to a minority with great satisfaction, saying ‘The nightmare is over!’, with excessive optimism. But I could also see that the results could lead to a repeat of the elections. I wrote:

“The June 7, 2015 general elections went down in Turkish history as a new victory for democracy. In the first victory in 1950, the people said ‘Enough!’ to the single-party regime. The 1983 elections pushed aside the project of being governed through parties loyal to the military that the military wanted to impose. The 2002 elections opened the way to the liquidation of the bureaucratic tutelage regime. The 2015 elections put an end to authoritarianism fed by the ballot box. We are learning liberal democracy by living it, internalizing it by living it. From now on, neither military-based nor ballot box-based authoritarianism will work; democracy based on human rights, rule of law, and respect for minorities will gradually take hold.

“The June 7 elections showed that Turkey is not as primitive a society as President Erdoğan thinks; that the people will not accept being herded like a flock by a single man who thinks himself their guardian. In an election where the AKP used all state resources to maintain its power, where a President who had taken an oath of neutrality openly ran the ruling party’s campaign, the people went to the polls with a high turnout rate of 87 percent, took away the AKP’s ability to govern alone; they gave an unforgettable lesson to a government drowning in corruption and spreading hatred to society.

“In Turkey, which has at least 65 years of multi-party life experience, the electorate once again embraced freedoms; once again embarrassed those who do not trust the people’s collective wisdom and common sense, those who say ‘There can be no democracy in a Muslim society…’ This election showed that the saying ‘You can fool some of the people all of the time, and all of the people some of the time, but you cannot fool all of the people all of the time…’ is also valid for Turkey.

“The AKP government, which was becoming increasingly arbitrary, corrupt, and authoritarian, came out successfully from the March 2014 local elections and the August 2014 presidential election using the ‘parallel structure’ fallacy, but in this election it was defeated by the ‘national will’; Erdoğan’s ambitions to become a one-man ruler were destroyed at the root. Erdoğan, whose legitimacy is beginning to be questioned, if he wants to complete his term as president, must from now on stop polarizing the country and spreading hatred toward his opponents; he must learn to know his limits, that is, to act within the boundaries drawn by the constitution and his oath. The AKP too, if it wants to prevent its gradual shrinking, must find a way to free itself from Erdoğan’s tutelage and from those who have tied their political careers to Erdoğan (especially Ahmet Davutoğlu, who tries to present a heavy defeat as an election victory and speaks as if unaware of the election results).

“Yes, the results may make a repeat of the elections inevitable. However, the opposition parties must keep the promise they made to the voters and never cooperate with the AKP. Parties that attempt to enter a coalition with the AKP should not forget that they will be condemned to a heavy defeat in the next election. As I underlined in my previous article, the opposition parties need to be able to come together on minimum common grounds to repair the great damage to the rule of law, and to form an alliance for this.

“In this context, it is essential: that the suspects of the December 17/25 investigation—the largest bribery and corruption investigation in Republican history—be brought before the judiciary; that the judicial and police officials who conducted the investigation be reinstated; that the criminal peace judgeships be abolished and those unjustly arrested by these courts be immediately released; that judicial independence be secured through changes to the HSYK and Court of Cassation laws; that press freedom be strengthened; that the threshold be reduced to at most 5 percent. It is certain that Turkey cannot continue on its way without repairing the great damage to the rule of law. On the other hand, a valuable lesson to be drawn from the corruption and authoritarianism caused by one-man, one-party rule is that Turkey should get used to being governed by coalition governments and succeed in this.

“One of the most important results of the June 7 elections is undoubtedly HDP under Selahattin Demirtaş’s leadership shattering the 10 percent threshold. I believe that HDP’s success under Demirtaş’s leadership paves the way for the peaceful and democratic resolution of the Kurdish issue and for securing Turkey’s integrity. The experiences gained with the IRA in Ireland, ETA in Spain, and the ANC in South Africa showed that for armed resistance against injustice and oppression to be directed toward a peaceful channel, in addition to opening peaceful-political struggle paths, it depends on the internal balance in the resistance movement shifting in favor of the civilian-unarmed-political wing. From now on, the party to peace negotiations must be HDP in Parliament. The nightmare is over! After June 7, Turkey can look to the future with optimism.” (Zaman, June 9, 2015)

How wrong I was!

## End to the ‘parallel’ fallacy

I also listed the lessons that should be drawn from the June 7 elections as follows:

“There are lessons that all parties should draw from the June 7 elections. At the head of these parties is undoubtedly the AKP. The electorate not only put an end to the ambition of President Tayyip Erdoğan—the de facto leader of the AKP—to become president and rule the country like a company; they also warned Erdoğan to know his limits, that is, not to exceed his constitutional powers. Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoğlu, who is legally the party chairman, himself admitted this: ‘We wanted to switch to a presidential system but the people did not give us the mandate…’ he said; referring to Erdoğan, he called on everyone to ‘do their duty within the scope of their powers and responsibilities.’

“The electorate not only said ‘no’ to Erdoğan; they also denied the AKP the possibility of governing alone. Within the AKP ranks, the debate ‘what did we do to lose power’ began. Davutoğlu expressed the extremely necessary need for debate by saying ‘We have to do our own internal reckoning…’ Many, including Abdullah Gül and Bülent Arınç among the party’s leading founders, are talking about the mistakes made. If this debate continues in a healthy way, that is, by facing the facts, both the AKP and the country will benefit from it.

“The first fact that AKP members must face is that their party completely turned its back in its third term in power on the policies of liberalization and democratization it had pursued in the first two terms. Can the AKP, which has become almost unrecognizable in terms of its cadres, give up turning its back on rights and freedoms? Can it give up covering up the December 17/25 investigation, which played a major role in its loss of power? It is difficult to give positive answers to these questions, but there is great benefit in AKP members, especially AKP voters, facing this fundamental truth.

“That December 17/25 was a ‘coup’ attempt against the elected government is complete nonsense. It is an investigation that revealed, purely and simply, that the rule of law that the AKP strengthened in its first two terms of power was working, and that the AKP’s top cadres were involved in bribery and corruption up to their necks. (Italics added later.) Gül (without answering the question of why he didn’t throw his weight in this direction at the time) says if I were at the head of the party I would have sent the suspects to the Supreme Tribunal. Arınç (without answering the question of why he didn’t express an opinion in this direction at the time) says the investigation can be reopened. If, as Gül and Arınç imply, there is ‘corruption,’ then ‘coup’ is a fallacy; the investigation should also be carried through to the end.

“A series of laws and regulations that devastated the rule of law, separation of powers, and judicial independence in Turkey were enacted to cover up the December 17/25 investigation—the largest bribery and corruption investigation in Republican history. Just as the claim that the investigation was a coup orchestrated by foreign powers who do not want Turkey to strengthen and implemented by the Hizmet Movement (smeared as ‘parallel structure’) is a complete fallacy, so is the claim that the Sledgehammer and Ergenekon cases were a ‘plot against the national army’ set up by the Hizmet Movement. Indeed, in the Sledgehammer coup attempt case, which was so obvious that it became the subject of a ‘which of us suppressed it’ debate between the Chief of General Staff and the Land Forces Commander of the time, the prosecution objected to the decision to acquit all defendants.

“The ‘parallel structure’ claim, produced to cover up the December 17/25 investigation and destroy the rule of law; used (in cooperation with the NSC) to revive February 28; put forward by almost all crime suspects to exonerate themselves, is nothing but a perception operation. There can certainly be those who have committed crimes within the Hizmet Movement. However, such claims cannot go beyond fallacy unless they are subject to a fair trial, not to courts established to declare them guilty. Leaving the entire Hizmet Movement under a vague accusation like ‘parallel structure,’ let alone a nonsensical accusation like ‘terrorist organization,’ is nothing other than the revival of the military tutelage supporters’ clamor about ‘religious reaction.’

“It is not possible to put the rule of law back on its feet as long as the ‘parallel’ fallacy does not end. This must be well understood not only by AKP members but by everyone, especially by those who claim to be committed to the rule of law.” (Zaman, June 16, 2015)

“Farewell to Shepherd Sülü”

Süleyman Demirel, one of the most important political actors of the post-1960 period—that is, the period I witnessed—passed away on June 16, 2015. I wrote the following afterwards:

“It can be said that multi-party political life in Turkey is divided into four increasingly shorter phases. The first phase is the military tutelage period starting from the 1950 elections that ended single-party rule and extending to the end of the 20th century, to the 2002 elections. The second phase is the period of (effectively) leaving behind military tutelage, extending from 2002 to 2011; the third phase is the period of the elected government’s increasing corruption, arbitrariness, and authoritarianism, extending from 2011 to the 2015 elections. It can be said that the fourth phase began with the 2015 elections, where we witnessed the birth pangs of leaving behind both military and civilian authoritarianism.

“The 9th President Süleyman Demirel, who passed away yesterday, was, together with Turgut Özal, one of the two most important politicians of the military tutelage period. He was one of the leading political representatives of the ‘periphery’ composed of civil society forces against the ‘center’ of the military-civilian bureaucracy that wanted to hold the reins of government with authoritarian Kemalism, that is, with an understanding of strict secularism and monoculturalism. As a pragmatic rather than ideological, conservative rather than reformist politician, Demirel’s main endeavor can be said to be keeping the military out of politics, sometimes through conflict and sometimes through compromise, and making civilian politics dominant. In this endeavor, he was sometimes successful and sometimes unsuccessful.

“Demirel had no sin in being forced to resign from the prime ministry on March 12, 1971. He was a victim of developments caused by a military coup attempt that would revive the single-party regime and remove Turkey from the alliance of Western democracies. His role in the execution of Deniz Gezmiş and his friends in 1972, however, will never be forgiven. His merit in recognizing that the import substitution development strategy that made the country ‘dependent on 70 cents’ had failed and pioneering the transition to an outward-oriented market economy with the January 24, 1980 decisions can be compared to his sin in paving the way for the September 12, 1980 military coup by rejecting Bülent Ecevit’s grand coalition proposal and insisting on early elections.

“If his opening the door to a peaceful solution by going to Diyarbakır and saying ‘We recognize the Kurdish reality’ upon his return to the prime ministry in 1991 can be written on the merit side, he committed a grave sin during his Presidency from 1993 to 2000 by supporting the deep state’s ‘solution through killing’ policies. His ensuring that Parliament remained open during the February 28 intervention can also be written on the merit side.

“His performance in the presidency can objectively be evaluated only by comparing it with Tayyip Erdoğan’s. The story of a peasant boy born in İslamköy, whose prime ministry began at age 41 and, with ups and downs, spanned 7 terms totaling 10 years, and then 7 years of presidency, is a success story of Demirel personally as well as of democracy in Turkey, with all its deficiencies and flaws.

“As I bid him farewell, I would like to share a memory of the late Demirel. Mainly due to my character, and partly because I pay attention to professional principles as a commentator, I have always stayed away from those holding political, administrative, and economic power. I met Demirel only once, in 2007, shortly after he left the presidency, on the occasion of a television program. Before the program, I went to him and introduced myself: ‘Mr. President, I am Şahin Alpay. I am a faculty member at such-and-such university, and I also write a column for such-and-such newspaper…’ I said. Demirel, with a rather mocking smile, said, ‘Mr. Alpay, I served as prime minister for ten years and president for 7 years in this country. I know who you are…’ He embarrassed me with his legendary memory.

“Like most of those, I think, who followed his long political career full of merits and sins, ups and downs, I too will remember Demirel as ‘Shepherd Sülü.’” (Zaman, June 18, 2015)

“Democracy is being murdered”

As a result of the June 7 elections, the expectation arose that CHP and MHP would form an HDP-supported coalition government and the AKP would fall from power. However, MHP leader Devlet Bahçeli had announced on the evening of June 7 that he would say “no” to all possible partnerships for a coalition and pointed to the need for new elections. Not only did he react against CHP leader Kılıçdaroğlu’s call of “Let him be prime minister if he wants,” he also opened the door for the AKP to elect the Speaker by refusing cooperation with opposition parties in the TBMM Speaker election. With this attitude, Bahçeli not only prevented the AKP from losing power but was also instrumental in its winning the repeat election to be held on November 1. President Erdoğan gave the task of forming a government to Davutoğlu, who was still serving as prime minister. No result came from Davutoğlu’s contacts. While no government could be formed, the country entered a rather dark period. This process developed step by step as follows:

- On July 15, the KCK announced that it had ended the resolution process, citing the construction of outposts and dams as justification.

- On July 20, in Suruç, ISIS carried out a suicide bomb attack against young people carrying toys for children in Kobani. 34 young people lost their lives.

- On July 22, two police officers stationed in Ceylanpınar were shot in the head and killed in their home. The PKK first claimed responsibility for the action, then announced it had no involvement. However, this incident, which still has not been fully clarified and in which all the names captured at the time were tried and acquitted, marked the end of the resolution process.

- On July 24, operations against the PKK and ISIS were launched on Prime Minister Davutoğlu’s orders. The operations meant that the “resolution process” had officially ended. On July 26, the PKK announced “The ceasefire has effectively ended.” On July 28, a major was martyred in a PKK attack; the next day, on July 29, President Erdoğan announced that the resolution process could no longer be carried out. With the start of PKK attacks, news of martyrs began coming from all directions. The TSK began bombing Kandil and its surroundings.

- On August 4, HDP Co-Chair Selahattin Demirtaş made a statement saying “The PKK should lay down arms, the government should end operations,” but his calls did not yield results. Demirtaş and HDP were accused of not openly taking a stance against the PKK.

- On August 12, a statement came from the KCK saying “We have declared democratic autonomy.” After this statement, “democratic autonomy has begun” announcements were made in many districts in the region. KCK groups that declared autonomy were arrested.

- When no result came from coalition negotiations, President Erdoğan did not assign anyone other than Davutoğlu the task of forming a government a second time and on August 26 decided that repeat elections should be held as required by the constitution.

- On September 7, 16 soldiers were martyred in a PKK attack in Dağlıca, and the next day 13 police officers were martyred in a PKK attack in Iğdır.

- On September 8, attacks were carried out against HDP buildings across the country. Davutoğlu’s statement “We are rising in the polls” created great controversy.

- On October 10, ISIS attacked a peace rally held in Ankara with two suicide bombers. 102 people lost their lives in this attack in front of Ankara Train Station. After the largest terrorist attack in Republican history, Davutoğlu made a “cocktail terrorism” statement. Davutoğlu pointed to the PKK along with ISIS for the massacre.

- Davutoğlu’s October 20 statement “If AKP goes, white Toros cars will come,” referring to the unsolved murders of the 1990s, created great controversy.

- In the repeat election on November 1, the AKP received 49.5% of the vote and became the single-party government again with 317 deputies. HDP, which lost votes, narrowly passed the threshold with 10.8% of the vote. MHP also lost votes, falling to 11.9%. CHP’s votes remained at 25%.

- The bloody process continued after the election as well. In January 2016, ISIS attacked foreign tourists in Sultanahmet. In February, the PKK carried out a bomb attack on shuttle vehicles carrying soldiers on Ankara’s Merasim Street; in March, a bomb attack was carried out on bus stops in Kızılay. Also in March, ISIS carried out a bomb attack on İstiklal Avenue. This was followed by the ISIS attack in Bursa in April. In the latter part of 2016, the PKK’s “trench operations” and security forces’ operations against them were launched. Operations in residential areas, especially in Cizre, Sur, and Yüksekova, continued for nearly a year. (See Gökçer Tahincioğlu, “What happened between the June 7 and November 1 elections?” T24, August 24, 2019.)

I commented on the events between June 7 and November 1 and the November 1 election results in the articles I quote below as follows:

“(…) The truth that emerged with the latest Dağlıca attack is this: Although two years ago Abdullah Öcalan said the period of armed struggle had ended; although PKK spokespeople have stated various times that there can be no armed solution to the Kurdish issue; although since the June 7 elections HDP has had the opportunity to take the lead in Turkey’s democratization; although HDP and all civil society organizations of the Kurdish-majority region, all tribal leaders have called on it to end its actions, the PKK does not hesitate in the slightest to support the murder of democracy in Turkey by escalating conflicts. President Erdoğan, who has effectively taken over the governance of the country, despite the increasing martyrs, despite the cries of families, can still say ‘…if a political party had reached a number that could get 400 deputies, the situation would be very different today…’ He can openly say ‘If you had made me president, all this suffering would not have happened’… By saying ‘According to our religion, martyrs don’t die, they continue to live…’ he can ignore the pain of parents, spouses, children, siblings. The general picture is this: both the government headed by President Erdoğan and the PKK do not hesitate to pave the way that could ultimately lead to the destruction of democracy once again in Turkey, that could take the country to civil war and disintegration. For the country’s sensible people, reasonable people, there seems to be no other way but to cry out once again, as our years of experience, our consciences, our future dictate: ‘Stop this violence; violence begets violence; problems can never be solved by killing, they can be solved by talking…’ (”Democracy is being murdered,” Zaman, September 8, 2015.)

“Who did this to us?”

“Last Saturday, the largest terrorist attack in Republican history took place in Ankara; 97 citizens were killed; 245 citizens, 65 of them in intensive care, are still being treated. Since the end of the ‘resolution process,’ the number of martyrs in clashes with the PKK has exceeded 150, hundreds of PKK militants have died, and the number of civilian deaths has reached 227. Turkey is bleeding internally. Starting with the Ankara massacre that brought the spiral of violence to its peak, we must ask the questions ‘Who did this to us? How can we get out of this bloody pit we have fallen into?’

“For now, we do not know for certain who planned and carried out the Ankara massacre. We can list what we know through open intelligence, that is, through news reflected in the media, as follows:

1) The bombs used at the HDP rally in Diyarbakır on June 5, in Suruç on July 20, and in the Ankara massacre on Saturday are identical. Whose work the Diyarbakır and Suruç massacres were has not been clarified to date. However, initial findings indicate that the Ankara massacre, like the others, may be the work of ISIS.

2) This is a strong possibility. Because Turkey, as of late July, not only opened its bases including İncirlik to US warplanes against ISIS, but the TSK also began striking ISIS positions. The attacks we have been subjected to may serve the purpose of ISIS, which is fighting the Kurds in Syria and Iraq, both to punish Turkey and to provoke Turkish-Kurdish conflict in Turkey.

3) As in the others, it is seen that there was a security failure in the Ankara massacre and that not all measures necessary to prevent the attacks were taken. It is estimated that the intelligence officers purged in the witch hunt the AKP government launched in the police force in response to the December 17/25 investigation played a role in the emergence of this failure. MIT’s success in ensuring the country’s internal and external security, which is its main task, has been seriously questioned at least since it emerged that 34 citizens who were smuggling in Uludere/Roboski were bombed by warplanes based on MIT intelligence that they were “terrorists.”

4) Information that the AKP government, until the last year, provided various forms of support to radical Islamist groups against the Bashar Assad regime, and at least turned a blind eye to their activities in Turkey, suggests that ISIS may have established a wide organizational network in Turkey.

5) Two AKP ministers and circles close to the government claimed that the Ankara massacre was carried out by the PKK for HDP to be successful in the election. It is not credible that the PKK, which generally attacks security forces, would target civilians, mostly HDP supporters. Moreover, the Ankara attack occurred on the day the PKK announced that it would not take action unless forced to defend itself.

6) The AKP government, headed first by Prime Minister and then President Tayyip Erdoğan, since the December 17/25 bribery and corruption investigation, and mainly after losing single-party power on June 7, has polarized the country to an unprecedented degree in its history by viewing everyone who does not support it as an enemy; by declaring them traitors, terrorists, or terrorist supporters. This environment has made the country vulnerable to all kinds of provocation.

7) The Syria policy pursued by the AKP government has dragged the country into great international isolation. There are many state and non-state actors in the region that could carry out covert activities to stir up Turkey from within.

It is certain that we need a government that will move the country away from polarization, ensure internal peace, end security failures, and pursue a foreign policy that considers strategic interests. The November 1 elections are a great opportunity to establish a coalition government that will heal the wounds. If this opportunity is wasted in one way or another, I don’t even want to think about what could happen to us.” (Zaman, October 13, 2015)

Unfortunately, a coalition government that would heal the wounds could not be established, and elections were repeated on November 1, 2015. In the election, the AKP increased its vote by 9% to 49.5% and, winning 317 parliamentary seats, gained the possibility of being in power alone again. CHP’s vote share and number of deputies remained stagnant at 25% and 134. The MHP, which had brought about the repeat election, saw its vote drop from 16% to 12% and its seats from 80 to 40. HDP’s votes also dropped from 13% to 11%, and its seats from 80 to 59.

## The November 1, 2015 disaster

I wrote two articles on the November 1 election results. In the first article I wrote:

“Undoubtedly, this is an electoral success for the AKP of a magnitude that neither party strategists nor public opinion pollsters could foresee. The voting, with participation reaching 85 percent and generally conducted with democratic maturity, is a satisfying situation both in terms of the people embracing their vote and in terms of the principle of government by election, one of the fundamental principles of democracy.

“However, it should now be better understood that democracy is not just about elections. Democracy is a regime where citizens’ fundamental rights and freedoms are secured as much as it is about government by election. The naked truth is that in the November 1 elections, approximately half of the voters approved the continuation of a government that was becoming increasingly arbitrary, authoritarian, and steeped in corruption up to its neck. Looking at past experiences, I believed that governments that do not respect rights and freedoms eventually lose in Turkey. The June 7 elections had also reinforced this conviction. However, November 1 badly proved me wrong. If we are to establish democracy with all its principles and institutions, we must first understand well the reasons for this unexpected result. In this context, the points that need to be underlined first are these:

“The polarization strategy pursued by the AKP government yielded results. The campaign of accusing the opposition of ‘treason, vileness, supporting terrorism, being an extension of terrorism, serving internal and external enemies’ played the leading role in consolidating voter support. The main implementers of this strategy were the judicial bodies placed under the government’s command and the pro-government media (‘pool media’) running a campaign of lies and slander. Public broadcasters TRT and AA functioned entirely as the government’s mouthpiece. Pressures intensifying during the election campaign on opposition media ranged from investigations, arrests, and censorship to the open seizure of İpek Media Group.

“It was also seen that the AKP administration was able to convince at least 8 percent of the electorate of its (completely unfounded) claim that stability could only be ensured by single-party government. The biggest role in this was played by the inability of the three opposition parties, which received 59 percent of citizens’ support in the June 7 elections, to come together and form a joint government, even for a short time, at least with the aim of repairing the damage done to the rule of law. The lion’s share of this failure certainly belongs to MHP, which treated HDP as ‘nonexistent’ and opened the way for repeat elections, virtually playing a buttress role for the government. Its loss of approximately 2 million votes on November 1 is clear evidence of this.

“On the other hand, it appears that the choices of Kurdish voters, who were caught between two fires (the state and the PKK) as the AKP government put the ‘resolution process’ in the ‘freezer’ and turned again to a military solution, and who were under the threat ‘if we go, white Toros cars (extrajudicial killings) will come,’ were somewhat affected by this situation. The fact that HDP, which could not even conduct a proper election campaign under pressure, still managed to pass the threshold and will maintain its place in Parliament with 59 deputies continues to be a source of hope for the resolution of the Kurdish issue. In this context, it should once again be seen that the PKK’s weapons are one of the most important obstacles to democratization in Turkey.

“As a result, yes, on November 1 the government problem was solved, but all the other problems of the country, especially authoritarianism, remain in place. Can Turkey, with a government that will effectively be run by President Erdoğan, overcome problems ranging from the Kurdish issue to judicial independence and freedom of expression, from economy to foreign policy? My answer in the next article.” (“Democracy is not just about elections,” Zaman, November 3, 2015)

## Polarization at its peak

In my article two days later, I wrote:

“I can summarize the main factors that played a role in the great electoral success of the AKP, effectively headed by President Erdoğan, on November 1 with 49 percent of the vote and (in the final count) 317 deputies as follows: The government polarizing society by declaring opponents ‘traitors’; turning facts upside down with the media under its command; with the help of the opposition, convincing a significant portion of the electorate that stability could only be ensured by single-party government; the MHP falling into the Bahçeli ‘trench,’ and the HDP into the PKK ‘trench.’

“Of course, in any country where government is determined by elections, for a party to collect around 49 percent of the vote is a great success. However, 49 or 59 percent of the vote alone cannot be a guarantee of either political or economic stability. Stability is possible only where citizens’ fundamental rights and freedoms are respected. Unfortunately, the main negative result of this election is that polarization in society has peaked with 49 percent approving authoritarianism. It is clear that the half of society that did not vote for the AKP feels a great reaction against Erdoğan’s administration, perhaps to a degree never seen in Republican history.

“Very different segments are extremely dissatisfied with the AKP government. No government that cannot win the hearts of the Kurds, who have resisted the denial of their identity since the founding of the Republic, can be long-lasting. Although the AKP government managed to regain the support of at least some Kurds, almost all of the Alevis, the country’s largest religious minority, have been very dissatisfied since at least the 1990s because their freedom of belief is restricted and they are being forced to adopt the Diyanet’s religion. The segment of society that perhaps constitutes Turkey’s largest minority in terms of lifestyle is extremely dissatisfied. Some devout Sunnis perceive the AKP government as a gang of interests that is an enemy of fundamental rights and freedoms, including freedom of belief, and that has turned its back on the most fundamental moral principles of Islam.

“Rising unemployment, inflation, declining exports, foreign and domestic investments, and declining economic growth rate are increasingly negatively affecting the living conditions of the segments of society that live by their labor. If the economic trend continues, an increase in dissatisfaction in this segment is inevitable. Under conditions where even the right to property is threatened, the segment of businessmen that does not receive the government’s support either remains silent for fear of facing wrath or grumbles silently. Not only are the dissatisfied spreading across a wide base, but groups from different political tendencies who had been opposed to each other until yesterday are tending to unite against the increasingly authoritarian government, setting aside their differences.

“In the face of the opposition parties’ powerlessness, the eyes of those hoping for the revival of the rule of law had turned to politicians within the AKP who seemed aware of the dangers of the direction of things, such as Abdullah Gül, Bülent Arınç, and Ali Babacan. Now the same eyes have turned to Prime Minister Davutoğlu because of his words in his ‘balcony’ speeches on the night of November 1 about being conciliatory and respecting rights and freedoms. (Arınç and Babacan, whom Erdoğan did not invite to the Palace on October 29, appeared right behind Davutoğlu on the ‘balcony.’)

“The point that seems to be being ignored is that both the AKP’s latest election victory and Davutoğlu himself are Erdoğan’s creation.
