The arrest of journalists the day after the election, ‘plot’ raids in 18 provinces, travel bans imposed on 54 judges and prosecutors, the Chief Prosecutor’s returning the Hrant Dink case indictment for the second time (allegedly to remove certain names from among the suspects) remind us of the saying that should never be forgotten: ‘A person’s work is their mirror, not their words.’ Another point that a narrower circle is trying to make us forget is that the ‘parallel structure’ fallacy is not being used to ‘fight all kinds of illegal structures within the state through legal means,’ but on the contrary, to demolish the rule of law.

“My conclusion from November 1 is that Turkey has taken another big step toward an ‘electoral autocracy.’ The defeat of military-based authoritarianism took at least half a century. That the defeat of ballot box-based authoritarianism will not take that long is, I think, the most optimistic comment I can make.” (Italics added later.) (Zaman, November 5, 2015)

Many more years will probably need to pass for this rather dark period in Turkish history between the two elections to be illuminated. However, the following points emerged with the November 1 election results: 1) MHP helped the AKP maintain power by refusing to join the government after the June 7 elections and insisting on early elections. It itself became the biggest loser of the election. 2) Between the two elections, the PKK and ISIS, above all, escalated terrorist actions to an unprecedented degree. (The PKK’s return to a low-intensity war strategy after several months of intense armed struggle raised questions.) 3) Voters frightened by the violence turned back to the AKP. The AKP increased its vote by approximately 9%, raising its number of deputies from 258 to 317 and regaining the possibility of governing alone.

## Last trip to the USA: September 2015

When my job at Bahçeşehir University was terminated, although I didn’t suddenly find myself “free as a bird,” I had more free time than I had in a long time. I had no work left other than writing columns three days a week for Zaman, one day for Today’s Zaman, and appearing one evening a week on the “Akıl Defteri” (Notebook of Wisdom) program on Mehtap TV. I had become able to take leave from my newspaper and television jobs and go on trips. At the invitation of Zaman representatives, in the last days of April I made a visit to Scandinavia (which would turn out to be the last). I spoke at meetings organized in Copenhagen, then in Gothenburg.

The Erdoğan government’s attacks on the Gülen movement and therefore on Zaman were increasing, and the circle surrounding the group was narrowing. I had begun to feel that troubles could befall me in the not-too-distant future. My close American friend Tor Krieger had come to Turkey three times to see me in 1963, 2005, and 2007; I had not been able to make a return visit even once. These days might be my last chance. In September, I got permission from Fatma to go to Tor. In August, I wrote to Tor that an opportunity had arisen for me to visit him, and that this might be my last chance. His response, though delayed, was positive.

When Tor came from Santa Rosa in northern California, where he had lived for a long time, to New York in the spring of 1998 just to see me, I had met Shan, his second legally married wife among his many wives. Now he was with his third legally married wife, Danelle. When they met me at the San Francisco airport on September 8, I learned the reason for Tor’s delayed response: considerable sorrow had been caused by the suicide about two weeks earlier of Danelle’s son from her first marriage, a very successful architect in his 30s (but whom Tor never liked because of his drug addiction). My coming to visit them provided an occasion for solace and was in a way good.

In the first five days of the visit, I stayed with Tor and Danelle. Our classmates from Webb School who lived nearby, Dick Power and John Trefethen, hosted us for dinners with their wives. Together with Tor, we toured the vineyards and wineries in the Napa Valley region, famous for northern California’s wines. One day we took a trip to the coast. On the way, we stopped at Bodega Bay, where Alfred Hitchcock’s famous 1963 film “Birds” was set. One evening, I gave a talk on political developments in Turkey and the world to a large group of friends at Tor’s house. Shan, the mother of Tor’s son Jess, also attended the meeting; we chatted briefly. I spoke by phone with my daughter Elvan and my granddaughter Defne, who were in Chicago at the time. This Santa Rosa visit, which I’ve described in some detail, took me out of the increasingly restrictive environment I was living in in Istanbul; it was good for me.

Before flying to San Francisco, I had contacted Hizmet’s representatives; I had informed them that I wanted to see its schools in California and that I could give talks to Americans about what was happening in Turkey. In this context, on September 16, I gave a talk titled “What went wrong in Turkey” at the Center for Middle Eastern Studies at UC Berkeley, one of the leading universities in the United States (<https:// www.youtube.com/watch?v=TuO6yMUSc4U>).

## Bilici instead of Dumanlı

When I returned to Turkey on September 18, the storm brewing around Zaman was growing.

The tension between the AKP government and the Gülen Community or Hizmet Movement, which began with the closure of the prep schools run by Hizmet, had greatly escalated with the December 17-25, 2013 “Corruption and Bribery Operation” in which public officials including four ministers were accused of abuse of office and bribery (allegedly initiated by prosecutors associated with Hizmet). Zaman newspaper editor-in-chief Ekrem Dumanlı and Samanyolu broadcasting group chairman Hidayet Karaca were detained on December 14, 2014; while Karaca was arrested on charges of establishing and running a terrorist organization (still in prison); Ekrem Dumanlı was released with a travel ban.

Dumanlı resigned on October 5, 2015 from the position he had held for 14 years. In his statement, he said, “I see that I cannot perform my duty as Editor-in-Chief due to the unlawful pressures applied to the press and to me personally in recent times.” (On November 11, 2015, an arrest warrant would be issued for him; it would become clear that he had fled abroad.) Following Dumanlı’s resignation, it was announced that Abdülhamit Bilici, the General Manager of Cihan News Agency, had been appointed to this position.

I had a more intimate relationship with Bilici than with Dumanlı. I was pleased that it was he, rather than someone else, who replaced Dumanlı. I visited him and wished him success in his new position, which he had assumed in a very difficult period. During this visit, we had a very interesting conversation. Bilici said that looking at developments in the Middle East and in Turkey in recent years, the Kemalists had been proven right, and complained that Islamism had turned the region and the country into a hell of oppression and violence. I objected. I said it should not be forgotten that what brought Islamists to power in Turkey, though not in the Middle East, was the oppression exerted by Kemalists on Muslims. Interestingly, a similar debate would take place between Hilmi Yavuz and myself some time later at a meeting where Zaman writers gathered. I objected to “Brother Hilmi’s” statement that Islam was incompatible with freedom and democracy. I argued that the problem stemmed not only from bigoted interpretations of Islam but also from imperialist and authoritarian pressures on Muslims. (As I write these lines, I think both factors need to be taken into account when trying to understand the Islamic world’s lack of accommodation for individual freedom.)

## Vietnam 50 years later

In mid-November, I went to Ankara at the invitation of Swedish Ambassador Lars Wahlund. I also visited the new and stylish building of Zaman and Today’s Zaman (which would be seized by the government before a year had passed). I met with the bureau chiefs of the two newspapers, Mustafa Ünal and Abdullah Bozkurt. (I would meet Ünal next in Silivri. This would be my last meeting with Bozkurt; I would learn that he had taken refuge in Sweden after July 15.)

November 29, 2015 was Fatma’s and my 50th wedding anniversary. When I suggested on this occasion that she could take a trip abroad of her choice, she chose a cruise to the Far East. With my elder sister Olcay and Fatma’s cousin Emine also joining, we flew to Singapore via Dubai on November 30 and from there boarded the ship for a trip that would last until December 13. The trip took us to Brunei in the north of Borneo island, from there to the Vietnamese cities of Nha Trang and Ho Chi Minh (former Saigon), to Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, and Koh Samui island, then back to our departure point, Singapore.

The stop that interested me most on this trip was, of course, Vietnam. In the article titled “Vietnam 50 years later” that I wrote for Zaman, I wrote: “Frankly, it never occurred to me that there would be such a great contrast between the Vietnam that adorned the dreams of my youth and the Vietnam I saw with my own eyes 50 years later. Yes, Vietnam is still under the authoritarian single-party rule of the Communist Party. However, it seems the very symbol of the fact that the only thing that doesn’t change in the world is change. (…)

Vietnam, which until that date had tried to establish a planned economy based on state ownership, seeing that this was not a way forward, from 1986 onwards (just like China) turned to establishing a (supposedly socialist) market economy based on private ownership under communist party rule.” (Zaman, December 19, 2015)

On December 12, while we were preparing to leave the ship, Fatma fell ill; she became unable to walk. We immediately went to the ship’s infirmary. The Australian doctor and nurses, bless them, showed warm concern. They said she was probably having a crisis due to fatigue and would recover after the injection they gave her. Indeed, that’s what happened. Perhaps because we disembarked late, the passport police delayed us for quite a while with questions. Skipping the Singapore city tour, we went straight to the airport. (If Fatma had had that crisis before leaving the ship, what would have become of us, which hospital would we have gone to, what would we have done if we had missed the plane? We were grateful for the timing of the crisis.) We returned to Istanbul via Dubai.

## Neither law nor logic remains

The article titled “Neither law nor logic remains” that I wrote upon returning from the Far East trip, which began with “I don’t remember an elected government in Turkey being as far from law and logic as it is today,” and ended with the sentence “This Turkey has ceased to be the country I was born and raised in, the country I knew; it is experiencing a state of madness,” in my opinion summarized well the point the country had reached at that time:

“I don’t remember an elected government in Turkey being as far from law and logic as it is today. The AKP government, which with EU reforms brought the country closer to the rule of law than ever before until 2011, has zeroed out the rule of law with the steps it has taken since then. The same government that in its first term was moving the country toward becoming a fortress of peace internally and externally now leaves the country facing the threat of war internally and externally. I have never felt as much as I do today that the country is being governed by a cadre devoid of competence and prudence. Those who govern Turkey today recognize neither law nor logic; not only the country’s law but also its accumulated wisdom and knowledge has been pushed aside.

“The most obvious, most painful proof of this is the conflicts growing in an increasingly alarming manner since the peace negotiations conducted with the PKK were unilaterally abandoned, saying ‘Oh, HDP won’t let me be elected president!’ The historical experience that neither the Kurdish issue nor the PKK issue—its product—can be solved by killing people; that it can only be solved through negotiation, through talking, has been completely thrown aside. The President says, ‘We must take the separatist terrorist organization out of action without showing the slightest tolerance…’ The Prime Minister is so focused on solution through killing that he addresses AKP youth saying ‘I see the love of martyrdom in your faces…’

“The Interior Minister proudly proclaims that 3,000 PKK members have been killed since the abandonment of the peace process; it is forgotten that dozens replace every PKK member killed. By subjecting the cities of the Kurdish region to an undeclared state of emergency, by imposing curfews, by forcing the population to migrate, by withdrawing public officials from the region, virtually everything necessary is being done to make the Kurds lose hope of living as equal citizens in Turkey. I don’t know if even the soldiers are convinced by the logic of solution through killing.

“In foreign policy conducted with reactive steps, we are constantly being tossed about. The downing of the Russian warplane left Ankara, which has been pursuing regime change since 2011, with no ability to influence Syria’s future. The no-fly zone it wanted established against Bashar Assad’s forces is now being implemented by Russia against Turkey. What Ankara feared is happening; Syrian Kurds, with Russia’s support as well, are advancing toward autonomy in the region stretching along the Turkish border. Despite saying ‘we won’t withdraw,’ Turkish soldiers in Iraq are being withdrawn at the demand of the Baghdad government, which is also supported by the US administration. The strained relations with Russia and the increasingly isolated situation in the region are forcing Ankara to get closer to the West, which it criticized saying ‘They don’t love us, they love our dead children,’ and to reconcile with Israel, which it accused of ‘committing genocide.’

“As for the internal situation: The revenge-motivated witch hunt conducted against the Hizmet movement on the claim that it was responsible for the December 17/25 bribery and corruption investigation has reached incredible dimensions. Perhaps all kinds of accusations can be made against its members, but neither sensible Turkey nor the world believes in the slightest the claim that Hizmet is an ‘armed terrorist organization.’ Efforts to pin all the dark murders committed in the country on the Hizmet movement in order to find support for this claim are the clearest evidence that the rule of law has been zeroed out.

“Just look at what happened in this last week: If an arrest warrant is issued for Cemal Uşak, Chairman of the Journalists and Writers Foundation, an intellectual who has earned almost everyone’s respect, on the grounds that he is an ‘armed terrorist’; if attempts are being made to link Police Chief Yakub Saygılı, who conducted the December 25 investigation, to the Zirve Publishing House massacre; if Hasan Cemal’s books are being confiscated on the grounds of terrorist organization propaganda, then we are at the point where words fail. This Turkey has ceased to be the country I was born and raised in, the country I knew; it is experiencing a state of madness.” (“Neither law nor logic remains,” December 22, 2015)

Gül: If not now, when?

In an environment where the country was heading toward increasingly darker days internally and externally, I felt the need to address President Gül and Bülent Arınç, who had given hope that he would be the party’s conscience. As follows:

“Exactly two years ago, I wrote an article titled ‘What is expected of Abdullah Gül and Bülent Arınç.’ The article ended as follows: ‘Both of them cannot fail to see that the Prime Minister has declared almost everyone who does not think like him a traitor; that he is polarizing society in a very dangerous way; that he is destroying the rule of law to cover up corruption; in short, that he is following a line incompatible with reason, judgment, and logic. It is obvious that where the Prime Minister is taking things will cause great harm to the country. The majority of society believes that the loyalty of these two leading politicians to the country’s interests is much stronger than what they feel toward the Prime Minister; they expect them to say stop to this direction that will cause great harm to both the country and the party.’ (February 13, 2014)

“Where Tayyip Erdoğan, the Prime Minister of the time, has brought the country in the two years that have passed is obvious. After being elected President, he declared that the constitution had been put in the ‘waiting room’ and that he was ‘effectively president.’ He ended the ‘resolution process.’ He turned to a military solution to the Kurdish issue, which cannot possibly yield results—to solution through killing. The PKK is gaining more and more supporters inside and more and more friends outside. The policy based on claiming to be a leader in the region has ultimately made Turkey completely ineffective in the region. While the country faces great dangers internally and externally, President Erdoğan is pursuing a ‘Turkish-style’ presidential regime by fueling polarization, as if all powers were not already in his hands, as if he couldn’t govern the country as he pleases, as if there were no other problems left. (…)

“Bülent Arınç has finally begun to raise his voice: ‘It won’t work with weapons, there must be a return to the resolution process; of course Erdoğan knew about the Dolmabahçe agreement with HDP,’ he said. ‘In the MIT trucks case, neither arrest nor conviction can be ordered,’ he said. ‘Such cases are being opened under the name of fighting the “parallel structure” that I want to take up lawyering again,’ he said. He didn’t heed the lynch campaign of ‘trolls and trollettes,’ he said ‘I stand by my words.’ Yes, he spoke ‘too late, too little,’ but he made us say ‘Better late than never…’ Former ministers Hüseyin Çelik, Sadullah Ergin, Suat Kılıç supported him. It seems others will too.

“And our 11th President Mr. Abdullah Gül? Although it was clear that he was not pleased with the situation internally and externally, he first signed all the laws that trampled on freedoms and the rule of law by acting like a ‘Çankaya notary’; then he remained completely silent, perhaps by putting party interests above everything, perhaps by saying ‘if there is a need my party will call me to duty…,’ perhaps with the expectation that ‘conditions will ripen.’ Yet if he shows the courage and determination to object to the bad direction, Gül could lead both the people and his party to put the country back on its feet. If nothing else, the respect he received from the majority of the people during his Presidency should encourage him to show this courage and determination.

“I wonder: If not now, when will Abdullah Gül say ‘Enough!’ and raise his voice against the country’s march toward chaos internally and externally?” (Zaman, February 6, 2016)

## Not paranoia but fallacy

I felt the need to defend the community against the characterization of the Gülen community or Hizmet movement as a “legal-looking illegal structure”:

“Murat Tokay has prepared a wonderful dossier for the latest (February 22-28, 2016) issue of Aksiyon magazine; the title is ‘Parallel paranoia’ (pp. 42-44). An instructive dossier in terms of showing how far the ‘parallel structure’ claim extends. Let me quote a few selections: ‘Parallel’ is responsible for the contraction in tourism. It deceived farmers and seized their cows and presented them as calves. It wiretapped underwater fiber optic cables with a team of 60 people. It shot down the Russian plane. It caused someone being tried for fraud to hit a cow with his car. It victimized tradespeople by opening the Bolu tunnel. It caused a crime of passion. And more…

“The dossier is truly instructive, but the title is misleading. Which paranoia? Are those who try to pin the crimes they commit on the Hizmet Movement, which they label as ‘parallel structure,’ suffering from paranoia? As is known, paranoia is a mental illness, defining people who, completely disconnected from reality, imagine that traps are being set for them. Those who put forward the ‘parallel structure’ claims, or in its developed expression ‘legal-looking illegal structure,’ have not the slightest connection to any mental illness. It is wrong to establish a connection between them and mental illness; because it implies that they could be excused, that they could not be held responsible.

“It is certain that those who put forward the ‘parallel structure, Fethullahist Gang, etc.’ claims do so with their mental-psychological balance fully intact, knowingly and willingly. Yes, their purposes may differ: Some use it as a tool to cover up the crimes they commit, some to oppress, frighten, and intimidate society; some do it to ingratiate themselves with those making the claims, to fawn. What we are dealing with is certainly not paranoia, but, as Honorary President of the Court of Cassation Sami Selçuk accurately diagnosed, ‘fallacy.’

“The claim that they were ‘victims of the parallel structure’s plot’ was first put forward by the defendants of the Sledgehammer and Ergenekon coup attempt cases. They claimed that they had committed no crime, and that the allegations against them were ‘fabricated’ by judiciary and police members implementing Fethullah Gülen’s instructions. It is true that in these cases, far too many people, involved or not, were made defendants, that detention turned into punishment, and that defense rights were violated. But neither the ECHR nor the Court of Cassation believed that the cases were fabricated.

“The AKP government, subjected to the December 17/25 major bribery and corruption investigation, immediately clung to the theses of the Sledgehammer and Ergenekon case defendants to cover up the investigation. It didn’t stop there; it turned to using the ‘parallel’ claim as a tool to purge public administration of those who don’t think like them, to oppress civil society, and to silence the opposition. McCarthyism and witch hunting peaked in Turkey. The ‘parallel’ claim extended to the absurdity of claiming that the Hizmet Movement was an ‘armed terrorist organization’ (like DAESH, PKK, DHKP-C, etc.).

“I understand very well those who cling to the ‘parallel’ claim to be cleansed of crime. What I have difficulty understanding is those who think they are protecting themselves from the AKP government’s wrath by clinging to it. Because it is certain that these people are aware of the following points: Crime is personal. If there is a suspect, they should be tried fairly and receive the punishment they deserve. But bringing people before courts established not to try them fairly but to convict them, with fabricated allegations, their being oppressed, pushed around, means the end of the rule of law… That people who know these things very well see no problem in aiding the destruction of the rule of law is another manifestation of the state of madness we are living in…” (Zaman, February 27, 2016)

## Last day at Zaman, last article

We did the last (477th) program of “Akıl Defteri,” which we had been conducting with Eser Karakaş and Mehmet Altan since 2006, on November 9, 2015. On November 15, all radio and television stations belonging to the Samanyolu group, including Mehtap TV, were removed from Türksat. On February 29, 2016, the broadcasts of Kanaltürk, Bugün TV, Bugün and Millet newspapers, and Kanaltürk Radio, which were under trustee management, were ended. On March 4, 2016, a trustee was appointed to Zaman. Anadolu Agency would report that this decision was made on the grounds that ‘there was strong evidence that the newspaper was being used within the scope of FETÖ/ Parallel State Structure’s activities and in a way to support organizational activities.’

I convey the subsequent developments from my notes:

On the night of March 3, I was feeling tired. Without looking at the news, I watched Beşiktaş’s 2-0 loss to Konya with annoyance and went to bed early. (Yet that day Cem Küçük and Abdurrahman Dilipak had written that Zaman would be seized.) On the morning of March 4, I woke up at 6 a.m. and until 8:30 a.m. reviewed the article titled ‘The wisdom of Herkül Millas,’ dealing with the issue of the Community’s transparency, to be published the next day. When I looked at email messages, I saw the message from page editor Buket Davulcu calling me to the newspaper. Then I read the headline story in Zaman titled “Trustee threat.” Around 9 a.m. Nazlı Ilıcak called, asking what was happening. I said I didn’t know; I advised her to call Abdülhamit Bilici. As usual, I took the Metrobus; I reached the Zaman building around 10:30. Buket said a trustee decision had been made about the newspaper, and it was unknown when the trustees would arrive. Then I went up to Bilici’s office: Mümtazer Türköne, Ahmet Turan Alkan, Bülent Keneş, Mehmet Kamış, Bülent Korucu, and, from Bugün, Nazlı Ilıcak and Turgay Oğur were there.

Morale was low. Bilici looked quite distressed. Alkan joked, “Now that Şahin Bey has come, the resistance is ready…” It was said the trustees might not come until their appointments appeared in the trade registry, and their arrival might be on Monday. I went downstairs and wrote a new article. I had managing editor Ali Akkuş read it: he said the sentence “President Erdoğan has become Turkey’s most dangerous person” could be dangerous. Upon learning that the trustees could arrive at any moment, I put the title on what was clearly going to be my last article: “Words don’t end.” I wrote:

## Words don’t end

“I am writing this article in the hours when Zaman Newspaper, where I have worked for 14 years and which is the fortress of free press in Turkey, faces the threat of being placed under trustee management and destroyed, just as happened to Bugün Newspaper before. Unfortunately, our great Turkey, our country that I dreamed would be a country where freedom and democracy reign, is being taken step by step toward a third world dictatorship. This is hard to believe!

“Unfortunately, it is so! While the AKP signed off on many reforms toward making Turkey a free and democratic country in its first two terms in power, I gave considerable support to Prime Minister Tayyip Erdoğan with my writings. I cannot help but be astonished that Mr. Erdoğan, as president, is managing the process of ruling all of Turkey alone; Turkey, which has behind it approximately two hundred years of rule of law and at least half a century of democratic accumulation; of reducing democracy to just elections; of destroying the rule of law at its root. However, if we close our eyes to the point Mr. Erdoğan has reached today and the impasse he has dragged the country into, we will have turned our backs on the principles and values we believe in.

“Mr. Erdoğan most recently says that the Constitutional Court violated the constitution by ruling that two journalists, Can Dündar and Erdem Gül, had suffered ‘rights violations.’ Admittedly, it is not an unseen thing in this country for the Constitutional Court to violate the constitution. My generation remembers as if it were yesterday that the Constitutional Court in this country bowed respectfully before the military administration that seized power through a coup. We also know that the current Constitutional Court played a role in the country reaching this point by approving the law concerning Criminal Peace Judgeships, which were established not to try fairly but to convict.

“However, I think that a legally compliant decision of the current Constitutional Court, which has no meaning beyond resulting in two journalists being tried without detention, being accused of ‘violating the constitution’ by a President who himself says ‘the constitution is on hold’ and that he is ‘effectively president’ rather than according to the constitution, is an event not encountered in any other country that could be considered a democracy to any degree. In a country claiming to be a democracy, the state’s seizure of the country’s best-selling, most-read newspaper, the fortress of freedom of expression, has never, ever been encountered.

“Unfortunately, Mr. President not only led the reversal of the gains of the first two terms of his government, but by excluding almost all of the founding cadres, he is transforming the AKP into a completely different party, the Tayyip Erdoğan Party. He turned his back on all the friendships he established while fighting against the enemies of democratization and won the friendship of his enemies. According to the constitution accepted by the people and the oath he took, the person who is supposed to represent all the people, who is expected to receive respect from everyone, viewing almost everyone who didn’t vote for him and who objects to the violation of law as an enemy, a traitor, must be one of the most dire situations that can befall a country. However, we are not at the point where words fail. We must say no to this direction that is taking our country toward the abyss. Turkey will not accept this direction.” (See: T24, March 5, 2016)

While we were waiting for the trustees, a crowd of readers and supporters, mostly community members, had begun to gather in the newspaper’s garden and in front. Administrators and writers were giving speeches to the crowd in the newspaper’s garden. I also got in line. Ali Bulaç addressed his former friends in the government, telling them to come to their senses; he warned supporters to conduct protests within the law. He spoke well. I also said in summary: “I am proud to have been writing for Zaman for 14 years. Zaman is the fortress of free press… In this country, we learn democracy and the value of freedoms by living them. We believed that the Erdoğan government would establish democracy in Turkey in its first two terms of power, and we supported it. The same government is taking the country toward a third world dictatorship. However, in a country at Turkey’s level of development, in Turkey which has 200 years of rule of law and 60-70 years of democracy experience, which is one of the oldest democracies in the world, it is not possible to establish an authoritarian regime. Every darkness ends with light…” Ali Bulaç said, “you spoke well.”

I went up to Bilici’s office again. I asked if there was any preparation for what to do after the closure. People had come to show solidarity with the newspaper: Orhan Birgit and Pınar Türenç from the Association were there. Photos were taken. I gave statements to Cihan News Agency and Can Erzincan TV. As Pınar Türenç was leaving, I went over to see her off. “We said from the beginning that things would come to this, but we couldn’t get through…” she said. She was implying that the support given to the AKP government was wrong. I didn’t say anything.

Around 6:30 p.m., I said goodbye to Bilici before leaving the newspaper with Ali Bulaç and Ahmet Turan Alkan. “Let’s not keep you any longer, brother,” he said. “Do I look very disheveled?…” he asked. I consoled him. As I was leaving the newspaper, I ran into Mehmet Kamış (one of the oldest acquaintances from the newspaper) at the entrance. “Don’t tell anyone, we have preparations for a new newspaper. This morning we talked with Sözcü and reached an agreement,” he said. After coming home and eating dinner, I watched on Can Erzincan TV the arrival of 4 CHP deputies at Zaman in solidarity; the police dispersing the crowd that had gathered in front of the newspaper around 10 p.m. with water cannons, tear gas, and smoke bombs, then breaking down the door and entering the newspaper around midnight.

Euronews reported the news as follows: “Police raided the building of Zaman Newspaper, one of Turkey’s leading media organizations. After the decision by Istanbul 6th Criminal Peace Judgeship to appoint a trustee to Feza Journalism, to which Zaman Newspaper belongs, riot police and police teams arrived in front of the newspaper building on Friday evening and clashed with newspaper employees and their relatives protesting the decision. Security forces, using pepper spray and water cannons to disperse the crowd, then broke through the chained doors and entered the building. Some journalists and photojournalists who resisted the police were removed.

“Zaman Newspaper Editor-in-Chief Abdülhamit Bilici is of the opinion that the decision is not legal but entirely political: ‘Unfortunately, for the last 3-4 years, those who speak against the government’s actions are either taken to court, imprisoned, or brought under government control. I think this is a dark process for our country and our democracy.’ On the other hand, the UK National Union of Journalists (NUJ) announced that they were ‘deeply concerned’ about the implemented decision. Zaman, Turkey’s best-selling newspaper with a circulation of 650,000, is known for its closeness to retired preacher Fethullah Gülen, founder of the Hizmet movement. It had been decided to appoint a trustee to Feza Journalism, which includes Zaman Newspaper, on the grounds that ‘there was strong evidence that it was being used within the scope of the Fethullahist Terrorist Organization / Parallel State Structure’s activities and in a way to support organizational activities.’”

# CHAPTER XVI / AFTER ZAMAN

Amid all these dramatic developments, Fatma’s health took a worrying turn. My beloved wife had been suffering from liver failure since 1986 and rheumatoid arthritis since 2000. After returning from our Far East trip, we began facing frequent episodes of her pulse racing. Several evenings we had to rush to Florence Nightingale Hospital, where medical interventions brought her pulse under control. When Fatma’s heart palpitations recurred in Izmir, where we were for her nephew Cenk’s wedding on March 18, we went to Alsancak State Hospital. Each time, injections would lower her pulse, but the episodes were becoming increasingly frequent.

When we returned to Istanbul, a friend strongly recommended that we consult Prof. Dr. Sabri Demircan from the Cardiovascular Diseases department at Florence Nightingale Hospital. Demircan had performed a procedure called ablation on our friend—entering the heart via catheter and burning specific tissues—achieving complete success in ending the palpitations. After examining Fatma, Demircan said he could succeed with 70 percent probability, not 100 percent, and Fatma decided without hesitation; she did not want to live with palpitations. On March 30, Fatma underwent the ablation procedure with very successful results. I was over the moon with happiness… I did not know how to thank Demircan enough…

We were leaving one problem behind only to face another. In early May 2016, we received news that Fatma’s elder sister Ayşe—three years her senior and our childhood friend—had undergone surgery at a private hospital in Izmir following a severe herniated disc crisis, so we flew to Izmir to visit her in the hospital. Unfortunately, Ayşe contracted what is called a “hospital infection”—a great misfortune for her and a shameful situation for the private hospital where she was staying—and passed away on May 16. This was another blow to Fatma’s morale.

“Why we could not establish democracy”

Starting from April 6, 2016, Zaman employees began publishing two daily newspapers, one named Yarına Bakış (Looking to Tomorrow) and the other Yeni Hayat (New Life). Upon invitation, I also began writing full-page articles once a week for Yarına Bakış starting April 21. Besides myself, Zaman writers such as Ali Bulaç, Hilmi Yavuz, Mümtazer Türköne, and Mustafa Ünal were contributing, along with renowned film critic Atilla Dorsay and constitutional law professor Levent Köker, who wrote for Yarına Bakış in solidarity with us.

In my first article titled “Why could we not establish democracy?”—a detailed analysis of the state the country had reached—I wrote:

“The Republic of Turkey transitioned to a multi-party system in 1950. It joined the Council of Europe in 1949 and NATO in 1952. It ratified the European Convention on Human Rights in 1954; in 1987 it recognized its citizens’ right to individual petition to the European Court of Human Rights; in 1990 it accepted the compulsory jurisdiction of the ECtHR. It signed an association agreement with the EEC in 1963; became an EU candidate in 1999; and began accession negotiations in 2005… Through this process that began at the end of World War II, under civilian governments ranging from the DP (Democrat Party) to the AKP (Justice and Development Party), Turkey became part of almost all international organizations formed by liberal democracies. Despite interruptions by military coups, we went through approximately 70 years of democratic experience during which restrictions on fundamental rights and freedoms gradually diminished.

“However, since the 2011 elections, Turkey has rapidly moved away from being a regime that could be called a democracy. It has become impossible to speak of rule of law, separation of powers, or judicial independence. All fundamental rights and freedoms—from freedom of expression, press, association, and belief to property and enterprise rights—are being trampled underfoot. Even elections have ceased to be fair. The ruling AKP is steering the country toward a one-man, one-party government with President Tayyip Erdoğan as its head. The country faces not only the danger of falling entirely under autocratic rule but also increasing instability and fragmentation.

“As citizens concerned about how we can stop this trajectory and get liberal and pluralist democracy back on track, we must reflect on these questions: Why could we not establish democracy and make it irreversible? How is it that despite all the democratization steps actually taken, we have arrived at where we are today? There are two main answers to these questions. One emphasizes ‘culture.’ According to nationalists (Ulusalcılar), socialists, and others who share an authoritarian understanding of secularism, the answer is roughly this: Religions in general, and Islam in particular, are incompatible with modernization, secularism (separation of religion and state), and democracy. This is because Islamic values do not instill respect for individual rights and diversity, which are necessary for democracy to take root. For this reason, democratic regimes that secure both elected government and fundamental rights and freedoms could not be established in Muslim-majority countries. In Turkey too, democracy essentially cannot take root for this reason.

“According to secular nationalists or Kemalists, without an authoritarian secularism of the kind envisioned by the Republic’s founding philosophy—where the state holds religion (Islam) under its monopoly and control and imposes restrictions on religious freedoms—neither secularism nor democracy can be institutionalized in Turkey. Only a democracy under the tutelage of military and civilian bureaucracy committed to Kemalism’s fundamental principles can survive. The ‘Islamist’ AKP boarded the democracy train in its first two terms to consolidate its power and push back the military tutelage it saw as an obstacle, but it got off the train when it judged that it had achieved its goal.

“The following main objections can be raised against the thesis summarized above—that democracy could not take root because of the people’s Islamic culture: No religion is compatible with secularism or democracy in theory, but interpretations compatible with both secularism and democracy in practice have been developed for all of them (including Islam). Except for fundamentalist Sunni Saudi Arabia and fundamentalist Shia Iran, the rest of the Muslim-majority states, including Turkey, were governed not by Islamic but by secular nationalist authoritarian regimes. Islamists, who claimed to bring an order that would be an alternative to capitalism and communism, tried but could not come to power in any of them. The reason these countries could not establish democratic regimes should be sought not in religion but in the perception of democracy as a colonial imposition and in subsoil resources feeding autocratic regimes.

“The findings of the World Values Survey indicate that prevalent values in Muslim-majority countries (except for gender equality) are not different from those in Western countries. Turkey, which took steps toward the rule of law and constitutional government in the 19th century, certainly has a unique place among Muslim-majority countries. In Turkey, Sufi (flexible, popular) interpretations of Islam rather than Salafi (fundamentalist) interpretations maintain their prevalence. Whether the values related to disrespect for diversity observed in some studies originate from Islam or from secular nationalist ideology is also quite debatable. If we look at our multi-party history, we see that parties defending citizens’ fundamental rights and freedoms received great support, and when they turned their backs on these, they gradually disappeared.

“The main examples are Menderes’s DP, Demirel’s AP (Justice Party), Ecevit’s CHP (Republican People’s Party) and DSP (Democratic Left Party), and Özal’s ANAP (Motherland Party). All major ruling parties came to power with promises of rights and freedoms. The AKP also came to power not because it was Islamist or promised one-man rule, but because it promised to establish a liberal and pluralist democracy, to end the military tutelage system that suppressed fundamental rights and freedoms, and to achieve EU membership. It owes the preservation of its power today not to being Islamist but to the services it rendered in both the economy and democracy during its first two terms in power. It should not be forgotten that support for EU membership in Muslim-majority Turkey climbed to 70 percent during the 2004-2005 period.

“The other, much more convincing answer to the question of why we could not establish a democratic regime emphasizes ‘institutional structure.’ According to this perspective, mostly shared by liberals, the problems stem from the failure of institutions that secure the rule of law, human rights, respect for minorities, and market economy to achieve stability. The reason for this should be sought essentially in the insistence on the founding principles of the Republic, which were designed for an authoritarian regime. The authoritarian mentality that we see becoming dominant again today draws its source from the single-party era. The roots of the mindset that equates opposition with treason and fuels intolerance of civil society are there. The origin of the understanding that restricts freedom of belief (both believing and not believing) and places religion under the monopoly and control of the state (the Diyanet, the Directorate of Religious Affairs) is there. The origin of disrespect for different religious and ethnic identities, and of the policies still insisted upon today—Turkifying Kurds, Sunnifying Alevis, keeping Sufis (Sufi orders and communities) under pressure—is also there.

“These were also the fundamental principles on which the military tutelage order that persisted throughout the second half of the 20th century was based. The AKP government set out with the promise of establishing the (universal) Copenhagen criteria, but turned its back on these criteria essentially as a result of prolonged absolute power corrupting absolutely. It is ultimately paying the price for this by surrendering to the ‘national and domestic’ Ankara criteria of the military-bureaucratic tutelage order. The discourse that the AKP is ‘Islamist’ is extremely misleading. The essential character of the AKP government is that it is nothing but a political and economic alliance of interests that, beneath a demagogic Islamic discourse on the surface, clings tightly to Kemalist policies at its core.

“Until now, no government that turned its back on citizens’ fundamental rights and freedoms could stay standing. This is also true for the AKP government. The first signs of this were seen in the June 7, 2015 elections. However, the AKP managed to monopolize power again by embracing Kemalist nationalism and by leaving the people facing instability and security concerns. But power protected in this way has a limited lifespan. On the other hand, we must understand that in order to establish democracy with its universal standards, not only the military-bureaucratic tutelage based on a minority but also the majority dictatorship that comes to power through elections must be defeated at the ballot box, by the people’s vote. This should be the next goal of struggle for those who believe in freedom.” (April 21, 2016)

In my second article published in Yarına Bakış, I referenced the recently published articles by Prof. Dr. Kemal Gözler, one of our leading constitutional law scholars whom I greatly admire, which listed the constitutional violations by the AKP government that had turned Turkey into a country where rule of law and democracy could not be spoken of. (“How was the Constitution shelved?”, April 28, 2016) The article by Gözler, a faculty member at Uludağ University, was so apt that I felt the need to get his phone number from his colleague and friend Prof. Ergun Özbudun to thank him. I called to congratulate him and said that it would be an honor for me to meet him. Gözler’s reply—that he had been following my writings for years and that it would actually be his honor to meet me—greatly pleased me. Gözler’s words were one of the most valuable rewards I received throughout my column-writing career.

## He finished off the party, the state is next

I maintained optimism in my articles published in Yarına Bakış. In the article titled “He finished off the party, the state is next,” I wrote: “Prime Minister Davutoğlu being forced to resign last week can be seen as the completion of Erdoğan’s project to turn the AKP into an ‘Erdoğan party’ under his absolute dominion… Yes, the task of turning the AKP into an ‘Erdoğan party’ has been completed, but there is still a way to go in turning Turkey into an ‘Erdoğan state.’” (May 12, 2016)

I also ended the article in which I asked “Why is the AKP still in power?” as follows: “The point where the AKP government is mistaken is this: ‘You can fool some of the people all of the time, and all of the people some of the time; but you cannot fool all of the people all of the time…’ It is not possible to keep the people asleep for long through brainwashing, or to hide the truth from the people for long. Governance by decrees coming from one person’s lips is doomed to failure always and everywhere. In Turkey, the fraud of bad governance has always, sooner or later, been exposed. The unsustainability of one-man rule will also be seen by the great majority sooner or later.” (May 19, 2016)

In the next article titled “How will the one-man state be prevented?”, I expressed the tough struggle that must be waged for Turkey to achieve liberal democracy: “Yes, the drift toward a one-man state is a great danger for what remains of democracy and for Turkey as we know it. We can only prevent this danger by mobilizing democratic means, by waging a struggle for democracy, and we must prevent it. Only when we defeat one-man rule—which is essentially a majority dictatorship—through the struggle for democracy, just as with the military tutelage regime—which is essentially a minority dictatorship—will it be possible to establish liberal and pluralist democracy.” (May 26, 2016)

In my next article titled “Erdoğan’s party and nation,” I expressed my conclusion about the nature of the AKP: “No, do not deceive yourselves: The Erdoğan (or the Chief’s) party, resembling neither the RP (Welfare Party) nor the AKP, having no goal other than preserving and perpetuating power, is not ideological but an opportunistic political and economic partnership of interests. It uses Islamist and Ottomanist discourse as seasoning, but it is not ‘Islamist, Ottomanist.’ If one insists on attributing an ideological quality to it, the Erdoğan party can be characterized as a ‘Religious (Sunni) Nationalist’ party. It embraces conservative Sunni Kurds but excludes other Kurds; it leaves Alevis out altogether. What the Erdoğan party calls ‘the nation’ consists only of those who vote for it.” (July 7, 2016)

## The one-man’s guarantee, the opposition’s wretchedness

In my final article titled “The one-man’s guarantee, the opposition’s wretchedness,” published one day before the July 15 coup attempt, I wrote:

“Except for June 7, 2015, the Erdoğan party, the AKP, won all elections since November 2002. On November 1, 2015, it regained the single-party government it had lost on June 7, through tactics of lies and intimidation (‘if I go, military tutelage will be resurrected; terror will increase, stability will be lost, there will be chaos’). If it dares, it will make the ‘Turkish-style’ presidential system (that is, one-man rule or autocracy) constitutional by renewing elections and/or through a referendum; if it does not dare, it will manage with the ‘Suspended constitution + De facto Presidency’ system. Indeed, one of the leading spokespeople of the one-man government declared: ‘No elections until 2019…’ It is being said that the possibility of changing government through elections has been reduced to zero. Not without justification, either…

“The one-man regime consolidated its alliance with the military tutelage advocates. (Doğu Perinçek declared the obvious: ‘Erdoğan has been captured by patriotic forces… He has surrendered to Kemalism…’) Nowadays, in accordance with its sole principle of ‘preserving and perpetuating power,’ it is putting new practices into effect. Some of these are: In the purging, under the ‘parallel’ nonsense, of public servants ‘incompatible with the government,’ the turn has now come to the TSK (Turkish Armed Forces). The judiciary is about to be made completely compatible with the government. According to the CHP leader, ‘judges are being summoned to the Palace at 03:00 in the morning…’

There will be no way to distinguish anymore whether the alleged crimes are real or fabricated. The print and visual media, with very few exceptions, were under the government’s control; now it is the turn of internet newspapers; they are being blacked out not by court decision but by prime ministry decree. (…)

“The factor that serves to keep the one-man regime standing, perhaps as effective as those listed above, is the wretchedness of the opposition. There are developments on that front as well. This wretchedness relates above all to the opposition parties’ inability to come together, to unite their forces, even to defend democracy (which is also the guarantee of their own survival). The second dimension of the wretchedness is that each of them is afflicted with internal divisions that are difficult to heal.

“Let us start with the MHP (Nationalist Movement Party): The Devlet Bahçeli leadership, knowingly or unknowingly, had opened the way to power for the AKP in 2002. Since last year, it has virtually been functioning as the AKP’s ‘Trojan horse.’ On June 7, it knowingly and willingly sabotaged the opportunity to get rid of one-man rule; on November 1, the party’s number of deputies was halved. To maintain its dominance, it tried open cooperation with the AKP, coalition flirtation. Now that the party majority has revolted against the slide below the threshold, it is trying to intimidate its opponents with the now thoroughly vulgarized ‘parallel’ nonsense; it is preventing the party congress from meeting with the support of the ‘compliant judiciary’; now the turn has come to expelling the dissidents.

“The revolt that broke out within the MHP, which until recently appeared to be Turkey’s most one-man party, is undoubtedly a sign that politics in Turkey maintains its vitality despite everything. As long as it cannot escape from the leader’s autocracy, the MHP will certainly continue to be one of the fundamental guarantees of Erdoğan’s power. Otherwise, could the MHP escape from being condemned to its marginal role limited to ethnic Turkish nationalism, assume a conservative party identity that resolutely defends democracy and the rule of law, and take on a more effective role in politics? This is certainly one of the most noteworthy questions regarding the future of Turkish politics. (Looking from today, it can be said that these lines foresaw the MHP - İyi Party split.)

“Perhaps since the 1960s when the ‘Left of Center’ movement emerged, the CHP continues to be captive to the tension between the ‘Ulusalcılar’ (secularist nationalists) who favor military-bureaucratic tutelage and authoritarian secularism and oppose the West on one side, and those who envision rebuilding the CHP as a social democratic party by Western standards on the other. This tension is also reflected in civil society organizations and media close to the party. (At Cumhuriyet, the disagreement that emerged in the 1980s between those who want to make it a liberal left-leaning newspaper of record that everyone can safely read and those who advocate clinging tightly to the role of spokesperson for ‘Ulusalcılık’ has flared up again.) This tension prevents the CHP from playing an effective role in national politics. There are indications that the MHP might escape from its ‘Trojan horse’ role, but there is yet no sign that the CHP can escape from the tension that holds it captive. As long as this situation continues, the CHP will certainly continue to be another insurance policy for Erdoğan’s power.

“The HDP (Peoples’ Democratic Party), which is the most feared opponent of the one-man government, has also fallen victim to the ‘confusion’ within the Kurdish political movement. HDP deputy Altan Tan best diagnosed the confusion revived by the escalating clashes between security forces and the PKK (Kurdistan Workers’ Party) since last July: ‘Are we going to establish a new democratic Republic of Turkey, or are we going to be divided by fighting, clashing, separating? Are we going to envision a Turkey and Middle East within the EU and Western bloc, or a Middle East on the Russia-Iran axis? Democratic autonomy: Are we going to achieve this with weapons, by fighting, by digging trenches, or by talking with Ankara, by making a new constitution?’ (Hürriyet, September 2, 2015) It is crystal clear that the Kurdish political movement settling on the first choices would lead Turkey toward democratization, while the second choices would lead to division.

“It is seen that some civil society organizations are making efforts to form a ‘Democracy Front’ against the autocratic regime and fragmentation that Erdoğan’s party is leading Turkey toward. For these initiatives to yield any results, as (former ECtHR judge and former CHP deputy) Rıza Türmen said, a union of forces must be realized in which ‘everyone without distinction who objects to the AKP’ participates and ‘differences are preserved.’ (A good example of this was given by those who ran the ‘Did you know: Journalism is not a crime…’ campaign.) Otherwise, it would take no prophet to say that nothing will come of these initiatives.”

The article concluded as follows: “The Ulusalcılar may be making calls for a return to military tutelage. However, military tutelage was tried in this country for many years; ultimately it paved the way for the disaster we face today. Our only way out is the struggle for liberal and pluralist democracy against autocracy. One hope still remains: a revival movement that could be initiated within the AKP for a return to the party’s ‘factory settings’ (the party program).” (July 14, 2016)

This article, which confirmed my stance against military rule, military intervention in politics, and military tutelage—positions I had maintained throughout almost my entire intellectual life—would, very ironically, be my last article before being locked up in Silivri on charges of supporting the July 15 coup attempt. One of the grounds on which the Constitutional Court’s ruling that characterized my detention as a rights violation was based would be the final paragraph of this article (which I have underlined).

# CHAPTER XVII / JULY 15 AND SİLİVRİ

I spent most of July with Fatma in Ayvalık. On the night of July 15, 2016, feeling tired, I wanted to go to bed early, around 10 PM. I had just lain down when Fatma got me up, saying, “Something is happening in Ankara…” The television was broadcasting news and footage of what appeared to be a thoroughly unconvincing military coup attempt. Soldiers had blocked the crossing from Asia to Europe on the Bosphorus Bridge, but traffic continued in the other direction. It was a very strange situation… I called Hasan Cemal, Eser Karakaş, and Seyfettin Gürsel; they knew no more than I did. My son Acar kept calling from İstanbul, asking what was happening. A friend calling from Ankara had arrived at Esenboğa Airport to fly to Edremit, but the plane was not taking off for unknown reasons. Others were calling too, asking: “What’s going on?…” I had no idea. After a while, when President Erdoğan appeared on television calling the people to take to the streets “against the coup attempt by FETÖ traitors,” I began to sense what was unfolding. The funeral prayers recited from the mosque right next to us until the early hours of morning—for those killed in the clashes in İstanbul and Ankara—created a demoralizing atmosphere unlike anything we had ever experienced. I was sleepy; I went to bed and slept.

In the early hours of July 16, we watched the news that “FETÖ’s coup attempt had been suppressed and Prime Minister Erdoğan was safe.” This bore no resemblance to any coup attempt we had known. And somehow it did not seem convincing. The news and commentary in the foreign press pointed in the same direction. When I went out in the morning to buy newspapers, I ran into a couple who had been planning to pay us a condolence visit that day on account of my sister-in-law’s death. I gathered they had cancelled the visit. As someone put it, on the night of July 15, “not only Turkey but the world had changed…” Looking at the newspapers, questions began swirling in my mind: Had Gülenist soldiers attempted a coup together with Kemalist and other opposition soldiers? Or was this a conspiracy against the Movement? Pro-government websites were writing that “members of FETÖ’s media wing” would be arrested, and my name was among them. It was plain as day that something was going to happen to me.

The evening before, we had arranged to meet Ayhan Aktar and Heath Lowry in Cunda. Sensing what was coming for me, they too were in low spirits; we cut the dinner and drinks short. I was receiving the news rather naively: “Yes, they might detain me, but it won’t last long,” I kept telling myself—and Fatma, who was anxious but maintained her usual composure with a “whatever will be, will be” attitude… If they were going to take me, it would be better for me to be in İstanbul. Besides, Fatma had doctor’s appointments.

When we arrived at Edremit airport on July 18 to fly to İstanbul, we were both wondering whether I would be able to board the plane. When I passed through the identity check without a hitch, we understood that the probable arrest warrant had not yet been put into effect. At least we would travel to İstanbul in peace. On the plane, we shared our troubles. How many times throughout our life together had I found myself in situations like this, where I did not feel safe.

Upon arriving in İstanbul, thinking I might be detained for a few months, I began making urgent visits to my doctors. One of them tried to console me, saying I would be locked up for a while but that this government could not last long. Another was of the opinion that Turkey had “entered a dark period that would last at least ten years.” (It has already been six years…) Fatma was going to see her doctor, my close friend Hasan Yazıcı. We went together. Hasan had just returned from Ankara; he was quite anxious. When he expressed the wish, “I hope you won’t be inside for too long…” we said goodbye with shared laughter. As we were leaving, Nazlı Ilıcak called from Bodrum, where she was staying, to ask what had happened to the newspapers we wrote columns for. Both had ceased publication. Ilıcak was even more naive in her outlook than I was. She said she had cancelled her planned trip to the Greek island across from Bodrum so that people would not say she had “fled.” “Don’t worry, my dear Şahin, Turkey changes quickly…” she said. The next day we watched the news of her detention in Bodrum. I called a lawyer friend to ask whether he could take on my representation; upon his positive reply, I had a power of attorney drawn up at the notary and mailed it to his address. When Sweden’s Consul General in İstanbul called to say it would be useful for us to meet, I went to see him. “The situation looks concerning. If you want to go to Sweden, we will support you there. If you prefer, you can also take refuge here, at the consulate…” he said. In reply, I said, “I am not thinking of going to Sweden or taking refuge at the consulate. In either case, they would take my family hostage… Even if I am arrested, I do not think I will be held for long…”

Once we had finished our business, we decided to return to Ayvalık via Edremit on the 2:20 PM flight on July 26, 2016. On the night of July 25, Fatma and I stuffed all the Fethullah Gülen books in my library into bags and threw them into the garbage containers a few streets away. Then, for a reason I cannot recall, we had to postpone the flight by one day. As it turned out, this was fortunate timing. On the morning of July 27, around 6 AM, three plainclothes police officers—one of them a captain—from Counter-Terrorism came and informed me that I was to be detained by court order. They did not search the house thoroughly. They confiscated my laptop, my desktop computer’s hard drive, my tablet, and my mobile phone. They had our building superintendent and his wife sign a report about what had taken place. One of the officers asked, with a touch of irony—or perhaps not really expecting it—whether I had any “one-dollar bills” on me. As I was leaving the house, Fatma showed her usual thoughtfulness; she pressed into my hands a bag containing the CPAP breathing device I had been using for twenty years on account of my sleep apnea, a blood pressure monitor, and the medications I took regularly. We said goodbye in the belief that our separation would not be long. We were wrong… During my detention, which would last far longer than we expected, I would come to appreciate the true worth of that bag.

I was put into a police car after passing through the courtyard of my apartment building, where reporters and plainclothes officers were taking photographs and shooting video. I remember calling out to the cameras recording my removal from home, “I have committed no crime!” (That footage would appear on screens countless times on various occasions.) In the police car taking us to the Gayrettepe Police Public Order Division, the captain returned my wallet along with the Metropolitan Municipality’s Free Transportation Card inside it, saying I would need it on the way home—which I took as a sign that he was overly optimistic about what lay ahead for me. (I should note here that throughout my life, the police officers I dealt with never thought the charges attributed to me suited me…) At the Public Order Division, before I was stuffed into barred compartments, they took away the belongings I had brought with me. By begging and pleading, saying I would die if I was not allowed to use it, I managed to keep my CPAP device: however, even though they were kind enough to provide an extension cord so I could plug it in, it would prove impossible for me to actually use the device. (That day, Fatma and my daughter Elvan had somehow learned that I had been taken to the Public Order Division and came there hoping to see me. Naturally, this would not be possible.)

When I arrived there, I recognized no one among the few people I saw. But as the hours passed, those we had expected to join us turned up one by one. Reporters from Zaman and the Cihan News Agency, along with many others, were brought in. Over a hundred of us were crammed into three small rooms; we sat on the floor, we lay on the floor and slept. We staved off our hunger with food we would never have touched under other circumstances. Ali Bulaç, Mümtaz’er Türköne, and Ahmet Turan Alkan—who had been brought from Bursa—ended up in the same room with me. We learned that Nazlı Ilıcak, Nuriye (Akman) Ural, and Lale Kemal were in the women’s detention facility in the adjacent building. Those detained at the Public Order Division were not only Zaman group employees. The number of people brought in kept growing, and the barred rooms became packed to capacity. Morale was low, but we tried not to show it, getting by through conversation.

The next day, July 28, Hilmi Yavuz, İhsan Dağı—brought from Ankara—Lale Kemal, and Mustafa Ünal (the Zaman bureau chief) also joined us. We were taken to Şişli Etfal Hospital for medical examinations. When we were brought out of Gayrettepe Public Order Division, we were led down the stairs handcuffed behind our backs, to be displayed for the press photographers waiting outside. (This was how I first made the acquaintance of the handcuffs that would be clamped onto my wrists every time I was taken out of Section 9 of Silivri prison, where I would spend approximately twenty months.) When my blood pressure was found to have risen to 220 at Şişli Etfal, I was given a sedative injection in the hip. When Ali Bulaç’s blood sugar spiked—he had had quadruple bypass surgery—he was made to rest for a while. That evening, eighty-year-old Hilmi Yavuz fell ill and was taken to the hospital; the next morning we learned he had been released thanks to the intervention of Culture and Tourism Minister Nabi Avcı. (I could not help wondering why Avcı—with whom I had quite an old and friendly relationship, and who had once remarked to me about the AKP government, “We have boarded an omen, heading for doomsday”—had not also secured my release.) As I learned after my own release, when a mutual friend of ours called Interior Minister Süleyman Soylu to ask why I had been detained, the answer he received was: “In these extraordinary circumstances, naturally the green wood burns along with the dry…” On July 29, we Zaman writers were put into a minibus without handcuffs and taken to Haseki Research Hospital on Vatan Avenue. There we underwent a psychological examination by a very kind female doctor. (That day, Fatma and Elvan had somehow learned where we had been taken and went there to hand over a bag full of clothes to the police to give to me. But that bag would never reach me.)

On the morning of July 30, we Zaman writers were taken to the Counter-Terrorism Division on Vatan Avenue—all except Mümtaz’er Türköne, for reasons we could not understand. As we were leaving Gayrettepe Public Order Division, a young plainclothes officer approached me and said I would be released. (Mümtaz’er, too, had seen me off saying, “You’ll celebrate your release tonight, brother…”) But, in truth, I was not hopeful at all. I thought I would be arrested and spend a few months in prison. After being hosted for a time in a private room at Vatan with offerings of tea, we were taken one by one for police interrogation. On our way, we saw that the detention ward cells were packed full of people staring at us anxiously. During my interrogation, a young female lawyer appointed by the İstanbul Bar Association was present, but she did not utter a word. A quite courteous plainclothes police official took my statement.

During the interrogation, I was taken aback when words I had uttered months earlier on the commentary program “Akıl Defteri” (Notebook of Reason)—which we did with Mehmet Altan and Eser Karakaş on Mehtap TV—were presented as though they had been spoken in July 2016. I had said them in utter astonishment upon first hearing the “FETÖ” allegation, to the effect of: “Fethullah Gülen is the world’s most peaceful Islamic scholar—how can he be a terrorist?…” Questions were put to me such as, “Did you know Fethullah Gülen? From whom were you receiving orders?…” The interrogating police officer said, “You may not believe it, but the Gülenists are a secret organization…” When he told another plainclothes officer, “We are not planning to hold these elderly ones for long—we will transfer them to Çağlayan,” we understood that we would be brought before a judge that very evening.

And indeed, in the evening hours we were taken to Çağlayan. First we were placed in the detention facility seven floors below the “Palace of Justice.” While waiting there, we tried to analyze what had happened to Turkey and to us. According to İhsan Dağı, from now on Turkey would follow China’s model, establishing a regime that provided bread but granted no freedom, and would gradually distance itself from the West. I objected: Turkey had no oil, unlike Russia or Iran. Its economy depended to a great extent on investment from the West and exports to the West. How could it leave NATO or the Council of Europe?… Ali Bulaç agreed with me: “Two hundred years of Westernization cannot be thrown in the trash,” he said. (Six years later, the answer to this question remains unclear.)

After a while, we were brought up to the 4th Criminal Court of Peace on one of the upper floors. Nazlı Ilıcak, Nuriye Akman, and Lale Kemal were also there. The lawyer Veysel Ok, whom the Platform for Independent Journalism (P24) had assigned for my defense, was waiting there. He told me that my wife Fatma and my children Elvan and Acar were waiting at the entrance to the building but had not been allowed inside. We gave our statements one by one to the judge of the 4th Criminal Court of Peace. In summary, I stated who I was; that until now I had only been able to see the positive face of the Movement; that I had contributed to the newspaper Zaman as an outside columnist; that throughout my career as a writer I had opposed military coups and the military’s role in politics; that I condemned everyone who had been involved in the July 15 coup attempt; and that a great evil had been inflicted upon the country.

While we waited for the decision, the lawyer Veysel Ok told me I might be released under judicial supervision, but I did not think it likely. The judge’s demeanor made us feel we would be arrested. One of the lawyers there voiced his pessimism: “Mr. Şahin, why did you come back from Sweden?…” And indeed, only İhsan Dağı—who had stopped writing for Zaman months earlier, alarmed by the way things were going—was released at the prosecutor’s request, while the rest of us were placed under arrest. Nazlı Ilıcak, Lale Kemal, and Nuriye Akman were taken to the women’s prison in Bakırköy; we reached Silivri prison in the early hours of July 31. We were processed and registered. I was deeply relieved that I was allowed to take the breathing device (CPAP), the blood pressure monitor, and the medication box from my bag into the cell. Ali Bulaç, Ahmet Turan Alkan, Mustafa Ünal, and I spent the first two nights together in a temporary cell. An elderly corrections officer treated us very well; he even brought a small table into the cell for me to set my CPAP on. On one hand, I was relieved to have escaped the detention facility where we had been held in dreadful conditions and to have been brought to Silivri; on the other, my heart grew heavy knowing I would be separated from Fatma, my children, and my grandchildren for a time.

On the morning of August 1, we were distributed among the cells of Section 9, which we had heard would hold three persons each. Ali Bulaç and I were placed in Block C5, Room 34; Ahmet T. Alkan and Mustafa Ünal were sent to a different cell. Since there was so much to talk about with him, I was very glad to be together with Bulaç. From here on, you can find—in the section that follows—the diary I kept almost every day for approximately twenty months, from August 3, 2016—the first day we were able to buy notebooks and pens from the canteen—until March 16, 2018.

# CHAPTER XVIII / THE LAST SIX MONTHS WITH FATMA

On March 17, 2018, around 2:30 in the morning, I was released from Silivri prison, where I had been detained for 20 months (600 days), to house arrest. A prison vehicle dropped me off at an intersection a few kilometers from the prison, where my wife Fatma, my daughter Elvan, my granddaughter Defne, as well as some news agency reporters were waiting. I embraced my loved ones… I had missed them so much…

Karin Karakasli, in her article published a few days later, inspired by the photograph of my reunion with my wife, wrote the following:

“Detained journalist Sahin Alpay, for whom the Constitutional Court ruled a rights violation for the second time, was released by Istanbul 13th High Criminal Court with a house arrest decision after 20 months of detention. The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) also ruled that Sahin Alpay and journalist and writer Mehmet Altan’s ‘rights to liberty, security, and freedom of expression were violated.’

After being released, Alpay, reunited with his family at the prison exit, expressed the common sentiment of many detainees: ‘I am extremely happy to be reunited with my family, but I cannot say I have regained my freedom. The 20 months were very difficult. Now that I am out, there are still thousands of people left behind who have no connection to terrorism or the coup. I believe that as long as they are not free, Turkey cannot be free either.’

Freedom is something else entirely. It exists in the necessity and naturalness of bread and water. Something that does not disappear with imprisonment, nor is regained by release. Connected to justice by an umbilical cord. For some of us.

Then a photograph came into my hands. A photograph of Mr. Sahin and his wife Mrs. Fatma… They are looking at each other. Deep into each other’s eyes. An indescribable smile on Mrs. Fatma’s face. The projection of a hardship that had to be overcome in a companionship tested by years. And something else. That nobility on Mrs. Fatma’s face. That thing which has now gone out of circulation, considered almost a hindrance rather than a moral value. A story of an era. Knowledge of old times, different places. A refinement. Something no school could teach…” (“What photographs tell us to see…”, Gazete Duvar, March 22, 2018)

Infinite thanks to Karin Karakasli for this article describing the great joy of reuniting with my loved ones and Fatma’s nobility.

A day or two after my release, my son Acar, my daughter-in-law Gokce, and my granddaughter Leyla, who was then only 3.5 years old, came from London where they had settled, adding joy to my happiness. As a family, we were able to come together for the first time in 20 months, even if only for a few days. I will never forget Leyla running and throwing her arms around my neck. The only other day in my life when I was this filled with joy was in January 1974, when Fatma came to Stockholm, where I had been living as an exile/refugee since November 1972, together with my daughter Elvan, whom I hadn’t seen for 3 years and who was 6 years old at the time.

House arrest meant, as the police officers at the Etiler station strictly warned, that I could not step outside the door of our apartment without permission from the court. From the first day of my house arrest, relatives and friends came to visit me in droves. We hosted them in three shifts: before noon, afternoon, and evening… As a result of consuming not only Fatma’s cooking that I had missed so much, but also the foods brought by visitors that I had longed for, I went from 84 kilos when I left Silivri to 93 kilos by the end of my house arrest.

Many friends, including those I hadn’t seen for years, even those I hadn’t been in touch with for a long time for various (now seemingly ridiculous) reasons, set aside past meaningless disputes and came to see me. The “get well” phone calls from CHP (Republican People’s Party) Chairman Mr. Kemal Kilicdaroglu and President Mr. Abdullah Gul greatly pleased me. Swedish Ambassador Lars Wahlund and Sweden’s Istanbul Consul General Therese Hyden, who attended all the hearings in my trial and to whom I owe gratitude, also visited our home.

When I left home with court permission for doctor visits for health checkups, I received “get well” wishes on the streets and in hospitals from many citizens I didn’t know. The solidarity I witnessed from society gave me the feeling that the great injustice I suffered—being accused of terrorism and coup involvement and imprisoned for nearly two years—was condemned in the public conscience; it consoled me to some extent.

During the house arrest days, the police officers, who behaved quite respectfully, came every evening to get my signature. Fatma always offered them a small treat (chocolate, Turkish delight, small pastries). Once when they came after midnight, after I had gone to bed, she scolded them: “If you come this late again, I won’t open the door!” and made them laugh too. We recalled the jokes of her late mother Leman Kaptan, who was originally from Surmene.

Fatma forbade me from talking about the days left behind or the possibility of being detained and imprisoned again. “From now on we will look forward and spend our remaining years thinking only of each other…” she said. I in turn promised her that from now on I would never disobey her, that I would never leave her side. We were finally together… The photograph that Elvan took, of Fatma and me holding hands, I think reflects our feelings in those days well.

Fatma told me about the fraud attempts she had experienced in my absence. Starting from November 2017, two people who introduced themselves as a prosecutor and a police captain began calling her by phone. They told her they could get me out of prison, but strictly warned her not to tell anyone about it, not even her children. Somehow, Fatma too (like a drowning person clutching at a snake) believed them, until they asked her to mortgage her olive groves in Ayvalik in exchange for these “services,” at which point she woke up and cut off contact with them… The fraud attempts didn’t end there. A person who presented himself on the phone as a Court of Cassation examining judge whom I knew, frequently called Fatma with promises of getting me out of prison. As Fatma told me these things, she was angry at herself, remembering how she had laughed at me years ago when she learned about the fraud attempt where someone playing the role of police and prosecutor had tried to swindle thousands of liras from me.

Undoubtedly, what was truly thought-provoking and instructive here was how widespread in Turkey’s society were these conscienceless people who felt no shame in trying to extort money by exploiting the vulnerabilities of suffering families.

The third hearing of the case in which I was being tried was held on April 5-6, 2018, in a courtroom in Silivri. In addition to Fatma and Elvan, my son Acar, who took three days off and came from London, also attended this hearing. This was my last trip to Silivri; because subsequent hearings (fortunately) were moved to the “Justice Palace” in Caglayan. At the fourth hearing held on May 10-11, 2018, we welcomed the lifting of house arrest with great joy!
