Instead, a requirement to sign in at the nearest police station on Sundays was imposed, but being able to go out on the street without court permission now felt like a step toward freedom.

My first task was to call Utku Cakirozer, a CHP parliamentarian and journalist colleague whom I greatly admired and loved, who had visited me in Silivri at least 5-6 times, to ask him when I could make a thank-you visit to him and Mr. Kilicdaroglu. Mr. Kemal had greatly boosted our morale by voicing the injustices done to us writers in group speeches and at almost every opportunity from the first days of our detention; he had made us feel that we were not alone. I have deep respect for him both for standing up for the rule of law and for this reason.

Cakirozer and I agreed to meet at the Turkish Grand National Assembly on Tuesday, May 15. We would have lunch at the parliament restaurant at 12:00, then go up to see Mr. Kemal before the group speech. At the restaurant, we ran into Adnan Keskin (whom I had met in 1993 when I was working as an advisor to the CHP chairman, and who was the party’s general secretary at the time). Mr. Adnan, bless him, immediately invited us to his table. Later, CHP parliamentarians Sezgin Tanrikulu and Musa Cam, who had long been my friends, also came and joined us. During the meal, some other CHP parliamentarians came to our table and said “get well.” Then we went up to see Mr. Kemal.

Kilicdaroglu greeted me by saying, “Welcome, you honor us…” (In his office, I met and embraced Deputy Group Chairman Ozgur Ozel.) During my visit, we took a photograph with Mr. Kemal and had a brief conversation. I conveyed my gratitude to him; I told him that our hope for the restoration of democracy and the rule of law lay with him. As Mr. Kemal was leaving us to attend the group meeting, Cakirozer told me, “It would be better if you don’t come; there are people there who don’t like you…” I interpreted this as a reflection of the state the CHP was in. I said goodbye to Cakirozer as well and returned to Istanbul that evening.

Between May 28-31, we had a wonderful vacation, simply marvelous, organized by Elvan. Fatma, Elvan, my granddaughter Defne, my elder sister Olcay, and I flew to Antalya; from there we went to Olympos Lodge in Kemer/Cirali. We stayed there for three days and three nights. Fatma was quite energetic and cheerful throughout the trip. Her state made me very happy. On our return to Istanbul, on June 1, we visited Prof. Dr. Hasan Yazici (my classmate from Robert College and one of my closest friends) at his clinic. Hasan found her well; he saw nothing unusual in her health.

The fifth hearing of the case in which I was being tried was held on June 7-8, 2018. The prosecutor read his opinion on the merits. He repeated the accusation that I had committed the crime of violating the constitution, but showing some mercy (!) he now requested that I be sentenced to life imprisonment once instead of three times, and additionally up to 15 years for allegedly being a member of an armed terrorist organization. In my statement, I simply said, “Mr. Presiding Judge, Honorable Members, I was detained for 20 months. I was kept under house arrest for about two months. I have been signing in at the police station for a month. There is no question of me fleeing or tampering with evidence. I request that you lift the judicial control measures against me.” My lawyer Aynur Yazgan Tuncel also said: “Two high courts have determined that there is no strong indication, which is the fundamental condition for detention as specified in Article 19 of the Constitution, regarding Sahin Alpay. Therefore, no form of judicial control can be applied where there is no condition for detention. I request the lifting of judicial control for our client for the reasons we have previously detailed in our petition.” Our request was denied.

On June 23, together with Fatma, Elvan, and Acar and Gokce who had come from London a week earlier, I attended the wedding ceremony of my nephew Cihan Alpay (son of my late elder brother Acar Alpay and brother of Umit Boyner) and Ece Vahapoglu. We voted in the general elections held on June 24: for the presidency, we voted for Muharrem Ince (reluctantly, because he was the CHP’s candidate), and for parliament, we voted for the HDP (Peoples’ Democratic Party).

On July 5-6, 2018, the sixth and verdict hearing was held. The prosecutor presented new “evidence” against me in his opinion on the merits; he repeated his request that I be sentenced to life imprisonment for violating the constitution and up to 15 years for membership in an armed terrorist organization. I responded to the prosecutor’s accusations point by point. In its decision announced on July 6, the court panel did not consider the accusation of violating the constitution, but ruled that I be sentenced to 8 years and 9 months in prison on the grounds that I was a “member of an armed terrorist organization,” that the judicial control requiring me to sign in at the police station every week be lifted, and that the ban on traveling abroad continue. One of the judges, in a dissenting opinion, argued that while I was not a member of an armed terrorist organization, I should be sentenced to life imprisonment for violating the constitution on the grounds that my writings had paved the way for the July 15 coup attempt.

The indictment had started with a request for three aggravated life sentences, and in the end I was sentenced to 8 years and 9 months, but I remained free due to two Constitutional Court decisions and one ECtHR decision ruling that my detention was a rights violation. Thinking of the tens of thousands of unjustly detained victims, we kept saying, “Let’s still be grateful for our situation…” When I expressed concern about being detained again, my dear Fatma wouldn’t give in to my pessimism, saying, “We must look forward now, we must forget what’s left behind…”

Fatma and Elvan went to Ayvalik on July 8. I stayed in Istanbul until July 11 to meet with my Swedish journalist colleague and friend Bitte Hammargren. On July 14, my son Acar, his wife Gokce, and my granddaughter Leyla also came to Ayvalik. That same day, Swedish Ambassador Lars Wahlund, who had been appointed to Dublin, came to Ayvalik with his sister Anna and son Leonard, and stayed for one night. I hosted them at a restaurant in Cunda.

On July 18, on the late Captain Guner’s veteran boat, we set out as a family for Ayvalik’s paradise islands for the first time in two years; we swam in the sea behind Maden Island. On July 20, we went to Istanbul as a family in Acar’s car to attend the wedding of Nazli, daughter of Fatma’s cousin Salim. Acar, Gokce, and Leyla returned to London on July 22. (Sadly, these days in Istanbul would be the last days Fatma would spend with her beloved son and granddaughter Leyla.)

My friend Mehmet Altan had been released about two months after me, on June 27, but I had only been able to talk with him by phone since; we finally got together on July 22 at a restaurant in Arnavutkoy. After the last “Akil Defteri” program on Mehtap-TV, I had only been able to see him in the corridors of Silivri prison or behind the glass of lawyer visiting rooms, greeting him from afar. Although sentenced to life imprisonment, he had been released pursuant to Constitutional Court and ECtHR decisions; but the requirement to sign in at the police station every week continued. (He would be acquitted at the end of the trial.) With Mehmet, we took stock of what had happened to us.

The next day, on the evening of July 23, my dear Fatma and I flew to Ayvalik. On July 26, we lived one of the most enjoyable days of that last summer we spent together. My elder sister and my nephew and niece Sinan and Sedef with their spouses were in Ayvalik, and we all went together to Ma’adra Winery on Mount Madra. We experienced a wonderful sunset there. Fatma greatly enjoyed this trip. On July 31, Fatma and I attended the traditional summer gathering of the Ayvalik International Music Academy, AIMA, of which our friend Filiz Ali was the president. It was only on that occasion that I was able to see many of our Ayvalik friends and acquaintances for the first time since Silivri. That night, Fatma was as beautiful and cheerful as always. On August 5, we had another boat trip with Captain Guner. Since a strong northeasterly wind was blowing, this time we went to the cove behind Ciplak (Naked) Island. Fatma was very well; she went swimming several times. (What would happen to her two months later was the farthest thing from our minds.) As always, she showed me great affection.

August and September were the last two months my dear Fatma and I lived happily together, just the two of us. At that time, taking into account the coming economic difficulties, I was trying to convince Fatma to vacate the apartment we had been renting in Istanbul for 33 years and settle in Ayvalik. I said we could go to Istanbul and stay with Elvan whenever necessary. My wish from then on was only to be together with my Fatma and to focus on writing my memoirs. However, one late afternoon, as we sat hand in hand on the terrace of our house in Camlik watching the sunset, she suddenly said, “I cannot stay here when the weather gets too cold to go out to the garden.” We agreed to rent a small apartment in Istanbul and spend the winter months there… A touching memory from those days, the photograph of us holding hands that Fatma’s niece Yesim took without our knowledge, seemed like a reflection of our hope and desire never to be separated again…

On August 20, our friends Nilufer (Kuyas) and her husband Tayfun (Ertan) came to Ayvalik and stayed with us for one night. Umit and Cem (Boyner) organized the traditional family dinner at their house in Cunda on August 22. On the way back, Fatma stepped into a hole and injured her ankle, but in general she looked quite healthy. On August 31, we took our last boat trip toward Maden Island with Captain Guner. My beloved enjoyed the sea. After “The Crown” and “Versailles,” the series we used to watch in the evenings when we were in Istanbul, we started watching “Breaking Bad” on Netflix. We were in good spirits.

Our friends Sefik (Yuksel) and his wife Idil (Biret) came to Ayvalik on August 29 and stayed until September 5. Sefik, who had been a close friend since middle school, and I met almost every morning at our house; I listened to his memories about me and noted them down to use in my autobiography. Idil had come, as she did every summer, to teach talented students at AIMA’s summer courses. And the courses, as every year, ended with a concert given by the students at the Ayvalik Municipality’s hall on the hilltop of Cunda (on the evening of September 4). Fatma greatly enjoyed this concert; she was extremely cheerful. (Who could have imagined that a month later she would bid us farewell forever…) Our days were never empty: On September 5, our friends Binnaz Toprak and Nursen Baydar came for a day visit from Yesilyurt village. On September 6, we had a dinner where we spent a very pleasant time with our friends Seyfi-Tulin (Gursel) and Ayhan (Aktar). On September 7, Vasif and Defne (Koryurek) were our guests for morning coffee.

On September 10, I went to Istanbul in the car of our friends and relatives Bulent and Simten (Comert) to meet with my lawyers. On the evening of September 12, we had dinner with Elvan and Defne at a restaurant in Nisantasi; we lamented that Fatma was not with us… On September 13, I attended the opening of an exhibition featuring works by alumni artists on the occasion of the 150th anniversary of the founding of Galatasaray High School, which Elvan also attended. After the exhibition, when I met for dinner with my journalist friend Michael Thumann from Die Zeit who had come from Germany, Seyfettin Gursel also joined us. On September 14, I returned to Ayvalik by plane. That evening we went to Altinova; we were guests of Fatma’s cousin Salim and Oya (Kaptan), and we had a lovely dinner at a restaurant on the beach. Two evenings later, we hosted them at a restaurant in Ayvalik.

Our friends Zeynel and Serpil (Celikel) were suggesting that we take a trip to the Black Sea region with their car. Fatma had never seen Vakfikebir and Surmene, where her mother and father were from. I wanted her to see those places. But as September progressed, we had begun to hesitate because it would be too strenuous a journey. When Fatma put her foot down, we postponed the trip; we would fly to Trabzon in the spring… The Trabzon trip had been postponed, but Fatma’s cousin Kemal (Kaptan), who lived in Antalya, had completed the preparations for a 3-4 day trip to Kas and its surroundings with a group of relatives.

Joining this trip was looming large in Fatma’s mind. In fact, when reports came in (which would turn out to be wrong) that the weather in the region would be rainy on the designated dates of September 27-30, she wanted to cancel the trip at one point. Then, perhaps because I had instilled this idea in Kemal’s mind, she said we should continue with the program so as not to be rude. Together with another cousin and our childhood friend Emine (Edremit), we drove to Izmir and flew from there to Antalya. On the way, Fatma had complained to Emine about shoulder pain, but she didn’t tell me anything.

Kemal met us at Antalya airport. After having dinner at a kebab restaurant, we set off for Kas in his car. I don’t recall Fatma making any complaints during the approximately three-hour journey. We arrived in Kas late in the evening and settled into a hotel at the tip of the peninsula. For the first time then, Fatma complained to me about the very humid weather and rheumatism pains. Since her pains would flare up from time to time and then subside, I honestly didn’t pay much attention. Her main complaint was about the breathing machine I used for sleep apnea. The air leaking from the device was bothering her. “Let’s have separate rooms now,” she said.

The next day, September 28, we took a trip by car covering Kalkan, Patara beach, and the ancient city of Xanthos. We had lunch at a trout farm in Islamlar village, at an altitude of 700 meters. Fatma had no complaints at all. She loved Patara. We had dinner at a beautiful restaurant overlooking the sea in Kas. Before dinner, Fatma went shopping and bought a white summer dress to wear on the boat trip the next day. Along the way, I kept telling the relatives how I would obey all of Fatma’s commands for the rest of my life, how she would direct me with her one-syllable commands. The relatives were having fun with me.

On September 29, we went to Kekova by car and set out to sea on a boat. The scenery and the sea were wonderful, and Fatma went swimming several times during the day; she was content with her life. She didn’t mention having pain even in the light rain that started in the afternoon. We had dinner at the hotel’s restaurant. After breakfast in the morning, we departed for Antalya in Kemal’s car to catch the flight to Izmir. We said goodbye to Kemal at the airport; we ate hamburgers while waiting for the flight. Fatma looked quite well.

PHOTO: My Fatma in the last photograph taken of her, wearing the white dress she bought in Kas…

In Izmir, we stopped by the house of Fatma’s niece Asli and her husband Ali (Ulker), and picking up Emine who was also returning to Izmir with them, we departed for Ayvalik by taxi. There was heavy rain throughout the journey. Fatma had begun complaining more intensely about the pain in her shoulder. Our mood had soured. When we arrived home late at night, she felt very tired and went to bed immediately. When I was preparing to move to a separate room as she had wanted, she stopped me; “stay with me,” she said. She must have been feeling an extraordinary weakness in herself.

The next day (October 1), I called our friend and her doctor Prof. Dr. Hasan Yazici. Fatma took the phone; it was noteworthy that she spoke directly about her complaints without any small talk… Hasan said she could take a mild painkiller 3-4 times a day. Fatma did so, but her pains were spreading. She asked me to rub Voltaren ointment on the left side of her back. The pains decreased somewhat with the medication, but Fatma was mostly lying down exhausted. Still, in the evenings, we were able to continue watching the “Breaking Bad” series on Netflix. The next day (October 2), I saw a large brown spot on the back of her right leg. There was yellowing on the front of her left leg. A large scab had also formed near her right wrist. I began to suspect that the liver insufficiency she had suffered from since the mid-1980s might have flared up. I called Hasan; I told him it would be good if he could see Fatma as soon as possible. “I’ll be expecting you at the hospital at 9:30 on Friday morning, October 5,” he said. He instructed that Fatma should come fasting for blood tests. On Thursday, October 4, I bought tickets for the Turkish Airlines flight departing from Edremit at 14:35.

When saying goodbye to her relatives in Ayvalik, she had said, “Hopefully I’ll return soon…” Holding hands, we had a good journey. She could only eat half of the toast we had bought at the start of the trip. She had very little appetite. We arrived at our home in Akatlar around 5 PM. She said she was very tired and went to bed immediately. Elvan came. We ordered cop sis (grilled meat skewers) for dinner. She could only eat a little without getting out of bed and then fell asleep. When I woke up around 4 AM, I found her in the dining room, eating some bread and cheese in the dark. “I was very hungry,” she said; and went back to bed right after. Honestly, I wasn’t very worried; I was thinking that Hasan would make the necessary intervention and we would get through this crisis too.

On the morning of October 5, she got up around 8:30. She went to the bathroom, washed, did her hair. As always, she dressed up beautifully, got ready. Around 9, I called for a taxi; there were no cars at any stand. It was only after about fifteen minutes that I was able to find a taxi and bring it to the front of the house. On her way to the taxi, she had run into our doorman and said, “I’m very tired…” As we were crossing the Bosphorus Bridge, I asked, “My dear Fatma, I always get confused about the hospital’s location, can you give directions to the driver?” Her answer was, “Use Yandex…” She was conscious. We reached the hospital in exactly 13 minutes. As she was getting out of the car, something unprecedented happened: Fatma dropped her bag on the ground; the contents spilled onto the road. I was surprised; I attributed it to her tiredness… It took me 5-10 minutes to complete the registration; during that time, she waited for me quietly, standing. Then we went to Hasan’s office.

Hasan would tell me later: When she entered the room, she wasn’t looking like the usual Fatma; this was like a different Fatma… Hasan began asking her questions. Her answers were broken and fragmented. She could barely sit on the examination table; it was as if she couldn’t fully control her body… Then she opened her hands and looked at them with wonder-filled eyes… She was seeing things we couldn’t see… Hasan measured her blood pressure and without saying what he saw, said let’s get some blood drawn. He called the nurse and requested a wheelchair be brought and blood to be drawn at the nearby emergency department. As Fatma struggled to sit in the wheelchair with the nurse’s help, her shoe came off her left foot. I felt the urge to bend down and kiss her foot… My worry was increasing. Something extraordinary was happening, but what was it?

At the emergency department, they laid her on her back and drew blood from her arm. She was no longer conscious. She started to retch; fearing she would vomit and choke, I called out to the staff to come quickly. They came running and turned her on her side. I saw that her mouth was full of blood. One of the orderlies said, “She must have bitten her tongue…” Then there was a flurry of activity in the emergency department. They closed the curtains around her bed. Hasan came; a little later, he left there and headed to his office, calling me to follow. He suspected a liver crisis. He called Fatma’s liver doctor Prof. Dr. Sabahattin Kaymakoglu. They agreed on transferring her to Florence Nightingale Hospital. I called Elvan and told her to come as soon as possible. An ambulance arrived, but the transfer was called off as Fatma’s condition was rapidly deteriorating. I was in complete shock. Hasan said a brain CT scan was being taken on the floor below; I could go down and check on the situation. I did so.

The doctor performing the CT scan didn’t take long to come out; “Unfortunately, we are facing a very severe case of brain hemorrhage; recovery is impossible, but we are still calling our neurosurgeon. We will take the patient to intensive care…” he said. By this time, Elvan had just managed to reach the hospital. Together, in deep anxiety, we began waiting for the neurosurgeon in front of the intensive care room. The neurosurgeon arrived and went in to see Fatma. When he came out, he said, “Unfortunately, brain death has occurred; the rest is a matter of time. There is nothing we can do, I’m afraid…” Together with Elvan, we went in to see her. My beloved was lying there as if nothing was wrong, as if she were just sleeping, with her usual beauty, her pink and white complexion… We understood that the time had come to say goodbye to her. I couldn’t stay by her side for long… Everything had happened so fast (in a span of about an hour) that I couldn’t comprehend what had befallen me…

I asked Hasan not to try to keep her alive. Her brain had died, meaning her selfhood had ended… Hasan said they would wait until Monday, and a decision would be made then. With our hearts bleeding, we left Fatma where she lay in intensive care, and Elvan and I returned home in a daze. That night, around 1:30 AM, Hasan called, “We’ve lost Fatma…” he said. I don’t remember how we conveyed the sad news to London, to my son Acar. Acar and Gokce had applied to the British authorities for an extension of their residence and work permits. Hasan had written a letter to the authorities requesting the urgent return of their passports, and we had immediately sent it to Acar.

While receiving Fatma’s death certificate from the hospital, the female clerk on duty offered her condolences; she told me that she too had lost her husband at a young age from a heart attack. “I understand what you’re going through… I couldn’t recover until a year and a half after my husband’s death…” she said. Would I ever be able to recover?..

We would take Fatma, who had been placed in the hospital morgue, to our hometown Ayvalik and bury her there. I contacted our relatives in Ayvalik and asked them to make the necessary preparations. For the transport of the body, I first called the Mayor of Ayvalik, our friend Rahmi Gencer, but when I learned that the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality also provided this service, I applied to them. On Sunday afternoon, October 7, at Karacaahmet Cemetery, Fatma was washed and shrouded under the supervision of her daughter Elvan. Around 6 in the evening, a refrigerated vehicle heading toward Izmir came and took her along with three other bodies. With our hearts bleeding, we watched her being loaded into the vehicle and setting off on her journey. I stood staring after her… Our 55 years together had come to an end.

Acar, Gokce, and Leyla were waiting for their passports to arrive from Liverpool before they could set off. That night and for two more nights until October 10, we had to keep Fatma waiting in the morgue of Ayvalik State Hospital.

On Monday morning, October 8, Hasan called. When he and his hematologist colleague examined Fatma’s final blood tests, they had concluded that the cause of death was, with 95 percent probability, a brain hemorrhage resulting from acute leukemia… We learned from acquaintances that there were others whom acute leukemia had killed within a week… When I returned to Istanbul, I spoke with Fatma’s cardiologist Prof. Dr. Sabri Demircan. He was very saddened by the news. He said that the blood-thinning pills that had been prescribed due to the ablation procedure performed on Fatma in April 2015 to treat her increasingly rapid heart palpitations could also cause brain hemorrhage “with a one in two hundred probability.”

The Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality Public Relations Directorate had called the day after Fatma was transported to Ayvalik; they had offered condolences on behalf of the Istanbul Mayor and told me to call them if there was anything they could do. The Ayvalik Municipality was also very helpful with the burial arrangements. I truly felt grateful for the attention and services provided by both municipalities.

During the days we spent waiting for Acar, our friends and loved ones showered us with condolence messages. Cengiz Candar, one of our closest friends, sent from Stockholm where he had been living for some time, an article he had written in memory of Fatma. I am including below Cengiz’s article, which was also published in T24 on October 11, 2018.

Cengiz Candar wrote about Fatma Alpay:

Could a person love another person as much as she loved Sahin?

https://media-cdn.t24.com.tr/media/stories/2018/10/page_cengiz-candar-fatma-alpayi-yazdi-onun-sahini-sevdigi-kadar-bir-insan-bir-baska-insani-sevebilir-miydi_011082388.jpg

“She was the only Fatma in my life. Given that the name Fatma is very common, it would not have been possible for her to be the only Fatma who had entered my life. But I didn’t know any other Fatma. Or she was such a dominant, powerful personality that even if I had known other Fatmas, I don’t remember them.

She was my only Fatma. And my most beautiful Fatma. She was a very beautiful woman. I used to compare her to Catherine Deneuve, but Tuba would say “No, Faye Dunaway.” Tuba was probably right. Even if she resembled Catherine Deneuve’s beauty, she was more like Faye Dunaway because she had nothing of her coldness. Or she was simply herself, Fatma Alpay.

Fatma was an impossible and entirely unique combination of the grandeur of strength and the unpretentiousness of humility. I knew Leman Kaptan. What a charismatic strong woman is, what it means to radiate power with her stance and a single glance without saying a word, I had seen that in Leman Kaptan. On the other hand, she was a familiar figure. Leman Kaptan had traits I recognized in my maternal grandmother from Thessaloniki. Fatma, beside her, would give the impression of being both her docile daughter and the heir apparent who would inherit Leman Kaptan’s throne as a powerful, commanding woman. She was different from her elder sisters. She was Leman Kaptan’s daughter. But incomparably more affectionate than her mother…

When I met Sahin, he was married. A university student and married. There were only one or two others like him in the entire Faculty of Political Science. But none as famous as Sahin. Fatma too had become famous through Sahin. If Mulkiye had a King, it must also have a Queen, and Fatma was exactly that. I understood as soon as I met her: she was not Queen merely because she was the King’s wife; she was Queen because she was a Queen.

As I write all this on the last day before she goes into the ground, it also occurs to me that I am a fortunate man. Even if I have never been free of trouble in my 70-year life, I believe I have lived a good and rich life. I have been thinking since October 5-6, 2018, that Fatma is among the foremost people who gave me this sense of richness. To know Fatma, to be one of the people she loved, to be among the people she loved - I understood better what an incredible wealth and what great fortune this has been for me.

I am a privileged intimate of the Fatma-Sahin-Elvan-Acar Alpay quartet. Fatma was the first to see Elvan, then Sahin, and very soon after, I did too. What a thing…

What luck that, when the Bahceli minibus coming from Cebeci stopped at the Kizilay stop and I got off, I came face to face with Sahin on the sidewalk, who had thrown himself onto the street to tell his loved ones about the birth of his daughter. I wasn’t one of his closest friends at that time, but some divine power must have planned our future, because Sahin excitedly said, “I have a daughter, come let me show you my daughter,” and took me to the nearby health center, I think, and we went up one or two floors and burst into Fatma’s room. Aside from being the first person other than her mother and father to see Elvan in Fatma’s arms, it was also the first time I had seen such a small creature since my sibling. I never forgot Fatma’s expression at that moment.

When I started going in and out of their home in Ankara, Elvan would wander among us as a mischievous little one. She was the first and youngest of our entire circle of friends. Then Cemo came. Elvan was Elvan, and through experiencing her in that tiny form, I experienced the love of small children within me.

Acar is also special to me. The elder Acar’s unexpected death had come right after some of Fatma’s very close relatives had perished in another traffic accident, between Balikesir and Susurluk. Acar came into existence with the elder Acar’s passing. He was wanted, planned, and born. We awaited him. After he was born, I experienced his early infancy in Ayvalik. I watched with excitement and curiosity as Fatma changed his diapers. If Elvan was the first newborn of my life, Acar was also one of the first whose infancy I observed closely.

In Elvan and Acar, I also came to know Fatma as a mother. She was a mother through and through. Authoritarian and at the same time completely affectionate, a mother through and through.

How many people Fatma was, all in one, with that calm manner of hers bringing together all her traits that seemed impossible to combine.

I wondered these past few days whether there could be a person of such powerful love on this earth. Could a person love another person as much as she loved Sahin?

In no period of Sahin’s life did any of his views become Fatma’s views. Fatma never became a Marxist, nor a Maoist, nor a Swedish Social Democrat, nor this, nor that; she never identified herself with the SHP (Social Democratic Populist Party), or the CHP, or Cumhuriyet newspaper, or Sabah, or Milliyet, or Zaman because of her husband. She had no allegiance to any of these. But she considered all the friends Sahin made in his changing circles as her own friends, showed them love.

What kind of thing is this!?? How else can this be explained except by an unparalleled love for Sahin? Why then did she love Sahin, whose views she never adopted? Why did she live this life, starting from the Camlik days, marrying him as a university student, waiting for him without knowing where he was during the period he went to Palestine, trying to raise Elvan, then going to Sweden where she wasn’t accustomed and standing by him, and afterward adopting without complaint the life he offered her in Istanbul?

Why?

Because she loved Sahin so much, had loved him so much, that she hadn’t even questioned any of this. Why did she love him so? Because Fatma loved Sahin’s essence, that incorruptible, uncorrupted, incorruptible pure essence.

She herself was so pure that such a pure person could only love someone with a pure essence this much, and Fatma loved Sahin like that. With a legendary love in the category of Asli loving Kerem, Leyla loving Mecnun, Juliet loving Romeo.

Remaining herself, she lived without the slightest reproach toward Sahin’s life, without a murmur, quietly, with great humility, and without giving up even an iota of her own rock-solid personality. What an incredible thing this is, how special and unique it makes Fatma.

And she had such an enormous heart that she loved Elvan, Acar, Defne, and Leyla as much as she loved Sahin. She loved all of Sahin’s close friends. I knew so well how much (and very much) she loved me, and I loved her so much too…

I realized how many memories I had accumulated with her. They all pass through my mind continuously like strips of film. While Sahin in Sweden was experiencing the hesitation of whether or not to return to Turkey, Fatma had come to Ankara to scout things out. We were sitting at Piknik, drinking our beers and eating sausage and french fries. That’s how it was done at Piknik in the 60s and 70s. When she asked, “What do you think, can Sahin return?” I had said, “Look Fatma, if he had returned, he would be the one drinking beer and eating sausage and french fries in my place.” What an enjoyable moment it was. We were talking, bursting with laughter. I was trying to convince her of something, I forgot what, she wasn’t accepting, “Why should I do that?” she asked; I mumbled something like “For the people, for the interests of the workers.” Fatma’s face, with all its dynamic and mischievous manner, rang before my eyes with “What do I care!” I paused for a second or two, it was my turn to laugh; “By God, the smartest and most Marxist among us is you, Fatma. You’re acting directly out of class interest. Of course, what do you care about all this…” I said, believing it. It was her turn to laugh - with that never-diminishing timbre of her laughter.

Fatma was a smart woman. Very smart. On top of such a beautiful, pure heart, a sparkling, crystal-clear mind. Tuba calls her “a woman of the earth” to emphasize her solidity, her personality solidity, her groundedness. When a pure heart meets a crystal-clear mind - not granted to every servant of God - a rock-solid, steel-like unbending personality emerges.

Both solid and dignified, head held high. Dignified in English. There was always “dignity” in her. Nobility… Both nobility in the sense of a Camlik aristocrat, and nobility of spirit.

To go to military service in Canakkale, I had come from Istanbul to Ayvalik. When setting off on the military path from the house in Ayvalik, it had fallen to Fatma to see both of us off to the army.

Ahh, how many memories we have accumulated with Fatma at the milestones, at the important turns of my life…

While Omer Madra and I had turned our military service into desertion and were perhaps having the longest summer vacation of our lives, Sahin, with an unnecessary discipline toward the end of his service, wouldn’t stick his nose out of the barracks. In one of those last weeks, Omer and I decided to desert to Ayvalik for the weekend. Omer was broke and was going to wring out whatever money was due to him from Madra olive oils, come what may. We were going to Ayvalik. We couldn’t convince Sahin, who was in love with his wife, to desert no matter what we did. We came to Ayvalik. Omer sat me on a bench overlooking the sea in Camlik and went to rescue the money. And of course, he came back with a small amount, unable to rescue it. What did we do? “Let’s go,” we said, “let’s go to Fatma. Let’s take Fatma out to dinner, let’s spend the money.” We did so. What a beautiful night it was. Fatma, Omer, and I. A night spent making fun of Sahin, continuing with Fatma’s laughter. We wished it would never end.

How much Fatma used to laugh. How much she would make us laugh without ever trying to be witty.

What a wonderful, what a unique person you were, Fatma!

What great wealth you were in my life, in our lives. How fortunate I am; to have been in this world for nearly half a century together with you, knowing you, knowing that I was someone loved by you.

Sahin, Elvan, Acar, never forget that you are among the luckiest people in the world; one of you is Fatma’s unparalleled love, one is her daughter, one is her son. What more could you want from this world.

How lucky a girl Defne is that she knew her grandmother. Acar, Leyla is only 4 years old, she may not remember; always tell her about her grandmother. Always.

Goodbye my dear Fatma. Perhaps someday somewhere we’ll meet…”

****

Fatma’s death notice published in Hurriyet newspaper on October 9 was as follows:

OBITUARY

Daughter of the late Leman Kaptan and the late Mustafa Lutfi Kaptan, of Ayvalik’s notable families; daughter-in-law of the late Sabiha Karatal and the late Ahmet Muharrem Alpay; sister of the late Hakki Kaptan and Suat Kaptan and the late Bingul Onen and Ayse Comert; paternal aunt of Yusuf Kaptan, Emine Edremit, and the late Ahmet Kaptan; maternal aunt of Ali Onen, Asli Ulker, Omer Onaran, Yesim Comert, and Cenk Comert; mother of Elvan Alpay and Acar Alpay; mother-in-law of Gokce Ozkaya Alpay; maternal grandmother of Defne Guler; paternal grandmother of Leyla Alpay; the love of Sahin Alpay

## Fatma Nur Alpay

(Isik High School class of 1961)

has passed away. Her funeral will be held on Wednesday, October 10, 2018, following the afternoon prayer at Ayvalik Saatli Mosque, and she will be buried in the family cemetery.

HER FAMILY

—————————————————————————

On Wednesday, October 10, 2018, at noon, we brought her to her home in Camlik. By her coffin, before a large gathering of friends and relatives, I gave the following speech:

## “Dear friends and relatives,

We have gathered to see my wife Fatma, whom we all loved very much, off on her last journey. Fatma was my love, my closest friend, the pillar of the family I built. That is why I want to say a few words in her memory.

I don’t need to describe her to you. You know her with all her beauty, her intelligence, her fortitude, her self-confidence, her personality free in thought and free in conscience.

I fell in love with her in elementary school, I declared my love in middle school, I won her in university. We married at 21. While I was swept away by the winds of my mind and emotions, she always stood firm. She protected the family we built.

She made me one of the happiest husbands in the world. She gave me my children and grandchildren whom I love more than my own life. She stood strong through all the hardships we went through and encouraged me to stand strong too. I want to thank her once again in your presence.

Of our 55 years together, I unfortunately spent three years in exile and two years in prison. I don’t forgive myself for the five years I spent away from her. I ask for her forgiveness once more in your presence.

Although she did not share my views or condone some of my behavior, what was the foundation of my happy union with Fatma that lasted so many years?

If you asked her, it was for the sake of our children that she didn’t leave me. According to some friends, she was pleased with my extraordinary personality. According to others, she was bound to me with love. Perhaps all of these were valid at once.

My only consolation as we bid her farewell is that she said goodbye to us in a manner befitting her dignity and personality. She neither suffered nor caused suffering…

She was very fond of her independence; she lived and died without being subject to anyone.

As you all know, living without Fatma will be very difficult for me…

I want to write the story of what we lived through together and then die.

Thank you all from the bottom of my heart for attending this farewell, for sharing our grief…”

Many of our friends and relatives from within and outside Ayvalik attended the funeral prayer held at Ayvalik Saatli Mosque during the afternoon prayer time. I am grateful to all of them. Heartfelt thanks to our friends and relatives who attended or could not attend Fatma’s funeral, who conveyed their condolences by sending wreaths or making donations.

We buried Fatma in our family cemetery at Ayvalik Cemetery, next to the place I had reserved for myself. Elvan and Defne decorated her grave with flowers. Acar, Gokce, and Leyla, who could only arrive from London the next day, joined us; my children and grandchildren and I visited her. We couldn’t believe she had left us…

When I search for consolations for myself, I find these: Yes, I couldn’t get enough of her and never would have anyway. How fortunate I am to have spent half a century with the most beautiful woman and the best person in the world! From the time she began coping with liver insufficiency in the mid-1980s, my prayer was that she would at least live to see 70. On her 70th birthday, she had told a friend, “I didn’t believe I would reach this age…” Every time she said to me, “I will die before you,” my answer was, “I would rather die first…” The fact that she lived until 74 despite the liver insufficiency diagnosed in 1986, the rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed in 2000, the palpitations that started in 2015 and the operation she had for them, and the dozen medications she had been taking for years is also a consolation. That she died without suffering is another… The fact that she passed away from a brain hemorrhage that began in the examination room of Prof. Dr. Hasan Yazici, her doctor of 20 years and our friend of 40 years, at a fully equipped hospital, does not allow me the remorse of feeling we didn’t do everything to save her. Finally, if she had died while I was in Silivri prison, if I had had to attend her funeral handcuffed and surrounded by gendarmes carrying machine guns, what would I have done?…

With Fatma’s death, my real life came to an end.

# CHAPTER XIX / FINAL WORDS: MY PRIVATE LIFE IS A COMPLETE SUCCESS STORY

I am writing this final chapter, which provides a general assessment of my life, in August 2022, after having completed writing my story: I lived through times, years when I suffered greatly, experienced much distress and sorrow. But when I look at it overall, I had a happy life; I will have no regrets when I say farewell. I owe this peace with myself primarily to what I experienced in my private life, to the family I was born into and the one I built with Fatma. The family I was born into, as I briefly described above, had been dragged into a deep crisis heading toward disintegration starting from when I was just one year old. My father, who was extremely devoted to his wife and children, an extremely affectionate father, unfortunately suffered a severe mental breakdown at just 33 years of age, attributed to various reasons, and gradually became estranged from our family.

It was my mother who held our family together and took all her children under her wing. We weathered as a family the potential negative consequences of what befell my father through my mother’s success in being both mother and father, especially to me as the youngest child but also to all her children, and by fostering our loving bond with each other. Perhaps because we grew up without a father, all siblings took the path of marrying at the earliest possible age to establish families of our own. Growing up in a fatherless, wounded family may have led me to seek a role outside the established order, while also causing me to develop self-confidence from an early age.

In the formation of my personality, I was influenced by my siblings as much as by my mother. My eldest sister Sumru had been a half-mother to me until she married and settled in Ayvalik when I was six years old, and it was not easy to accept why I had to be separated from her. She was a monument of character. Having lost her father when she was just one year old, she grew up with a stepfather who loved her dearly, found happiness in the family she built, in her husband and children, and weathered life’s storms with great fortitude. She experienced every twist of fate, from being the child and then daughter-in-law of one of Ayvalik’s wealthiest families to complete poverty, and took it upon herself not to be happy but to make others happy. She raised her children with great affection expecting nothing in return; she sheltered her husband, her youthful love, with deep devotion through two years of imprisonment and then ten years of suffering from Alzheimer’s. May she rest in peace.

Olcay, the younger of my two elder sisters, is, fortunately, the sibling I had the most opportunity to be together with, first in Ankara between 1964-71 and after 1980 in Istanbul. What her classmates wrote about her when she graduated from the girls’ section of Robert College describes her character well. Her presence leaves a “spring breeze” effect in every environment she is in. Although she is nine years older than me, since she became as close as a friend over time, it felt more appropriate to address her as “Olcay” rather than “sister.” She perhaps experienced most deeply the negative effects that our father’s depression had on our family; for this reason, like all of us siblings, she too became tightly attached to her husband and children. We celebrated my marriage to Fatma at her home; we shared all our joys and troubles with her. I am very fortunate that she was always by my side in good and bad times, during my time as a fugitive and in prison, never withholding her love and solidarity.

If I have been able to reach this age and can say that I have generally lived a happy life, I owe this significantly to the sacrifices my late elder brother Acar undertook. If I have certain qualities as a literate person, I acquired them through his guidance and his example. If, during the March 12 period, he had not risked everything solely because he was my elder brother and enabled my escape abroad, I would not have had anything I came to possess afterwards. If luck had not been on our side and I had been caught, not only my life but his could have been ruined; I could have been devastated by the harm I caused him, his wife, and children… He was the unluckiest member of our family. His greatest misfortune was undoubtedly losing his life at a very young age, just when he had found peace, in an impossible, unbelievable traffic accident. I was devastated that he said farewell to us at such a young age, before I could have enough of him, before I could find the opportunity to show him all my love and solidarity. I am even more saddened that he departed from among us without seeing the successes of his daughter Umit, who would become one of the most successful female executives not just in Turkey but in the world. Because of the deep love he showed me and the risks he took for me, I lived indebted to him, and I will die indebted.

If I can say “I generally had a good, happy life; I will have no regrets when I say farewell,” I owe this primarily to my Fatma, who was my beloved, my wife, and my friend for 55 years, to my children she gave me, and to my grandchildren. During the days I spent in Silivri, I wrote the following letters to Fatma (which unfortunately I never had the chance to show her) and to my children she gave me, Elvan and Acar.

## Letter to Fatma from Silivri

“My beloved, my life, my soul… Before being imprisoned in Silivri, I thought I had generally lived a full, rich, happy life, and I would say I wouldn’t mind dying. But after spending more than 15 months here, my outlook on life has changed. Now, with the longing I feel for you, I want to live for many more years and be able to enjoy being with you. I pray for this.

Now I look back at our past life with regret. I say if only I hadn’t been so headstrong, if only I had been fully aware of what a gift from God you were to me, if only I had lived only for you and with you; if only we had four children instead of two; if only we had more grandchildren than two… At least, I say, if only after returning from Sweden, or failing that, after Milliyet, I had listened to her, if only I had set up a bookstore-publishing house and charted a path where I’d still be occupied with books and ideas but wouldn’t end up a prisoner and once again far from Fatma… Unfortunately, regret is useless. Now I am burning only with the hope that I will be released in the not too distant future and will be reunited with you. Now perhaps I am more in love with you than ever…

I always think about the unique role you played in my life. You made me experience every kind of emotion. What passionate love, jealousy, anger, losing, winning, longing, the joy of reunion means, what it means to be forgiven… I learned all of these from you. The history of my love for you extends back to 1953, when we were just nine years old, to the days when we studied third grade together at Ayvalik Cumhuriyet Elementary School. That year, my getting upset and making up were the first expressions of my passion for you. When I heard that your late father had passed away in a traffic accident in 1956, thinking “my father-in-law has died…” is one of my most vivid childhood memories. And I never forget how, when I said “I think I’m falling in love with you…” in 1960 when I finished middle school, you responded with surprise saying “That’s just how it seems to you…”

The year I started high school, I was burning with jealousy. Somehow that summer, in the summer of 1961, I had managed to attract your attention. I went to the USA with a burning heart, suffering. During the first months there, I didn’t know how I would bear missing you. I consoled myself saying a year will pass quickly, then I’ll be reunited with you and never be separated again. I wrote passionate love letters. Your responses became increasingly infrequent and after a while stopped altogether. In the summer of 1962 when I returned from the USA, I didn’t even want to see you, but my passion for you had only turned to embers. This smoldering ember began to burn again with all its heat the following summer. When you made me feel you might perhaps return to me, the world was mine. I couldn’t bear to lose you once more. I immediately gave up going to college in New York with the scholarship I had won. This was the best decision I ever made in my life. I lived the most beautiful days of my life in the period from the summer of 1963 to the fall of 1965 when we got married. When we married on November 29, I achieved my greatest ideal.

Unfortunately, during these happiest days when I was united with you, the paths that would lead me to much suffering were also being laid. I remember the spring of 1966 with regret: The ambition to have a cause was preparing the troubles I would experience. In the summer following March 1968 when our daughter was born, with the publication of Aydinlik magazine, I found myself caught between two fires: On one side my love for you and our daughter, on the other my intellectual, political ideal. Here I remember what your late mother said about me: “He has intelligence, but no sense…” There could be no better description of my state.

I could see that you were gradually cooling toward me, distancing yourself; while on one hand I struggled to prevent this, on the other I could see we were heading toward the end of our togetherness. The most painful day of my life was the day in June 1972 when I said goodbye to you before disappearing from sight. During the nearly nine months I spent within the Palestinian resistance movement, I sought death; I hoped it would find me and put an end to the pain I was suffering.

But I must be a servant whom God favors, for I did not die, I did not end up in prison; just as I managed to seek refuge in Sweden through my brother’s great sacrifice, I was able to persuade you to come together with me again under one roof. I was aware that I owed this essentially to the existence of our daughter Elvan. Your agreeing to come to Sweden, and coming with Elvan, gave me extraordinarily happy days again. Feeling that I was winning your heart again was like returning to life for me.

After returning to the country with the 1974 amnesty and completing my military service, I had to struggle greatly to obtain a passport, but in the end it became possible for me to return to Stockholm and begin my doctorate. Your acceptance to marry me again convinced me that I had won your heart back… Then we gained the strength to bear the pain of the successive deaths that deeply shook us - first your mother, then your maternal aunt, your elder sister and brother-in-law, then my elder brother - by holding on to life with the birth of our son Acar. The birth of our son gave us great happiness, just like the birth of our daughter ten years earlier.

If you had loved Sweden, I probably wouldn’t have thought of returning to the country as soon as my work (doctorate) was finished. But your preference was more important than everything. However, we rushed. At the end of 1978, you took the children and returned to the country; I focused on finishing the doctorate with all its difficulties. If we had returned together, it might have been better for us and for Elvan. On the other hand, if we had delayed, our courage to return might have been broken, considering the hell that was being experienced in Turkey in the late 1970s.

When I finished my doctorate and returned to Turkey in 1981, I couldn’t find the opportunity to work at a university. I was forced to turn to journalism. I became increasingly unhappy at Cumhuriyet. I exhausted you greatly by sharing this distress. Then I got a herniated disc; I was bedridden for months. The burden of caring for me in this state also fell on you. I upset and exhausted you greatly once again. Until I moved to Sabah in 1994, I worked for barely enough to get by. Weekends were spent on jobs I did for extra income; I couldn’t spare proper time for you or the children. That our children grew up to be good people and good citizens is almost entirely your achievement. Not being able to give them enough attention is one of my greatest regrets.

Then your health problems caught up with us. First liver insufficiency, then rheumatoid arthritis, then heart palpitations… Thank God we found the means to cope with all of these. I cannot describe how much your ailments upset and worried me. I attributed your ability to cope with these to my prayers. When I went to Japan in 1987, I believed that hanging the amulet I got from a Shinto shrine at the head of your bed protected you.

I know our feelings are not mutual. Now, while lying in prison at 73, I feel more in love with you than ever. Recently, during a visit, you expressed your feelings about me as follows: Both love and anger… You are right to be angry at me for all I put you through. But no one could love you as much as I loved you. Therefore, I console myself thinking I deserve whatever love you have.

My beloved, if one aspect of my love for you relates to your personality, the other aspect certainly relates to your womanhood. Nothing in life made me as happy as being with you. Just looking at you was the greatest of happinesses. You gave me two children as precious as the world, two grandchildren as beloved as the world. All the virtues of our children are your creation. For this I owe you gratitude.

Let me confess that I was perhaps not the only but the most important obstacle preventing you from having a profession, a career where you could utilize your intelligence and talents. By promising you that you would be a happy diplomat’s wife, I even blocked you from graduating from university. I am sorry for this. But this is also a fact: we were able to sustain our 52-year marriage, our 54-year togetherness until now (despite painful separations) thanks to this.

My beloved, you made me taste every kind of emotion in life. Passionate love, jealousy, longing, losing, winning, the pain of separation, the joy of reunion, being forgiven despite everything… I am not in love with you only as a woman/wife; as a human being, I have not known anyone more valuable than you. Intelligence, common sense, character, honor, courage, elegance, nobility, fortitude, standing tall, understanding, compassion, sacrifice - I found all virtues in you. If my family has remained standing, I owe it to you.” (Silivri, November 13, 2017)

## Letter to Elvan

My dear daughter, I am writing this letter to you from Silivri prison. This is a kind of letter thanking you for existing and at the same time apologizing to you.

You are the product of my love with Fatma, of our most beautiful days together. You were born on March 31, 1968. From August of that year, I (unfortunately) began pursuing my other passion, my search for a political cause, and the difficult days of our family began. I will never forget the day you were born: My mother, who had come to Ankara for Fatma’s delivery, had gone to a “women’s matinee” that morning with my mother-in-law and my elder sister Olcay. Then Fatma began showing signs of labor. I called her doctor from the grocery store across the street; he said “come to the maternity hospital without delay.” And so we did.

When we arrived at Yenisehir Health Center on Selanik Avenue in the heart of Kizilay, the (well-known) doctor whose name I no longer remember was waiting for us, and they immediately took your mother to the delivery room. Shortly after, perhaps 15-20 minutes later, the door to the room where I was waiting excitedly for you opened and the nurse said, “Congratulations, you have a daughter!” (This was a surprise. In those years, the gender of the baby could not be known in advance. Your mother was trying to discover the gender by swinging a ring tied to a string over her belly.) Until they brought your mother, we were alone together for quite a while. You weren’t making a sound; your eyes were open and you were looking at me as if trying to recognize your father. I cannot describe the happiness I felt in those minutes. I was face to face with a stunningly beautiful baby. On one hand I was thinking of the beautiful days we would live together, on the other I was experiencing an anxiety (still very deep down) because I was unemployed and because of uncertainties about my future.

Some time after they brought your mother to the room, I rushed out to convey the news to the family. By coincidence, the first person I encountered was Cengiz. Excitedly saying “I have a very beautiful daughter, come see,” I called him inside. Therefore, after your mother and father, Cengiz was the first to see you. Later, to share my joy, I ran to the house of my closest friend at the time, Nuri Colakoglu, who lived on nearby Izmir Avenue. He wasn’t home. I wrote a note saying “I have a daughter!” and hung it on the door. (Nuri kept that note for years but could never manage to get it to me. I’ll ask for it when I get out of here.)

When you were born, we were living in our first home, a small one-bedroom apartment on the seventh floor of Gunes Apt. in Maltepe. Later, toward the end of 1968, we would move to an apartment in a ramshackle building across from your Aunt Olcay on Kizilirmak Street, an apartment your mother never liked. In early 1970, we would settle in Cim Apt. on Tunus Avenue, which your mother acquired with the money from selling the three-story apartment building in Ayvalik, under whose roof both of us were born. (Throughout our marriage, we lived by selling off the things we inherited. Among the things we sold, of course later, the one I was most sorry about was the apartment building in Ayvalik.) You brought me luck. In May 1968, for the first time I had a seemingly solid job. Through Dogu Perincek’s mediation, I was hired as an assistant at Ankara University Faculty of Education. However, this job neither resembled the assistantship at SBF (the Faculty of Political Sciences) that I actually wanted, nor seemed like it would lead anywhere with the revolutionary fervor increasingly taking hold of me…

Shortly after your birth, you developed jaundice. You almost became a victim of my revolutionary enthusiasm. Sevim Hanim, the wife of Mihri Belli whom I had met in those days and whom I considered very important in my own way, was a pediatrician. I insisted that we must have her examine you. Despite all your mother’s resistance, we did so. (I cannot forget Fatma’s reluctance and uneasiness during this doctor visit.) From those days on, our preferences began to diverge and clash, unfortunately. But we both deeply regretted it. When Sevim Hanim said your blood needed to be changed, your mother said, “I’m going to take my daughter to a proper doctor,” and we did. The doctor would say that this type of jaundice can be seen in newborn babies, that it would pass with time, and required no treatment. (Your mother had been right, as she always would be.)

I have many memories about your infancy. Here I will talk about the most unforgettable ones. We celebrated your first birthday at our home on Kizilirmak Street, your second birthday at our home on Tunus Avenue. When you reached two years of age, your most unforgettable characteristic was your dislike of sleep. I would put you to bed and sit by you until you fell asleep. If I thought you were asleep and tried to leave, you would immediately jump to your feet in bed and raise a ruckus. I would both get angry at you and adore your sweetness.

My not paying enough attention to you began in those very days. Though I had a wife I was passionately attached to, a daughter I loved as much as my own life, I don’t know how I could have entered a path that would separate me from you, how I could have sunk so low as to say to Fatma, “If the revolution requires it, if my comrades want it, I can abandon you…” I remember taking you to nearby Kavaklidere (Kugulu) Park on weekends. You were a chubby, pink and white, wonderfully beautiful baby. The photographs we had taken on your first birthday describe it well. You had a blue hooded coat. When I put the hood on, your cheeks would bulge out as if to say kiss me. And I would embrace and kiss you over and over. Your standing on the garden wall on the short little street descending from Tunali Hilmi to Tunus is engraved in my mind.

I lived one of the worst days of my life during our last visit to Kugulu Park together. The awareness that I wouldn’t see you for a long time (perhaps never again) was painful. The March 12 military intervention had happened; I expected it would have a cost for me. Indeed, when my name appeared on the first “wanted” list published in May, I began hiding in the homes of some acquaintances. The pain of separation from our home, from your mother, from you was great. The most painful part was that I had knowingly and willingly put myself in this situation…

In May 1971, we separated for this reason; our reunion would come in January 1974. In the years in between, I very much wanted to die to escape the irreconcilable conflict between my passions. But God, Fate, or Fortune did not permit it; it gave me the opportunity to reorganize my life in Sweden. I owe our being able to reunite essentially to you. If you hadn’t existed, your mother would not have given me another chance. And she would have been right. I owe being reunited with your mother, whom I passionately loved, to you as well. As for me, I left you fatherless perhaps in the years when you needed me most. I have a great sin against you. How fortunate that you did not grow cold toward me because of this.

Just like our last time alone together at Kugulu Park in May 1971, I remember with all its vividness our first day alone together in Stockholm in January 1974: I had bought a big doll to make you happy, we were talking together on the bus going to Lappis. I was so happy in those days that I had been able to bring my family together. Perhaps more than I had ever been… We immediately got a color television for the house. I remember your mother and you asking “What’s he saying?… What’s he saying?…”

and asking me to translate what was being said into Turkish, as if it were yesterday.

However, you quickly began learning Swedish. At the daycare you started attending, although new children were expected to come with their parents for at least the first week, your saying “Daddy, you can go now!” at the end of the very first day had greatly surprised the plump and very sweet caretaker Else Marie. Your surprising adaptation ability (and therefore your intelligence) had emerged there in all its brilliance. The result of quickly learning Swedish was this: We laughed a lot at how you gave away our family secrets by saying in Swedish to those who called asking for me, “Pappa inte hemma han stadar / Daddy’s not home, he went to clean…”

In the first days after you arrived in Stockholm, we visited together the home of my American friend Fred Krimgold in Slussen, where I had also lived for a while. I think Fred took your first photographs in Stockholm there. My Swedish friend Klas also came to visit us at Lappis one day and took those wonderful photographs of us that we still keep and gave them to us as a gift.

In Stockholm, you attended daycare for one year and elementary school for three years. Because of my return to Turkey with the amnesty and then struggling for six months to get a passport after completing military service, you could only start in January 1976 at the elementary school that had opened in August. Despite this, we were extremely happy whenever we heard from your very sweet class teacher Babba (Barbro) that you were very successful in your classes. The navy blue down jacket and white hood you wore when going to elementary school are still before my eyes. At the beginning of the summer of 1978 when we decided to return to the country for good, we sent you to Turkey with a friend. In the days close to your departure, when we visited the home of my doctoral thesis advisor Tomas (Hammar) and his wife Stina, they were saying that you spoke Swedish like a true Stockholmer.

Shortly after the birth, on March 11, 1978, of your brother Acar, who came almost exactly ten years after you, we returned to the country. The result of our decision to return for good was dragging you from place to place again. You attended third grade at Ayvalik Sakarya Elementary School. You made the transition from one of Stockholm’s most select schools to Ayvalik Sakarya Elementary School; from being entirely among Swedes to entirely among Turks. While your mother and you children spent the winter of 1978-79 in Ayvalik, I went back and forth to Stockholm to complete my doctorate; I left the responsibility of both our children on your mother’s shoulders. If the family I built remained standing, it was possible thanks to your mother’s sacrifices, common sense, and love for her children. In the winter of 1979-80, we moved to Istanbul. You attended fifth grade at Levent Elementary School with a class teacher you almost hated. I found consolation thinking that these radical environment changes, despite some drawbacks, essentially gave you a high adaptation/adjustment ability.

In later years, you would say you felt resentment toward us for not entering you in the entrance exams for American middle schools in Istanbul. There were two considerations your mother and I took into account when entering you in the Galatasaray High School exam: That GS High School was a free public school was an advantage for our family budget. On the other hand, with the assumption that you would learn English anyway, we thought learning French would also be beneficial. Unfortunately, you never really warmed to GS High School. Fortunately, in your second year of high school, through a connection that your Aunt Ayla helped us establish, finding the opportunity to spend that year as a guest with a family in Rochester, New York State, USA, and to attend senior year of high school there was, I think, a great, enriching experience for you. Coming to the USA years later on an invitation and visiting you in Rochester was very exciting for me.

The Rochester experience opened another door for you. Again thanks to contacts your Aunt Ayla established, we found the opportunity to have the equivalency of your American high school diploma approved. Unlike other fields, universities in the fine arts fields you wanted to study were accepting students through talent exams that year. You didn’t get into Mimar Sinan University which you really wanted, but you passed the exam for Marmara University Faculty of Fine Arts. You were never very satisfied with the education you received there, but thanks to your natural talents, the path to becoming one of Turkey’s most recognized, most valued visual artists was thus opened.

In 1994, you married Altan. This marriage started happily, but unfortunately did not continue that way. But from this marriage a great happiness was born for us: In 1997, our Defne came into the world. The days we spent in Princeton in the spring of 1998, witnessing Defne’s first steps on the Princeton lawn, are among my happiest memories. Your mother and I, thinking of our Defne, expected you to do everything you could to maintain your marriage, but when you came one day and said you couldn’t do it (just as when you said you wanted to get married), we supported you. How fortunate that you managed to stand on your own two feet with your extraordinary artistic talent. I admire your art… In my view, its clear, open, and distinct message is: the beauty of nature, and therefore of life. (I liken the clarity in your paintings to that of my writings.) That you couldn’t establish a harmonious family always saddened me. For if I am going to die happy, I owe this primarily to the togetherness I managed to build with your mother.

Since your mother and I also came from broken families (one due to death, the other to divorce), we didn’t want the divorce to have negative consequences for Defne, but the consequences of an unhappy marriage could have been heavier for her. How fortunate that my Defne has superior intelligence and language and expression abilities that can make her free and happy. The experiences abroad that she gained at a young age (first Lyon, then Chicago) did not turn out as expected, but I am sure they helped her know herself and the world, and develop her ability to adapt to different conditions.

And we come to what happened to me with July 15. I think you understand the reasons we experienced this. The conflict between my love for my wife and children on one side, and my search for giving meaning to my life on the other, unfortunately led to my imprisonment in Silivri for quite a long time, to being far from you. Let me confess to you that if I could have foreseen that the result would be this (imprisonment at 73), I probably would have thought of giving meaning to my life in a different way…

You, my wife, my children, and my grandchildren, are paying the price of my imprisonment. Here the greatest burden fell on you, my dear Elvan. Just as I abandoned you at three years old and didn’t see you for three years, now too I left you alone with an imprisonment whose end date is unknown. I cannot describe how sorry I am for this. Sometimes I think, “it would have been better if I had died, they would have recovered by now,” but immediately afterwards, thinking that these days will pass and I will be reunited with you, I pull myself together and find the strength to endure captivity.

I owe you gratitude for forgiving me despite all the wrongs I did against you, all the offenses I committed, and for not just forgiving but always supporting me with great affection. You are one of life’s greatest gifts to me. Because you exist, I don’t feel alone. I apologize to you for all the sorrows I caused. (Silivri, December 6, 2017)

## Letter to Acar

My beautiful son in every way. I am writing this letter to you on perhaps the most distressing, gloomy day of my imprisonment, which has reached its 500th day. I was hoping to be released and be able to spend a few days with you, with Gokce, with my dear Leyla before your move to London. It didn’t happen. I cannot describe the longing I felt while looking at you from afar at yesterday’s hearing. I hadn’t intended to start my letter with such sad lines, but it was unavoidable for it to be a sincere address. I wish you and your family healthy, successful years in London.

Let me come to what I really want to say to you… We had been deeply shaken by the unexpected, tragic deaths of your maternal aunt in 1976 and your paternal uncle in 1977. We thought a new baby would connect us to life again. Indeed, your birth enabled us to embrace life again with all our might. (I calculate that you were conceived in July 1977, during the days we stayed at the Efes Hotel in Izmir. In this, I am inspired by the famous astronomer Joseph Keller. According to what I recently read, he calculated exactly which day he was conceived in his mother’s womb and noted it in his diary!

Your mother was at the peak of her beauty during her pregnancy with you. You can look at the photographs I took in those days, in her burgundy velvet maternity dress.)

Of course I remember the day you came into the world on March 11, 1978, in all its details. When your mother’s labor pains started, Uncle Sait (Kocas) drove us in his car to Danderyd’s Sjukhus, perhaps one of the finest hospitals in Stockholm that we were registered with. When your mother’s contractions began to intensify, they took her to the delivery room and invited me in as well. Therefore, while excitedly watching you emerge from your mother’s belly, I held your mother’s hand and prayed for a healthy delivery. (Your birth was not as easy as Elvan’s; your mother suffered quite a lot of pain this time, but everything went well.)

In those years, the gender of the baby could not be known in advance. There was a very exciting aspect to this… The nurse gave the good news, “En pojke, en snygg pojke! / A son, a handsome boy!” We had a daughter; now we were blessed with a son too; I was flying with happiness. The nurse first put you in an incubator to maintain your body temperature; then took you out and gave you your shots. You and your mother stayed in the hospital for two nights; I went home, to Elvan who was waiting excitedly and joyfully for news of her little sibling.

One of the most vivid memories of those joyful days is this: We had laid our son, who was about a month old, between us in our bed. Your mother was expressing her admiration for you, saying “My God, is this beautiful boy really mine?!” On March 31, our stunningly beautiful daughter had turned 10, and our stunningly beautiful son was 20 days old. (I had started telling my friends “Elvan is my pre-revolution child, Acar is my post-revolution child.”) Following your birth, my mother went abroad for the first time and came to Stockholm. My mother and I had put you in the baby carriage that Gulder and Sait gave us, Ceren’s baby carriage, and strolled with you along the seaside of Lappis. That too is one of the most vivid memories of our family story for me.

A few months after your birth, we decided that the time had come to return to the country. For three reasons: 1) Ecevit had formed the government in December 1977 by transferring 12 members of parliament from the Justice Party; he was promising to end terrorism and bring order to the economy, raising hopes that things in the country would get on track. 2) Your mother had decided she did not want to live in Sweden and wanted to return to the country. 3) My doctoral work was nearing its end. In October 1978, when you were just 6 months old, we made our final return to the country.

However, this was a decision made much too early: 1) Ecevit couldn’t do anything beyond talking frequently and at length, and when he lost the by-elections in June 1979 he resigned, Demirel formed a minority government. 2) We settled in Ayvalik, in your maternal grandmother’s stove-heated house in Camlik. That winter was especially cold and very difficult for your mother. She almost regretted returning. My dear son burned his hand by pressing it against the stove. I was very upset. 3) I had thought that being alone in Stockholm would let me work more productively and return to the country sooner. The plan didn’t work out, the opposite happened: I suffered a lot, I came to Ayvalik at every opportunity missing you all, my work dragged on.

After Elvan completed fourth grade in Ayvalik, in the fall of 1979 we moved to the apartment in Zerrin building on Peker Street, Levent, Istanbul. Even finding this house had been very difficult. That winter the country’s economy hit rock bottom, heating fuel (fuel oil) had become impossible to find. We had to set up a wood stove in the living room. That winter too had been harsh. You loved playing with snow in the garden and you remained a snow-lover always. My strongest memories of 1-2 year old Acar in Zerrin apartment are these: Your starting to talk saying “Ba.. ku… / Look… bird…” Your playing with straight pins (without ever pricking your hand)… When you reached 5-6 years old, you and Cengiz playing football inside the house…

In the fall of 1985, we moved to Akatlar, to Hayran Apartment on Meydan Street. You started at Levent Elementary School. You were much luckier than Elvan when it came to your teacher. Yours was a very sweet, well-intentioned person with strong human qualities. My instilling Besiktas fandom in you happened around that time. When I saw a Galatasaray inclination developing in you with Elvan starting at GS High School, at the first opportunity I took you to a BJK match and outfitted you with a BJK beret and flag. This (what luck!) happened to coincide with the match on October 15, 1989, when BJK beat Adana Demirspor 10-0 at Ali Sami Yen stadium. From that date on, you became a fervent Besiktas fan. We had celebrated your elementary school graduation at a restaurant on the Bosphorus. When the man sitting at the piano started in a bland voice “Long live Fenerbahce…”, I was delighted as your classmates, who made up the great majority there, silenced the man with chants of “Besiktas! Besiktas!”

Until second year of high school, you received your secondary education at Atanur Oguz College in Balmumcu. My most vivid memories about you from those years are these: Although you were an extremely well-behaved and calm child at home, teachers complained about your wildness at school. This made me happy, because I would say “My son will be a gentleman, but he will never let himself be trampled on.” My sad memory, however, was when you were asked to write a composition introducing your father in English class, you wrote about me “He is fat and nervous…” (This may have been influenced by my troubles in work life in those days. Otherwise I was an affectionate father…)

Just as I couldn’t be a guide for Elvan, unfortunately I couldn’t be one for you either. I couldn’t do the things I should have done to help develop your knowledge and culture, like taking you to movies, theater, museums, concerts, bookstores. I had my own excuse; I had to work hard. When you reached second year of high school, your mother, who had taken on the main responsibility for raising our children, became alarmed. She wanted you to transfer to Isik High School in senior year to increase your chances of getting into a good university. This way, if you wanted, the path to continuing at Isik University could be opened. Since your mother’s classmates were on the school’s board of trustees, arranging this transfer was not difficult. You weren’t very enthusiastic because you didn’t want to be separated from your classmates, but you didn’t object. You finished high school at Isik. I was moved at the graduation ceremony; for the first time in many years, tears poured from my eyes.

When we learned that Bilkent University Faculty of Fine Arts would be accepting students through talent exams, we were very happy. You too, like your sister, had artistic inclinations. An opportunity had arisen for you to study at a good university, in a field you had talent in, in a civilized environment. Indeed, you passed the graphic design department exam and studied happily at Bilkent until you graduated in 2002.
