We decided you should take advantage of the opportunity to do short-term reserve officer service. You did your military service during the winter period (December - June) at the Infantry Training Brigade in Sivas.

At the oath ceremony, tears poured from both your mother’s and my eyes. During the six months you spent there, your mother and I came to Sivas three times to see you. Since there were no flights to Sivas at that time, we first flew to Ankara, then to Kayseri, and reached there by bus. On our second and third visits, you were allowed to stay with us at the hotel. On the first visit, I cannot forget the sight when you came to the hotel and took off your socks. Your feet had literally turned green with moss from walking in the snow. You did your military service under harsh conditions, but as always, you adapted and never complained.

After military service, it was time to find a job. Around that time, a close friend of mine, Fuat Atalay, had been appointed general manager of IKEA Turkey. Through him you started working at IKEA, but since it was a job that didn’t allow you to develop your talents, you were rightfully uneasy from almost the first day; a few months later, with our support as well, you resigned. However, the few months you spent at IKEA were a great gain for you. You met Gokce there, who would become your wife, whom we also loved dearly, who had studied interior design at GS University. You found a job suitable to your education at an advertising agency in Bahariye, Kadikoy. Then when she too left IKEA and started working at an architecture firm, you and Gokce rented a place near us and started living together. Later we celebrated your engagement at a restaurant in Akaretler with both families. I had worked together with Gokce’s eldest sister Yonca at Cumhuriyet. Her other elder sister, Yesim, was a very warm person. Her maternal uncle had done the layout for Cumhuriyet. I was very pleased that you became son-in-law to a family suited to us.

You didn’t want a wedding, but your mother’s wish prevailed. My Fatma said, “I didn’t have a wedding, my daughter didn’t either, I’m going to have a wedding for my son.” When you said “In that case, let it at least be in Ayvalik,” it crossed my mind, “Could it be in Umit and Cem’s garden in Cunda?” When my Fatma called Umit and said “Make sure you’re in Ayvalik on July 25, 2009,” didn’t Umit immediately say “Let’s do it in our garden…”!!!… I had sensed it…

In the Boyners’ garden, in my opinion the most beautiful wedding ever held in Ayvalik took place. Yesim - Cenk Co. took on the garden organization and refreshments, and Omer - Elcin Co. took on the wedding cake. It was a very pleasant celebration with about three hundred guests. In my speech celebrating your marriage, I commemorated your paternal uncle. It was very touching for me, but unavoidable. Your wedding also reflected family solidarity (just as between my elder brother and me, among you cousins). Gokce’s late mother, her paternal uncle, and her nieces and nephews; my close friends Mehmet (Atakan), Cengiz, Sabetay, Zeynel, Oguz, Seyfettin, and Nuri (Yildirim) also attended the wedding. It was one of the happiest events of my life. We loved our daughter-in-law, as I said in my speech at the wedding, “like our own daughter.”

After the wedding, you moved to an apartment in Nisantasi. You started working at a PR agency in Levent, but you weren’t satisfied because you couldn’t show your creativity, though you had reached a good position. You had waited quite a while to have a child, but on November 20, 2014, we had such a grandchild that it seemed there couldn’t be one sweeter, more beautiful, more lovable than her. While thanking Gokce for giving birth to my Leyla, I asked, “Did you expect her to be this sweet?” She said, “I was sure she would be sweet, but I didn’t expect this much”…

The day my Leyla was born, I was in Thessaloniki, where I had gone to teach for a week at a university. We celebrated my Leyla with friends from the university at a tavern. The next evening, as soon as I landed in Istanbul, I rushed to Florence Nightingale hospital to see my Leyla. You know how much I have adored and been devoted to her since that day. I am very happy that I suggested her name be Leyla and convinced Gokce of it. She is my Leyla, and I am her Majnun grandfather. I am writing these lines in Silivri prison. Unfortunately, I could only be together with my Leyla until she was 2.5 years old. In the spring months of 2016, as if sensing that I would be left longing for her, almost every day I put her in her stroller and walked to Taksim, to Taslik.

In this morning’s visit, I perhaps saw you for the last time before your migration to England. As I have said repeatedly, your primary responsibility is not to your mother and father, but to your wife and daughter. I wish you had gone after I was released (?), but it’s not clear when that will be. Yes, our hopes for the ECtHR and the Constitutional Court continue, but hopes can also turn out to be empty.

My Acar, in my view you are the world’s most gentlemanly, most intelligent, most talented, best, most honest person. From your birth, you gave us so much happiness. I embrace you over and over and wish you success in your new life in London. My greatest wish is to be released without too long a delay, to be reunited with you, and for you to bring my Leyla to me right away. (Silivri, December 9, 2017)

My Public Life, on the Other Hand, Is a Complete Story of Defeat

My private life, that is, the family I built with Fatma, what I experienced with my children and grandchildren, when looked at overall despite all the hardships I put myself through along the way, all the troubles and sorrows I brought upon myself, is a complete success story. In short, I will die content with my private life. In contrast, my public life, that is, my life as an educated citizen, an intellectual concerned with the country’s political problems, when looked at from the perspective of what I wanted to do but couldn’t accomplish, is in every sense a story of failure.

Thanks to my mother’s fortitude, during my formative years I received the best education possible in the country. I attended elementary school at Nilufer Hatun Elementary School in Nisantasi, Istanbul, middle school at the English High School for Boys in Nisantasi, high school at Robert College in Bebek and with an AFS scholarship at Webb School of California in the USA, with great success. I gave up going to Columbia University in New York, one of the most select universities in the USA where I had won a four-year scholarship, but I graduated from the Diplomacy and Foreign Relations division of Ankara University Faculty of Political Sciences, one of Turkey’s foremost higher education institutions at the time.

Perhaps due to the effect of growing up in a family that fell apart encountering various problems, perhaps with the subconscious belief that I could only distinguish myself in a different Turkey, from my early youth I was in search of a different order for Turkey. In 1962, when returning to Turkey from the USA where I had spent a year, the fundamental question in my mind was why Turkey was so poor and weak while the USA was so rich and powerful. Before long, with the help of the Workers’ Party of Turkey founded in those years and the developing leftist discourse, I found the answer: Because Turkey was a country exploited, “kept backward” by Western imperialist countries, primarily the USA… This understanding (or paradigm) that settled in my mind led me to start from a Kemalist nationalist discourse and gradually arrive at an increasingly totalitarian worldview. By the late 1960s, I had become convinced that Turkey’s “liberation from the yoke of imperialism; establishing an equal, free, and prosperous society” was only possible through a Marxist-Leninist-Maoist revolution.

However, when I looked from the perspective of the Marxist-Leninist theory I had adopted at that time, both the socio-economic conditions of Turkish society and the consciousness level of the people seemed very far from achieving such a revolution. The “objective and subjective conditions” of the revolution did not exist; a very long and difficult preparation process was needed, a process of raising the people’s consciousness. My trust in the friends I had set out with, especially Dogu Perincek, had also been shaken. But one had to start somewhere. When my commitment to the revolutionary ideal combined with the conditions of the March 12 period when I started being sought by security forces, I decided to abandon my wife whom I loved and my beloved daughter who was only three years old, and walk the path of revolution.

I thought that socialist revolution could not happen through the struggle of a handful of intellectuals and students without the workers and peasants wanting it, but I couldn’t abandon the cause, I couldn’t tarnish my valor. Dogu Perincek, just as he made me a member of the illegal Revolutionary Workers’ and Peasants’ Party of Turkey he had established with his friends (despite my not being convinced of its necessity), decided to send me to the Palestinian resistance movement so I could rid myself of my bourgeois tendencies and attachments (which, presumably, he didn’t see in himself) and prepare for the armed struggle I intellectually advocated. My warning that the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP), led by Naif Hawatmeh, which I was deemed fit to join, was a Trotskyist organization was not taken into account by my “comrade” Halil Berktay who conveyed the assignment, on the grounds that I could “bring them to the correct revolutionary line” (!).

As I described in detail above, during the approximately nine months I spent in Palestine, in an environment where my commitment to the revolutionary ideal conflicted with my awareness of how far we were from its conditions and with my longing for my wife and daughter, I tried to be an exemplary militant as best I could. To escape the torment of the conflict in my consciousness, I also volunteered to take part in an operation against Israel. After returning to Turkey nine months later and investigating for a short time whether there were possibilities to continue the struggle, I concluded (with my thinking at the time) that the idea of revolution was extremely valuable but completely disconnected from Turkish reality, and I took refuge with my family. My elder brother risked his life, fortune smiled on us, and in the end I took refuge in Sweden. As the years passed, it would become abundantly clear how far Turkey was from socialist revolution, and socialist countries would also be seen to abandon socialism.

In Sweden, where I managed to escape to and obtain asylum at the end of 1972, after quite some time I concluded that although socialist revolution might be an ideal, I no longer had any connection with this ideal, and I found the opportunity to do a doctorate in political science at Stockholm University. Over time, the Marxist paradigm in my mind gave way to a Popperian, liberal paradigm. Turkey needed a libertarian democracy and social market economy modeled on Sweden. To correct the wrongs I had done in the past, I decided to serve this ideal from now on.

It was patently obvious that neither the Kemalist, secular nationalism widespread in one part of society, nor the Islamism developing in reaction to it in the other part, was compatible with my ideal of a liberal democratic Turkey. Kemalist nationalism needed to be transformed into liberal social democracy, and Islamism needed to be reconciled with pluralistic democracy. Now, it seems ridiculous, but (as I described above) for quite a long time (together with a handful of like-minded friends) I believed these transformations could be possible. Unfortunately, I probably only fully grasped that the ideal of establishing a liberal democratic regime in Turkey was just as far from reality as the ideal of establishing a Marxist-Leninist-Maoist regime when I found myself in Silivri Prison.

So how was it that in roughly the first half of my adult life I could believe in a Marxist-Leninist, even Maoist Turkey, and in the second half in a liberal social democratic Turkey, the exact opposite? How was it that I, who had received quite a distinguished education by Turkey’s standards, could adopt ideals both of which were so far from the country’s realities, so disconnected, having no validity? And I spent my life for these ideals? I can list the explanations that come to mind as follows.

1) My Family: I mentioned above that having been born into a troubled family and grown up without a father may have directed me toward the belief that I couldn’t be successful in the established order and toward the search for an alternative order.

2) My Subculture: My origins go back to a family established by those who came and settled in Turkey through population exchange, forced migration from Greece, in short, by those of Rumelian origin. At least as far as I know, this subculture group, as I described in detail above, carries cultural characteristics quite different from the Turkish and Muslim people of Anatolia. It has characteristics whose summary might be found in Kemalist nationalism: It is Muslim but its religious beliefs are superficial. It has a culture of approaching differences with understanding, brought by centuries of coexisting with different religions and cultures. Ayvalik, where I was born and grew up, perhaps most intensely carried the characteristics of this subculture, at least in the years I was raised. Not only the cultural structure of Ayvalik but also its sociological structure where class differences were very pronounced may have affected me; growing up in a relatively affluent family and environment may have strengthened my reaction against socio-economic inequalities and may have directed me toward the search for a more just order.

3) My Education: In the formation of my personality and thoughts, undoubtedly the schools I attended played as great a role as, perhaps an even greater role than, the family and social environment I grew up in. I think having done my secondary education at English and American schools made me a bit too Western, to some extent foreign to society. Having done my higher education at Mulkiye may have led me to become overly engaged with Turkey’s political problems. (The slogan at the SBF I attended was “Today at Mulkiye, tomorrow in Turkey”; that is, it was believed that graduates of our school would shape the country.) Having done my doctorate at Stockholm University may also have undoubtedly led me to start seeing Sweden as an example/model country. Whatever the influence of Mulkiye was on my “Maoism” in my youth, it can be said that my “social democracy” in my mature age originated from my years at Stockholm University. In the sum of all these influences, it can be seen that I belong to a subculture group quite foreign, quite marginal to Turkish society.

4) Turkey’s Complexity: The diversity and plurality of Turkish society in which I was born and grew up (the divisions between Native - Immigrant, Sunni - Alevi, Turk - Kurd, secular - religious subcultures), alongside the rapid socio-economic change it underwent during the years I lived through (increases in both population and urbanization and average income levels), may have made my efforts to understand society difficult. These difficulties, as much as the education I received and the values I acquired from the schools I attended, may have led me to rely on imitative solutions that saw first China, then Sweden as examples/models, rather than creative solutions to problems.

Because I remained quite foreign to Turkish society for the fundamental reasons I listed above, although I sincerely advocated libertarian and pluralistic democracy, it can be said that I ultimately found myself in Silivri prison on the accusation of advocating a military coup. In summary I can say that, primarily thanks to my attachment to my late wife Fatma, I generally led a happy, worthwhile life; when looked at from the perspective of my political ideals that separated me from her, however, I was completely disappointed. The “Maoism” I advocated in my youth was completely remote from intellectual creativity and completely disconnected from reality. The “liberal social democracy” I advocated in my mature age, although it expresses the political values I am still committed to, is unfortunately as foreign to Turkish reality as “Maoism.” If it is possible to extract an essence from all the complexity of Turkish politics, as far as I can see, it can be said that Turkish politics today is shaped around the struggle between a kind of secular nationalism with its nuances on one side and a kind of Islamic/religious nationalism with its nuances on the other. Of course, Kurdish nationalism with its different interpretations, which conflicts with both, must also be added to these.

THE END

This memoir, originally published in 2024 by Lejand in two volumes as Bir Hikâyem Var and Hikâyemin Sonu, appears here with a machine translation produced by Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.5 and revised by Claude Fable 5, from a manuscript provided by the author.

John MacFarlane orchestrated the translation and typeset it in facing English and Turkish paragraphs, using LuaLaTeX and the reledmac package.
